steps.label: Bowel gas pattern
steps.detail: Assess distension and persistent focal loops on serial films.
findings: Diffuse bowel distension.
Persistent fixed dilated loop in the [right lower quadrant].
Gasless abdomen.
steps.look: Serial supine radiographs; a persistent loop that does not change between radiographs is an ominous sign of necrosis.

steps.label: Pneumatosis and wall
steps.detail: Look for intramural gas and wall abnormalities.
findings: Pneumatosis intestinalis in the [right lower quadrant / diffuse].
Thickened / thinned bowel wall on ultrasound.
steps.look: Bubbly or linear lucency in the bowel wall on radiographs; ultrasound for wall thickness and echogenic dots.
steps.tip: Bubbly pneumatosis can look like stool; compare with the clinical picture and serial films.

steps.label: Portal venous gas
steps.detail: Assess branching gas in the liver on radiograph or echogenic moving foci on ultrasound.
findings: Branching lucencies over the liver (portal venous gas).
Echogenic foci moving in the portal vein on ultrasound.
steps.look: Right upper quadrant on radiograph; portal vein on ultrasound.

steps.label: Free air and fluid
steps.detail: Look for pneumoperitoneum, ascites and collections.

normal.PERITONEAL FINDINGS: No free air or complex fluid.

findings: Pneumoperitoneum (football / Rigler sign): perforation.
Complex ascites with debris.
Localised collection.
steps.look: Horizontal-beam or left-side-down decubitus view; ultrasound for complex fluid.
steps.tip: Perforation is a surgical emergency; a horizontal-beam view is the most sensitive radiograph.

steps.label: Ultrasound and evolution
steps.detail: When obtained, assess perfusion and peristalsis, and describe change over time.

normal.ULTRASOUND AND EVOLUTION: Ultrasound not performed. No interval change.

findings: Absent bowel wall perfusion in the [ ] (necrosis).
Worsening since [time].
Improving pattern.
steps.look: Doppler of bowel wall; comparison with previous films.

steps.label: Compartment and thymus
steps.detail: Localise the mass and distinguish it from normal thymus.

normal.COMPARTMENT: Normal thymus for age; no mediastinal mass.

findings: Anterior mediastinal mass separate from normal thymus.
Middle mediastinal cyst adjacent to the carina.
Posterior mediastinal paravertebral mass.
steps.look: Anterior mediastinum: normal thymus is soft, conforms to adjacent structures and does not compress the airway or vessels.
steps.tip: Normal thymus never compresses the airway or vessels; a mass that does is not normal thymus.

steps.label: Composition
steps.detail: Assess soft tissue, fluid, fat and calcification.
findings: Homogeneous soft-tissue mass __ mm (lymphoma pattern).
Fat, fluid and calcification (germ cell tumour / teratoma).
Fluid-filled cyst (bronchogenic / foregut duplication cyst).
Calcified paravertebral mass (neuroblastoma pattern).
steps.look: CT attenuation or MRI signal.

steps.label: Airway
steps.detail: Describe tracheobronchial displacement or narrowing.
findings: Tracheal narrowing to __ mm (cross-sectional area reduced by about __%).
Compression of the [left main] bronchus with distal air trapping.
steps.look: Axial and coronal CT at the narrowest airway; minimum intensity projections.
steps.tip: Significant airway compression by an anterior mass is a major anaesthetic risk; communicate it directly.

steps.label: Vessels and spinal canal

normal.VESSELS AND SPINE: No vascular compression; no intraspinal extension.

findings: Compression of the superior vena cava.
Extension through the neural foramina into the spinal canal.
steps.look: Superior vena cava and pulmonary arteries; neural foramina on MRI.

steps.label: Nodes and spread

normal.NODES AND THORACIC SPREAD: No lymphadenopathy, effusion or other lesion.

findings: Bulky mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy.
Pleural / pericardial effusion.
steps.look: Hilar and mediastinal nodes; pleural and pericardial effusions.

steps.label: Suture inventory
steps.detail: Assess the metopic, sagittal, both coronal and both lambdoid sutures individually.
findings: Fused sagittal suture; other sutures patent.
Fused [right] coronal suture.
Fused metopic suture with a ridge.
steps.look: Axial CT source images and 3D rendering; ultrasound for sutures in young infants.
steps.tip: The metopic suture normally closes in infancy; a closed metopic suture alone is not trigonocephaly.

steps.label: Extent of fusion
steps.detail: Describe the affected segment, length of fusion, ridge or sclerosis and confirm on source images.
findings: Complete fusion of the sagittal suture with ridging.
Partial fusion of the [posterior] third of the sagittal suture.
steps.look: Source images along each suture; 3D rendering can hide thin patent sutures.
steps.tip: 3D segmentation can erase a thin patent suture or create an apparent gap; confirm on source images.

steps.label: Vault shape
steps.detail: Describe the skull shape pattern, asymmetry and compensatory growth.
findings: Scaphocephaly (long narrow skull) from sagittal synostosis.
Trigonocephaly with a triangular forehead from metopic synostosis.
Anterior plagiocephaly from unilateral coronal synostosis.
Parallelogram shape without suture fusion (positional plagiocephaly).
steps.look: Vertex view of the 3D rendering; cephalic index with named landmarks if used.
steps.tip: Positional plagiocephaly gives a parallelogram shape with the ear moved forward; lambdoid synostosis gives a trapezoid with the ear moved back.

steps.label: Orbits and skull base
steps.detail: Assess orbital asymmetry, cranial fossae and skull-base findings.
findings: Harlequin-eye deformity of the [right] orbit.
Hypotelorism (metopic synostosis).
steps.look: Frontal and basal views; orbital shape (harlequin eye in coronal synostosis).

steps.label: Intracranial and associated findings
steps.detail: Describe ventricles and other visible abnormality, and whether the pattern is single-suture or multisuture.

normal.INTRACRANIAL AND ASSOCIATED FINDINGS: No intracranial abnormality within the limits of the study; single-suture pattern.

findings: Multisuture synostosis, raising concern for a syndromic form.
Copper-beaten appearance of the inner table (raised intracranial pressure to be considered).
Chiari I malformation.
steps.look: Brain window of the CT or MRI.

steps.label: Standard plane
steps.detail: Confirm a valid standard coronal plane before measuring.

normal.TECHNICAL LANDMARKS: Standard plane obtained on both sides.

findings: Standard plane not obtained on the [ ] side; measurements are not reliable.
steps.look: Straight horizontal iliac line, lower limb of the ilium, and the acetabular labrum all visible (Graf standard plane).
steps.tip: Measurements from an invalid plane misclassify the hip; do not categorise without the standard plane.

steps.label: Bony roof (alpha angle)
steps.detail: Assess acetabular morphology and measure the alpha angle.

normal.BONY ROOF: Right alpha angle __°, left __°; good bony roof.

findings: Alpha angle __° (50–59°): physiologically immature under 3 months (Graf IIa) or delayed ossification over 3 months (IIb).
Alpha angle __° (43–49°): critical hip (Graf IIc) or decentring (D).
Alpha angle below 43°: decentred hip (Graf III / IV).
steps.look: Alpha angle between the baseline (iliac line) and the bony roof line.
steps.tip: An alpha angle of 60° or more is normal (Graf I).

steps.label: Cartilaginous roof
steps.detail: Assess the labrum and cartilaginous coverage (beta angle if used).

normal.CARTILAGINOUS ROOF: Cartilaginous roof covers the femoral head; labrum in normal position.

findings: Beta angle __°.
Labrum everted (Graf III) / inverted (Graf IV).
steps.look: Cartilage roof line from the bony rim to the labrum.

steps.label: Femoral head position
steps.detail: Describe centring and femoral head coverage.

normal.FEMORAL HEAD POSITION: Femoral heads centred with coverage of 50% or more.

findings: [Left] femoral head coverage __%, decentred.
steps.look: Proportion of the femoral head medial to the iliac line.

steps.label: Stability and classification
steps.detail: Record stability only if examined, and interpret morphology with age.

findings: [Left] hip subluxable on stress.
Dynamic assessment not performed.
Graf type [ ] at age [ ] weeks.
steps.look: Stress manoeuvre in the transverse flexion view when performed.

steps.label: Alignment and development
steps.detail: Assess joint alignment and age-appropriate ossification, comparing both hips.

normal.ALIGNMENT AND DEVELOPMENT: Normal alignment and ossification; symmetric hips.

findings: Klein line does not intersect the [left] femoral epiphysis (slipped capital femoral epiphysis).
Asymmetric ossification of the femoral heads.
steps.look: AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral; Klein line along the superior femoral neck.
steps.tip: The frog-leg lateral is more sensitive for early slipped capital femoral epiphysis than the AP view.

steps.label: Epiphysis and physis
steps.detail: Assess femoral head contour, physis width and displacement.
findings: Flattening, sclerosis and fragmentation of the [right] femoral epiphysis (Perthes disease).
Widened irregular physis with posteromedial slip of the epiphysis.
steps.look: Epiphyseal height and density; physis width compared with the other side.

steps.label: Effusion
steps.detail: Describe effusion and synovial findings, comparing both sides.
findings: [Right] hip effusion (capsule-to-neck distance __ mm; __ mm more than the other side).
Synovial thickening with hyperaemia.
steps.look: Anterior sagittal ultrasound along the femoral neck; compare capsule distance with the other hip.
steps.tip: An effusion alone cannot separate transient synovitis from septic arthritis; aspiration is guided by the clinical picture.

steps.label: Bone and marrow
steps.detail: Review osseous change and MRI marrow findings if obtained.
findings: Metaphyseal marrow oedema with periosteal reaction (osteomyelitis).
Reduced epiphyseal enhancement (ischaemia).
Avulsion of the [anterior inferior iliac spine / ischial apophysis].
steps.look: Radiographs for lucency and periosteal reaction; MRI for marrow oedema and epiphyseal perfusion.

steps.label: Soft tissues and comparison
steps.detail: Inspect adjacent muscles and collections and note change over time.

normal.SOFT TISSUES AND COMPARISON: No soft-tissue collection; no change since [date].

findings: Intramuscular abscess in the [obturator internus].
Interval progression since [date].
steps.look: Periarticular muscles and fascial planes on ultrasound or MRI.

steps.label: Ventricles
steps.detail: Measure ventricular size with a named method and compare with an age chart and prior scans.

normal.VENTRICLES: Ventricles normal in size and symmetric.

findings: Ventricular index __ mm (above the 97th centile for gestational age).
Progressive ventricular dilatation since [date].
steps.look: Coronal view at the level of the foramen of Monro for the ventricular index; sagittal views for the anterior horns.
steps.tip: Serial measurements with the same method and chart matter more than a single value.

steps.label: Germinal matrix and intraventricular haemorrhage
steps.detail: Inspect the caudothalamic grooves and ventricular contents.

normal.GERMINAL MATRIX AND VENTRICULAR BLOOD: No germinal matrix or intraventricular haemorrhage.

findings: Germinal matrix haemorrhage at the [right] caudothalamic groove (grade I).
Intraventricular haemorrhage filling less than half of the ventricle (grade II).
Intraventricular haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation (grade III).
steps.look: Coronal and parasagittal views of the caudothalamic groove.

steps.label: Parenchymal injury
steps.detail: Assess periventricular echogenicity, cysts and focal haemorrhagic infarction.
findings: Periventricular echogenicity (flaring) — follow up to assess evolution.
Periventricular cysts (cystic periventricular leukomalacia).
Periventricular haemorrhagic infarction on the [ ] side.
steps.look: Parasagittal views of the periventricular white matter compared with the choroid plexus.
steps.tip: Periventricular flaring is only significant if it persists or evolves into cysts on follow-up.

steps.label: Midline and deep structures
steps.detail: Review midline anatomy and the deep grey matter.

normal.MIDLINE AND DEEP STRUCTURES: Normal midline structures and deep grey matter.

findings: Cavum septi pellucidi and cavum vergae (normal variant).
Linear echogenic lenticulostriate vessels (mineralising vasculopathy).
Absent corpus callosum.
steps.look: Midsagittal view: corpus callosum, cavum septi pellucidi, cerebellar vermis; coronal views of the basal ganglia.

steps.label: Posterior fossa, extra-axial spaces and limitations
steps.detail: Assess the posterior fossa via the mastoid window, extra-axial spaces and coverage limits.

normal.POSTERIOR FOSSA AND LIMITATIONS: Normal posterior fossa and extra-axial spaces.

findings: Cerebellar haemorrhage.
Widened subarachnoid spaces (benign enlargement in macrocrania).
Posterior fossa not assessed.
steps.look: Mastoid fontanelle for the cerebellum and fourth ventricle; high-frequency probe for extra-axial spaces.

measurements.name: Conus level
measurements.method: State vertebral body/disc level and how levels were counted.
measurements.pitfall: Miscounting from a transitional vertebra can falsely imply a low conus.

measurements.name: Filum thickness
measurements.method: Measure in a true transverse plane at a named level in mm if visible.
measurements.pitfall: Obliquity, an adjacent nerve root or poor resolution can overestimate thickness.

measurements.name: Tract/mass
measurements.method: Measure lesion dimensions and trace any spinal-canal communication.
measurements.pitfall: Failure to see a tract on limited ultrasound does not exclude one.

pitfalls: A simple coccygeal pit differs from a higher or complex cutaneous marker; use the clinical description.
Tethering is not diagnosed from a single uncertain conus level without morphology and clinical context.
impression_prompts: Is conus position and motion appropriate with reliable numbering?
Is there a tract, lipoma or other dysraphic abnormality?
Is MRI or specialist assessment needed because of findings or limitations?
escalation: Promptly refer a concerning dermal sinus/canal connection, low fixed cord or other significant dysraphism through the appropriate pathway.

steps.label: Levels and window
steps.detail: Establish vertebral levels with reproducible landmarks and describe the acoustic window.

normal.LANDMARKS AND NUMBERING: Levels counted from [ ]; good acoustic window.

findings: Transitional anatomy; counting uncertain.
Limited window above [ ].
steps.look: Count from the last rib-bearing vertebra or up from the coccyx and sacrum; mark the skin.

steps.label: Conus medullaris
steps.detail: Describe the conus level, shape, position and motion.

normal.CONUS: Conus terminates at [L1–L2] with normal tapering shape and normal pulsation.

findings: Conus terminates low at [L3], with reduced motion (tethering to be considered).
Blunted conus terminus.
steps.look: Longitudinal midline images; real-time pulsation of the cord and roots.
steps.tip: A conus at or above the L2–L3 level is normal in a newborn; a low, fixed conus suggests tethering.

steps.label: Filum and cauda equina
steps.detail: Assess filum thickness, echogenicity and root mobility.

normal.FILUM AND CAUDA EQUINA: Filum under 2 mm, normal echogenicity; mobile nerve roots.

findings: Thickened (__ mm) echogenic filum (fibrolipoma / fatty filum).
Nerve roots clumped and immobile.
steps.look: True transverse image of the filum; real-time root motion.

steps.label: Cutaneous tract and posterior elements
steps.detail: Trace any tract from the skin marker and assess posterior element defects.

normal.CUTANEOUS TRACT AND POSTERIOR ELEMENTS: No sinus tract; posterior elements intact.

findings: Dorsal dermal sinus tract from the skin to the [spinal canal / dura].
Posterior element defect at [ ].
Simple coccygeal pit ending blindly below the canal.
steps.look: Longitudinal and transverse images at the skin marker.
steps.tip: A tract entering the spinal canal is a risk for infection and needs prompt referral.

steps.label: Associated anomalies and limitations
steps.detail: Review lipoma, split cord, syrinx and limitations requiring MRI.

normal.ASSOCIATED DYSRAPHISM: No lipoma, split cord or syrinx.

findings: Intraspinal lipoma __ × __ × __ mm.
Split cord (diastematomyelia).
Dilated central canal / syrinx.
MRI recommended because of [limitation / finding].
steps.look: Transverse images of the cord; the lumbosacral canal.

module_contract.goal: Use a simple container to separate what is visible from what is hidden.
learning_outcomes: Describe the outside of an object without guessing its hidden contents.
Use inside and outside to describe positions.
Update a prediction when new evidence appears.

lesson.overview: We can often see the outside of a closed box while its contents are hidden. Saying 'the box is blue' describes something we can see. Saying 'there is a bear inside' is a guess until we get more evidence. Opening a pretend-play box with a grown-up can show what was hidden. A drawing may show the outside, or the artist may draw an opened view to help us imagine the inside. The drawing is a model of the box, not the box itself.
lesson.worked_example: A closed toy box has a picture of a ball on its lid. Sam guesses there is a ball inside. A grown-up opens it and shows a scarf. The lid picture was a clue about the box, but it did not prove what was inside today. Sam changes the guess after looking.
lesson.activity: Ask a grown-up to hide one large familiar toy in a safe box. Name two things you can see about the closed box. Say 'I guess...' before naming what might be inside. Open it together, then draw the outside and the inside as two different pictures.
lesson.reflection: What did you know before the box opened, and what did opening it help you learn?

module_contract.goal: Notice how a blocked light makes a shadow and how a picture can leave things out.
learning_outcomes: Place a blocker between a light and a wall.
Distinguish an object from its shadow.
Notice that a shadow does not show every detail.

lesson.overview: A lamp sends light toward a wall. Put a cardboard shape in the way and less light reaches part of the wall. That darker patch is a shadow. The cardboard is the object; the patch on the wall is a picture made by blocked light. A shadow can show an outline, but it may hide the object's color, marks and the side facing away. Looking at a picture and looking at the object are different ways to explore.
lesson.worked_example: Two cardboard circles are the same size. One is red and one is blue. Hold each in the same place between a small lamp and a wall. Their shadows can look the same even though the cards have different colors. The shadow alone does not tell us which colored card made it.
lesson.activity: With a grown-up, use an ordinary cool flashlight, a large cardboard shape and a wall. Keep the light away from eyes. Put the card between the light and the wall, then move it out of the way. Point to the light, card and shadow. Let the grown-up help you name one detail the shadow leaves out.
lesson.reflection: Could two different toys make similar shadows? What could you look at next to find out more?

lesson.overview: A picture depends on where you look from. A drinking cup may look like a circle from above and a tall curved shape from the side. Neither view alone shows every feature. curriculum_modules.title: Locate a Boundary with an Echo

module_contract.goal: Reason from round-trip sound time to distance in a simple, nonclinical model.
learning_outcomes: Explain why echo timing measures an outward and a return journey.
Calculate depth from a stated sound speed and round-trip time.
Recognize that speed assumptions and weak echoes limit a distance estimate.

lesson.overview: Sound is a traveling disturbance in a material. At a boundary, some sound may return as an echo. If a pulse goes straight to a stationary boundary and back along the same route, the round-trip distance is twice the depth. With constant sound speed c and return time t, depth d = c × t / 2. Ultrasound imaging uses sound at frequencies above ordinary human hearing and analyzes returning signals. The simple formula assumes a known speed and one direct path. Real materials, weak echoes and multiple paths complicate the estimate. A rope-wave model can show repeating wave features, but sound in fluid mainly involves compression along the travel direction.
lesson.worked_example: In an ideal water-tank exercise, assume c = 1,500 m/s. A pulse returns after 0.004 s. Its total path is 1,500 × 0.004 = 6 m. The boundary is 3 m away because the sound traveled there and back. This invented example is for arithmetic, not setting up or interpreting a medical scan.
lesson.activity: Draw a source and a wall on paper. Trace an outward arrow and a return arrow. Use an invented speed of 10 drawing-units per second and round-trip times of 2, 4 and 6 seconds. Compute the three depths and explain what stays fixed in this model.
lesson.reflection: If a return is late, could the boundary be farther away, the sound slower, or the path longer? What would you need to know to decide?

module_contract.goal: Connect image grids to real-world measurements and distinguish display enlargement from new detail.
learning_outcomes: Convert a calibrated pixel distance into an object distance.
Distinguish sampling size from display zoom.
Explain why an image may not separate two nearby features.

lesson.overview: A digital image stores numbers on a grid. A pixel is one cell of a two-dimensional image; a voxel represents a small volume in a three-dimensional dataset. If the spacing is calibrated at 2 millimetres per pixel, a distance spanning 5 pixel intervals represents 10 millimetres in the pictured object. This conversion needs the scale and the measurement direction. Zooming makes stored cells larger on a screen but does not recover detail that was never recorded. Pixel spacing also does not guarantee resolving power: blur, motion and noise can hide smaller features. A voxel containing two materials may store a mixed value, an effect called partial volume.
lesson.worked_example: A toy image has 2 mm spacing between neighboring pixel centers. Two marked centers are 6 intervals apart, so their represented separation is 6 × 2 = 12 mm. Enlarging the display threefold does not make the object 36 mm across. The same image data still represent 12 mm.
lesson.activity: Make a 6-by-6 grid and draw a tiny dark shape using filled cells. Label the spacing 2 mm per cell interval. Measure two marked cell centers using intervals, then redraw each cell twice as large. Compare what changed on the page with what changed in the underlying data.
lesson.reflection: If a small feature is missing, what evidence would distinguish an absent feature from one too small or blurred to see?

module_contract.goal: Use an ideal attenuation model to explain why one projection cannot uniquely locate hidden material.
learning_outcomes: Compute transmission through repeated ideal layers.
Separate incident intensity from transmitted intensity.
Explain the ambiguity of one path-total measurement.

lesson.overview: A transmission measurement compares the signal entering an object with the signal that reaches a detector after passing through it. In an ideal uniform absorber, I = I₀ exp(−μx), where I₀ is incident intensity, x is path length, and μ is an attenuation coefficient. The model assumes a fixed beam energy and ignores scatter. For a simple layer exercise, each identical layer transmits half the incoming signal, so two layers transmit one quarter and three transmit one eighth. A single projected measurement combines effects along a path; it does not uniquely say where along that path each contribution occurred. X-ray transmission imaging uses this general principle with more complex physics and calibrated equipment.
lesson.worked_example: Start with 80 arbitrary signal units. Three ideal half-transmitting layers leave 40, then 20, then 10 units. Swapping these identical layers changes no total. Even two different layers with transmission fractions 1/2 and 1/4 give 1/8 in either order. This toy measurement cannot reveal which layer came first.
lesson.activity: On paper, send 80 units through pairs of fictional filters with transmission fractions 1/2, 1/4 and 1. Multiply the fractions and compare two possible orders. Sketch another viewing direction that could pass through the filters differently. This is a calculation using invented filters, with no radiation equipment.
lesson.reflection: Why can a very precise measurement still leave the location of material uncertain? Which different measurement could reduce that ambiguity?

40 units
26.7 units

quiz.prompt: What does I₀ represent in the attenuation equation?
choices: The final image pixel count
The distance between all detectors
The incident intensity before the object
quiz.answer: The incident intensity before the object
quiz.explain: I₀ is the input intensity against which transmission is compared.

quiz.prompt: In I = I₀ exp(−μx), increasing x with μ positive does what?
choices: Has no effect
Reduces transmitted intensity
Always increases transmitted intensity
quiz.answer: Reduces transmitted intensity
quiz.explain: A longer absorbing path decreases the exponential transmission factor.

quiz.prompt: A half-transmitting layer followed by a quarter-transmitting layer transmits what fraction?
choices: One eighth
Three quarters
One half
quiz.answer: One eighth
quiz.explain: Multiply the fractions: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

quiz.prompt: Reversing those two ideal layers changes their combined transmission to what?
choices: One quarter
One sixteenth
Still one eighth
quiz.answer: Still one eighth
quiz.explain: Multiplication is commutative, so this measurement cannot recover the order.

quiz.prompt: What does one path-total measurement directly establish?
choices: The identity of every object
Combined effects along that path under the measurement model
The unique position of every absorber
quiz.answer: Combined effects along that path under the measurement model
quiz.explain: A projection combines contributions; it does not uniquely locate them.

quiz.prompt: Why might a second projection angle help?
choices: It measures different paths through the object
It automatically removes all uncertainty
It changes all materials into air
quiz.answer: It measures different paths through the object
quiz.explain: Different paths can supply independent spatial constraints.

quiz.prompt: Which assumption belongs to the simple exponential model used here?
choices: All radiation has zero interaction
Every object has the same thickness
Fixed beam energy and negligible scatter
quiz.answer: Fixed beam energy and negligible scatter
quiz.explain: The lesson model omits several effects present in real equipment.

quiz.prompt: If incident intensity doubles and transmission fraction is unchanged, the detected signal does what?
choices: Stays fixed
Doubles
Halves
quiz.answer: Doubles
quiz.explain: I is proportional to I₀ when attenuation is unchanged.

quiz.prompt: Two arrangements have equal path totals. A more precise measurement on that same path may still fail to do what?
choices: Distinguish the two arrangements
Measure the total accurately
Record an input intensity
quiz.answer: Distinguish the two arrangements
quiz.explain: Precision does not eliminate ambiguity caused by insufficient independent information.

quiz.prompt: A fictional beam starts with 160 signal units and passes through four ideal layers, each transmitting half of what reaches it. How many units reach the detector?
quiz.explain: Four successive halvings give 160 → 80 → 40 → 20 → 10. The combined transmission is 1/16.

module_contract.goal: Compare transmission, echo and magnetic-resonance measurements without treating an image as a literal photograph.
learning_outcomes: Identify the measured signal behind three imaging methods.
Separate image appearance from the physical quantity measured.
Distinguish ionizing X-rays from sound and radiofrequency signals.

lesson.overview: An image is a spatial display made from measurements. X-ray projection imaging records transmission along paths; CT combines measurements from many directions to reconstruct cross-sections. Ultrasound uses returned sound signals. MRI uses magnetic fields, radiofrequency excitation and detected resonance signals, with spatial encoding and computation. Their brightness values therefore need not mean the same thing. X-rays are ionizing electromagnetic radiation; ultrasound is sound, while MRI uses non-ionizing radiofrequency signals and magnetic fields. Non-ionizing does not mean that equipment has no hazards. This comparison concerns physical principles and does not select a scan for a person or interpret disease.
lesson.worked_example: Imagine two grayscale images of a fictional sample. In one, a bright region is assigned to stronger transmission; in the other, it represents a stronger returned echo. Equal brightness on the screens does not show equal physical measurements. Even within one method, changing display mapping can change appearance while the recorded data stay fixed.
lesson.activity: Make three cards headed Transmission, Echo and Magnetic resonance. Under each, write the excitation or source, what is detected, and one processing step. Add a separate Display card to each chain. Mark which statements describe data and which only describe screen appearance.
lesson.reflection: What information about acquisition and display would you ask for before comparing brightness across two images?

Sound echoes

Sound echoes
MRI radiofrequency signals

The detectors must use the same signal
Their measured physical quantities may still differ

quiz.prompt: Can a display mapping change image appearance without changing the stored measurements?
choices: Only if the object changes
Yes
No, every appearance change requires another scan
quiz.answer: Yes

choices: The slice uses multiple measurements and a reconstruction model
The slice must be a photograph of a physical cut
The projection always contains more location information
quiz.answer: The slice uses multiple measurements and a reconstruction model

quiz.prompt: Does non-ionizing imply that an imaging machine has no hazards?
choices: Yes, there can be no physical interactions
Yes, if its screen is gray
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Non-ionizing describes radiation properties, not the complete safety of equipment.

choices: Which file name is shortest?
What physical signal and display mapping produced each?
Which picture has the prettier frame?
quiz.answer: What physical signal and display mapping produced each?
quiz.explain: Acquisition and display information give brightness its meaning.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly limits this physics lesson?
choices: It explains signals rather than selecting a clinical examination
It proves which scan every patient needs
It lets any viewer diagnose disease from brightness
quiz.answer: It explains signals rather than selecting a clinical examination
quiz.explain: Understanding a measurement principle is different from clinical decision-making.

quiz.prompt: Why is equal brightness in two different imaging methods insufficient to show an equal physical measurement?
quiz.answer: Each method detects a different signal, so its measurement represents a different physical quantity. A display mapping turns recorded values into brightness; equal screen brightness does not guarantee equal underlying measurements.
quiz.explain: Identify both the acquisition signal and the display mapping before interpreting a shade. Screen appearance alone does not identify the measured quantity.

curriculum_modules.title: Reconstructing an Image as an Inverse Problem

module_contract.goal: Solve a small measurement system and explain nonuniqueness, noise and regularization in reconstruction.
learning_outcomes: Express a toy imaging problem as y = Ax + noise.
Identify whether measurements uniquely determine unknowns.
Explain how a regularization penalty stabilizes an estimate while introducing assumptions.

lesson.overview: A forward model predicts measurements from an object: y = Ax + ε, where x holds unknown object values, A describes the measurement process, and ε represents error. Reconstruction runs the reasoning in reverse, estimating x from y. Consider two unknown cells a and b. The single sum a + b = 10 allows many solutions, such as (4, 6) and (7, 3). Adding 2a + b = 14 gives an independent constraint and yields (4, 6). Real systems may be noisy, incomplete or ill-conditioned, so small data errors can produce large changes in the estimate. Least squares minimizes a residual such as ||Ax − y||². Regularization adds a penalty, for example λ||Lx||², encoding a preference such as smoothness. That can stabilize the estimate but can also suppress genuine features. A reconstruction is consequently a model-dependent estimate, not a unique truth merely because it looks plausible.
lesson.worked_example: Subtract a + b = 10 from 2a + b = 14 to obtain a = 4, then b = 6. If the second equation were instead 2a + 2b = 20, it would repeat the first constraint and leave the split unknown. Two recorded equations are not necessarily two independent pieces of information.
lesson.activity: List three nonnegative pairs satisfying a + b = 10. Test each against 2a + b = 14. Then replace that second measurement by 2a + b = 14.2 and compare the solution. Explain why a smoothness preference for a close to b could alter the chosen reconstruction when data are incomplete.
lesson.reflection: Which assumptions come from the measurements and which come from the regularizer? How could you test whether a small reconstructed feature is supported by data?

quiz.prompt: In y = Ax + ε, what does A represent?
choices: The forward measurement model
Only the final display color map
An automatic diagnosis
quiz.answer: The forward measurement model
quiz.explain: A relates unknown object values to predicted observations.

quiz.prompt: With only a + b = 10, which statement is correct?
choices: Only a = 5 and b = 5 is possible
Neither value can be nonnegative
Many pairs can satisfy the measurement
quiz.answer: Many pairs can satisfy the measurement
quiz.explain: One equation for two unknowns generally leaves a family of solutions.

quiz.prompt: Solve a + b = 10 and 2a + b = 14.
quiz.explain: Subtract the equations to get a = 4, then substitute to get b = 6.

quiz.prompt: Why does 2a + 2b = 20 add no new constraint to a + b = 10?
choices: It is twice the same equation
It has more symbols
It uses a different unit automatically
quiz.answer: It is twice the same equation
quiz.explain: Linearly dependent measurements do not identify a new degree of freedom.

quiz.prompt: What is the residual Ax − y?
choices: The true object with no uncertainty
Only the number of pixels
Predicted measurements minus recorded measurements
quiz.answer: Predicted measurements minus recorded measurements
quiz.explain: The residual measures disagreement in measurement space.

quiz.prompt: What does ordinary least squares minimize here?
choices: The total number of real objects
The sum of squared residuals
The number of displayed colors
quiz.answer: The sum of squared residuals
quiz.explain: The objective ||Ax − y||² penalizes squared prediction errors.

quiz.prompt: What is a role of λ||Lx||² in regularized reconstruction?
choices: To penalize structures according to an added modeling preference
To create independent measured data
To guarantee every small feature is real
quiz.answer: To penalize structures according to an added modeling preference
quiz.explain: A regularizer constrains the estimate using a preference beyond direct measurements.

quiz.prompt: What trade-off can a strong smoothness penalty introduce?
choices: Perfect recovery without any bias
More measured viewing angles
Less noise but loss of real fine structure
quiz.answer: Less noise but loss of real fine structure
quiz.explain: Smoothing can stabilize estimates while suppressing genuine boundaries or small features.

quiz.prompt: What does ill-conditioned mean in this setting?
choices: Every model has exactly one integer solution
Small measurement errors can cause large changes in the solution
The screen cannot show grayscale
quiz.answer: Small measurement errors can cause large changes in the solution
quiz.explain: Sensitivity to input perturbations is the central issue.

quiz.prompt: A reconstruction looks plausible. What is still needed?
choices: Checks against data, assumptions and independent validation
A claim of certainty based only on appearance
A brighter display to prove accuracy
quiz.answer: Checks against data, assumptions and independent validation
quiz.explain: Visual plausibility does not establish measurement support or accuracy.

quiz.prompt: A two-cell reconstruction satisfies a + b = 13 and 2a + b = 18. What is a?
quiz.explain: Subtract the first equation from the second: a = 18 − 13 = 5. Substitution gives b = 8 and checks both measurements.

module_contract.goal: Design a reproducible nonclinical imaging evaluation using known objects, held-out conditions and explicit error measures.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish bias, repeatability and the ability to resolve nearby features.
Design a test using known dimensions and held-out conditions.
Report errors and limits without claiming clinical competence.

lesson.overview: An imaging phantom is a test object with known features or materials used to assess a measurement system. A toy phantom might be a printed grid of known spacing. Repeated measurements of a 10 mm feature could cluster tightly around 12 mm: repeatability is good, but the 2 mm systematic offset indicates bias. Resolution concerns separating nearby structures and is not identical to small pixel spacing. A fair comparison specifies the task, known reference, acquisition conditions, processing and error measure. A reconstruction method tuned and tested on the same examples may overfit; held-out objects or conditions test whether improvement generalizes. Report uncertainty and failure cases alongside averages. Success on a classroom phantom does not establish clinical performance on people.
lesson.worked_example: A known feature is 10 mm wide. Method A reports 11.9, 12.0 and 12.1 mm; Method B reports 9, 10 and 11 mm. A is tightly repeatable but its mean has a +2 mm bias. B has zero mean error for these three trials but greater spread. Which method is useful depends on the task and acceptable error, and three trials do not establish performance everywhere.
lesson.activity: On paper, define a phantom with two line spacings and a known width. Specify what counts as resolving the lines and how width error will be calculated. Create separate tuning and test cases with different contrast or noise. Write a short report naming reference values, results, uncertainty, processing settings and one condition not tested.
lesson.reflection: Could an attractive image hide a biased measurement? Which changed object or acquisition condition would most seriously test your conclusion?

quiz.prompt: What makes a phantom useful for evaluating an imaging system?
choices: Known features provide a reference for comparison
It is guaranteed to match every patient
Its name removes uncertainty
quiz.answer: Known features provide a reference for comparison

quiz.prompt: A 10 mm feature repeatedly measures about 12 mm with little spread. What is the main pattern?

Poor repeatability with no bias
Good repeatability with positive bias
quiz.answer: Good repeatability with positive bias
quiz.explain: Clustering describes repeatability; deviation from the reference indicates bias.

quiz.prompt: What is the mean error of measurements 11.9, 12.0 and 12.1 mm against 10 mm?
choices: −2 mm
+2 mm
0 mm
quiz.answer: +2 mm
quiz.explain: The mean is 12 mm, so estimated minus reference is +2 mm.

quiz.prompt: Measurements 9, 10 and 11 mm have which property against a 10 mm reference?
choices: Zero mean error in this sample, with nonzero spread
Every individual measurement is exact
No uncertainty can remain
quiz.answer: Zero mean error in this sample, with nonzero spread

To guarantee zero error
To check generalization beyond the tuning examples
quiz.answer: To check generalization beyond the tuning examples

The measurement task and error metric
Only the display frame and title
quiz.answer: The measurement task and error metric

Yes, no resolution test is needed
Only if the image is saved twice

So failure cases can be omitted

A limited result for the tested task and conditions

quiz.answer: A limited result for the tested task and conditions

Only the most attractive reconstructed picture
Only the best result without its conditions
quiz.answer: Reference, errors, variability, settings and failure conditions

source.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria — Relative Radiation Level designations

approach.step: State the question as a physical property
approach.detail: Attenuation, proton behaviour, acoustic impedance, glucose metabolism, receptor expression. A modality can only answer a question that maps onto what it measures.

approach.step: Rule out the modality the physics forbids
approach.detail: Ultrasound cannot see through bone or gas — a soft tissue/air interface reflects nearly the whole beam and leaves a shadow. CT cannot separate two tissues of the same attenuation whatever the window. Structural imaging cannot report metabolism.

Ultrasound and MRI are relative radiation level O across every ACR variant table: transabdominal, transvaginal, duplex Doppler and endoscopic ultrasound, and MRI with or without contrast including MRCP. If one of them answers the question, the radiation debate does not arise.

approach.step: Count the contrast cost separately from the radiation cost
approach.detail: They are independent. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast and without contrast both sit at ☢☢☢; doing both moves the patient to ☢☢☢☢. MRI without contrast and MRI with contrast are both O.

PET resolution is limited by the 2–3 mm the positron travels before annihilation and by detector element size; FDG sensitivity and specificity fall below 7 mm. Do not send a 5 mm question to a functional study.

approach.step: Decide whether you need anatomy with the function
approach.detail: PET and SPECT data are noisy and poorly resolved, which is why they are hybridised with CT. Scintigraphy is planar and two-dimensional; SPECT and PET reconstruct in three.

approach.step: Say why the alternative was not chosen
approach.detail: The line that makes a recommendation useful is not "CT is recommended" but "ultrasound cannot answer this because the target lies behind bowel gas".

measure.cutoff: Water 0 HU · air −1000 HU · cortical bone > 1000 HU · metal > 3000 HU

measure.how: Set by positron range before annihilation and by detector element size.
measure.cutoff: Positron travels 2–3 mm before annihilation; photons detected at 511 keV

measure.how: Below this, a negative PET is weak evidence.
measure.cutoff: Sensitivity and specificity fall below 7 mm

measure.what: Radiation cost of adding a phase
measure.how: Compare the single-phase and multiphase entries in the same ACR variant table.
measure.cutoff: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast ☢☢☢ → without and with contrast ☢☢☢☢

classify.note: RRL bands: O is 0 mSv, ☢ under 0.1 mSv, ☢☢ 0.1–1, ☢☢☢ 1–10, ☢☢☢☢ 10–30, ☢☢☢☢☢ 30–100 mSv in adults. Paediatric bands are roughly threefold lower. Examples are taken from ACR Appropriateness Criteria variant tables; two rows are left unbanded because the sources consulted did not give a figure — do not fill them from memory.

pitfalls: Choosing the modality by availability and then reasoning backwards. If the physics cannot answer the question, a normal study means nothing.

Treating contrast and radiation as the same trade. Unenhanced and contrast-enhanced CT of the same region occupy the same radiation band; it is the extra phase, not the contrast, that raises the dose.
Sending a small nodule to PET. Both sensitivity and specificity deteriorate below 7 mm, so the answer will not be actionable either way.
Assuming ultrasound has failed when it has been defeated. Bowel gas and bone shadow the beam by physics, not by operator error — say which structure was obscured so the next test is chosen properly.
Reading a functional study without its anatomical partner. PET and SPECT are noisy and poorly resolved; the hybrid CT exists because localisation is otherwise guesswork.
Recommending a test without saying what it will change. The value of the recommendation lies in naming the question the chosen modality can answer and the ones it cannot.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain and tenderness an hour after fatty meals. The overnight team ordered a contrast CT of the abdomen, which is reported as showing no stones, and the referrer now considers the gallbladder cleared. What is the strongest objection to that conclusion?
choices: Many gallstones match bile in attenuation on CT
The gallbladder empties before a CT is acquired
Contrast in the wall hides stones in the lumen
Stones under one centimetre fall below CT resolution
quiz.answer: Many gallstones match bile in attenuation on CT
quiz.explain: CT forms its image from differences in X-ray attenuation, and a cholesterol stone sitting in bile often has almost the same attenuation as the bile around it, so a substantial minority of gallstones are invisible on CT however good the scanner. Ultrasound does not measure attenuation at all: it listens for sound reflected at boundaries where acoustic impedance changes, and the step from bile to a stone is large enough to send back a bright arc with a clean shadow behind it, moving as the patient rolls. Ultrasound also delivers the rest of the answer in the same minute, with wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign obtained under the probe. The resolution option inverts the physics: CT resolves well under a millimetre, and ultrasound routinely shows 2 mm stones, so what CT lacks here is contrast, not detail.

quiz.prompt: An ultrasound machine assumes a speed of sound in soft tissue of 1540 metres per second. A pulse leaves the transducer and its echo returns 130 microseconds later. At what depth does the machine place that reflector? Answer in centimetres to the nearest whole number, with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The pulse travels to the reflector and back, so the depth is half the round trip: 1540 multiplied by 130 microseconds is 0.2002 metres of travel, and half of that is 0.100 metres, or 10 cm. Two things follow. First, the machine is assuming 1540 m/s for every tissue, and where sound actually travels more slowly, through fat at roughly 1450 m/s, the echo is placed too deep, which is one origin of the duplication and refraction artefacts seen at fat interfaces. Second, depth costs time, because the machine has to wait for the deepest echo before firing again; imaging deeper therefore lowers the frame rate, and that is why a cardiac study narrows its sector to keep the images moving.

quiz.prompt: A 16-year-old presents three hours after sudden severe left testicular pain, with a high-riding tender testis. The on-call team debates imaging. Which property of ultrasound makes it the test that settles this question fastest?
choices: It shows blood flow in real time at the bedside
It penetrates gas and bone better than CT does
It measures tissue attenuation in absolute units
It separates tissues by their water content alone
quiz.answer: It shows blood flow in real time at the bedside
quiz.explain: Torsion is a perfusion question, and the finding that answers it is absent or asymmetrically reduced flow inside the testis, which Doppler shows in minutes at the bedside while the greyscale changes of infarction are still hours away. The other three describe things ultrasound does badly or not at all: gas and bone reflect almost the whole beam rather than transmitting it, absolute attenuation in calibrated units is what CT measures, and separating tissues by their water and fat content is the business of MRI. The clinical rider matters as much as the physics: where the diagnosis is clinically obvious, imaging must not delay exploration, because the salvage rate falls steeply with each hour of ischaemia, and normal Doppler flow does not exclude intermittent torsion in a convincing history.

quiz.prompt: A bedside ultrasound in a large-bodied patient with abdominal pain returns 'pancreas not visualised, obscured by bowel gas'. The requesting doctor asks why the same gas that hides the pancreas from ultrasound does nothing to a CT taken minutes later. Answer in terms of what each machine detects.
quiz.answer: Ultrasound builds its image from sound reflected at boundaries between tissues of differing acoustic impedance, and the impedance step from soft tissue to gas is so large that almost the entire pulse is reflected at the first bowel surface it meets. Nothing is left to travel deeper, so the pancreas behind the gas returns no signal at all, and the thick body wall attenuates the beam further, forcing a lower frequency and coarser resolution. CT does not listen for echoes: it measures how much of a transmitted X-ray beam is absorbed along each path through the body, and gas absorbs very little, so a gas-filled loop is simply a low-attenuation structure that is imaged rather than a barrier standing in front of everything behind it. Body habitus costs CT noise for a given dose rather than access, which is why the retroperitoneum is CT territory and the gallbladder, thyroid and testis are ultrasound territory.
quiz.explain: The two machines fail in different ways because they detect different things. Ultrasound is a reflection technique and therefore has a hard geometric requirement: an unobstructed acoustic window. Anything with an impedance far from soft tissue, meaning gas or bone, reflects the pulse almost totally and casts a shadow behind it, which is why the lungs, the bowel and the adult skull are barriers. CT is a transmission technique, so it does not need a window, and a structure that transmits nearly everything is imaged as a very low number rather than as an obstacle. This is also why the same physics that defeats ultrasound in the abdomen makes it excellent at the pleural surface, where the barrier itself is the finding.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old has anatomical snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand. Radiographs at presentation and again at ten days are normal, and the wrist is still painful. MRI is chosen ahead of CT. What does MRI show that makes it the better test here?
choices: Marrow oedema at the fracture, before any displacement
Finer bone detail than CT achieves in the same wrist
The scapholunate ligament, which fractures alongside
Cortical breaks that radiographs are too coarse to show
quiz.answer: Marrow oedema at the fracture, before any displacement
quiz.explain: An undisplaced trabecular fracture need not alter the cortical outline at all, which is why the radiographs are normal and why a repeat film ten days later can stay normal. What changes immediately is the marrow, which bleeds and swells: water content rises, so the site becomes bright on fluid-sensitive sequences and dark against normal fatty marrow on T1. MRI is treated as the reference standard for the occult scaphoid fracture for exactly that reason, and it shows the differential in the same acquisition, including bone bruise, ligament injury and a distal radial fracture. The second option is backwards, since CT resolves cortical and trabecular bone better than MRI does, and the fourth describes what CT is good at, which is the fracture that MRI is being called in to find when CT has nothing to show.

quiz.prompt: Plain radiographic interpretation rests on a small number of basic densities. Put these five in order of increasing X-ray attenuation, from the one that appears blackest on the image to the one that appears whitest.
quiz.answer: air fat soft-tissue bone metal
quiz.explain: Attenuation rises with physical density and, in the energy range used for imaging, very steeply with effective atomic number, because photoelectric absorption depends on it. Air is thin and light and removes almost nothing from the beam, so it blackens the image; fat is slightly less attenuating than the water-like soft tissues around it, which is what makes fat planes visible at all; muscle, blood, solid organs and fluid all cluster together as one soft-tissue density, which is precisely why a radiograph cannot separate them; calcium-rich bone removes far more; and metal removes almost everything. Every plain film sign is a consequence of this ladder, from the silhouette sign, where two structures of the same density in contact lose their border, to the visibility of a pneumothorax, which exists because air has been placed next to soft tissue. CT keeps the same ordering but assigns each tissue a number instead of a shade.

quiz.prompt: Take soft tissue to attenuate ultrasound by 0.5 decibels per centimetre per megahertz, in one direction. A 5 MHz probe images a structure 8 cm deep. Counting the outward path and the return path together, how many decibels has the echo lost by the time it arrives back at the transducer? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The path length is 8 cm out and 8 cm back, so 16 cm in total; 0.5 dB per centimetre per megahertz at 5 MHz is 2.5 dB per centimetre, and 16 centimetres of that is 40 dB, a fall in intensity by a factor of ten thousand. This one line of arithmetic governs probe selection. Doubling the frequency to 10 MHz doubles the loss to 80 dB, which no amount of receiver gain recovers without amplifying noise as well, so high frequencies are confined to superficial work. Frequency is also what sets resolution, since a shorter pulse resolves two reflectors closer together, so every ultrasound examination trades resolution against depth: 3 to 5 MHz for an abdomen, 12 to 15 MHz for a thyroid or a testis, and a large body habitus forces the operator further down that scale exactly when the anatomy is deepest.

quiz.prompt: A supine trauma patient is hypotensive. The portable anteroposterior chest radiograph is read as normal. Bedside ultrasound of the anterior chest is then performed and lung sliding is absent on the left. Why did the radiograph miss what ultrasound found?
choices: Free air collects anteriorly in a patient lying supine
Portable radiographs are exposed at too low a voltage
The pleural line lies outside the radiographic field
Air in the pleural space attenuates as much as lung
quiz.answer: Free air collects anteriorly in a patient lying supine
quiz.explain: On an upright film pleural air rises to the apex and outlines a visceral pleural line against the chest wall. Supine, it collects anteriorly and basally instead, where it is projected through aerated lung and produces only indirect signs such as a deep lateral sulcus or an unusually crisp cardiac border. Ultrasound looks at the pleural interface itself rather than through the chest: air in the pleural space stops the beam at that surface, so the shimmering movement of the two pleural layers against one another is lost, and the point where sliding returns marks the edge of the pneumothorax. Absent sliding is sensitive but not specific, since pleurodesis, dense consolidation, apnoea and a main-stem intubation abolish it too, so the finding is read alongside the clinical picture. The fourth option inverts the physics, because pleural air attenuates the X-ray beam far less than lung tissue does.

quiz.prompt: A junior notices that on MRI the cortex of the femur is a black line while the marrow inside it is bright, and that on the plain radiograph of the same femur the cortex is the whitest structure in the image. Explain both appearances from what the two machines detect.
quiz.answer: MRI detects a radiofrequency signal from hydrogen nuclei that are mobile enough to precess freely and still be giving signal when the sequence reads out, so brightness tracks the mobile water and fat in a voxel. Cortical bone is dense mineral with very few mobile protons and an extremely short T2, so its signal has decayed to nothing before a conventional readout and it appears as a signal void; the marrow inside it is fat and water and is therefore bright. A radiograph detects the transmitted X-ray beam, and attenuation rises with physical density and steeply with effective atomic number, so the calcium-rich cortex removes far more photons than the fatty marrow beside it and leaves that part of the detector unexposed, which prints white. The two machines are answering different questions about the same bone: the radiograph maps mineral, MRI maps the water and fat around it, which is why a fracture invisible on the radiograph can be obvious as marrow oedema on MRI, and why a lytic lesion must destroy a substantial fraction of the cortex before a radiograph shows it.
quiz.explain: The general rule is worth carrying: X-ray-based imaging sees electron density and atomic number, so it sees mineral and iodine well and water badly; MRI sees mobile hydrogen and its chemical environment, so it sees water, fat and marrow well and mineral not at all. Both statements are two sides of one fact. It also explains their blind spots. MRI is poor at cortical detail and at calcification, which is why a suspected fracture line or a calcified matrix goes to CT, and why lung parenchyma, being mostly air, is difficult on MRI. X-ray imaging is poor at separating soft tissues that differ only in water content, which is why iodinated contrast exists.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old is brought in 40 minutes after sudden dense right hemiparesis and aphasia. Non-contrast CT of the head is obtained immediately and is normal. The team proceeds to thrombolysis. What was the CT for?
choices: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
To confirm the infarct that the deficit already suggests
To measure the volume of tissue already infarcted
To grade the collateral supply to the affected side
quiz.answer: To exclude haemorrhage before a thrombolytic is given
quiz.explain: At 40 minutes an ischaemic infarct is usually invisible on CT, and a normal scan is the expected result rather than evidence against the diagnosis. What CT does deliver within minutes, anywhere, in a patient who may be restless and vomiting, is the one finding that turns a life-saving treatment into a lethal one: intracranial haemorrhage. It also excludes some structural mimics. Measuring infarct core and grading collaterals are real tasks with real consequences for thrombectomy selection, but they belong to CT perfusion and CT angiography acquired in the same visit, after the haemorrhage question is settled. Diffusion-weighted MRI would show the infarct within minutes, and where it is available immediately it is used, but availability and speed decide this at 40 minutes.

quiz.prompt: A metal fabricator is booked for a lumbar spine MRI. Screening reveals that a fragment was removed from his eye at work some years ago, with no imaging performed at the time. He has no ocular symptoms now. What should happen before he enters the scan room?
choices: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
A slit-lamp examination on the morning of the scan
A written declaration that his vision is normal now
A reduced specific absorption rate for the study
quiz.answer: Orbital radiographs to look for a retained fragment
quiz.explain: A ferromagnetic intraocular foreign body is one of the few hard exclusions in MRI screening, because the static field can rotate or translate a fragment lying against the retina and cause blindness in a patient who came in for a back problem. Two plain radiographs of the orbits, or CT where radiography is equivocal, are the accepted screen, and a negative screen clears the patient. Symptoms and visual acuity do not settle it, since a small retained intraocular or intraorbital fragment is often asymptomatic, and a self-reported history of an injury years ago is exactly the situation the screen exists for. Specific absorption rate governs radiofrequency heating of tissue and is the wrong lever here, since the hazard is mechanical force from the static field, which is present from the moment he walks through the door.

approach.detail: Ask what the answer will change. An unjustified exposure cannot be optimised into an acceptable one, and the zero-dose alternatives — ultrasound and MRI — carry no ionising radiation at all.

approach.step: Place the study on the relative radiation level scale
approach.detail: Work in bands, not in decimal points. Ultrasound and MRI are O. A chest radiograph is one symbol. Single-phase body CT is three. A multiphase CT or an embolisation procedure is four.

approach.step: Drop the phases you do not need
approach.detail: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast sits at ☢☢☢; adding a non-contrast phase moves the same patient to ☢☢☢☢. Each extra pass is a doubling you have to justify by name.

As low as reasonably achievable — or ALARP in the UK — while still producing image quality adequate for the diagnosis. Reducing dose below diagnostic quality is not optimisation, it is a wasted exposure.

approach.step: Audit against the diagnostic reference level, not against the patient
approach.detail: DRLs are set from audit data across many patients — DAP and entrance skin dose in radiography and fluoroscopy, CTDI and DLP in CT. They are not limits and they are not applied to an individual. Consistent excursion above or below one triggers an investigation of technique or equipment.

approach.step: Ask about pregnancy, and about age
approach.detail: The embryo is extremely radiosensitive because of rapid proliferation, migration and differentiation. Children carry the same disadvantage plus more years in which a stochastic effect can appear — the paediatric dose bands sit roughly threefold below the adult ones for the same level of concern.

approach.step: Put the risk in proportion when you counsel
approach.detail: Most diagnostic x-ray and nuclear medicine examinations are under 50 mSv and have not been shown to affect fetal growth or development. Up to 100 mSv the risk is deemed low against the background risks of pregnancy — the spontaneous incidence of abnormality is about 6%.

measure.how: Sum of organ equivalent doses weighted by tissue weighting factors. Use it for order-of-magnitude comparison between techniques only — it ignores age, sex and size and is not meaningful for an individual patient.
measure.cutoff: Always lower than the equivalent dose of the same partial-body exposure

measure.how: Median (not mean) of audited patient doses for a named procedure, locally or nationally.
measure.cutoff: ESD and DAP in radiography and fluoroscopy · CTDI and DLP in CT

measure.how: Compare the study's effective dose against the thresholds below before you refuse it.
measure.cutoff: Most diagnostic studies < 50 mSv · risk deemed low up to 100 mSv

measure.how: All-or-nothing: intrauterine death and resorption, usually undetected, or a normal pregnancy.
Deterministic risk of congenital malformation, most of it CNS. Growth restriction can occur beyond 4 weeks gestation.
measure.cutoff: Probable threshold > 100 mSv; malformation especially at 20–40 days

measure.how: Little malformation risk; the concerns shift to IQ and to childhood cancer.
measure.cutoff: Reduced IQ mainly 8–25 weeks · childhood cancer mainly after 25 weeks

classify.name: ACR relative radiation level bands
columns: Examples verified from ACR variant tables
rows: Ultrasound (transabdominal, transvaginal, duplex Doppler, endoscopic); MRI with or without contrast, including MRCP
CT chest with, without, or without and with contrast; CTA chest; CT abdomen and pelvis with or without contrast; CT pelvis with or without contrast
CT abdomen and pelvis without and with contrast; CT pelvis without and with contrast; bronchial arteriography with embolisation
classify.note: Where patient dose varies too much with body region or guidance technique to band it, the ACR designates the examination "Varies". Bands marked — had no example in the variant tables consulted; do not fill them from memory.

pitfalls: Quoting an effective dose to a patient as their personal risk. It is a rough whole-body equivalence built on arbitrary weighting factors that ignore age, sex and size — good for comparing techniques, meaningless for one person.
Treating a diagnostic reference level as a dose limit. It is an optimisation aid derived from audit; the patient in front of you may legitimately need more.
Assuming a lower dose is always better. Below diagnostic image quality the exposure delivers risk and no answer, which is the worst possible trade.

Refusing a justified CT in pregnancy. Diagnostic examinations sit well below the ≈100 mSv thresholds at which deterministic fetal effects begin; interventional pelvic procedures and radiotherapy are the exposures that can reach them.
Adding an unenhanced phase by habit. It moves a body CT up a whole radiation level for the same clinical question.

Forgetting that children are not small adults for dose. The ACR paediatric band for a given level of concern is roughly a third of the adult figure, and there are more years ahead in which a stochastic effect can appear.
