quiz.prompt: A patient is transferred with abdominal pain and brings a disc containing a CT of the abdomen performed at the referring hospital two days ago. The images are awkward to import, and the receiving team asks for the scan to be repeated so that it sits on the local system. What is the correct response?
choices: Import the outside study rather than repeat the scan
Repeat the scan, since local images are read faster
Repeat it with a lower dose protocol to compensate
Repeat the single phase that the local team wants
quiz.answer: Import the outside study rather than repeat the scan
quiz.explain: Justification asks whether this exposure will change what happens to this patient. An exposure that duplicates a diagnostic study performed two days ago delivers the whole of the risk and almost none of the information, and avoidable repeat imaging is a recognised source of population dose that departments are expected to design against. Optimisation is the answer to a different question, namely how to keep the dose as low as reasonably achievable once an examination has been justified, and a lower-dose protocol cannot rescue an exposure that failed the prior test of whether to expose at all. Repeating a single phase is the same argument in a smaller package. The right work here is administrative rather than radiological: import the disc, or ask the referring department to push the study, and escalate the interoperability problem so that it stops generating exposures.

quiz.prompt: During a fluoroscopically guided procedure the scattered dose rate one metre from the patient is 360 microsieverts per hour. Scatter falls with the square of the distance from the patient. What is the dose rate three metres from the patient, in microsieverts per hour? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three times the distance means a ninth of the rate, so 360 becomes 40 microsieverts per hour. The patient is the source as far as staff are concerned, because the scattered beam coming off the irradiated tissue, not the primary beam, is what reaches the room. Distance is therefore the cheapest protection available: it costs nothing, needs no equipment, protects the eyes and the hands as well as the trunk, and it does not alter the patient's dose by a microsievert. Lead of 0.35 to 0.5 mm equivalent attenuates most of the scattered beam but protects only what it covers and is worn all day, and the other classical levers are time, meaning short fluoroscopy runs at low pulse rates, and shielding, meaning ceiling-suspended screens and table drapes.

quiz.prompt: Your department is asked why a 4-year-old having a CT of the abdomen is not simply scanned on the adult protocol with the milliampere setting turned down. Give the reasons that make dose in a child a separate problem, covering both how much dose the child receives and what that dose then does.
quiz.answer: Two separate things are at stake. First, the delivered dose differs: a small body attenuates far less of the beam, so an adult technique deposits a substantially higher absorbed dose in a child's organs, and those organs sit closer together and closer to the surface, so more of them lie within the primary beam and fewer are spared by depth. A paediatric protocol therefore changes tube current and tube potential together, restricts the scan length to the anatomy the question needs, drops phases that add nothing, and adapts to the size of the child rather than to the age on the request card. Second, the same absorbed dose carries more risk: growing tissues divide rapidly and are more radiosensitive, and a young child has many more years ahead in which a stochastic effect such as a radiation-induced cancer can appear. Justification therefore bites harder in children, which is why ultrasound and MRI are preferred wherever they can answer the same question.
quiz.explain: Turning one dial down is not a paediatric protocol, and the reason is that two independent multipliers are working against the child at once. The physical one is attenuation: less tissue means more of the beam reaching the far side, and a lower fraction absorbed does not translate into a lower dose when the same output is used. The biological one is radiosensitivity multiplied by remaining lifespan, which is why the risk per millisievert is estimated to be several times higher in early childhood than in late adulthood. The practical corollary is the one to remember at the request stage: the single largest dose reduction available in a child is usually the scan that is not performed, followed by the modality that uses no ionising radiation at all.

quiz.prompt: Effective dose weights the absorbed dose to each organ by a tissue weighting factor before summing. Put these four tissues in order of increasing ICRP 103 tissue weighting factor, from the smallest weight to the largest.
quiz.answer: skin thyroid gonads breast
quiz.explain: ICRP Publication 103 assigns skin 0.01, thyroid 0.04, the gonads 0.08 and breast 0.12, the last shared with red bone marrow, colon, lung and stomach. The ordering carries a practical message: a scan that puts the breast in the primary beam, such as a chest CT in a young woman, spends its dose on heavily weighted tissue, which is one argument behind breast shielding debates, behind organ-based tube current modulation, and behind preferring perfusion scintigraphy to CT in some pregnant patients. Two cautions belong with the numbers. Effective dose is a protection quantity, averaged across both sexes and all ages, designed for setting standards and comparing protocols rather than for estimating the risk to the individual in front of you. And the weights are for stochastic risk, so they say nothing about tissue reactions such as skin injury, where the absorbed dose to the skin itself is what counts.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old at nine weeks of pregnancy has pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and hypoxia. Leg ultrasound shows no thrombus. The team is reluctant to expose the fetus and proposes treating on suspicion alone. What is the better course?
choices: Image the chest and let the result direct treatment
Anticoagulate for six months without any imaging
Defer chest imaging until the second trimester
Repeat the leg ultrasound daily for three days
quiz.answer: Image the chest and let the result direct treatment
quiz.explain: The fetal dose from CT pulmonary angiography, and from perfusion scintigraphy, is far below the levels at which fetal harm has been demonstrated, and both examinations are accepted in pregnancy. What is not acceptable is committing a young woman to months of anticoagulation, to the bleeding risk around delivery and to the label in every future pregnancy, on suspicion alone, when untreated pulmonary embolism remains a leading cause of maternal death. A negative leg ultrasound reduces the probability but does not exclude embolism, since the clot may have embolised entirely. Choosing between CT angiography and perfusion scintigraphy turns on the chest radiograph and on which dose is being minimised, because CT delivers more to the maternal breast and scintigraphy a little more to the fetus, and both are small; the conversation with the patient about that trade is part of the examination.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old with ileal Crohn disease will need repeated assessment of disease activity over decades. The team asks for CT enterography each time, because it is quicker to schedule. What is the better standing arrangement?
choices: MR enterography for the repeated assessments
CT enterography with a reduced-dose protocol
Abdominal radiographs between the CT studies
CT enterography at half the usual scan length
quiz.answer: MR enterography for the repeated assessments
quiz.explain: The decision that matters here is not made scan by scan but over a lifetime: a relapsing disease diagnosed at 22 means decades of repeat imaging, and cumulative exposure in inflammatory bowel disease is a recognised problem concentrated in the young patients who are scanned most often. MR enterography answers the same questions, being mural thickening, mural enhancement, strictures, fistulae and collections, with no ionising radiation, and it adds a cine assessment of peristalsis that CT cannot give. Bowel ultrasound is increasingly used in the same surveillance role and is quicker still. Optimising the CT protocol is worth doing and buys a real reduction, but it still spends dose at every visit, and shortening the scan length sacrifices the anatomy the question needs. CT keeps its place for the acute complication, where speed and the search for free air or an abscess decide.

quiz.prompt: Take the effective dose of a posteroanterior chest radiograph as 0.02 mSv and that of a CT of the abdomen and pelvis as 10 mSv. How many chest radiographs deliver the same effective dose as one such CT? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Ten divided by 0.02 is 500. The arithmetic is trivial and the scale is the point: the two examinations sit orders of magnitude apart, so the mental habit of treating any imaging as roughly equivalent breaks down immediately. Natural background is a few millisieverts a year in most countries, which puts a chest radiograph at a few days of background and an abdominal CT at a few years of it, and those comparisons are useful for a conversation with a patient. Use them to inform rather than to reassure, for two reasons: effective dose is a protection quantity averaged over a reference population rather than a personal risk figure, and the actual dose of a given CT varies severalfold with the patient's size, the protocol and the number of phases, so the 10 mSv in the question is a typical value and not a constant.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after a long fluoroscopically guided embolisation, a patient reports a well-demarcated red patch of skin on the back, roughly square and about the size of the image field. What does this represent?
choices: A tissue reaction from skin dose above a threshold
A delayed allergic response to the iodinated agent
A stochastic effect of the radiation on skin cells
A pressure injury from lying still on a hard table
quiz.answer: A tissue reaction from skin dose above a threshold
quiz.explain: The shape gives it away: a sharply squared patch matching the collimated field is a dose map, not a disease. Skin injury is a deterministic effect, or tissue reaction, with a threshold in the region of 2 Gy for transient erythema, above which severity rises with dose through epilation and desquamation to dermal necrosis, and the latency lengthens as the severity increases. That is why long interventional procedures track cumulative skin dose, vary the beam angulation to spread the entrance point, set notification levels and arrange follow-up above them. A stochastic effect has no threshold and rises in probability rather than severity with dose, appearing as a cancer years later rather than as a field-shaped patch at three weeks. A contrast reaction does not respect the edges of a collimated field, and a pressure injury sits over a bony prominence rather than in a rectangle.

quiz.prompt: A general practitioner requests lumbar spine radiographs for six weeks of non-specific low back pain in a 35-year-old with no red flags. Draft the substance of your reply, using justification and optimisation as two separate ideas.
quiz.answer: The request fails justification, which is the prior question of whether this exposure will change what happens to this patient. In non-specific back pain without red flags the radiographs will either be normal or show degenerative change that is common in people of the same age who have no pain at all, so management is unchanged either way while the patient acquires a label and a reason to believe the spine is damaged. The dose is not trivial either, because a lumbar spine series delivers an effective dose many times that of a chest radiograph, to the abdomen and gonads. Optimisation is a separate idea and comes second: it asks how to keep the dose as low as reasonably achievable once an examination has been justified, through collimation, projection choice, exposure factors, shielding where it helps and avoiding repeat exposures. A well-optimised examination that should not have happened is still an unjustified exposure, so the reply should offer what does change management: conservative treatment with review, and imaging reserved for red flags, for failure to improve, or for a planned intervention.
quiz.explain: The two principles are ordered, and the order is what trainees most often lose. Justification is a judgement about this patient and this question, made jointly by the referrer and the practitioner who authorises the exposure, and it can only be answered yes or no. Optimisation is an engineering exercise applied afterwards, and it is continuous rather than binary. Running them together produces the two characteristic errors: agreeing to an unhelpful examination because the dose is small, and refusing a helpful one because the dose is large. The third principle, dose limitation, does not enter at all here, because dose limits do not apply to the medical exposure of patients.

quiz.prompt: A radiographer refuses a third CT this year in a patient with metastatic disease, saying that the patient has used up the annual dose limit. How should this be answered?
choices: Dose limits are set for staff and the public, not patients
The limit resets on the anniversary of the first study
The limit applies once three studies have been done
The limit is set per organ, so the chest is exempt
quiz.answer: Dose limits are set for staff and the public, not patients
quiz.explain: The system of radiological protection applies dose limits to occupational and public exposure, where the person exposed receives no direct benefit from the exposure. Medical exposure of a patient is controlled differently, through justification for that patient and optimisation of that examination, with diagnostic reference levels as the audit tool for the department rather than a cap on the individual. There is therefore no annual patient allowance to exhaust, and inventing one would deny imaging to precisely the patients whose illness makes imaging most valuable, which in this case is a patient whose treatment decisions depend on measuring the disease. The radiographer's instinct is still worth having and should be spent on the questions that do apply: will this scan change management, has the interval since the last one been long enough to show a change, and could a shorter or lower-dose protocol answer it.

quiz.prompt: An operator wants to cut personal dose on a busy fluoroscopy list. Which single change lowers the operator's dose while leaving the dose to the patient exactly as it was?
choices: Standing a metre further back during acquisitions
Pulsing the fluoroscopy at half the frame rate
Collimating tightly to the region of interest
Removing the anti-scatter grid for small patients
quiz.answer: Standing a metre further back during acquisitions
quiz.explain: The operator is irradiated by scatter from the patient, so distance acts on the operator alone: the rate falls with the square of the separation, and a single step back is worth more than most equipment. The other three are all good practice, and all of them work by making less radiation in the first place, so each reduces the patient's dose as well and therefore does not answer the question as put. Halving the pulse rate roughly halves the fluoroscopic dose, tight collimation reduces both the irradiated volume and the scatter it produces, and removing the grid in a small patient lowers the entrance dose needed for the same image. The other protections that spare the operator without touching the patient are the ceiling-suspended screen, the table drape, lead glasses and, where geometry allows, keeping the tube under the table so that the densest scatter goes downwards.

module_contract.goal: Read an acute abdominal CT for free gas, obstruction and inflammation, find the transition point, and tell mechanical obstruction from ileus.

approach.detail: First confirm or exclude the most common disease for that presentation. Then screen for general signs of pathology.

approach.step: Let the quadrant set the first question
approach.detail: Right lower quadrant — appendicitis. Left lower quadrant — sigmoid diverticulitis. Right upper quadrant — cholecystitis. Left upper quadrant is rare, and gastric pathology is the usual answer.

approach.step: Look for free air on lung windows
approach.detail: Always examine the images on lung settings. Free intraperitoneal air is proof of bowel perforation and a surgical emergency. Perforated gastric ulcer and colonic diverticulitis are the commonest causes.
Dilated loops followed by collapsed loops mean mechanical obstruction. An ileus with no normal bowel loops anywhere strongly suggests a paralytic cause such as general peritonitis.
A smooth transition from dilated to collapsed small bowel with no mass suggests adhesions — 60–80% of cases.

approach.step: Use the small bowel faeces sign
approach.detail: Gas and particulate material within a dilated small bowel loop marks the obstruction site.
Maximum outer-to-outer diameter over 6 mm with surrounding fat inflammation.

measure.how: Maximum outer-to-outer diameter, with the periappendiceal fat.
measure.cutoff: Normal ≤ 6 mm; inflamed > 6 mm with fat inflammation

measure.how: Smooth transition from dilated to collapsed small bowel with no mass or hernia.

classify.name: Quadrant to first question
rows: Appendix > 6 mm outer diameter with periappendiceal fat inflammation
Inflamed diverticulum with pericolic fat stranding
Distended gallbladder, thickened wall, pericholecystic inflammation
Gastric wall or perigastric change; free air on lung windows
classify.note: Then screen for the general signs regardless of quadrant: free air, free fluid, obstruction, fat stranding, abnormal enhancement.

TECHNIQUE
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, portal venous phase. Reviewed on soft-tissue, lung and bone settings.

FINDINGS

Free fluid: [absent / present — distribution, attenuation].
Bowel calibre: small bowel [n] mm, colon [n] mm.
Pattern: [normal / mechanical obstruction — dilated proximal to collapsed distal / paralytic ileus — no normal bowel loops].
Transition point: [none / at (site)], [smooth with no mass — adhesion / hernia / mass].
Small bowel faeces sign: [absent / present at (site)].
Appendix: [normal, n mm / inflamed, n mm with fat inflammation / not visualised].
Colon: diverticula [ ], pericolic inflammation [ ].
Gallbladder and biliary tree: [ ]. Pancreas: [ ]. Solid organs: [ ]. Vessels: [ ].
Abdominal wall and hernial orifices: [ ].

IMPRESSION
1. [Primary diagnosis.]
2. [Free air / obstruction with transition point / ischaemia — what the surgeon must act on.]
3. [Secondary findings.]
pitfalls: Not looking at lung windows. A small pneumoperitoneum is invisible on soft-tissue settings, and free air is proof of perforation.
Calling mechanical obstruction when no bowel anywhere is of normal calibre. That pattern points to a paralytic cause.
Answering only the clinical question. Confirm or exclude the common disease, then screen for the general signs — the second step is where the surprise lives.
Reporting obstruction without the transition point. It is the sentence the surgeon reads.
Missing hernial orifices. An incarcerated hernia at a groin or a Spigelian defect is a mechanical obstruction with a named cause.

quiz.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph is taken on the intensive care unit for distension. Gas outlines both the inner and the outer surface of a loop of bowel in the right upper quadrant, and a thin vertical line runs to the right of the midline from the liver towards the umbilicus. What do these two findings together indicate?
choices: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
Gas within the portal venous branches of the liver
Gas confined to the wall of the ascending colon
Colon interposed between liver and diaphragm
quiz.answer: Free intraperitoneal gas, visible on a supine film
quiz.explain: Both signs need gas outside the lumen. Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of the bowel wall, which can only happen when free gas lies against the serosa while luminal gas lies against the mucosa; the vertical line is the falciform ligament, visible because free gas has outlined it. That both appear on a supine film matters, because a supine film is often all a ventilated patient can manage and the classic erect view is unavailable. Portal venous gas is branching and lies within the liver, reaching its periphery, rather than tracing a bowel wall. Pneumatosis alone gives a curvilinear lucency in the wall but produces no falciform sign, and it is exactly what Rigler's sign is contrasted against. Colonic interposition, Chilaiditi's appearance, mimics free gas beneath the right hemidiaphragm on an erect film, but haustral folds run through the lucency and it does not outline anything from outside. Where doubt remains, CT settles it, and a left lateral decubitus film is the fallback where CT is not to hand.

quiz.prompt: A CT for abdominal distension measures the small bowel at 2.6 cm, the transverse colon at 7.2 cm and the caecum at 9.4 cm, each outer wall to outer wall. Taking the conventional 3, 6 and 9 cm calibre limits for those three segments, how many of the measurements exceed their own limit? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Small bowel at 2.6 cm is within its 3 cm limit; transverse colon at 7.2 cm exceeds 6; caecum at 9.4 cm exceeds 9. Two of the three. The caecum is the one to watch: it is the widest part of the colon, and by Laplace's law wall tension at a given pressure rises with radius, so it is where a distal large bowel obstruction perforates when the ileocaecal valve stays competent and turns the colon into a closed loop. Treat the numbers as a prompt to look rather than as a diagnosis. Calibre says only that bowel is distended; whether that distension is mechanical depends on finding a point where the calibre changes, and a colon dilated evenly through to the rectum is far more likely to be ileus or acute colonic pseudo-obstruction than a blockage.

quiz.prompt: A CT is reported for a suspected closed-loop small bowel obstruction. Put these steps of the search in the order that first identifies the closed loop and then judges whether it is still viable.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops first-transition second-transition mesenteric-whirl wall-enhancement
quiz.explain: Recognise dilated small bowel; track it distally to the point where calibre drops, which is the first transition; then look immediately around that point for a second transition, because a closed loop is bowel obstructed at two points close together, usually where a band or a hernial neck catches it. The C-shaped or U-shaped loop between them has its own mesentery, and following that mesentery back shows the vessels converging and twisting, the whirl. Only then ask about viability, on wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric fluid and venous engorgement. The order is not arbitrary: viability is judged on the loop you have identified, and a reader who starts by hunting for signs of ischaemia across the whole abdomen finds thickened bowel everywhere and localises nothing. A closed loop is the configuration that strangulates, so finding the second transition is what converts an overnight obstruction into a theatre case.

quiz.prompt: Four days after an open colectomy a patient is distended and not passing flatus. CT shows small bowel loops to 3.4 cm, several air-fluid levels and mildly oedematous folds, and no point at which the bowel calibre changes. Which single further observation would most strongly support ileus rather than mechanical obstruction?
choices: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
Fluid levels at different heights in one loop
Circumferential thickening of the dilated wall
A collapsed segment of distal small bowel
quiz.answer: Gas and faecal residue reaching the rectum
quiz.explain: The absence of a transition point is a negative finding, and negatives are weak: a transition can be subtle, and a low-grade or intermittent obstruction hides one. The positive finding is that content is still moving the whole way through. Gas and residue in a non-dilated rectum say the lumen is patent from duodenum to anus, which no complete mechanical obstruction permits. A collapsed segment of distal small bowel is the opposite observation, and is precisely what a transition point looks like. Differential air-fluid levels within a single loop have been taught for decades as a sign of obstruction; they are neither sensitive nor specific enough to decide a case, but they lean towards a mechanical cause rather than away from it. Wall thickening happens in both and comments on oedema or perfusion, not on mechanism. Postoperative ileus settles with time and correction of electrolytes and opiates; the reason to keep looking is that early postoperative mechanical obstruction, from adhesions or an internal hernia, is indistinguishable at the bedside.

quiz.prompt: CT in a patient with three days of vomiting shows dilated jejunal and proximal ileal loops. In the 20 cm of ileum immediately upstream of a calibre change there is mottled, particulate material mixed with gas that resembles colonic content. What does that material signify?
choices: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
Ischaemia of the wall of the obstructed segment
Reflux of colonic content across the ileocaecal valve
Bacterial overgrowth producing a functional ileus
quiz.answer: Stasis in obstructed small bowel, marking the level
quiz.explain: This is the small bowel faeces sign: undigested residue mixed with gas from bacterial fermentation, in a segment where water has been resorbed during prolonged stasis. Its practical value is topographic. It tends to sit just proximal to the transition, so on a study where the calibre change is hard to see, following the mottled material distally leads to it. It says the obstruction has been present for a while rather than that it is severe, and it appears in chronic partial obstruction too. It is not a sign of ischaemia: that question is answered by wall enhancement, mesenteric fluid and vascular engorgement, and a reader who takes the faeces sign as reassurance or as alarm has read it for the wrong thing. Nor is it retrograde colonic content, which does not cross a competent ileocaecal valve in this fashion.

quiz.prompt: A closed-loop small bowel obstruction is confirmed on CT. The loop is thick-walled, there is fluid in the adjacent mesentery, the mesenteric vessels converging on the twist are engorged, and one part of the loop takes up less contrast than the rest of the bowel on the portal venous phase. Which of these observations is the most specific for strangulation?
choices: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
Free fluid tracking through the adjacent mesentery
Circumferential thickening of the obstructed wall
Engorgement of the vessels running to the twist
quiz.answer: Enhancement of the wall reduced against other loops
quiz.explain: Reduced or absent mural enhancement is the sign that speaks directly to perfusion, and it is the most specific of the four for strangulation; where it is unequivocal, the bowel in question is at risk now. The other three are sensitive and unspecific. Mesenteric fluid, mural thickening and vascular engorgement all follow venous congestion, which begins long before arterial supply fails and is present in plenty of obstructions that recover without resection. The trap is the reverse of the usual one: their absence is reassuring, but their presence is not damning, and a report that lists them without commenting on enhancement has answered the easy question. Two cautions on the enhancement itself. Compare like with like, against non-obstructed loops on the same phase, since a hypotensive patient enhances poorly everywhere; and remember that a thin, poorly enhancing wall can look deceptively normal on a single phase, which is why the finding is sought on the portal venous phase where mural enhancement is at its most uniform.

quiz.prompt: A CT in a 26-year-old with right iliac fossa pain shows an appendix of 7 mm outer diameter with a normal thin wall, no periappendiceal fat stranding, no free fluid, and gas throughout its lumen. The registrar wants to report appendicitis on the diameter alone. Set out why the diameter by itself will not carry that report, and say what you would look for instead.
quiz.answer: A diameter above about 6 mm is sensitive but poorly specific: normal appendices are distensible and commonly measure between 6 and 10 mm, particularly when gas-filled, so 7 mm on its own separates nothing. The findings that make the diagnosis are the secondary ones, and they should be sought together: mural thickening with hyperenhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding, free fluid, an appendicolith, thickening of the adjacent caecal apex, and failure of the lumen to fill with gas or with oral contrast. An appendix that is gas-filled along its length, thin-walled and surrounded by clean fat is very unlikely to be inflamed whatever its calibre, and a report should say so rather than hedge.
quiz.explain: The 6 mm figure entered practice from graded-compression ultrasound, where the appendix is compressed and a distended one cannot be flattened. Transposed to CT, where nothing compresses the appendix, the same number keeps its sensitivity and loses much of its specificity, because a normal appendix filled with gas or with a little fluid readily exceeds it. That is why every published CT series reads diameter alongside secondary signs, and why the confident negative report rests on gas through the lumen, a thin wall and clean surrounding fat rather than on a measurement. The corollary matters for the report a surgeon can act on: hedging over a normal-looking appendix at 7 mm generates observation, repeat imaging and sometimes an operation, all of which cost more than a clear statement supported by the findings actually present.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free gas remote from the colon and free fluid across the peritoneum; at laparoscopy there is generalised purulent contamination with no faeculent soiling. Which modified Hinchey stage does that describe? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The modified, imaging-based Hinchey scheme runs: stage I, inflammation confined to the pericolic tissues, with Ia a phlegmon and Ib a pericolic abscess; stage II, a pelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess; stage III, generalised purulent peritonitis; stage IV, generalised faecal peritonitis. Purulent contamination without faecal soiling is III. The grades are not a taxonomy for its own sake. I and II are usually managed with antibiotics and, where the collection is large enough to warrant it, percutaneous drainage; III and IV go to theatre, and whether the peritoneum contains pus or faeces separates the two operative grades and tracks with mortality. Free gas by itself does not fix the stage: a small locule beside an inflamed segment sits comfortably within stage I, and it is the distribution of gas and fluid, read against the state of the patient, that says how far the perforation has spread.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has left iliac fossa pain. CT shows sigmoid wall thickening with numerous diverticula and pericolic fat stranding. Which additional finding would shift the reading furthest towards carcinoma rather than diverticulitis?
choices: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
Fluid tracking at the root of the sigmoid mesentery
Engorged vasa recta feeding the thickened segment
Inflammation out of proportion to the wall thickening
quiz.answer: Enlarged pericolic nodes beside a short thick segment
quiz.explain: The two diseases share the sigmoid, the wall thickening and, often enough, the diverticula, and a carcinoma can perforate and inflame exactly as diverticulitis does. The features that discriminate are the length of the abnormal segment and the company it keeps. A short segment with shouldered, abrupt margins and enlarged pericolic nodes is the carcinoma pattern; a long segment, more than about 10 cm, with fat stranding out of proportion to the degree of mural thickening, engorged vasa recta and fluid at the root of the sigmoid mesentery is the diverticulitis pattern. The three distractors are all diverticulitis findings, which is what makes them tempting to a reader who has already settled on the diagnosis. Carry away the limit of the exercise: none of these signs is decisive, CT cannot exclude a carcinoma hidden in an inflamed segment, and that is why an episode of complicated diverticulitis is followed by colonoscopy once the inflammation has resolved.

quiz.prompt: Five days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy a well, afebrile patient with a soft abdomen has an erect chest radiograph for a cough, and gas is seen beneath both hemidiaphragms. Explain how you would interpret that film, and what would make you treat the same finding as a leak.
quiz.answer: Gas introduced at surgery is absorbed over days, and how long it takes varies with the volume left behind, with the route of surgery and with the patient's build, so the interval alone cannot separate residual gas from a fresh perforation. In a patient who is well, afebrile and has a soft abdomen, a small volume at this stage is expected, and the useful next step is comparison with earlier films rather than an intervention. What changes the reading is the trend and the company the gas keeps: a volume that is increasing rather than shrinking across serial films, a new or unexpectedly large collection of gas, free fluid, a collection with an enteric or biliary character, or any of pain, fever, tachycardia and rising inflammatory markers. Then the study to do is CT, and the object is to find the leak itself rather than to count the gas.
quiz.explain: This is a question about what a finding means rather than about what it is, and the answer is that free gas after an operation is uninterpretable in isolation. The single most useful piece of information is the previous film, because a shrinking volume of gas in a patient who is improving needs nothing at all, while the same volume growing in a patient who is not is an anastomotic leak until proved otherwise. Note which way the error runs in practice: the common mistake is not calling a leak free gas, but calling a leak nothing because the patient has recently been operated on. The clinical state carries most of the weight, and radiology's job is to say whether the gas is accompanied by fluid, by a collection, or by a defect, and to compare it with what was there yesterday.

quiz.prompt: An abdominal CT in a hypotensive septic patient shows branching lucencies within the liver that extend to within 2 cm of the capsule, together with curvilinear gas in the wall of a segment of small bowel. Which reading of the hepatic gas fits its distribution, and why?
choices: Portal venous gas, since portal flow runs outward
Biliary gas, since bile drains towards the hilum
Abscess gas, since abscesses form peripherally
Arterial gas, injected during line insertion
quiz.answer: Portal venous gas, since portal flow runs outward
quiz.explain: Distribution settles it. Portal venous flow is centrifugal, from the hilum outwards, so gas carried in it reaches the subcapsular branches and appears within 2 cm of the liver edge. Bile flows the other way, towards the hilum, so pneumobilia collects centrally and characteristically stops short of the periphery; that 2 cm rule is the discriminator, and it is worth having, because the two look otherwise identical. An abscess produces a focal collection of gas with a wall, not branching lucencies following vessels. Read the finding with its companion: gas in the bowel wall together with portal venous gas in a hypotensive septic patient is bowel ischaemia until proved otherwise, and the pair is what earns an urgent surgical conversation. The caution is that either finding alone can be benign. Pneumatosis occurs with chronic obstructive lung disease, steroids, chemotherapy and after endoscopy, and portal venous gas after instrumentation or in a patient with none of the clinical picture. It is the physiology, not the gas, that decides.

quiz.prompt: Appendicitis is usually described as an obstructed appendix failing in stages. Put these events in the order in which they occur.
quiz.answer: luminal-obstruction appendiceal-distension mural-hyperenhancement periappendiceal-stranding extraluminal-abscess
quiz.explain: An appendicolith, lymphoid hyperplasia or, in older patients, a tumour obstructs the lumen; continued mucus secretion distends it past 6 mm; rising intraluminal pressure inflames the wall, which thickens and hyperenhances; transmural inflammation spreads into the periappendiceal fat and produces free fluid; and finally the wall gives way, with extraluminal gas, a phlegmon or a walled-off abscess. The reason to hold the sequence is that the findings appear in that order on imaging. A distended appendix with a normal wall and clean fat is either very early or not appendicitis at all, while stranding without an enlarged appendix should send you looking for another cause, such as right-sided diverticulitis, epiploic appendagitis, terminal ileitis or a perforated caecal tumour. One inversion is worth expecting: hyperenhancement is lost rather than gained once a segment becomes gangrenous, so a focal defect in an otherwise enhancing wall is a late and serious finding, not a reassuring one.

module_contract.goal: Read a chest radiograph to a fixed search pattern, localise disease by the silhouette sign, and separate a technically poor film from a diseased one.

approach.detail: Rotation, inspiration, penetration and projection before you say anything about disease — a technically poor film mimics pathology.
"The most important radiograph is the old film." Nothing here is interpretable in isolation.
Position and calibre. Deviation implies mass effect or volume loss, not the diagnosis itself.
Mediastinal contour for widening, cardiothoracic ratio, aortic arch.
Size, position and density of each hilum; compare the two for asymmetry.
Each zone for opacity, lucency, consolidation, nodules, interstitial pattern, effusion, pneumothorax, pleural thickening.

approach.step: Diaphragm, bones, soft tissue, upper abdomen
approach.detail: Hemidiaphragm height and contour, costophrenic angles, then work outward to the chest wall and visible upper abdomen.

measure.how: Widest transverse cardiac diameter over widest internal thoracic diameter, on an erect PA film only.

classify.name: The silhouette sign — localising disease by the border it erases
classify.note: Loss of a border means the two structures share the same density at that interface — it does not itself name the disease.

pitfalls: Reading a rotated film as cardiomegaly or a shifted mediastinum — check clavicle-to-spinous-process symmetry before you measure anything.
Measuring the cardiothoracic ratio on a supine or AP film; magnification inflates the heart size and the 0.5 cutoff no longer applies.
Calling consolidation without checking the silhouette sign to localise it — the lobe you can name changes the differential.
Skipping the comparison film. A stable abnormality and a new one look identical on a single study.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with cough and fever has a PA chest radiograph. The right heart border can no longer be traced against the adjacent lung, while the right hemidiaphragm stays sharp along its whole length. On the lateral there is a wedge of increased density overlying the heart, bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the front half of the oblique fissure. Where does the disease sit?
choices: The right middle lobe
The right lower lobe
The anterior mediastinum
The lingular segments
quiz.answer: The right middle lobe
quiz.explain: A border is drawn on a radiograph wherever soft tissue meets air-filled lung along the beam. The right middle lobe is the only lung that touches the right heart border, so consolidation there erases it, and the two fissures that bound the wedge on the lateral are the middle lobe's own boundaries. The right lower lobe sits posteriorly against the diaphragm: it would rub out the hemidiaphragm and leave the heart border intact, which is the reverse of what is described, and it is the commonest wrong answer because both lobes project over the lower zone on the frontal film. The lingula does the same job on the left, so it erases the left heart border. An anterior mediastinal mass does obscure the right heart border, but it displaces structures rather than filling a fissure-bounded wedge, and on the lateral it fills the retrosternal clear space instead of overlying the heart.

quiz.prompt: A supine AP radiograph of an intensive care patient shows the left hemithorax uniformly greyer than the right. Pulmonary vessels can still be traced through the grey to the periphery, there are no air bronchograms, the left hemidiaphragm is indistinct and the mediastinum is central. What accounts for it?
choices: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
Consolidation of the whole left lung
Collapse of the left lower lobe
Air trapped anterior to the lung
quiz.answer: Pleural fluid layering behind the lung
quiz.explain: Supine, fluid runs to the dependent posterior pleural space and spreads as a sheet behind the whole lung, so the beam passes through fluid and aerated lung in series. The result is a veil of increased density with the vascular markings preserved through it, because the lung behind the veil still contains air. Consolidation replaces that air, so it obscures the vessels and usually shows air bronchograms. Lobar collapse loses volume, and the mediastinum and hilum would shift toward the opacity rather than staying central. Anterior air makes a hemithorax blacker, not greyer. The point that survives the case is that a supine film hides an effusion in plain sight: what would be a meniscus on an erect film becomes a whole-lung haze, and an erect or decubitus view, or five seconds of ultrasound, settles it.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient becomes suddenly hypotensive as airway pressures rise. The supine AP film shows the left costophrenic sulcus extending abnormally low and lucent towards the flank, an unusually crisp left heart border and pericardial fat pad, and no visible pleural line anywhere.
choices: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
Emphysema of the left lower lobe
A left-sided diaphragmatic rupture
Loculated fluid in the left fissure
quiz.answer: Air in the pleural space anteriorly
quiz.explain: In a supine patient the least dependent part of the pleural space is anterior and basal, not apical, so pneumothorax collects in front of the lung and runs down into the costophrenic sulcus. That gives the deep sulcus sign, a hyperlucent upper abdominal quadrant, and mediastinal and diaphragmatic borders that look sharper than they should because air rather than lung now abuts them. The absent pleural line is the trap: the visceral edge is only seen where the beam runs tangential to it, and here it does not, so waiting for a white line means missing a tension pneumothorax in a patient whose blood pressure is already falling. Lower lobe emphysema does not appear in minutes, a ruptured hemidiaphragm displaces abdominal contents into the chest, and loculated fluid is dense rather than lucent.

quiz.prompt: A ward PA film reported quickly is described as showing a widened upper mediastinum and a prominent right hilum, and a CT is requested on that basis. Reviewing the film, the spinous processes at T3 lie far closer to the medial end of the right clavicle than to the left, and the posterior ribs are noticeably longer on one side. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
Proceed to contrast CT of the mediastinum
Add a lateral to confirm the hilar mass
Arrange a follow-up radiograph in six weeks
quiz.answer: Repeat the radiograph with the patient square
quiz.explain: The spinous processes should sit midway between the medial ends of the clavicles; when they do not, the patient is rotated and the mediastinum is being projected obliquely. An obliqued mediastinum casts a wider shadow, and one hilum is thrown clear of the spine while the other is buried in it, so both of the reported abnormalities are manufactured by geometry. A repeat film costs one exposure and a minute, and it either removes the finding or confirms it. The discipline generalises: technique is assessed before findings, because every technical fault has a disease that it imitates. The one qualification worth carrying is that rotation is an explanation, not an excuse. In a patient after significant trauma, a mediastinum that still looks wide clinically goes to CT whatever the rotation.

quiz.prompt: A frontal radiograph shows a smooth ovoid opacity in the right superior mediastinum. Its lateral margin stays crisply outlined against aerated lung as it is traced upward, remaining sharp well above the level of the clavicles. What does that tell you, and where should the next examination look?
choices: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
It lies anteriorly, so assess the thymic bed
It lies within the neck, so scan the thyroid
It lies in the middle mediastinum, near the trachea
quiz.answer: It lies posteriorly, so image the neural foramina
quiz.explain: The anterior lung stops at the clavicles, while the posterior pleural apex extends several centimetres higher into the thoracic inlet. A mass in the anterior mediastinum therefore runs out of adjacent lung at the clavicle and its border dissolves there, meeting the soft tissues of the neck; a mass sitting posteriorly still has aerated lung beside it above the clavicle and keeps a sharp edge. That is the cervicothoracic sign, and it is a depth judgement made from a single projection. The reading changes what is looked for: a posterior mediastinal mass in this position is most often neurogenic, so the follow-up study is directed at the neural exit foramina and the cord, which usually means MRI. A retrosternal goitre, the classic anterior candidate, loses its border at the clavicle and is traced up into the neck instead.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with night sweats has a PA film in which the cardiac silhouette looks grossly enlarged. Both hilar vascular shadows are still clearly visible, roughly 2 cm inside the lateral border of the enlarged shadow, and the left heart border is sharp. What does that tell you?
choices: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
The left atrium is enlarged behind the heart
There is a large pericardial effusion present
The pulmonary arteries are dilated centrally
quiz.answer: The enlarged shadow is not the heart itself
quiz.explain: This is the hilum overlay sign, and it is the silhouette sign used in reverse. Structures that touch each other efface each other; structures separated in depth are simply superimposed, and both are still seen. Hilar vessels visible well inside the border of a large central opacity therefore mean the opacity is not in contact with them, so it lies in front of or behind the hilum rather than arising from it. A genuinely enlarged heart, and a pericardial effusion filling the same outline, would abut the hila and push them laterally rather than leaving them projected within the shadow. In a young adult with night sweats the anterior mediastinum is where the answer lies, and the film has already told you to look there rather than at the heart.

quiz.prompt: A febrile patient's frontal film looks unremarkable. On the lateral view the thoracic vertebral bodies become progressively denser and whiter as they are followed downward towards the diaphragm, rather than progressively darker.
choices: Consolidation in a lower lobe
Consolidation of the lingula
A large anterior mediastinal mass
Air trapping in both lower lobes
quiz.answer: Consolidation in a lower lobe
quiz.explain: Descending the thoracic spine on a lateral film, there is progressively less shoulder girdle and soft tissue in the beam, so the vertebrae normally look blacker the further down you go. Anything that adds density in front of the lower spine reverses that gradient, and lower lobe consolidation is the usual cause: the spine sign. It matters because the lower lobes hide behind the heart and the diaphragm on the frontal view, which is exactly why the retrocardiac zone is a named review area and why the lateral is worth its dose. Lingular consolidation is anterior and would erase the left heart border instead. An anterior mediastinal mass fills the retrosternal clear space at the other end of the film. Air trapping makes lung blacker, not whiter.

quiz.prompt: An erect PA chest radiograph taken at full inspiration shows a maximum transverse cardiac diameter of 16.4 cm and a maximum internal transverse thoracic diameter, measured at the level of the domes of the diaphragm, of 29.8 cm. What is the cardiothoracic ratio? Give it to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 16.4 divided by 29.8 is 0.5503, so 0.55, and a ratio above 0.50 on a film of this kind is cardiomegaly. Each qualifier in the question is load-bearing. Erect, because supine increases pulmonary blood volume and widens the mediastinum. PA, because in an AP projection the heart lies far from the detector and is magnified. Full inspiration, because a shallow film raises the diaphragm and splays the heart transversely, which can add several centimetres of apparent width to a normal heart. And the ratio only measures a transverse shadow: concentric hypertrophy can leave it normal, a pericardial effusion can raise it with a structurally normal heart, so it is a screening observation rather than a diagnosis, and echocardiography is what settles the question.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film is exposed with the x-ray source 100 cm from the detector, and the centre of the heart lies 20 cm in front of the detector. Treating the heart as a point object on the central ray, by what factor is its width magnified compared with an object lying against the detector? Give the factor to two decimal places. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Magnification is the source-to-detector distance divided by the source-to-object distance, that is 100 divided by 80, which is 1.25. The heart on this film is a quarter wider than it truly is, which is why a cardiothoracic ratio measured from a portable AP study routinely overcalls cardiomegaly and should not be quoted as one. Compare a departmental erect PA at 180 cm with the heart almost against the detector, perhaps 7 cm away: 180 divided by 173 is about 1.04, a four per cent magnification that the 0.50 threshold was built to tolerate. Two variables drive the difference, the shorter distance and the reversed geometry, and both are properties of the portable machine rather than of the patient.

quiz.prompt: A left lower lobe consolidation lies directly behind the heart, yet the left heart border stays sharp; a lingular consolidation of the same size erases it. Explain the physical rule that produces this difference, and state the one thing the sign gives you that a single frontal projection otherwise cannot.
quiz.answer: A border appears on a radiograph only where two tissues of different attenuation lie in contact along the path of the beam, and in the chest that means soft tissue against aerated lung. Consolidated lung has essentially the attenuation of soft tissue, so where it touches the heart the interface vanishes and the border is lost. The lingula lies immediately lateral to and in contact with the left heart border, so lingular consolidation effaces it. The left lower lobe lies posterior to the heart, and aerated lung still intervenes at the border itself, so the outline survives even though solid lung lies behind it. The sign therefore supplies depth: it localises disease to the lobe or segment that touches the effaced structure, which is anatomical information a single frontal projection has no other way to give.
quiz.explain: The rule is about contact, not about superimposition, and that is the whole of it. Disease behind a structure is superimposed on it and adds density without removing the edge; disease against a structure removes the edge. Run the map in both directions and it becomes a localiser: right heart border to middle lobe, left heart border to lingula, right hemidiaphragm to right lower lobe, left hemidiaphragm to left lower lobe, ascending aorta and superior vena cava to the anterior segment of the right upper lobe, aortic knuckle to the apicoposterior segment on the left. The same logic warns you off the two failure modes: a border that is lost because the film is rotated or under-inspired rather than because lung is diseased, and a normal variant in which a hemidiaphragm border is faint because of an interposed colon.

quiz.prompt: A portable AP film in a septic 70-year-old is reported as showing cardiomegaly with bibasal pulmonary oedema. Before accepting that report, name four technical features of the film you would assess, and for each say how it can manufacture that appearance in a normal chest.
quiz.answer: Projection: an AP portable film magnifies the anteriorly placed heart by around a fifth to a quarter, so the cardiothoracic ratio is not valid and a normal heart looks big. Inspiration: a shallow film, with fewer than five to six anterior or nine to ten posterior ribs above the hemidiaphragm, raises the diaphragms, crowds the lower zone vessels into apparent basal shadowing and splays the heart transversely. Position: supine, blood redistributes to the upper zones and mimics the upper lobe diversion of cardiac failure, and any pleural fluid layers posteriorly as a diffuse haze rather than as a meniscus. Rotation: an obliqued mediastinum looks wide and one hilum looks prominent. Exposure and penetration: an underexposed film makes lungs look uniformly opaque and adds interstitial markings that are not there, and an overexposed one erases them. The remedy is to compare with a previous film of comparable technique, and to state the technical limitation in the report rather than to report through it.
quiz.explain: Every technical fault on a chest radiograph has a disease it imitates, which is why technique is assessed first and not as a courtesy at the end. The four faults here converge on one clinical picture, and a single film carrying all four will show a big heart, upper zone vessels, hazy bases and a wide mediastinum in a patient with normal lungs. Reading in the other direction is just as important: the same faults hide disease, since a shallow film buries a lower lobe behind the diaphragm and an overexposed one erases a fine reticular pattern. What makes the report defensible is the comparison. Serial portable films in the same patient are read as a series against each other, and a change in technique between two of them is the commonest reason a chest appears to have changed overnight.

quiz.prompt: A chest radiograph reported as normal is shown three months later to have contained a 2 cm cancer. Name four review areas where an overlying structure hides lung, and for each give one finding it characteristically conceals.
quiz.answer: The apices, where the clavicles, the first ribs and the overlying soft tissues obscure lung: an apical tumour or a small pneumothorax hides here. The retrocardiac region, where the heart overlies the left lower lobe: consolidation, a collapsed left lower lobe behind the heart, and a hiatus hernia are missed here, and the lateral view rescues them. Below the diaphragms, which are part of the film: free subphrenic gas, a raised hemidiaphragm and basal disease projected below the domes. The hila, where normal vessels are dense enough to hide a nodal mass or a central tumour, and where comparison of size, density and position between the two sides is the only defence. Beyond those four, the bones and soft tissues carry rib and shoulder lesions, absent breast shadows and surgical emphysema, and the lung periphery beyond the lung markings carries the pleural line of a small pneumothorax. The common feature is that all of them are looked at after the reader believes they have finished.
quiz.explain: Satisfaction of search is the real mechanism behind most missed lesions, and a fixed review sequence is the only reliable countermeasure, because it runs whether or not the reader has already found something. The areas are not arbitrary. They are precisely the places where a dense structure is superimposed on lung, so that a lesion has to be more conspicuous than usual to be seen. Two practical additions make the sequence work: comparing the two sides directly, since the chest is nearly symmetrical and asymmetry is easier to see than abnormality, and always comparing with the oldest available previous film rather than only the most recent, since a nodule that grew slowly is invisible against yesterday and obvious against three years ago.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral chest radiograph, at the level of the mid-heart, put these structures in order from the most anterior to the most posterior.
quiz.answer: sternum right-ventricle left-atrium descending-aorta vertebral-body
quiz.explain: The lateral view exists to supply the depth the frontal view cannot. Behind the sternum lies the retrosternal clear space, which should be dark down to the level where the right ventricle meets the anterior chest wall; a filled retrosternal space is an anterior mediastinal mass until proven otherwise. The right ventricle forms the anterior cardiac border, the left atrium the posterosuperior one, and behind them the descending aorta runs down in front of the spine, with the retrocardiac clear space between the posterior heart border and the spine. That anterior-to-posterior sequence is what turns a lateral into a localiser: an opacity that overlies the vertebral bodies and stops them darkening downward is posterior, one that fills the space behind the sternum is anterior, and one that does neither but obscures the heart border is beside the heart.

module_contract.goal: Decide when contrast changes the answer, choose the agent for the question and the patient, and manage the reaction and the kidney.

approach.step: Name the phase the question needs
approach.detail: Decide before you inject which phase answers the question — a hypervascular lesion is found in the late arterial phase and lost in the portal phase.

approach.step: Set the volume from the weight
approach.detail: Contrast volume scales with body weight. A fixed 100 mL under-opacifies a large patient.

approach.step: Set the rate from the cannula
approach.detail: The injection rate you can use is limited by the access you have. Check the gauge before promising an arterial study.

approach.step: Time the scan, do not guess it
approach.detail: Use bolus tracking with the ROI in the target vessel, or a test bolus, rather than a fixed delay when circulation time is unpredictable.
A saline chaser pushes the tail of the bolus out of the arm veins and into the circulation, so less contrast is wasted in the injection line.

measure.how: Standard adult volume.
Scaled up to maintain enhancement.
Scaled up again; this is the recommended ceiling.
Through an 18-gauge catheter. Used for all indications, and particularly GI bleeding, liver tumour characterisation, pancreatic carcinoma and pulmonary embolism.
Through a 20-gauge catheter, when a higher rate is not possible or only the late portal phase is needed.
ROI in the target vessel — the pulmonary trunk for a PE study — scanning starts when the threshold is reached.

classify.name: CT phases and scan delay after injection
rows: Arteries opacified; little or no parenchymal enhancement. CT angiography.
Peak enhancement of hypervascular lesions. Also called the arterial or hepatic arterial phase.
Peak hepatic parenchymal enhancement via the portal vein — hypovascular liver metastases are most conspicuous.
Renal medulla and cortex enhance uniformly; the phase for renal lesions.
Washout and late retention — fibrous tissue, cholangiocarcinoma, urothelium.

pitfalls: Giving every patient 100 cc. Volume is set by weight, up to a maximum of 150 cc; a 95 kg patient scanned on a standard volume gives a study you cannot call negative.
Promising an arterial study through a 20-gauge cannula. At 3–4 cc/sec you will get a late portal phase, not a 5 cc/sec arterial bolus — check the access before the patient is on the table.
Using the portal venous phase to look for a hypervascular lesion. Peak hypervascular enhancement is at 35–40 sec; by 70–80 sec the lesion is isodense to liver.
Using a fixed delay in a patient with poor cardiac output. Circulation time is the variable that ruins timing — bolus track on the target vessel instead.
Scanning the kidneys in the arterial phase. The nephrogenic phase at 100 sec is the one in which a renal lesion is either there or is not.
