quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old woman has six weeks of hand stiffness worst in the morning. Radiographs show fusiform soft-tissue swelling around the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints on both sides, reduced bone density around those joints, and small erosions at the radial margins of the metacarpal heads. The distal interphalangeal joints are normal and there is no new bone. What does the film support, and what should follow?
choices: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
Psoriatic arthritis; look for nail pitting and hidden skin plaques
Erosive osteoarthritis; treat symptomatically and repeat the film
Gouty arthropathy; aspirate the joint for crystal analysis
quiz.answer: Early rheumatoid arthritis; request MRI or ultrasound of the hands
quiz.explain: Four features move together here. The distribution is bilateral, symmetric and proximal — metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists — with the distal interphalangeal joints spared, which is close to the opposite of psoriatic disease. The density is reduced periarticularly, because hyperaemic synovitis resorbs the adjacent trabecular bone. The erosions sit at the margin, at the bare area between the edge of the articular cartilage and the capsular insertion, where synovium lies against unprotected bone. And there is no new bone at all, which is what separates rheumatoid arthritis from every spondyloarthritis. The action matters as much as the label: a visible radiographic erosion is already a late finding, so ultrasound or MRI, which show synovitis and bone marrow oedema before the cortex is breached, is what changes treatment inside the window in which treatment works best.

quiz.prompt: A 39-year-old man has one swollen, sausage-shaped fourth finger. The radiograph shows erosion at the fourth distal interphalangeal joint with irregular, ill-defined new bone along the adjacent phalangeal shaft and resorption of the terminal tuft. Bone density is normal, the other fingers are unaffected and the wrist is normal. What does the combination indicate?
choices: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
Rheumatoid arthritis presenting atypically in a single finger
Erosive osteoarthritis, which favours the distal finger joints
Chronic tophaceous gout eroding the terminal phalanx
quiz.answer: Psoriatic arthritis, with erosion and proliferation in one ray
quiz.explain: Psoriatic arthritis destroys and builds at the same time, and the coexistence of erosion with fluffy periosteal new bone beside it is close to diagnostic; rheumatoid arthritis erodes without ever laying down new bone. The distribution is the second half of the argument: disease running along one digit through all its joints, asymmetrically, is a ray pattern, whereas rheumatoid disease picks out the same row of joints on both hands. Preserved bone density, distal rather than proximal predominance, tuft resorption and the swollen whole digit all belong to the same picture, and the advanced form gives the pencil-in-cup deformity and arthritis mutilans. Erosive osteoarthritis does favour the distal joints but erodes centrally and appears in an older patient alongside osteophytes; gout would preserve the joint space and produce a corticated erosion with an overhanging edge next to a soft-tissue tophus, not periostitis.

quiz.prompt: An untreated seropositive rheumatoid wrist and hand are radiographed at intervals over fifteen years. Put these radiographic changes in the order in which they first appear.
quiz.answer: soft-tissue-swelling periarticular-osteopenia marginal-erosion joint-space-narrowing carpal-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Synovitis comes first and shows as fusiform periarticular soft-tissue swelling; the hyperaemia that accompanies it resorbs trabecular bone next to the joint, giving periarticular osteopenia. Pannus then reaches the bare area at the joint margin, where no cartilage protects the bone, and erodes it. Only after that does the pannus thin the cartilage across the whole joint, which is why the narrowing of rheumatoid arthritis is uniform rather than confined to a loaded compartment as in osteoarthritis. Deformity, subluxation and finally bony ankylosis — commonest in the carpus — end the sequence. The order is the argument for imaging early with a modality that sees synovium: by the time the radiograph shows the third step, the damage that treatment was meant to prevent has happened.

quiz.prompt: A woman with twenty years of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is listed for a general anaesthetic, and the anaesthetist asks for flexion and extension lateral cervical radiographs before intubation. On the flexion view the distance is measured between the posterior cortex of the anterior arch of the atlas and the anterior cortex of the odontoid peg. Above how many millimetres is this distance abnormal in an adult? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres is the upper limit of the anterior atlanto-dental interval in an adult; up to five is accepted in a child, whose ligaments are laxer and whose odontoid is incompletely ossified. Beyond the adult limit the transverse ligament has been destroyed by pannus and the atlas slides forward on the axis in flexion, which is precisely what happens when an anaesthetist positions a head for laryngoscopy. The interval that predicts neurological injury, though, is the one behind the peg — the space left for the cord between the odontoid and the posterior arch — because as the anterior gap opens, that posterior space closes. Radiographs answer the question of movement; MRI is what shows pannus, cord compression and cord signal change, and vertical migration of the peg through the foramen magnum is the more dangerous and easily missed second pattern.

quiz.prompt: A hand radiograph in a 58-year-old woman shows erosions at several distal interphalangeal joints. Set out the features that separate erosive osteoarthritis from psoriatic arthritis on the radiograph alone.
quiz.answer: Erosive osteoarthritis erodes centrally. The subchondral plate collapses in the middle of the joint while osteophytes hold up the margins, producing the gull-wing outline on the frontal view, and sometimes a saw-tooth appearance where the opposing surface is remodelled. It sits in a hand that shows osteoarthritis elsewhere — first carpometacarpal and proximal interphalangeal involvement, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts — with normal bone density and no periosteal reaction. Psoriatic arthritis erodes at the margins, where the bare area lies, and then lays down new bone: ill-defined fluffy periosteal reaction along the shaft next to the erosion, ossification at entheses, and in advanced disease pencil-in-cup deformity and acro-osteolysis of the tuft. Its distribution is asymmetric and follows a whole ray rather than a row of equivalent joints, the soft tissues may show a uniformly swollen digit rather than a joint-centred swelling, and bone density is preserved. Neither shows the periarticular osteopenia of rheumatoid arthritis, and neither spares new bone the way rheumatoid arthritis does.
quiz.explain: The two questions that settle almost every eroding hand are where in the joint the erosion sits and whether the bone is reacting. Central erosion with marginal osteophytes is a degenerative process eating through a thinned subchondral plate; marginal erosion with adjacent proliferation is an enthesis-driven inflammatory one. Distribution is the cross-check: osteoarthritis, erosive or not, picks out the same joints on both hands in a recognisable pattern, whereas psoriatic disease is asymmetric and runs down a ray. Where the film is genuinely equivocal, the clinical examination — nail pitting and onycholysis, a scalp or natal cleft plaque, dactylitis, enthesitis at the heel — usually decides it faster than more imaging will.

quiz.prompt: A 72-year-old has wrist pain and swelling. The radiograph shows a thin band of calcification in the triangular fibrocartilage and in the intercarpal cartilage, narrowing of the radiocarpal joint with subchondral cysts, and widening of the scapholunate interval with proximal migration of the capitate. The metacarpophalangeal joints are normal and bone density is preserved. What does the pattern indicate?
choices: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
Rheumatoid arthritis with carpal collapse and ligament failure
Primary osteoarthritis of the wrist following an old injury
Haemochromatosis arthropathy of the second and third heads
quiz.answer: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition with scapholunate collapse
quiz.explain: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, and the triangular fibrocartilage is one of the four places worth looking for them, with the knee menisci, the symphysis pubis and the acetabular labrum. Their arthropathy is degenerative in character — narrowing, sclerosis and prominent subchondral cysts — but it appears in joints that primary osteoarthritis has little reason to visit, and the radiocarpal joint is the classic one: crystal-driven failure of the scapholunate ligament lets the interval widen and the capitate migrate proximally between scaphoid and lunate. Rheumatoid disease also destroys the carpus, but with periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions and erosion of the ulnar styloid rather than chondrocalcinosis. Haemochromatosis is the important companion diagnosis and produces chondrocalcinosis too, but its signature is hook-like osteophytes on the radial aspect of the second and third metacarpal heads, and those joints are stated to be normal here.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old man has had inflammatory back pain for two years. The anteroposterior pelvis shows erosion and sclerosis on the iliac side of the right sacroiliac joint with irregular widening of the joint space, and a normal left joint. Under the modified New York criteria, a unilateral abnormality must reach at least which sacroiliitis grade to satisfy the radiographic criterion? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The grading runs from 0 for a normal joint, through 1 for suspicious change, 2 for minimal sclerosis or small erosions without any alteration of joint width, 3 for unequivocal abnormality with erosion, sclerosis, widening, narrowing or partial ankylosis, to 4 for total ankylosis. The radiographic criterion is met by grade 2 or more on both sides, or grade 3 or 4 on one side alone, which is why a convincing unilateral change has to reach grade 3 while a milder bilateral change need only reach grade 2. The reason the whole exercise has been overtaken clinically is worth knowing: radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear, and MRI showing bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone of the sacroiliac joints identifies active inflammation long before, which is what allows a diagnosis of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis to be made at all. Grading a plain film also has poor interobserver agreement, and oblique or dedicated views add little over a good frontal view.

quiz.prompt: The lumbar spine of a man with ankylosing spondylitis is followed on lateral radiographs from his twenties into his fifties. Put these vertebral appearances in the order in which they develop.
quiz.answer: shiny-corner vertebral-squaring syndesmophyte bridging-ankylosis
quiz.explain: Inflammation begins at the enthesis where the outer annulus inserts into the vertebral corner. Erosion there provokes reactive sclerosis, and the dense corner against a normal body is the shiny corner of the Romanus lesion. Continued erosion of the anterior corners flattens the normal anterior concavity of the body, which is squaring. Ossification then advances vertically through the outer fibres of the annulus as a thin, marginal syndesmophyte, and successive syndesmophytes meet to bridge the disc, ending in the fused bamboo spine. The whole sequence is the argument for the distinction that matters on a spine film: the syndesmophyte of ankylosing spondylitis is thin, vertical and marginal because it follows the annulus, while the bulky, asymmetric, non-marginal paravertebral ossification of psoriatic and reactive arthritis does not, and the flowing anterior ossification of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis spares the sacroiliac joints and the disc heights altogether. A fused spine also fractures like a long bone, which is why new pain in this patient means CT rather than reassurance.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has medial knee pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show loss of the medial tibiofemoral joint space with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes on the medial tibial plateau, a normal lateral compartment, and no erosion or periarticular osteopenia. A supine film taken a year earlier had been reported as normal. What accounts for the difference between the two studies?
choices: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
The earlier film was taken before any of the cartilage was lost
The osteophytes had not yet formed when the first film was taken
Sclerosis obscured the joint space on the earlier projection
quiz.answer: Load is needed to bring the worn compartment surfaces together
quiz.explain: Cartilage is radiolucent, so joint space is inferred from the gap between two cortical surfaces, and that gap closes to its true minimum in a worn compartment only when the joint is loaded. A supine knee film can therefore show a preserved space in a knee with advanced cartilage loss, which is why the standing anteroposterior view is the standard, and why a flexed posteroanterior weight-bearing view is added when the posterior femoral condyles are the suspected site, since that is where cartilage wears first. The rest of the description is a compact statement of osteoarthritis and its difference from an inflammatory arthritis: one compartment rather than the whole joint, new bone in the form of osteophytes and sclerosis, normal bone density, and no erosions.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old man has pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The radiograph shows a well-corticated erosion on the medial aspect of the metatarsal head with a thin spur of bone overhanging an adjacent soft-tissue mass, a preserved joint space and normal bone density. Argue from the film why this is gout rather than rheumatoid arthritis, and say what would confirm it.
quiz.answer: Three features argue against rheumatoid arthritis. The erosion is punched out with a sclerotic rim and an overhanging edge of bone, because a tophus enlarges slowly enough for the adjacent bone to react and to be lifted rather than simply destroyed, whereas the rheumatoid marginal erosion has neither a sclerotic margin nor an overhanging edge. The joint space is preserved, because urate deposits in and beside the joint and erodes bone long before it destroys cartilage, while rheumatoid pannus thins cartilage across the whole joint and narrows it early and uniformly. Bone density is normal, whereas periarticular osteopenia is an early rheumatoid sign. The soft-tissue mass is the tophus itself, occasionally containing dense internal calcification, particularly in renal impairment. Confirmation: ultrasound shows the double contour sign of urate deposited on the surface of the hyaline cartilage and hyperechoic aggregates within a tophus, dual-energy CT colour-codes urate deposits volumetrically, and aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light remains the definitive test.
quiz.explain: Gout is the arthritis that breaks the usual coupling between erosion and joint destruction, and that dissociation — substantial erosion with a joint space that still looks reasonable and bone that is still dense — is what should bring it to mind on any hand or foot film. The distribution helps: the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the midfoot, the olecranon bursa, the knee and the hands in longstanding disease, characteristically asymmetric. Two cautions on confirmation: the double contour sign and dual-energy CT are much less sensitive in the first attack than in established disease, so a negative study does not exclude gout in an acute joint, and an eroded joint with a soft-tissue mass that turns out to have no urate needs a different explanation, including infection.

quiz.prompt: Two men in their thirties have inflammatory back pain. The first has thin vertical ossifications running from the corner of one vertebral body to the corner of the next, with symmetric erosion and sclerosis of both sacroiliac joints. The second has bulky coarse ossification bridging vertebrae away from the disc margin, skipping levels, with sacroiliitis on one side. What separates them?
choices: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
The first is psoriatic disease; the second, ankylosing spondylitis
Both are ankylosing spondylitis at different stages of the disease
Both are diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not inflammation
quiz.answer: The first is ankylosing spondylitis; the second, psoriatic disease
quiz.explain: Where the ossification runs tells you which structure is ossifying. In ankylosing spondylitis it is the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus, which run vertically from one vertebral corner to the next, so the syndesmophyte is thin, vertical and marginal, and the disease is symmetric — including its sacroiliitis, which is bilateral and equal. In psoriatic and reactive arthritis the ossification forms in the paravertebral tissues away from the disc margin, so it is bulky, coarse, asymmetric and often skips levels, matching an asymmetric or unilateral sacroiliitis. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is the third pattern and the one most often confused with the second: flowing ossification along the anterior longitudinal ligament across four or more contiguous vertebrae, with the disc heights preserved and the sacroiliac joints and facet joints uninvolved, which is why the sacroiliitis described here excludes it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a hot, swollen, painful knee for ten days. The radiograph shows loss of the entire joint space compared with a film taken three weeks earlier, ill-defined erosion of both articular surfaces, a large effusion, and no osteophytes. What must be excluded before anything else?
choices: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
Rheumatoid arthritis; start disease-modifying therapy promptly
Rapidly progressive osteoarthritis of the femorotibial joint
Neuropathic arthropathy from long-standing diabetic neuropathy
quiz.answer: Septic arthritis; aspirate the joint before treatment is started
quiz.explain: The tempo is the diagnosis. Bacterial enzymes and the host response destroy cartilage over days, so the whole joint space disappears at once and both articular surfaces erode, with no time for the new bone that any chronic arthropathy would have produced. Nothing else on the list moves that fast: rheumatoid arthritis does not destroy a knee in three weeks and is rarely monoarticular at onset, rapidly progressive osteoarthritis is a real but slower entity and a diagnosis of exclusion, and a neuropathic joint shows the triad of increased density, debris and dislocation with abundant fragmentation, in a patient whose pain is characteristically less than the film suggests. Aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals comes before antibiotics wherever possible, since an aspirate taken afterwards may not grow the organism — and crystals and infection can coexist, so finding crystals does not close the question.

source.title: BI-RADS for Mammography and Ultrasound (BI-RADS v2025 Manual)

approach.step: Describe the finding in lexicon terms before assigning a category
approach.detail: Mass: shape (oval, round, lobulated, irregular), margin (circumscribed, obscured, indistinct, spiculated) and density (fat-containing, low, equal, high). Calcifications: morphology and distribution. Asymmetry: asymmetry, focal asymmetry or global asymmetry.

approach.step: Work up before you finalise a screening call
approach.detail: Category 0 is only for the screening context, when the study is neither negative nor definitively benign and needs a complete diagnostic work-up before a final category can be given.

approach.step: Reserve Category 3 for a genuinely complete diagnostic evaluation
approach.detail: Category 3 (probably benign) is assigned only after a complete diagnostic imaging evaluation, not from a screening study alone.

approach.step: Match the category to the action, not the adjective
approach.detail: The category exists to name the next step — routine screening, short-interval follow-up, or biopsy — pick the category that matches what actually needs to happen next.
Category 6 is for a lesion already proven malignant by biopsy, used for staging or monitoring before definitive therapy — not a diagnostic call in its own right.

classify.name: BI-RADS assessment categories (v2025)
rows: Screening finding that is neither negative nor definitively benign
e.g. calcified fibroadenoma, skin calcifications, surgical clips, fat-containing masses
≤ 2% likelihood of malignancy; assigned only after a complete diagnostic evaluation
Short-interval follow-up imaging at 6, 12 and 24 months
Tissue diagnosis; a benign biopsy result is discordant and must be acted on
Used after tissue diagnosis, before definitive therapy
classify.note: Version on the page is the BI-RADS v2025 Manual. If your reporting habit still calls Category 3 'six-month follow-up' only, note the v2025 wording specifies short-interval follow-up at 6, 12 AND 24 months. Category 4 is subdivided because the biopsy conversation differs across it: 4A, 4B and 4C all get a needle, but a benign result is concordant in 4A and discordant in 4C.

modifiers.meaning: Oval (elliptical), lobulated (undulating contour), round, irregular (numerous angular/deep lobulations).
Circumscribed (sharp, abrupt transition), obscured (hidden by dense tissue), indistinct (poorly defined), spiculated (radiating lines).
Fat-containing (mostly benign), low, equal, or high density — a high-density mass carries about a 70% likelihood of malignancy.
Skin, vascular, coarse ('popcorn'), round, large rod-like, layering (milk of calcium).
Amorphous, coarse heterogeneous, fine pleomorphic, fine linear/branching.
Diffuse, regional (>2 cm), grouped (typically ≥5 within 1–2 cm), linear, segmental (triangular, apex toward the nipple).
Asymmetry (one projection only); focal asymmetry (two projections, <1/4 of the breast); global asymmetry (>1/4 of the breast, no contralateral match).

pitfalls: Assigning Category 3 from a screening mammogram without completing diagnostic views first.
Using Category 0 as a default 'unsure' bucket outside the screening context, where it does not belong.
Calling a high-density mass low-suspicion — density above the surrounding fibroglandular tissue carries a meaningfully higher malignancy likelihood.
Under-reading a segmental calcification distribution as merely 'grouped' — segmental distribution follows a duct system and changes the differential toward DCIS.
Treating Category 6 as a diagnostic decision rather than a staging label for an already biopsy-proven cancer.

quiz.prompt: A screening mammogram in a 54-year-old shows a new group of calcifications in the upper outer left breast that were not present two years ago. The reader is tempted to call them probably benign and repeat the study in six months. Explain what must happen first, and how the category is then chosen.
quiz.answer: The screening study is incomplete, so the correct assessment is category 0 and a recall for further imaging rather than a probably-benign category assigned from a screening film. The further imaging is magnification views in the craniocaudal and true lateral projections, which resolve the morphology of individual particles and let milk of calcium layer into teacup shapes on the horizontal-beam lateral, with ultrasound if an underlying mass is suspected. Probably-benign is an assessment made after a complete diagnostic workup, precisely because magnification so often reclassifies a group in one direction or the other. Once the morphology and distribution are seen, typically benign forms such as vascular, coarse, large rod-like, round, rim, layering and suture calcifications take category 2 and routine screening. A group of round calcifications with no suspicious feature may take category 3 with the six-month follow-up protocol. Amorphous, coarse heterogeneous, fine pleomorphic and fine linear or fine-linear branching morphologies are suspicious and take category 4, rising through the subcategories with more suspicious morphology and with a linear or segmental rather than grouped distribution, and are sampled by stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy, with a specimen radiograph to prove the calcifications were retrieved and a marker clip left at the site.
quiz.explain: Category 0 exists because the screening examination and the diagnostic examination are different tests with different purposes, and a suspicion level cannot honestly be assigned until the second one has been done. The workup is not a formality: magnification changes the apparent morphology of calcifications more than any other manoeuvre in mammography, turning apparently grouped amorphous particles into either unmistakable milk of calcium or unmistakable fine pleomorphic ones. The specimen radiograph and the marker clip are the two steps most often forgotten and the two that determine whether the pathology result can be trusted and whether the surgeon can find the site again.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these calcification distribution descriptors in their BI-RADS v2025 lexicon sequence, from widespread patterns to ductal patterns. This is not a fixed malignancy-risk ladder.
quiz.answer: diffuse regional grouped linear segmental
quiz.explain: The lexicon sequence is diffuse, regional, grouped, linear, segmental. Interpret distribution with morphology and interval change; it does not independently assign a category or universal malignancy probability. The v2025 manual removed the previous distribution-risk table.

quiz.prompt: At diagnostic workup a woman has a solitary, circumscribed, oval, non-calcified mass that is not palpable, and the radiologist assigns BI-RADS 3 with a six-month follow-up rather than a biopsy. That category carries an agreed ceiling on the likelihood of malignancy. What is that ceiling, as a percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Probably benign means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than two per cent — low enough that surveillance is safer than biopsying every such lesion, but not low enough to ignore. The obligation the category carries is a protocol, not a vague plan: a unilateral study at six months, then bilateral at twelve and twenty-four months, and stability across two to three years permits a downgrade to benign. Three constraints go with it. The category should be assigned after a complete diagnostic workup rather than from a screening study, it is not appropriate for a palpable finding or where the patient cannot or will not comply with follow-up, and the findings for which the evidence supports it are few: a solitary circumscribed non-calcified mass, a focal asymmetry that effaces on spot compression, and a group of round or punctate calcifications. A finding that enlarges or changes during surveillance is biopsied.

quiz.prompt: On the mediolateral oblique view a small mass sits in the upper half of the breast; the craniocaudal view places it laterally. A true lateral mediolateral view is then taken to establish its position for biopsy. Compared with the oblique, where should the mass lie if the craniocaudal reading is correct?
choices: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
Higher on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
At the same height, since both are lateral projections
Further from the nipple on the true lateral projection
quiz.answer: Lower on the true lateral than on the oblique projection
quiz.explain: Rotating the tube from the oblique to a true lateral swings the lateral part of the breast downwards and the medial part upwards, so a lateral lesion drops and a medial lesion rises — the aide-memoire is that lead sinks and muffins rise. Watching the lesion move in the predicted direction is how you prove that the two views show the same object rather than two different ones, which is the whole point of triangulation and the reason a mass seen on one view alone gets a second projection before anything else. The true lateral also supplies the vertical coordinate a biopsy or wire localisation needs, and it is the projection on which milk of calcium layers into teacup shapes that the craniocaudal view shows only as smudges.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old presents with a palpable lump. Targeted ultrasound at the site of the lump shows a 15 mm anechoic structure with a circumscribed margin, an imperceptible wall, posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal vascularity or mural nodule. What follows?
choices: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
Assess as probably benign and repeat the scan in six months
Aspirate the lesion and send the fluid for cytological study
Take a core biopsy, since a palpable lump requires tissue
quiz.answer: Assess as benign and reassure; no biopsy or imaging follow-up
quiz.explain: A structure meeting every criterion for a simple cyst is a category 2 finding, and imaging follow-up adds nothing; the criteria have to be met in full, though, because it is the combination of anechoic contents, an imperceptible wall, a circumscribed margin and posterior enhancement that gives the near-perfect negative predictive value. Aspiration is a treatment for a symptomatic cyst rather than a diagnostic step, and clear or greenish fluid from a simple cyst is discarded rather than sent for cytology, which has a poor yield and a real false-positive rate. The categories that do require action are the neighbours: a complicated cyst with homogeneous low-level internal echoes is followed or aspirated, and a complex cystic and solid mass with a thick septation or a vascularised mural nodule is biopsied. In a woman of this age ultrasound is the right first test for a palpable lump, with mammography added when the ultrasound is suspicious or the clinical concern persists.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated irregular mass with associated fine-linear branching calcifications and overlying skin retraction is worked up, and the radiologist must decide between category 4C and category 5 before the multidisciplinary meeting. For a finding to be placed in category 5, the likelihood of malignancy must be at least what percentage? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Category 4C runs from above fifty per cent to below ninety-five; category 5 begins at ninety-five per cent and means the imaging alone is close to diagnostic. The distinction is not cosmetic, because the category changes what happens after the biopsy. A benign core biopsy result against a category 5 finding is by definition discordant and obliges repeat sampling or surgical excision, whereas a benign result against a 4A finding may reasonably be accepted with imaging follow-up. Category 5 is also the level of confidence at which definitive surgical and oncological management can be planned around the biopsy result before it returns. Category 6 sits outside this scale altogether: it is reserved for a malignancy already proved by biopsy and awaiting definitive treatment, and it is not a way of expressing very high suspicion.

quiz.prompt: A spiculated mass with an irregular margin in the upper outer quadrant is assessed as category 5. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy returns fibrocystic change with no atypia, and the pathologist confirms that representative breast tissue was sampled. What should be done?
choices: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
Accept the benign result and return her to routine screening
Accept the result but repeat the mammogram in six months
Repeat the core biopsy under stereotactic guidance instead
quiz.answer: Treat the result as discordant and proceed to excision biopsy
quiz.explain: Radiological-pathological concordance is the last step of every image-guided biopsy and the one that catches the sampling error. A finding carrying at least a ninety-five per cent likelihood of malignancy cannot be explained by fibrocystic change, so the benign result is discordant whether or not the pathologist is confident about what is on the slide, and the pathway is repeat sampling or, more usually at this level of suspicion, surgical excision. Accepting it and returning the patient to screening is the failure mode this check exists to prevent. Repeating the biopsy stereotactically is the wrong technique for a mass that ultrasound can see, and short-interval mammography leaves a probable cancer in place. The same discipline governs the lesions that are excised despite a benign core result because of their upgrade rate at excision — atypical ductal hyperplasia, a radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, papillary lesions, and a discordant result of any kind.

quiz.prompt: A multidisciplinary meeting reviews six mammograms, each assigned a different BI-RADS assessment category. Put the categories in order of increasing likelihood of malignancy.
quiz.answer: category-2 category-3 category-4A category-4B category-4C category-5
quiz.explain: Each category is a probability band, and each band names an action. Category 1 and category 2 both carry an essentially zero likelihood and both mean routine screening; category 2 differs only in that a benign finding has been described. Category 3 is above zero but no more than two per cent and means short-interval surveillance. The three category 4 subdivisions run above two to ten, above ten to fifty, and above fifty to below ninety-five per cent, and all three mean tissue diagnosis — the subdivision guides how the result is then handled rather than whether to biopsy. Category 5 is ninety-five per cent or more. Two categories deliberately sit outside this ladder: category 0 is not a suspicion level at all but a statement that the workup is incomplete, and category 6 is a cancer already proved by biopsy.

quiz.prompt: Comparison with prior mammograms shows a focal asymmetry in the right breast that is larger and denser than on the study two years earlier, visible on both projections, containing no mass and no calcification. Spot compression shows it persists rather than effacing, and targeted ultrasound of the area is normal. What should be done?
choices: Biopsy it, because a new or increasing focal asymmetry carries real risk
Return to routine screening, since ultrasound was normal here
Assess as probably benign and reimage the area in six months
Report it as summation of normal tissue on both projections
quiz.answer: Biopsy it, because a new or increasing focal asymmetry carries real risk
quiz.explain: An asymmetry that is new or has increased, is visible on both projections and persists on spot compression has a positive predictive value high enough to demand tissue, and it is one of the presentations of invasive lobular carcinoma, the type that most often grows without forming a mass. A normal ultrasound does not overturn that, because a lesion with no discrete mass frequently has no sonographic correlate; it changes only the technique used to sample it, which becomes stereotactic or tomosynthesis-guided rather than ultrasound-guided, or MRI-guided if MRI is used to localise. Tomosynthesis is the tool that separates a true asymmetry from summation of overlapping normal tissue, and summation is precisely what a finding that persists on spot compression is not.

quiz.prompt: Five years after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a mammogram shows a spiculated density at the upper outer quadrant with overlying skin thickening. It lies exactly at the surgical site with surgical clips within it, and it has been unchanged over four annual studies, having been denser on the earliest of them. What should be done?
choices: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
Assess as suspicious and take a core biopsy from the density
Request MRI, since a scar and a recurrence look the same
Assess as probably benign and reimage the breast in six months
quiz.answer: Report the postsurgical scar and continue annual surveillance
quiz.explain: Four things identify a scar: it is at the operative site, marked by clips; it changes shape markedly between the two projections, because it is a plane of fibrosis rather than a mass; it has no central density; and above all it becomes less conspicuous or stays stable over successive studies, since scar tissue and post-radiotherapy oedema regress. Recurrence does the opposite — a scar that becomes denser, develops a central mass, or acquires new calcifications is the finding that triggers biopsy. MRI is genuinely useful where the mammogram is equivocal, because mature scar beyond about a year typically enhances little while recurrence enhances, but ordering it against a four-year stable appearance buys false positives rather than information. Comparison with the previous films is the whole of the argument here, which is why the prior studies are part of the examination and not an optional extra.

quiz.prompt: A 47-year-old has a biopsy-proven invasive lobular carcinoma of the left breast, and the mammogram shows only a subtle architectural distortion, so the extent of disease is uncertain. Separately, a 30-year-old whose mother and sister had premenopausal breast cancer asks whether she should be screened by MRI instead of mammography. Give the reasoning in each case.
quiz.answer: In the first case MRI earns its place. Lobular carcinoma grows in single-file strands without forming a discrete mass or a desmoplastic reaction, so it is the type that mammography most often misses or underestimates, particularly in dense tissue; MRI has the highest sensitivity of any breast technique for invasive disease and is used here to measure the extent of the tumour, to look for multifocal or multicentric disease and for a contralateral cancer that would change the operation. The condition attached is that MRI also finds lesions that prove benign, so any additional finding that would alter surgery is biopsied first, usually under ultrasound after a targeted second-look scan, rather than acted on directly. In the second case supplemental MRI is offered to women at high lifetime risk — carriers of a pathogenic BRCA1, BRCA2 or comparable variant and their untested first-degree relatives, women whose family history puts their lifetime risk above roughly a fifth on a model that accounts for it, and women irradiated to the chest in adolescence or early adulthood — but it is an addition to mammography rather than a replacement, because MRI is poor at showing calcifications, which is how a large share of ductal carcinoma in situ presents. Current ACR guidance does not require routine menstrual-cycle scheduling; repeat imaging for a genuinely limited examination is individualised.
quiz.explain: The two halves are the same argument used in opposite directions. MRI's strength is sensitivity to enhancing invasive tumour, so it is worth doing where the question is how much invasive disease there is and mammography cannot answer it, and where a woman's prior risk is high enough that the extra cancers found outweigh the extra benign biopsies. Its weakness is calcification, which is why it supplements rather than replaces mammography in screening, and why an MRI-detected finding is a hypothesis to be tested rather than a diagnosis. Second-look ultrasound and image-guided tissue confirmation help make additional MRI findings actionable.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old whose screening mammogram was reported as normal, with the density assessed as extremely dense, presents nine months later with a 2 cm palpable invasive cancer. On review of the earlier film the unit finds nothing to see even in retrospect. What does the case say about mammographic density?
choices: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
Dense tissue masks cancer but carries no risk of its own
Dense tissue is a reader effect and not a property of tissue
Dense tissue lowers sensitivity but raises specificity to match
quiz.answer: Dense tissue masks cancer, and it also raises the risk itself
quiz.explain: Fibroglandular tissue attenuates x-rays much as a tumour does, so a cancer surrounded by it has little contrast against its background and mammographic sensitivity falls with increasing density — the masking effect that produced this interval cancer. Separately and independently, high breast density is itself a risk factor for developing breast cancer, so the two effects compound rather than offset. That is the argument for supplemental imaging in dense breasts: tomosynthesis raises cancer detection and lowers recall by separating overlapping tissue, and supplemental ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography and MRI each find additional cancers, with MRI shown to reduce the interval cancer rate in extremely dense breasts. The honest caveat is that a mortality benefit from supplemental screening has not been demonstrated, and every additional test brings false positives with it. Density is a qualitative judgement made on the current study and can change over time, with hormonal status and with weight.

curriculum_modules.title: Head Injury: Selecting, Timing and Reading the Trauma CT

module_contract.goal: Decide which head injury is scanned and when it is scanned again, and read the trauma study for axonal injury, herniation and fracture-related vascular injury.

approach.detail: Lentiform versus crescentic tells you epidural from subdural before you think about anything else.
Traumatic SAH sits in the sulci and the Sylvian fissure, not centred on the basal cisterns.

approach.step: Then the coup and contrecoup sites
approach.detail: Contusions cluster frontobasally and in the anterior temporal lobes, against the skull.

approach.step: Then the midline and the brainstem
approach.detail: Subfalcine, uncal and parahippocampal herniation, and the small linear Duret haemorrhages in the midbrain and upper pons that follow downward displacement.

approach.step: Reconsider a normal CT in a poor GCS
approach.detail: CT is insensitive to diffuse axonal injury. If the deficit and the scan disagree, the answer is MRI.

approach.step: Date the subdural before you call it acute
approach.detail: Hyperdense acutely, isodense at 3–21 days, hypodense after 21 days — and an isodense bilateral collection is easy to miss.

classify.name: Traumatic haemorrhage by compartment
rows: Usually does not cross suture lines
Between inner dural layer and arachnoid
Cannot cross the midline; spreads along falx and tentorium
Follows the subarachnoid space, e.g. the Sylvian fissure
Downward brainstem displacement through the tentorial hiatus
classify.note: Subdural density with age: hyperdense acute, isodense 3–21 days, hypodense beyond 21 days. Risk factors for subdural are anticoagulation, age and alcoholism with atrophy.

measure.how: Graded on MRI by how deep the lesions go.
measure.cutoff: 1 lobar white matter · 2 corpus callosum · 3 brainstem

measure.how: Worth stating in the impression, because it carries the prognosis the clinician needs.
measure.cutoff: Odds of unfavourable outcome ×3 per grade

measure.how: Read against grey matter.
measure.cutoff: Hyperdense acute · isodense 3–21 d · hypodense > 21 d

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Non-enhanced CT head[, CT angiography].

FINDINGS
Extra-axial: epidural [none / site, lentiform, n mm]. Subdural [none / site, crescentic, n mm, density — hence — days].
Subarachnoid blood: [none / sites].
Contusions: [none / frontobasal, anterior temporal, n and size].
Intraventricular blood: [none / present].
Brainstem: [normal / linear Duret haemorrhage in midbrain and upper pons].
Mass effect: midline shift [n] mm; [subfalcine / uncal / parahippocampal] herniation; basal cisterns [patent / effaced].
Skull: [no fracture / site, depressed n mm, crossing a suture or vascular groove].

IMPRESSION
1. [Dominant injury and compartment.]
2. Mass effect: [midline shift, herniation, cisterns].
3. [If GCS is disproportionate to the CT, recommend MRI for diffuse axonal injury.]
4. Discussed with [name] at [time].
pitfalls: Calling a normal CT a normal brain. CT is insensitive to diffuse axonal injury; a poor GCS with a clean scan needs MRI.
Missing a bilateral isodense subdural. Between 3 and 21 days it matches cortex, and with symmetrical collections there is no side to compare against.
Using 'crosses the suture' as the only test. Epidural is usually bounded by sutures, but it is not absolute — shape and compartment come first.
Reading a Duret haemorrhage as a primary brainstem injury. It is a consequence of downward displacement, and the herniation is the finding to report.
Reporting the blood and not the mass effect. Midline shift, the state of the basal cisterns and the herniation pattern are what the surgeon acts on.

checklist.detail: Identify epidural, subdural and subarachnoid blood and its distribution.

checklist.label: Parenchymal injury
checklist.detail: Inspect inferior frontal/temporal surfaces, contrecoup sites and grey-white junctions.

checklist.label: Pressure
checklist.detail: Assess ventricles, cisterns, shift and herniation.

checklist.label: Fracture
checklist.detail: Trace calvarial/skull-base fractures and relation to vascular canals, sinuses and air spaces.

checklist.label: Secondary findings
checklist.detail: Check pneumocephalus, scalp injury, visible orbits and device position.

measurements.name: Haematoma thickness
measurements.method: Measure extra-axial blood perpendicular to the adjacent skull in mm.
measurements.pitfall: A tangential plane overestimates thickness.

measurements.name: Shift and contusions
measurements.method: Measure shift at a named level; document dominant contusion in three dimensions.
measurements.pitfall: Early contusions can enlarge; unchanged shift does not mean stable blood volume.

pitfalls: CT can miss diffuse axonal injury and small nonhaemorrhagic lesions.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old fell from standing while drunk, was briefly dazed, and has vomited once. In the department her GCS is 15 at two hours, there is no scalp wound, no sign of a base of skull injury, and she remembers everything up to the moment she fell. She takes no medication. The nurse asks whether to book a CT head.
choices: No scan on these features, but observe and rescan if any of them changes
Scan now, because a single episode of vomiting is itself sufficient
Scan now, because alcohol makes the clinical assessment unreliable
No scan and no observation, since the decision rule has been satisfied
quiz.answer: No scan on these features, but observe and rescan if any of them changes
quiz.explain: The Canadian CT Head Rule applies exactly here: minor injury, witnessed loss of awareness or amnesia, and a GCS that has returned to 15. Its high-risk features are GCS below 15 at two hours after injury, suspected open or depressed vault fracture, any sign of a base of skull fracture, two or more episodes of vomiting, and age sixty-five or over; its medium-risk features are retrograde amnesia of thirty minutes or more and a dangerous mechanism. She has none of them, so the rule does not call for imaging. What the rule does not do is discharge her: it selects a scan, not a disposition, and any rule loses its validity the moment the patient drifts outside the population it was derived in - so a second vomit, a drop to 14, a new headache or a raccoon eye all reopen the question. Alcohol is a reason to observe rather than an automatic reason to irradiate, though a patient too intoxicated to be assessed at all cannot be risk-stratified and is usually scanned for that reason. Note that the rule was derived excluding anticoagulated patients, which is why they are handled separately.

quiz.prompt: A head-injured man opens his eyes only when you press on his nail bed, makes incomprehensible groaning sounds, and withdraws his arm from that same painful stimulus without localising it. What is his total Glasgow Coma Scale score? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds score 2, and withdrawal from pain scores 4, giving 8. Report the three components rather than only the sum, because 8 can be assembled several ways with very different meanings - E1 V1 M6 in a fitting patient is not the same clinical problem as this one. Eight is the conventional threshold at which the airway is considered unprotected and intubation is planned, and a patient at or below it is in the severe band, so the imaging question shifts from whether to scan to how fast, and a low GCS with a bland CT should send you to look for axonal injury rather than to relax. The commonest scoring error is scoring localisation when the patient merely withdraws: localising means the hand crosses to the site of the stimulus, and the difference of one point sits exactly on the decision line.

quiz.prompt: An 84-year-old on apixaban for atrial fibrillation tripped and hit her forehead. She is fully alert, GCS 15, with no focal signs and no vomiting. A CT head performed within the hour shows no intracranial haemorrhage.
choices: Observe for a delayed bleed rather than discharging on the negative scan
Discharge directly, since an early negative CT excludes late haemorrhage
Book a routine repeat CT at six weeks to look for a chronic subdural
Request MRI now, because CT cannot exclude blood in the elderly brain
quiz.answer: Observe for a delayed bleed rather than discharging on the negative scan
quiz.explain: Two separate things make the anticoagulated elderly patient a special case. Age alone is a high-risk feature in the Canadian rule, so she was always going to be scanned; and anticoagulation means a bleed that had not started at one hour can still appear later, which the rule was never designed to address. The practical response is a period of observation with a low threshold for a repeat scan on any change - new headache, vomiting, drowsiness, a fresh focal sign - rather than either reflexive rescanning of every patient or discharge on the strength of one early film. Direct oral anticoagulants and warfarin are not equivalent: warfarin can be reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K guided by the INR, while a factor Xa inhibitor has its own agent and dabigatran has idarucizumab, and knowing which drug the patient takes changes the phone call you make when the scan is positive. Antiplatelet agents raise risk far less than anticoagulants, and aspirin alone least of all. MRI would be more sensitive but is the wrong tool in an acute trauma pathway.

quiz.prompt: A three-year-old fell from a sofa, cried immediately, and is now playing normally with a small boggy swelling over the left parietal region and a GCS of 15. A parent asks for a CT scan to be certain. Set out how the calculus differs from the adult one and what you would offer.
quiz.answer: The calculus differs on three counts. First, the child is more radiosensitive and has decades of life ahead for a stochastic malignancy to appear, so the dose of a CT head carries more weight than it does in an adult and the threshold to image should be correspondingly higher. Second, the clinical predictors are different and paediatric rules are validated separately, using features such as altered mental status, a palpable or basal skull fracture, a severe mechanism, a non-frontal scalp haematoma in an infant, prolonged loss of consciousness and persistent vomiting, and a well child at low risk can be observed instead of scanned. Third, observation is itself a validated strategy in this group, because deterioration is what identifies the few who need imaging. I would explain that a structured period of observation is safer than an immediate scan here, scan promptly if anything changes, and consider whether the history and the injury match, since a discrepant account is the first sign of an inflicted injury.
quiz.explain: The dose argument is the one that is most often waved away as theoretical, but it is the reason paediatric rules exist at all: the aim is not to detect fewer injuries but to detect the same injuries with far fewer scans. Two paediatric particulars are worth carrying. A non-frontal scalp haematoma in a child under about two years is a real predictor of underlying fracture and bleed, because the infant skull is thin and the child cannot report symptoms - so the boggy swelling matters more the younger the child. And skull radiographs, long abandoned in adults, retain a place in the skeletal survey for suspected inflicted injury, where the question is the fracture itself rather than the brain. If imaging is needed for a suspected inflicted injury, CT answers the acute question and MRI is added for the age of collections and for parenchymal injury.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stages of an untreated expanding supratentorial mass by the rostrocaudal order in which the herniations appear.
quiz.answer: subfalcine central-transtentorial uncal tonsillar
quiz.explain: The cingulate gyrus slips under the free edge of the falx first, because the falx is the nearest boundary and the shift is horizontal. As volume grows, the diencephalon is pressed downward through the tentorial incisura - central transtentorial herniation - and the medial temporal lobe, the uncus, follows over the tentorial edge. Finally the cerebellar tonsils are forced through the foramen magnum onto the medulla, which is the terminal event. The sequence is worth holding because each step has a signature: subfalcine herniation threatens the anterior cerebral artery under the falx and infarcts the medial frontal lobe with contralateral leg weakness; transtentorial herniation compresses the third nerve to give a fixed dilated pupil and the posterior cerebral artery against the tentorial edge to infarct the occipital lobe; tonsillar herniation gives apnoea and death. A lateral temporal mass can reach the uncus before the diencephalon has moved much, so the order is the typical progression of a diffuse or convexity mass rather than an invariable law, and the tonsils are always last.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a large right hemisphere swelling and a fixed dilated right pupil is taken for a repeat CT. There is now a small ovoid haemorrhage in the central pons and midbrain, with no other new blood and no vascular injury on the angiographic images.
choices: Brainstem perforators torn by downward displacement of the midbrain
A hypertensive pontine haemorrhage arising from a perforating vessel
A cavernous malformation in the pons that has bled during the admission
Basilar artery occlusion with haemorrhagic transformation of an infarct
quiz.answer: Brainstem perforators torn by downward displacement of the midbrain
quiz.explain: This is a Duret haemorrhage, the mechanical consequence of descending transtentorial herniation rather than a disease of the brainstem itself. The basilar artery is anchored below while the midbrain is driven downwards, so the perforating branches supplying the central pons and midbrain are stretched and torn; the resulting haemorrhage lies centrally and paramedian in the tegmentum, appears in the context of an obvious supratentorial mass, and is an agonal sign rather than an independent problem to treat. The value of naming it is that it changes nothing about the operation but a great deal about the conversation with the family and the intensive care team. A hypertensive pontine bleed occurs without a supratentorial mass and in a hypertensive patient, a cavernoma has a haemosiderin rim and popcorn heterogeneity on prior imaging, and haemorrhagic transformation of a brainstem infarct would follow a demonstrable arterial occlusion and an established infarct.

quiz.prompt: A twenty-year-old is deeply unconscious after a motorcycle crash. The CT head shows no collection, no shift and no fracture; a few scattered dense dots sit at the lobar grey-white junction. The team wants to know why the scan and the patient do not match, and what to do about it.
quiz.answer: The mismatch is the signature of diffuse axonal injury. Rotational acceleration and deceleration shear axons where tissues of different stiffness meet, and most of those lesions are non-haemorrhagic, so a CT that images density sees almost nothing while the patient is comatose; the few dense dots are the haemorrhagic minority of a far larger burden. The answer is MRI. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is the sequence that changes the study, because it exploits the field distortion around deoxygenated blood products and shows microhaemorrhages that gradient echo underestimates and CT misses entirely, while diffusion-weighted imaging shows non-haemorrhagic lesions as restricted foci in the first week. Grade the depth: lobar grey-white junction alone, then involvement of the corpus callosum, then the dorsolateral midbrain and upper pons, with prognosis worsening as the lesions go deeper. Timing matters, since the susceptibility lesions persist for months while the diffusion changes fade.
quiz.explain: The sites follow the mechanics. The corpus callosum is tethered against the falx and the dorsolateral midbrain against the tentorial edge, so both are shearing planes; grey-white junctions shear because myelinated white matter and cortex have different densities and so different inertia. That is also why the injury is a feature of rotational mechanisms - a fall from standing rarely produces it, a high-speed rotational deceleration commonly does. The clinical use of the scan is threefold: it explains a coma no other finding accounts for, it supplies prognostic information for the family and the rehabilitation team, and it provides objective evidence in the medico-legal account of a patient whose CT was called normal. It is not an emergency study; the patient is stabilised first, and MRI in a ventilated trauma patient is planned rather than rushed.

quiz.prompt: A young man struck on the side of the head is alert. CT shows an undisplaced linear fracture of the right temporal bone that runs forward across the floor of the middle cranial fossa and through the wall of the carotid canal. There is no intracranial collection and he has no neurological deficit.
choices: Add CT angiography of the neck and skull base before he leaves the scanner
Repeat the unenhanced CT head in six hours and image no further
Arrange outpatient MRI of the brain in the next two weeks
No further imaging, since he is neurologically intact after the injury
quiz.answer: Add CT angiography of the neck and skull base before he leaves the scanner
quiz.explain: A fracture crossing the carotid canal is one of the accepted screening criteria for blunt cerebrovascular injury, alongside fractures extending into the foramen transversarium, cervical spine fractures particularly of the upper three levels or with subluxation, Le Fort II and III facial fractures, a basal skull fracture, severe closed head injury, and clinical clues such as a cervical bruit, an expanding neck haematoma or a neurological deficit unexplained by the brain images. The whole point of screening is that these patients are asymptomatic: dissection or pseudoaneurysm is silent until it embolises, and the strokes that follow occur hours to days later and are largely preventable with antithrombotic treatment. CT angiography is the screening test in practice, and the injury is graded on the Biffl scale from intimal irregularity through dissection with a haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, occlusion, to transection. A fracture crossing a venous sinus groove poses the venous version of the same question, and CT venography is what answers it. Deferring to outpatient MRI wastes the interval in which the stroke happens.

quiz.prompt: A patient assaulted the previous evening has clear fluid dripping from the left nostril, bruising confined to both eyelids with sharp margins at the orbital rims, and reduced hearing on the left. The CT head is reported as showing no haemorrhage, and the reporting radiologist has looked only at soft tissue windows.
choices: Review bone windows and thin reformats for a fracture of the skull base
Request lumbar puncture to confirm the source of the nasal discharge
Repeat the CT head after twenty-four hours on soft tissue windows
Attribute the findings to soft tissue swelling from the facial assault
quiz.answer: Review bone windows and thin reformats for a fracture of the skull base
quiz.explain: Periorbital bruising held within the orbital rims, cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea and conductive hearing loss are clinical signs of a base of skull fracture, and the clinical signs frequently arrive before the fracture is seen - retroauricular bruising and haemotympanum complete the set, and the retroauricular sign typically takes a day or two to appear. Base fractures are missed because they are undisplaced, oriented obliquely, and invisible at soft tissue windows: they are found on thin-section bone algorithm images with coronal and sagittal reformats, and their surrogate signs are pneumocephalus, an opacified or fluid-filled sphenoid sinus, and mastoid or middle ear opacification. Each site brings its own complication - a cribriform or posterior frontal sinus fracture brings a cerebrospinal fluid leak and meningitis, a petrous fracture brings facial nerve injury and hearing loss, and a fracture across the carotid canal or a sinus groove brings a vascular question. A lumbar puncture answers nothing here and is contraindicated thinking in a head injury.

quiz.prompt: In the Canadian CT Head Rule, what is the minimum duration of retrograde amnesia before the impact, in minutes, that counts as a medium-risk criterion for imaging? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Thirty minutes or more of retrograde amnesia - memory lost for events before the blow, not after it - is one of the two medium-risk criteria, the other being a dangerous mechanism such as ejection from a vehicle, a pedestrian struck by a car, or a fall from more than about a metre or five stairs. The medium-risk criteria were derived to identify clinically important brain injury rather than injury needing an operation, which is why the rule is sometimes applied with only its high-risk criteria when the question is strictly neurosurgical. The distinction that trips people is retrograde against anterograde: patients volunteer post-traumatic amnesia readily, but the criterion asks what they have lost from before, so it must be asked for directly. Remember also who the rule excludes - patients on anticoagulants, those with a coagulopathy, seizure after the injury, focal deficit, age under sixteen, and no loss of consciousness or amnesia at all - because applying a rule outside its derivation population is the commonest way it fails.

quiz.prompt: A CT head done four hours after a fall shows a 3 mm right frontal contusion and no shift. Twelve hours later the patient is more drowsy though still obeying commands, and a repeat scan shows the contusion is now 20 mm with surrounding oedema and 4 mm of shift.
choices: Contusions expand over the first day, so early imaging understates the injury
The initial study was misreported and the contusion was always this large
A second impact has occurred between the two scans and caused the growth
Rebleeding indicates an underlying vascular malformation beneath the contusion
quiz.answer: Contusions expand over the first day, so early imaging understates the injury
quiz.explain: Contusions blossom. What begins as scattered petechial haemorrhage in bruised cortex coalesces and enlarges over roughly the first six to twenty-four hours, with oedema following, so the scan done in the first hours of a trauma call systematically shows the injury at its smallest. This is the single most useful fact about timing a head injury CT: a scan is a snapshot of a moving process, and the report should say when it was performed relative to the injury. The practical rule is to repeat the scan for a reason - clinical deterioration, an unexplained failure to improve, coagulopathy or anticoagulation, or a finding whose growth would change the plan such as a contusion abutting the tentorium - rather than reflexively at a fixed interval, since routine rescanning of stable patients with a normal examination rarely changes management and adds dose and transfers. A vascular malformation is a consideration in spontaneous rather than traumatic contusional bleeding.

quiz.prompt: You are reporting the CT of a head-injured patient overnight and the ward is busy. List the trauma findings you would telephone rather than leave in a written report, and give the principle that decides which findings qualify.
quiz.answer: The principle is that a finding must be telephoned when it needs an action within a shorter time than the report will realistically be read, and when the receiving team cannot see it for themselves. On that basis I would telephone any extra-axial collection with mass effect or midline shift, any evidence of herniation of any kind, an expanding or actively bleeding haematoma showing a swirl within the clot, obstructive hydrocephalus, a depressed or open vault fracture, a fracture crossing the carotid canal or a venous sinus groove because of the vascular injury it implies, a base of skull fracture with pneumocephalus or a cerebrospinal fluid leak, and any suspicion of inflicted injury in a child. The call is documented in the report with the time, the name of the person told, and what was said.
quiz.explain: Critical results communication is part of the report rather than an optional courtesy, and it is where trauma reporting most often fails in practice: the finding is correct, written, and read four hours later. Two refinements are worth adding. First, tell the person who can act - the neurosurgical registrar for a collection needing evacuation, the trauma team leader for the rest - rather than whoever answers. Second, the threshold falls at night and in a district hospital without on-site neurosurgery, because the action needed is a transfer and transfers take hours; a small extradural in a patient who is well is precisely the finding that turns dangerous while the report sits unread. Suspected inflicted injury in a child is on the list for a different reason: the action needed is protective as well as medical, and it cannot wait for the morning.

quiz.prompt: A seventeen-year-old rugby player concussed a week ago, still headachy, took a further blow in training today and collapsed within minutes. CT shows diffuse cerebral swelling with effaced basal cisterns and only a thin subdural collection quite out of proportion to the swelling.
choices: Catastrophic swelling after a second impact during symptomatic recovery
A rapidly expanding subdural haematoma driving the swelling mechanically
Post-traumatic epilepsy with prolonged seizure and secondary oedema
Global hypoxic-ischaemic injury from an unwitnessed cardiac arrest
quiz.answer: Catastrophic swelling after a second impact during symptomatic recovery
quiz.explain: Second-impact syndrome is the label for diffuse malignant cerebral swelling that follows a further head injury while a young athlete is still symptomatic from an earlier one, and its imaging signature is exactly this mismatch: swelling far out of proportion to any collection, effaced cisterns, and a very rapid collapse. The mechanism is presumed to be loss of cerebrovascular autoregulation, which is why the swelling is vascular and immediate rather than the delayed cytotoxic oedema of an ischaemic insult. It is rare and it remains contested as an entity, so report the findings you can see - the swelling, the cistern effacement, the thin collection - and offer the syndrome as the clinical context rather than the diagnosis. Its whole value is preventive, and it is the argument behind graduated return-to-play protocols that keep a symptomatic player out. A thin subdural does not mechanically cause diffuse swelling, and hypoxic injury spares no territory and would show loss of grey-white differentiation in the deep grey matter with a reversal sign.

module_contract.goal: Name the elementary HRCT patterns from the images, use nodule distribution and an expiratory series to narrow the cause, and place a fibrotic scan into the UIP categories.

approach.detail: Reticular, nodular, high-attenuation (ground glass, consolidation), or low-attenuation (cystic, low-density/mosaic) — pick the one pattern that organises the rest of the reading.
Perilymphatic (pleura, fissures, peribronchovascular), centrilobular (spares the pleura, 5–10 mm off the fissures), or random.
Upper vs lower zone, central vs peripheral, subpleural vs bronchovascular — this narrows the differential more than the pattern alone.
Subpleural, multilayered, thick-walled cystic spaces — the pathological signature of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), distinct from paraseptal emphysema.

approach.step: Run an expiratory series when air trapping is possible
approach.detail: Expiratory images separate genuine air trapping (obstructive small-airways disease) from infiltrative causes of mosaic attenuation.
Pleural effusion, lymphadenopathy, traction bronchiectasis — each shifts the differential for the primary pattern.

measure.how: A true cyst has a thin, usually regular wall; distinguish from a cavity by wall thickness.
measure.cutoff: Cyst < 4 mm wall · cavity > 4 mm wall

measure.how: Hazy increased opacity that does NOT obscure the underlying vessels — if vessels are obscured, call it consolidation instead.

classify.name: Elementary HRCT patterns
rows: Excess linear opacities from interlobular septal thickening or fibrosis
Small, thick-walled cystic spaces of fibrous tissue, subpleural, in multiple contiguous layers
Hazy increase in opacity, vessels still visible through it
Increased opacity that obscures the vessels, with air bronchograms
Nodules along pleura, fissures and peribronchovascular interstitium
Nodules sparing the pleura, centred 5–10 mm from the fissures
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, respiratory bronchiolitis, endobronchial TB spread
No relation to any lobular structure
Miliary TB, fungal infection, haematogenous metastases
Density difference between adjacent lung regions
Infiltrative disease or air trapping — resolve on expiratory images

pitfalls: Calling honeycombing when it is paraseptal emphysema — honeycombing is subpleural and layered in more than one row of cysts; a single row of larger, thin-walled spaces without fibrosis elsewhere is emphysema.
Missing air trapping because no expiratory series was run when the inspiratory scan showed mosaic attenuation.
Ignoring ground-glass as "probably nothing" — the majority of GGO represents active, potentially treatable disease, not an artefact.
Assigning a random-pattern differential (miliary, metastases) to nodules that are actually centrilobular and airway-related.
