quiz.prompt: A 3 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a single FDG-avid node of 12 mm short axis in the left lower paratracheal region, with no other abnormality on PET-CT. The team asks whether lobectomy should still go ahead.
choices: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
It is N2, so proceed to mediastinoscopy
It is N1, so proceed to lobectomy as planned
It is M1a, so treat as metastatic disease
quiz.answer: It is N3, so sample it before abandoning surgery
quiz.explain: Station 4L is contralateral mediastinum for a right-sided primary, and contralateral mediastinal nodes are N3, which takes a patient off a primary surgical pathway. But avidity is not tissue. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all FDG-avid, and the positive predictive value of PET in the mediastinum is only moderate, so the single finding that would convert a resectable patient into an unresectable one is exactly the finding that must be proved. Endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 4L, and a negative needle result in a node with this much riding on it is followed by surgical staging rather than accepted. The converse discipline is just as important: normal-sized, PET-negative mediastinal nodes still conceal metastasis in a minority, which is why central tumours, large tumours and N1 disease go to invasive staging even after a clean PET-CT.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a right lower lobe carcinoma has an enlarged pretracheal node. It lies anterior to the trachea, its centre is a little to the left of the midline of the body, but it lies entirely to the right of the left lateral border of the trachea. How is it classified on the IASLC map?
choices: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
Station 4L, and therefore N3 disease
Station 3a, and therefore N2 disease
Station 10R, and therefore N1 disease
quiz.answer: Station 4R, and therefore N2 disease
quiz.explain: The IASLC map deliberately does not use the body midline to divide right from left paratracheal nodes. For stations 2 and 4 the boundary is the left lateral border of the trachea, so a node in front of the trachea and to the right of that line is 4R however it looks against the anatomical midline. The consequence is not academic: for a right-sided tumour, 4R is ipsilateral mediastinal, N2, and remains within a multimodality plan that can be given with curative intent, while 4L would be N3. Station 3a is prevascular, anterior to the great vessels and not in contact with the trachea. Station 10R is hilar, beginning below the lower border of the azygos vein where station 4R ends, and hilar nodes are N1. Naming the station rather than describing the node loosely is what lets the next person choose a sampling route.

quiz.prompt: A 4.5 cm left lower lobe squamous carcinoma has a small ipsilateral pleural effusion on CT, with no visible pleural nodularity or thickening. The plan is surgery or chemoradiotherapy depending on stage. What does the effusion require?
choices: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
Nothing, because it lacks pleural nodularity
Drainage, because it will limit radiotherapy
Repeat CT, because it may resolve on its own
quiz.answer: Sampling, because it may make the disease M1a
quiz.explain: A malignant pleural or pericardial effusion, and pleural or pericardial nodules, are M1a, which removes curative resection from consideration, so this is one of the highest-consequence findings on a staging CT. Most effusions in lung cancer are malignant, and the absence of visible nodularity does not exclude pleural deposits, which are commonly a few millimetres and below the resolution of the study. The classification is explicit about the exception: where the fluid is not blood-stained, is not an exudate, and repeated cytology is negative, and where clinical judgement attributes it to something else such as obstructive pneumonitis or cardiac failure, the effusion is excluded as a staging element. So cytology decides, not CT, and in an otherwise operable patient with repeatedly negative cytology, thoracoscopy is the next step rather than an assumption in either direction.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT in a patient with a 3.5 cm lung cancer shows a 2.4 cm left adrenal nodule and nothing else outside the chest. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
Call it M1b and treat as stage IV disease
Biopsy the adrenal gland under CT guidance
Proceed to surgery and monitor the adrenal
quiz.answer: Measure its unenhanced attenuation first
quiz.explain: Adrenal nodules are common in the general population, and most adrenal nodules in patients with lung cancer are still adenomas. An unenhanced attenuation of 10 HU or less establishes a lipid-rich adenoma; chemical-shift MRI answers the same question when unenhanced CT is unavailable, and contrast washout characterises a lipid-poor adenoma. Getting it right matters more here than in an incidental setting, because a solitary adrenal metastasis is the difference between a treatment given with curative intent and palliative systemic therapy. The M1b category exists because single-lesion, single-organ metastatic disease behaves differently from widespread disease, and an oligometastatic patient may have both sites treated radically. Biopsy is reserved for a lesion that imaging cannot characterise, and phaeochromocytoma should be considered before a needle is put into an adrenal gland.

quiz.prompt: A 2.5 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma is accompanied by a solitary 9 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe, biopsied and shown to be the same tumour type, with no nodal or distant disease. How does the second nodule count?
choices: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
M1a, so systemic treatment is indicated
T3, because it sits in the same lung
N1, because spread is intrapulmonary
quiz.answer: T4, still within a curative-intent plan
quiz.explain: Separate tumour nodules are graded by where they sit relative to the primary: the same lobe is T3, a different ipsilateral lobe is T4, and the contralateral lung is M1a. A T4 arrived at this way is not the same animal as a T4 by invasion of the mediastinum or a great vessel. With N0 disease this configuration is resectable and potentially curable, and it is one of the places where the stage label and the surgical reality diverge, which is a good reason to report the anatomy rather than only the letter. The other trap is assuming the second nodule is a metastasis at all. Synchronous second primaries are common in this population, and comparing histological subtype and molecular profile can turn one T4 tumour into two early-stage tumours, with quite different treatment.

quiz.prompt: A superior sulcus tumour abuts the subclavian artery and the T1 nerve root on CT, with an equivocal fat plane at both sites. Which examination best answers the resectability question, and what is it looking for?
choices: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
PET-CT, for occult nodal and distant disease
CT angiography, for subclavian artery invasion
Bone scan, for invasion of the first two ribs
quiz.answer: MRI, for brachial plexus and vertebral invasion
quiz.explain: At the lung apex the questions that decide the operation are soft-tissue ones: the brachial plexus, the subclavian vessels, the vertebral body, the neural foramina and the spinal canal. MRI with coronal and sagittal planes shows all of them, and CT, whatever its spatial resolution in bone, is poor at the plexus. Tumour reaching the plexus above the T1 root, encasing rather than abutting the subclavian artery, or invading the vertebral body extensively or entering the canal, is generally beyond resection; involvement of the T1 root and below, of the ribs, or of a limited portion of a vertebral body is within the scope of en-bloc resection after induction chemoradiotherapy at experienced centres. PET-CT is still needed, because a superior sulcus tumour is staged for nodal and distant disease like any other, but it does not answer the local question this patient's operability turns on.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a 5 cm tumour and ipsilateral mediastinal nodal disease has a PET-CT that shows no extrathoracic uptake, and has no neurological symptoms. What is still required before treatment is planned?
choices: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
A repeat PET-CT after chemotherapy
A bone scan for skeletal metastases
No further imaging before treatment
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain
quiz.explain: Normal cerebral cortex takes up FDG avidly, so a metastasis sits against a bright background and PET-CT is unreliable intracranially. Dedicated brain imaging is recommended separately for locally advanced disease and for anyone with neurological symptoms, and contrast-enhanced MRI is substantially more sensitive than CT for small and posterior fossa deposits. The reason to do it before treatment is planned rather than afterwards is that the result changes the plan in either direction: an occult brain metastasis can convert a radical chemoradiotherapy plan into systemic therapy, or, if it is solitary and the thoracic disease is limited, into radical treatment of both sites with stereotactic radiosurgery or resection. A bone scan adds nothing after a PET-CT, which covers the skeleton with better sensitivity and specificity.

quiz.prompt: A peripheral part-solid adenocarcinoma measures 2.4 cm overall on lung windows, with a solid component of 1.8 cm, and there is no nodal or distant disease. Which of those measurements in centimetres is used to assign the clinical T category? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The ninth edition retains the solid-component rule introduced in the eighth: a part-solid tumour is staged on the size of its solid component on CT, and at pathology on the size of the invasive component, because the ground-glass, lepidic part does not carry the same prognosis as invasive tumour of equal size. So 1.8 cm makes this T1b, where the whole-lesion measurement of 2.4 cm would have made it T1c. Both numbers belong in the report, since the referrer needs the total size to follow the lesion and the solid size to stage it. The same logic runs to the bottom of the scale: a pure ground-glass lesion up to 3 cm with no invasive component is staged as in situ disease, and one with an invasive component of 5 mm or less as minimally invasive. It runs upward too, in that growth of the solid component is what constitutes progression in a subsolid lesion.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with a left upper lobe tumour, an enlarged node lies in the space bounded above by the lower border of the aortic arch, below by the upper border of the left main pulmonary artery, and lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Which IASLC station number is that? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: That is station 5, the subaortic or aortopulmonary window node, and left upper lobe tumours drain there characteristically. It is ipsilateral mediastinal for a left-sided primary, so N2. The practical weight of naming it correctly lies in access: neither cervical mediastinoscopy nor endobronchial ultrasound reaches station 5, so tissue requires a parasternal mediastinotomy, a video-assisted thoracoscopic approach or an extended cervical procedure. Station 6, the para-aortic node lying anterior and lateral to the ascending aorta and the arch, is equally out of reach of those routine techniques. This is the concrete reason a report should name the station rather than describe a node loosely as being in the upper mediastinum: the station determines who can biopsy it and how, and a vague description costs the patient an extra clinic visit or the wrong procedure.

quiz.prompt: Explain why an FDG-avid mediastinal node should be sampled before a patient is told that surgery is off, and set out which stations the two standard needle routes reach and which they do not.
quiz.answer: PET is sensitive but only moderately specific in the mediastinum: granulomatous disease, anthracosilicotic nodes, infection, and nodes reacting downstream of an obstructed bronchus are all avid, so an avid node in an otherwise operable patient is a hypothesis rather than a stage. Nodal upstaging can change the treatment plan, so a finding that would rule out surgery needs tissue confirmation. N2 disease does not automatically preclude surgery: selected patients remain candidates for multimodality treatment after specialist review. Endobronchial ultrasound with transbronchial needle aspiration, EBUS-TBNA, reaches the paratracheal stations 2R, 2L, 4R and 4L, the subcarinal station 7, and the hilar and interlobar stations 10 and 11. Endoscopic ultrasound from the oesophagus reaches 4L, 7, 8 and 9, and can also sample the left adrenal gland and the left lobe of the liver. Neither reaches the subaortic station 5 or the para-aortic station 6, which need a parasternal mediastinotomy or a thoracoscopic approach. The converse error also matters: a negative needle result in a node with a high pretest probability does not exclude disease, and surgical staging follows.
quiz.explain: The rule underneath all of this is that a finding gets proved in proportion to what it costs the patient if it is wrong. A PET-positive node that merely confirms disease already evident elsewhere changes nothing and needs nothing; a PET-positive node that alone takes away an operation is worth an invasive test. Two extras are worth carrying. First, the two needle routes are complementary rather than alternatives, because they approach the mediastinum from opposite sides, and combining them raises the yield in the posterior and inferior stations that bronchoscopy cannot see. Second, the ninth edition of the classification, in force since 2025, subdivides N2 into single-station N2a and multi-station N2b disease because they carry different prognoses, which raises the value of a report that names each involved station rather than reporting mediastinal nodal disease in aggregate.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT reports no enlarged mediastinal nodes, and the team treats that as N0. Explain the two ways that inference can be wrong, and what determines whether invasive staging is needed anyway.
quiz.answer: The CT criterion is a short-axis diameter of 10 mm or more, and it fails in both directions. Nodes enlarge reactively in obstructive pneumonitis, infection and old granulomatous disease, so a good proportion of enlarged nodes are benign; and metastatic deposits sit inside normal-sized nodes, so a normal CT does not exclude N2 disease, with sensitivity around half. PET-CT improves on both figures without solving either, since deposits below its resolution are missed and lepidic adenocarcinoma and carcinoid tumours are poorly avid, while inflammatory nodes are avid. What determines whether invasive staging is done anyway is the pretest probability of mediastinal disease: a central tumour, a large tumour, enlarged or avid N1 nodes, and adenocarcinoma histology all raise it enough that a negative PET-CT is not accepted at face value, and endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) with or without surgical staging is performed before resection. A small peripheral tumour with a clean PET mediastinum carries a low enough residual risk to proceed directly to surgery.
quiz.explain: Size is a poor surrogate for tumour because it measures a consequence that inflammation produces just as readily. That is why nodal staging is a sequence of tests with rising invasiveness and rising accuracy, rather than a single measurement, and why the sequence is entered at the point the pretest probability justifies. The reporting habit that follows is to describe nodes by station, short-axis size and avidity, and to state the pretest features that raise concern, rather than issuing a bare N category from CT alone: the radiologist's job at this step is to set the probability that the next test is chosen against. The same reasoning explains why a positive result is confirmed when it removes an operation, and a negative result is confirmed when the probability was high to begin with.

quiz.prompt: Put these IASLC nodal stations in order of the level at which they are found, from the most cranial to the most caudal.
quiz.answer: station-2R station-4R station-7 station-8 station-9
quiz.explain: Station 2R is the upper paratracheal node, running down to the level where the caudal border of the left brachiocephalic vein crosses the trachea; 4R is the lower paratracheal node below that, down to the lower border of the azygos vein; 7 is subcarinal; 8 is paraoesophageal below the level of the carina; and 9 lies in the inferior pulmonary ligament, the most caudal mediastinal station of all. Two structural facts make the map worth learning rather than looking up each time. Station 1 is low cervical/supraclavicular and is N3 on either side. Ipsilateral mediastinal and subcarinal nodes are N2; contralateral mediastinal nodes are N3. Ipsilateral stations 10 to 14 are N1. And the boundaries are defined by structures visible on CT, precisely so that a radiologist and a surgeon assigning the same node from the same images arrive at the same number.

quiz.prompt: A single 3 cm peripheral lung cancer is being staged. Taking each site of direct invasion on its own, put them in order of the T category that site alone would confer, from the lowest to the highest.
quiz.answer: visceral-pleura chest-wall vertebral-body
quiz.explain: Invasion of the visceral pleura makes a tumour at least T2 whatever its size. Invasion through it into the parietal pleura or the chest wall makes T3, in company with the phrenic nerve and the parietal pericardium. Invasion of a vertebral body makes T4, in company with the mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and carina. What is worth carrying is how badly CT performs at each of these boundaries. Contact with the pleura, loss of an extrapleural fat plane, and even a broad interface between tumour and chest wall do not prove invasion; the findings that do are frank rib destruction and an extrapleural soft-tissue mass. The step from T3 to T4 changes the operation and often the intent of treatment, so equivocal cases go to MRI, to careful review of sagittal and coronal reformats, or to assessment at thoracotomy, and the report should say which of those is being asked for.

module_contract.goal: Select target lesions, compute the sum of diameters, assign a RECIST 1.1 category, and recognise growth on immunotherapy that needs confirming rather than acting on.

source.title: RECIST 1.1 — the basics, the criteria and examples

approach.detail: Identify the study the trial calls baseline, and the nadir — the smallest sum of diameters achieved so far on treatment. Percentage change is measured against baseline for response and against nadir for progression.

Lymphoma has Lugano, GIST on imatinib has Choi, HCC has mRECIST, immunotherapy has iRECIST. RECIST 1.1 is not barred in those settings, but the trial or MDT will usually expect the disease-specific system — say which you applied.
Up to two per organ and five in the whole study, measurable and reproducible. Once a target lesion, always a target lesion — the selection never changes.

approach.step: Measure the targets and sum them
approach.detail: Longest diameter for solid lesions, short axis for nodes. Add them to a single sum of longest diameters (SLD).
Present, absent, or unequivocally progressed. Do not measure them routinely — but unequivocal non-target progression is progressive disease however the targets behave.
Any new lesion is progressive disease, however small and however good the target response looks.
Combine target response, non-target status and new lesions into one overall category, and state the percentage change you based it on.

measure.how: Longest diameter of the whole lesion, including any necrotic centre, in the same imaging plane as at baseline.
measure.cutoff: ≥ 10 mm on CT or MRI · ≥ 20 mm on chest radiograph

measure.how: Short axis, not long axis. Nodes are the commonest place people measure the wrong dimension.
Pathological but not big enough to be a target — record presence, do not add to the sum.
Chosen at baseline and fixed thereafter, spread across the involved organs.
measure.cutoff: Max 2 per organ · max 5 in total

measure.how: Add the diameters of all target lesions. Compare to baseline for response, to nadir for progression.
measure.cutoff: Baseline SLD and nadir SLD both recorded

measure.what: A target that becomes too small to measure
measure.how: Do not drop it from the sum. Assign a default value reflecting CT slice thickness.
If the lesion splits, sum the diameters of the fragments. If lesions merge, measure the merged mass only.
measure.cutoff: Sum fragments · measure the merged mass

classify.name: RECIST 1.1 — target lesion response
rows: Disappearance of all target lesions; any pathological lymph node < 10 mm short axis
No measurable disease left. Non-target lesions must also have resolved for an overall CR.
Neither response nor progression. The default when nothing else is met.
≥ 20% increase in SLD and an absolute increase of ≥ 5 mm; or any new lesion; or unequivocal non-target progression
Progression. Both the percentage and the 5 mm absolute increase are required for progression by size.
classify.note: Not applicable to lymphoma, GIST on imatinib, hepatocellular carcinoma or malignant brain tumours — each has dedicated criteria.

NON-TARGET LESIONS
[list] — [absent / present, unchanged / unequivocal progression].

NEW LESIONS
[None / describe: site, size, series and image].

OTHER FINDINGS
[Incidental and treatment-related findings.]

IMPRESSION
1. RECIST 1.1: [CR / PR / SD / PD], based on a [n]% [decrease from baseline / increase from nadir] in the sum of diameters [and an absolute increase of [n] mm] [/ a new lesion at [site] / unequivocal non-target progression].
2. [Plain-language restatement of what has changed.]
3. [Anything needing action independent of the response category.]
pitfalls: Measuring a nodal target on its long axis. Nodes are assessed by short axis throughout — ≥ 15 mm to be a target, and < 10 mm before a complete response can be called.
Calling progression on percentage alone. A ≥ 20% rise from nadir also needs an absolute increase of at least 5 mm; a small sum can cross 20% on noise.
Comparing progression against baseline instead of nadir. Response is measured from baseline, progression from the smallest sum achieved on treatment.
Dropping a target that has become too small to measure. It stays in the sum at a default 5 mm — remove it and the arithmetic is wrong in the patient's favour.

Calling complete response while a pleural effusion or sclerotic bone lesion persists. That is not CR unless those are proven non-viable by FDG-PET or cytology — and sclerotic bone metastases becoming more sclerotic on treatment is a favourable response, not progression.
Choosing targets in a previously irradiated or loco-regionally treated field, or picking a pure sclerotic bone lesion. Neither is eligible.

classification.name: RECIST
classification.applicability: Measurable solid-tumour response when the clinical or trial pathway specifies RECIST.
classification.summary: PR requires ≥30% reduction from baseline; target PD requires ≥20% increase from nadir plus ≥5 mm absolute increase. New and non-target disease affect overall response.

pitfalls: A suspicious but equivocal new focus is not automatically unequivocal progression.
Do not substitute RECIST for an indication requiring a different named response system.
impression_prompts: State the selected criteria and overall response.
Provide current sum and change against the relevant reference.
Identify the finding that determines progression or the uncertainty preventing categorisation.

criteria_table.title: RECIST 1.1 response anchors
criteria_table.scope: Use the protocol-defined target set and comparison dates. Overall response also integrates non-target disease and new lesions. Immunotherapy-specific iRECIST is a separate framework.

rows.criteria: Target lesions disappear; pathological nodes become <10 mm short axis.
rows.report_note: Non-target disease and new lesions still affect overall response.

rows.criteria: Sum decreases ≥30% from baseline.
rows.report_note: Apply confirmation requirements when the study protocol requires them.

rows.criteria: Sum increases ≥20% from nadir and by ≥5 mm absolutely.
rows.report_note: The nadir includes baseline if it is the smallest sum.

rows.criteria: Neither sufficient decrease for PR nor increase for PD.
rows.report_note: Check protocol timing and response history.

rows.criteria: Unequivocal new malignant lesion or unequivocal non-target progression can establish PD.
rows.report_note: An uncertain new finding needs resolution, not automatic progression.

quiz.prompt: A baseline CT for a trial shows a 12 mm short-axis mediastinal node and a 22 mm liver metastasis, and the reader must decide whether the node can serve as a target lesion. What short-axis measurement in millimetres must a lymph node reach before RECIST 1.1 allows it to be selected as a target? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Nodes are the exception to the ten-millimetre rule, because normal nodes are visible and measurable and a ten-millimetre node may be entirely healthy. The bands are: 15 mm or more in short axis is measurable and may be selected as a target; 10 mm up to 15 mm is pathological but goes on the non-target list; under 10 mm is regarded as non-pathological and is not recorded at all. Short axis is used because it is the dimension least dependent on the plane of section, and it is the short axis that enters the sum of diameters - the one place in the system where the sum mixes two different measurements, longest diameter for everything else and short axis for nodes. One consequence follows directly: since a node's contribution can never fall below its normal size, a complete response requires target nodes to fall below 10 mm rather than to disappear.

quiz.prompt: At follow-up a reader records a target mediastinal node as 24 mm, having measured its long axis; at baseline the same node was recorded as 18 mm short axis. The sum of diameters accordingly rises and the software flags progression. What is the primary problem with this assessment?
choices: The node was measured in a different axis from baseline
The node should have been dropped as a target lesion
Nodal disease is recorded as non-target in this system
The reader should have used the mean of the two axes
quiz.answer: The node was measured in a different axis from baseline
quiz.explain: Reproducibility is the entire value of a response criterion: the number matters far less than the fact that it was obtained the same way every time. A node's long axis can be twice its short axis, so switching axes between timepoints can manufacture a 20 per cent rise out of a node that has not changed at all, and the consequence is a patient taken off a working treatment. The rule is that a node is measured in short axis at every timepoint, on the same imaging technique, ideally by the same reader with the same window settings, and that a target lesion once chosen is followed to the end even if it becomes difficult to measure. When a lesion genuinely becomes unmeasurable - it fragments, or is obscured - that is stated and handled explicitly, rather than fixed by quietly measuring something else.

quiz.prompt: The baseline sum of target diameters is 92 mm. The sum falls to 45 mm at the best response and then measures 54 mm on the current scan, with no new lesions and no change in non-target disease. Calculate the percentage increase from the nadir, to the nearest whole number. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 54 minus 45 is 9 mm, and 9 divided by 45 is 20 per cent. Progression requires two criteria to be met together: a relative increase of at least 20 per cent above the nadir, and an absolute increase of at least 5 mm. Both are satisfied here, at exactly 20 per cent and 9 mm, so this is progressive disease. Notice which number is the reference. Progression is judged against the nadir, the smallest sum recorded at any point including baseline, not against baseline itself - measured against the 92 mm baseline this patient is still 41 per cent down and would look like a continuing partial response. Using the wrong reference in this direction keeps patients on treatments that stopped working months ago.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a single target lesion has a nadir sum of 15 mm; on the current scan it measures 19 mm, with no new lesions and no change in the non-target disease. The trial coordinator reports progression on the strength of the 27 per cent rise. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Stable disease, as the absolute rise is under five millimetres
Progressive disease, as the relative rise is above twenty per cent
Progressive disease, as growth from the nadir was unequivocal
Not evaluable, as one target lesion is too few to assess
quiz.answer: Stable disease, as the absolute rise is under five millimetres
quiz.explain: The absolute five-millimetre requirement exists exactly for this situation. On a small lesion a percentage is treacherous: a 4 mm change on a 15 mm lesion is 27 per cent, and it is also well within the disagreement of two competent readers measuring the same lesion on the same scan, or of the same reader on a different day. Requiring both criteria stops measurement noise being reported as biology. The distinction between the two progressive-disease options is worth sitting with, because both invoke real rules - relative growth from the nadir, and unequivocal worsening - and neither rescues a 4 mm change. A single target lesion is entirely permissible, though it makes the assessment more fragile, which is one reason protocols prefer several. Progression could still arrive by another route on the same scan: a new lesion, or unequivocal progression of non-target disease, either of which would give progressive disease whatever the sum did.

quiz.prompt: A patient entering a trial has, at baseline: three liver metastases of 34, 22 and 12 mm; a 25 mm lung mass previously irradiated and unchanged since; two lung nodules of 11 and 9 mm; a 17 mm short-axis para-aortic node; sclerotic deposits in the right ilium; and a 30 mm simple renal cyst. Say which lesions you would take as targets, and justify the selection rules you applied.
quiz.answer: Take four targets: the 34 mm and 22 mm liver metastases, the 11 mm lung nodule and the 17 mm short-axis para-aortic node. The rules that produce this list are these. A lesion must be measurable, which on CT with 5 mm slices means at least 10 mm in longest diameter, or at least 15 mm in short axis for a node, so the 9 mm lung nodule is excluded, and the simple renal cyst is excluded outright because it is not tumour. No more than five targets in total and no more than two per organ, which is why only two of the three liver lesions are taken - the 34 mm and 22 mm, ahead of the measurable but smaller 12 mm lesion - chosen as the largest and the most reproducibly measurable, not merely the largest. Targets should represent all the involved organs, so a lung lesion and a node are included rather than filling the quota from the liver. A previously irradiated lesion is treated as non-measurable unless it has demonstrably progressed since, so the 25 mm lung mass moves to the non-target list, as do the sclerotic bone deposits, which have no measurable soft tissue component. Everything not selected is still recorded and followed qualitatively as non-target disease.
quiz.explain: Target selection is where most of the error in a trial dataset is introduced, because it happens once, early, and is never revisited. Two of the exclusions here are frequently forgotten. A previously irradiated lesion is unreliable because fibrosis holds its size regardless of what the tumour inside it is doing, so it neither shrinks convincingly nor grows convincingly; it becomes eligible again only if it has already progressed. Sclerotic bone deposits are unmeasurable for a related reason - the sclerosis is the healed bone reaction, and it may increase as the tumour responds, so a blastic lesion that gets denser is not growing disease. Choosing reproducibly measurable lesions matters more than choosing large ones: a lesion abutting the diaphragm or the heart border, or one bisected by an artefact, will generate spurious change at every timepoint.

quiz.prompt: Put these four RECIST 1.1 overall response categories in order, from the greatest reduction in tumour burden to the greatest increase.
quiz.answer: complete-response partial-response stable-disease progressive-disease
quiz.explain: Complete response is the disappearance of the target lesions, with any pathological node falling below 10 mm short axis. Partial response is a fall of at least 30 per cent in the sum of diameters, measured against baseline. Progressive disease is a rise of at least 20 per cent from the nadir together with an absolute rise of at least 5 mm, or a new lesion, or unequivocal progression of non-target disease. Stable disease is the wide middle ground - anything that is neither a 30 per cent fall nor a 20 per cent rise. The bands are deliberately asymmetric and deliberately broad, because most of what lies between them is measurement noise rather than biology; a system with narrow thresholds would report a great deal of change that no reader could reproduce. Stable disease is a category in its own right and not a failure to categorise, and in most protocols it carries a minimum duration before it can be claimed.

quiz.prompt: A protocol asks the reader to state whether a patient has met the criterion for a partial response. The baseline sum of target diameters was 80 mm. What is the largest current sum, in millimetres, that still qualifies as a partial response? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A partial response requires a decrease of at least 30 per cent from the baseline sum, so the ceiling is 80 multiplied by 0.7, which is 56 mm: a sum of 56 qualifies and 57 does not. Two features of the arithmetic deserve holding together. Partial response is measured against baseline while progression is measured against the nadir, so the two categories use different reference points and a patient can be simultaneously well below baseline and unequivocally progressing. And because the criterion is applied to a sum, shrinkage in one lesion can offset growth in another, which is part of why a new lesion counts as progression whatever the sum is doing. Where response rate is the primary endpoint of a non-randomised trial, a response must additionally be confirmed on a repeat assessment at least four weeks later.

quiz.prompt: After six cycles the liver and lung target lesions are no longer identifiable. The single target node, 21 mm short axis at baseline, now measures 8 mm short axis. The reader is minded to record a complete response and asks whether the residual node prevents it. What is the correct assessment?
choices: Complete response, as the node is below ten millimetres
Partial response, as measurable nodal tissue still remains
Complete response, as node size is disregarded on follow-up
Stable disease, as the node has not entirely disappeared
quiz.answer: Complete response, as the node is below ten millimetres
quiz.explain: Nodes do not vanish - healthy people have them - so the system sets the bar for a target node at below 10 mm in short axis rather than at zero. This node at 8 mm has cleared that bar, and with every other target lesion gone the target response is complete. Two riders keep the bookkeeping honest. The node's 8 mm is still recorded in the sum of diameters at each timepoint, so the sum of a patient in complete response is not zero, which surprises readers who expect the arithmetic to bottom out. And the overall response depends on more than the targets: any non-target disease must also have resolved, with any pathological nodes below 10 mm and tumour markers back within the normal range, before an overall complete response can be recorded.

quiz.prompt: The sum of target diameters has fallen from 96 mm to 55 mm, a 43 per cent reduction. The same scan shows a 7 mm enhancing liver lesion that was unequivocally absent before, is not explicable as artefact, and lies within a region imaged identically at baseline. What is the overall response?
choices: Progressive disease, because a new lesion has appeared
Partial response, as the new lesion is not measurable
Stable disease, pending a confirmatory scan in six weeks
Partial response, with the new lesion recorded separately
quiz.answer: Progressive disease, because a new lesion has appeared
quiz.explain: A new lesion is progression in its own right, regardless of what the sum of diameters has done, and this is one of the few places where the criteria abandon arithmetic entirely. The new lesion need not be measurable and it is not added into the sum; its existence is the finding. What the criteria demand instead is that it be unequivocal, and the qualifications matter: a small node visible only because this scan was reconstructed more thinly, a lesion in an area not previously imaged, or a finding attributable to infection or collapse is not a new lesion. Where a finding is genuinely equivocal the reader says so, treatment continues, and the next timepoint decides - and if it is then confirmed, the date of progression is backdated to the earlier scan. Immunotherapy is precisely where this rule strains, and it is why the immune-adapted criteria place new lesions in a separate compartment rather than treating them as an automatic endpoint.

quiz.prompt: A patient's target sum has fallen 22 per cent, but the previously mild peritoneal disease is now sheet-like with a new moderate volume of ascites, and the patient has deteriorated clinically. Explain how RECIST 1.1 handles non-target disease of this kind and what standard the change has to meet.
quiz.answer: Non-target disease is not measured; it is judged qualitatively and can only be recorded in one of three ways - complete response, non-complete-response with non-progressive-disease, or unequivocal progression. Unequivocal progression is a deliberately high bar. The worsening must be substantial enough that, taken with the whole picture, the overall tumour burden has increased to a degree that would justify stopping treatment, even though the target lesions are stable or shrinking. A modest apparent increase in a non-measurable deposit does not qualify, precisely because non-target assessment is subjective and the target sum is the quantitative anchor that keeps the whole system reproducible. Sheet-like peritoneal disease with new ascites in a deteriorating patient does meet that bar, and the case is recorded as progressive disease despite the 22 per cent fall in the sum. Where the reader is unsure, the honest course is to seek a second opinion or to wait for the next timepoint rather than to let an impression overrule a falling sum.
quiz.explain: This provision exists because a purely measurement-driven system would otherwise be blind to the disease it cannot measure - peritoneal and pleural disease, leptomeningeal spread, lymphangitis, diffuse bone marrow involvement - and those are common patterns of failure. But the same subjectivity that makes the provision necessary makes it dangerous, which is why the wording sets the bar at a change that would itself justify discontinuing treatment. The practical test to apply is whether an oncologist shown these images alone, without knowing the target sum, would stop the drug. If the answer is a confident yes, it is unequivocal progression; if it requires argument, it is not, and the next scan will settle it. Note that ascites and effusions are treated with particular caution, since both have non-malignant causes and both can be induced by treatment.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks into pembrolizumab for melanoma, a scan shows the target sum up 28 per cent from the nadir with an absolute rise of 9 mm, and one new subcutaneous nodule. The patient feels well, is gaining weight, and has no new symptoms. Explain what may be happening biologically, and how the response assessment should proceed.
quiz.answer: This may be pseudoprogression. Checkpoint blockade recruits lymphocytes into the tumour, so a lesion can enlarge with inflammatory infiltrate and oedema rather than with tumour cells, and deposits that were previously subclinical can become visible for the same reason. It is uncommon - of the order of a few per cent, more often seen in melanoma than in most other tumours - so it is a hypothesis to be tested rather than assumed. Under conventional RECIST 1.1 this scan is progressive disease. Under the immune-adapted criteria it is unconfirmed progression, and in a patient who is clinically stable treatment continues with a confirmatory scan in four to eight weeks. If that scan shows further growth - a further increase in the target sum of at least 5 mm, or further growth of the new lesion - progression is confirmed and is dated to the first scan. If instead the disease is stable or has shrunk, the unconfirmed progression is reset and the patient continues on treatment. The clinical state is part of the assessment: a patient who is deteriorating is not left on a drug for another eight weeks on the strength of a hypothesis.
quiz.explain: The reason a second set of criteria was needed is that the original ones were built for cytotoxic drugs, where growth means growth. With immunotherapy an early increase in size can precede a durable response, and a rigid application of the original rules would discontinue treatment in the patients about to benefit most. The safeguard against the opposite error - keeping everyone on a failing drug in the hope of a late response - is the confirmation requirement plus the clinical condition, which is why 'clinically stable' is written into the rule rather than left to judgement. Two further points for the radiologist. Related patterns exist elsewhere: enlarging nodes on immunotherapy may be sarcoid-like reaction rather than metastasis, and a growing lesion after chemoradiotherapy or ablation may be treatment effect. And in high-grade glioma the same trap has its own rule, where new enhancement within the radiation field in the first weeks after chemoradiotherapy is treated as pseudoprogression unless proven otherwise.

quiz.prompt: A trial site submits a baseline CT reconstructed at 8 mm slice thickness. The reader identifies a 12 mm liver lesion and wants to take it as a target lesion. What does RECIST 1.1 require here?
choices: The lesion must be at least twice the slice thickness
The lesion must be re-measured in the coronal plane
The lesion may be used if it is seen on three slices
The lesion counts, as twelve exceeds the ten limit
quiz.answer: The lesion must be at least twice the slice thickness
quiz.explain: The ten-millimetre rule assumes slices of 5 mm or less. Where slices are thicker, the minimum measurable size becomes twice the slice thickness, so at 8 mm the lesion must be at least 16 mm and this 12 mm lesion is non-measurable and goes on the non-target list. Partial volume is the reason. A lesion smaller than about twice the slice thickness may never be caught in a slice that contains its true maximum diameter, so its apparent size depends on where the slices happened to fall relative to it - and that dependence reappears at the next timepoint as change that is purely an artefact of positioning. The general lesson outlives the specific number: response criteria are only as reproducible as the acquisition beneath them, which is why trials fix the technique - slice thickness, contrast phase, reconstruction kernel, timing - and require the same one at every visit.

quiz.prompt: Two infants are tachypnoeic in the first hours of life. The first, born at term by caesarean section without labour, has a film showing fluid in the horizontal fissure, prominent perihilar streaking and normal to slightly increased lung volumes. The second, born at 29 weeks, has uniformly low volumes, a fine granular pattern throughout both lungs and air bronchograms extending to the periphery. Interpret each film and say how the next 48 hours should differ.
quiz.answer: The first is transient tachypnoea of the newborn: fetal lung fluid that would normally be cleared during labour and the first breaths is still in the interstitium and the lymphatics, so it collects in the fissures and around the hila while the alveoli remain aerated, which is why the lung volumes are preserved or even increased. It is managed supportively, with oxygen if needed, and it clears as the fluid is absorbed, typically within 24 to 48 hours, so the follow-up film should look better rather than worse. The second is surfactant deficiency: without surfactant the alveoli collapse at end-expiration, so the volumes are low, the fine granularity is the summation of countless airless acini, and the air bronchograms are conspicuous because aerated bronchi stand out against airless lung. Untreated it worsens over the first day or two rather than clearing, and it is treated with exogenous surfactant and respiratory support, after which the film can clear strikingly and sometimes asymmetrically. Two cautions belong with the pair: group B streptococcal pneumonia can be radiographically indistinguishable from surfactant deficiency, so antibiotics are started while cultures are awaited, and a sudden deterioration on a ventilator should prompt a search for pulmonary interstitial emphysema or a pneumothorax rather than a change in the underlying diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Lung volume is the discriminator that does most of the work on a neonatal chest film, because it follows directly from where the abnormality sits. Fluid in the interstitium leaves the air spaces open and the lungs large; absent surfactant collapses the air spaces and makes the lungs small. Everything else — gestation, mode of delivery, the tempo over the following two days, and the response to surfactant — is confirmatory. The pair also illustrates why the neonatal film is read alongside the gestational age and the clinical course rather than in isolation: the same granular pattern in a term infant should raise pneumonia, and coarse patchy shadowing with hyperinflation in a term or post-term infant with a history of stained liquor points instead to meconium aspiration.

quiz.prompt: A radiograph of a preterm infant shows one umbilical catheter that dips into the pelvis, turns and ascends to the left of the vertebral bodies, with its tip at the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra. A second catheter runs directly cephalad from the umbilicus with its tip at the level of the ninth thoracic vertebra. How should the lines be reported?
choices: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
Both need withdrawal; the tips lie within the heart itself
The lines are swapped; the ascending one is the arterial line
The venous line is in the portal vein and must be pulled back
quiz.answer: Both are well sited; the descending course marks the artery
quiz.explain: The course identifies the vessel before the tip is judged. The umbilical artery runs caudally to the internal iliac artery before turning up the aorta, so an initial dip into the pelvis is the signature of an arterial catheter; the umbilical vein runs straight up through the falciform ligament and the left portal vein into the ductus venosus, so a catheter that only ascends is venous. Acceptable arterial tip positions are high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae — above the coeliac axis and below the ductus arteriosus — or low, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, below the renal arteries; the intervening stretch is avoided because it lies across the origins of the visceral vessels. The venous tip should sit at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium, around the eighth or ninth thoracic level. The two failures worth knowing are a venous tip that stops short in the liver, which risks portal vein thrombosis and extravasation of hypertonic infusate into the parenchyma, and a tip advanced into the right atrium, which risks arrhythmia, thrombus and pericardial tamponade.

quiz.prompt: A preterm infant on the neonatal unit has serial abdominal radiographs during an episode of necrotising enterocolitis. Put these radiographic findings in order of increasing severity.
quiz.answer: dilated-loops pneumatosis portal-venous-gas pneumoperitoneum
quiz.explain: Dilated, separated loops with a loss of the normal polygonal gas pattern are the earliest and least specific finding, and by themselves they support only a suspicion. Intramural gas — a bubbly or curvilinear lucency within the bowel wall, produced by gas-forming organisms in a damaged mucosa — is the finding that establishes the diagnosis. Branching lucencies over the liver are that gas carried back in the portal venous system, and they mark more extensive disease and a worse prognosis. Free intraperitoneal gas means the bowel has perforated and is the one finding that is an absolute indication for surgery; it appears as gas outlining the falciform ligament on the supine film, as both sides of the bowel wall becoming visible, or as a lucency over the liver on a left lateral decubitus view, which is the projection to request in an infant too unwell to be sat up. A loop that stays in the same position and the same shape across serial films is a further sign of a segment that is no longer viable, and ultrasound adds bowel wall thickness, perfusion and free fluid that the radiograph cannot show.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate aged three days vomits bile. Put the steps of the emergency pathway in the order in which they are carried out.
quiz.answer: nasogastric-decompression abdominal-radiograph upper-GI-contrast laparotomy
quiz.explain: Bile-stained vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise, and the whole pathway is built around how quickly the midgut dies once its vascular pedicle twists. Resuscitation and a nasogastric tube come first, both to decompress the stomach and to confirm the character of the aspirate. The plain film is quick and can show a double bubble, a gasless abdomen or dilated loops — but it is very often normal, so it can raise the suspicion and cannot lower it. The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the reference standard: it shows where the duodenojejunal flexure lies, which should be to the left of the left-sided pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb, and in volvulus it shows a corkscrew or beaked duodenum. A twisted midgut then goes straight to a Ladd procedure. Ultrasound showing the superior mesenteric vein lying anterior or to the left of the artery, or a whirlpool of vessels wrapping the pedicle, is increasingly used and can make the diagnosis quickly, but in most units a normal ultrasound does not by itself exclude malrotation.

quiz.prompt: A 5-week-old boy has non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium. Ultrasound of the pylorus is performed in the right lateral decubitus position with a high-frequency linear probe. At or above what single-wall muscle thickness, in millimetres, is the pylorus regarded as hypertrophied? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Three millimetres of single muscle wall thickness, measured on the short-axis image away from the near-field, together with a pyloric channel length of about fifteen to seventeen millimetres or more, defines the hypertrophied pylorus. The measurements matter less than the dynamic observation that accompanies them: the study is watched for several minutes, and in true hypertrophic pyloric stenosis vigorous gastric peristalsis fails to drive fluid through the channel, whereas pylorospasm relaxes and lets fluid pass. A borderline pylorus in a young infant is rescanned rather than operated on. The surgical point is that this is not a surgical emergency but a medical one: the persistent vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and that must be corrected before an anaesthetic, because alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea. Ultrasound has replaced the contrast meal, and no ionising radiation is involved at all.

quiz.prompt: A neonate with trisomy 21 vomits in the first hours of life. The supine abdominal radiograph shows two gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen, one under the left hemidiaphragm and one to its right, with no gas anywhere beyond them. What does the absence of distal gas indicate?
choices: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
Midgut volvulus twisting a patent duodenum shut
A duodenal web with a central perforation in it
Annular pancreas causing a partial obstruction
quiz.answer: Complete duodenal obstruction, most likely an atresia
quiz.explain: The two bubbles are the distended stomach and the dilated duodenal cap proximal to the obstruction, and what discriminates among the causes is whether any gas has passed beyond them. Complete absence of distal gas means a complete obstruction, and in a neonate with trisomy 21 that is duodenal atresia, which needs no contrast study before surgery. Gas beyond the second bubble means the obstruction is incomplete — a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas, or malrotation with Ladd bands — and those do need a contrast study, both to define the anatomy and because malrotation carries the risk of volvulus. The trap to hold on to is the converse: a neonate vomiting bile whose film is normal or near-normal still needs an urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because a midgut volvulus can produce very little to see on a plain film and is the one diagnosis here that cannot wait.

quiz.prompt: A previously well 9-month-old has episodes of screaming with drawing up of the legs, and a sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm structure with concentric rings in the transverse plane. The abdomen is soft, there is no peritonism and the child is well perfused. What should follow?
choices: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
Immediate laparotomy, since ultrasound has already made the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to search for a lead point
Observation with intravenous fluids, since most reduce spontaneously
quiz.answer: Fluoroscopically guided air enema reduction, with surgery on standby
quiz.explain: Ileocolic intussusception at this age is usually idiopathic, following lymphoid hypertrophy after a viral illness, and ultrasound is both sensitive and specific enough to be the diagnostic test — the target on the transverse image and the pseudo-kidney on the longitudinal one. Reduction by air, or by fluid under ultrasound guidance, is the treatment, and it succeeds in the large majority. It is done with a surgeon informed and theatre available, because of the small risk of perforation during the procedure and because a failed reduction goes on to operation. The contraindications are perforation, peritonitis and shock, none of which is present here. CT adds radiation to a child and delays a treatment that is already available; a lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, a duplication cyst, lymphoma or the bowel wall haematoma of Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is looked for in children outside the typical age range or after repeated recurrence. A short small-bowel-only intussusception found incidentally is usually transient and needs no intervention.

quiz.prompt: A girl born in the breech position at term has a normal hip examination at birth, and is referred for imaging because of the breech presentation alone. Coronal hip ultrasound is performed by the Graf method. At or above what alpha angle, in degrees, is the bony acetabular roof regarded as normal? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The alpha angle lies between the vertical line of the iliac wing and the slope of the bony acetabular roof, and sixty degrees or more is a mature hip. Between fifty and fifty-nine the roof is deficient, which may be physiological immaturity in the first weeks or genuine dysplasia depending on the infant's age; below fifty the hip is dysplastic and the femoral head is subluxed or dislocated. Two points about timing follow. Ultrasound is the technique before the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months, because the cartilaginous head and roof are invisible on a radiograph; after that an anteroposterior pelvis takes over, read with Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines, with the ossific nucleus expected in the lower inner quadrant, together with Shenton's line and the acetabular index. And a risk-factor scan of this kind is deferred to about six weeks of age, because physiological laxity in the first weeks produces findings that resolve on their own and would lead to over-treatment. An infant with an abnormal clinical examination is a different matter and is imaged and referred sooner.

quiz.prompt: A girl born at term in the breech position has a normal hip examination at birth. At two weeks of age the department receives a request for an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph to screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip. What should the department do?
choices: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
Perform the radiograph, which shows the cartilage well enough
Perform hip ultrasound at once, before the laxity settles down
Perform MRI of the hips under sedation to assess the labrum
quiz.answer: Perform hip ultrasound instead, and book it at about six weeks
quiz.explain: Both halves of the answer matter. The modality is wrong because the femoral head is entirely cartilaginous until around four to six months, so a neonatal radiograph shows an empty acetabulum and unreliable landmarks, while ultrasound images the cartilaginous head and the acetabular roof directly and adds a dynamic assessment of stability under stress. The timing is wrong because physiological ligamentous laxity in the first weeks of life produces immature-looking hips that resolve spontaneously, so scanning too early converts normal newborns into patients; a scan at around six weeks is the compromise that finds the hips that need treating without treating the ones that do not. This applies to screening on the basis of a risk factor — breech presentation, a first-degree family history, oligohydramnios — in an infant whose examination is normal. An infant with a positive Ortolani or Barlow test is imaged and referred to orthopaedics sooner, and a frankly dislocated irreducible hip is discussed immediately.

quiz.prompt: A term neonate has not passed meconium by 48 hours and the abdomen is distended. The radiograph shows many dilated bowel loops throughout the abdomen. A water-soluble contrast enema shows a small-calibre colon with a change in calibre at the rectosigmoid junction, and the rectum narrower than the sigmoid above it. What does the enema indicate?
choices: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
Meconium ileus; inspissated pellets fill an unused colon
Ileal atresia; the colon is unused and small along its length
Functional immaturity of the colon in an infant of a diabetic
quiz.answer: Hirschsprung disease; the aganglionic rectum stays narrow
quiz.explain: In a normal neonate the rectum is the widest part of the large bowel, so a rectum narrower than the sigmoid — a rectosigmoid index below one — is abnormal in itself, and a transition in calibre above it marks the boundary between the aganglionic distal segment, which cannot relax, and the dilated ganglionic bowel proximal to it. Suction rectal biopsy is what confirms the diagnosis; the enema shows where to expect the transition and how much bowel is involved. Two technical points determine whether the study works: it is done without a preceding rectal examination or washout, either of which can decompress the transition zone and hide it, and delayed films are taken, since retention of contrast beyond 24 hours supports the diagnosis. The alternatives differ in the calibre of the colon along its whole length: meconium ileus gives a microcolon with filling defects in the terminal ileum and points to cystic fibrosis, ileal atresia gives an unused microcolon with no pellets, and small left colon syndrome shows an abrupt calibre change at the splenic flexure in an infant of a diabetic mother and resolves without surgery.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old who is not yet crawling is brought in with a swollen thigh, and the radiograph shows a transverse mid-shaft femoral fracture. The parents describe a roll from a sofa onto a carpeted floor. Set out the imaging that should follow and the findings that would raise the concern further.
quiz.answer: The starting point is that the injury is not explained by the history: a femoral shaft fracture requires substantial force, and in an infant who cannot yet crawl, cruise or weight-bear, a short fall of this kind is an inadequate mechanism. The mismatch between the injury, the mechanism offered and the child's motor development is itself the concerning feature. A full skeletal survey to a national standard is indicated in any child under two years with suspected physical abuse: a defined set of collimated, coned, high-detail views of the whole skeleton rather than a single film of the entire baby, reported by a radiologist experienced in the work, and a limited follow-up survey at about eleven to fourteen days shows healing periosteal reaction at sites that were invisible acutely. Neuroimaging is added in an infant, because occult abusive head trauma is common at this age and clinical signs are unreliable. The findings carrying the highest specificity are classic metaphyseal lesions at the ends of the long bones, posterior and posteromedial rib fractures, and scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures; fractures of clearly different ages, multiple fractures, and any fracture whose mechanism does not match the history or the developmental stage add further weight. The imaging is one contribution to a multi-agency safeguarding assessment made with the clinical team, and is not a verdict on its own.
quiz.explain: The single most useful question in this area is whether the injury fits what the child is physically capable of doing. Fractures in non-ambulant infants are uncommon and are the group in which inflicted injury is most frequent, which is why the developmental history is recorded before the film is reported. The survey is a protocol rather than an ad hoc set of films because its purpose is to find fractures that are clinically silent, and the follow-up survey exists because callus makes visible what the acute study could not — particularly rib and metaphyseal injuries. The last sentence is the one that is easiest to get wrong in either direction: imaging can describe the injuries and their probable ages and mechanisms, and it can say whether the account offered fits, but the determination is made by the safeguarding process rather than by the radiologist alone.

quiz.prompt: A skeletal survey in an 8-month-old, carried out after a reported fall from a bed, shows a healing fracture of the posterior sixth left rib near the costovertebral junction, a linear parietal skull fracture and a mid-clavicular fracture. The parents point out that the child was resuscitated by a paramedic at the scene. How should the rib fracture be weighed?
choices: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
Adequately explained by the chest compressions given at the scene
A common birth injury at this age, and of no further concern
Of no more weight than the skull fracture in the same survey
quiz.answer: Highly specific for abuse; chest compressions seldom fracture there
quiz.explain: Posterior and posteromedial rib fractures arise when an infant is gripped around the chest and squeezed front to back, levering the rib over the transverse process, and they are among the findings with the highest specificity for inflicted injury. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation does fracture ribs in a small minority of infants, and the fractures it produces are predominantly anterior or anterolateral, although posterior fractures after resuscitation have been reported with the two-thumb technique; a documented resuscitation is therefore weighed as a possible contributor rather than accepted as a complete explanation, and it does not on its own dispose of the finding. The other two fractures illustrate the difference between specificity and presence. A linear parietal skull fracture is common and non-specific, follows an ordinary household impact as readily as an inflicted one, and cannot be dated, because the skull heals without callus. A clavicular fracture is the commonest birth injury but would have remodelled long before eight months, and in any case is non-specific. Classic metaphyseal lesions carry specificity comparable to posterior rib fractures and are the other finding to hunt for on the survey.

module_contract.goal: Measure an incidental nodule to the Fleischner convention, judge solid from subsolid, and give the follow-up the guidance recommends or say why it does not apply.

source.title: BTS Guideline for the Investigation and Management of Pulmonary Nodules

approach.step: Confirm it is a true nodule, not a perifissural lymph node
approach.detail: A typical perifissural nodule is attached to a fissure, homogeneous, solid, smooth-margined — it needs no follow-up at all.

approach.step: Measure by convention — and keep to one pathway
approach.detail: This block is the BTS pathway: size by volumetry where your PACS supports it, otherwise maximum diameter. Fleischner 2017 instead averages the long and short axis. Do not mix them — averaging against BTS thresholds systematically undersizes the nodule.
Subsolid nodules (pure ground-glass or part-solid) are staged and followed differently from solid nodules, and behave more indolently.
Nodules under the guideline's minimum size need no follow-up; above it, follow-up or risk modelling applies.

approach.step: Run the Brock model where the nodule warrants it
approach.detail: Age, smoking status, nodule size, location, spiculation, family history and emphysema feed a malignancy probability for solid nodules over the threshold, and for subsolid nodules once they have proven stable at 3 months.

approach.step: Add PET-CT and the Herder model selectively
approach.detail: When the Brock score reaches the intermediate range, FDG-avidity on PET-CT refines the probability further (Herder model).

approach.step: Judge growth on volume, not diameter, where volumetry is available
approach.detail: Volume change is a more sensitive growth signal than a change in linear diameter, and shortens the necessary follow-up duration.

measure.how: Manual 2D diameter or 3D volumetry.
Percentage change in volume between two scans on the same technique.
Calculated from two volumetric measurements a known interval apart.
measure.cutoff: > 600 days — consider discharge · < 400 days — treat as higher risk of malignancy

measure.how: Total surveillance period depends on the measurement method used.
measure.cutoff: 1 year with volumetry · 2 years with manual 2D measurement

classify.name: BTS pathway for the incidental solid nodule
rows: Discharge. A perifissural nodule > 10 mm or with atypical features warrants consideration of follow-up.
Apply the Brock model for malignancy risk
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm persistence, then apply the Brock model if it persists

pitfalls: Following a typical perifissural nodule — it is a lymph node, not a nodule to survey, and BTS says so explicitly.
Judging stability by eye on the diameter alone when volumetry is available — a nodule can grow 25% in volume with almost no visible change in diameter.
Running the Brock model on a subsolid nodule before it has proven persistent at 3 months — transient infective or haemorrhagic nodules are excluded first.
Stopping surveillance at 1 year on manual 2D measurements — that duration is only validated for volumetric follow-up; 2D measurement needs the full 2 years.

Reaching for a Lung-RADS category — Lung-RADS is a US lung-cancer-screening scheme, not part of this guideline or the Fleischner 2017 incidental-nodule guideline; do not mix the two frameworks in one report.
