quiz.prompt: A department rewrites its CT reports to follow the standard section headings used in structured reporting. Put those five headings in the order they appear, from the top of the report.
quiz.answer: indication technique comparison findings impression
quiz.explain: The order is not decorative; each section exists so that a later reader can tell what question was asked, what was done to answer it, and what the answer was. The indication frames the study and is what makes an incidental finding incidental. The technique records contrast, phases and reconstruction, so that a reader in six months knows what the study could and could not have shown - a non-contrast scan reported as showing no liver lesion means something different from a portal-venous one. The comparison names the prior studies actually reviewed, and naming them is a claim that they were opened. The findings are the observation, and the impression is the answer. The impression is the part that is read, quoted in the notes and acted on, which is why it goes last and why it has to stand alone.

quiz.prompt: A CT report on a patient with weight loss runs to eleven lines of findings, one of which records a 3 cm hypoenhancing pancreatic mass with upstream duct dilatation. The impression reads, in full: 'Abnormal appearances as described above. Clinical correlation advised.' The surgeon telephones the next day to ask whether the scan showed anything to explain the symptoms. What is the substantive failure in this report?
choices: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
The findings should have opened with the pancreatic mass
The mass needed a stated differential in the findings
The report should have advised a repeat scan at 3 months
quiz.answer: The impression did not answer the clinical question asked
quiz.explain: The mass was seen, measured and recorded, and still the report failed, because the section the referrer reads contained nothing. 'As described above' asks a clinician who has not seen the images to do the synthesis, and 'clinical correlation advised' hands back the decision the study was requested to inform. A usable impression names the finding, gives the most likely explanation, ranks the alternative worth acting on, and states the next step with a modality and an interval. The near-miss about ordering the findings is a real point of style - leading with the abnormality that matters does help - but a perfectly ordered findings section under an empty impression still leaves the surgeon telephoning. Nor is a differential in the findings section the fix: the findings section is for what was seen, and interpretation belongs in the impression where it will be read.

quiz.prompt: A diagnostic workup characterises a circumscribed, oval, non-calcified mass, and the radiologist assigns BI-RADS 3, probably benign, with short-interval follow-up rather than biopsy. What is the upper limit of the likelihood of malignancy, as a percentage, that this category permits? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: BI-RADS 3 means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than 2 per cent, and that number is the whole content of the category: it is the risk at which surveillance - typically at 6, 12 and 24 months - is judged safer than a needle. Category 4A begins immediately above it, at more than 2 up to 10 per cent, so a lesion the reader privately puts at 5 per cent is not a 3, however benign it looks. The bands continue: 4B more than 10 to 50 per cent, 4C more than 50 to less than 95, and category 5 at 95 per cent or above, where a benign biopsy result is disbelieved rather than accepted. Two disciplines follow. A category 3 may be given only after a complete diagnostic evaluation, never off a screening study, and the patient's own circumstances - a planned pregnancy, an unreliable route back for follow-up, or a patient who will not tolerate the wait - can still justify sampling a lesion the imaging calls probably benign.

quiz.prompt: A screening mammogram shows an asymmetry seen on the craniocaudal view only. No spot compression views, no ultrasound and no prior films have been obtained. The reporting radiologist writes 'BI-RADS 4, suspicious, biopsy recommended'. Why is that assessment wrong even if the lesion later proves malignant?
choices: The workup is incomplete, so the assessment is category 0
A one-view asymmetry is category 2 until it is proven
Category 4 is reserved for lesions with a mass on ultrasound
A screening study permits category 1 or category 2 alone
quiz.answer: The workup is incomplete, so the assessment is category 0
quiz.explain: An assessment category is a statement about a completed evaluation, and category 0 exists to say that the evaluation is not finished and to name what is needed - additional views, ultrasound, or the prior films. Being lucky about the eventual outcome does not rescue a category that misdescribes the state of the workup, for two reasons. The patient is sent to biopsy without the cheap steps that resolve most one-view asymmetries as summation of normal tissue, and the unit's own audit is corrupted, because positive predictive value is computed from these codes and a 4 assigned before workup pollutes the denominator that the department is judged on. The distractor pinning category 4 to an ultrasound correlate inverts the logic: a mammographic finding with no sonographic correlate is not thereby benign, and a lesion may be sampled under stereotactic or tomosynthesis guidance instead.

quiz.prompt: An emergency department patient with abdominal pain has a CT reported four hours after they were discharged home. It shows a 4 mm non-obstructing renal stone and, incidentally, a 3.5 cm saccular aneurysm of the splenic artery. The referring emergency physician's shift ended two hours ago. Describe how this result should be handled and what has to appear in the record.
quiz.answer: Treat it as an actionable finding that the report alone will not carry safely, because the clinician it is addressed to has no further contact with the patient. Reach a person who can act - the on-call clinician who has taken over that shift's patients, or the patient's named responsible clinician - by direct person-to-person contact rather than by leaving the result in an electronic inbox, and confirm that they have understood what is being asked of them. Close the loop by establishing that a named individual accepts responsibility for arranging vascular referral and for informing the patient, since a message that is delivered but not accepted is not closure. Then document in the report itself, as an addendum, who was contacted, at what time, by what means, and what was agreed. The written record is the durable part: a telephone call that nobody documented is indistinguishable, months later, from a call that was never made.
quiz.explain: Actionable findings sort roughly into three tiers by how fast someone must act: findings that threaten life within minutes, such as a tension pneumothorax or a ruptured ectopic, which demand immediate voice contact; findings that need action within hours or days, such as this aneurysm; and incidental findings that need outpatient follow-up. Counterintuitively, it is the third tier that is most often lost, and discharge is the classic failure mode, because the report lands with a clinician whose episode of care has ended. Notice also what is not the answer: adding a strong recommendation to the report changes nothing if nobody reads it, and telling the patient alone offloads the follow-up onto the person least able to arrange it. The durable fix is systemic - a tracked register of communicated results with acknowledgement, rather than a radiologist's memory - and the documented addendum is what feeds it.

quiz.prompt: An audit of one unit's CT reports finds the phrase 'infection or infarction cannot be entirely excluded' in a third of them, with no ranking of the two possibilities and no recommendation attached. What is the practical cost of this habit to the referring team?
choices: The decision the report was meant to inform is handed back
The report becomes too long for a clinician to read
The differential given is too narrow for the appearances
The findings section duplicates what the impression says
quiz.answer: The decision the report was meant to inform is handed back
quiz.explain: Hedging is sometimes the honest thing: genuine uncertainty must be stated, and a report that manufactures confidence it does not have is worse than one that admits doubt. The failure here is unranked uncertainty with no exit. Two diagnoses with opposite treatments are offered with no statement of which is more likely, no feature that separates them, and no test that would. The workable form gives the favoured diagnosis, names the alternative that is worth acting on, and says what would discriminate - a specific test at a specific interval, or a specific piece of clinical information. 'Correlate clinically' becomes meaningful only when it names the correlation sought: a white cell count, a lactate, a travel history, the date of the last chemotherapy. Length is not the problem; a two-line impression can be entirely unhelpful, and a controlled lexicon exists precisely so that agreed words carry agreed meanings between readers.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT for haematuria that incidentally shows a single solid 4 mm pulmonary nodule and no other lung abnormality. Applying the 2017 Fleischner Society recommendations for incidental nodules, at how many months is the optional follow-up CT offered to a patient at this level of risk? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: A solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about 1 per cent, so no routine follow-up is recommended in a low-risk patient; in a high-risk patient - heavy smoking, upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, older age - the guidance offers an optional single CT at 12 months, and if it is unchanged nothing further is needed. Hold the neighbouring bands beside it, because the intervals are not intuitive: a single solid nodule of 6 to 8 mm is imaged at 6 to 12 months and then considered again at 18 to 24 months, while a nodule over 8 mm earns CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling, since at that size the pre-test probability justifies the intervention. Equally important are the recommendations' boundaries: they apply to incidental nodules in patients aged 35 and over, and not to lung cancer screening, which has its own system, nor to the immunosuppressed, nor to patients with a known primary malignancy.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old on tacrolimus after renal transplantation has a CT showing three new solid 5 mm pulmonary nodules. A trainee proposes discharging the finding under the Fleischner recommendation that nodules under 6 mm need no routine follow-up. Why is that reasoning unsound here?
choices: This patient sits outside the population the guidance covers
Three nodules exceed the number the guidance permits
The guidance requires thin-section CT to have been used
The guidance applies to nodules found on screening CT
quiz.answer: This patient sits outside the population the guidance covers
quiz.explain: Two exclusions bite at once. The recommendations are written for patients aged 35 and over, below which granuloma and resolving infection dominate and a lifetime of surveillance radiation is a real cost; and they explicitly exclude immunosuppressed patients, in whom a new nodule may be fungal or bacterial infection that needs treating this week, not a lesion to be watched for a year. Known primary malignancy is the third exclusion, for the mirror-image reason. The distractor about screening inverts the truth and is worth naming: this framework is for incidental nodules, while nodules found in a lung cancer screening programme are handled by the screening system, whose thresholds are calibrated to a population enriched for cancer. The right action here is short-interval CT with a discussion about infection, plus attention to whether the nodules are new against any prior imaging.

quiz.prompt: Your hospital board asks why the breast unit reports in BI-RADS categories while the general CT service writes free text, and whether the categories add anything beyond jargon. Give the argument in terms of what a category does that a paragraph of prose does not.
quiz.answer: A category is a controlled term that carries a defined probability of disease and a single recommended action, so the same word means the same thing to every reader and to every referrer. That buys three things prose does not. It removes ambiguity, because 'probably benign' becomes a stated risk band rather than one radiologist's confidence on one day. It ties the report to management, since the recommendation follows from the category rather than from individual habit, which reduces the variation between readers that is otherwise invisible to everyone outside the reporting room. And it makes the output auditable: because every study leaves a coded outcome, the unit can link its categories to the eventual pathology and measure its own positive predictive value, recall rate and cancer detection rate, then feed those numbers back into practice. The cost is real and should be conceded: a rigid category can flatten an unusual case, which is why these systems keep an explicit route for the reader who needs to depart from them, and why the departure has to be justified in the report.
quiz.explain: The board's scepticism is reasonable and the weak answer - that categories are clearer - does not survive it, since a well-written paragraph is clear too. What a paragraph cannot do is be counted. A coded assessment turns every report into a data point, and once the data exist the unit can discover that one reader's recall rate is twice another's, or that its own category 4A biopsies come back malignant at a rate far from the published band, which is a signal no amount of eloquent prose generates. This is also why the systems tie a recommendation to each category: it converts a probability estimate into a decision, and it makes divergence between the category and the advice visible as an error rather than as a style. The honest caveat is that the categories are only as good as the criteria beneath them, which is why they are versioned and periodically revised against outcome data.

quiz.prompt: A liver MRI in a cirrhotic patient describes a 2.5 cm observation with non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement, non-peripheral washout and an enhancing capsule, and concludes: 'LI-RADS 4, probably hepatocellular carcinoma; recommend follow-up MRI in six months.' The hepatologist queries the report. What is the internal inconsistency?
choices: The features listed already meet the criteria for LR-5
The washout must be seen in the portal venous phase
A capsule is not a feature this system recognises
An observation this size is reported without a category
quiz.answer: The features listed already meet the criteria for LR-5
quiz.explain: In a patient at risk, an observation of 20 mm or more with non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement plus at least one additional major feature - non-peripheral washout, an enhancing capsule, or threshold growth - is LR-5, definite hepatocellular carcinoma, and LR-5 is the category on which many programmes treat without a biopsy. Two errors compound here. The category understates what the reader's own description establishes, and the recommendation then contradicts even the understated category, since neither LR-4 nor LR-5 is followed with routine six-month surveillance. That second error is the one worth generalising: in a reporting system the recommendation belongs to the category, not to the reader's mood, and a report whose advice disagrees with its own code is more dangerous than free text because it wears the uniform of a standard. The washout distractor contains a real technical point - with extracellular agents washout may be assessed in the portal venous or delayed phase, while with a hepatobiliary agent it is judged in the portal venous phase only - but it is a caveat about acquisition, not the inconsistency in this report.

quiz.prompt: Rewrite the sentence 'Small lung nodule noted, follow-up as clinically indicated' into a recommendation that can actually be acted on and tracked, and set out the elements that make the difference.
quiz.answer: Something of the form: '5 mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe, apical segment, unchanged from the CT of 12 March 2024. Recommend non-contrast chest CT at 12 months; no further imaging if it remains stable.' The elements are a measurement and a specific location, so that the next reader finds the same nodule rather than a different one; a comparison that states whether it is new, stable or growing and against which study by date; a named modality and technique, so the follow-up can actually answer the question; a specific interval rather than a discretionary one; an endpoint that says when surveillance stops, which prevents a nodule being followed indefinitely by inertia; and clarity about who arranges it. 'As clinically indicated' fails every one of these: it passes the decision to a clinician who has not seen the images, leaves nothing for a tracking system to key on, and cannot be audited afterwards, because no one can say whether the recommendation was followed.
quiz.explain: The test of a recommendation is whether an administrator with no clinical training could book the right study from it, and whether an auditor could later decide whether it happened. Vague advice fails both. There is a second reason to state the endpoint: surveillance that never terminates accumulates radiation, cost and anxiety, and generates its own incidental findings, so the exit condition is part of the clinical decision rather than an afterthought. Where a published framework governs the finding, citing it by name and version does additional work, because it tells the referrer that the interval comes from evidence rather than from the reader's preference, and it lets a future radiologist see which rule was applied when the rules change.

curriculum_modules.title: CT in Abdominal Trauma and AAST Grading

module_contract.goal: Choose and interpret the phases of a trauma abdominal CT, grade solid organ injury by the AAST scale, and separate the findings that go to the angiography suite from those that go straight to theatre.

approach.step: Get the phases right before you read
approach.detail: Arterial phase as a roadmap for the interventional radiologist or surgeon and for vascular injury; portal venous at 70 seconds for the organ injuries; delayed at 7–10 minutes when a collecting system, ureteric or bladder injury is suspected.

approach.step: Take the solid organs in turn
approach.detail: Spleen, liver, kidneys, pancreas, adrenals. Separate contusion — vague ill-defined hypodense areas — from laceration, which is linear, and haematoma, which is oval or round.

approach.step: Decide what any contrast blush is
approach.detail: Measure it. Density within ten HU of the nearby vessel or the aorta is vascular. Contrast beyond the borders of the organ must be extravasation.

approach.step: Use the delayed phase to tell the two apart
approach.detail: Active arterial extravasation persists or increases on the delayed images. A pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula washes away with the bloodstream.
Bowel wall thickening, unexplained intraperitoneal fluid, interloop fluid, mesenteric stranding. Extravasated oral contrast or bowel content is specific but rare.

approach.step: Step back for the hypoperfusion complex
approach.detail: Diffuse bowel wall thickening in a severely injured patient may be shock bowel from active bleeding rather than direct injury.

measure.how: The primary phase for solid organ injury.
Acquired when a collecting system, ureteric or bladder injury is suspected.
Region of interest on the blush and on the nearby vessel or aorta in the same phase.
Subcapsular haematomas are graded by the proportion of surface area they cover; intraparenchymal haematomas by maximal dimension. Portal venous phase.
measure.cutoff: Subcapsular > 50% of surface area, or ruptured, or intraparenchymal > 10 cm = AAST grade III · grade IV is parenchymal disruption of 25–75% of a lobe

classify.name: AAST renal injury scale
rows: Laceration < 1 cm without collecting system injury
Laceration > 1 cm without collecting system injury
Collecting system violation or large laceration
Urology involvement; delayed phase mandatory. In penetrating trauma, collecting system violation is an operative finding
classify.note: The 2018 AAST revision adds vascular injury — pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula — and active extravasation as grade-raising findings for spleen, liver and kidney. Report both explicitly, whatever the parenchymal grade.

modifiers.meaning: Vague, ill-defined hypodense area within the parenchyma.
Linear-shaped hypodense area.
Oval or round hypodense area; subcapsular or intraparenchymal.
Pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula — contained, washes away on delayed imaging. Goes to angioembolisation.
Contrast beyond the organ borders that persists or increases on delayed imaging. Angioembolisation if contained and the patient is stable; theatre if enormous or the patient is unstable.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Trauma CT: arterial phase, portal venous phase at 70 s[, delayed excretory phase at 7–10 min for collecting system assessment].

FINDINGS
Spleen: [normal / contusion / laceration n cm / subcapsular haematoma n cm] — AAST grade [ ].
Liver: [ ] — AAST grade [ ]. Subcapsular haematoma [n] cm.
Kidneys: [ ] — AAST grade [ ]. Collecting system: [intact / violated — contrast extravasation on the excretory phase].
Pancreas, adrenals: [ ].
Vascular injury (pseudoaneurysm / AV fistula): [absent / present — organ, size]; behaviour on delayed phase [washes out].
Active extravasation: [absent / present — organ, within / beyond the organ borders, persists or increases on delayed phase].
Bowel and mesentery: wall thickening [ ], interloop fluid [ ], mesenteric stranding [ ], free extraluminal gas [ ].
Free fluid: [absent / present — volume, distribution, attenuation].
Hypoperfusion complex: [absent / present].

IMPRESSION
1. [Organ] injury, AAST grade [ ].
2. [Active extravasation / contained vascular injury] — [angioembolisation / laparotomy].
3. [Bowel or mesenteric injury.] [Discussed with (trauma team) at (time).]
pitfalls: Calling every blush active bleeding. A contained pseudoaneurysm washes away on delayed imaging; extravasation persists or grows. Acquire the delayed phase before you decide.
Split-bolus economy. Combining arterial and venous phases cuts dose but can compromise the demonstration of contrast extravasation — know which protocol you are reading.
Trusting pneumoperitoneum as proof of bowel injury. Air transmitted from the chest in pneumothorax is its commonest cause in trauma.
Ignoring unexplained free fluid with no solid organ injury. Interloop fluid in particular is very suggestive of bowel injury.
Reading diffuse bowel wall thickening as injury in a hypotensive patient. That is shock bowel, and the finding to chase is the bleed causing it.
Omitting the delayed phase when the kidney is injured. Without it you cannot say whether the collecting system is violated, and that is the grade IV threshold.

quiz.prompt: A stable 30-year-old is scanned after a high-speed collision. The radiographer asks whether a single portal venous phase will do, or whether an arterial phase should be added. What is the best answer and its justification?
quiz.answer: Add an arterial phase where arterial bleeding is likely, because it separates arterial from venous bleeding and shows the embolisation target
choices: Use the portal venous phase alone in blunt trauma, because an added arterial phase raises dose without changing management decisions
Use an arterial phase alone in blunt trauma, because parenchymal lacerations and free fluid are shown at least as well on those images
Add a delayed phase rather than an arterial phase in routine practice, because it demonstrates the source of arterial bleeding far more reliably
Add an arterial phase where arterial bleeding is likely, because it separates arterial from venous bleeding and shows the embolisation target
quiz.explain: The portal venous phase at around 70 seconds is the workhorse: it shows parenchymal lacerations and haematomas, bowel wall enhancement, mesenteric injury and free fluid, and it is the phase on which AAST grading is largely done. An arterial phase adds real value where arterial haemorrhage is likely, which in practice means high-grade solid organ injury and pelvic fractures, because it distinguishes brisk arterial extravasation from a slow venous ooze and shows the vessel the interventional radiologist will target. A delayed phase, at three to five minutes, is a problem-solver rather than a routine, used to separate active extravasation from a contained vascular injury and to show urinary tract leak. Split-bolus techniques let some units combine phases and hold the dose down.

quiz.prompt: A splenic injury shows a rounded 8 mm focus of contrast within the parenchyma on the arterial phase, matching the aorta in attenuation. On the three-minute delayed images the focus is smaller, still round and sharply marginated, and it now matches the attenuation of the splenic vein. How do you interpret this and what do you advise?
quiz.answer: A contained pseudoaneurysm rather than active bleeding, since it stays discrete and follows the blood pool; advise angiographic embolisation
choices: Active extravasation, since a focus that matches aortic attenuation on the arterial phase represents haemorrhage escaping into the parenchyma
A contained pseudoaneurysm rather than active bleeding, since it stays discrete and follows the blood pool; advise angiographic embolisation
A calcified splenic artery branch, since the density persists across phases and vascular calcification is common at any adult age
An arteriovenous fistula requiring laparotomy, since early venous filling of this kind cannot be dealt with by endovascular means
quiz.explain: The delayed phase is what separates these. Active extravasation grows, changes shape, spreads irregularly and stays dense as more contrast pours out; it also usually enlarges beyond the organ or into the peritoneum. A contained vascular injury, that is a pseudoaneurysm or an arteriovenous fistula, stays round and well defined and washes out in step with the blood pool because it is still in continuity with the circulation. Calcification is distinguished by being present on the unenhanced series, if you have one, and by not changing at all. The management implication is that both active bleeding and a contained pseudoaneurysm in a stable patient are indications for angiography and embolisation, but a pseudoaneurysm may declare itself late, which is why it must be named in the report rather than dismissed as a blush.

quiz.prompt: A stable adult has a splenic laceration 4 cm deep, an intraparenchymal haematoma of 6 cm, and a 6 mm pseudoaneurysm within the parenchyma with no contrast beyond the splenic capsule. Give the AAST organ injury grade for the spleen under the 2018 revision. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The 2018 revision of the AAST spleen scale made vascular injury an explicit upgrader. Any splenic injury containing a vascular injury, meaning a pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula, or active bleeding that remains confined within the splenic capsule, is grade IV, whatever the size of the laceration. Grade V is reserved for a shattered spleen, or a vascular injury with active bleeding extending beyond the spleen into the peritoneum. Without the pseudoaneurysm this injury would have been grade III on the laceration depth of more than 3 cm and the haematoma of 5 cm or more. This is exactly why the arterial phase earns its place: a grade III becomes a grade IV, and a stable patient who might have been observed goes to the angiography suite instead.

quiz.prompt: A stable patient kicked by a horse has a right renal laceration extending into the collecting system, with contrast in the perinephric space on the excretory phase, a normal renal artery and vein, and the haematoma confined within Gerota fascia. Give the AAST renal injury grade under the 2018 revision. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Under the 2018 AAST kidney scale, a laceration involving the collecting system with urinary extravasation is grade IV, as are renal pelvic laceration or ureteropelvic disruption, a segmental vessel injury with a devascularised segment, and active bleeding extending beyond Gerota fascia. Grade III is a laceration deeper than 1 cm without collecting system involvement, or vascular injury and bleeding contained within Gerota fascia. Grade V means a shattered kidney or main renal artery or vein avulsion with a devascularised kidney. Note that the grade does not dictate the operation here: most grade IV renal injuries with urinary extravasation in a stable patient are managed without surgery, with a ureteric stent if the leak persists. This is also the injury you will miss without an excretory phase.

quiz.prompt: You have acquired arterial and portal venous phases in a stable patient with a renal and a splenic injury. Justify adding a delayed phase: what two distinct questions does it answer?
quiz.answer: It separates active extravasation, which enlarges and spreads, from a contained pseudoaneurysm, which stays discrete and washes out with the blood pool; and as an excretory phase it shows urinary leak from the collecting system or ureter.
quiz.explain: The delayed acquisition earns its dose twice. First, the behaviour of a hyperattenuating focus over time is the only reliable way to tell continuing haemorrhage from a contained vascular injury, and the two do not have identical urgency even though both point towards angiography. Second, at three to five minutes contrast has reached the collecting system, so a laceration communicating with the pelvicalyceal system or a ureteric injury shows as extraluminal excreted contrast; without this phase a grade IV renal injury can be graded as a III. Restrict the delayed acquisition to the region of interest rather than repeating the whole abdomen, and remember that it does not fill the bladder adequately, so it does not substitute for a retrograde CT cystogram.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these trauma CT acquisitions in the order they are performed within a single sitting.
quiz.answer: arterial-phase portal-venous-phase excretory-phase CT-cystography
quiz.explain: The arterial phase comes first, timed by bolus tracking, and answers the question of arterial haemorrhage and vascular injury. The portal venous phase at around 70 seconds is the diagnostic backbone for parenchymal injury, bowel and free fluid. The excretory phase at three to five minutes then serves two purposes: it resolves extravasation against pseudoaneurysm, and it opacifies the collecting systems and ureters. CT cystography comes last because it needs the bladder filled retrogradely through the catheter, and because the excreted contrast already in the system would otherwise confuse the picture. Not every patient needs all four; the sequence is a menu that the mechanism and the findings select from, and each added phase must be justified against dose in what is often a young patient.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a seat-belt mark across the abdomen has CT showing a segment of jejunum with discontinuous wall, adjacent extraluminal gas locules, a mesenteric haematoma and moderate free fluid. He is haemodynamically stable. What should you recommend?
quiz.answer: Immediate laparotomy: bowel wall discontinuity with adjacent extraluminal gas is a specific sign of perforation and is not managed expectantly
choices: Immediate laparotomy: bowel wall discontinuity with adjacent extraluminal gas is a specific sign of perforation and is not managed expectantly
Angiography and embolisation: the mesenteric haematoma is the dominant lesion here, and endovascular haemorrhage control should precede any operation
Admission for serial abdominal examination: stability makes bowel injury unlikely and repeat CT at 24 hours will settle the question
Oral contrast study and repeat CT: gas locules of this kind are usually artefactual and need confirmation before an operation
quiz.explain: Signs of blunt bowel injury divide into specific and suggestive. The specific ones, meaning discontinuity of the bowel wall, extraluminal gas adjacent to bowel, and extraluminal enteric or oral contrast, mandate laparotomy in a patient with the right mechanism. The suggestive ones, being focal bowel wall thickening, abnormal wall enhancement, mesenteric fat stranding, mesenteric haematoma, and interloop free fluid without solid organ injury, are individually unreliable but powerful in combination and warrant close observation and often surgery. Active mesenteric arterial extravasation is itself an indication for laparotomy or embolisation. Stability is no reassurance here: bowel and mesenteric injuries kill through delayed peritonitis rather than through haemorrhage, and every hour of delay after the first eight increases morbidity.

quiz.prompt: A stable adult with a seat-belt mark has moderate free fluid in the pelvis and both paracolic gutters on CT, with entirely normal liver, spleen, kidneys and pancreas. What is your interpretation and what do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Free fluid without solid organ injury after blunt trauma points to a bowel or mesenteric injury; scrutinise for bowel wall thickening, abnormal enhancement and mesenteric haematoma, and either take the patient to laparotomy or admit for serial examination with a low threshold for repeat imaging.
quiz.explain: Unexplained free fluid is one of the highest-yield observations on a trauma scan, because the fluid has to have come from somewhere. In a blunt-injured adult, the leading explanations are bowel or mesenteric injury, a bladder injury, and bleeding from an injury you have not yet seen. Small volumes of simple fluid in the pelvis of a woman of reproductive age can be physiological, and a modest amount may follow aggressive crystalloid resuscitation, but moderate or large fluid deserves a formal answer. Measure the attenuation: fluid at 30 to 45 Hounsfield units is blood, while low attenuation suggests bowel content, bile or urine. Do not sign off a normal report with unexplained free fluid on it.

quiz.prompt: A man with a pelvic fracture has CT cystography showing contrast tracking into the prevesical space and along the anterior abdominal wall, with none outlining bowel loops or reaching the paracolic gutters. He has no peritonism. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: An extraperitoneal rupture, which is usually treated by catheter drainage alone unless fracture fixation or a bladder neck injury forces repair
choices: An intraperitoneal rupture, which requires urgent operative repair, because urine within the peritoneal cavity causes a chemical peritonitis and sepsis
A urethral injury, which requires a retrograde urethrogram and precludes any attempt at urethral catheterisation before repair
An extraperitoneal rupture, which is usually treated by catheter drainage alone unless fracture fixation or a bladder neck injury forces repair
A normal study, since perivesical contrast after pelvic fracture reflects passive leakage around the catheter rather than a tear
quiz.explain: The two patterns are separated by where the contrast goes. Extraperitoneal rupture, which is far more common and nearly always accompanies a pelvic fracture, leaks into the prevesical space of Retzius and can track into the anterior abdominal wall, thigh or scrotum, producing the molar tooth appearance around the bladder base. Intraperitoneal rupture occurs at the dome, typically in a distended bladder struck by a direct blow, and contrast outlines bowel loops and fills the paracolic gutters; it needs surgical repair. Combined injuries occur and are managed surgically. The technique caveat is essential: the bladder must be filled retrogradely and distended with dilute contrast, since a passively filled bladder is the classic reason a rupture is missed.

quiz.prompt: A man arrives after a fall from height with a systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg that does not improve after two units of blood. FAST shows fluid in Morison pouch and the pelvis. The registrar wants a trauma CT before deciding. What should be advised?
quiz.answer: Take him to theatre for laparotomy: with a positive FAST and no response to resuscitation, CT delays definitive haemorrhage control
choices: Scan him first with a portal venous phase alone, since an abbreviated protocol is quick enough to be safe even in a shocked patient
Take him to the angiography suite first: catheter angiography is faster than CT and can control any source of abdominal bleeding
Repeat the FAST in fifteen minutes: a single positive study is not sufficient grounds for laparotomy in blunt abdominal trauma
Take him to theatre for laparotomy: with a positive FAST and no response to resuscitation, CT delays definitive haemorrhage control
quiz.explain: CT is a test for the stable patient and for the transient responder in a department set up to scan them safely, ideally with the scanner in or beside the resuscitation room. A non-responder with free fluid needs the bleeding stopped, and the operating theatre does that; every minute in the scanner is a minute of ongoing haemorrhage, and the shocked patient is also the one who arrests on the table. Angiography has a defined role in pelvic arterial bleeding, often alongside packing, but it does not control splenic hilar or mesenteric haemorrhage in a crashing patient. Recognise the hypoperfusion complex when you do scan such patients: a flat inferior vena cava, intense bowel wall and adrenal enhancement, and a shocked pancreas.

quiz.prompt: A stable 25-year-old has a hepatic injury with parenchymal disruption of about 40 per cent of the right lobe and a focus of active contrast extravasation extending beyond the liver capsule into the peritoneum. The hepatic veins and inferior vena cava are intact. What is the appropriate recommendation?
quiz.answer: Grade IV liver injury; while he remains stable, hepatic angiography with embolisation is preferred to laparotomy for the active bleeding
choices: Grade III liver injury; parenchymal disruption below 50 per cent of a lobe means observation alone, with a repeat scan at 48 hours to reassess
Grade IV liver injury; while he remains stable, hepatic angiography with embolisation is preferred to laparotomy for the active bleeding
Grade V liver injury; extravasation beyond the capsule always denotes juxtahepatic venous injury and demands immediate laparotomy
Grade II liver injury; extravasation contained within the peritoneum without venous injury does not change the grade or the plan
quiz.explain: On the 2018 AAST liver scale, parenchymal disruption involving 25 to 75 per cent of a hepatic lobe is grade IV, as is active bleeding extending beyond the liver parenchyma into the peritoneum. Grade V is disruption of more than 75 per cent of a lobe or a juxtahepatic venous injury involving the retrohepatic inferior vena cava or the central major hepatic veins. Vascular injury contained within the parenchyma sits at grade III. Management has moved decisively towards non-operative care with angioembolisation for arterial bleeding in stable patients, because the liver is difficult to operate on and most venous bleeding tamponades. Anticipate the delayed complications you will be asked to image: biloma, abscess, haemobilia and delayed rupture of a subcapsular haematoma.

quiz.prompt: You are asked to perform CT cystography on a patient with a pelvic fracture and frank haematuria. Describe how you would fill the bladder and explain why clamping the catheter and relying on excreted contrast fails.
quiz.answer: Instil roughly 300 to 400 millilitres of dilute contrast retrogradely through the urethral catheter under gravity until the bladder is distended, then scan; passive antegrade filling with excreted contrast does not distend the bladder enough, so small tears stay apposed and the leak is missed.
quiz.explain: The whole sensitivity of the test lies in distension. A bladder that is not stretched keeps the edges of a tear in contact, and dilute urinary contrast simply sits in the dependent part without ever pressurising the wall, which is why the passively filled study has a well-earned reputation for false negatives. Fill retrogradely by gravity with dilute contrast, typically around 300 to 400 millilitres or until the patient reports discomfort, and scan through the pelvis; a post-drainage image helps where extraperitoneal leak is subtle. One absolute precaution: if there is blood at the meatus, a high-riding prostate or a suspected urethral injury, a retrograde urethrogram comes first, because passing a catheter through a partial urethral tear can complete it.

quiz.prompt: A hypotensive 7-year-old scanned after a road collision shows diffuse intense enhancement of thickened small bowel wall, a slit-like inferior vena cava, avid adrenal enhancement and a hypoenhancing pancreas, with no laceration or free gas. How should this be reported?
quiz.answer: As the hypoperfusion complex of hypovolaemic shock; it calls for urgent resuscitation and a search for bleeding, not laparotomy for bowel injury
choices: As diffuse blunt small bowel injury; the wall thickening and the abnormal enhancement together mandate laparotomy without any further resuscitation
As mesenteric venous thrombosis; the combination of bowel wall thickening with a collapsed vena cava indicates acute venous outflow occlusion
As the hypoperfusion complex of hypovolaemic shock; it calls for urgent resuscitation and a search for bleeding, not laparotomy for bowel injury
As a normal paediatric study; bowel wall enhancement and a narrow vena cava are expected findings at this age and carry no significance
quiz.explain: The hypoperfusion complex, sometimes called shock bowel, is a physiological pattern rather than an injury, and it is commonest in children. Low cardiac output produces a flattened inferior vena cava and small aorta, splanchnic vasoconstriction with intense mucosal enhancement and fluid-filled thickened bowel, avid adrenal enhancement, and reduced enhancement of the spleen, pancreas, liver and kidneys. Recognising it does two things. It stops the report from calling a diffuse enhancement pattern a bowel injury and sending a child who needs blood to theatre for the wrong operation. And it is an alarm: the child is decompensating on the table, so the scan should be curtailed, resuscitation intensified, and the bleeding source found. The pattern reverses within hours of adequate volume replacement.

module_contract.goal: Characterise an adrenal lesion using its actual anatomy, composition and acquired CT/MRI findings; separate imaging uncertainty, endocrine function and framework-specific management.

approach.detail: Confirm adrenal origin on multiplanar imaging: identify residual gland limbs, displacement and organ interfaces; exclude a renal, pancreatic, splenic, vascular or retroperitoneal mimic. Static planes do not show motion.

For a homogeneous lesion, use a representative unenhanced ROI covering most of the lesion (ESE/ENSAT Table 4 specifies at least 75%) without surrounding-tissue contamination. Record heterogeneity; do not select a reassuring component to classify the entire heterogeneous mass.

ESE/ENSAT 2023: a homogeneous mass with true unenhanced attenuation ≤10 HU needs no further imaging, but endocrine assessment is separate. Homogeneous 11–20 HU and <4 cm without significant hormone excess: additional imaging or 12-month noncontrast CT/MRI. Seow 2025 proposes a different ≤20 HU/<4 cm true-incidentaloma pathway; do not blend the frameworks or extend it to oncology/endocrine presentations.

approach.step: Use chemical shift MRI for indeterminate lesions
approach.detail: Compare actual matched in-phase and opposed-phase MRI and check motion, field strength and acquisition details. Signal loss supports intracellular lipid; it is not a universal adenoma diagnosis and heterogeneous masses cannot be classified from a reassuring component.

approach.step: Reserve washout CT for genuinely indeterminate lesions
approach.detail: Washout is not a definitive diagnosis. Historical 60% absolute/40% relative criteria overlap with phaeochromocytoma and other tumours. ESE/ENSAT 2023 allows selected additional imaging with weak washout evidence; Seow 2025 proposes no washout for true incidentalomas. State the actual protocol, framework and endocrine/oncology context.

Assess size together with homogeneity, unenhanced attenuation, invasion and context. ESE/ENSAT 2023 follow-up of indeterminate masses uses >20% AND ≥5 mm growth in maximum diameter over 6–12 months; size alone is not a universal malignant diagnosis or surgery instruction.

Imaging characterises anatomy and composition but cannot establish hormonal function or every histological diagnosis. State uncertainty, framework and specialist discussion where appropriate. Biopsy needs exclusion of phaeochromocytoma, unresolved imaging and a result that would alter management.

measure.how: For a homogeneous lesion, use a representative unenhanced ROI covering most of the lesion (ESE/ENSAT Table 4 specifies at least 75%) without surrounding-tissue contamination. Record heterogeneity; do not select a reassuring component to classify the entire heterogeneous mass.
measure.cutoff: Homogeneous mass, true unenhanced ≤10 HU: benign imaging features under ESE/ENSAT 2023; not unique adenoma histology or endocrine clearance.

measure.how: True unenhanced CT; record whole-lesion homogeneity, size and clinical/endocrine context.
measure.cutoff: ESE/ENSAT 2023: 11–20 HU and <4 cm, without significant hormone excess, suggests additional imaging or 12-month CT/MRI. Seow 2025 proposes a distinct true-incidentaloma pathway.

measure.how: (Enhanced HU - delayed HU) / (Enhanced HU - unenhanced HU) x 100.
measure.cutoff: Historical ≥60%; overlapping tumour patterns prevent a standalone adenoma diagnosis.

measure.how: (Enhanced HU - delayed HU) / Enhanced HU x 100, used when no unenhanced phase is available.
measure.cutoff: Historical ≥40%; ESE/ENSAT Table 4 lists >58% with weak evidence and caution. No standalone diagnosis.

measure.how: Longest diameter on the plane that best shows the lesion, compared with any prior study.
measure.cutoff: ESE/ENSAT indeterminate-lesion follow-up: >20% AND ≥5 mm over 6–12 months. Size, attenuation, homogeneity and clinical context assessed together.

classify.name: ESE/ENSAT 2023 imaging categories — endocrine and clinical context remain separate
rows: Benign imaging features, independent of size
No further adrenal imaging; endocrine function assessed separately
Usually benign; not conclusively lipid-poor adenoma from attenuation alone
Without significant hormone excess, additional imaging or interval CT/MRI at 12 months
Expert multidisciplinary assessment, staging and individualized management
Expert discussion and additional imaging selected for the actual clinical question
classify.note: The Seow 2025 ≤20 HU/<4 cm true-incidentaloma proposal is distinct from ESE/ENSAT 2023; do not apply its eligibility or follow-up rules silently to cancer staging or suspected adrenal disease.

pitfalls: Hormonal activity cannot be excluded by benign imaging morphology.
Washout overlap occurs in non-adenomas; do not diagnose an adenoma from washout alone in a discordant lesion.
A low-attenuation homogeneous adrenal lesion can be benign without proving adenoma histology; a nonenhancing cyst and a fat-predominant myelolipoma require their own composition assessment.
Small foci of macroscopic fat do not uniquely establish myelolipoma, and chemical-shift signal loss is not a universal adenoma or nonfunctioning-lesion diagnosis.
Keep ESE/ENSAT 2023 recommendations separate from the Seow 2025 proposed pathway adopted by the updated source; record the framework and its incidentaloma/endocrine eligibility.

Before considering biopsy, exclude phaeochromocytoma, confirm imaging remains indeterminate and confirm histology would change management. Suspected adrenocortical carcinoma needs expert assessment rather than routine biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT in a woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer shows a 1.8 cm left adrenal nodule. It is round, homogeneous, and a generous region of interest gives a mean of 6 HU on the true unenhanced series. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: No further adrenal imaging: an unenhanced attenuation of 10 HU or less identifies a lipid-rich adenoma
choices: No further adrenal imaging: an unenhanced attenuation of 10 HU or less identifies a lipid-rich adenoma
A dedicated washout study now, since attenuation is unreliable when a patient has a known primary
FDG PET-CT, since a nodule of this size in a patient with cancer has to be presumed a metastasis
Percutaneous biopsy, since histology is the way to separate an adenoma from a metastasis at this size
quiz.explain: The 10 HU rule is one of the most dependable numbers in body imaging: a homogeneous adrenal nodule measuring 10 HU or less on a true unenhanced acquisition is a lipid-rich adenoma, with a specificity around 98 per cent, and that holds in a patient with a known malignancy. Adrenal metastases do not contain intracytoplasmic lipid. The limitation is sensitivity, not specificity, since roughly 30 per cent of adenomas are lipid-poor and measure above 10 HU, which is why a higher value does not mean cancer. Measure properly: place the region of interest over about two-thirds of the lesion, away from the edges, on a genuine unenhanced series rather than a low-dose localiser. Then remember the part imaging does not answer, which is whether the adenoma secretes anything.

quiz.prompt: A 2.4 cm right adrenal nodule is homogeneous and measures 26 HU on the unenhanced series. The patient is normotensive, has no known malignancy, and the nodule was found on a CT for abdominal pain. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Endocrine assessment and an individualized additional imaging plan, such as chemical-shift MRI, with the selected framework stated
choices: Endocrine assessment and an individualized additional imaging plan, such as chemical-shift MRI, with the selected framework stated
A repeat unenhanced CT in twelve months, since attenuation just above 10 HU can be watched
FDG PET-CT, since attenuation above 10 HU makes a cortical carcinoma the leading diagnosis
Percutaneous biopsy, the usual next test once an adrenal nodule measures more than 10 HU
quiz.explain: A homogeneous 26 HU lesion is indeterminate by unenhanced attenuation. ESE/ENSAT 2023 supports expert discussion and additional imaging chosen for the question and local expertise. The Seow 2025 proposal questions washout for true incidentalomas. Neither framework makes historical washout thresholds a definitive adenoma diagnosis, and endocrine function remains a separate assessment.

quiz.prompt: A 5 cm right mass is confirmed to arise from the adrenal and is predominantly macroscopic fat (minus 45 HU), with small strands of soft tissue. There is no calcification, invasion or symptom attributable to it. What does the imaging support, and what remains separate?
quiz.answer: A fat-predominant adrenal lesion compatible with myelolipoma; assess discordant components and clinical/endocrine context separately
choices: A fat-predominant adrenal lesion compatible with myelolipoma; assess discordant components and clinical/endocrine context separately
A lipid-rich adenoma: the negative attenuation reflects the intracytoplasmic lipid these tumours contain
An adrenal liposarcoma: fat within an adrenal mass of this size should be presumed malignant until proved
A retroperitoneal teratoma: fat-containing adrenal lesions arise from germ cell rests displaced in development
quiz.explain: Confirmed adrenal origin and predominant macroscopic fat support myelolipoma. Small fat foci alone are not diagnostic: other adrenal or retroperitoneal tumours may contain fat. Whole-lesion soft tissue, haemorrhage, mass effect and clinical context affect assessment; no blanket endocrine or management clearance follows from fat alone.

quiz.prompt: A patient taking warfarin presents with right upper quadrant pain. CT shows a new 4 cm right adrenal mass measuring 58 HU on the unenhanced series, with stranding in the surrounding fat and no measurable enhancement on the portal venous phase. What do you report and advise?
quiz.answer: Adrenal haematoma: repeat imaging in two to three months to confirm it shrinks and conceals no underlying mass
choices: Adrenal haematoma: repeat imaging in two to three months to confirm it shrinks and conceals no underlying mass
Lipid-poor adenoma: proceed to a dedicated washout study during this admission to confirm the diagnosis
Adrenal metastasis: the high attenuation reflects tumour cellularity, so staging should be completed now
Adrenocortical carcinoma: the size and the density together make a primary cortical tumour most likely here
quiz.explain: High unenhanced attenuation, absent enhancement and periadrenal stranding in a patient who is anticoagulated, septic, stressed or recently injured is adrenal haemorrhage. It is more often right-sided after trauma, where the short adrenal vein and compression against the cava do the damage. The reason it always needs follow-up is that tumours bleed: phaeochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma and metastases can all present as a haematoma, and only resolution over two to three months proves there was nothing underneath. Washout figures are meaningless in a lesion that does not enhance, so the study offered in the second option would produce numbers you could not use. Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage is a different emergency, since it can cause acute adrenal insufficiency and needs treating as such before anyone worries about the imaging follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A 7 cm left adrenal mass is heterogeneous with central necrosis and a few flecks of calcification, enhances avidly and irregularly, and a tongue of enhancing tissue extends into the left renal vein. The patient has no known primary malignancy. What follows?
quiz.answer: Urgent expert multidisciplinary assessment, endocrine work-up and staging for a suspicious adrenal mass with venous extension
choices: Urgent expert multidisciplinary assessment, endocrine work-up and staging for a suspicious adrenal mass with venous extension
Arrange a washout study, because a high washout figure would settle matters and spare an operation
Arrange interval imaging at six months, since heterogeneity by itself is not enough to act on here
Arrange image-guided biopsy first, since histology should precede any discussion of adrenal surgery
quiz.explain: A large heterogeneous mass with enhancing venous extension is suspicious, including for adrenocortical carcinoma, but imaging is not histological proof. Expert staging and endocrine assessment guide management and surgical planning. Routine biopsy is not the default for suspected adrenocortical carcinoma.

quiz.prompt: A patient with clinical Cushing syndrome and a raised plasma ACTH has CT showing both adrenal glands diffusely thickened, with smooth limbs, the normal adreniform shape preserved and no discrete nodule on either side. What do you report, and what should be imaged next?
quiz.answer: Bilateral hyperplasia driven by excess ACTH: image the pituitary, and the chest if an ectopic source is suspected
choices: Bilateral hyperplasia driven by excess ACTH: image the pituitary, and the chest if an ectopic source is suspected
Bilateral adenomas below the resolution of CT: proceed to adrenal vein sampling to find the dominant side
Bilateral metastases: diffuse enlargement of both glands is their usual appearance, so seek an occult primary
Bilateral haemorrhage: gland enlargement with a preserved contour is characteristic of bleeding under steroid excess
quiz.explain: Hyperplasia thickens the gland while keeping its shape, so the limbs look plump and smooth, commonly above about 5 mm in width, and the adreniform outline survives. That appearance in the presence of a raised ACTH tells you the adrenals are responding, not driving, and the search moves upstream: a pituitary corticotroph adenoma accounts for the great majority, with ectopic ACTH from a small cell lung cancer or a bronchial carcinoid the main alternative, which is why the chest is imaged when the biochemistry or clinical picture suggests it. If ACTH were suppressed instead, the source would be adrenal, and you would look for a unilateral adenoma, a carcinoma or bilateral macronodular disease. Metastases, by contrast, are discrete nodular masses that distort the gland rather than enlarging it evenly.

quiz.prompt: On a dedicated adrenal CT, a nodule measures 12 HU on the unenhanced series, 78 HU at 60 seconds and 32 HU at 15 minutes. Calculate the absolute percentage washout and state it as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Absolute washout is (78−32)/(78−12)×100 = 69.7%. This arithmetic does not diagnose adenoma. Record matched ROIs and actual acquisition timing; historical cutoffs overlap with phaeochromocytoma and other tumours, and apply only in an explicitly selected clinical framework.

quiz.prompt: An adrenal study was performed without an unenhanced series. The nodule measures 64 HU at 60 seconds and 30 HU at 15 minutes. Calculate the relative percentage washout and state it as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Relative washout is (64−30)/64×100 = 53.1%. Without a true unenhanced acquisition, absolute washout and unenhanced lipid criteria cannot be calculated. Historical relative 40% and the cautious ESE/ENSAT >58% evidence are different criteria; neither is a standalone histological diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: On chemical shift MRI an adrenal nodule has a mean signal of 480 on the in-phase images and 336 on the opposed-phase images, while the spleen is unchanged between the two. Calculate the adrenal signal intensity index as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The signal intensity index is the in-phase signal minus the opposed-phase signal, divided by the in-phase signal, times one hundred: 480 minus 336, over 480, which is 30.0 per cent. Values above roughly 16.5 per cent indicate intracytoplasmic lipid and therefore an adenoma, and in practice a confident visual drop measured against an internal reference does most of the work. The reference should be the spleen rather than the liver, because a fatty liver also loses signal on opposed-phase images and would mask a genuine adrenal drop. Two caveats to keep. Clear cell renal carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma both contain intracellular lipid, so their adrenal metastases can drop signal and imitate an adenoma. And nodules with high unenhanced CT attenuation rarely show any drop, so a negative result there is uninformative rather than reassuring.

quiz.prompt: An indeterminate 4 cm adrenal mass in a patient with lung cancer is booked for percutaneous biopsy to resolve staging. State what must be done before the needle goes in, and why.
quiz.answer: Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded biochemically first, with plasma free metanephrines or urinary metanephrines, because biopsying an unblocked phaeochromocytoma can precipitate a hypertensive crisis; if it proves to be one, the patient needs alpha blockade before any intervention.
quiz.explain: Before biopsy, establish that the lesion is hormonally inactive (especially exclude phaeochromocytoma), remains indeterminate on imaging and that histology would alter clinical management. Specialist planning is required; suspected adrenocortical carcinoma is not a routine biopsy indication.

quiz.prompt: Give two circumstances in which you should refuse to call an adrenal nodule an adenoma on the strength of its washout figures, and say what you would rely on instead.
quiz.answer: Washout is unreliable in hypervascular lesions, since phaeochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma and metastases from renal or hepatocellular carcinoma can all wash out above the thresholds, and it is unreliable when the nodule barely enhances, because a small enhancement value makes the percentage unstable; rely instead on the unenhanced attenuation, chemical shift MRI, biochemistry, PET or interval stability.
quiz.explain: Hypervascular tumours may show adenoma-like washout. Small enhancement denominators amplify measurement noise, and heterogeneous masses must not be classified from one reassuring component. Actual timing and matched ROIs are essential; follow the selected clinical framework rather than an automatic washout threshold. Unenhanced composition, MRI, endocrine assessment, specialist review or contextual follow-up may answer different parts of the question.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with resistant hypertension and hypokalaemia has a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio. CT shows a 1.1 cm low-attenuation left adrenal nodule and a normal-looking right gland. The surgeon asks whether the left gland can be taken on this basis. State your answer and its reason.
quiz.answer: Not on the CT alone, because non-functioning adenomas are common at this size and the true source may be the other gland or bilateral hyperplasia, so adrenal vein sampling is needed to lateralise aldosterone secretion before adrenalectomy.
quiz.explain: Adrenal incidentalomas are found in around 4 per cent of abdominal CT studies and become commoner with age, so the presence of a small nodule beside a positive biochemical screen does not establish that the nodule is the culprit. Bilateral hyperplasia is a frequent cause of primary aldosteronism and may look normal or near normal on CT, and a genuine aldosteronoma can be smaller than the scanner can resolve. Adrenal vein sampling remains the reference standard for lateralisation and regularly contradicts the CT. The recognised exception is a young patient, usually under 35, with florid biochemistry and an unequivocal unilateral adenoma. This is the general lesson of the adrenal: imaging characterises tissue, while function is a separate question answered by an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, plasma metanephrines and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

quiz.prompt: For the specified historical dedicated washout protocol using a 15-minute delay, arrange its three acquisitions. This is protocol recall, not a recommendation to perform routine incidentaloma washout CT.
quiz.answer: unenhanced portal-venous-60-seconds delayed-15-minutes
quiz.explain: This specified protocol uses unenhanced, approximately 60–75-second enhanced and 15-minute delayed acquisitions. Preserve actual timing and matched ROIs. Other delay protocols exist; thresholds cannot be transferred without validation. ESE/ENSAT notes timing evidence is uncertain, while Seow 2025 proposes abandoning washout in true incidentalomas.

curriculum_modules.title: Airway Disease: Bronchiectasis, Small Airways and the Large Airway

module_contract.goal: Diagnose bronchiectasis on criteria that will survive scrutiny, use distribution and expiratory imaging to work out a cause, distinguish the emphysema subtypes, and assess the large airway for fixed narrowing and for dynamic collapse.

approach.step: Describe the narrowing's length and shape
approach.detail: Focal versus diffuse, and the cross-sectional shape (hourglass, circumferential, horseshoe-sparing-posterior-wall) points to a specific cause before you name one.

approach.step: Take the history into the report
approach.detail: Prior intubation or tracheostomy, radiotherapy field, and systemic disease (relapsing polychondritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, amyloidosis) each produce a recognisable pattern.
A fixed stricture does not change between inspiration and expiration; tracheomalacia and tracheobronchomalacia narrow further, or collapse, on expiration.

approach.step: Characterise a focal airway lesion by tissue
approach.detail: Fat density suggests a hamartoma, a pedunculated lesion suggests a lipoma, a smooth-muscle origin suggests a leiomyoma; an irregular invasive mass suggests squamous cell carcinoma, submucosal spread suggests adenoid cystic carcinoma, a well-defined hypervascular lesion suggests carcinoid.

approach.step: Turn to the small airways separately
approach.detail: Assess for mosaic attenuation on the inspiratory series, then confirm air trapping with a matched expiratory series — the two together separate obstructive small-airways disease from an infiltrative process.

classify.name: Large airway disease by pattern
rows: Focal hourglass stricture at the cuff site
Irregular invasive mass; submucosal spread; well-defined hypervascular lesion
Squamous cell carcinoma; adenoid cystic carcinoma; carcinoid
Horseshoe thickening sparing the posterior wall; irregular calcified thickening; circumferential thickening
Relapsing polychondritis; amyloidosis; granulomatosis with polyangiitis

pitfalls: Missing a horseshoe pattern that spares the posterior membranous wall — that distribution is specific for relapsing polychondritis and is easy to mistake for a nonspecific thickened trachea.
Calling any expiratory narrowing tracheomalacia without a true expiratory series — inspiratory technique alone cannot make this diagnosis.
Reporting mosaic attenuation as "infiltrative" without an expiratory series to check for air trapping — the two causes need opposite work-ups.
Attributing a smooth, tapered post-intubation stricture to malignancy because of its location, rather than to the cuff or stoma site and the patient's ventilation history.
