quiz.prompt: On an axial HRCT image the internal diameter of a right lower lobe segmental bronchus is 6.0 mm and the adjacent pulmonary artery measures 4.0 mm. Calculate the broncho-arterial ratio. Answer as a decimal, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Six divided by four is 1.5, so the bronchus is half as wide again as its companion artery and the pair form the signet ring. A ratio above one is the classical criterion, but on its own it over-diagnoses: the ratio rises with age, at altitude, in chronic hypoxaemia and in pulmonary arterial hypoplasia, all of which shrink the artery rather than widen the bronchus, and it rises artefactually on expiratory images and on oblique cuts through a bronchus. The more specific findings are failure of the bronchus to taper over one to two centimetres of its course, and bronchi visible within about a centimetre of the costal pleura or touching the mediastinal pleura. Measure perpendicular to the bronchial axis, and always ask whether the patient has the symptoms to match.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old has a broncho-arterial ratio of about 1.1 in both lower lobes. The bronchi taper normally along their course, none is visible within a centimetre of the costal pleura, and the walls are not thickened. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: The ratio alone is insufficient here and bronchiectasis should not be diagnosed
choices: The ratio alone is insufficient here and bronchiectasis should not be diagnosed
The ratio exceeds one, which establishes cylindrical bronchiectasis in both bases
The ratio suggests traction bronchiectasis and a fibrotic process should be sought
The ratio is diagnostic once an expiratory acquisition has confirmed air trapping
quiz.explain: A mildly raised broncho-arterial ratio in an elderly patient with normal tapering, normal wall thickness and no peripheral bronchial visibility is far more likely to reflect an age-related fall in arterial calibre than a diseased airway. Tapering is the sign to lean on, because it is a property of the bronchus itself rather than of the ratio between two structures. The cost of getting this wrong runs in both directions. Over-calling commits a patient to lifelong airway clearance, sputum surveillance and repeated antibiotic courses, and it anchors every subsequent reader. Under-calling in someone producing sputum daily misses a diagnosis with real treatment. Traction bronchiectasis is a different animal, occurring inside fibrotic lung with reticulation and volume loss around it, and the fibrosis is the finding to report first.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old with poorly controlled asthma has central upper lobe bronchiectasis packed with mucus, and on the unenhanced study some of the mucus plugs are denser than the paraspinal muscle. What should be done next?
quiz.answer: Send total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE, since this pattern suits allergic aspergillosis
choices: Send total IgE and Aspergillus-specific IgE, since this pattern suits allergic aspergillosis
Send sputum for mycobacterial culture, since this pattern suits atypical mycobacterial disease
Send a sweat chloride test and genotype, since this pattern suits late presenting cystic fibrosis
Send immunoglobulin subclasses, since this pattern suits common variable immunodeficiency
quiz.explain: Mucus that is denser than muscle without contrast is high-attenuation mucus, and in a bronchiectatic asthmatic it is close to specific for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, reflecting calcium and metal salts within inspissated secretions. The distribution supports it: central and perihilar bronchiectasis with relatively normal peripheral airways, upper zone predominant, sometimes with finger-in-glove opacities from impacted branching bronchi. Confirmation is serological, resting on a raised total IgE with Aspergillus-specific IgE or immediate skin reactivity in a patient with asthma or cystic fibrosis, and treatment is corticosteroids with or without itraconazole. The alternatives all cause bronchiectasis with a different distribution: cystic fibrosis is upper zone but diffuse with hyperinflation, mycobacterial disease favours the middle lobe and lingula with tree-in-bud nodules, and immunoglobulin deficiency favours the lower zones with chronic sinus disease.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old lifelong non-smoking woman has cylindrical bronchiectasis confined to the right middle lobe and the lingula, with clusters of tree-in-bud nodules in the same regions. Say what you suspect and what would confirm it.
quiz.answer: This nodular bronchiectatic distribution suggests nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease, usually Mycobacterium avium complex. Confirmation needs repeated sputum samples sent for mycobacterial culture, or lavage culture if she cannot expectorate.
quiz.explain: Cylindrical bronchiectasis with tree-in-bud nodularity restricted to the middle lobe and lingula in an older, slim, non-smoking woman is the nodular bronchiectatic form of nontuberculous mycobacterial disease. Tree-in-bud tells you the small airways are filled, so the process is spreading endobronchially, and the same appearance occurs in aspiration and in post-infective bronchiolitis. The distinction matters because treatment is a multi-drug regimen lasting a year or more beyond culture conversion, with real toxicity, so imaging alone never starts it. The accepted microbiological requirement is two separate positive sputum cultures, or one positive bronchial lavage, alongside compatible symptoms and imaging. The other form, cavitary fibronodular disease in the upper lobes, occurs in older men with emphysema and looks much more like tuberculosis.

quiz.prompt: A patient two years after lung transplantation is breathless with a falling FEV1, and the inspiratory CT looks nearly normal apart from mild bronchial wall thickening. Say what acquisition you would add and what it would show if the small airways are the problem.
quiz.answer: Add an expiratory acquisition. Lobular or geographic regions that fail to increase in attenuation on expiration, giving mosaic attenuation with air trapping alongside bronchial dilatation, indicate constrictive bronchiolitis, the imaging counterpart of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome.
quiz.explain: Constrictive bronchiolitis narrows and obliterates membranous bronchioles that are below the resolution of CT, so the inspiratory study is often unremarkable and the disease is diagnosed by what the lung fails to do rather than by what it shows. On expiration the affected lobules cannot empty and stay lucent while normal lung becomes denser, producing sharply bordered geographic air trapping, usually with bronchial wall thickening and eventually bronchial dilatation. The causes are worth carrying: chronic lung allograft dysfunction, chronic graft-versus-host disease after stem cell transplantation, rheumatoid arthritis, post-viral disease in children, and inhalational injury. Check the expiratory series is genuine by looking for forward bowing of the posterior tracheal membrane, and discount the small volume of physiological trapping seen in dependent lung, the lingula and the superior segments of the lower lobes.

quiz.prompt: A 42-year-old who has never smoked has uniform low attenuation with a strikingly sparse vascular tree in both lower lobes, rather than discrete punched-out holes. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Measure the alpha-1 antitrypsin level, because basal panlobular destruction suggests deficiency
choices: Measure the alpha-1 antitrypsin level, because basal panlobular destruction suggests deficiency
Measure the diffusing capacity alone, because basal low attenuation is a normal finding at this age
Arrange bronchoscopy urgently, because basal low attenuation of this kind indicates large airway obstruction
Arrange a ventilation study first, because basal low attenuation reflects redistribution of lung perfusion
quiz.explain: The three emphysema subtypes separate on distribution and on what is destroyed. Centrilobular emphysema destroys the lobular core, gives discrete lucencies with the central artery still visible as a dot, and is upper zone predominant in smokers. Panlobular emphysema destroys the whole lobule uniformly, favours the lower zones, and is the pattern of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, also seen after intravenous methylphenidate use. Paraseptal emphysema sits subpleurally and along the septa. Panlobular disease is the one most often missed, because there is no hole to point at: the give-away is simplification of the vascular tree, an oddly empty-looking lower lobe. Testing changes several things at once, since deficiency brings augmentation therapy into play, makes smoking cessation urgent, prompts family screening, and calls for liver surveillance.

quiz.prompt: A tall 24-year-old man presents with a second right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax. CT after drainage shows a single row of thin-walled subpleural lucencies in both apices, with normal lung between them and elsewhere. What is the significance?
quiz.answer: Apical paraseptal emphysema and blebs, which carry a real risk of further pneumothorax
choices: Apical paraseptal emphysema and blebs, which carry a real risk of further pneumothorax
Apical honeycombing from fibrosis, which calls for a full interstitial disease work-up
Apical cavitating infection, which calls for sputum culture before any further imaging
Apical cystic lung disease, which calls for screening for lymphangioleiomyomatosis now
quiz.explain: Paraseptal emphysema occupies the subpleural lung and the lung along the interlobular septa, and on CT it is a single layer of lucencies with thin or barely visible walls, favouring the apices and the paramediastinal regions. It is the substrate for apical blebs and bullae in tall young men, and the reason this matters is recurrence: after a second ipsilateral pneumothorax the risk of a third is high enough that surgical pleurodesis with bullectomy is usually offered, so the CT finding feeds directly into an operative decision. Do not confuse the single subpleural row with honeycombing, which is stacked in layers, thick walled, basal and surrounded by reticulation. Cystic lung diseases such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis give round, walled cysts distributed throughout the lung rather than only under the pleura.

quiz.prompt: On a dynamic expiratory CT the tracheal lumen at a fixed level measures 240 mm squared at end-inspiration and 96 mm squared during forced expiration. Calculate the percentage reduction in cross-sectional area. Answer as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The lumen falls by 144 of 240 square millimetres, which is 60.0 per cent. The conventional threshold for tracheobronchomalacia is expiratory collapse of more than half the cross-sectional area, and it is best demonstrated on dynamic imaging during forced expiration or coughing rather than on a static end-expiratory acquisition, which underestimates it. Two qualifications keep this honest. Healthy volunteers can exceed fifty per cent on forced expiration, which is why some groups use a higher cut-off and why nobody should make the diagnosis without symptoms to match. And malacia frequently coexists with other airway disease: it is common in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, after prolonged intubation or tracheostomy, and in relapsing polychondritis, and it is a recurring explanation for the patient whose obstruction does not respond to bronchodilators.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have tracheal narrowing with wall thickening that at first glance looks circumferential. Say which single feature of the tracheal wall you would use to separate relapsing polychondritis from tracheal amyloidosis, and what that feature reflects.
quiz.answer: Look at the posterior membranous wall. Relapsing polychondritis thickens the anterior and lateral walls and spares the posterior membrane because the disease attacks cartilage, whereas amyloid is deposited circumferentially, involves the posterior membrane and often calcifies.
quiz.explain: The posterior wall of the trachea has no cartilage, so it sorts the differential of tracheal narrowing into two groups. The cartilage diseases spare it: relapsing polychondritis, which thickens and later collapses the anterolateral wall, and tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica, which studs the same walls with calcified submucosal nodules. The infiltrative and inflammatory diseases involve it: amyloidosis, which thickens the wall circumferentially with calcification, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, classically as a short subglottic stenosis, and post-intubation or post-tracheostomy stenosis. Relapsing polychondritis also declares itself outside the chest, in auricular and nasal chondritis and audiovestibular symptoms, and airway involvement drives its mortality, so add dynamic expiratory imaging: fixed narrowing and malacia often coexist, and only the second explains sudden collapse on coughing.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an intrathoracic trachea whose coronal diameter is half its sagittal diameter, with normal wall thickness and a normal extrathoracic segment. What should the report state?
quiz.answer: A sabre-sheath configuration related to COPD, needing no specific airway intervention
choices: A sabre-sheath configuration related to COPD, needing no specific airway intervention
A fixed tracheal stenosis from prior intubation, needing bronchoscopic reassessment
Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica, needing biopsy of the submucosal nodules
Extrinsic compression by mediastinal fibrosis, needing contrast-enhanced reassessment
quiz.explain: Side-to-side narrowing with preservation of the front-to-back diameter, confined to the intrathoracic trachea and sparing the cervical segment, with a coronal to sagittal ratio of two thirds or less and a normal wall thickness, is the sabre-sheath trachea of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is a marker of the disease rather than a lesion needing treatment, and reporting it as a stenosis sends the patient for an unnecessary bronchoscopy. The alternatives look different: post-intubation stenosis is a short hourglass segment at cuff or stoma level and often involves the cervical trachea, osteochondroplastica produces nodular anterolateral wall thickening that spares the posterior membrane, and extrinsic compression displaces as well as narrows. Do look for coexisting malacia, which is common in the same patients and does change management.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old had a witnessed choking episode. The inspiratory frontal film looks symmetrical, but on the expiratory film the right lung remains lucent and large while the left deflates, and the mediastinum shifts to the left. What does this indicate?
quiz.answer: Ball-valve obstruction of the right main bronchus with air trapping on that side
choices: Ball-valve obstruction of the right main bronchus with air trapping on that side
Complete obstruction of the right main bronchus with collapse of the right lung
A left-sided pneumothorax decompressing across the anterior junction on expiry
A normal paediatric expiratory film, since the mediastinum swings in small children
quiz.explain: Most inhaled foreign bodies in children are organic and radiolucent, so the radiograph is read for their effect rather than for the object. The commonest effect is obstructive hyperinflation, not collapse: the object acts as a ball valve, letting air past on inspiration when the airway widens and trapping it on expiration when the airway narrows. So the affected lung fails to deflate, stays lucent and large, and pushes the mediastinum away from it on the expiratory film. The right main bronchus is the more frequent site because it is wider and more vertical. In a child who cannot cooperate with expiration, lateral decubitus films substitute: the dependent lung should deflate, and a dependent lung that stays inflated implicates that side. A normal film never excludes a foreign body.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these investigations for a clinically stable child with a suspected inhaled foreign body in order of increasing invasiveness, as you would escalate when each proves unhelpful.
quiz.answer: inspiratory-radiograph expiratory-radiograph low-dose-CT rigid-bronchoscopy
quiz.explain: The ladder exists to keep children out of a general anaesthetic they do not need. A frontal inspiratory radiograph comes first and may show a radio-opaque object, collapse or hyperinflation. An expiratory film, or lateral decubitus films in a child too young to cooperate, is added when the inspiratory film is unremarkable, because air trapping is a functional sign and only appears on expiration. Low-dose CT sits next: it can show a non-opaque object directly and resolve the equivocal case at a modest dose. Rigid bronchoscopy is last on this ladder because it needs anaesthesia, but it is also the only step that treats as well as diagnoses. The ladder is for the stable, equivocal child; with a witnessed choking episode and unilateral signs, the child goes straight to bronchoscopy.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old with a lifelong productive cough has bronchiectasis concentrated in the middle lobe and both lower lobes, chronic pansinusitis, and dextrocardia with a right-sided gastric bubble. What should be pursued?
quiz.answer: Testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia, since situs inversus accompanies this distribution
choices: Testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia, since situs inversus accompanies this distribution
Testing for cystic fibrosis, since sinus disease accompanies this pattern of bronchiectasis
Testing for immunoglobulin deficiency, since sinus disease dominates this clinical picture
Testing for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, since lower zone disease dominates this picture
quiz.explain: Bronchiectasis in the middle lobe and lower lobes, chronic sinus disease and situs inversus is primary ciliary dyskinesia, and the combination with situs inversus is Kartagener syndrome, present in roughly half of these patients because embryonic nodal cilia determine laterality. Confirmation runs through nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy of ciliary beat and genetic testing. Distribution does most of the sorting among the causes of diffuse bronchiectasis: cystic fibrosis is upper zone predominant and diffuse with hyperinflation and mucus plugging, and presents far earlier; antibody deficiency such as common variable immunodeficiency gives lower zone bronchiectasis with sinus disease but no laterality defect, and is worth excluding in any unexplained case because immunoglobulin replacement changes the course. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes basal emphysema rather than bronchiectasis.

quiz.prompt: An anal squamous carcinoma measures 3.4 cm in its longest plane, without adjacent-organ invasion. Which T category fits?
choices: T1
T2
T3
T4
quiz.answer: T2
quiz.explain: Anal T category depends principally on maximum dimension until adjacent-organ invasion establishes T4. Use the longest dimension across planes and state the staging edition.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm anal tumour extends into the external sphincter without invading another organ. What should the report do?
choices: Call T4 solely because the external sphincter is involved
Omit the sphincter because it cannot affect planning
Describe sphincter involvement without automatically assigning T4
Replace the maximum dimension with wall thickness
quiz.answer: Describe sphincter involvement without automatically assigning T4
quiz.explain: Sphincter and pelvic-floor mapping informs treatment planning, but sphincter involvement by itself is not adjacent-organ invasion for anal T4 classification.

quiz.prompt: Suspicious inguinal nodes accompany an anal canal primary. Which statement is correct?
choices: They automatically represent distant metastases
Only their total number matters
They are irrelevant below the dentate line
Their station must be recorded as regional nodal disease
quiz.answer: Their station must be recorded as regional nodal disease
quiz.explain: Anal nodal staging depends on involved stations. Record side, compartment, size and morphology rather than importing the rectal-cancer node-count rule.

quiz.prompt: A pelvic MRI maps the anal tumour well, but the referral asks for complete staging. What remains necessary?
choices: Assessment for disease beyond the pelvic MRI coverage
No additional assessment because MRI excludes all metastases
Replacing MRI with a lumbar radiograph
Using tumour length to estimate lung involvement
quiz.answer: Assessment for disease beyond the pelvic MRI coverage
quiz.explain: Local MRI and distant staging answer different questions. Chest and abdominal assessment and, where indicated, metabolic imaging complement the local examination.

quiz.prompt: Soon after chemoradiotherapy, the tumour bed remains thickened but has decreased substantially. What is the most defensible report?
choices: Certain treatment failure from thickness alone
Describe interval change, diffusion findings and treatment interval
Complete response solely because the tumour is smaller
No response assessment until a new tumour appears
quiz.answer: Describe interval change, diffusion findings and treatment interval
quiz.explain: Early inflammatory change and fibrosis complicate interpretation. Integrate morphology, diffusion, comparison and clinical timing; persistent thickness alone does not establish viable tumour.

quiz.prompt: An anal tumour measures 1.8 cm axially, 3.1 cm sagittally and 5.6 cm coronally, without adjacent-organ invasion. Which measurement governs the size-based T category, and what category does it support?
quiz.answer: Use the longest reproducible tumour dimension across the available planes: 5.6 cm. This supports a size-based T3 category. Record the plane and all useful dimensions, and separately describe sphincter, pelvic-floor and adjacent-organ relationships rather than allowing an axial measurement alone to understate extent.
quiz.explain: The largest dimension may be craniocaudal. A reproducible measurement and anatomical description make the stage auditable.

quiz.prompt: A draft anal MRI report imports a rectal-cancer template and assigns the nodal category solely from the number of abnormal nodes. Explain how you would repair the report.
quiz.answer: Keep the observed nodes but reorganise them by anatomical station and side, including regional inguinal and pelvic stations and any nonregional nodes. Describe size and suspicious morphology, then use the anal-cancer staging system and named edition for the category. Do not substitute the rectal node-count rule.
quiz.explain: A reporting template carries assumptions from its disease. Reusing its layout is reasonable only after checking that its classification rules apply.

quiz.prompt: MRI shows an anal lesion extending from 2 to 6 o'clock through the internal and external sphincters. There is no adjacent-organ invasion. Which details should survive in the impression even though they do not automatically make this T4?
quiz.answer: Preserve the circumferential involvement, craniocaudal extent and which sphincter layers or pelvic-floor structures are involved. State any extension to perianal skin or rectum and the absence of demonstrated adjacent-organ invasion. Assign the T category from the appropriate size and organ-invasion criteria, independently of this anatomical map.
quiz.explain: The category compresses information. Treatment planning still needs the location and structural relationships that the category does not encode.

quiz.prompt: After treatment, an anal tumour bed is smaller and predominantly low signal on T2, but a focal area remains indeterminate on diffusion imaging. How would you describe response without forcing a binary result?
quiz.answer: Describe the interval reduction and fibrotic appearance, then localise and measure the remaining indeterminate focus. State the diffusion limitation or concern, treatment interval, and change in regional nodes. Give a calibrated assessment of possible residual disease and recommend correlation with the clinical response assessment rather than declaring either complete response or failure from one sequence.
quiz.explain: Response reporting should explain both the favourable change and the unresolved evidence. This is more useful than concealing uncertainty inside a category.

quiz.prompt: The pelvic MRI is degraded by motion and does not reliably separate tumour from the anterior adjacent organ. A previous report described a preserved plane. Explain how comparison should influence, but not override, the current conclusion.
quiz.answer: The prior examination supplies a baseline but cannot prove that the current plane remains intact. State that anterior organ involvement is indeterminate because of motion, describe any assessable interval change, and identify the unanswered staging question. Further targeted imaging or multidisciplinary correlation may be needed before treatment decisions depend on that boundary.
quiz.explain: Comparison cannot repair missing current information. Carrying forward a previously normal relationship as a present finding creates unsupported certainty.

curriculum_modules.title: Ankle Fractures and the Painful Foot

module_contract.goal: Decide who needs an ankle or foot radiograph, classify an ankle fracture in the terms that predict instability, and work up the tendon, midfoot and heel causes of a painful foot.

approach.step: Find the fibular fracture and place it against the syndesmosis
approach.detail: Below it, at it, or above it. That single decision is the Weber letter and it drives everything after.
A medial malleolar fracture, a medial avulsion, or a widened medial clear space all mean the same thing — the medial restraint has failed.

approach.step: Read the posterior side on the lateral view
approach.detail: A posterior malleolar (tertius) fragment is a linear lucency or density that is easy to walk past. As an isolated finding it is very uncommon, so if you see one look again at the fibula.
Each ring of injury you can see implies the ones before it. Stage 1 lesions are usually invisible but assumed present once a higher stage is found.
Weber A stage 2, Weber B stages 3–4 and Weber C stages 3–4 are unstable. Two or more rings broken means unstable.

approach.step: Check you have the whole fibula
approach.detail: An isolated medial or isolated posterior malleolar fracture with no lateral fracture means a Maisonneuve until the proximal fibula has been imaged.

measure.how: On the mortise view, between the medial malleolus and the talus; normally equal to the tibiotalar distance above the dome.
measure.cutoff: Should not exceed 4 mm; ≥ 6 mm requires medial collateral disruption

measure.how: From the medial border of the fibula to the lateral border of the posterior tibia, measured 1 cm above the tibial plafond.
AP with the foot internally rotated until the lateral malleolus sits at the same height as the medial malleolus.
Foot position at the moment of injury, inferred from the pattern.

classify.name: Weber and Lauge-Hansen — the fibula against the syndesmosis
rows: Below the syndesmosis, which stays intact
1 lateral collateral rupture or avulsion below the syndesmosis · 2 oblique medial malleolar fracture (uncommon)
At the level of the syndesmosis, with partial or total rupture. About 60% of ankle fractures
1 anterior syndesmosis ruptures · 2 oblique fibular fracture · 3 posterior syndesmosis ruptures or posterior malleolar fracture · 4 medial malleolar avulsion or deltoid rupture
Above the syndesmosis, which is completely torn. About 20% of ankle fractures, and the hardest to diagnose

1 medial collateral rupture or medial malleolar avulsion · 2 anterior syndesmosis ruptures · 3 fibular fracture above the syndesmosis (Maisonneuve if high) · 4 posterior syndesmosis rupture or posterior malleolar avulsion
classify.note: Exorotation accounts for 75–80% of ankle injuries, so SER/Weber B is what you will mostly be reading. Weber A runs medially last; Weber B and C run medially first or last depending on supination or pronation — that is the whole difference.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Ankle radiographs: AP, mortise ([n]° endorotation) and lateral.

FINDINGS
Fibula: [no fracture / fracture at [level], described against the syndesmosis as infra- / trans- / suprasyndesmotic]. [Oblique / transverse / spiral], [displaced n mm / undisplaced].
Medial malleolus: [intact / fracture — transverse avulsion or oblique].
Posterior malleolus: [intact / fragment on the lateral view, occupying approximately [n]% of the articular surface].
Medial clear space: [n] mm.
Tibiofibular clear space 1 cm above the plafond: [n] mm.
Talar dome and shift: [congruent / talus displaced [direction]].
Proximal fibula: [imaged and normal / not imaged].

IMPRESSION
1. Weber [A/B/C], Lauge-Hansen [SA / SER / PER / PA] stage [1–4].
2. [Stable / unstable] — [number] of the four rings disrupted.
3. [Maisonneuve suspected: proximal fibular radiographs required.]
pitfalls: Missing the posterior malleolus. It is a faint line or a band of increased density on the lateral view, and it is almost never isolated — finding one should send you back to the fibula.

Stopping at the ankle in a Weber C pattern. A high fibular fracture is invisible on an ankle series; an isolated medial or isolated posterior malleolar fracture is a Maisonneuve until the whole fibula has been seen.
Calling a normal study because the malleoli are intact. Medial swelling with no visible fracture is still a Maisonneuve pattern.
Reading the medial clear space off the AP rather than the mortise view. Without 15–25° of endorotation the malleoli overlap the talus and the space is unmeasurable.
Reporting the Weber letter and stopping. The letter is the level; the stage is the stability, and the stage is what the surgeon acts on.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old inverted her ankle stepping off a kerb. She is tender over the base of the fifth metatarsal and describes midfoot pain. There is no tenderness over either malleolus, and she walked four steps in the department without help. What imaging follows from the Ottawa rules?
quiz.answer: Radiograph the foot but not the ankle, since only the midfoot criterion is met
choices: Radiograph the foot but not the ankle, since only the midfoot criterion is met
Radiograph the ankle but not the foot, since weight bearing has been preserved
Request no radiograph at all, because she managed to take four steps unaided
Radiograph the foot and ankle together with a whole-length view of the fibula
quiz.explain: The Ottawa rules are two separate rules sharing a structure. A foot radiograph is indicated when there is midfoot pain plus bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or at the navicular, or an inability to take four steps both at the time of injury and in the department. An ankle radiograph is indicated when there is malleolar pain plus bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus over its distal 6 cm, or the same weight-bearing failure. Here the fifth metatarsal base is tender with midfoot pain, so the foot rule fires and the ankle rule does not. The rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures, which is why a negative result is safe to act on, but their specificity is low, so a positive result simply means imaging is justified rather than that a fracture is likely.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has a spiral fracture of the distal fibula beginning at the level of the tibial plafond. The medial malleolus is intact but the medial clear space measures 6 mm on the mortise view. How should this be reported and what does it imply?
quiz.answer: Weber B with medial-sided injury, so the ankle is unstable and needs fixation
choices: Weber B with medial-sided injury, so the ankle is unstable and needs fixation
Weber B with an intact deltoid ligament, so a walking cast will be sufficient
Weber A, below the syndesmosis, and therefore a stable avulsion-type injury
Weber C, above the syndesmosis, with an obligate proximal fibular fracture
quiz.explain: Weber classifies by the level of the fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis. Type A is below it, typically a transverse avulsion from supination and adduction, with the syndesmosis intact and the injury usually stable. Type B is at the level of the syndesmosis, typically a spiral fracture from external rotation, and stability is the open question. Type C is above it, and the syndesmosis is torn up to the level of the fracture. The Weber grade alone does not settle treatment for a type B: what settles it is the medial side. A widened medial clear space, above about 4 mm and wider than the superior joint space, means the deltoid ligament has failed, giving a bimalleolar-equivalent injury with a talus free to shift. That combination is unstable and goes for fixation, whereas an isolated Weber B with an intact medial side can be treated non-operatively.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these injuries in the order that the Lauge-Hansen sequence predicts for a supination and external rotation ankle injury.
quiz.answer: anterior-tibiofibular-ligament spiral-fibular-fracture posterior-malleolus medial-malleolus
quiz.explain: Lauge-Hansen names the position of the foot first and the direction of the deforming force second, and each mechanism fails in a fixed order, so the classification is genuinely predictive rather than merely descriptive. Supination with external rotation is the commonest pattern. Stage 1 tears the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, sometimes avulsing the Tillaux-Chaput or Wagstaffe fragment. Stage 2 produces the characteristic spiral fibular fracture running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior at the level of the plafond. Stage 3 involves the posterior structures, either the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament or a posterior malleolar fragment. Stage 4 completes the ring medially, with a transverse medial malleolar fracture or deltoid rupture. The practical value is that finding a late stage obliges you to look for the earlier ones, and finding an early stage tells you which structures to scrutinise before calling the ankle stable.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks which radiographic measurements you use to judge the syndesmosis on ankle films. Give them and say where they are taken.
quiz.answer: Measured 1 cm above the plafond, the tibiofibular clear space should be under 6 mm on both anteroposterior and mortise views, tibiofibular overlap should be present, and the medial clear space should be under 4 mm and no wider than the superior joint space.
quiz.explain: All three syndesmotic measurements are taken at the same level, 1 cm proximal to the tibial plafond, and they are read together rather than singly. The tibiofibular clear space, the gap between the lateral border of the posterior tibial malleolus and the medial border of the fibula, is the most reliable because it varies least with rotation of the limb; under 6 mm is normal. Tibiofibular overlap is generous on the anteroposterior view and much narrower on the mortise view, and it disappears as the syndesmosis opens, but it is rotation-sensitive so a lone abnormal value warrants a repeat with correct positioning. The medial clear space reports the talus rather than the syndesmosis itself. Normal static films do not exclude a dynamic syndesmotic injury, so external rotation stress views or weight-bearing CT are the next step when the clinical suspicion is high.

quiz.prompt: A 35-year-old has a transverse medial malleolar fracture with a widened medial clear space. The ankle series shows no fibular fracture at all, and on re-examination the patient is tender high over the proximal calf. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Image the whole fibula; a proximal fracture with syndesmotic rupture is likely
choices: Image the whole fibula; a proximal fracture with syndesmotic rupture is likely
Repeat the ankle series in ten days to look for an occult distal fibular fracture
Treat as an isolated medial malleolar injury in a below-knee walking cast
Arrange an MRI of the ankle first to assess the deltoid before further radiographs
quiz.explain: The ankle behaves as a ring, and a ring rarely breaks in only one place. A medial injury with a widened mortise and no lateral fracture at the ankle means the force escaped proximally, and that is the Maisonneuve pattern: the extreme of the pronation and external rotation mechanism, in which the interosseous membrane and syndesmosis tear from the ankle upwards to a spiral fracture of the proximal fibula, often near the neck. It is missed whenever the radiograph is coned to the ankle, which is why palpating the whole leg and imaging the full length of the fibula is the standing rule in any medial-sided injury without a lateral fracture. It matters because the syndesmosis needs stabilisation and the fracture itself may need nothing, and because the common peroneal nerve runs around the fibular neck and can be injured.

quiz.prompt: After a forced inversion injury, a 28-year-old has persistent ankle pain. MRI shows a shallow, wafer-shaped osteochondral fragment at the anterolateral corner of the talar dome with a thin line of fluid signal along its deep surface. What is the correct characterisation?
quiz.answer: A lateral talar dome lesion, typically traumatic, shallow and prone to displace
choices: A lateral talar dome lesion, typically traumatic, shallow and prone to displace
A medial talar dome lesion, typically atraumatic, deeper and cup-shaped in profile
A subchondral insufficiency fracture of the talus in a low bone density patient
An accessory ossicle below the lateral malleolus of no clinical consequence here
quiz.explain: Talar dome osteochondral lesions divide by location and behave differently. Lateral lesions sit anterolaterally, are shallow and wafer-shaped, and are nearly always traumatic, following inversion with dorsiflexion; because they are thin and lie at the edge, they detach and displace more readily. Medial lesions sit posteromedially, are deeper and cup-shaped, and are more often atraumatic and degenerative in origin. The stability of the fragment is what the surgeon wants, so look for the features that suggest it has lifted: a continuous high signal line along the interface on fluid-sensitive sequences, subchondral cysts, a breach of the overlying cartilage, or a displaced fragment in the joint. A stable lesion is treated conservatively, whereas an unstable or displaced one goes to fixation, microfracture or grafting. An os subfibulare lies below the malleolus, outside the joint surface, with a corticated margin.

quiz.prompt: A 45-year-old felt a blow to the back of the calf during squash and cannot push off. Ultrasound shows complete discontinuity of the Achilles tendon 5 cm above its calcaneal insertion, with retraction of the torn ends and blood filling the gap. What is the most useful thing to add to the report?
quiz.answer: A mid-substance rupture in the hypovascular zone; state the gap in plantar flexion
choices: A mid-substance rupture in the hypovascular zone; state the gap in plantar flexion
Insertional tendinopathy with a Haglund deformity and retrocalcaneal bursal fluid
A partial tear of the plantaris tendon with the Achilles tendon itself intact
Oedema in the Kager fat pad after a sprain, with a normal underlying tendon
quiz.explain: Most Achilles ruptures occur 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, in the relatively hypovascular watershed segment, which is also where mid-substance tendinopathy sits. The diagnosis is usually clinical; the imaging question is what the treating team cannot get from examination, and that is the size of the gap and whether it closes. Ultrasound answers it dynamically: measure the separation between tendon ends in neutral and again in plantar flexion, because a gap that apposes in equinus supports functional non-operative management in a boot, whereas a gap that stays wide favours repair. Note the tendon ends themselves, since frayed, degenerate ends behave differently from clean ones. Insertional disease is a separate entity at the calcaneus, associated with a Haglund prominence and retrocalcaneal bursitis. An intact plantaris tendon running medially is a common finding beside a ruptured Achilles and should not be mistaken for intact fibres.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old has chronic lateral ankle pain after repeated sprains. Axial images at the level of the lateral malleolus show the peroneus brevis tendon splayed into a C shape wrapped around peroneus longus, with a small avulsed fragment from the posterolateral fibular rim. What do you report?
quiz.answer: A peroneus brevis split tear with injury of the superior peroneal retinaculum
choices: A peroneus brevis split tear with injury of the superior peroneal retinaculum
A peroneus longus tear at the os peroneum with retraction of the proximal stump
A normal low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly sitting within the fibular groove
Tenosynovitis alone, with a trace of physiological fluid within the tendon sheath
quiz.explain: Peroneus brevis lies directly against the fibula in the retromalleolar groove and is the tendon that splits, taking on a C or boomerang shape that partly envelops peroneus longus on axial images. The mechanism is chronic subluxation over the sharp posterolateral fibular ridge, so the superior peroneal retinaculum is nearly always implicated, and a fleck of bone avulsed from the fibular rim is direct evidence of retinacular failure. Report both, because repairing the tendon without addressing the retinaculum invites recurrence. Look also for predisposing anatomy: a low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly extending below the tip of the malleolus, or an accessory peroneus quartus, both of which crowd the groove. A small volume of fluid in the peroneal sheath is normal; fluid that exceeds the calibre of the tendons, or that is present without any tendon abnormality, needs care in interpretation.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old crushed the midfoot when a load fell on it. The non-weight-bearing anteroposterior radiograph shows the medial border of the second metatarsal base lying 2 mm lateral to the medial border of the middle cuneiform, and a tiny bone fragment sits in the interval between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base. What follows?
quiz.answer: A Lisfranc injury; the fleck and malalignment need weight-bearing views or CT
choices: A Lisfranc injury; the fleck and malalignment need weight-bearing views or CT
A normal variation in tarsometatarsal alignment as seen on non-weight-bearing films
An avulsion at the peroneus brevis insertion on the base of the fifth metatarsal
A navicular stress fracture, which would account for the small cortical fragment
quiz.explain: Two alignment rules carry most of the diagnosis. On the anteroposterior view the medial border of the second metatarsal base should line up with the medial border of the middle cuneiform; on the oblique the medial border of the fourth metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the cuboid. The fleck sign, a small avulsed fragment lying in the Lisfranc interval between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal base, represents avulsion of the Lisfranc ligament and is close to pathognomonic. These injuries are missed on a substantial proportion of initial radiographs because a non-weight-bearing film lets a subluxed midfoot reduce itself. Weight-bearing or comparison views unmask it, and CT shows the fracture pattern for planning. Missing it leads to midfoot collapse and post-traumatic arthritis, so the threshold for further imaging should be low.

quiz.prompt: Comparison weight-bearing views are obtained. The gap between the medial cortex of the second metatarsal base and the lateral cortex of the medial cuneiform measures 4.6 mm on the injured side and 1.9 mm on the uninjured side. Report the side-to-side difference in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 4.6 minus 1.9 is 2.7 mm. Absolute widths at the first and second metatarsal interval vary considerably between individuals, which is exactly why the contralateral weight-bearing film is worth the extra exposure: it makes each patient their own control. A side-to-side difference greater than about 2 mm indicates diastasis and an unstable Lisfranc injury, and a difference of 2.7 mm on weight bearing takes this out of the equivocal zone and towards fixation, whether by open reduction and internal fixation or primary arthrodesis. If the patient cannot bear weight, the alternatives are stress views under anaesthesia or weight-bearing CT where available. Report the measurement itself rather than only the conclusion, since the surgical decision hangs on the number and the treating team will want to see it.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old fell three metres from scaffolding and landed on both heels. On the lateral radiograph of the right foot, Bohler angle measures 12 degrees and there is a broadened, sclerotic heel. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A depressed intra-articular fracture; add CT and image the thoracolumbar spine
choices: A depressed intra-articular fracture; add CT and image the thoracolumbar spine
A normal Bohler angle, so no imaging beyond the standard ankle series is needed
An extra-articular anterior process avulsion, treatable in a below-knee cast
A calcaneal stress fracture of the type seen in runners, best assessed with MRI
quiz.explain: Bohler angle is formed by a line from the highest point of the anterior process to the highest point of the posterior facet and a line from that point to the superior aspect of the tuberosity. It normally measures 20 to 40 degrees, and it flattens when the posterior facet is driven downwards, so 12 degrees indicates a depressed intra-articular fracture. Two things follow. CT with coronal reformats defines the posterior facet, which is what the Sanders classification grades and what determines whether the fracture is reconstructable. And the mechanism obliges a wider search: axial loading fractures the calcaneus but also transmits force up the axial skeleton, so bilateral heels and the thoracolumbar spine should be imaged, with spinal fractures accompanying roughly one in ten calcaneal fractures. The critical angle of Gissane, normally about 120 to 145 degrees, is the second measurement to check.

quiz.prompt: On a lateral radiograph, relative to the highest point of the posterior facet, the highest point of the anterior process lies 40 mm anterior to it and 10 mm below it, and the superior point of the tuberosity lies 30 mm posterior to it and 10 mm below it. Bohler angle is the sum of the inclinations of these two lines to the horizontal. Calculate Bohler angle in degrees, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The anterior limb falls 10 mm over a horizontal run of 40 mm, so its inclination is the arctangent of 0.25, which is 14.0 degrees. The posterior limb falls 10 mm over 30 mm, giving the arctangent of 0.333, which is 18.4 degrees. Their sum is 32.5 degrees, comfortably within the normal range of 20 to 40 degrees, so the posterior facet has not been depressed. Working it out this way is worth doing once, because it shows why the measurement behaves as it does: depression of the posterior facet lifts the apex out of the angle and flattens both limbs together, which is why the value falls so sharply with even modest impaction. It also shows why positioning matters, since an obliquely projected lateral distorts both limbs. Compare with the uninjured side when the value sits near the boundary.

quiz.prompt: A 50-year-old runner has heel pain that is worst on the first steps of the morning. Say what you would look for on ultrasound and MRI, and what you would say about the heel spur seen on the radiograph.
quiz.answer: I would look for thickening of the plantar fascia beyond about 4 mm at its calcaneal origin with loss of the normal fibrillar pattern on ultrasound and perifascial oedema on MRI, and I would report the heel spur as an incidental degenerative finding rather than the cause of the pain.
quiz.explain: Plantar fasciitis is a degenerative enthesopathy rather than an inflammatory one, and the imaging findings mirror that. On ultrasound the proximal fascia at the medial calcaneal tuberosity thickens beyond roughly 4 mm, loses its tight fibrillar echotexture, becomes hypoechoic, and may show neovascularity on Doppler. On MRI the same segment thickens with intermediate signal, surrounded by perifascial oedema and often with marrow oedema in the adjacent calcaneus. Compare with the asymptomatic side, since fascial thickness varies. The spur is the finding to be careful with: plantar calcaneal spurs sit within the flexor digitorum brevis origin, occur in a large fraction of asymptomatic feet and are found in only some symptomatic ones, so calling it the cause misleads the patient about what treatment should target. In a young patient with bilateral enthesopathy and erosive change, consider seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

quiz.prompt: On a forefoot MRI there is a small mass in the third intermetatarsal space. Say how you would distinguish a Morton neuroma from intermetatarsal bursitis.
quiz.answer: A Morton neuroma lies plantar to the intermetatarsal ligament, is teardrop-shaped and stays low in signal on T2 because it is fibrous, whereas intermetatarsal bursitis sits dorsal to the ligament and follows fluid, appearing bright on T2.
quiz.explain: Two features separate them and both are visible on a single coronal fluid-sensitive image. Position relative to the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament comes first: a Morton neuroma arises from the plantar digital nerve and therefore sits plantar to the ligament, whereas the intermetatarsal bursa lies dorsal to it. Signal comes second: the lesion is perineural fibrosis rather than a true neuroma, so it stays intermediate to low on T2 and enhances, while a bursa follows fluid and is uniformly bright. Neuromas favour the third intermetatarsal space, then the second. Ultrasound is a good alternative and adds the dynamic Mulder manoeuvre, in which squeezing the forefoot displaces the lesion plantarwards with a palpable and visible click. The two conditions coexist often enough that finding one should prompt a look for the other, since injection targets differ.

module_contract.goal: Protocol and read the CT for suspected acute aortic syndrome, classify what it shows, and say what that commits the patient to.

approach.detail: Read it before the contrast phase — it is how you see intramural haematoma, which the contrast phase can hide.
Type A involves the ascending aorta and arch, with or without the descending aorta. Type B is confined to the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery.
Locate the primary intimal tear and any re-entry point; both change the endovascular plan.

True lumen is smaller, often rimmed by displaced intimal calcification, shows the beak sign, and usually gives origin to the coeliac trunk, SMA and right renal artery. False lumen is larger, circular, outer-curve, delayed-enhancing, may contain thrombus and cobwebs, and usually gives origin to the left renal artery.
For every major branch, say which lumen it arises from and whether it is patent, compromised or occluded.
Correlate branch findings with end-organ appearances — bowel, kidneys, spinal cord, lower limbs.
Rupture, pericardial effusion, coronary ostial involvement, aortic regurgitation, neurological deficit.

measure.cutoff: > 5 cm predicts worse outcome in intramural haematoma

measure.how: Maximum wall thickness on the non-enhanced series.
measure.cutoff: > 2 cm predicts higher mortality; < 2 cm more often regresses (up to 80%)

measure.how: IMH can progress to classic dissection.

rows: Involves the ascending aorta and aortic arch, with or without the descending aorta
Confined to the thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian artery

classify.note: DeBakey (I ascending+arch+descending, II ascending only, III descending only) is superseded by Stanford but still appears in referrals.

modifiers.meaning: The dissection flap itself extends into and narrows the feeding artery. Treated by stenting the branch.
A mobile flap prolapses across the branch ostium like a curtain, without extending into it. Treated by fenestration of the flap.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Non-enhanced series followed by ECG-gated / non-gated CT angiography, [right] arm injection to reduce arch artifact. [n] mL contrast at [n] mL/s.

FINDINGS
Stanford type: [A / B].
Entry tear: [location]. Re-entry: [location / none identified].
True lumen: [location, calibre]. False lumen: [location, calibre, thrombosed / patent].
Branch vessels: coeliac, SMA, renal arteries, iliacs — [lumen of origin, patency] for each.
End-organ perfusion: bowel, kidneys, lower limbs — [normal / malperfusion, specify].
Pericardium: [effusion absent / present, size].
Aortic root: [regurgitation, coronary ostial involvement].
Maximum aortic diameter: [n] mm at [level].
Iliofemoral access vessels: [calibre, calcification, tortuosity] for endovascular planning.

IMPRESSION
1. [Type A / Type B] acute aortic dissection [or intramural haematoma / penetrating ulcer].
2. [Malperfusion present/absent — organ, mechanism].
3. [Complications — rupture, effusion, regurgitation].
4. Recommend: [emergency surgery / medical management with surveillance / endovascular referral].
pitfalls: Skipping the non-enhanced series. Intramural haematoma is a non-enhanced-phase diagnosis and is easy to miss on the angiographic phase alone.
Left arm injection artifact mimicking or obscuring an intimal flap at the arch — inject from the right arm where possible.
Expecting to see the intimal flap in every case — it is visible in only about 70% of dissections; absence does not exclude one.
Confusing a thrombosed false lumen with simple mural thrombus in an aneurysm — look for displaced intimal calcification, which points to dissection.
Reporting the type without the malperfusion and branch-vessel detail the surgeon actually needs to plan the case.

quiz.prompt: A CT for suspected acute aortic syndrome is acquired as three passes through the chest. Put those passes in the order the protocol runs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced arterial delayed
quiz.explain: The unenhanced pass comes first, and it is the one most often skipped to save dose. An intramural haematoma appears on it as a crescent of attenuation higher than the unopacified lumen, and once the lumen holds iodine at three hundred Hounsfield units or more that crescent is invisible against it. The same pass shows displaced intimal calcification, a hyperattenuating crescent within aneurysm thrombus, and fresh blood in the pericardium or mediastinum. Then the arterial acquisition, which is the diagnostic pass and which should be electrocardiogram-gated through the chest so that root pulsation cannot imitate a flap. The delayed pass answers slow-flow questions - a false lumen that fills late, a contained leak, an endoleak after repair - and is the one that can reasonably be dropped when the arterial phase has already answered the question and the dose is worth saving.

quiz.prompt: A non-gated CT angiogram of the chest shows a thin linear lucency in the ascending aorta at the level of the sinotubular junction, running from the right anterior to the left posterior wall, present on two adjacent slices, with no separate enhancing lumen and no extension into the arch. The patient's pain has settled. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Repeat the acquisition with electrocardiogram gating
Report a limited dissection of the ascending aorta
Obtain a delayed acquisition through the aortic root
Report a chronic dissection and arrange surveillance
quiz.answer: Repeat the acquisition with electrocardiogram gating
quiz.explain: Every feature here is the signature of motion rather than disease: the right anterior to left posterior orientation, confinement to the root, presence on only a couple of slices, no second lumen and no extension. The aortic root swings through systole, and an ungated helical acquisition catches it in different positions on adjacent rotations, producing a line that mimics a flap almost exactly. Gating freezes it, and the repeat is cheap against the alternative, which is sending a well patient to sternotomy. A true flap runs over a length of aorta, separates two lumens that enhance differently, and usually extends beyond the root; it should also have a correlate on the unenhanced series in the form of displaced calcification or mural haematoma. Where gating is unavailable, demand that the line be reproducible over more slices, and consider transoesophageal echocardiography, which is not troubled by this artefact at all.

quiz.prompt: CT shows an entry tear 3 cm beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery, with the flap extending distally to the coeliac axis and also retrogradely around the arch to involve the ascending aorta. A registrar codes it Stanford type B on the grounds that the tear is distal to the arch. What does the surgical team need to be told?
choices: Type A, because the ascending aorta is involved
Type B, because the entry tear sits beyond the arch
Type B, with the arch component reported separately
Indeterminate, pending transoesophageal confirmation
quiz.answer: Type A, because the ascending aorta is involved
quiz.explain: The Stanford division rests on whether the ascending aorta is involved, and deliberately not on where the tear is, because involvement of the ascending aorta is what determines the operation. A dissected ascending aorta threatens the coronary ostia, the aortic valve and the pericardium, and untreated it carries a mortality of the order of one to two per cent per hour over the first day or two, so it goes to theatre; an uncomplicated type B is managed medically. Retrograde type A is exactly the case the classification exists to catch, and the trap is real, because the eye anchors on the entry tear once it has found it. DeBakey does classify by origin and extent - type I ascending and beyond, type II ascending alone, type III descending - and handles this pattern less cleanly, which is one reason Stanford dominates the acute conversation. The newer reporting standards keep A and B but add the zone of the entry tear and the proximal and distal extent, so the report states where the disease starts and stops rather than which of two boxes it fits.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with tearing chest pain has a CT angiogram; no intimal flap is seen, but there is a smooth crescent of thickening in the wall of the descending aorta with an intimal calcification displaced inward. The unenhanced series was skipped to save dose. Explain what is likely present, how the omitted series would have settled it, and what the finding commits the patient to.
quiz.answer: The appearances are those of an intramural haematoma: blood within the aortic media with no demonstrable intimal tear and no flow in a false lumen, seen as a crescentic thickening that keeps a constant circumferential relationship to the wall rather than spiralling as a dissection flap does, and that displaces intimal calcification inward, so the calcium lies at the inner margin of the crescent. The unenhanced series is where it declares itself, as a crescent of attenuation higher than the unopacified lumen - of the order of fifty to seventy Hounsfield units acutely - a contrast that is destroyed once the lumen is filled with iodine, where the same crescent looks merely like mural thrombus or a thickened wall. The distinction matters because the management is that of dissection rather than that of atheroma: an intramural haematoma of the ascending aorta is treated as a type A event and usually operated on, while a descending one is managed medically with impulse control and close interval imaging, since a substantial minority progress to frank dissection, to ulceration or to rupture.
quiz.explain: Two features separate an intramural haematoma from atheromatous mural thrombus, and both are visible here. The haematoma lies outside the intima, so intimal calcification is pushed inward and sits at the crescent's luminal edge, whereas thrombus lies inside the intima with the calcification at its outer margin. And the haematoma has a smooth luminal surface and a constant circumferential relationship along the vessel, while thrombus is irregular, tends to sit on an ectatic atherosclerotic aorta, and varies in position from slice to slice. Attenuation settles it on the unenhanced series, which is the whole argument for that pass. Its appearance evolves: at a few days the haematoma loses attenuation and, on later imaging, an unenhanced study can no longer make the distinction - so a scan without the unenhanced series is not merely incomplete now, it forecloses the diagnosis retrospectively.

quiz.prompt: A patient with an uncomplicated type B dissection is admitted for medical management, and the first order is intravenous beta-blockade titrated towards a heart rate target. Below what heart rate, in beats per minute, is that titration conventionally aimed? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: Impulse control targets the rate of rise of pressure as much as the pressure itself, because it is the shearing force on the flap with each ejection that propagates the dissection. Convention is a heart rate below 60 and a systolic pressure in the region of 100 to 120 mmHg, as far as perfusion of brain, kidneys and gut allows. The sequence of drugs matters as much as the targets: the beta blocker goes in before any vasodilator, because a vasodilator given alone provokes reflex tachycardia and raises the very quantity being treated - the classic error on the ward. Analgesia is part of the haemodynamic treatment rather than a comfort measure, since pain drives catecholamines and with them both numbers. For the radiologist, the relevance is that this treatment is the reason an uncomplicated type B does not go to theatre, and the reason the follow-up scan exists.

quiz.prompt: In a chronic type B dissection the interventional team asks which lumen the landing zone lies in. On the axial images one lumen is larger, meets the outer wall at an acute angle where the flap inserts, and contains thin linear strands crossing it. Which lumen is it, and which feature is the most reliable indicator?
choices: The false lumen, indicated by the acute beak-shaped angle
The true lumen, indicated by the strands that cross it
The false lumen, indicated by its larger cross-section
The true lumen, indicated by its thin surrounding wall
quiz.answer: The false lumen, indicated by the acute beak-shaped angle
quiz.explain: The beak sign - the acute, wedge-shaped angle between the flap and the outer wall at the edge of the lumen - is the most reliable single indicator of the false lumen, because it is the leading edge of the haematoma prising the media apart. The true lumen, bounded by intima, meets the wall at an obtuse angle. Cobwebs, those thin strands of incompletely sheared media, are highly specific for the false lumen but are seen in only a minority of cases, so they confirm when present and prove nothing when absent. Size is the least dependable of the three: the false lumen is usually the larger in chronic dissection, but acutely a compressed true lumen and a small false lumen are both common, so the sign misleads in both directions. The most secure method is not a sign at all - follow the lumen proximally into undissected aorta, and the one continuous with it is true. The consequence of getting this wrong is a stent graft deployed into the false lumen, occluding every branch that arises from the true one.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old with an acute type B dissection is on intravenous beta-blockade with the pain settled. Six hours later the serum lactate rises and the abdomen becomes tender; repeat CT shows the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery arising from a true lumen compressed to a slit at that level. What does this change?
choices: It makes the dissection complicated and needs intervention
It reflects the expected course and medical therapy goes on
It is treated by deepening the blood pressure reduction
It calls for anticoagulation to protect the mesenteric flow
quiz.answer: It makes the dissection complicated and needs intervention
quiz.explain: Malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain and refractory hypertension are the features that convert a type B dissection from a medical problem into an interventional one, most often thoracic endovascular repair to cover the entry tear and let the true lumen re-expand. Recognise the mechanism, because it dictates the treatment: this is dynamic obstruction, in which the mobile flap prolapses across the branch origin as the true lumen collapses, and it is relieved by restoring pressure and flow in the true lumen. Static obstruction, where the flap extends into the branch itself, may need a stent in that branch instead, and the two often coexist. Note that the intuitive move is the harmful one - lowering the pressure further collapses the true lumen and worsens dynamic malperfusion. This is also why the protocol runs to the femoral heads: the question is never only what the arch looks like but what every branch from the coronaries downwards is being perfused by.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old with a known 6.2 cm infrarenal aneurysm attends with two days of back pain and stable observations. On the unenhanced series a crescent of attenuation higher than the psoas muscle lies within the peripheral thrombus of the sac; there is no periaortic fat stranding and no extraluminal contrast. What should the report say?
choices: Impending rupture; discuss with vascular surgery now
Chronic contained leak; arrange elective repair
Mural thrombus; back pain is unrelated to the sac
Infected aneurysm; obtain blood cultures and MRI
quiz.answer: Impending rupture; discuss with vascular surgery now
quiz.explain: The hyperattenuating crescent sign is acute blood dissecting into the mural thrombus or the aneurysm wall, and it is one of the recognised signs of impending rupture, alongside focal discontinuity of intimal calcification, the draped aorta sign in which the posterior wall loses its convexity and drapes over a vertebral body, and periaortic stranding. It is visible only on the unenhanced series, since against an opacified lumen and an enhancing wall it disappears - the second reason that pass exists. Reference the attenuation against psoas muscle, which is the standard comparator. Stable observations are not reassurance: a contained retroperitoneal leak can be haemodynamically quiet for hours before it is not. The elective repair threshold, around 5.5 cm in men, has no bearing here, because a symptomatic aneurysm is treated on its symptoms and its signs rather than on its diameter.

quiz.prompt: A screening ultrasound finds an asymptomatic infrarenal aortic aneurysm in a 72-year-old man, and the vascular clinic explains that repair is offered once the maximum diameter reaches a threshold. Give that threshold in centimetres, to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: 5.5 cm is the long-standing threshold in men: the diameter at which the annual risk of rupture overtakes the risk of the operation. Below it the aneurysm is watched with ultrasound at intervals that shorten as the diameter grows. Three qualifications belong with the number. Many services intervene at a smaller diameter in women, whose aortas are smaller to begin with and who appear to rupture at smaller absolute diameters. Rapid expansion - conventionally more than about a centimetre in a year - is an indication in its own right, whatever the absolute size. And a symptomatic aneurysm of any diameter is a different problem altogether, treated urgently. One measurement discipline underlies all of it: measure perpendicular to the centreline of the vessel, because an axial diameter through a tortuous aorta cuts it obliquely and overstates the true size, and a patient can be referred for surgery by a measurement artefact.

quiz.prompt: A hypertensive 74-year-old with heavy aortic calcification has a focal outpouching of contrast extending beyond the expected line of the lumen into the wall of the mid descending aorta, with adjacent wall thickening. Describe the lesion, say what distinguishes it from a saccular aneurysm and from a dissection, and explain what determines whether it is treated.
quiz.answer: This is a penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer: an atheromatous plaque that has ulcerated through the internal elastic lamina, letting blood into the media, so that contrast projects beyond the intimal line into the wall itself. It occurs on a background of heavy atheroma, typically in the mid to distal descending aorta, is focal rather than longitudinal, and the adjacent wall thickening is an intramural haematoma at its base. A saccular aneurysm is an outpouching of an intact if abnormal wall, without disruption of the intima and without surrounding haematoma. A dissection has a flap propagating longitudinally and separating two lumens that both carry flow, whereas an ulcer stays local. Treatment is driven by symptoms and behaviour rather than by the finding alone: persistent or recurrent pain, an enlarging associated haematoma, growth in depth or diameter on interval imaging, a new pleural effusion or signs of rupture push towards repair, usually endovascular, while an incidental ulcer in a well patient is managed with blood pressure control and interval imaging.
quiz.explain: Dissection, intramural haematoma and penetrating ulcer form one family, united by a media that has been breached, and they interconvert: an ulcer can produce a haematoma, a haematoma can develop an ulcer-like projection, and either can progress to frank dissection, pseudoaneurysm or rupture. That is why they are read together and why interval imaging is the common thread in management. One distinction is worth guarding. A de novo penetrating ulcer, in an atherosclerotic aorta with a focal contrast outpouching through calcified plaque, is not the same as an ulcer-like projection arising within an established intramural haematoma, which is a marker of instability in a lesion already being followed. The imaging appearance overlaps; the history separates them, which is one more argument for naming the prior studies in the report.

quiz.prompt: A department's chest pain protocol covers the aortic arch to the diaphragm with a single gated arterial phase, and a patient with a proven type A dissection is taken to theatre on that study. The surgeon asks for the scan to be repeated before the anaesthetic. What is the surgeon most likely to be missing?
choices: The extent of the flap and the state of the iliac vessels
The calibre of the pulmonary arteries at the hilum
The pattern of coronary calcification in the septum
The volume of contrast in the collecting systems
quiz.answer: The extent of the flap and the state of the iliac vessels
quiz.explain: A type A repair is done on cardiopulmonary bypass and needs an arterial cannulation site, so the surgeon needs the whole aorta down to the femoral vessels, and needs to know which of them is perfused by the true lumen. They also need the arch branches, since a flap in the innominate or a carotid changes the perfusion strategy and predicts stroke; the coronary ostia; the pericardium; and the aortic valve and root dimensions. The recommended range for suspected acute aortic syndrome is therefore from the thoracic inlet through to the femoral heads, with gating at least through the chest. Extending the range costs one more spiral and some dose, and it saves a second scan on a patient who has no time to spare for one. The general lesson is to protocol for the question rather than for the region where the pain is: the anatomy the referrer must act on is nearly always larger than the anatomy the symptom points to.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old presents with severe chest pain and inferior ST elevation. The cardiology team is preparing for primary percutaneous coronary intervention when the chest radiograph is reported as showing a widened mediastinum, and the blood pressure is found to differ by 30 mmHg between the arms. Set out the concern, and what it changes about the immediate plan.
quiz.answer: The concern is a type A dissection extending into a coronary ostium, most often the right, which is why the electrocardiogram shows inferior infarction: the dissection is the cause and the infarct is its complication. It matters because the reflex treatment for that electrocardiogram - thrombolysis, or dual antiplatelet therapy with heparin before angiography - is close to lethal in a dissected aorta that may already be leaking into the pericardium. The plan changes to immediate cross-sectional confirmation before any antithrombotic treatment: an electrocardiogram-gated CT angiogram from the thoracic inlet to the femoral heads, or transoesophageal echocardiography if the patient is too unstable to move, with cardiac surgery alerted in parallel rather than afterwards. The clinical features that should trigger that pause are the pressure or pulse differential between limbs, the widened mediastinum, pain that was maximal at onset or that has migrated, a new diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, and any focal neurological deficit.
quiz.explain: This is the highest-stakes overlap in acute cardiac imaging, and it runs in both directions: a dissection can present as an infarct, and the treatment for one is dangerous in the other. The right coronary is involved more often than the left because the dissection commonly propagates along the greater curvature of the ascending aorta towards it, which is why inferior ST elevation is the pattern to be suspicious of. The radiologist's contribution is to protect the pause - a chest radiograph reported promptly, and a gated CT that answers the aortic question and the coronary question on the same acquisition. Be aware of the counter-risk, since it is what makes the decision hard: delaying reperfusion in a genuine infarct costs myocardium, so the pause is justified by the specific clinical features above, not by generalised caution in every inferior infarct.

approach.step: Find the appendix and follow it to the tip
approach.detail: Base at the confluence of the taeniae on the caecum, then along its whole length. A normal proximal appendix with an inflamed tip is still appendicitis.
Outer-to-outer, on the short axis, at the widest point.
Periappendiceal fat stranding on CT, non-compressible hyperechoic inflamed fat on ultrasound. Fat changes carry more weight than a borderline diameter.

approach.step: Look for an appendicolith and for wall hyperaemia
approach.detail: Colour Doppler hypervascularity of the appendix wall on ultrasound; caecal apical thickening on either modality.

approach.step: If the appendix is normal, work the differential
approach.detail: Terminal ileum and caecum, the mesenteric nodes, the fat adjacent to the colon, the right colonic diverticula, the ovaries and the ureter.

pitfalls: Stopping at the first normal-looking segment. Tip appendicitis is missed by a scan that does not follow the appendix to its end.
Deciding on diameter alone. Around a quarter of normal appendices measure 6 mm or more — the fat, the compressibility and the Doppler signal are what separate them.
Missing early appendicitis on ultrasound: severe pain, minimal local findings, no inflamed fat, only a dilated lumen.
Reporting 'appendix not visualised' as reassurance. Normal appendices are seen in only 20–30% of asymptomatic people, so non-visualisation says very little.
Calling a fatty right-sided inflammatory lesion appendicitis. Look for the hyperattenuating ring of epiploic appendagitis before anyone books a theatre.
