quiz.prompt: During graded compression ultrasound of the right iliac fossa a tubular structure is found at the caecal pole. Under gentle, progressive pressure it flattens completely, peristalsis is seen passing along it, and no blind end can be demonstrated. What follows from these three observations?
quiz.answer: This is small bowel rather than the appendix, and the search for a blind-ending tube should continue.
choices: This is small bowel rather than the appendix, and the search for a blind-ending tube should continue.
This is a normal appendix, and the study can be reported as having excluded acute appendicitis.
This is an inflamed appendix that has decompressed after perforating into the adjacent pelvis.
This is a mesenteric node imaged in its long axis, and the finding supports mesenteric adenitis.
quiz.explain: Three features identify the appendix and all three are needed: it ends blindly, it does not peristalse, and it arises from the caecal pole where the taeniae converge. A tube that peristalses is small bowel, and calling it a normal appendix is how a false negative is manufactured. Graded compression is the technique that makes the search possible — steady, increasing pressure with the linear probe displaces gas-filled bowel out of the field and brings the appendix closer, which both improves resolution and tests compressibility. The inflamed appendix is non-compressible, aperistaltic, over 6 mm outer-to-outer, often with an echogenic hyperaemic halo of inflamed fat around it. A perforated appendix may indeed decompress, but it does not acquire peristalsis. Nodes are ovoid with an echogenic hilum, not tubular in continuity along their length.

quiz.prompt: On graded compression ultrasound a blind-ending, aperistaltic, non-compressible tube arises from the caecal pole. Measured in true cross section, the near wall is 2.1 mm, the lumen 4.6 mm and the far wall 2.1 mm. Give the outer-to-outer diameter in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 2.1 plus 4.6 plus 2.1 gives 8.8 mm. The measurement that matters is outer wall to outer wall in a true transverse section, not the lumen and not an oblique cut through a curving appendix, both of which mislead. The conventional upper limit of normal is 6 mm, but the threshold behaves poorly on its own: a normal appendix can distend to 7 mm with gas or faecal material, and diameters between 6 and 8 mm are a genuine grey zone in which secondary signs decide — non-compressibility, mural hyperaemia on colour Doppler, an appendicolith, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, and focal tenderness under the probe. At 8.8 mm with non-compressibility the diagnosis is secure. Beware the opposite error too: pressing too hard flattens the measurement and can talk you out of a real appendicitis.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old woman has had right iliac fossa pain for 30 hours. Ultrasound is careful and prolonged, but the appendix is not seen; there is no free fluid, no enlarged nodes and no echogenic fat. Write the conclusion you would put in the report, and say what happens next.
quiz.answer: Report that the appendix was not visualised, that this does not exclude appendicitis, and that the absence of secondary signs makes it less likely. If pain persists, proceed to CT - or MRI if she turns out to be pregnant - or re-examine clinically within a few hours.
quiz.explain: A non-visualised appendix is a common and honest result, and the report must say plainly that it is not a negative study. The causes are worth knowing because several are correctable: a retrocaecal or deep pelvic position, overlying gas, obesity, guarding that defeats compression, a perforated appendix that has decompressed, and inexperience with the technique. What softens the result is the complete absence of secondary signs — no free fluid, no echogenic fat, no nodes, no tenderness under the probe — which lowers the probability but never to zero. The next step depends on the patient in front of you: CT in a non-pregnant adult whose pain persists or whose inflammatory markers are rising, MRI in pregnancy, and structured clinical reassessment where the story is settling. What is not acceptable is a conclusion that reads as though appendicitis has been excluded.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 38-year-old man with two days of vague right-sided pain shows an appendix of 7 mm outer diameter, filled with gas along its whole length, with a thin wall, no periappendiceal stranding and no free fluid. What is the most defensible report?
quiz.answer: A borderline calibre appendix, gas-filled throughout with no periappendiceal change, argues against appendicitis.
choices: A borderline calibre appendix, gas-filled throughout with no periappendiceal change, argues against appendicitis.
A 7 mm appendix exceeds the accepted threshold, so acute appendicitis should be diagnosed and surgery advised.
Gas within the appendiceal lumen indicates perforation here, and urgent surgical exploration should be advised.
The study is uninterpretable at this calibre, and magnetic resonance imaging should be arranged the same day.
quiz.explain: Diameter alone is the weakest of the CT criteria. A normal appendix distended with gas or faecal material commonly measures 6 to 8 mm, so a 7 mm appendix is not a diagnosis. What resolves the equivocal case is the company it keeps. Against appendicitis: gas or oral contrast passing along the full length of the lumen, a thin non-enhancing-thickened wall, and clean surrounding fat. In favour: mural thickening beyond about 3 mm, mural hyperenhancement, periappendiceal fat stranding, an appendicolith, thickening of the caecal apex funnelling towards the base, and adjacent free fluid. Intraluminal gas is reassuring rather than alarming; extraluminal gas is the perforation sign. Reporting an equivocal appendix well means saying which secondary signs you looked for and did not find, so the clinician can weigh it against the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old girl has right iliac fossa pain. Ultrasound shows a compressible 4 mm blind-ending tube at the caecal pole, mild terminal ileal wall thickening, and three ileocolic nodes with short-axis diameters of 4 mm, 6 mm and 8 mm. Using a short-axis threshold of 5 mm, how many of these nodes count as enlarged? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Two nodes — those of 6 mm and 8 mm — meet a 5 mm short-axis threshold. A commonly used working definition of mesenteric adenitis asks for three or more right iliac fossa nodes of at least 5 mm in short axis together with a normal appendix, sometimes with mild ileal or caecal wall thickening, so on this study the label is not fully earned even though the picture fits. That nuance matters less than the discipline behind it: nodes are non-specific, they are common in children and they are frequently present in appendicitis itself, so enlarged nodes never exclude an inflamed appendix. The finding that carries the weight here is the appendix — compressible, 4 mm, blind-ending — which is a genuinely normal appendix. Always measure nodes in short axis; long-axis measurements make reactive nodes look pathological.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old boy with a high body mass index has right-sided abdominal pain. CT shows a 7 cm heterogeneous, whorled fat-density mass lying between the ascending colon and the anterior abdominal wall, without a hyperattenuating rim, and a normal gas-filled appendix. What should be recommended?
quiz.answer: Conservative management with analgesia, since an omental infarct of this kind resolves without antibiotics or surgery.
choices: Conservative management with analgesia, since an omental infarct of this kind resolves without antibiotics or surgery.
Laparoscopy and excision, because a fatty mass of this size will not resolve and risks progressing to an abscess.
Antibiotics for a contained appendiceal phlegmon, with interval appendicectomy planned about six weeks later.
Staging CT of the chest and pelvis, since a fat-containing mesenteric mass of this size suggests a liposarcoma.
quiz.explain: Omental infarct and epiploic appendagitis are the two self-limiting fat lesions that imitate appendicitis and diverticulitis, and CT separates them confidently. Omental infarct is the larger of the two, typically over 5 cm, heterogeneous and whorled, sited between the colon and the anterior abdominal wall — most often on the right — and it is disproportionately a disease of children and of obese adults. Epiploic appendagitis is smaller, oval, under about 5 cm, with a thin hyperattenuating rim and sometimes a central dot representing a thrombosed vein, and it hugs the colonic serosa, usually the sigmoid. Neither needs antibiotics or an operation; both settle over weeks with analgesia. The normal appendix here rules out the phlegmon option. Liposarcoma is a mass with nodular soft tissue components in a patient without acute pain, not an inflamed omental fat lesion of sudden onset.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old man of East Asian background has right iliac fossa pain and tenderness. CT shows a normal, gas-filled 5 mm appendix, and a single inflamed outpouching arising from the caecum with focal adjacent wall thickening and pericolic stranding. What should the report advise?
quiz.answer: Solitary caecal diverticulitis: treat medically, since appendicectomy would not address the inflamed segment.
choices: Solitary caecal diverticulitis: treat medically, since appendicectomy would not address the inflamed segment.
Early appendicectomy, because the appendix is unreliably assessed on CT once the caecum is inflamed.
Right hemicolectomy, because focal caecal wall thickening at this age usually indicates a carcinoma.
Percutaneous drainage, because caecal diverticulitis nearly always harbours a drainable collection.
quiz.explain: Right-sided diverticulitis is clinically indistinguishable from appendicitis — same site, same age group, same tenderness — and it is relatively more common in patients of East and South-East Asian descent, in whom the diverticula tend to be solitary, true and right-sided. CT settles it by showing an inflamed outpouching with surrounding stranding and a demonstrably normal appendix. Most cases respond to antibiotics and supportive care, and the value of making the diagnosis before the operation is that it avoids a needless appendicectomy or, worse, an over-extensive resection of an inflamed caecum that the surgeon cannot distinguish from a tumour at the table. Carcinoma does deserve consideration when the wall thickening is asymmetric and shouldered rather than centred on a diverticulum, particularly in older patients — but at 32, with a visible inflamed diverticulum, medical treatment with later colonic assessment is the proportionate advice.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 29-year-old shows a dilated appendix with a focal defect in its enhancing wall, a 4.5 cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection containing gas, and a calcified body lying outside the appendiceal lumen. Say what has happened, and how it changes management.
quiz.answer: The appendix has perforated: there is a wall defect, an extraluminal appendicolith and a periappendiceal abscess. A collection of this size is generally managed with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage rather than immediate appendicectomy, with interval surgery considered afterwards.
quiz.explain: The signs of perforation on CT are a focal defect in the enhancing appendiceal wall, extraluminal gas, an extraluminal appendicolith and a rim-enhancing collection; a phlegmon is the same process without a drainable cavity. The distinction changes the operation rather than the diagnosis. A well-formed abscess of a few centimetres or more is usually treated first with antibiotics and image-guided percutaneous drainage, because immediate appendicectomy in a hostile, inflamed right iliac fossa carries a higher complication rate and sometimes forces a caecal resection. A phlegmon or small collection is treated with antibiotics alone. Interval appendicectomy afterwards is a matter of local policy and patient factors. Report the extraluminal appendicolith explicitly: one left behind after drainage is a recognised cause of recurrent abscess, and the surgeon needs to know it is there.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old with three months of loose stool has right iliac fossa pain. CT shows 20 cm of terminal ileum with mural thickening and layered enhancement, engorged vasa recta combed along the mesenteric border, fibrofatty proliferation, and a normal appendix. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Refer to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy with biopsy, and consider MR enterography to map disease extent.
choices: Refer to gastroenterology for ileocolonoscopy with biopsy, and consider MR enterography to map disease extent.
Refer for urgent appendicectomy, since terminal ileal change at this site is secondary to appendiceal inflammation.
Treat as infective ileitis with antibiotics alone, and repeat the CT at six weeks to confirm that it has resolved.
Arrange a barium follow-through as the definitive investigation before any endoscopic or cross-sectional imaging.
quiz.explain: A long segment of terminal ileum with mural stratification, engorged vasa recta along the mesenteric border and proliferation of the surrounding fat, in a young patient with months of diarrhoea, is ileocolic Crohn disease until proven otherwise. Diagnosis is made by endoscopy and histology, and the imaging job afterwards is mapping — MR enterography for disease length, activity, strictures, fistulae and abscesses, which spares a young patient repeated CT over decades of follow-up. Infective ileitis from Yersinia, Campylobacter or Salmonella can look identical on a single acute study, which is precisely why the history and the endoscopy matter rather than a repeat scan. Barium studies have been superseded for this indication. The normal appendix in a case like this is a finding to report positively, since it is what keeps the patient off the emergency list.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the imaging tests for suspected appendicitis in a 20-week pregnant woman in the order they should be attempted.
quiz.answer: ultrasound MRI CT
quiz.explain: Ultrasound comes first: no ionising radiation, immediately available, and in the first two trimesters graded compression still reaches the appendix in a useful proportion of women. As the uterus enlarges the appendix is displaced upwards and laterally and the success rate falls. MRI is second, performed without gadolinium, and it is very good at this question: an appendix above about 7 mm with wall thickening, periappendiceal fluid or high signal in the surrounding fat supports the diagnosis, while a normal appendix below 6 mm filled with gas is reassuring. CT is third rather than forbidden. The dose from a limited abdominopelvic study is well below the level associated with deterministic fetal injury, and a perforated appendix carries a far greater risk to the pregnancy than the scan. The pathway must keep moving to a decision.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old woman has sudden right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm oedematous right ovary with follicles displaced to the periphery and a twisted vascular pedicle, and a normal appendix. Arterial flow is still detectable within the ovary. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Refer for emergency gynaecological surgery, since detectable arterial flow does not exclude ovarian torsion.
choices: Refer for emergency gynaecological surgery, since detectable arterial flow does not exclude ovarian torsion.
Reassure and rescan in 24 hours, since detectable arterial flow makes ovarian torsion improbable here.
Treat empirically for pelvic inflammatory disease, and arrange outpatient follow-up imaging in two weeks.
Proceed to contrast-enhanced CT, which is considerably more sensitive than ultrasound for this diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Preserved arterial flow is the classic trap in ovarian torsion. The ovary has a dual supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries, torsion is often intermittent and partial, and venous outflow fails before arterial inflow does — so Doppler can look deceptively normal in a torted ovary. The diagnosis rests on the grey-scale findings: a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, an abnormal position of the ovary near the midline or above the uterus, a whirlpool of the twisted pedicle, and often a lead-point cyst or dermoid. Salvage depends on how fast detorsion happens, so this is a telephone call, not a routine referral. CT may be the study that happens to be done first in an undifferentiated abdomen, but ultrasound with Doppler is the test of choice, and a normal appendix does not close the case.

quiz.prompt: A 64-year-old man has CT-proven acute appendicitis. At the appendiceal base the caecal wall is asymmetrically thickened over about 3 cm with a shouldered margin, and there are two 8 mm pericolic nodes. State what you must add to the report, and why.
quiz.answer: Recommend colonoscopy after recovery, or interval imaging: appendicitis in an older patient may be caused by a caecal or appendiceal tumour obstructing the appendiceal orifice, and asymmetric shouldered caecal thickening with nodes is suspicious.
quiz.explain: Appendicitis is a disease of luminal obstruction, and in a patient over about 50 the thing doing the obstructing may be a neoplasm — a caecal carcinoma at the appendiceal orifice, or a mucinous neoplasm of the appendix itself. The clue is that the findings extend beyond what appendicitis alone explains: asymmetric caecal wall thickening with shouldered margins rather than symmetrical funnelling of the caecal apex, a soft tissue mass at the base, disproportionate lymph nodes, or a distended mucin-filled appendix with mural calcification. The report should name the concern and recommend colonoscopy or CT after the acute episode has settled, because that recommendation is often the only thing that carries the patient into a cancer pathway. Saying only 'acute appendicitis' in this situation is technically true and clinically incomplete.

quiz.prompt: A slim, cooperative 7-year-old boy has 18 hours of right iliac fossa pain and a raised C-reactive protein. Which pathway exposes him to the least harm while still answering the question?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound first, reserving CT or MRI for the child whose appendix is not seen and whose pain persists.
choices: Ultrasound first, reserving CT or MRI for the child whose appendix is not seen and whose pain persists.
Contrast-enhanced CT first, since ultrasound is too operator dependent to be relied upon in children.
Serial clinical review without imaging, since imaging seldom changes management in a child of this age.
MRI as the first test, since out-of-hours access to MRI matches ultrasound in most district hospitals.
quiz.explain: Children are the ideal ultrasound patients: thin abdominal walls, little intervening fat, and a short distance to the appendix, so a competent operator visualises it in a high proportion of cases. Radiation risk is also at its most consequential in a long life expectancy, which makes ultrasound first the right default. The pathway must not stall there, though. If the appendix is not seen and the child stays symptomatic, the options are a repeat ultrasound in experienced hands, MRI where it is genuinely available and the child will lie still, or CT. Withholding CT from a deteriorating child in order to avoid a dose is a false economy — perforation, abscess and sepsis are the greater harm. Out-of-hours MRI access is rarely comparable to ultrasound, which is why it cannot be the standing first test.

curriculum_modules.title: Biliary Obstruction, Stones and the Thickened Gallbladder

module_contract.goal: Investigate a tender or jaundiced right upper quadrant, state the level and likely cause of biliary obstruction, and separate the inflamed gallbladder from the merely thick-walled one.

approach.step: Measure the wall and note the distension
approach.detail: The normal wall is a pencil-thin echogenic line. Thickness varies with distension, and a non-fasting gallbladder thickens on its own.
Diffuse thickening sends you looking for a systemic or hepatic cause; focal thickening sends you looking for adenomyomatosis or carcinoma.
Obstructing stone, hydropic distension, sonographic Murphy sign, pericholecystic fluid and inflammation, wall hyperaemia on Doppler.

Intramural cystic spaces with characteristic comet-tail reverberation support adenomyomatosis. Assess the complete lesion, wall layers and hepatic interface; one artefact does not exclude a coexisting or mimicking malignancy.

approach.step: If thickening is secondary, find the cause
approach.detail: Cirrhosis, hepatitis, cardiac failure and pancreatitis may cause secondary wall oedema. Correlate the actual clinical/examination pattern and look for coexisting primary gallbladder disease rather than making an automatic no-surgery judgement.

Follow the actual duct tree and variants to each transition; report stricture site, length, margin, upstream distribution and associated tissue. Length alone does not distinguish PSC, other inflammatory disease and malignancy.

measure.how: On ultrasound, perpendicular to the anterior wall, with the gallbladder distended after fasting.
measure.cutoff: Conventionally thickened >3 mm in an adequately distended gallbladder; measurement quality, contraction/fasting and clinical context remain essential. Thickness alone is not a diagnosis.

measure.how: Along the duct on MRCP or CT, from shoulder to shoulder.
measure.cutoff: Source examples describe shorter PSC and longer malignant strictures, but there is no universal length-only diagnostic cutoff; source images, morphology and clinical context remain necessary.

classify.name: The thickened gallbladder wall
rows: Obstructing stone, hydropic distension, positive sonographic Murphy sign, pericholecystic fluid, wall hyperaemia on Doppler
Clinical/laboratory correlation and timely specialist assessment when acute disease is suspected; imaging alone is not the full diagnosis or severity grade.
Intramural cystic spaces with characteristic reverberation support adenomyomatosis; assess the whole lesion for discordant tissue and interfaces.
When confidently characterized, management depends on symptoms and context; uncertainty or suspicious/coexisting features require further assessment.
Polypoid lesion through to infiltrating mass, invasion of adjacent structures, bile duct dilatation, metastases
Raised portal pressure and low osmotic pressure; layered oedematous wall
Assess the systemic cause and exclude coexisting primary gallbladder disease; no automatic operative verdict from wall oedema.
Diffuse reversible thickening with the hepatitic picture
Assess the systemic cause and exclude coexisting primary gallbladder disease; no automatic operative verdict from wall oedema.
Raised systemic venous pressure, often with other congestive signs
Assess the systemic cause and exclude coexisting primary gallbladder disease; no automatic operative verdict from wall oedema.
Direct spread of inflammation to the gallbladder wall
classify.note: Contraction/postprandial state may cause apparent thickening. Record limitations and repeat under suitable conditions when clinically appropriate; do not delay urgent assessment to obtain a fasting image.

measurements.name: CBD calibre
measurements.method: Measure inner-to-inner diameter perpendicular to the duct at a named level.
measurements.pitfall: Interpret with age, surgery and symptoms; calibre alone does not establish obstruction.

measurements.name: Gallbladder wall

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old with right upper quadrant pain has gallstones and a common bile duct of 9 mm on ultrasound, but the distal duct is obscured by duodenal gas. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are raised. State the next investigation you would recommend, and why.
quiz.answer: MRCP, because ultrasound is insensitive for stones in the distal common bile duct where duodenal gas obscures it; a dilated duct with obstructive liver tests needs direct imaging of the duct before cholecystectomy.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound is excellent for stones in the gallbladder — sensitivity comfortably above 90 per cent for a mobile shadowing echogenic focus — and poor for stones in the duct, where reported sensitivity is around half or less. The reason is anatomical: the retroduodenal and intrapancreatic segments lie behind gas-filled bowel, and small stones bathed in bile may not shadow at all. So a duct that is dilated with obstructive biochemistry is an indication for direct duct imaging, not for repeating the ultrasound. MRCP is the usual first choice; endoscopic ultrasound is more sensitive for stones under 5 mm where it is available, and ERCP is reserved for treatment rather than diagnosis. CT is a poor stone test, because many calculi are cholesterol-predominant and isodense with bile.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old with no previous biliary surgery has an incidentally noted common bile duct. Using the common convention that the upper limit of normal is 6 mm at 60 years and rises by 1 mm for each subsequent decade, calculate the upper limit for this patient. Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Two decades beyond 60 adds 2 mm to the 6 mm baseline, giving 8 mm. Treat this as a convention rather than a law: the duct does tend to widen with age as its wall loses elastin, but the number is a reporting aid, and it should always be read alongside the liver enzymes and the symptoms. A duct at the upper limit in an asymptomatic patient with normal biochemistry rarely repays pursuit, while a 6 mm duct with a rising bilirubin certainly does. Two further adjustments matter in practice. After cholecystectomy the duct takes over some reservoir function and up to about 10 mm may be normal. And opiates cause sphincter of Oddi spasm, so a duct measured on a patient who has just had morphine can be transiently wide. Measure inner wall to inner wall, perpendicular to the duct, at the porta.

quiz.prompt: A patient is scanned after an appropriate period of fasting and the gallbladder is distended. Above what anterior gallbladder wall thickness, measured on ultrasound, is the wall conventionally regarded as thickened? Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: More than 3 mm is the conventional wall-thickening threshold in an adequately distended gallbladder with perpendicular anterior-wall measurement. Contraction and poor measurement may mislead; an isolated thick wall is nonspecific. Describe supporting imaging findings and actual tenderness/Doppler assessment, then integrate local and systemic clinical evidence rather than diagnosing or grading acute cholecystitis from thickness alone.

quiz.prompt: A 72-year-old diabetic with four days of pain has a distended gallbladder containing stones, a thick wall with hypoechoic striations, sloughed intraluminal membranes, and a negative sonographic Murphy sign. What should you report and recommend?
quiz.answer: Gangrenous cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign is not reassuring, and urgent surgical review is needed
choices: Gangrenous cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign is not reassuring, and urgent surgical review is needed
Chronic cholecystitis; the negative Murphy sign makes acute inflammation unlikely at this presentation
Gallbladder carcinoma; recommend a staging CT and referral to the hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team
Adenomyomatosis; the intramural findings are Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses and no intervention is needed
quiz.explain: The trap sits in the negative Murphy sign. In gangrenous cholecystitis the wall is necrotic and its innervation destroyed, so focal tenderness is often lost — precisely in the patients who are sickest. Diabetes, age and analgesia compound this. The findings that make the diagnosis are the striated, heterogeneous wall, intraluminal membranes from sloughed mucosa, focal wall defects, and, on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, segments of wall that do not perfuse. It matters because gangrene multiplies the risk of perforation and death and pushes management towards urgent cholecystectomy, or a percutaneous cholecystostomy if the patient is too unwell for theatre. Adenomyomatosis produces comet-tail reverberation from crystals in intramural sinuses in a gallbladder that is not tender, and carcinoma produces focal irregular solid thickening with invasion of the liver interface rather than membranes.

quiz.prompt: An unwell diabetic man has a CT showing curvilinear gas within the gallbladder wall, a few gas bubbles in the lumen, and pericholecystic fat stranding. Write what you would say when you telephone the surgical team.
quiz.answer: This is emphysematous cholecystitis, with gas in the gallbladder wall from gas-forming organisms; it carries a high risk of gangrene and perforation, so it needs immediate antibiotics and urgent cholecystectomy or percutaneous cholecystostomy.
quiz.explain: Gas in the wall means gas-forming organisms — commonly Clostridium perfringens or Escherichia coli — growing in an ischaemic gallbladder. The associations are diabetes and male sex, and roughly half the cases have no stones at all. Mortality is several times that of ordinary calculous cholecystitis and perforation is far more likely, so this is a telephone call, not a report line. Ultrasound is treacherous here: intramural gas produces bright echoes with dirty shadowing and ring-down that can be mistaken for a stone-packed gallbladder or overlying bowel, and if the lumen cannot be resolved at all the correct move is a CT rather than a confident report. Two look-alikes to keep separate. Porcelain gallbladder is mural calcification, dense and cleanly shadowing, with none of the dirty reverberation. Pneumobilia is central and branching, following the ducts towards the hilum.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient on day 12 of an intensive care admission after major burns develops a rising bilirubin. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a 6 mm wall and pericholecystic fluid, no stones, and sedation prevents any Murphy sign being elicited. What is the most appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Treat as acalculous cholecystitis; consider cholescintigraphy and percutaneous cholecystostomy
choices: Treat as acalculous cholecystitis; consider cholescintigraphy and percutaneous cholecystostomy
Attribute the findings to hypoalbuminaemia; no biliary imaging or intervention is warranted
Arrange MRCP to exclude a common bile duct stone before any biliary drainage is considered
Arrange urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, since medical management is contraindicated here
quiz.explain: Acalculous cholecystitis is a disease of the critically ill — burns, sepsis, major trauma, prolonged parenteral nutrition, mechanical ventilation — driven by bile stasis and gallbladder wall ischaemia, and it gangrenes and perforates more readily than calculous disease. The difficulty is that intensive care itself produces every individual finding: hypoalbuminaemia and positive-pressure ventilation thicken the wall, fluid overload gives pericholecystic fluid, and fasting distends the gallbladder. So the diagnosis is a judgement built on the whole picture, supported where needed by cholescintigraphy showing non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 minutes with morphine augmentation, or by a wall perfusion defect on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is frequently chosen over surgery because these patients tolerate anaesthesia and laparotomy badly, and drainage buys time for the underlying illness to be treated.

quiz.prompt: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis and gross ascites has a 7 mm gallbladder wall, no stones, no tenderness over the gallbladder, and normal liver enzymes. Explain what you would report and why.
quiz.answer: Report the wall thickening as non-specific, most likely secondary to hypoalbuminaemia, ascites and portal hypertension rather than cholecystitis, since there are no stones, no focal tenderness and no obstructive biochemistry.
quiz.explain: A thick gallbladder wall is a finding, not a diagnosis, and the list of causes that are not cholecystitis is long: the physiologically contracted post-prandial gallbladder, hypoalbuminaemia of any cause, right heart failure and raised central venous pressure, cirrhosis and portal hypertension, acute hepatitis, renal failure, pancreatitis, adenomyomatosis and carcinoma. In cirrhosis the wall is thick for two reasons at once — low oncotic pressure and venous congestion — and Doppler may show varices within it. What should raise suspicion instead is focal rather than diffuse thickening, an irregular solid component, loss of the interface with adjacent liver, and internal vascularity, all of which point at gallbladder carcinoma. Writing this out matters: an unqualified line about a thickened wall in a cirrhotic patient generates surgical referrals and occasionally an operation that nobody needed.

quiz.prompt: A non-tender gallbladder has a focally thickened fundal wall containing tiny echogenic foci, each throwing a narrow V-shaped reverberation artefact that widens away from the transducer. There are no stones and no pericholecystic fluid. What should you conclude?
quiz.answer: Findings favour adenomyomatosis; confirm intramural spaces and assess the complete wall for discordant features
choices: Findings favour adenomyomatosis; confirm intramural spaces and assess the complete wall for discordant features
Chronic cholecystitis; the echogenic foci are tiny calculi embedded within a fibrotic scarred wall
Gallbladder carcinoma; focal fundal thickening of this kind warrants urgent staging and biopsy
Emphysematous cholecystitis; the artefacts arise from small volumes of gas within the gallbladder wall
quiz.explain: Characteristic intramural spaces and comet-tail reverberation support adenomyomatosis, but one artefact is not a universal cancer exclusion. Examine the complete wall, other compartments and hepatic interface for a coexisting or mimicking lesion. Confidently characterized benign disease and uncertain/symptomatic or suspicious cases need different clinical decisions; no blanket instruction to stop assessment follows from the artefact alone.

quiz.prompt: MRCP performed after a previous endoscopic sphincterotomy shows two rounded signal voids within the common bile duct. Both lie along the anterior, non-dependent wall, and both bloom on the gradient-echo sequence. What is the correct interpretation?
quiz.answer: Air bubbles introduced at sphincterotomy: non-dependent position and blooming distinguish them from stones
choices: Air bubbles introduced at sphincterotomy: non-dependent position and blooming distinguish them from stones
Two calculi: rounded filling defects within an instrumented duct should be treated as stones until disproved
Flow artefact from the right hepatic artery crossing the duct and producing a rounded signal void
Surgical clips from the earlier cholecystectomy, projected over the duct on the coronal acquisitions
quiz.explain: Pneumobilia is the classic MRCP mimic after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or stent placement. Two features separate it from a stone. Gas rises to the non-dependent surface — anterior in a supine patient — while a stone falls to the dependent wall; and gas blooms on gradient-echo sequences because of its susceptibility effect, whereas a stone does not. If real doubt persists, gas is unmistakable on CT. Other MRCP traps are worth carrying: pulsation of the right hepatic artery crossing the common hepatic duct makes a linear void, susceptibility from clips or a metal stent can obliterate a whole segment of duct, stones under about 5 mm are readily missed, and a calculus impacted at the ampulla can be mistaken for normal distal tapering. When the clinical suspicion is strong and MRCP is negative, endoscopic ultrasound is the more sensitive next step.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these levels of the biliary tree in order from within the liver towards the duodenum, as used when stating the level of an obstruction.
quiz.answer: intrahepatic-ducts hilar-confluence common-hepatic-duct common-bile-duct ampulla
quiz.explain: Stating the level narrows the differential more sharply than almost any other sentence in a biliary report, because the cause tracks the level. Intrahepatic and hilar obstruction, with dilated intrahepatic ducts and a collapsed, empty gallbladder, points to a hilar cholangiocarcinoma, to nodal disease at the porta, or to metastatic compression. Obstruction below the insertion of the cystic duct allows the gallbladder to distend, which is the anatomical basis of the old observation that a palpable, painless gallbladder in a jaundiced patient favours malignancy over stones. Distal and ampullary obstruction dilates both the bile duct and the pancreatic duct, which is where the double duct sign comes from. So work down the tree on the coronal images, find the last normal-calibre segment, and say where the transition is and whether it is abrupt or tapered.

quiz.prompt: A jaundiced 70-year-old has dilatation of both the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct, with an abrupt cut-off of both at the pancreatic head, and no visible calculus. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A pancreatic head or ampullary tumour until proven otherwise; pancreatic protocol CT and MDT referral
choices: A pancreatic head or ampullary tumour until proven otherwise; pancreatic protocol CT and MDT referral
Chronic pancreatitis with a benign stricture; recommend a repeat MRCP in six months to reassess
A common bile duct stone that has already passed; recommend ERCP with sphincterotomy and clearance
Primary sclerosing cholangitis; recommend colonoscopy and serial liver function testing thereafter
quiz.explain: The double duct sign in a jaundiced older patient carries a high probability of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma, and next of ampullary or distal bile duct carcinoma. Chronic pancreatitis can produce it too, but usually with parenchymal calcification, a beaded and irregular pancreatic duct, and a long history. The essential point is that the sign obliges dedicated imaging even when no mass is visible, because a proportion of small head tumours are isoattenuating to pancreas on portal venous phase images alone. That means a pancreatic protocol CT with a late arterial pancreatic parenchymal phase and a portal venous phase, and endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling where the CT remains negative. Read the morphology of the cut-off as well: abrupt and shouldered is the malignant pattern, whereas a smooth gradual taper over a centimetre or two favours a benign stricture.

quiz.prompt: Two patients each have a stricture of the distal common bile duct. In the first the duct narrows over about 2 cm with a smooth gradual taper; in the second it stops abruptly with an irregular shouldered margin and there is subtle adjacent soft tissue. State what you conclude in each case and what you would do next.
quiz.answer: The smooth gradual taper favours a benign stricture — post-inflammatory, post-operative or from chronic pancreatitis — and can go to ERCP with brushings and follow-up; the abrupt shouldered narrowing with soft tissue favours malignancy and needs pancreatic protocol CT, endoscopic ultrasound with biopsy, and MDT referral.
quiz.explain: Stricture morphology is one of the few reliably discriminating observations in biliary imaging. Benign strictures are the product of diffuse fibrosis and taper gradually with preserved, concentric mucosal contour; the usual causes are chronic pancreatitis, previous surgery or instrumentation, ischaemia after transplantation, IgG4-related disease and passed stones. Malignant strictures are the product of a growing mass and end abruptly, with irregular shouldered margins, asymmetry, a long segment of involvement, associated periductal soft tissue and enhancement, and often upstream ductal wall thickening. Neither pattern is absolute, and brush cytology has poor sensitivity, so a persistent stricture with a negative brushing is not cleared — repeat sampling, cholangioscopy or resection may still be needed. State the length, the margin, and the presence or absence of enhancing soft tissue, because those three data points drive the next decision.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with ulcerative colitis has MRCP showing multifocal short strictures with intervening mildly dilated segments throughout the intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts. Two years later one stricture has lengthened and there is now 2 cm of enhancing periductal soft tissue with new upstream dilatation. What should you report?
quiz.answer: Suspected cholangiocarcinoma arising in sclerosing cholangitis; urgent MDT review and tissue sampling
choices: Suspected cholangiocarcinoma arising in sclerosing cholangitis; urgent MDT review and tissue sampling
Progression of sclerosing cholangitis alone; continue annual MRCP and liver function monitoring
Recurrent bacterial cholangitis; recommend a course of antibiotics and repeat imaging in six weeks
Secondary sclerosing cholangitis from ischaemia; correlate with the state of the hepatic artery
quiz.explain: The new enhancing periductal tissue and upstream change are concerning for cholangiocarcinoma in this clinical setting, but imaging is not histological proof. Urgent specialist MDT assessment should plan further imaging and appropriate sampling. Inflammatory disease can overlap, and a negative brushing does not exclude malignancy; do not classify every changing stricture as proven malignant.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain has a CT showing thickened enhancing bile duct walls, periportal oedema, patchy ill-defined arterial hyperenhancement of the liver, and a calculus impacted in the distal common bile duct. The blood pressure is 85/50. What does the report need to drive?
quiz.answer: Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP, alongside resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
choices: Urgent biliary decompression by ERCP, alongside resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
Elective ERCP on the next available list, once the blood cultures have been reported
Percutaneous drainage of the hyperenhancing hepatic areas, which are developing abscesses
Urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with operative cholangiography and peritoneal washout
quiz.explain: Clinical infection, jaundice, obstruction and hypotension require urgent communication, resuscitation, antibiotics and specialist drainage assessment. Patchy hepatic enhancement alone is not a drainable abscess. TG18 diagnosis integrates systemic inflammation, cholestasis and imaging; severity is assessed clinically. A low blood-pressure reading alone does not prove TG18 Grade III cardiovascular dysfunction: that criterion requires dopamine ≥5 micrograms/kg/min or any norepinephrine dose. Other defined organ dysfunction can independently establish Grade III. Imaging does not assign the grade, and urgent care should not wait for a morphology-based label.

module_contract.goal: Plan an image-guided biopsy or drainage that is safe to perform - the right modality, a defensible tract, haemostasis corrected to the right threshold, the right catheter, and a team that knows what to do when it goes wrong.

approach.step: Place the procedure in a bleeding-risk category first
approach.detail: Everything downstream — whether you screen, what you correct to, which drugs you hold — follows from low, moderate or high risk. Decide it before you look at the drug chart.

approach.step: Weigh the thrombotic risk against the bleeding risk, explicitly
approach.detail: Three things go into the decision: the procedure's bleeding risk, the drugs altering coagulation or platelet function, and the patient's own thromboembolic risk. Skipping the third is how a stent thromboses for a thyroid biopsy.

High risk: INR, aPTT, platelet count and haematocrit. Moderate risk: INR routinely. Low risk: no routine testing. Screen anyone with unexplained previous haemorrhage, renal, liver or haematological disease whatever the category.

approach.step: Correct to the target for the category, then stop
approach.detail: Low risk INR < 2.0. Moderate and high risk INR < 1.5 with aPTT < 1.5 × control. Platelets transfused below 50,000/μL at every level.

approach.step: Ask who else has to agree
approach.detail: Cardiology for previous PCI, mechanical valves or high-risk atrial fibrillation. Haematology for thrombophilia, coagulopathy or reversal. The operator and the departmental guideline outrank any general table, including this one.

approach.step: Plan the tract before the needle
approach.detail: Choose the modality that shows the lesion in real time, then choose a route that avoids bowel, pleura and major vessels — bearing in mind that a new tract, as in biliary intervention, is itself what makes a procedure high risk.

approach.step: Fix the restart before the patient leaves
approach.detail: Aspirin at 24 hours. ADP inhibitors at 24–48 hours. Warfarin at 12–24 hours. DOACs at 24–48 hours. Write it on the plan, because the omitted restart causes as much harm as the omitted hold.

measure.how: Correct before proceeding.

measure.what: Coagulation target, moderate and high-risk procedure
measure.how: Correct before proceeding.
measure.cutoff: INR < 1.5 · aPTT < 1.5 × control · transfuse platelets if < 50,000/μL

measure.how: Withhold for high-risk procedures; generally continue for low and moderate. Only platelet transfusion or desmopressin expedites reversal.
Withhold for low, moderate and high risk, though some continue for low risk where stopping is itself hazardous.
measure.cutoff: Hold 5 days (7 days for high-risk procedures) · restart 24–48 h

measure.how: Greater platelet inhibition than the other ADP inhibitors.
Generally only for high-risk procedures; the hold follows the agent's half-life.
measure.cutoff: Short half-life (diclofenac, ibuprofen) 24 h · medium (naproxen, celecoxib) 2–3 days · restart 24 h

measure.how: Withhold and confirm the INR. Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate for faster reversal.
measure.cutoff: Low risk: hold 3–5 days to INR < 2.0 · moderate/high: hold 5 days to INR < 1.5 · restart 12–24 h

measure.how: Withhold for moderate and high-risk procedures; renally excreted, so extend with impaired function.
Withhold for moderate and high-risk procedures.
Withhold for moderate and high-risk procedures.
No hold needed for low-risk procedures.
measure.cutoff: Moderate/high: hold 12–24 h · restart at 24 h

measure.how: Monitor with anti-factor Xa; aPTT is unreliable.
measure.cutoff: Low risk: hold 12–24 h, restart 6 h · moderate/high: hold 24 h, restart 24–48 h

measure.how: Withhold for all risk levels; check aPTT; protamine reverses rapidly.
measure.cutoff: Hold 4 h · aim aPTT < 1.5 × control · restart 6–48 h

measure.what: Unfractionated heparin, subcutaneous prophylactic (5000 U 8–12 hourly)
measure.how: Withhold for moderate and high-risk procedures.

measure.what: Dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary stenting
measure.how: Do not interrupt inside these windows without a cardiology opinion.
measure.cutoff: Bare metal stent: at least 6 weeks, ideally 3 months · drug-eluting stent: 6–12 months

TECHNIQUE

Tract: [described — structures deliberately avoided].
Device: [needle gauge / catheter size and type]. Passes: [n]. Specimens: [n] to [histology / microbiology / cytology].

POST-PROCEDURE
Immediate imaging: [no complication / describe].

pitfalls: Categorising by how the procedure feels rather than by the list. A renal biopsy and a nephrostomy are high risk; a liver biopsy is moderate; a thyroid biopsy is low. The instinct that all biopsies are alike is wrong.

Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy inside the stent window. Bare metal stents need at least 6 weeks and ideally 3 months uninterrupted; drug-eluting stents 6–12 months. Ask cardiology before you touch it.

Using the INR to check that a DOAC has worn off. It is not a reliable measure — a normal or slightly raised aPTT for dabigatran, or anti-Xa activity for rivaroxaban and apixaban, is the reassurance available, and none of it is a true reversal assay.
Forgetting renal function when holding a DOAC. All are renally excreted; rivaroxaban goes from 3–4 days to 7 days in CKD stage 4.
Monitoring LMWH with the aPTT. It does not reflect the effect; the anti-factor Xa assay does.

Bridging by reflex. Bridging is for mechanical valves, high-risk atrial fibrillation (CHADS2 5–6), VTE within 3 months or severe thrombophilia, and recent coronary stenting after a cardiology opinion — the BRIDGE and PERIOP2 trials have cast doubt on the practice more widely, and DOAC patients almost never need it.
Holding aspirin for everything. It can generally be continued for low and moderate-risk procedures, and once stopped it takes 5 days, with only platelets or desmopressin to shorten that.

quiz.prompt: A 3 cm lesion sits high and posteriorly in segment VIII of the liver, just under the dome. Ultrasound demonstrates it only through an intercostal window that crosses the costophrenic recess. What is the best plan?
quiz.answer: Plan on CT and take a subcostal, angled tract below the recess
choices: Plan on CT and take a subcostal, angled tract below the recess
Go through the recess in held expiration, accepting the risk
Abandon biopsy and manage on imaging features and follow-up
Use a fine needle rather than a core to make a pleural pass safe
quiz.explain: Crossing the pleural reflection turns a liver biopsy into a chest procedure: pneumothorax, and if the lesion is infected or contains bile, empyema or a bilious effusion. The variables you can actually change are respiratory phase and approach angle. In held expiration the diaphragm rises and the recess descends, which is the wrong direction; in held inspiration the liver descends below the costal margin, and an angled subcostal tract directed cephalad reaches segment VIII while staying extrapleural. That route also crosses a cuff of normal parenchyma, which tamponades the tract and is why a directly subcapsular or exophytic approach is avoided when a parenchymal one exists. Needle calibre changes bleeding risk, not the anatomy of a pleural pass. And abandoning a biopsy that would change management is a decision with its own harms - it is not the cautious option, merely the passive one.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm presacral collection after anterior resection needs drainage, and CT shows the only percutaneous window is transgluteal. Where should the needle pass?
quiz.answer: Medially, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
choices: Medially, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
Laterally, close to the greater trochanter and above piriformis
Through the mid-gluteal region at the level of the sciatic notch
Through the ischiorectal fossa, angling upwards to the collection
quiz.explain: The sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels leave the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and run laterally, so the safe corridor is the medial one: as close to the sacrum as the sacrospinous ligament permits, and inferior to piriformis, which keeps the needle medial and caudal to both structures. A lateral or mid-gluteal pass at the level of the notch is precisely where the nerve and the superior gluteal artery lie, and an arterial injury there is difficult to compress and may need embolisation. Two practical corollaries. Transgluteal drains hurt, and the patient deserves to be warned and given adequate analgesia, since pain is a common reason these catheters are pulled early. And where a transrectal or transvaginal route under ultrasound is available for a low pelvic collection, it is often shorter, less painful and avoids the gluteal anatomy altogether.

quiz.prompt: A patient with cirrhosis needs a percutaneous core biopsy of a liver lesion. The INR is 1.9 and the platelet count is 42 x 10^9/L. What does the SIR 2019 consensus support before proceeding?
quiz.answer: Correct the INR towards 1.5-1.8 and transfuse platelets above 50
choices: Correct the INR towards 1.5-1.8 and transfuse platelets above 50
Proceed as things stand; both values are acceptable for this case
Transfuse platelets above 20 and accept an INR of up to 3.0 here
Defer indefinitely; the coagulopathy of cirrhosis is not correctable
quiz.explain: The 2019 Society of Interventional Radiology consensus sorts procedures into low and high bleeding risk and attaches different thresholds to each. Percutaneous core biopsy of a solid organ, including the liver and the kidney, sits in the high-risk group, where the recommendation is an INR at or below 1.5 to 1.8 and platelets at or above 50 x 10^9/L. The lower thresholds - platelets above 20, INR tolerated up to 2.0 to 3.0 - belong to the low-risk list: thoracentesis, paracentesis, superficial aspiration and biopsy, and most catheter exchanges. The point worth carrying beyond the numbers is that in cirrhosis the INR is a poor predictor of bleeding, because procoagulant and anticoagulant factors fall together and the assay only sees one side. Transfusing plasma to chase a number adds volume and portal pressure; a transjugular route, which also measures the pressure gradient, is often the better answer.

quiz.prompt: A loculated abscess drains poorly through an 8 French catheter and you consider upsizing to 12 French. Treating the catheter as a rigid tube with laminar flow, so that flow varies with the fourth power of the internal radius, by what factor would the flow rate increase? Answer as a number, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The radius ratio is 12 over 8, which is 1.5, and 1.5 to the fourth power is 5.06, so about a fivefold gain from what looks like a modest change of catheter. Since three French equals one millimetre of outer diameter, 8 F is 2.7 mm and 12 F is 4.0 mm. Poiseuille's law is why doubling the French number multiplies flow sixteenfold, and why arguing about a single French size is rarely worth it. Real pus is not a Newtonian fluid, though, and in practice a side-hole blocked by fibrinous debris stops flow long before the physics becomes relevant, which is why the decision is driven by what came back on the aspirating syringe. Thin serous fluid drains happily through 8 to 10 F; frank pus, old haematoma or necrotic debris wants 12 to 14 F or larger, plus regular saline flushing to keep the side holes open.

quiz.prompt: In a service where 20 per cent of CT-guided lung biopsies are complicated by pneumothorax, and one quarter of those pneumothoraces require a chest drain, how many drains would you expect across 200 consecutive biopsies? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty per cent of 200 is 40 pneumothoraces, and a quarter of those is 10 drains, which is a drain rate of 5 per cent. Those proportions are representative: series of CT-guided lung biopsy report pneumothorax in roughly 15 to 25 per cent, with drainage needed in around 5 per cent of biopsies overall. The distinction matters for consent, because the two numbers mean different things to the patient. A pneumothorax that is small, asymptomatic and stable changes nothing about her day; a drain means admission. Quote the number that maps onto the consequence. The risk rises with emphysema anywhere along the tract, with small and deep lesions, with crossing a fissure, with larger needles and, above all, with the number of separate pleural passes - which is the argument for coaxial technique, where one pleural puncture yields several cores.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of Seldinger-technique catheter placement into an abdominal abscess in the order they are performed.
quiz.answer: access-needle guidewire tract-dilatation catheter-advancement wire-removal
quiz.explain: The whole safety argument for Seldinger over trocar technique lives in step two: once the wire is coiled in the cavity, access is secured and everything afterwards is done over it, so a dilator or catheter that will not pass can be exchanged without losing the target. Trocar technique - catheter, stiffening cannula and needle advanced as one assembly in a single pass - is faster and reasonable for a large, superficial, easily seen collection, but it gives you one attempt and no wire to fall back on. Practical points around the sequence: aspirate a sample for microbiology before you flush anything in, dilate only to the size you intend to place, keep the wire under vision as the dilators go, and form and lock the pigtail as the wire comes out. Then confirm the position, secure the catheter properly, and record the volume and character of what drained.

quiz.prompt: A patient on clopidogrel following a drug-eluting stent placed eight weeks ago needs a percutaneous renal biopsy for suspected glomerulonephritis. What is the right approach?
quiz.answer: Discuss with cardiology before any hold, and consider a transjugular route
choices: Discuss with cardiology before any hold, and consider a transjugular route
Hold the clopidogrel for five days and proceed, as SIR 2019 advises
Proceed on clopidogrel, since renal biopsy is a low bleeding risk case
Hold clopidogrel for seven days and bridge with heparin in the interval
quiz.explain: Both halves of the naive answer are individually defensible and together they are wrong. SIR 2019 does classify renal biopsy as high bleeding risk and does suggest withholding clopidogrel for five days. But a drug-eluting stent at eight weeks is inside the period where interrupting dual antiplatelet therapy risks stent thrombosis, an event whose case fatality is far higher than that of a renal haematoma. This is a decision that belongs to a conversation, not to a protocol, and the cardiologist may say the biopsy can wait a month. If it cannot, a transjugular renal biopsy lets the tract be tamponaded or coiled from within the vein, which is why it exists for exactly this patient. Heparin bridging is the classic error: it substitutes for warfarin, which acts on the coagulation cascade, and does nothing for a platelet-mediated mechanism.

quiz.prompt: You are planning a CT-guided biopsy of a retroperitoneal node. Using that case as the example, set out what makes a tract unsafe, naming at least four structures or features you would refuse to cross and saying why each one matters.
quiz.answer: The criterion is the safest path, not the shortest. I would not cross bowel, because a needle through colon or small bowel seeds the retroperitoneum with organisms and can produce an abscess or a fistula. I would not cross a major vessel - the aorta, cava, renal or mesenteric vessels - and I would use intravenous contrast or Doppler to be sure a suspected node is not an aneurysm or a vascular tumour. I would not cross the pancreas, because a needle tract through it risks pancreatitis and a pancreatic fistula. I would not cross the pleura or the costophrenic recess for an upper retroperitoneal target, because that converts the complication list into pneumothorax and empyema. And I would avoid a nerve or the neurovascular bundle running at the inferior margin of a rib, entering over the superior edge instead. Where a choice exists, passing through a cuff of normal solid organ that will tamponade is safer than a free peritoneal route.
quiz.explain: A safe window is a positive thing you construct, not the absence of an obvious obstacle. Build it from four questions. What is between the skin and the target on every slice of the planned angle, in the respiratory phase the patient will actually hold? What will bleed, and can it be compressed or tamponaded if it does? What is contaminated, and what would contamination cost here? And what could I not fix in this room? Two anatomical details repay memorising: the intercostal artery is protected in the costal groove laterally but runs unprotected and tortuous within about 6 cm of the midline posteriorly, and in the elderly it can wander mid-space; and a hypervascular lesion, a hydatid cyst or a phaeochromocytoma is a reason not to put a needle in at all until the diagnosis has been considered.

quiz.prompt: A 19 year old has a destructive lytic lesion of the distal femur with aggressive periosteal reaction and a soft tissue mass. The local orthopaedic team asks you to biopsy it on tomorrow's list. What do you do, and why does the position of the tract matter more here than almost anywhere else?
quiz.answer: I would not biopsy it locally. I would complete the imaging first - MRI of the whole bone and staging - and refer the patient to the regional sarcoma centre so that the biopsy is performed there, or at least along a tract agreed with the surgeon who will operate. The reason is that a biopsy tract through a suspected primary bone sarcoma is contaminated with tumour and must be excised en bloc with the specimen at the definitive resection. A tract placed through the wrong compartment, through a neurovascular bundle's plane, or transversely across the limb, can make that excision impossible and convert a limb-sparing operation into an amputation. Getting the biopsy technically right is worth nothing if the route has closed off the operation.
quiz.explain: This is the strongest version of a general rule: before the needle, ask who will treat this and what your tract does to their options. Primary bone and soft tissue sarcoma is the classic, and the evidence that unplanned local biopsy worsens outcomes is why national pathways route these lesions to specialist centres. Two neighbouring rules belong with it. A testicular mass is never approached percutaneously - it is explored inguinally with cord control, because a scrotal route changes the lymphatic drainage. And elsewhere, tract seeding is real but rare: cumulative rates of the order of a few per cent are reported for hepatocellular carcinoma, and mesothelioma is the other name usually cited. Rare is not the same as ignorable, which is why coaxial technique and a route that a future resection could take are good habits everywhere, not just in the femur.

quiz.prompt: Aspiration of a 9 cm post-appendicectomy collection returns thick, foul, particulate pus that barely moves through the 18 gauge needle. What catheter would you place?
quiz.answer: A 14 French locking pigtail, with regular saline flushes
choices: A 14 French locking pigtail, with regular saline flushes
An 8 French locking pigtail, upsized later if it blocks
A 6 French pigtail, since the tract should stay narrow
A 10 French straight catheter without a locking loop
quiz.explain: The character of the aspirate decides the calibre, not the size of the cavity. Fluid that will not pass an 18 gauge needle will not pass an 8 French side hole for long, and planning to upsize later means a second procedure for a patient who is already septic. Thin serous fluid drains through 8 to 10 F; viscous pus, haematoma or necrotic debris needs 12 to 14 F or more. The locking loop is not a detail: catheter dislodgement is the commonest reason a drain stops working, and a straight catheter in a mobile patient is asking for it. Prescribe flushing - typically 10 mL of saline two or three times a day - and record the output. If output falls while the patient stays septic, image before concluding the abscess has resolved: a blocked or displaced catheter, an undrained locule, or an enteric fistula are the usual explanations.

quiz.prompt: A 78 year old on home oxygen is having a painful drainage under conscious sedation with midazolam and fentanyl. Two minutes after a top-up she is unrousable, her respiratory rate is 6 and her saturations are 84 per cent on 4 litres. What comes first?
quiz.answer: Open the airway, give high flow oxygen and support ventilation
choices: Open the airway, give high flow oxygen and support ventilation
Give flumazenil 200 micrograms and repeat until she rouses
Give naloxone 400 micrograms intravenously and then reassess
Call the arrest team and begin chest compressions immediately
quiz.explain: Airway and breathing before pharmacology. A head tilt and chin lift, an airway adjunct, high-flow oxygen and bag-mask ventilation fix the physiology immediately, while any drug takes a minute or two to work and may not be the right drug. Reversal agents come second and with caveats: naloxone should be titrated in small increments of 100 micrograms or so and has a shorter half-life than fentanyl, so re-sedation follows and the patient must be watched; flumazenil can precipitate seizures and is avoided in anyone on long-term benzodiazepines. She has a pulse and a rhythm, so compressions would be wrong. The part that actually prevents this is upstream: continuous capnography, one person whose only task is monitoring the patient, reduced doses for age and for chronic respiratory disease, and small increments with enough time between them to see the effect before giving more.

quiz.prompt: Set out what should happen to a patient in the four hours after a CT-guided lung biopsy in a day-case service, and state two circumstances in which you would not discharge them that afternoon.
quiz.answer: Immediately after the needle comes out, roll the patient puncture-site down to help seal the pleural breach, then observe with regular observations and pulse oximetry. An erect chest radiograph at about one hour is the key check, since most pneumothoraces are apparent by then. If it is satisfactory and the patient is comfortable, continue observation for a further two to three hours before discharge with written advice on what to do if breathlessness or chest pain develops, and with a responsible adult to stay overnight within reasonable reach of a hospital. I would not discharge if the radiograph shows a pneumothorax that is enlarging or symptomatic, or has needed a drain; and I would not discharge if the social criteria fail - nobody at home, or a long journey from any emergency department - however good the radiograph looks. More than a trace of haemoptysis is a third reason to keep them.
quiz.explain: British Thoracic Society guidance built this pathway around one observation: the great majority of post-biopsy pneumothoraces declare themselves within the first hour, but a minority appear later, which is why the advice sheet and the accompanying adult are as much a part of the safety net as the radiograph. Two refinements worth knowing. The rollover manoeuvre and, in some services, a blood patch or saline instilled through the coaxial cannula as it is withdrawn, aim to reduce the leak at the moment of maximal risk. And a small, stable, asymptomatic pneumothorax does not need a drain: it needs a repeat film and a patient who understands what to watch for. Systemic air embolism is the rare catastrophe to know about - sudden neurological deficit or arrest during or just after the biopsy - managed with 100 per cent oxygen, head-down left lateral positioning and urgent hyperbaric referral.

quiz.prompt: The team is scrubbed and the patient is draped for a renal biopsy. The pause immediately before the needle goes in exists chiefly to catch one of the following. Which one?
quiz.answer: That the side on the consent form matches the side on the images
choices: That the side on the consent form matches the side on the images
That the histopathology request card has been completed correctly
That the sedation drugs have been drawn into labelled syringes
That the post-procedure observation chart is at the bedside ready
quiz.explain: All four are good practice, and three of them belong earlier in the checklist. The pause immediately before the needle exists for the never-events: wrong patient, wrong side, wrong site, wrong procedure. Laterality is the classic failure and it is not a failure of care but of geometry and assumption - images can be displayed flipped, a referral can name the wrong kidney, the prone patient's left is on your right, and by this point the patient is draped and sedated and can no longer correct you. So the pause is spoken aloud, by the whole team, against two independent sources: the signed consent form and the images on the screen. Add allergies, the coagulation results and antibiotic prophylaxis to the same thirty seconds. Consent itself belongs earlier and unsedated, with the specific numbers for this procedure - here, the risk of significant bleeding and of needing transfusion or embolisation.

module_contract.goal: Assign a VI-RADS category from a multiparametric bladder MRI, defend it when the sequences disagree, and stage urothelial carcinoma beyond the bladder wall and into the upper tract.

approach.detail: VI-RADS is built from a structural (T2W), a diffusion (DWI) and a contrast-enhanced (DCE) category — score each, then combine.

approach.step: Trace the muscularis propria on T2W
approach.detail: Look for a continuous low-signal line under the tumour. Interruption is the key structural sign of invasion.

approach.step: Check for early focal enhancement on DCE
approach.detail: Early enhancement that extends focally into or through the muscularis propria tracks with invasion.
A continuous intermediate-to-low signal line under the tumour argues against invasion; focal extension into or through it argues for it.
Size above or below 1 cm separates VI-RADS 1 from 2 when the muscularis propria line is otherwise intact.
Combine the three categories into the single VI-RADS score, then stage any disease beyond the bladder wall separately.

measure.how: Longest diameter on T2W.
measure.cutoff: < 1 cm favours VI-RADS 1 · > 1 cm favours VI-RADS 2 when the muscularis propria line is intact

classify.name: VI-RADS
rows: Continuous low-signal muscularis propria line, lesion < 1 cm
Continuous intermediate signal line of muscularis propria
No early enhancement of the muscularis propria line
Lesion > 1 cm, papillary with a stalk and/or high signal intensity
Continuous intermediate signal line in lesions > 1 cm
Low-signal muscular layer, no early enhancement
No stalk in a papillary tumour, but the low-signal line is still continuous
Continuous low-signal line of the muscularis propria
No focal early enhancement of the muscularis propria
Interruption of the low-signal muscularis propria line
Focal extension into the muscularis propria
Focal early enhancement extending into the muscularis propria
Tumour extends into the peri-vesical fat
Extension throughout the bladder wall and into the extravesical fat
Early enhancement into the extravesical adipose tissue
classify.note: VI-RADS 1-2 argue against muscle invasion; 4-5 argue for it. Category 3 is the genuinely equivocal group where the three sequences do not agree cleanly.

FINDINGS

pitfalls: Scoring on an underdistended bladder. Wall thickening from an empty or non-distended bladder mimics tumour and disrupts the muscularis propria assessment.
Letting a single discordant sequence override the other two. VI-RADS is a synthesis of T2W, DWI and DCE — do not anchor on whichever one looks worst.
Missing early enhancement because the dynamic series was not truly early. Delayed post-contrast imaging cannot distinguish focal early enhancement from generalised bladder wall enhancement.
Applying VI-RADS to a bladder with recent instrumentation or biopsy. Post-procedural change mimics invasion on all three sequences.
Stopping at the VI-RADS category without staging locoregional and upper-tract disease when the category is 4 or 5.
