quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old man with painless visible haematuria has a 2.5 cm broad-based tumour on the left lateral bladder wall at cystoscopy. The urologist asks for multiparametric MRI before taking him to theatre. Which management question is the MRI being asked to answer?
quiz.answer: Whether tumour extends into the muscularis propria, since that separates transurethral resection from cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy
choices: Whether tumour extends into the muscularis propria, since that separates transurethral resection from cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Whether the tumour is high grade, since that separates simple surveillance from a course of intravesical BCG after resection
Whether the histology is urothelial rather than squamous or glandular, since that changes which systemic agents are chosen
Whether residual papillary tumour will be left at the base, since that decides if a second-look resection is required
quiz.explain: Bladder cancer splits into two diseases at one anatomical line. Non-muscle-invasive disease (Ta, Tis, T1) is managed endoscopically with intravesical therapy and surveillance; muscle-invasive disease (T2 and above) earns neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy and radical cystectomy or bladder-preserving chemoradiation. That single question is what VI-RADS was built to answer, and it is the one thing cystoscopy cannot settle, because the scope sees only the luminal surface. Grade and histological subtype come from the pathologist, not from MRI. Residual tumour at the base is a resection-quality question answered by re-resection. And note the sequencing: TURBT itself causes oedema, granulation and enhancement at the base, so the most informative MRI is the one done before the resection, not after it.

quiz.prompt: Your bladder MRI protocol asks patients not to void for one to two hours before the scan. State the degree of bladder filling you are aiming for, and say what goes wrong on the images when the bladder is under-filled and when it is over-filled.
quiz.answer: Aim for moderate distension. An under-filled bladder produces apparent diffuse wall thickening and can hide a small tumour against the crumpled wall; an over-filled bladder stretches and thins the wall, flattens an exophytic tumour against it, and provokes movement from discomfort.
quiz.explain: VI-RADS rests on seeing a continuous low-signal muscularis propria, and that line only behaves predictably in a moderately distended bladder. Empty the bladder and the wall folds on itself: it looks thickened everywhere, a small sessile tumour disappears into the folds, and the dark muscle line becomes impossible to follow. Fill it too far and the wall is stretched thin, a papillary tumour is pressed flat and loses its stalk, and the patient cannot lie still for a diffusion series. The practical instruction is to void, then wait one to two hours, or to drink a measured volume beforehand. If the study is done at either extreme, say so in the report — a VI-RADS category assigned on an under-distended bladder is not the same evidence as one assigned on a good study.

quiz.prompt: A bladder multiparametric MRI is technically good on all three sequences. The T2 structural category is 3, the diffusion-weighted score is 4 and the dynamic contrast-enhanced score is 4. Give the overall VI-RADS category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: VI-RADS scores each of the three sequences from 1 to 5 and then combines them into one category, but the combination is not an average and not a majority vote. Diffusion is the dominant sequence, with dynamic contrast enhancement second and T2 providing the structural framework. Here diffusion and the dynamic series both say 4, so the overall category is 4 — muscle invasion is likely — and the T2 score of 3 does not pull it down. VI-RADS 4 means the low-signal muscularis propria is breached on the sequences that matter, and it should push the team towards staging for muscle-invasive disease rather than towards a purely endoscopic plan. Most published series use a cut-off of VI-RADS 3 or above to call muscle invasion, gaining sensitivity; a cut-off of 4 or above trades some of that sensitivity for specificity.

quiz.prompt: A 1.8 cm papillary bladder tumour is bright on high b-value diffusion imaging, while the stalk at its base is dark on diffusion and bright on ADC. The low-signal muscularis propria beneath the tumour is unbroken on T2, on diffusion and on the early dynamic images. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Muscle invasion is unlikely: this reads as VI-RADS 2, and complete transurethral resection with sampling of the base is the appropriate step
choices: Muscle invasion is unlikely: this reads as VI-RADS 2, and complete transurethral resection with sampling of the base is the appropriate step
Muscle invasion is likely: restricted diffusion within the tumour itself makes this VI-RADS 4 regardless of what the muscle line does
Muscle invasion is equivocal: a dark stalk on diffusion is a post-resection change, so the study should be reported as VI-RADS 3
The study is not interpretable: a stalk that is dark on diffusion means the b-value was too low, and the sequence needs repeating
quiz.explain: This is the inchworm sign, and it is one of the most useful patterns in bladder MRI. A papillary tumour has a fibrovascular submucosal stalk. The tumour is cellular and restricts diffusion, so it is bright on high b-value images with a low ADC; the stalk is loose oedematous connective tissue, so it is dark on high b-value images and bright on ADC. The bright cap sitting on a dark base gives the arched look of an inchworm, and its presence tells you the tumour is exophytic on a stalk with the wall beneath it intact — the picture of non-muscle-invasive disease. Restricted diffusion inside a urothelial tumour is expected and says nothing about stage on its own; what matters is whether the dark muscle line is interrupted. Under VI-RADS, an exophytic tumour with a stalk and an intact muscle line scores 1 if under 1 cm and 2 at 1 cm or more.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the tissue planes that a bladder tumour crosses as its T category rises, working from the luminal surface outward.
quiz.answer: urothelium lamina-propria muscularis-propria perivesical-fat prostatic-stroma
quiz.explain: The T categories of bladder cancer are simply a list of the layers a tumour has eaten through. Ta and Tis sit in the urothelium; T1 breaches the basement membrane into the lamina propria; T2 is in the muscularis propria, split into T2a for the inner half and T2b for the outer half; T3 reaches perivesical fat, microscopically as T3a and as a visible extravesical mass as T3b; T4a is direct contiguous invasion of an adjacent organ such as prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina, and T4b is pelvic or abdominal wall. Knowing the ladder tells you where imaging is strong and where it is weak. MRI is good at the muscularis propria step, which is the step that changes treatment. It cannot see microscopic perivesical spread, so it cannot reliably separate T2b from T3a — a limitation worth stating in the report rather than papering over.

quiz.prompt: A bladder MRI is excellent on T2 and on the dynamic contrast series, but the diffusion-weighted images are wrecked by susceptibility artefact from a right hip replacement. Say which sequence now carries the VI-RADS assessment, and what the report must state.
quiz.answer: The dynamic contrast-enhanced series carries it. Diffusion is normally the dominant sequence, and the dynamic series takes over when diffusion is non-diagnostic. The report must say that the diffusion images are unusable, that the category rests on the DCE and T2 findings, and that confidence is correspondingly reduced.
quiz.explain: The VI-RADS hierarchy is diffusion first, dynamic contrast second, T2 as the structural scaffold — but the hierarchy assumes each sequence is diagnostic. Echo-planar diffusion is the sequence most easily destroyed by metal, bowel gas and motion, and a hip prosthesis on the side of interest will do it. When diffusion fails, the dynamic series inherits the decision: on early dynamic images tumour and the inner layer enhance before the muscularis propria does, so an intact non-enhancing dark muscle band in that early window is reassuring, and early enhancement extending into the muscle is not. Say this explicitly in the report. A category assigned without its dominant sequence carries less weight, and the urologist deciding between resection and cystectomy is entitled to know which evidence the number rests on.

quiz.prompt: An MRI is requested six days after transurethral resection because the specimen contained no muscle. At the resection base there is wall thickening, restricted diffusion and early enhancement that would otherwise read as VI-RADS 4. What is the right response?
quiz.answer: Report the appearance but state that post-resection change cannot be separated from residual tumour here, and advise reassessment at least two weeks after the resection
choices: Report the appearance but state that post-resection change cannot be separated from residual tumour here, and advise reassessment at least two weeks after the resection
Report VI-RADS 4 at face value, since restricted diffusion at a resection base reflects residual tumour rather than granulation tissue in most patients
Report VI-RADS 2, since enhancement and restricted diffusion this soon after a resection are granulation tissue and carry no diagnostic weight at all
Report the bladder as normal for the interval, since wall thickening at a resection base always settles and no further imaging is warranted
quiz.explain: A fresh resection bed does everything a tumour does. Granulation tissue is cellular and hyperaemic, so it restricts diffusion and enhances early; oedema and haemorrhage thicken the wall and blur the dark muscle line; a perforation of the detrusor during resection may leave inflammatory change tracking into perivesical fat that mimics T3. This is the single commonest cause of overstaging on bladder MRI. The VI-RADS recommendation is to scan before resection wherever possible, and if the study must follow a resection, to leave an interval of at least two weeks so the acute inflammatory phase settles. Neither of the confident extremes is defensible: calling it tumour risks a cystectomy on granulation tissue, and calling it nothing risks missing residual disease. Report what you see, state the confounder, and give the interval at which the question can be answered.

quiz.prompt: A woman on maintenance intravesical BCG for high-grade T1 disease has surveillance MRI. There is smooth diffuse wall thickening around the whole bladder with early enhancement and mildly restricted diffusion, and no focal mass anywhere. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Read it as granulomatous inflammatory change from BCG, report the absence of any focal mass, and correlate with cystoscopy and urine cytology
choices: Read it as granulomatous inflammatory change from BCG, report the absence of any focal mass, and correlate with cystoscopy and urine cytology
Read it as diffuse carcinoma in situ, assign VI-RADS 4, and recommend cystectomy on the strength of the enhancement and diffusion findings
Assign VI-RADS 3 to the bladder as a whole, since diffuse enhancement is equivocal and that category conveys the uncertainty faithfully
Repeat the study in 48 hours with a fuller bladder, since diffuse thickening of this degree is an artefact of poor distension alone
quiz.explain: Intravesical BCG sets up a granulomatous cystitis. The wall thickens, enhances and shows mild diffusion restriction, often circumferentially and often for months after the last instillation. VI-RADS was designed for, and validated on, a bladder containing a visible tumour that has not been recently instilled or resected; applied to a diffusely inflamed bladder it will overcall. The discriminator is focality and asymmetry — a discrete mass with its own stalk or a segmental interruption of the dark muscle line means something, while smooth symmetrical change does not. Carcinoma in situ is flat and is essentially invisible on MRI, which is precisely why cystoscopy with biopsy and urine cytology remain the arbiters of BCG failure. Report the pattern, name the confounder, and hand the question back to the endoscopist rather than manufacturing a category the system was not built to give.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a muscle-invasive bladder cancer shows a 12 mm short-axis left obturator node and a 9 mm short-axis right common iliac node. There is no nodal disease above the aortic bifurcation. Give the N category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: Bladder nodal staging is anatomical before it is numerical. N1 is a single node in the true pelvis — perivesical, obturator, internal iliac, external iliac or sacral. N2 is multiple nodes within that same true pelvic group. N3 is disease in a common iliac node, which sits above the true pelvis but is still regional. Anything higher, in the retroperitoneum, is no longer nodal staging at all: it counts as distant disease. Here the obturator node alone would be N1, but the common iliac node overrides it and makes the case N3. Size thresholds are conventions rather than rules — 8 mm short axis is commonly used for pelvic nodes and 10 mm above the bifurcation — and shape, necrosis and clustering matter as much as the caliper. The distinction is not academic: N3 disease remains within the field a radical lymphadenectomy or a radiotherapy volume can cover.

quiz.prompt: A bladder tumour at the trigone extends through the full thickness of the wall, and there is intermediate-signal tumour replacing the adjacent prostatic stroma in direct continuity with the bladder mass. The pelvic side walls and obturator internus are clear. How should T be reported?
quiz.answer: T4a, since tumour spreading contiguously from the bladder into prostatic stroma is what that category describes and it still points towards radical surgery
choices: T4a, since tumour spreading contiguously from the bladder into prostatic stroma is what that category describes and it still points towards radical surgery
T3b, since extension of any degree towards the prostate beyond the detrusor is graded simply as macroscopic extravesical disease
T4b, since involvement of a neighbouring pelvic organ by direct spread is the category used to denote surgically unresectable disease
T2b, since the prostatic stroma lies deep to the outer half of the detrusor and is therefore staged together with the muscle layer
quiz.explain: T4 divides into two very different prognoses. T4a is contiguous invasion of an adjacent organ — prostatic stroma, seminal vesicles, uterus or vagina — and remains resectable, so it belongs in the radical cystectomy conversation. T4b is fixation to the pelvic side wall or abdominal wall, and that is the category that generally takes surgery off the table. T3b is a macroscopic perivesical soft tissue mass without organ invasion, which is not what is described here. One nuance to keep: prostatic stromal invasion counts as T4a when tumour reaches it directly through the bladder wall, but urothelial carcinoma spreading along the prostatic urethra and into the stroma from within is staged under the urethral rules instead. On MRI, look for intermediate-signal tumour replacing the normally heterogeneous prostatic tissue rather than merely abutting it.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with previously treated bladder cancer presents with fresh right-sided haematuria and a CT urogram is booked. Say which acquisition on that study answers the upper tract question, and what you are hunting for in the collecting system.
quiz.answer: The excretory or delayed acquisition, taken several minutes after injection once the collecting systems and ureters are opacified. Look for a fixed filling defect, focal urothelial thickening or an enhancing soft tissue mass, an irregular stricture, and hydronephrosis or calyceal dilatation above the level of the lesion.
quiz.explain: CT urography is a multiphase study and each phase does a different job. Unenhanced images find calculi and give a baseline density. The nephrographic phase, at around 100 seconds, is where renal parenchymal tumours are seen. Only the excretory phase, obtained several minutes later, distends and opacifies the urothelium so that a filling defect can be identified — and upper tract urothelial carcinoma lives in the urothelium. The three appearances to know are a filling defect, focal or circumferential wall thickening, and an infiltrative stricture with upstream obstruction. Enhancement is what separates tumour from clot: a clot does not enhance, and it moves between phases or between studies. Compare the two sides on the same image, because subtle asymmetric thickening reads far better as a comparison than as an absolute measurement.

quiz.prompt: The CT urogram shows a 1.5 cm enhancing filling defect in the right renal pelvis with mild upstream calyceal dilatation, alongside the separately confirmed bladder tumour. What does this add to the plan?
quiz.answer: It signals a synchronous upper tract primary that needs ureteroscopy and its own staging, since the urothelium behaves as a single field at risk
choices: It signals a synchronous upper tract primary that needs ureteroscopy and its own staging, since the urothelium behaves as a single field at risk
It most likely represents blood clot shed from the bladder tumour, so a repeat urogram in three months is the proportionate response here
It represents a metastasis from the bladder primary, so systemic chemotherapy replaces any local treatment of the renal pelvic lesion
It has little staging consequence, since the bladder tumour drives management and the renal pelvic lesion is treated only if it obstructs
quiz.explain: Urothelium runs continuously from renal calyx to urethra and is exposed to the same carcinogens along its whole length, so urothelial carcinoma is characteristically multifocal in space and metachronous in time. A patient with a bladder tumour and a separate enhancing renal pelvic lesion has two primaries until proved otherwise, and the upper tract one is staged and treated in its own right — ureteroscopy with biopsy, and radical nephroureterectomy including a bladder cuff for high-risk disease, or kidney-sparing treatment for low-risk lesions. Enhancement is the point that excludes clot, which is avascular and mobile. The field effect also runs the other way: after nephroureterectomy for an upper tract tumour, bladder recurrence is common enough that cystoscopic surveillance is routine. Report the lesion, its length and site, the degree of obstruction, and the contralateral kidney, because renal function shapes whether cisplatin is an option.

curriculum_modules.title: Bone Tumours: Lytic, Sclerotic and Cartilage

module_contract.goal: Read a bone lesion in order of age, site, margin, periosteal reaction and matrix, and decide what to leave alone, what to follow and what must reach the sarcoma unit before anyone puts a needle in it.

approach.detail: The most important clinical clue in differentiating bone tumours. Under 30 the field is primary lesions; over 40 metastases and myeloma have to be in the differential of anything.
The most reliable indicator of whether an osteolytic lesion is benign or malignant. Narrow and sharply drawn means benign; wide and imperceptible means aggressive.

Epiphysis, metaphysis or diaphysis, and centric or eccentric within the bone. An epiphyseal lesion abutting the articular surface in a skeletally mature patient is a giant cell tumour until proven otherwise.
Thick, wavy and uniform is chronic irritation and benign. Multilayered, lamellated, perpendicular to the cortex, or a Codman triangle is aggressive.
Judge it but do not trust a normal-looking cortex: small round cell tumours can grow permeatively through the Haversian channels while the cortex still looks nearly normal.
Chondroid mineralises as rings-and-arcs, popcorn, stippled or flocculent. Osteoid is trabecular in benign lesions and cloud-like or ill-defined amorphous in osteosarcoma.
Leave alone, follow, or refer. Anything with a wide zone of transition, aggressive periosteal reaction or a soft tissue mass goes to the sarcoma unit before anyone puts a needle in it.

measure.how: The single strongest prior. Apply it before you describe anything.
Longest dimension of a chondroid lesion, used to decide whether it needs follow-up.
Measured on axial slices as the proportion of the lesion circumference affected.
Thickness of the cap on fluid-sensitive MRI or CT.
measure.cutoff: WHO criterion 2 cm — resect above this to exclude chondrosarcoma

classify.name: Reading the lesion — margin, periosteum, matrix
rows: Narrow, sharply definable, with or without a sclerotic rim
The most reliable single indicator of benign versus malignant
Thick, wavy, uniform callus from chronic irritation
Multilayered or lamellated, or bone formed perpendicular to the cortex; Codman triangle
A Codman triangle is periosteum lifted off the cortex, meeting bone at an angle
Destroyed — or deceptively normal with permeative growth through the Haversian channels
A normal-looking cortex does not exclude a small round cell tumour
Rings-and-arcs, popcorn, focal stippled or flocculent
Same mineral, with cortical destruction, periostitis, soft tissue mass or perilesional marrow oedema
Mineral type names the tissue; the surrounding features grade it
classify.note: Well-defined lytic lesions run through FEGNOMASHIC: fibrous dysplasia, enchondroma, giant cell tumour, non-ossifying fibroma, osteoblastoma, metastases, aneurysmal bone cyst, solitary bone cyst, hyperparathyroidism (brown tumour), infection, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma. Under 30, ABC, SBC, NOF, eosinophilic granuloma and chondroblastoma dominate; over 40, add metastasis and plasmacytoma to every list.

IMPRESSION

pitfalls: Describing the lesion before asking the age. Age is the most important clue and it reorders the differential more than any imaging feature does.
Trusting an intact cortex. Small round cell tumours grow permeatively through the Haversian channels and the cortex can look almost normal on the radiograph.

Grading a cartilage lesion on mineral alone. Rings-and-arcs say chondroid, not benign — it is cortical destruction, periostitis, a soft tissue mass or perilesional oedema that separates high-grade chondrosarcoma from an atypical cartilaginous tumour.
Biopsying locally. A lesion with a wide zone of transition or aggressive periosteal reaction reaches the sarcoma unit before the needle, because the tract has to be planned into the resection.
Forgetting metastasis and myeloma over 40. Any lytic lesion in that age group carries them in the differential regardless of how the margin looks.

quiz.prompt: Two incidental lesions arrive on the same list. A 14-year-old has an eccentric, lobulated lucency in the distal tibial metaphysis with a thick sclerotic rim and an intact cortex, seen after a sprain. A 61-year-old has a lucency in the femoral diaphysis with a wide zone of transition and a moth-eaten margin. How should each be handled?
quiz.answer: Leave the first alone without follow-up, and stage and refer the second one urgently
choices: Leave the first alone without follow-up, and stage and refer the second one urgently
Follow the first with radiographs at six months, and follow the second in the same way
Biopsy both, since a lucent lesion in bone is not characterised on radiographs alone
Refer both to the sarcoma unit, since the age of the patient is not a discriminator
quiz.explain: The margin is the best radiographic index of how fast a lesion is growing, because it shows whether the bone has had time to wall the lesion off. A thick sclerotic rim around an eccentric metaphyseal lucency in a teenager is a non-ossifying fibroma, a lesion that involutes and needs nothing, not even a follow-up film; putting a note in the report that it requires no action is more useful than a date. A moth-eaten margin with a wide zone of transition means destruction is outrunning repair, and in a patient past 40 the leading candidates are metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma, with primary sarcoma less common but still on the list. Age is the strongest single prior in bone tumours, which is why it belongs at the top of the read rather than in the clinical details you skipped. Biopsying the first lesion would be an avoidable operation on a normal variant.

quiz.prompt: A 17-year-old has months of night pain in the mid-femur, relieved within half an hour of taking ibuprofen. The radiograph shows a fusiform band of dense solid periosteal new bone along the cortex, with no soft tissue mass and no destruction. What imaging should follow, and why?
quiz.answer: Thin-slice CT of the segment, to find the small lucent nidus buried inside the reaction
choices: Thin-slice CT of the segment, to find the small lucent nidus buried inside the reaction
Contrast-enhanced MRI alone, since the reactive marrow oedema will localise the lesion
Radiographs of the opposite femur, to compare the thickness of the two cortices
A whole-body isotope scan, to establish that the lesion is solitary before any biopsy
quiz.explain: Dense, solid, uninterrupted periosteal new bone is the signature of a slow process, and combined with night pain that responds to a non-steroidal drug in a teenager, it points to an osteoid osteoma with its nidus hidden inside the thickened cortex. Thin-slice CT is the test that finds the nidus, typically under 15 mm and often with a central density. MRI is the classic trap here: the florid marrow and soft tissue oedema around the lesion can be read as infection or as an aggressive tumour, and the small nidus is lost inside it, which is why CT rather than MRI settles the diagnosis. The report should state where the nidus sits, whether it is intracortical, subperiosteal or intramedullary, and how far it lies from skin and neurovascular structures, because thermal ablation is the usual treatment and those are the numbers the operator needs. Isotope imaging is sensitive but non-specific.

quiz.prompt: A 12-year-old has three weeks of pain and fever, and radiographs of the femoral diaphysis show a permeative pattern with lamellated periosteal reaction. MRI shows an enhancing soft tissue mass encircling the shaft that is considerably larger than the area of bone destruction, with no rim-enhancing collection. What is the most useful conclusion for the referrer?
quiz.answer: A solid mass out of proportion to the bone destruction favours tumour over infection here
choices: A solid mass out of proportion to the bone destruction favours tumour over infection here
The permeative pattern with fever makes acute osteomyelitis much the likelier diagnosis
The lamellated periosteal reaction is specific for infection and excludes a bone sarcoma
No useful comment is possible until an aspirate has been taken and sent for culture
quiz.explain: Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis overlap almost completely on the plain film in this age group: both are diaphyseal, both are permeative, both raise inflammatory markers, and both can produce fever and a lamellated reaction. The discriminator is what MRI shows outside the bone. Ewing sarcoma builds a solid, enhancing, circumferential mass that is often far larger than the bone destruction that produced it, spreading through the cortex without destroying much of it. Osteomyelitis produces oedema, subperiosteal pus and a rim-enhancing abscess, sometimes with a sequestrum, and the soft tissue change is inflammatory rather than mass-like. The practical output is not a diagnosis but a route: this child should reach the sarcoma service before anyone aspirates, because a tract or a drain placed for a presumed abscess contaminates compartments and can convert a limb-sparing resection into something larger.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT in a woman with breast cancer shows a 9 mm sclerotic focus in the L2 vertebral body. It has spiculated margins that blend into the surrounding trabeculae, and it was present and unchanged on a CT from four years ago. What do you report, and what evidence do you use to justify it?
quiz.answer: Report it as a benign bone island needing no follow-up: it has been stable for four years, its brush-border margins interdigitate with the surrounding trabeculae, and its uniform very high attenuation is greater than an osteoblastic deposit would show; if there had been no prior study, absent or minimal uptake on a bone scan would carry the same argument.
quiz.explain: Three lines of evidence separate an enostosis from an osteoblastic deposit, and the strongest is an old study: a sclerotic focus that has not changed over years is not a metastasis. Morphology is the second, since an enostosis has the thorny brush border that merges with normal trabeculae, while a deposit tends to have a rounded, ill-defined edge that pushes trabeculae aside. Attenuation is the third: enostoses are very dense and homogeneous, and published CT thresholds of roughly 885 HU for the mean and 1060 HU for the maximum have been used to separate them from osteoblastic deposits, which are typically less dense. On MRI an enostosis is low signal on every sequence with no surrounding marrow oedema, and on isotope imaging it is usually cold, although a large one can take up a little tracer. The trap in an oncology patient is the healing deposit that has sclerosed under treatment, which is another reason the old films matter.

quiz.prompt: MRI of the proximal humerus shows a lobulated cartilage lesion. On the axial images the adjacent cortex measures 6 mm thick, and the deepest endosteal scalloping measures 4.5 mm. Express the depth of scalloping as a percentage of the cortical thickness. Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Four and a half divided by six is 0.75, so the scalloping is 75 per cent of the cortical thickness, and that clears the commonly used threshold of two thirds, or about 67 per cent, which is one of the features that shifts a cartilage lesion out of the enchondroma category. It rarely stands alone. The others worth measuring or describing are length beyond about 5 to 6 cm, cortical expansion or remodelling, periosteal reaction, any soft tissue extension, and pain arising from the lesion itself rather than from the rotator cuff or the joint. Nomenclature matters when reporting: in the long bones of the arms and legs, a low-grade cartilage tumour is now called an atypical cartilaginous tumour and is often managed by curettage or by surveillance, whereas identical histology in the pelvis, scapula, ribs or spine is treated as chondrosarcoma because it behaves worse. Enchondromas in the hands are the standing exception, since they scallop and expand while remaining benign.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old has a 7 cm lobulated lesion with rings-and-arcs mineralisation in the proximal femoral diaphysis, with deep endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening, and localised pain at that site with no history of injury. What is the right course?
quiz.answer: Refer to the sarcoma service for staging and biopsy, since these features suggest malignancy
choices: Refer to the sarcoma service for staging and biopsy, since these features suggest malignancy
Report an enchondroma and reassure, since rings-and-arcs mineralisation indicates benignity
Arrange a repeat radiograph in twelve months, since cartilage lesions change very slowly
Arrange a local curettage, since low-grade cartilage lesions are cured by curettage alone
quiz.explain: Rings and arcs tell you the matrix is cartilage and nothing whatever about its grade, since enchondroma and chondrosarcoma mineralise in the same way. The features that carry the weight here are size beyond 5 to 6 cm, deep endosteal scalloping, cortical thickening or remodelling, and unexplained pain localised to the lesion: in a long bone that combination is a chondrosarcoma until histology says otherwise. Local curettage would be the wrong operation performed by the wrong team, and it also spills tumour into the surrounding tissue. Twelve-month surveillance is a reasonable strategy for a small, asymptomatic, incidental cartilage lesion, which this is not. Once the lesion is referred, remember that cartilage tumours are heterogeneous, so a biopsy from a low-grade area of a high-grade tumour under-grades it, and the imaging appearances have to be weighed against the histology rather than being overruled by it.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with anaemia, renal impairment and a paraprotein has a normal skeletal survey. The haematologist needs to know whether there is bone disease before deciding whether to treat. What imaging do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Whole-body low-dose CT or whole-body MRI, both far more sensitive than the skeletal survey
choices: Whole-body low-dose CT or whole-body MRI, both far more sensitive than the skeletal survey
An isotope bone scan, which detects myeloma deposits earlier than the skeletal survey
A repeat skeletal survey in three months, which will demonstrate progression of the lysis
Targeted radiographs of each painful area, which match cross-sectional imaging for yield
quiz.explain: Myeloma destroys bone through osteoclast activation while suppressing the osteoblastic response, which has two consequences for imaging. First, the isotope bone scan depends on osteoblastic activity and is characteristically cold, so it is the wrong test. Second, a radiograph needs a large proportion of trabecular bone to be lost before a lesion becomes visible, so a normal skeletal survey excludes very little. Whole-body low-dose CT and whole-body MRI have replaced it, and current International Myeloma Working Group criteria count one or more osteolytic lesions of 5 mm or more on radiograph, CT or PET-CT as myeloma-defining bone disease, while more than one focal marrow lesion of 5 mm or more on MRI is itself a myeloma-defining event under the SLiM additions to the CRAB criteria. MRI is also the only way to see the diffuse infiltration pattern, which destroys no cortex at all and is invisible on CT.

quiz.prompt: A patient with metastatic disease is about to start systemic treatment. Baseline CT with 5 mm slices shows lung nodules of 14 mm, 12 mm and 8 mm, liver deposits of 20 mm and 15 mm, and one purely sclerotic deposit in the ilium with no soft tissue component. Applying RECIST 1.1, how many of these lesions may be selected as target lesions? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Four: two lung nodules and two liver deposits. Under RECIST 1.1 a non-nodal lesion is measurable when its longest diameter is at least 10 mm on CT with a slice thickness of 5 mm or less, so the 8 mm nodule is non-measurable and is recorded as non-target disease. At most two target lesions are chosen per organ and five in total, so both liver deposits and the two larger lung nodules qualify and the count sits comfortably under the ceiling. A purely blastic bone deposit is non-measurable in RECIST 1.1, whereas a lytic or mixed deposit with an identifiable soft tissue component of 10 mm or more can be selected. For completeness, lymph nodes are the exception that is measured on the short axis and are only measurable at 15 mm or more. Everything not selected still has to be followed, since unequivocal progression of non-target disease is progression regardless of what the targets do.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps in the work-up of a suspected primary bone sarcoma of the femur, from the first investigation to definitive treatment.
quiz.answer: radiograph sarcoma-referral staging-MRI planned-biopsy resection
quiz.explain: The radiograph comes first and still carries most of the diagnostic information, since age, site, margin, periosteal reaction and matrix are all read from it. Referral comes next, before any needle is passed, because the tract has to be chosen by the surgeon who will later resect it. Local staging MRI of the whole bone follows, and it must precede the biopsy: haemorrhage and tract oedema degrade the images afterwards and can lead to over-staging of marrow and soft tissue extent. The biopsy is then performed at the treating centre along the line of the planned incision, ideally by or with the operating surgeon, with cores taken from viable tumour rather than from necrotic centre or reactive rim. Resection removes the tumour and the tract in one piece. Staging of distant disease, principally CT of the chest, is added around the same time and does not change this order.

quiz.prompt: A general radiologist is asked by an orthopaedic colleague to biopsy a destructive proximal tibial lesion this afternoon, before the sarcoma meeting has seen it. Give the reason to decline, in terms the colleague will accept.
quiz.answer: The needle tract is seeded with tumour and has to be excised in one piece with the specimen, so it must run through tissue the surgeon plans to remove and along the line of the planned incision; a tract chosen elsewhere can cross an uninvolved compartment or a neurovascular plane and turn a limb-sparing resection into a much larger operation, which is why the biopsy belongs to the treating unit.
quiz.explain: Everything the needle passes through is contaminated, and haematoma spreads that contamination along fascial planes, so the tract is treated as part of the tumour and is resected with it. That is why the position of the skin entry, the angle and the muscles crossed are surgical decisions rather than technical conveniences: a transverse entry, a tract crossing from one compartment into another, or one that runs alongside the neurovascular bundle can each remove the option of saving the limb. Published series comparing biopsies performed at referral centres with those done elsewhere have repeatedly found more complications, more changes of plan and more unnecessary amputations in the latter group, which is the argument that carries weight in a corridor conversation. The practical steps are to agree the tract with the surgeon, mark and record the entry point, use image guidance, and take enough cores from viable tissue to allow grading and molecular work.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old has knee pain. Radiographs show an eccentric lucent lesion in the distal femur that extends to the subchondral bone, with a narrow but non-sclerotic margin, no mineralised matrix, and thinning of the adjacent cortex. What should the report conclude and advise?
quiz.answer: A giant cell tumour is most likely, so refer for local staging, biopsy and surgical treatment
choices: A giant cell tumour is most likely, so refer for local staging, biopsy and surgical treatment
A simple bone cyst is most likely, so nothing beyond a repeat radiograph is required here
A chondroblastoma is most likely, since this age and this site are typical for that lesion
An osteoblastic metastasis is most likely, so look for the primary tumour before doing more
quiz.explain: The combination that matters is a lesion reaching the subchondral plate in a skeletally mature adult between 20 and 40, eccentric, with a narrow but non-sclerotic margin and no matrix. That is a giant cell tumour, and its margin, geographic but unsclerosed, marks it as locally aggressive rather than indolent. Chondroblastoma occupies the epiphysis of a patient whose physis is still open, usually with a thin sclerotic rim and often with chondroid matrix, so the age here is wrong for it. A simple bone cyst is central and metaphyseal in a child, most often in the proximal humerus or femur. An osteoblastic metastasis would be sclerotic, not lucent, and metastasis in this age group is uncommon. Report also whether there are fluid-fluid levels, since secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change is common, and whether the cortex is breached, since these tumours recur locally and occasionally seed to the lungs.

quiz.prompt: You are staging a distal femoral osteosarcoma with MRI before neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Which set of observations most changes the operation the surgeon plans?
quiz.answer: Whole-bone extent, skip lesions, joint involvement and contact with the popliteal vessels
choices: Whole-bone extent, skip lesions, joint involvement and contact with the popliteal vessels
Matrix signal intensity, degree of enhancement and apparent diffusion coefficient values
Extent of surrounding oedema, amount of periosteal new bone and marrow fat percentage
Number of vessels within the mass, its enhancement curve and its calcified proportion
quiz.explain: Local staging is an anatomical exercise done for the surgeon. The resection level is planned from the proximal extent of marrow replacement measured against a fixed landmark such as the joint line, which is why the whole bone is imaged rather than the lesion alone, and imaging the whole bone is also how skip metastases in the same bone are found. Transphyseal spread, intra-articular extension and involvement of the popliteal vessels and nerve are the findings that decide between an endoprosthetic replacement and an amputation. Judge marrow extent on T1, where tumour replaces fat, since peritumoural oedema on fluid-sensitive sequences will over-estimate it. The tissue characterisation measurements are interesting but do not move the operation, and response to chemotherapy is judged mainly on the percentage of necrosis in the resected specimen rather than on any change in size. Staging is completed with CT of the chest.

quiz.prompt: Two lytic lesions in the same bone are compared. The first has a fine sclerotic rim you could trace with a pencil; around the second you could not draw a line at all. What does the difference in margin tell you, and what does it not tell you?
quiz.answer: The margin measures the speed of the lesion against the speed of bone repair: a sclerotic rim means the bone has had time to wall the lesion off, so growth is slow, whereas a wide zone of transition means destruction is outrunning repair and the lesion is aggressive. It does not tell you whether the lesion is malignant, since infection and eosinophilic granuloma can look aggressive while some metastases and myeloma deposits look slow.
quiz.explain: Lodwick built his grading on exactly this observation: grade IA is geographic with a sclerotic margin, IB geographic and well defined without sclerosis, IC geographic with an ill-defined margin or partial cortical destruction, grade II is moth-eaten and grade III permeative. The scale is a measure of growth rate, not of histology, and that is both its strength and its limit. It is why the differential is assembled from age plus site plus margin rather than margin alone: a permeative lesion in a child brings up Ewing sarcoma, leukaemia, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and osteomyelitis together, while the same pattern past 40 brings up metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma. Assess the margin on the radiograph rather than on CT or MRI, since the radiograph averages the whole thickness of bone and shows the transition zone better than a cross-section through part of it.

curriculum_modules.title: Bowel Ischaemia and Wall Thickening Patterns

module_contract.goal: Separate the four mechanisms of bowel ischaemia on CT, read wall thickening and enhancement against the phase you acquired, and decide when intramural gas means the patient needs an operation tonight.

approach.detail: Arterial occlusive, venous occlusive, non-occlusive (NOMI), or strangulation from a mechanical cause. The four behave differently on CT and lead to different operations.
SMA and coeliac origins for embolus or thrombus; SMV and portal vein for thrombus; a small-calibre aorta and diffusely narrowed mesenteric vessels for NOMI.
Venous occlusion and reperfusion thicken the wall. Pure arterial occlusion classically gives a paper-thin wall — advanced necrosis often looks unimpressively normal.

approach.step: Read enhancement against the phase you acquired
approach.detail: Hyperenhancement suggests viable bowel; hypoenhancement or absent enhancement means compromised perfusion and possible necrosis. Judge it against a normal loop on the same series.
Pneumatosis intestinalis and portal venous gas together indicate transmural necrosis and a poor prognosis. Window for gas, not for soft tissue.

approach.step: Use the attenuation pattern to place the differential
approach.detail: White, grey, water target, fat target or gas — each pattern has its own short list.

measure.how: Along the bowel on coronal reformats; length narrows the differential more than thickness does.
Compare the suspect segment with a normal loop on the same series and phase.
measure.cutoff: Hyper = viable · Hypo or absent = compromised

classify.name: CT attenuation pattern of bowel wall thickening
rows: Acute inflammatory bowel disease, shock bowel, intramural haematoma
Thick wall with poor enhancement despite a good bolus
Chronic fibrotic Crohn disease, mesenteric ischaemia, adenocarcinoma, lymphoma
Enhancing mucosa and muscularis propria with oedematous submucosa between
Pseudomembranous colitis, portal hypertension, typhlitis, infectious colitis, ischaemia
Obesity, chronic inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, chemotherapy effect
Pneumatosis intestinalis — gas within the bowel wall
Mesenteric ischaemia, obstruction, trauma, incidental in COPD or asthma
classify.note: Segment length narrows it further: under 5 cm with shouldering favours adenocarcinoma; 5–10 cm fits diverticulitis, Crohn disease and ischaemia; 10–30 cm includes submucosal haemorrhage; diffuse colonic involvement fits ulcerative colitis or a systemic cause.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, [arterial and] portal venous phase.

FINDINGS
Mechanism: [arterial occlusive / venous occlusive / non-occlusive / strangulation from (cause)].
Vessels: coeliac [ ], SMA [ ], SMV and portal vein [ ].
Involved segment: [site], length [n] cm.
Wall: [thickened n mm / paper-thin]; attenuation pattern [white / grey / water target / fat target / gas].
Enhancement: [hyper- / normal / hypo- / absent] compared with adjacent normal bowel.
Pneumatosis: [absent / present — site]. Portal venous gas: [absent / present].
Mesentery: [oedema / stranding / fluid]. Ascites: [absent / present].

IMPRESSION
1. Bowel ischaemia of the [segment], mechanism [ ].
2. [Pneumatosis and/or portal venous gas — transmural necrosis, poor prognosis.]
3. [Direct call to the surgical team.]
pitfalls: Expecting a thick wall. In arterial occlusion the necrotic bowel is paper-thin, and the scan can look almost normal.
Judging enhancement without a reference. Compare the segment with a normal loop on the same phase before calling it hypoenhancing.
Reading pneumatosis in isolation. It is a sign of ischaemia, but also of obstruction, trauma, and it occurs incidentally in COPD and asthma — the company it keeps decides.
Missing shock bowel. Diffuse white mural enhancement in a hypotensive patient is hypoperfusion, not primary bowel disease.
Skipping the venous side. SMV and portal vein thrombus produces markedly thickened, poorly enhancing bowel and is easy to overlook if you only check the arteries.

Congestion, oedema and venous clot reflect blocked outflow.
Closed-loop geometry plus threatened wall demands urgent action.

Review wall thickness, dilation and pneumatosis.
Review mesenteric oedema, ascites and portal venous gas.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old in atrial fibrillation has abdominal pain far out of proportion to a soft abdomen. CT angiography shows a sharply marginated filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery about 5 cm beyond its origin. The proximal jejunal branches and the middle colic opacify normally, the aorta is smooth with little calcification, and the mid ileal loops are thin-walled and barely enhance. What does that configuration point to?
quiz.answer: Embolus beyond the first branches, so the proximal jejunum is spared
choices: Embolus beyond the first branches, so the proximal jejunum is spared
Ostial thrombosis on plaque, so collaterals should have been visible
Low-flow ischaemia with a patent artery, so no clot will be retrieved
Venous outflow block, so the arterial defect is a timing artefact
quiz.explain: The level of the defect is the whole message. An embolus travels until the calibre steps down, which is typically a few centimetres beyond the origin and beyond the first jejunal branches and often the middle colic, so the proximal jejunum and the transverse colon are spared while the mid gut infarcts. Thrombosis behaves differently: it forms on an ostial plaque in a heavily calcified aorta, in a patient who has usually had months of post-prandial pain and weight loss, and by the time it occludes there are collaterals to see, through the arc of Riolan and the marginal artery. Low-flow ischaemia leaves the artery patent, so there is nothing to retrieve. Venous occlusion thickens the wall rather than thinning it. The distinction is operative: an embolus is taken out through the artery, whereas ostial thrombosis needs stenting or a bypass, and the surgeon plans differently for each.

quiz.prompt: Two patients arrive within the hour, both with infarcting bowel. In the first, the ileal loops are dilated, paper-thin and hypoenhancing, with almost no mesenteric fluid. In the second, the loops are thick-walled and layered, the mesenteric fat is oedematous and there is free fluid. What accounts for the difference in wall thickness?
quiz.answer: Arterial cut-off thins the wall; venous obstruction floods it with oedema
choices: Arterial cut-off thins the wall; venous obstruction floods it with oedema
The first is earlier in its course; both will look identical by day two
The second is inflammatory rather than ischaemic; look for an enteritis
Wall thickness follows the segment involved, not the vessel obstructed
quiz.explain: Thickening needs a delivery route. When the artery is cut off, nothing arrives: the wall loses tone, the loop dilates, and the wall becomes thin and unenhancing, which is why a paper-thin loop is one of the most ominous findings in the abdomen rather than a reassuring one. When the vein is obstructed, arterial inflow continues against a blocked outflow, so plasma and blood are driven into the wall and the mesentery: marked stratified thickening, mesenteric fat oedema, engorged vessels and ascites. Time modifies this but does not abolish it, because an arterial occlusion that reperfuses will then thicken and hyperenhance, which is a different appearance again and one worth naming in the report. The practical habit is to read wall thickness and the state of the mesentery together, and to ask which vessel would produce both.

quiz.prompt: On the unenhanced series a segment of ileal wall measures 64 HU. On the portal venous phase the same segment measures 71 HU, while an adjacent normal loop rises from 32 HU to 96 HU. By how many Hounsfield units does the abnormal segment enhance? Answer in Hounsfield units, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Seven Hounsfield units is not enhancement, it is noise. The adjacent loop, acquired in the same breath and at the same circulation time, gains 64 HU, which is the internal control that makes the comparison trustworthy: absolute mural attenuation depends on injection rate, cardiac output and phase, so a remembered number is a poor referee while the loop next door is an excellent one. Notice too that the 64 HU baseline is itself a finding. Wall that is already dense before contrast contains blood, and intramural haemorrhage is the signature of venous occlusion or reperfusion injury. Had the unenhanced series been omitted, the 71 HU wall could easily have been read as enhancing normally, and the diagnosis would have been missed twice over.

quiz.prompt: To save dose, your department proposes reducing the protocol for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia to a single portal venous acquisition. Name the findings that a dropped unenhanced series would cost you, and say what each would be mistaken for.
quiz.answer: Intramural or mesenteric haemorrhage, which on a single portal venous series is read as wall enhancement, and mural or vascular calcification and hyperdense thrombus in the vessel wall, which vanish once the lumen and vessels are opacified.
quiz.explain: A dense bowel wall after contrast has two explanations, and only the unenhanced series separates them: a wall that was already dense contains blood, and a wall that was not contains contrast. Getting this backwards inverts the diagnosis, since intramural haemorrhage belongs to venous occlusion, strangulation or reperfusion, whereas true hyperenhancement suggests inflammation or an early reperfused segment. The same series carries the vascular calcium that tells you whether an ostial defect sits on chronic plaque, and hyperdense thrombus in the mesenteric vein, both of which disappear once the lumen opacifies. The accepted protocol therefore acquires unenhanced, arterial and portal venous phases; the dose argument is real, but the phase to negotiate away is not the unenhanced one.

quiz.prompt: Thirty-six hours after a cardiac arrest, a 62-year-old on high-dose noradrenaline develops a rising lactate and a distended abdomen. CT shows a patent superior mesenteric artery and vein with no filling defect, branch vessels alternately narrowed and dilated, and thick-walled, poorly enhancing right colon and distal ileum. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Correct the shock and cut the vasopressors; consider an intra-arterial vasodilator
choices: Correct the shock and cut the vasopressors; consider an intra-arterial vasodilator
Take the patient for surgical embolectomy of the superior mesenteric artery
Start therapeutic anticoagulation for an occult mesenteric venous thrombosis
Treat this as an infective colitis, since the mesenteric vessels are patent
quiz.explain: This is non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia: splanchnic vasoconstriction in a low-output state, seen after cardiac arrest or cardiac surgery, in dialysis patients and with vasopressor or digoxin use. The vessels are patent, which is precisely why there is nothing to embolectomise, and the branch calibre alternates because the vasoconstriction is segmental. The treatment is haemodynamic: raise cardiac output, restore volume, withdraw the vasoconstrictor if the blood pressure allows, and in selected patients infuse a vasodilator such as papaverine into the superior mesenteric artery. Anticoagulation treats a clot that is not there. The trap is that the patient looks like every other unwell intensive care patient and the CT has no dramatic occlusion to point at, so the diagnosis rests on the pattern plus the physiology. Laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis or established infarction, and mortality remains high.

quiz.prompt: A 60-year-old with iron deficiency anaemia has two abnormal segments. One is 4 cm of jejunum with eccentric, homogeneous soft tissue thickening, abrupt shouldered margins and no layering. The other is a long ileal segment with symmetrical thickening and a low-attenuation middle layer. What should each be reported as?
quiz.answer: Short shouldered segment neoplastic; long stratified segment oedematous
choices: Short shouldered segment neoplastic; long stratified segment oedematous
Short shouldered segment ischaemic; long stratified segment neoplastic
Both segments neoplastic, one infiltrative and the other polypoid
Both segments oedematous, the shorter one simply less distended
quiz.explain: Two questions do most of the work: how long is it, and is the wall layered? Preserved stratification, with a water-attenuation middle layer between an enhancing mucosa and an enhancing serosa, means fluid has entered an intact wall, which is oedema from inflammation, ischaemia, venous congestion or hypoalbuminaemia, and it argues strongly against tumour. Tumour replaces the wall rather than swelling it: short, eccentric, homogeneous soft tissue, abrupt shoulders, loss of layering, sometimes with nodes or upstream obstruction. Length matters because infiltrating processes tend to be long and neoplasms short, with the notable exception of lymphoma, which can involve a long segment and dilate rather than obstruct it, replacing the muscularis and its nerve plexus. So a long aneurysmal segment with lost layering is not reassurance, it is a lymphoma until proven otherwise.

quiz.prompt: The middle layer of a thickened colonic wall measures about -40 HU. Say what that layer is made of and what it tells you about how long this disease has been present.
quiz.answer: It is fat laid down in the submucosa, a marker of long-standing disease such as chronic inflammatory bowel disease, so it is not an acute finding and does not support a diagnosis of acute ischaemia.
quiz.explain: Negative attenuation is the discriminator. In the target or halo pattern of acute disease the middle layer is water attenuation, roughly 0 to 20 HU, because it is oedema. At around -40 HU the submucosa contains fat, which takes time to accumulate: it is seen in long-standing ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, and also without any bowel disease at all in obesity, after steroids, after transplantation, and in the normal rectum and caecum of some patients. So it is a chronicity marker rather than a diagnosis, and its practical value is defensive. When an acutely unwell patient has a thickened colon with a fatty submucosa, some of that thickening predates today, and calling acute ischaemia on wall thickness alone would be an error.

quiz.prompt: Two patients have intramural gas. The first is a 70-year-old on chemotherapy, systemically well, with bubbly cystic gas in the descending colon wall, no portal or mesenteric gas and a normal lactate. The second is shocked, with linear gas in the wall of a dilated non-enhancing ileal segment, branching lucency at the liver periphery and gas in the mesenteric veins. How should they be handled?
quiz.answer: The first can be observed and treated medically; the second needs urgent surgery
choices: The first can be observed and treated medically; the second needs urgent surgery
Both need laparotomy, because intramural gas indicates a breached mucosa
Both can be observed, because intramural gas is a poor predictor of outcome
The first needs laparotomy for perforation risk; the second is drug-related
quiz.explain: Intramural gas is a sign, not a diagnosis, and the company it keeps decides its meaning. Bubbly, cystic, submucosal gas in a comfortable patient is the benign end: pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, chemotherapy and immunosuppression, steroids, chronic lung disease, connective tissue disease, recent endoscopy, or bowel proximal to a stenosis. Linear or curvilinear gas following the contour of a loop that does not enhance, in a shocked and acidotic patient, is transmural infarction. Portal venous gas obeys flow, so it appears as fine branching lucency within a couple of centimetres of the liver capsule, which is what separates it from pneumobilia sitting centrally near the hilum. Portal gas alone is not a death sentence either, since it follows endoscopy and severe gastric distension, but portal gas with mural hypoenhancement and rising lactate is.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with a previous appendicectomy has a U-shaped, fluid-filled dilated ileal segment, radially converging mesenteric vessels and a whirl of twisted mesentery. To call this a closed loop rather than a simple obstruction, how many transition points must you identify at the same site? Answer with a whole number.
quiz.explain: A closed loop is a segment obstructed at two adjacent points by a single lesion, most often an adhesive band, a hernia neck or a volvulus, so the two transitions lie side by side and can be within a centimetre of each other. Finding both is what converts a description of dilated bowel into a surgical emergency, because the same twist that closes the loop catches its mesentery, and venous return fails inside a compartment that cannot decompress in either direction. The supporting signs are the C-shaped or U-shaped loop, beaks at each transition, radially converging vasa recta, the whirl of twisted mesenteric vessels, and disproportionate fluid within the closed segment. A closed loop with impaired mural enhancement goes to theatre even when the patient looks comfortable, because the abdomen lags behind the bowel.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the events of a strangulating closed-loop obstruction in the order they occur.
quiz.answer: venous-outflow-occlusion mural-oedema-and-haemorrhage arterial-inflow-failure transmural-infarction
quiz.explain: The sequence explains everything you see. Thin-walled veins collapse first at the twisted neck, while the thicker-walled artery keeps delivering, so blood and plasma are pushed into a wall that cannot drain: mural thickening, high attenuation from haemorrhage on the unenhanced series, mesenteric fat oedema, engorged vasa recta and fluid in the mesentery. Rising interstitial pressure then defeats arterial inflow, and only at that point does the wall stop enhancing and the bowel begin to die. This is why the earliest CT signs of strangulation are mesenteric, not mural, and why a thick dense wall early and a thin unenhancing wall late can both be strangulation at different hours of the same illness. Reading enhancement without reading the mesentery loses the early window, which is the only window that saves bowel.

quiz.prompt: A hypotensive patient has segmental colonic wall thickening from the splenic flexure to the mid descending colon, with a normal rectum. Explain why that distribution is expected, and say what you would reconsider if the rectum were involved too.
quiz.answer: The splenic flexure is the watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories and fails first in low flow, while the rectum has a dual supply that includes branches of the internal iliac and is usually spared, so rectal involvement argues against simple arterial ischaemia and towards infection, an inflammatory colitis, or occlusion low in the aorta or iliac vessels.
quiz.explain: Ischaemic colitis follows perfusion boundaries. The splenic flexure sits where the superior and inferior mesenteric territories meet, and the rectosigmoid junction sits where the inferior mesenteric supply meets the internal iliac branches, so both are vulnerable when flow falls. The rectum escapes because it draws on the middle and inferior rectal arteries from the internal iliac as well as the superior rectal artery, which is a genuinely dual supply. That escape is diagnostically useful: a thickened rectum in a hypotensive patient should send you looking for pseudomembranous or infective colitis, an inflammatory bowel disease, radiation change, or a low aortic or bilateral iliac occlusion, rather than accepting the ischaemic label. The corollary is that ischaemic colitis is usually segmental with an abrupt normal boundary, so pancolitis is also a reason to think again.

quiz.prompt: In an 80-year-old, ischaemic colitis involves the caecum and ascending colon rather than the left colon, and CT angiography shows ostial disease of the superior mesenteric artery. What does the right-sided distribution change?
quiz.answer: It carries a worse outcome and a higher chance of needing surgery
choices: It carries a worse outcome and a higher chance of needing surgery
It usually resolves faster because the right colon is thin walled
It makes an embolic source unlikely and suggests a venous cause
It runs the same course as left-sided disease and changes nothing
quiz.explain: Left-sided ischaemic colitis is usually a mucosal insult in a watershed, resolves with supportive care, and is often managed without a surgeon in the room. Isolated right colonic ischaemia is a different disease: it lies in the superior mesenteric territory, so it keeps company with small bowel ischaemia, with proximal arterial occlusion, and with the low-flow states of dialysis and cardiac failure. It carries a substantially higher rate of colectomy and death, so it justifies imaging the mesenteric vessels and involving surgery early rather than treating conservatively and reviewing in the morning. The other options invert the point: a thin wall does not aid recovery, and an arterial cause becomes more likely, not less, when the right colon alone is affected.

source.title: Closed loop in small bowel obstruction

approach.detail: Dilated loops followed by collapsed loops. An ileus with no normal-calibre bowel anywhere strongly suggests a paralytic cause.
Follow the dilated bowel to where it becomes collapsed. A smooth transition with no mass suggests adhesions, which account for 60–80% of cases.

approach.step: Use the small bowel faeces sign
approach.detail: Gas and particulate material within a dilated small bowel loop marks the level of obstruction — a useful pointer straight to the transition zone.

approach.step: Ask whether the loop is closed
approach.detail: Two points along the bowel obstructed at a single location. Look for a U- or C-shaped loop, a beak at the obstruction, and a radial array of dilated loops with mesenteric vessels converging to a central point.
Wall thickening, abnormal enhancement — decreased, absent, or paradoxically increased — mesenteric oedema, ascites, and dilated mesenteric veins.

approach.step: Name the afferent and efferent limbs
approach.detail: Which loop is dilated and which is collapsed determines the operative approach and the urgency. Use multiplanar reformats to show the strangulation point.

measure.how: Context for the phone call rather than a measurement on the images.
A smooth transition from dilated to collapsed small bowel with no mass or hernia.

classify.name: Signs of a closed loop and of strangulation
rows: A dilated loop whose two ends converge at one point
Dilated small bowel loops radiating with mesenteric vessels converging to a central point
Tapered beak-like narrowing at the obstruction site
The transition point of the closed loop
Gas and particulate material within a dilated loop
Marks the obstruction level, helping localise the transition zone
Decreased, absent, or paradoxically increased mural enhancement
Fluid and haziness in the mesentery of the involved loop, free fluid
Engorged veins draining the involved loop
Venous outflow obstruction within the closed loop
classify.note: Closed loop obstruction is obstruction with vascular compromise and requires urgent surgery. Reformat in multiple planes: the strangulation point is often only obvious off-axial.

Mesentery: [normal / oedematous]. Ascites: [absent / present]. Mesenteric veins: [normal / dilated].

IMPRESSION
1. [Mechanical small bowel obstruction / paralytic ileus], transition point at [ ], cause [ ].
2. [Closed loop obstruction — present / absent.]
3. [Signs of strangulation — present / absent.] [Discussed with (surgeon) at (time).]
pitfalls: Reporting obstruction without naming the transition point. The surgeon plans the incision from it.
Reading only axial images. The U- or C-shaped loop and the converging mesenteric vessels of a closed loop often appear only on coronal and sagittal reformats.
Taking increased mural enhancement as reassurance. Paradoxically increased enhancement is one of the abnormal patterns in strangulation.
Calling a distended abdomen mechanical when no bowel is of normal calibre anywhere — that pattern points to a paralytic cause such as general peritonitis.
Treating the small bowel faeces sign as a diagnosis. It is a signpost to the transition zone, not a cause.

long_description.takeaway: The transition point explains both the obstruction and the threat to bowel viability.
