quiz.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph shows the widest small bowel loop at 3.6 cm, the transverse colon at 5.2 cm and the caecum at 11.0 cm. Using the conventional 3 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm upper limits of normal, how many of these three measurements are abnormal? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Two: the small bowel at 3.6 cm and the caecum at 11.0 cm. The transverse colon at 5.2 cm is within normal limits. The 3/6/9 rule — 3 cm for small bowel, 6 cm for colon, 9 cm for caecum — is a crude but durable bedside aid, and the caecal figure is the one that carries urgency. By Laplace's law, wall tension rises with radius, so the caecum, the widest and thinnest-walled segment, is where an obstructed colon perforates first, typically without any warning from the pain score. A caecum beyond about 12 cm is widely treated as demanding decompression. Radiographic measurement is approximate: magnification, projection and overlapping loops all distort it, so confirm on CT, where you can also assess wall enhancement and look for the cause.

quiz.prompt: CT in a 58-year-old woman with vomiting shows dilated fluid-filled jejunum and proximal ileum to 3.8 cm, collapsed distal ileum and colon, and an abrupt calibre change in the right iliac fossa with no mass, no hernia and no wall thickening at that point. She had an appendicectomy at 15. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with a right iliac fossa transition point and no current signs of strangulation.
choices: Adhesive small bowel obstruction with a right iliac fossa transition point and no current signs of strangulation.
Small bowel ileus, since an abrupt calibre change without a visible mass is not evidence of mechanical obstruction.
An obstructing small bowel tumour, which should be presumed whenever no external hernia can be demonstrated.
Gallstone ileus, which is the usual explanation for an abrupt ileal transition point in this particular age group.
quiz.explain: Adhesions cause most small bowel obstruction in adults with previous surgery, and they are diagnosed by what is absent: an abrupt transition with nothing at it — no mass, no wall thickening, no hernia, no intussusception, no inflammatory process. That makes the diagnosis a duty rather than a shrug. Before accepting it you must inspect every hernial orifice including femoral and obturator, look for a beak within the mesentery suggesting an internal hernia, and check for a lesion at the transition on thin reformats. Ileus is excluded here by the collapsed distal bowel and colon: an ileus dilates everything without a calibre change. Gallstone ileus has its own triad of pneumobilia, obstruction and an ectopic stone. The final clause — no signs of strangulation — is the part the surgeon reads first, because it is what permits a trial of conservative management.

quiz.prompt: A CT report on a small bowel obstruction lists five findings: mesenteric fluid, reduced small bowel wall enhancement, the small bowel faeces sign, pneumatosis of a dilated loop, and moderate ascites. How many of these five are recognised signs of strangulation? Answer as a whole number, with no units.
quiz.explain: Four. Mesenteric fluid and oedema, reduced or absent wall enhancement, pneumatosis and ascites all belong to the strangulation family, along with mural thickening, a hyperattenuating wall on the non-contrast series from haemorrhagic infarction, mesenteric venous engorgement and portal venous gas. Reduced wall enhancement is the most specific of them and the one to hunt for deliberately, comparing the suspect loop against a normal loop on the same image and on the same window. The small bowel faeces sign is the odd one out: it reflects stasis and delayed transit, not compromised perfusion. It is more common in higher-grade and longer-standing obstruction, which is why it feels ominous, but it does not by itself justify an emergency laparotomy. Grading the CT by how many of the real signs are present is how you communicate urgency.

quiz.prompt: In a patient with high-grade small bowel obstruction, a segment of dilated bowel immediately proximal to the calibre change contains particulate material mixed with gas bubbles. How should this influence what you do?
quiz.answer: Use it to point you towards the transition zone; by itself it says nothing about the blood supply of the loop.
choices: Use it to point you towards the transition zone; by itself it says nothing about the blood supply of the loop.
Treat it as an early sign of strangulation, and escalate the patient directly to an emergency laparotomy.
Take it as evidence against mechanical obstruction, since particulate content implies transit is preserved.
Take it as proof of a distal colonic cause, since particulate material can only originate within the colon.
quiz.explain: The small bowel faeces sign is gas bubbles suspended in particulate debris within dilated small bowel, produced by stasis, water resorption and bacterial overgrowth in a segment whose contents have not moved. Its practical value is topographical: it sits just proximal to the transition point, so when the transition is hard to find, follow the faecalised segment distally and it will usually take you there. It also tells you the obstruction is not brand new. What it is not is an ischaemia sign, and reading it as one leads to overcalling. It appears in Crohn disease, in some chronic strictures and occasionally without obstruction at all. Judge urgency on wall enhancement, mesenteric oedema, closed-loop configuration and the patient's physiology, and use the faeces sign for what it is good at — finding the level.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a C-shaped, fluid-filled dilated small bowel loop with two transition points at a single site, mesenteric vessels radiating towards that point, mesenteric oedema, and reduced enhancement of the loop wall. Say what you are describing and how quickly the surgical team needs to hear it.
quiz.answer: A closed-loop small bowel obstruction with signs of strangulation. Telephone the surgical team immediately rather than leaving a written report - the loop is at risk of infarction and this needs an emergency laparotomy, not a trial of conservative management.
quiz.explain: A closed loop is a segment obstructed at two points close together, usually by a single adhesive band or a hernial neck, and it is the configuration most likely to strangulate because the mesentery is caught in the same twist. Recognise it by the shape — a C or U-shaped, fluid-filled, disproportionately dilated loop — by two transition points converging at one site, and by mesenteric vessels stretched and radiating towards that point, sometimes with a whirl. Then look specifically for the viability signs: reduced or absent wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric oedema and fluid, ascites, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. The report is not the communication. A closed loop with reduced enhancement is a phone call in minutes, because the interval between venous occlusion and transmural infarction is measured in hours and the operation is different if the bowel has to be resected.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the four questions to work through when reading a CT for suspected bowel obstruction, in the order they should be answered.
quiz.answer: confirm-dilatation locate-transition identify-cause assess-viability
quiz.explain: The sequence is forced by logic. First establish that bowel is genuinely obstructed rather than merely dilated: dilated proximal bowel with collapsed distal bowel and colon, against the 3/6/9 calibre limits. Second, find the transition point by following the dilated loops to where calibre changes, using coronal reformats, since the level determines whether this is a small or large bowel problem. Third, work out what is at the transition — adhesion, hernia, tumour, intussusception, volvulus, gallstone, inflammatory stricture — because the cause decides whether conservative management is even an option. Fourth, and never omitted, assess viability: wall enhancement, mural thickness, mesenteric fat and fluid, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. Viability comes last in the reading order but first in the conversation with the surgeon, because it is the finding that changes the timing of the operation rather than only its nature.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old has an obstructing sigmoid carcinoma. CT shows colonic dilatation from the caecum to the tumour, a caecum measuring 10.5 cm, no small bowel dilatation, and a thin caecal wall enhancing normally. What is the significance of the undistended small bowel?
quiz.answer: The ileocaecal valve is competent, making this a closed loop with the caecum at risk of perforating.
choices: The ileocaecal valve is competent, making this a closed loop with the caecum at risk of perforating.
The obstruction is incomplete, so the patient can safely wait for an elective operating list next week.
The tumour is more likely benign, since malignant strictures decompress into the small bowel early.
The caecal dilatation is passive, and the measurement therefore carries no prognostic weight here.
quiz.explain: A competent ileocaecal valve converts a distal colonic obstruction into a closed loop between the valve and the tumour. Nothing can escape proximally into the ileum or distally past the tumour, so the colon — and above all the caecum — takes the whole pressure. Because wall tension rises with radius, the caecum is the segment that ruptures, and it can do so with a deceptively comfortable abdomen. Paradoxically, the absence of small bowel dilatation is therefore the worrying feature, not the reassuring one: decompression into dilated small bowel means an incompetent valve and a lower immediate perforation risk. Report the caecal diameter as a number, comment on caecal wall enhancement and any pericaecal fluid or pneumatosis, and flag it for urgent decompression, whether by stent, defunctioning stoma or resection. This is not an elective list problem.

quiz.prompt: An 84-year-old nursing home resident with chronic constipation has gross distension. The radiograph shows an inverted U-shaped loop arising from the pelvis with its apex in the right upper quadrant and no rectal gas; CT confirms a whirl of twisted sigmoid mesentery with normal wall enhancement and no free gas. What is the appropriate first treatment?
quiz.answer: Endoscopic decompression with placement of a flatus tube, holding surgery for failure or for ischaemia.
choices: Endoscopic decompression with placement of a flatus tube, holding surgery for failure or for ischaemia.
Immediate laparotomy with sigmoid resection, since detorsion is seldom successful in this age group.
Water-soluble contrast enema for therapeutic reduction, which succeeds in the majority of volvulus cases.
Fluids and laxatives alone, since a sigmoid volvulus in a frail patient generally untwists without help.
quiz.explain: Sigmoid volvulus is a disease of the elderly, the immobile and the chronically constipated, and the classic radiograph is an enormously dilated inverted U arising from the pelvis, its apex often reaching above the transverse colon and pointing towards the right upper quadrant, with absent rectal gas. CT confirms it with a whirl of twisted mesentery and two beaks at the point of torsion, and — crucially — assesses viability. With enhancing wall and no free gas, first-line management is endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube left in place, which succeeds in most patients and converts an emergency into a planned procedure. Recurrence is high, so elective sigmoidectomy is usually considered afterwards. Perforation, peritonitis or CT evidence of ischaemia overrides all of this and sends the patient straight to theatre. Contrast enema is diagnostic at best and has been overtaken by CT.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old has acute distension and vomiting. CT shows a hugely dilated gas-filled loop in the left upper quadrant with a beak and a whirl of mesentery in the right iliac fossa, dilated small bowel, an empty right iliac fossa and a collapsed distal colon. State the diagnosis and why endoscopy is not the answer.
quiz.answer: This is a caecal volvulus. Unlike sigmoid volvulus it is rarely reduced endoscopically and recurs if it is, so it needs surgery - usually right hemicolectomy, or caecopexy in the unfit - and delay risks caecal infarction.
quiz.explain: Caecal volvulus needs a congenitally mobile caecum on an unfused mesentery, so it affects a much younger population than sigmoid volvulus. The giveaways are the empty right iliac fossa, the dilated caecum displaced towards the left upper quadrant, dilated small bowel proximal to it because the obstruction sits at the ileocaecal level, and a collapsed distal colon. On CT, look for the whirl of the twisted ileocolic pedicle and then for wall enhancement. The management diverges sharply from sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic reduction is technically difficult, frequently fails and recurs, so the answer is operative — right hemicolectomy where the patient can take it, caecopexy or caecostomy where they cannot. Say the diagnosis explicitly in the report rather than describing a distended loop, because the word caecal is what routes the patient to theatre instead of to endoscopy.

quiz.prompt: On day three after an open hysterectomy a woman is distended and not passing flatus. CT shows dilated small bowel and dilated colon with gas reaching the rectum, no calibre change anywhere, and no wall thickening or mesenteric fluid. State your conclusion and what it changes.
quiz.answer: Post-operative ileus rather than mechanical obstruction: bowel is dilated throughout with gas down to the rectum and no transition point. Management is conservative - nasogastric decompression, fluids, correcting electrolytes and reducing opiates - rather than a return to theatre.
quiz.explain: The distinction rests on one question: is there a transition point? An ileus dilates the whole gut uniformly, small bowel and colon together, with gas carried through to the rectum and no calibre change; mechanical obstruction dilates proximally and collapses distally around a discrete transition. Ileus follows surgery, electrolyte disturbance — especially hypokalaemia — opiates, sepsis, retroperitoneal inflammation and spinal injury, and it is treated by removing the cause. The trap is early post-operative mechanical obstruction, from an internal hernia or a tight closure, which can masquerade as a slow ileus and only declares itself when someone looks specifically for a transition point. So report the absence of a transition as a positive finding, and set a threshold: if the picture does not settle over the next couple of days, or the patient becomes tender or tachycardic, rescan and look again.

quiz.prompt: CT in a septic 70-year-old shows branching gas within the liver extending to within 1 cm of the capsule in the left lobe, together with gas in the wall of a dilated small bowel loop. What should be conveyed to the referring team?
quiz.answer: Gas of this peripheral distribution is portal venous, and with pneumatosis it points to infarcted bowel.
choices: Gas of this peripheral distribution is portal venous, and with pneumatosis it points to infarcted bowel.
Gas of this distribution within the liver is biliary, and is explained by a previous sphincterotomy.
The intramural gas is probably benign pneumatosis, so the hepatic gas can reasonably be disregarded.
The appearances suggest a gas-forming hepatic abscess, and image-guided aspiration should be arranged.
quiz.explain: Direction of flow separates the two. Portal blood runs from the hilum outwards, so portal venous gas is peripheral, fine and branching, typically reaching within 2 cm of the liver capsule and favouring the left lobe in a supine patient. Bile flows towards the hilum, so pneumobilia is central, coarser, and clusters around the porta — the expected finding after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or an incompetent sphincter. Portal venous gas together with pneumatosis in a septic patient is bowel infarction until proven otherwise and warrants immediate surgical discussion. The nuance to hold alongside it is that pneumatosis on its own is not always ischaemic: it occurs in chronic lung disease, with corticosteroids and some chemotherapy agents, after endoscopy, and in connective tissue disease. The company it keeps, and the patient, decide the meaning.

quiz.prompt: An 81-year-old inpatient recovering from a fractured neck of femur develops gross abdominal distension. CT shows dilatation of the entire colon including the rectum, a caecum of 12 cm, no transition point, no mass, and normal wall enhancement. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: correct electrolytes and drugs, and consider neostigmine or endoscopic decompression.
choices: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction: correct electrolytes and drugs, and consider neostigmine or endoscopic decompression.
Mechanical obstruction of the distal colon, with a water-soluble contrast enema needed before any decompression.
Immediate laparotomy and subtotal colectomy, since a caecum of this diameter has by definition already infarcted.
Sigmoid volvulus, with urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy and placement of a flatus tube as the first intervention.
quiz.explain: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is massive colonic dilatation with no mechanical cause, typically in an elderly inpatient after surgery, trauma or acute illness, and often with electrolyte disturbance, opiates or anticholinergics contributing. The distinguishing features on CT are gas carried right through into the rectum and the absence of any transition point — a sigmoid volvulus would show a whirl and beaks, and a tumour would show a shouldered stricture. First-line treatment is conservative: stop the offending drugs, correct potassium and magnesium, decompress nasogastrically, mobilise. Neostigmine under cardiac monitoring is effective in many patients, with colonoscopic decompression where it fails or is contraindicated. Report the caecal diameter and wall enhancement each time, because a caecum beyond about 12 cm, or one with pneumatosis, thinning or pericaecal fluid, is the trigger for escalation to surgery.

quiz.prompt: An 86-year-old thin woman with no previous abdominal surgery has a small bowel obstruction and pain radiating down the medial thigh. CT shows a loop of ileum passing between the pectineus and obturator externus muscles, with the transition point at that loop. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Refer urgently for surgical repair of an obturator hernia, stating the high risk of strangulation.
choices: Refer urgently for surgical repair of an obturator hernia, stating the high risk of strangulation.
Manage conservatively with a nasogastric tube, since hernias at this site usually reduce spontaneously.
Attribute the obstruction to adhesions, since the pelvic appearance is a recognised anatomical variant.
Book an outpatient hernia clinic appointment once the obstruction has settled with intravenous fluids.
quiz.explain: When there is no history of previous surgery, the transition point is far more likely to be a hernia than an adhesion, so the hernial orifices deserve a deliberate pass on the coronal images every time. The obturator hernia is the one most often missed: it occurs in thin, elderly, often multiparous women, the bowel passes through the obturator canal between pectineus and obturator externus, and compression of the obturator nerve produces pain referred to the medial thigh or knee — the Howship-Romberg sign. The neck is narrow and rigid, so strangulation is common and the reported mortality is high; this is an urgent operation, not a conservative trial. Check the femoral canals, the umbilicus, old incisions, and the mesenteric windows for internal hernias in the same sweep. Naming the hernia in the report changes both the urgency and the surgical approach.

module_contract.goal: Localise a brain lesion to its arterial or venous territory from cross-sectional images, and say what that territory tells you about the vessel, the deficit and the mechanism.

approach.detail: Cortex plus the subcortical white matter under it is a branch territory. Deep grey and internal capsule alone is a perforator.
Match the shape to ACA, MCA, PCA, anterior choroidal or a cerebellar artery before you name a mechanism.
Infarct sitting at ACA/MCA or MCA/PCA junctions, or as a chain in centrum semiovale and corona radiata, is hypoperfusion — go and look at the carotids.

approach.step: Check whether it respects an arterial map at all
approach.detail: Bilateral parasagittal or bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia change in a non-arterial distribution is venous until proven otherwise.
An enlarged Virchow-Robin space follows CSF on every sequence. A lacune does not.
Cortical territory means embolic or large vessel; borderzone means hypoperfusion; a single deep penetrator means lacunar.

classify.name: Arterial territories and what they imply
rows: Medial frontal and parietal lobes, anterior corpus callosum, parts of basal ganglia and internal capsule
Medial lenticulostriates (A1, recurrent artery of Heubner)
Anteromedial caudate head, anteroinferior internal capsule
Lateral hemispheric surface, sparing medial frontoparietal and inferior temporal lobe
Superior caudate head and body, globus pallidus, putamen, internal capsule
Inferomedial temporal lobe, occipital pole, visual cortex, splenium
Hippocampus, posterior limb of internal capsule, region lateral to the posterior cella media
Small vessel off the ICA — deficit out of proportion to size
Medulla and pons, sharply defined paramedian territories that do not cross the midline
Perforator occlusion; a lesion crossing the midline is not this
Inferior occipital surface of the cerebellum; territory inversely proportional to AICA
Superior and tentorial surfaces of the cerebellum
ACA/MCA and MCA/PCA junctions, cortex and subcortical white matter
Deep white matter of centrum semiovale and corona radiata
classify.note: Lacunar infarcts account for about 25% of ischaemic strokes.

pitfalls: Calling a borderzone infarct embolic. The cortical and internal borderzone patterns should send you to the carotids, not to the heart.
Reading bilateral thalamic or bilateral parasagittal change as arterial. It fits no artery; it fits the deep venous system or the superior sagittal sinus.
Mistaking enlarged perivascular spaces for lacunes. Virchow-Robin spaces follow CSF signal on every sequence.
Assuming a fixed PICA territory. PICA and AICA trade territory — one is large when the other is small.
Missing deep cerebral venous thrombosis in a young woman with mild symptoms; the page calls it underdiagnosed.

measurements.pitfall: Oblique reformats or pre-existing asymmetry can mislead.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old develops weakness of the right leg with only trivial arm involvement, a normal face, and striking abulia. CT at 24 hours shows hypoattenuation confined to the medial surface of the left hemisphere, running from the genu of the corpus callosum back to the paracentral lobule. Which occlusion best accounts for this?
quiz.answer: Occlusion of the left pericallosal artery, the A2 continuation of the anterior cerebral artery
choices: Occlusion of the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery in the sylvian fissure
Occlusion of the recurrent artery of Heubner arising at the left A1–A2 junction
Occlusion of the left pericallosal artery, the A2 continuation of the anterior cerebral artery
Occlusion of the left anterior choroidal artery just beyond the posterior communicating origin
quiz.explain: The homunculus is the whole argument. The leg and perineum sit on the medial surface at the paracentral lobule, and that surface, together with the genu and body of the corpus callosum and the medial frontal cortex, is anterior cerebral artery territory carried by the pericallosal and callosomarginal branches. Leg-dominant weakness with a spared face is therefore ACA until proven otherwise, and the abulia comes from the medial frontal and cingulate involvement. The middle cerebral artery's superior division supplies the lateral convexity, so it gives face and arm weakness with sparing of the leg — the mirror image. Heubner's recurrent artery supplies the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule; it produces a small deep infarct with facio-brachial weakness and dysarthria, not a strip of medial cortex. The anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, optic tract and medial temporal structures, classically hemiplegia with hemianaesthesia and hemianopia. When you see a medial strip, look next at the A1 segments and the anterior communicating complex, because a single dominant A1 can infarct both medial hemispheres at once.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with a 90% left internal carotid stenosis is found on the ward after a hypotensive episode. Diffusion imaging shows a chain of three small round infarcts strung in a line through the left corona radiata and centrum semiovale, with a normal cortical ribbon and no cardiac source found. What does this pattern tell you?
quiz.answer: Internal borderzone infarction from haemodynamic failure behind a tight proximal internal carotid stenosis
choices: Internal borderzone infarction from haemodynamic failure behind a tight proximal internal carotid stenosis
Cortical borderzone infarction from cardioembolic showers reaching the distal anterior cerebral branches
Chronic small vessel disease of the perforators, unrelated to the carotid stenosis on this study
Distal middle cerebral artery branch occlusion producing a wedge of cortical and subcortical infarct
quiz.explain: There are two borderzones and they mean different things. The external, or cortical, borderzone lies between the surface branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries and infarcts as a wedge running from the ventricle to the cortex; it is often embolic, with hypoperfusion impairing washout of emboli. The internal, or deep, borderzone lies between the lenticulostriate perforators from below and the long medullary branches descending from the cortical arteries above, in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale. It infarcts as a linear string of small lesions parallel to the lateral ventricle — the rosary bead appearance — and it is the most haemodynamic of all stroke patterns. A normal cortical ribbon argues against embolism, and diffusion restriction argues against old small vessel disease, which would be T2 hyperintense without restriction. The management consequence is the point: this patient needs perfusion assessment and an urgent decision about revascularising the carotid, plus avoidance of further hypotension, not simply another antiplatelet.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old is brought in with abrupt coma, a vertical gaze palsy and dense amnesia. MRI shows restricted diffusion in both paramedian thalami and a small V-shaped lesion on the anterior surface of the midbrain. State the arterial variant that explains this, and the one alternative diagnosis you must exclude before you commit to it, and how you would exclude it.
quiz.answer: This is the artery of Percheron: a single dominant thalamoperforator arising from one P1 that supplies both paramedian thalami and often the rostral midbrain. Before committing, exclude deep cerebral venous thrombosis by inspecting the internal cerebral veins, vein of Galen and straight sinus, with a CT or MR venogram if there is any doubt.
quiz.explain: Bilateral thalamic signal change is one of the few patterns in neuroradiology with a short and dangerous differential. The artery of Percheron is a normal variant in which both paramedian thalamic territories hang off a single perforator from one P1 segment, so one small occlusion infarcts both thalami; involvement of the rostral midbrain gives the V-shaped anterior mesencephalic lesion. The clinical triad of depressed consciousness, vertical gaze palsy and memory loss follows from the intralaminar nuclei and the rostral interstitial nucleus. The mimic that must not be missed is thrombosis of the deep venous system, because the internal cerebral veins drain exactly this territory and its treatment is anticoagulation, not stroke pathway care. Venous infarction tends to be more oedematous, less sharply diffusion-restricted, often haemorrhagic, and extends into the basal ganglia; the giveaway is a dense straight sinus or vein of Galen on the unenhanced CT. Top-of-the-basilar embolism and Wernicke encephalopathy round out the list, the latter favouring the medial thalami around the third ventricle with the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey.

quiz.prompt: Consider these five structures: the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic tract, the head of the caudate nucleus, the lateral geniculate nucleus, and the occipital cortex. How many of them lie within the usual territory of the anterior choroidal artery? Answer as a whole number, counting structures.
quiz.explain: The anterior choroidal artery arises from the supraclinoid internal carotid just distal to the posterior communicating artery and runs backwards along the optic tract into the temporal horn. Its territory is small but strategically dense: the posterior limb of the internal capsule (its inferior and posterior part), the optic tract, the lateral geniculate nucleus, the medial temporal structures including the uncus and part of the hippocampus, and the choroid plexus of the temporal horn. That gives three of the five listed. The caudate head belongs to the recurrent artery of Heubner and the medial lenticulostriates, and the occipital cortex belongs to the posterior cerebral artery. The reason to hold this territory in mind is the classical triad it produces — contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and homonymous hemianopia — from a lesion no larger than a lacune. If you see a small capsular infarct and the patient has a field defect, look for optic tract and geniculate involvement rather than assuming a second lesion.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old has sudden vertigo and vomiting, ipsilateral facial weakness of lower motor neurone type, ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss, ipsilateral limb ataxia and contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss in the trunk and limbs. Which vessel does this combination point to?
quiz.answer: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery, which also supplies the labyrinth through the internal auditory artery
choices: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery, which supplies the lateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum
The superior cerebellar artery, which supplies the dorsolateral pons and the superior cerebellar surface
A paramedian basilar perforator, which supplies the ventromedial pons and the descending corticospinal fibres
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery, which also supplies the labyrinth through the internal auditory artery
quiz.explain: Hearing loss is the discriminator. The internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery usually arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, so AICA is the one posterior circulation territory in which cochlear and vestibular failure sits alongside brainstem signs. Add lower motor neurone facial weakness from the facial nucleus in the caudal pons, ataxia from the middle cerebellar peduncle and flocculus, and crossed sensory loss from the spinothalamic tract, and the lateral pontine syndrome is complete. PICA gives the lateral medullary syndrome: vertigo, hoarseness and dysphagia from the nucleus ambiguus, Horner syndrome, crossed sensory loss — but hearing is preserved and the facial weakness, if any, is not of lower motor neurone type. SCA gives ataxia, dysarthria and sometimes a contralateral fourth nerve palsy, without hearing loss. A paramedian perforator gives a ventral pontine syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and no vestibulocochlear features. In practice, sudden isolated deafness with vertigo in a vasculopath is an AICA warning and deserves urgent posterior circulation imaging rather than a labyrinthitis label.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these vessels in the order that blood drains from the deep grey structures of the brain to the neck.
quiz.answer: internal-cerebral-vein vein-of-Galen straight-sinus confluence-of-sinuses transverse-sinus sigmoid-sinus internal-jugular-vein
quiz.explain: The deep venous system is a fixed chain and knowing it lets you predict which structures swell when one link fails. The thalamostriate and septal veins meet at the venous angle behind the foramen of Monro to form the paired internal cerebral veins, which run back in the velum interpositum. They join the basal veins of Rosenthal, carrying blood from the medial temporal lobes and midbrain, to form the great cerebral vein of Galen beneath the splenium. The vein of Galen meets the inferior sagittal sinus to become the straight sinus, which runs in the falco-tentorial junction to the confluence of sinuses, then out through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein. Thrombosis anywhere from the internal cerebral veins to the straight sinus produces bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia oedema, often haemorrhagic — the venous mimic of the artery of Percheron. Thrombosis further downstream, in a transverse or sigmoid sinus, is far more often silent or presents with raised pressure, because the cortical veins and the opposite side can compensate.

quiz.prompt: A 60-year-old has a painless isolated right abducens palsy. There is no proptosis, orbital movements are otherwise full, V1 sensation is intact and the optic nerve function is normal. On the thin-section post-contrast MRI you are about to report, which compartment deserves the closest scrutiny, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: The cavernous sinus, because the sixth nerve runs free within it alongside the internal carotid artery
choices: The superior orbital fissure, because the sixth nerve passes outside the annulus of Zinn on its way to the orbit
The cavernous sinus, because the sixth nerve runs free within it alongside the internal carotid artery
Meckel's cave, because the sixth nerve traverses it before entering the orbit through the fissure
The internal auditory canal, because the sixth nerve accompanies the facial nerve out of the pons
quiz.explain: The anatomy explains the clinical pattern. In the cavernous sinus the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves are embedded in the lateral dural wall, insulated to some degree from what is happening in the venous channel itself. The abducens nerve is the exception: it runs free inside the sinus, immediately lateral to the cavernous internal carotid artery. Anything that expands or infiltrates the venous compartment — tumour, thrombosis, a carotid–cavernous fistula, inflammatory pseudotumour — therefore tends to strike the sixth nerve first, and an isolated abducens palsy with an otherwise quiet orbit should send you to thin-section coronal images of the cavernous sinuses before anywhere else. In the superior orbital fissure the sixth nerve is inside the annulus of Zinn, not outside it, and a fissure lesion would rarely spare the third and fourth nerves. Meckel's cave contains the trigeminal ganglion, not the sixth nerve, and the internal auditory canal carries the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. Do not forget raised intracranial pressure, which stretches the sixth nerve at Dorello's canal and is a false localising sign.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows a small acute infarct confined to the posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule on the left, with the putamen and globus pallidus entirely normal. Say which artery you would suspect, and give one additional finding on the same study that would support your suspicion.
quiz.answer: Suspect the left anterior choroidal artery rather than a lenticulostriate perforator, because the lentiform nucleus is spared. Support it by looking for extension into the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus or the medial temporal lobe and uncus, and by asking the team to test for a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
quiz.explain: Two vessels can infarct the internal capsule and telling them apart changes what you look for and what you predict. The lateral lenticulostriate perforators arise from M1 and supply the putamen, most of the globus pallidus, the caudate body and the superior part of the posterior limb; if the lentiform nucleus is normal, they are unlikely to be the culprit. The anterior choroidal artery, from the supraclinoid carotid, supplies the inferior and posterior part of the posterior limb and continues to the optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus and medial temporal structures. So the extra finding you hunt for is downstream: signal change tracking along the optic tract or into the uncus, and a homonymous field defect on examination. This matters because the anterior choroidal origin is an atheromatous carotid segment and is also vulnerable during aneurysm clipping and coiling near the posterior communicating artery, so a fresh anterior choroidal infarct should turn your attention to the carotid, not to isolated small vessel disease.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old speaks fluently but with frequent paraphasias and cannot follow a two-step command. There is no limb weakness and no facial asymmetry. Formal fields show a right superior quadrantanopia. CT perfusion shows a deficit over the left posterior temporal and inferior parietal region sparing the precentral gyrus. Which occlusion fits?
quiz.answer: Occlusion of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
choices: Occlusion of the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
Occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery M1 segment proximal to the lenticulostriate origins
Occlusion of the inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery beyond the bifurcation
Occlusion of the left posterior cerebral artery P2 segment beyond the thalamogeniculate branches
quiz.explain: The middle cerebral artery bifurcates in the sylvian fissure into a superior and an inferior division, and the two produce almost opposite clinical pictures in the dominant hemisphere. The superior division feeds the frontal operculum and precentral cortex: expect face and arm weakness with a non-fluent, effortful aphasia and relatively preserved comprehension. The inferior division feeds the posterior temporal and inferior parietal cortex: expect fluent, paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension, often with no weakness at all, and a superior quadrantanopia because Meyer's loop sweeps forward through the temporal lobe. An M1 occlusion proximal to the lenticulostriates would add deep grey infarction and a dense hemiparesis. A P2 occlusion would give a homonymous hemianopia, usually complete or inferior, with alexia without agraphia if the splenium goes, but not this language pattern. The practical trap is that a patient with a pure inferior division occlusion has a high NIHSS driven almost entirely by language, looks unimpaired at the bedside on limb testing, and can still have a large vessel occlusion worth treating.

quiz.prompt: A skull base tumour is reported as filling the right jugular foramen and extending anteromedially into the right hypoglossal canal. Counting only nerves that traverse those two openings, how many cranial nerves are at risk on that side? Answer as a whole number, counting nerves.
quiz.explain: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, along with the internal jugular vein and the inferior petrosal sinus; the hypoglossal canal, just anteromedial and inferior to it in the occipital bone, transmits the twelfth nerve alone. A lesion occupying both therefore threatens four nerves — IX, X, XI and XII — which together make up the classical Collet–Sicard pattern, and the clinical consequence is a patient who cannot protect their airway. That is why this specific extension deserves an explicit sentence in your report rather than a general statement about skull base involvement. Keeping the neighbouring openings straight is worth the effort: the internal auditory meatus carries VII and VIII, the foramen ovale carries V3, the foramen rotundum carries V2, the optic canal carries II with the ophthalmic artery, and the superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI. When a mass sits at the pars nervosa or pars vascularis, look also for the vertical segment of the carotid and for a high jugular bulb before anyone contemplates biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old on the combined oral contraceptive pill has a right temporal haemorrhagic lesion that does not conform to any arterial territory, with surrounding oedema out of proportion to its size. The right transverse sinus does not opacify on the venous phase. Which vein's drainage territory matches the lesion?
quiz.answer: The vein of Labbé, the inferior anastomotic vein draining the temporal convexity to the transverse sinus
choices: The vein of Trolard, the superior anastomotic vein draining the convexity to the superior sagittal sinus
The basal vein of Rosenthal, draining the medial temporal region into the great cerebral vein of Galen
The internal cerebral vein, draining the deep grey structures into the great cerebral vein of Galen
The vein of Labbé, the inferior anastomotic vein draining the temporal convexity to the transverse sinus
quiz.explain: Venous infarcts announce themselves by disobeying arterial boundaries, by bleeding early, and by having oedema disproportionate to the infarct. Once you suspect one, work out which vein and then look at the sinus it empties into. The vein of Labbé drains the lateral temporal convexity backwards into the transverse sinus, so a transverse or sigmoid sinus thrombosis produces exactly this temporal haemorrhagic lesion, sometimes with a rapid decline as the temporal lobe swells against the tentorium. The vein of Trolard runs upwards to the superior sagittal sinus and matches parasagittal high convexity lesions, which is why superior sagittal sinus thrombosis gives bilateral parasagittal haemorrhages. Rosenthal's basal vein and the internal cerebral veins belong to the deep system and produce thalamic and basal ganglia oedema instead. The next step here is a dedicated venogram and anticoagulation, which is given even in the presence of venous haemorrhage — the bleeding is a consequence of the outflow obstruction, not a contraindication to relieving it.

quiz.prompt: A referrer asks whether a left medial occipital infarct with an ipsilateral posterolateral thalamic infarct in the same patient means one vessel or two. Explain the single arterial configuration that accounts for both, and state the one variant on the CTA that would change where you look for the embolic source.
quiz.answer: One vessel: the posterior cerebral artery, whose P2 segment supplies the medial occipital cortex through its cortical branches and the posterolateral thalamus through the thalamogeniculate perforators. Look for a fetal origin of that posterior cerebral artery from the internal carotid, because it moves the search for an embolic source to the anterior circulation.
quiz.explain: It is tempting to call two lesions two events, but the posterior cerebral artery supplies both cortex and deep grey, and a single P2 occlusion can take out the calcarine cortex and the lateral thalamus together. The thalamic supply is regional: the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating artery, the paramedian thalamoperforators from P1, the thalamogeniculate branches from P2 to the posterolateral thalamus, and the posterior choroidal arteries to the pulvinar and geniculate bodies. A posterolateral thalamic plus medial occipital pattern is the P2 signature. The variant that changes management is a fetal posterior cerebral artery, present in roughly a fifth to a quarter of hemispheres, in which the PCA arises from the internal carotid through a dominant posterior communicating artery with a hypoplastic or absent P1. In that patient an occipital infarct is a carotid territory event, so the carotid bifurcation, not the vertebrobasilar system, is where the workup belongs — and it also matters when planning any carotid intervention.

quiz.prompt: A patient with progressive right hemifacial numbness and wasting on chewing has an enhancing mass replacing the normal fat of the right Meckel's cave and reaching the skull base foramen immediately below it. Having found that, what should you do next in reading the study?
quiz.answer: Follow V3 through the foramen ovale and look for denervation change in the muscles of mastication
choices: Follow V2 through the foramen rotundum and look for a mass filling the pterygopalatine fossa
Follow V3 through the foramen ovale and look for denervation change in the muscles of mastication
Follow the facial nerve through the stylomastoid foramen and look for a mass in the parotid gland
Follow the lower cranial nerves through the jugular foramen and look for a carotid space mass
quiz.explain: Meckel's cave is a cerebrospinal fluid-filled dural pouch in the petrous apex holding the trigeminal ganglion, and it is a junction box: the ophthalmic division leaves through the superior orbital fissure, the maxillary division through the foramen rotundum, and the mandibular division through the foramen ovale into the masticator space. Because the patient has both sensory loss and weakness of chewing, the motor fibres travelling with V3 are involved, so the foramen ovale is the route to follow. The specific sign to hunt for is denervation of the masseter, temporalis and pterygoids — oedematous and T2 bright in the subacute phase, fatty and atrophic later — which can be the only clue that a small perineural tumour is present. Perineural spread from a skin or parotid malignancy classically travels this way, and it upstages disease and changes the radiotherapy field, so it is worth an explicit statement in the report. The maxillary route matters for palatal and midface tumours, and the facial and lower cranial nerve routes belong to different clinical pictures altogether.

module_contract.goal: Place an intracranial mass in the intra-axial or extra-axial compartment, then narrow it with enhancement, diffusion and perfusion.

approach.detail: Look for a CSF cleft, displaced subarachnoid vessels, grey matter between lesion and white matter, a widened subarachnoid space, a broad dural base or dural tail, and bony change. Any of these makes it extra-axial.
Under 2, first decade and adult each have a different shortlist; the age narrows the differential more than any sequence does.
Skull base, sella and suprasellar, CPA, pineal, intraventricular, fourth ventricle, cortical. The compartment is the differential.
Multiple points to metastases, lymphoma, multicentric GBM, gliomatosis, CSF seeding — or a phacomatosis.
None, homogeneous, patchy or ring. Ring enhancement in particular is a short and specific list.
Most tumours do not restrict, even where they are necrotic or cystic. Restriction means abscess, epidermoid or acute infarct.
Perfusion correlates with tumour grade better than the amount of contrast enhancement does.

classify.name: Enhancement pattern and the lesions that give it
rows: Metastasis, lymphoma, germinoma, pituitary macroadenoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, haemangioblastoma, ganglioglioma, meningioma, schwannoma
Metastasis, high-grade glioma, abscess, some MS plaques
classify.note: Extra-axial: 80% are meningioma or schwannoma. Intra-axial in adults: 75% are metastasis or astrocytoma. Overall roughly one third metastatic, one third glioma, one third non-glial.

measure.how: Work through the short list that shortens T1: haemorrhage or subacute haematoma, melanin, fat, some calcification, slow flow.
Reads as hypercellularity — CNS lymphoma, PNET and medulloblastoma — or calcification, haemosiderin, a very dense meningioma, melanin.
An arachnoid cyst is isointense to CSF on every sequence. Tumour necrosis never is completely.
Treat as a positive finding pointing away from tumour: abscess, epidermoid cyst, acute infarct.

pitfalls: Settling the compartment on size or signal rather than the interface. The CSF cleft, the displaced subarachnoid vessels and the dural tail are what decide it.

Forgetting that a midline-crossing lesion has its own short list: GBM through the corpus callosum, meningioma along the meninges, lymphoma, epidermoid, MS.

quiz.prompt: A rounded 4 cm mass sits against the right frontal convexity. Between the mass and the brain there is a thin rim of cerebrospinal fluid containing vessels, the cortical grey matter is displaced inwards away from the inner table, and the underlying white matter is buckled rather than expanded. Where has the mass arisen?
choices: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
Within the cortex of the frontal lobe
Within the subcortical white matter
Inside the frontal horn of the ventricle
quiz.answer: Outside the brain, from the dural surface
quiz.explain: The compartment question is answered before any question of histology, because it halves the differential at a stroke. The extra-axial signs are all displacements: a cerebrospinal fluid cleft, pial vessels running between the mass and the brain, grey matter pushed inwards so that the cortical ribbon lies between the mass and the white matter, buckling of the white matter, a widened subarachnoid space, and reaction in the adjacent bone. An intra-axial mass does the opposite - it expands cortex or white matter, effaces the subarachnoid space, and has brain rather than fluid at its margin. Being systematic matters because a large extra-axial mass invaginating deeply can look intra-axial on a single axial image; coronal images and the position of the cortical ribbon resolve it. The differentials then diverge completely: meningioma, dural metastasis, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma and lymphoma outside the brain; glioma, metastasis, abscess and demyelination within it.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old treated for breast cancer three years ago has headache. MRI shows four separate dural-based enhancing masses over both convexities and along the falx, and CT shows lytic destruction of the inner table beneath the largest, with no hyperostosis. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
Multiple meningiomas in a predisposed patient
Neurosarcoidosis involving the pachymeninges
IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis
quiz.answer: Dural metastatic deposits from the breast primary
quiz.explain: Multiplicity alone does not settle it, since meningiomas are multiple in neurofibromatosis type 2, after cranial radiation, and occasionally sporadically - but the bone does. Meningioma provokes bone: hyperostosis, a thickened sclerotic inner table, sometimes a permeative sclerotic pattern with tumour inside it. Metastasis destroys bone. Add a treated breast primary, the commonest source of dural metastases, and the diagnosis follows. The near-misses are worth holding: sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease thicken the dura in a more sheet-like, less nodular fashion and come with other clues - in sarcoid, leptomeningeal enhancement around the basal cisterns and involvement of the infundibulum and cranial nerves - and neither destroys bone. Solitary fibrous tumour, the entity that absorbed haemangiopericytoma, is the trap for a solitary lesion: narrow dural attachment, prominent internal flow voids, and bone erosion rather than hyperostosis. Saying this out loud in the report matters, because dural metastases change the whole management conversation and 'dural-based masses, likely meningiomas' closes it down.

quiz.prompt: A convexity mass has a tapering rim of thickened enhancing dura extending from each of its margins, and the neurosurgeon takes this as confirming a meningioma. Explain what this sign does and does not establish, and why it still matters to the operation.
quiz.answer: The tapering enhancing dural thickening - the dural tail - establishes that the mass is extra-axial and dural-based, which is genuinely useful, but it does not establish histology. It is seen in most meningiomas and also in dural metastases, lymphoma, solitary fibrous tumour, schwannoma, sarcoidosis and other pachymeningeal disease, so it is sensitive rather than specific. Histologically the tail may be tumour infiltrating the dura or merely reactive, hypervascular, oedematous dura, and imaging cannot separate the two. It matters to the operation because the tail may contain tumour: completeness of resection of the dural attachment is what the Simpson grading records and what predicts recurrence, so the surgeon plans to excise or coagulate the involved dura rather than the mass alone, and the report should state how far the tail extends and what it runs into, such as a venous sinus.
quiz.explain: What a sign is worth depends on the population it is used in. In a series of convexity masses the dural tail is common in meningiomas and uncommon in gliomas, so it is a good compartment sign; among dural-based masses, where every lesion has one, it discriminates nothing. That is the general lesson: a sign that separates two categories well can be useless one level further down the tree, and the tail is the neuroradiological example. The other half of the lesson is surgical. Simpson grade 1 resection - the mass, its dural attachment and any abnormal bone - carries the lowest recurrence rate, and grades rise as attachment is left behind, so the extent of the tail is an operative planning measurement rather than a descriptive flourish.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old with fever and a recent dental extraction has a 3 cm ring-enhancing left frontal lesion with surrounding oedema. The enhancing rim is smooth, thin, and thinner on the side facing the ventricle, and the centre is markedly bright on diffusion-weighted imaging with an apparent diffusion coefficient well below that of normal white matter. What is the lesion?
choices: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
A metastasis with a necrotic centre
A glioblastoma with central necrosis
A tumefactive demyelinating lesion
quiz.answer: A pyogenic abscess containing pus
quiz.explain: Pus is viscous, cellular and protein-rich, so water motion within it is genuinely restricted: the cavity is bright on diffusion with a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and this is among the most reliable signs in neuroimaging for separating an abscess from a necrotic tumour. Tumour necrosis is liquefied and acellular and has a high coefficient. Two further clues sit in the stem. An abscess rim is smooth and thin and is characteristically thinner along its deep margin, because the deep white matter is less well vascularised than the cortex - which is also why abscesses rupture into the ventricle rather than outwards - and it is often low in signal on T2, sometimes with a dual rim on susceptibility imaging. A glioblastoma rim is thick, irregular and nodular. Cautions: a treated abscess loses its restriction, some tumours restrict after haemorrhage, and spectroscopy adds amino acids, acetate and succinate to the argument, so the clinical trajectory stays in the reasoning rather than being replaced by one sequence.

quiz.prompt: A solitary ring-enhancing mass in the right parietal lobe is surrounded by extensive T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity. Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion shows relative cerebral blood volume markedly elevated in the enhancing rim, and moderately elevated in the non-enhancing hyperintense region beyond it. What does the perfusion of the region beyond the enhancement favour?
choices: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
A solitary metastasis with vasogenic oedema
An abscess with surrounding cerebritis
Radiation necrosis of the white matter
quiz.answer: A glioma infiltrating past the enhancing margin
quiz.explain: Enhancement marks where the blood-brain barrier has failed, which in a high-grade glioma is only the core; the tumour cells themselves extend well beyond it along white matter tracts, into brain that looks merely oedematous. Those infiltrated regions carry neovascularity with them, so relative cerebral blood volume in the peritumoural T2 signal is raised. Around a metastasis the same region is pure vasogenic oedema - plasma driven out through leaky capillaries into the extracellular space, with no tumour cells in it - and its blood volume is low. That difference is one of the few imaging tools that separates a solitary metastasis from a glioblastoma when the conventional images look alike, and it is why the surgical margin and the radiotherapy volume differ so much between the two diagnoses. Caveats worth carrying: the sequence needs preload and leakage correction, because contrast escaping through a broken barrier corrupts the estimate; susceptibility from blood products and from skull base bone degrades the maps; and the finding shifts a probability rather than settling a diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion of a cerebral mass gives a leakage-corrected cerebral blood volume of 5.8 mL per 100 g in the most vascular part of the lesion, while a region of interest in normal-appearing contralateral white matter gives 1.6 mL per 100 g. What is the relative cerebral blood volume ratio? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 5.8 divided by 1.6 is 3.6. The ratio is what gets reported rather than the absolute value, because absolute blood volume from this technique depends on the arterial input function, the injection, the sequence and the vendor, and only the comparison against the patient's own normal white matter is stable across studies. Ratios of roughly 1.75 are commonly used to separate high-grade from low-grade glioma, and 3.6 sits well into the high-grade range - but the threshold shifts with technique and with the leakage correction applied, so it belongs in a report as a supporting argument rather than as a grade. Two traps: sample the most vascular part of the tumour, since a single large region of interest across a heterogeneous mass averages the answer away, and do not sample a vessel, which turns any tumour into a high-grade one instantly. The standing exception is the oligodendroglioma, which often has high blood volume from its dense capillary network despite being low-grade.

quiz.prompt: Rank these five tissues by their typical apparent diffusion coefficient, from the lowest value to the highest.
quiz.answer: abscess-pus lymphoma glioblastoma vasogenic-oedema cerebrospinal-fluid
quiz.explain: The apparent diffusion coefficient measures how freely water moves, so the sequence runs from the most crowded and most viscous compartment to free fluid. Pus is viscous and packed with inflammatory cells, debris and protein and sits at the bottom. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is the most cellular of the common tumours - small round cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and scant extracellular space - so its coefficient is low, generally below that of gliomas and below normal white matter, which is why a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with a low coefficient in an immunocompetent adult is lymphoma until proved otherwise. The solid part of a glioblastoma is cellular but heterogeneously so, and sits in the middle. Vasogenic oedema is extracellular water in a widened extracellular space and diffuses more freely than normal brain. Cerebrospinal fluid is essentially free water and is the highest, which is why it is dark on the high-b image and bright on the map. The practical rule that follows: read the map, not the diffusion-weighted image, because T2 shine-through makes anything T2-bright look restricted.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after completing chemoradiotherapy for an MGMT-methylated glioblastoma, the MRI shows new enhancement at the resection margin with more surrounding FLAIR signal. The patient is clinically well and on a reducing dose of dexamethasone. Explain the two possibilities, what favours each, and what you would do.
quiz.answer: The two possibilities are true progression and pseudoprogression, a treatment effect in which radiation and temozolomide cause endothelial injury, inflammation and increased permeability, producing new or enlarging enhancement without tumour growth. Pseudoprogression is favoured here by the timing, since most cases appear within three months of finishing chemoradiotherapy; by MGMT promoter methylation, which is strongly associated with it; and by a patient who is clinically stable or improving. True progression is favoured by clinical deterioration, by enhancement appearing outside the high-dose radiation field, and by elevated relative cerebral blood volume, whereas pseudoprogression tends to show low blood volume; diffusion, spectroscopy and amino-acid PET add weight but none is definitive. The action is not to declare progression: continue treatment and repeat the MRI at a short interval of about four to eight weeks, since the RANO framework does not call progression within twelve weeks of radiotherapy unless the new enhancement lies outside the high-dose field or there is histological proof.
quiz.explain: The mirror image of this error is worth learning at the same time. Under an antiangiogenic agent such as bevacizumab, the drug restores the blood-brain barrier and the enhancement melts away within days without the tumour having shrunk - pseudoresponse - which is why response on such treatment is judged on the non-enhancing T2 and FLAIR component rather than on the enhancing volume. Both errors have one root: enhancement is a property of the barrier, not of tumour cells, so any drug or injury that changes the barrier changes the picture without changing the disease. The clinical stakes are real in both directions, since calling pseudoprogression as progression stops an effective treatment early, and calling progression as pseudoprogression leaves a growing tumour untreated for two more months.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old presents with a first seizure. MRI shows a non-enhancing, expansile mass in the left frontal lobe that is homogeneously and markedly hyperintense on T2, while on FLAIR the same lesion is suppressed centrally with a bright peripheral rim. What does this appearance favour?
choices: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
An oligodendroglioma, 1p/19q codeleted
An IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, grade 4
A tumefactive demyelinating plaque
quiz.answer: An IDH-mutant astrocytoma, not codeleted
quiz.explain: The T2-FLAIR mismatch sign - homogeneous high T2 signal with relative FLAIR suppression except at the rim - is among the most specific signs in neuro-oncology, approaching complete specificity for IDH-mutant astrocytoma without 1p/19q codeletion, while its sensitivity is low, so its absence says nothing at all. The likely substrate is the loosely structured, microcystic, water-rich matrix of these tumours: free water is bright on T2 and is nulled by the FLAIR inversion pulse, whereas the rim contains more cellular infiltrated tissue that resists nulling. Oligodendrogliomas, the other IDH-mutant tumour, are heterogeneous, frequently calcified, tend to involve the cortex, and characteristically lack the sign. A glioblastoma in a 32-year-old is possible but would usually enhance and rarely look this homogeneous. Under the 2021 WHO classification these molecular groups are the diagnosis rather than a refinement of it, so a sign that predicts the group changes the conversation before the biopsy. Apply the criteria strictly: the mismatch must involve most of the lesion, and a focal or cystic mismatch does not count.

quiz.prompt: An immunocompetent 68-year-old has a periventricular mass that is hyperattenuating on unenhanced CT, enhances homogeneously and avidly, has a low apparent diffusion coefficient, and shows strikingly little necrosis for its size. Neurosurgery plans a biopsy in four days, and the medical team wants to start dexamethasone now for the surrounding oedema. What is the strongest objection?
choices: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
Steroids raise the risk of bleeding at biopsy
Steroids will mask the restricted diffusion
Steroids promote leptomeningeal spread here
quiz.answer: Steroids can make the biopsy non-diagnostic
quiz.explain: The imaging describes primary central nervous system lymphoma: dense on unenhanced CT because the tumour is so cellular, homogeneously enhancing, low in apparent diffusion coefficient for the same reason, periventricular and abutting the ependyma, and with little necrosis in an immunocompetent patient - necrosis and ring enhancement being the rule in the AIDS-related form instead. Lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive: corticosteroids are lympholytic and can dissolve the enhancing mass within days, the old 'ghost tumour', leaving a biopsy that shows reactive gliosis and debris and forcing either weeks of waiting for the tumour to return or a second procedure. The radiologist's job when this pattern appears is therefore to say in the report that lymphoma leads the differential and that steroids should be withheld until tissue is obtained, unless impending herniation makes them unavoidable. The distractors fail in different ways: steroids do not cause bleeding, do not abolish the low coefficient of the tissue that remains, and do not disseminate the tumour.

quiz.prompt: A diffuse glioma in a young adult does not enhance at all, while the pituitary gland, the choroid plexus and a small meningioma in the same patient enhance intensely. Explain what enhancement is actually measuring, and what follows for judging whether a lesion is benign.
quiz.answer: Gadolinium enhancement measures delivery of contrast into the extracellular space, which requires that contrast can leave the vasculature. It therefore maps where the blood-brain barrier is absent or broken, not where tumour is. The pituitary, choroid plexus, pineal gland, dura and area postrema lie outside the barrier and have fenestrated capillaries, so they enhance normally, as does a meningioma, which is fed by dural vessels that never had a barrier. A diffuse glioma grows through brain whose capillaries retain intact tight junctions, so it can be extensive and still not enhance at all. It follows that absence of enhancement is not evidence that a lesion is benign - a non-enhancing diffuse astrocytoma is still a tumour that infiltrates and eventually progresses, and its grade is set by histology and molecular findings rather than by enhancement - and that enhancement in a treated tumour may reflect a barrier damaged by surgery, radiation or infarction rather than tumour itself.
quiz.explain: The consequences run in both directions and both are common errors. Reading enhancement as a proxy for malignancy under-calls the non-enhancing diffuse gliomas, which under the 2021 WHO classification may reach grade 4 on molecular grounds alone - homozygous deletion of CDKN2A/B in an IDH-mutant astrocytoma, for instance, makes it grade 4 without necrosis or microvascular proliferation being present. Reading it the other way over-calls, because a subacute infarct, an area of demyelination, radiation injury and postoperative granulation tissue all enhance briskly. The practical habit is to describe enhancement as a finding about the barrier, then argue about the cause using the company it keeps: territory, diffusion, perfusion, time course and what the patient has already been treated with.

quiz.prompt: An incidental convexity meningioma measured 24 mm in maximum diameter three years ago and measures 31 mm on the current study. Treating the lesion as a sphere, by what factor has its volume increased? Give the answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Volume scales with the cube of a linear dimension, so 31 over 24 cubed is 2.2: a 29 per cent increase in diameter is a 116 per cent increase in volume. That is why a surveillance report reading 'minimally increased, 24 to 31 mm' can be so misleading - the tumour has more than doubled. It is also why measurement error deserves respect, since 2 mm of interobserver variation on a 24 mm lesion swings the implied volume by more than a quarter; growth should be judged against the earliest available study rather than the immediately preceding one, and measured on the same plane and sequence each time. For meningiomas specifically, a demonstrable growth rate, T2 hyperintensity, absence of calcification, peritumoural oedema and younger patient age all favour a tumour that will keep growing, and a growing meningioma in an operable location is treated before it becomes a symptomatic one.

module_contract.goal: Read a group of breast calcifications by morphology and distribution together, decide whether it needs sampling, and carry a stereotactic biopsy through to a concordant result.

approach.detail: The form of the calcifications is the single most important factor in separating benign from malignant — read shape before distribution.
Diffuse/scattered and regional patterns favour benign; grouped, linear and especially segmental distributions raise suspicion.

approach.step: Do not lean on stability alone
approach.detail: Stability over time is reassuring for a probably-benign morphology, but roughly 25% of malignant calcification clusters were stable for 8–63 months in the literature this page cites — morphology outranks stability.

approach.step: Look for the tattoo sign before calling something skin calcification
approach.detail: Skin calcifications should have an identical configuration on orthogonal views — confirm this rather than assuming location from one view.
Amorphous and coarse heterogeneous calcifications are typically larger (>0.5 mm); fine pleomorphic and fine linear/branching are typically smaller (<0.5 mm) and carry the higher malignancy risk.

classify.name: Calcification morphology and malignancy risk
rows: Round or oval, lucent-centred; identical on orthogonal views (tattoo sign)
Coarse, irregular, rod-shaped, ductal — plasma cell mastitis, >1 mm
Layers on the horizontal-beam lateral view
Thin, irregular lines following a ductal distribution

pitfalls: Reassuring on stability alone when the morphology itself is suspicious — a quarter of malignant clusters are stable for years.
Confusing coarse heterogeneous with fine pleomorphic by eye rather than by size and conspicuity — the distinction changes the reported risk band.
Calling calcifications 'skin' without confirming the tattoo sign on a second view.
Under-reading a segmental distribution as regional — segmental distribution (a duct system, apex toward the nipple) is the pattern that most needs full-field sampling.
