choices: Report benign layering calcifications in microcysts and return her to routine screening
Report fine pleomorphic calcification and book a stereotactic biopsy this week
Report amorphous calcification and offer six-month short-interval magnification views
Report dystrophic calcification and retrieve the previous operation note first
quiz.explain: This is the one appearance that is defined by how it changes between projections. Calcium sediments to the bottom of tiny cysts, so with the vertical beam of a craniocaudal view you look down the column and see a smudge that can mimic amorphous calcification; with the horizontal beam of a 90-degree lateral you look across it and see a meniscus, the teacup. The mediolateral oblique is not good enough, because its angled beam blurs the layering; ask specifically for a true lateral. The v2025 descriptor is layering (formerly milk of calcium), a typically benign finding assessed as category 2. The trap runs the other way too: if the group looks identical on both projections, the layering argument is not available to you and the morphology must stand on its own.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has a new 2.5 cm run of calcifications extending back from the nipple in a wedge that points to the nipple. On magnification they are thin, of varying calibre, some branching in a dot-dash pattern. How do you assess and act?
quiz.answer: Category 4C: biopsy now, and warn the team that high-grade DCIS is likely
choices: Category 4C: biopsy now, and warn the team that high-grade DCIS is likely
Category 3: repeat magnification views in six months, since it has not changed
Category 2: benign secretory calcification, so return her to routine screening
Category 0: add ultrasound and MRI before any decision on this group is taken
quiz.explain: Fine linear and fine-linear-branching calcification carries the highest positive predictive value of any morphology in the BI-RADS 5th edition atlas, around 70 per cent, which places it above the 50 per cent floor of subcategory 4C. Category 5 is reserved for at least 95 per cent likelihood and would need supporting features such as an associated mass or skin change. The segmental distribution compounds the suspicion because it follows a duct system, exactly the territory high-grade comedo DCIS necrosis casts. Category 3 is not available for suspicious morphology; it is reserved for findings with a 2 per cent ceiling. Tell the surgeon the span, because the calcification often maps the disease better than any other test and drives the choice between wide excision and mastectomy.

quiz.prompt: Your unit biopsies 40 groups of fine-linear-branching calcification over a year. For this calculation, assume the local positive predictive value is 70 per cent. How many benign results should you expect? Answer as a whole number of biopsies.
quiz.explain: If 70 per cent are malignant, 30 per cent are benign: 0.30 x 40 = 12. This supplied probability is an arithmetic assumption, not a universal risk for every calcification group. Consider morphology, distribution and clinical context, then assess imaging-pathology concordance after sampling.

quiz.prompt: In the BI-RADS v2025, what is the minimum likelihood of malignancy a finding must carry before it may be assessed as category 5? Answer as a whole-number percentage.
quiz.explain: BI-RADS 5 denotes a malignancy likelihood of at least 95 per cent and requires tissue diagnosis. A benign biopsy result must be treated as discordant and resolved. Imaging suspicion does not itself replace histological confirmation.

quiz.prompt: You perform a stereotactic vacuum-assisted biopsy for grouped amorphous calcification. The specimen radiograph clearly shows calcification in three cores, but histology reports fibrocystic change with no calcification identified. In one or two sentences, say what you do next and why.
quiz.answer: Treat this as discordant: ask the pathologist to cut deeper levels and to examine the block under polarised light for calcium oxalate, and if calcification still cannot be matched to the histology, repeat the sampling or proceed to excision.
quiz.explain: Radiological-pathological concordance is the safety net of the whole calcification pathway, and it fails silently if nobody checks it. Two things can go wrong here. The calcium may simply lie in a part of the block that has not yet been sectioned, which deeper levels solve. Or it may be calcium oxalate, which is transparent on routine haematoxylin and eosin staining and only becomes visible as a birefringent crystal under polarised light; oxalate tends to accompany benign processes, while the calcium phosphate of hydroxyapatite is what malignancy usually produces. If neither manoeuvre finds calcium, the pathologist has not examined the lesion you targeted, and a benign report tells you nothing about it. Say so explicitly in the report rather than filing the case.

quiz.prompt: A surgeon challenges you at the multidisciplinary meeting: why keep biopsying calcification when the clinical examination and the ultrasound are both normal? In one or two sentences, explain what calcification contributes to the detection of DCIS.
quiz.answer: Most DCIS is impalpable and invisible on ultrasound, so calcification is frequently the only sign it produces, and it is the morphology and distribution of that calcification that let mammography find the disease before it becomes invasive.
quiz.explain: DCIS is confined within the duct, so it usually creates no mass to feel and no hypoechoic lesion to see. What it does create is necrotic debris and secretory material that mineralises inside the duct lumen, which is why calcification is its dominant, and often its sole, imaging manifestation. The pattern reflects the grade: high-grade comedo necrosis casts the duct and gives fine linear and branching forms, while low-grade cribriform and micropapillary disease produces rounder, finer, more amorphous granules that are much easier to dismiss. This is also the honest answer to the overdiagnosis question the surgeon is really asking: calcification detection is why screening finds DCIS at all, and the debate about which DCIS needs treating is a separate one from whether we can see it.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these calcification distribution descriptors in their BI-RADS v2025 lexicon sequence, from widespread patterns to ductal patterns. This is not a fixed malignancy-risk ladder.
quiz.answer: diffuse regional grouped linear segmental
quiz.explain: The lexicon sequence is diffuse, regional, grouped, linear, segmental. Interpret distribution with morphology and interval change; it does not independently assign a category or universal malignancy probability. The v2025 manual removed the previous distribution-risk table.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of a stereotactic vacuum-assisted biopsy for calcification in the order you would carry them out.
quiz.answer: magnification-views stereotactic-pair vacuum-sampling specimen-radiograph clip-deployment post-biopsy-mammogram
quiz.explain: Each step protects the one after it. Magnification craniocaudal and true lateral views come first because they establish morphology, extent and the best approach, and they are much harder to obtain once a cavity and a haematoma exist. The stereotactic pair at plus and minus 15 degrees provides the depth coordinate. Sampling follows, then the specimen radiograph, which is the only proof that the calcification is in the pot rather than still in the breast; if it is absent, you resample now, not next week. The clip is deployed once you know the target has been hit, since it marks the site for the surgeon and for future comparison. The two-view post-biopsy mammogram closes the loop by recording where the clip actually ended up, and how much calcification remains.

quiz.prompt: Three years after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a woman's mammogram shows a new 2 cm cluster of coarse irregular calcifications at the scar, several with lucent centres, alongside an oval fat-density lesion with a thin calcified rim. What is your report?
quiz.answer: Benign coarse postsurgical calcifications and an oil cyst; complete the routine annual mammogram
choices: Benign coarse postsurgical calcifications and an oil cyst; complete the routine annual mammogram
Suspicious pleomorphic calcification at the scar; arrange stereotactic biopsy of the group
Probably benign findings; bring her back for magnification views of the scar at six months
Incomplete assessment; obtain contrast-enhanced MRI of both breasts before deciding
quiz.explain: Fat necrosis writes itself into the mammogram in a recognisable way. Coarse calcification is the v2025 descriptor, incorporating the older dystrophic terminology for these postsurgical changes. The oval fat-density lesion with a thin calcified rim is an oil cyst, and a lesion containing fat is benign; that is one of the few genuinely reliable rules in breast imaging. Recurrent disease at a scar tends to produce fine pleomorphic calcification, an enlarging mass, or increasing distortion rather than lucent-centred coarse particles. What earns a second look is any part of the group whose particles are thin, of varying calibre and without lucent centres, because dystrophic and malignant calcification can coexist at an operated site.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old has dense, smooth, rod-shaped calcifications more than a millimetre wide scattered through both breasts, several with lucent centres, all oriented along lines converging towards the nipples. Some branch, but each limb is continuous and smooth. What is the right report?
quiz.answer: Secretory calcification of duct ectasia: benign, with no further imaging required
choices: Secretory calcification of duct ectasia: benign, with no further imaging required
Comedo DCIS spanning both breasts: stereotactic biopsy of the densest group
Vascular calcification: report the cardiovascular risk and repeat imaging in a year
Skin calcification: confirm with tangential views before returning her to screening
quiz.explain: This is the benign appearance most often mistaken for high-grade DCIS, because both fill ducts and both can branch. The discriminators are calibre and continuity. Secretory, or plasma-cell mastitis, calcification is large and rod-like, typically over half a millimetre wide, smooth-edged, of even thickness along its length, often with a lucent centre because the calcium coats the duct wall around retained secretions, and it is usually bilateral and roughly symmetrical in an older woman. Malignant fine linear calcification is thin, irregular in calibre, discontinuous in a dot-dash rhythm, and confined to one segment. Vascular calcification runs as parallel tram-tracks that do not converge on the nipple, and skin calcification is polygonal with lucent centres and sits in the skin line on a tangential view.

quiz.prompt: On both screening projections a 42-year-old has a group of small lucent-centred polygonal calcifications that keep the same relationship to one another and lie close to the medial skin surface on each view. What is the most useful next step?
quiz.answer: A tangential view of the marked skin site, to project the group into the skin line
choices: A tangential view of the marked skin site, to project the group into the skin line
A stereotactic vacuum biopsy of the group with a marker clip left at the site
Targeted ultrasound of the medial breast, with biopsy of any correlate found
Six-month magnification follow-up of both breasts to establish that it is stable
quiz.explain: Dermal calcification is a classic false alarm, and it is cheap to exclude. The clue is the fixed internal arrangement: because the group lies in a flat sheet of skin rather than in three-dimensional breast tissue, the particles keep the same pattern relative to one another whatever the projection, whereas deep calcification changes its configuration as the breast is compressed differently. The particles themselves are small, polygonal and lucent-centred, lying in sweat glands. The confirmatory manoeuvre is an alphanumeric grid localisation of the skin surface followed by a tangential projection, which throws the group into the skin line where it becomes unmistakable. Ultrasound will not show them, and biopsying skin calcification is an avoidable harm that a single extra view prevents.

quiz.prompt: A 51-year-old's mammogram shows hundreds of amorphous calcifications scattered randomly and roughly symmetrically through both breasts, with no group standing out and no associated mass or distortion. How should you assess this?
quiz.answer: The bilateral random scatter makes them benign; return her to routine screening
choices: The bilateral random scatter makes them benign; return her to routine screening
Amorphous morphology stays suspicious wherever it lies; biopsy the largest group
Assess as probably benign and repeat magnification views of both breasts at six months
Assess as incomplete and add tomosynthesis and ultrasound of both breasts today
quiz.explain: Morphology and distribution are read together, never in isolation, and this is the case that proves it. Amorphous calcification carries a positive predictive value of roughly 21 per cent in the BI-RADS 5th edition atlas when it is grouped, which is squarely biopsy territory. Spread diffusely and bilaterally, the same particles reflect fibrocystic change, sclerosing adenosis or involuting lobules, and biopsy of one arbitrarily chosen area answers no question, because there is no reason to think the sampled millilitre differs from the rest. What would change this is asymmetry: a group that is denser, more numerous, or newer than the surrounding background, or one that has appeared since the last round. Compare with the previous films before you settle on diffuse.

quiz.prompt: After an uneventful stereotactic vacuum biopsy of an upper outer quadrant calcification group, the two-view post-biopsy mammogram shows the marker clip lying about 3 cm away from the residual calcification and biopsy cavity. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Clip displacement is common; record the offset so that localisation still targets the calcification
choices: Clip displacement is common; record the offset so that localisation still targets the calcification
The clip is correctly sited, which means the device removed all of the calcification
Repeat the biopsy today, because the wrong quadrant has clearly been sampled instead
No action is needed, since the surgeon will locate the cavity by palpation at operation
quiz.explain: The clip is deployed while the breast is compressed. When compression is released the tissue re-expands like a concertina and the clip can travel several centimetres along the axis of compression, most often towards the skin; this is the accordion effect, and it is a property of the technique rather than an error. The post-biopsy two-view mammogram exists precisely to document it. What matters is that the report states where the residual calcification actually lies, so that a subsequent wire or seed is placed to the calcification rather than to the clip. Assuming the clip marks the target is how a wrong-site excision happens. Absence of visible residual calcification does not confirm complete removal either, and does not change the need for surgical clearance if the histology is malignant.

quiz.prompt: An MRI is requested solely for suspected silicone implant rupture. Which protocol choice answers that question?
choices: Routine dynamic contrast imaging alone
A dedicated non-contrast implant protocol with silicone-sensitive sequences
Only diffusion images
Only a thoracic spine localiser
quiz.answer: A dedicated non-contrast implant protocol with silicone-sensitive sequences
quiz.explain: Implant integrity depends on shell and silicone assessment. Contrast-enhanced breast imaging addresses a separate question, such as malignancy, and is added when indicated.

quiz.prompt: MRI demonstrates collapsed implant-shell lines within the fibrous capsule, without silicone outside that capsule. Which category fits?
choices: Extracapsular rupture
A definite implant-associated lymphoma
Intracapsular rupture
A malignant breast-parenchymal mass
quiz.answer: Intracapsular rupture
quiz.explain: The distinction depends on whether silicone extends beyond the fibrous capsule. Normal folds and other mimics require multiplanar review before diagnosing rupture.

quiz.prompt: Years after implantation, a patient develops a new unilateral peri-implant effusion. What should the interpretation prompt?
choices: Routine reassurance from fluid signal alone
Assume all late fluid represents mechanical rupture
Ignore the capsule if the implant shell appears intact
Targeted assessment for implant-associated disease, including tissue or fluid sampling when indicated
quiz.answer: Targeted assessment for implant-associated disease, including tissue or fluid sampling when indicated
quiz.explain: A delayed symptomatic collection merits evaluation of fluid, capsule, any mass and nodes. Imaging alone cannot diagnose or exclude implant-associated lymphoma.

quiz.prompt: A man has tender subareolar tissue with a fan-shaped pattern centred on the nipple. Which diagnosis is favoured?
choices: Gynaecomastia
A simple lipoma outside the breast
Invasive carcinoma in every case
A collapsed breast implant
quiz.answer: Gynaecomastia
quiz.explain: Typical gynaecomastia is centred behind the nipple. Correlate with examination, medications and symptoms rather than applying the female breast differential unchanged.

quiz.prompt: A man has an eccentric irregular solid breast mass and nipple retraction. What is the appropriate imaging conclusion?
choices: Male sex makes carcinoma implausible
A suspicious lesion requiring breast assessment and tissue diagnosis
Gynaecomastia regardless of morphology
A benign lesion unless bilateral
quiz.answer: A suspicious lesion requiring breast assessment and tissue diagnosis
quiz.explain: Eccentric location and malignant morphology are not explained by ordinary gynaecomastia. Use a diagnostic breast pathway and a clear assessment category.

quiz.prompt: An implant-integrity MRI shows no rupture. The referral also mentions a new palpable breast lump, but no dedicated parenchymal assessment was performed. Explain what the result does and does not establish.
quiz.answer: The result addresses implant integrity within the acquired protocol. It does not exclude a breast-parenchymal cause of the palpable lump. State that separate question explicitly and arrange or recommend the appropriate diagnostic breast assessment, with imaging targeted to the palpable site and clinical correlation.
quiz.explain: An implant and the surrounding breast are different targets. A normal answer to one should not be allowed to close the other.

quiz.prompt: Silicone-sensitive images show silicone beyond the implant capsule and in an axillary node. What anatomical details belong in the report before discussing management?
quiz.answer: Describe the side, implant type and position if known, shell appearance, and extracapsular silicone distribution. Localise affected breast or chest-wall tissues and the axillary finding, noting any associated mass or fluid. Separate evidence of silicone migration from assessment of unrelated suspicious breast findings.
quiz.explain: The distribution matters more than the rupture label alone. Mapping the findings allows the clinical team to connect symptoms, implant history and possible treatment.

quiz.prompt: A patient develops swelling years after implantation. Ultrasound shows a new effusion and an indeterminate capsular nodule. How would you communicate the concern without diagnosing lymphoma from imaging?
quiz.answer: Report the delayed effusion, nodule location and size, capsular findings and relevant nodes. State that implant-associated disease is a concern requiring specialist breast assessment and appropriate fluid or tissue evaluation. Imaging cannot determine whether the process is malignant, inflammatory or another cause on these findings alone.
quiz.explain: The concern should trigger the correct investigation while retaining diagnostic uncertainty. A named serious possibility is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A man has typical subareolar glandular tissue, but examination identifies a separate hard lump lateral to the nipple. What error would occur if the report ended at gynaecomastia?
quiz.answer: It would leave the separate palpable abnormality unexplained. Correlate the exact lump location with targeted imaging, document whether a distinct lesion is present, and assess its morphology independently. Gynaecomastia can coexist with another lesion and should not be used to dismiss a discordant clinical finding.
quiz.explain: One correct diagnosis may be incomplete. Concordance requires explaining the finding that prompted the referral, not merely finding a benign abnormality nearby.

quiz.prompt: A male breast lesion is irregular and eccentric, but the draft recommends observation because male breast cancer is uncommon. Explain the reasoning error and improve the conclusion.
quiz.answer: Low background frequency does not make suspicious morphology benign. Describe the lesion and associated nipple, skin or nodal findings, assign the appropriate diagnostic assessment, and recommend tissue evaluation through the breast pathway. The conclusion should reflect this lesion's evidence rather than reassurance based only on sex.
quiz.explain: Population frequency informs prior probability. It does not override a concerning individual finding or remove the need for diagnostic concordance.

module_contract.goal: Choose breast MRI and ultrasound for the situations in which they change surgical management, and interpret enhancement, kinetics, nodes, implants and the treated breast accordingly.

approach.detail: Problem-solving for a finding not resolved on mammography/ultrasound, high-risk screening, staging a new cancer (it changes management in 15–30% of cases), or monitoring response to chemotherapy.
Focus/foci (<5 mm, too small to characterise further), mass (a 3-D lesion — describe shape, margin, enhancement pattern) or non-mass enhancement (no distinct 3-D shape).
Round, oval or lobulated margins are lower risk; irregular shape carries about 32% malignancy and a spiculated margin about 80%.

Dark, non-enhancing internal septations are typical of a fibroadenoma; enhancing internal septations, rim enhancement (~40% malignant if not a simple cyst), and central enhancement (associated with high-grade cancer) all push toward malignancy.

approach.step: Read the kinetic curve on the delayed phase
approach.detail: Persistent (Type 1, still rising) carries about 6% malignancy risk; washout (Type 3, rises then drops) carries 29–77%; plateau (Type 2) sits in between.

approach.step: Correlate with ultrasound before recommending biopsy
approach.detail: An MRI-detected finding needs a second-look ultrasound correlate whenever one is plausible, so that sampling can be done under ultrasound rather than MRI guidance.

classify.name: Kinetic curve type and malignancy risk
rows: Slow initial rise, continued rise through the delayed phase
Initial rise followed by a plateau (±10%) in the delayed phase
Rapid initial rise, then a drop-off (washout) in the delayed phase

measure.how: Measure the enhancing lesion's largest diameter.
measure.cutoff: < 5 mm = focus, too small to characterise by shape/margin

pitfalls: Calling washout kinetics diagnostic on its own — a benign lesion can wash out and a cancer can occasionally show a persistent curve; combine kinetics with morphology.
Missing enhancing internal septations because dark septations (typical of fibroadenoma) set the expectation.
Reporting a mass without stating shape and margin — spiculated margin alone carries a very different risk (~80%) from a round, circumscribed one.
Recommending MRI-guided biopsy by default instead of first attempting a targeted second-look ultrasound.

TECHNIQUE

FINDINGS

quiz.prompt: Four women are referred to your breast unit asking about supplemental MRI screening. Which of them should be offered annual contrast-enhanced breast MRI alongside mammography?
quiz.answer: A 31-year-old who had mantle radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma when she was seventeen
choices: A 31-year-old who had mantle radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma when she was seventeen
A 47-year-old whose mother developed a breast cancer at the age of seventy-four
A 52-year-old with heterogeneously dense breasts and no relevant family history
A 39-year-old whose fibroadenoma was surgically excised six years ago and confirmed
quiz.explain: Chest irradiation between roughly ages 10 and 30 confers a lifetime breast cancer risk approaching that of a BRCA carrier, which is why supplemental MRI is recommended, usually beginning about eight years after treatment and not before age 25. The threshold in general use is a lifetime risk of 20 to 25 per cent or more, which also captures BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers and their untested first-degree relatives, TP53, PTEN, CDH1 and PALB2. A single second-degree or late-onset first-degree relative does not reach that threshold. Dense tissue alone raises risk modestly and lowers mammographic sensitivity, but it is handled by supplemental ultrasound or contrast-enhanced mammography in most services rather than by MRI. Excised benign fibroadenoma confers no meaningful excess risk at all.

quiz.prompt: On a high-risk screening MRI a 6 mm mass is dark on T2, has an irregular margin and heterogeneous internal enhancement, and its kinetic curve rises steeply then falls away after two minutes. Nothing is visible on the mammogram. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Assess as suspicious, arrange second-look ultrasound, and biopsy under whichever guidance shows it
choices: Assess as suspicious, arrange second-look ultrasound, and biopsy under whichever guidance shows it
Assess as benign, since persistent type 1 kinetics permit return to annual screening
Assess as probably benign and repeat the whole examination at six months for stability
Assess as artefactual, re-shim the magnet, and repeat the dynamic series after re-injection
quiz.explain: A steep initial rise with a fall after the two-minute mark is a type 3 washout curve, the most worrying of the three delayed patterns, and here it agrees with a morphology that is already suspicious: irregular margin, heterogeneous internal enhancement, and low T2 signal. When morphology and kinetics disagree, morphology wins, because plenty of malignancies, particularly DCIS and invasive lobular carcinoma, show type 1 persistent enhancement, and plenty of fibroadenomas wash out. The practical route is second-look targeted ultrasound of the correct quadrant and depth, which finds a correlate for a substantial minority of MRI-detected lesions and makes biopsy quicker, cheaper and better tolerated. If nothing is found, biopsy under MRI guidance rather than downgrading the lesion because ultrasound was negative.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old having high-risk screening MRI has background parenchymal enhancement that limits confidence. A trainee proposes that all premenopausal breast MRI must be booked on cycle days 7-14. Is that a current requirement, and how should this limited examination be handled?
quiz.answer: No. Current ACR guidance does not require routine menstrual-cycle scheduling. Document the actual limitation and individualise any repeat or further assessment with the breast imaging team; cycle timing alone does not guarantee a diagnostic examination.
quiz.explain: Background parenchymal enhancement should be reported, but its degree alone does not establish that an examination is non-diagnostic. Routine scheduling by menstrual phase has not reliably improved diagnostic performance. Decide further assessment from the actual image limitation and clinical question, without an automatic cycle-related delay.

quiz.prompt: A woman with silicone implants has MRI for a change in breast shape. On silicone-selective sequences several curvilinear low-signal lines float within the silicone, well away from the periphery, and no silicone lies outside the fibrous capsule. In one or two sentences, report the finding and its consequence.
quiz.answer: This is the linguine sign of intracapsular rupture: the elastomer shell has collapsed inside an intact fibrous capsule, so the silicone remains contained and she needs elective implant exchange rather than urgent surgery.
quiz.explain: Implant imaging turns on two boundaries: the implant's own elastomer shell and the fibrous capsule the body builds around it. When the shell tears but the capsule holds, silicone escapes the shell yet stays inside the capsule, and the collapsed shell floats within it as the wavy dark lines of the linguine sign. Lesser degrees give the subcapsular line, or the keyhole and teardrop signs where a little silicone tracks into a radial fold. Radial folds alone, with no silicone between the layers, are a normal finding and the commonest source of overcalling. Extracapsular rupture is the different and more consequential diagnosis: silicone outside the capsule, in the parenchyma or in axillary nodes, giving the snowstorm appearance of dirty shadowing on ultrasound.

quiz.prompt: On a dynamic breast MRI a lesion has a signal intensity of 180 before contrast and 468 on the first post-contrast acquisition. Calculate the initial percentage enhancement. Answer as a whole-number percentage.
quiz.explain: Initial enhancement is the rise divided by the baseline: 468 minus 180 is 288, and 288 divided by 180 is 1.6, so 160 per cent. The number matters because the initial phase, before roughly two minutes, is graded slow, medium or rapid, and the fast rise of a malignancy reflects leaky neovascular capillaries with wide endothelial gaps. Curve typing then uses the delayed phase after that point: type 1 continues to rise, type 2 plateaus, type 3 falls away. Do the arithmetic on a region of interest placed in the most avidly enhancing part of the lesion, avoiding necrosis and avoiding the edge, because a region straddling normal tissue flattens the curve. Absolute signal intensities are not comparable between scanners, but the ratio is.

quiz.prompt: On axillary ultrasound before breast cancer surgery, above what uniform cortical thickness is a node conventionally regarded as suspicious and worth sampling? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Cortical thickness above about 3 mm is the threshold most units use, but the shape of the thickening matters as much as the number. Tumour arrives through the afferent lymphatics and first deposits in the subcapsular sinus, so the earliest sign is a focal eccentric bulge of cortex, not uniform thickening, and a node with an eccentric 5 mm lobe and a perfectly preserved fatty hilum can still be involved. Later changes are loss of the hilum, rounding with a shortened long-to-short axis ratio, non-hilar peripheral vascularity, and matting. Sensitivity is moderate at best, so a normal axillary ultrasound does not replace sentinel node biopsy; a positive needle sample, however, changes the operation and can spare the patient a two-stage procedure.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the acquisitions of a standard dynamic contrast-enhanced breast MRI in the order they are obtained and processed.
quiz.answer: localiser t2-weighted pre-contrast-t1 first-post-contrast delayed-post-contrast subtraction-images
quiz.explain: The order is not arbitrary. T2-weighted imaging is acquired before contrast because it must be uncontaminated: it is what tells you a mass is a cyst, a lymph node with a fatty hilum, or a T2-bright fibroadenoma with dark internal septations. The pre-contrast T1 series is the arithmetic baseline for everything that follows, so patient movement between it and the post-contrast series is what ruins subtractions. The first post-contrast acquisition, obtained within about 90 seconds of injection, carries most of the diagnostic weight because that is when malignant enhancement peaks against a still-quiet background; delayed acquisitions out to five or seven minutes define the curve type. Subtraction images are computed last, and should always be read alongside the source images rather than instead of them.

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm enhancing mass is seen only on MRI, and targeted ultrasound of the correct quadrant finds no correlate. Arrange the steps of the resulting work-up in the order they occur.
quiz.answer: mri-detection second-look-ultrasound mri-guided-biopsy clip-placement post-biopsy-mammogram
quiz.explain: Second-look ultrasound comes before MRI-guided biopsy for practical reasons: it is quicker, cheaper, better tolerated and available on any list, and it succeeds in a useful proportion of cases if you scan the right quadrant at the right depth with the MRI open beside you. When it fails, the lesion must still be sampled under MRI guidance rather than dismissed, because a negative second look does not downgrade a suspicious enhancing mass. A clip is deployed through the biopsy device before the patient leaves the magnet, since the lesion may be invisible by any other means and enhancement can vanish once the lesion has been sampled. The two-view post-biopsy mammogram records the clip position for future localisation and for comparison at follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old has a firm mobile lump. Ultrasound shows an 18 mm oval hypoechoic mass, wider than tall, circumscribed with three gentle lobulations, homogeneous internally, with mild posterior enhancement and no vascular distortion. What is the appropriate management?
quiz.answer: Probably benign: document it and offer six-month ultrasound follow-up, or biopsy if she prefers
choices: Probably benign: document it and offer six-month ultrasound follow-up, or biopsy if she prefers
Suspicious: perform a core biopsy today, because a palpable mass at any age needs tissue
Malignant features: arrange staging MRI and axillary ultrasound before taking a biopsy
Simple cyst: aspirate it under ultrasound guidance and discard the fluid if it is clear
quiz.explain: Every feature here is on the benign side of the BI-RADS ultrasound lexicon: oval shape, parallel orientation, circumscribed margin with no more than three gentle lobulations, homogeneous hypoechoic internal echoes, and posterior enhancement rather than shadowing. That combination in a woman of this age fits a fibroadenoma and carries a malignancy risk of around 2 per cent or less, which is category 3 territory. The features that would overturn it are a taller-than-wide orientation, an angular, microlobulated or spiculated margin, an echogenic halo, posterior acoustic shadowing, or internal calcification. A palpable mass is not itself a reason to biopsy, but it is a reason to take the woman's preference seriously, and many will choose tissue diagnosis over two years of surveillance.

quiz.prompt: Staging ultrasound in a woman with a 15 mm invasive carcinoma shows a level I axillary node with a preserved fatty hilum but an eccentric 5 mm bulge of cortex on one side. What is the right course?
quiz.answer: Sample the node with a needle and mark it with a clip before any systemic treatment
choices: Sample the node with a needle and mark it with a clip before any systemic treatment
Report it as reactive, since the fatty hilum is preserved throughout the whole node
Proceed directly to axillary node clearance without needle sampling of the node first
Repeat the axillary ultrasound once the primary tumour has been surgically removed
quiz.explain: An eccentric cortical bulge with a preserved hilum is the earliest morphological sign of metastasis, because deposits land in the subcapsular sinus and expand the cortex focally long before they efface the hilum. Preserved hilar fat is therefore reassuring only in a node whose cortex is uniformly thin. A fine needle or core sample of the most abnormal node converts imaging suspicion into a fact that changes the operation and the sequence of treatment. Marking the sampled node with a clip is what makes targeted axillary dissection possible if she has neoadjuvant chemotherapy, because a node that responds completely becomes impossible to find again. Clearance without sampling overtreats the substantial proportion of morphologically abnormal nodes that prove reactive.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a biopsy-proven 12 mm invasive ductal carcinoma has staging MRI. Beyond the mass, enhancement extends 5 cm posteriorly in a wedge converging on the nipple, with a clustered ring internal pattern. How should this change the plan?
quiz.answer: It suggests DCIS extending well beyond the mass: discuss wider excision or mastectomy
choices: It suggests DCIS extending well beyond the mass: discuss wider excision or mastectomy
It is benign fibrocystic enhancement: proceed with the planned wide local excision
It is background parenchymal enhancement: repeat the study in the second week of her cycle
It is post-biopsy change: attribute it to the recent core biopsy and disregard it entirely
quiz.explain: Non-mass enhancement is described by distribution and by internal pattern, and both are informative here. A segmental distribution occupies the territory of a single duct system, which is precisely how DCIS spreads. The clustered ring internal pattern, thin rings of enhancement around ducts filled with non-enhancing debris, is the most specific of the internal patterns for malignancy; homogeneous and heterogeneous patterns are far less discriminating. Background enhancement is bilateral and symmetrical rather than confined to one segment, and post-biopsy change is focal around the tract. Before converting a woman to mastectomy on MRI alone, obtain histology from the far end of the segment, because MRI overestimates extent often enough that a single wide excision plan should not be abandoned on imaging alone.

quiz.prompt: Fourteen months after wide local excision and radiotherapy, a woman has an area of nodular enhancement at the lumpectomy bed with a washout curve. The mammogram shows scarring only, and there is no fat signal within the enhancing tissue. What is your interpretation?
quiz.answer: Nodular washout enhancement at this interval is recurrence until histology proves otherwise
choices: Nodular washout enhancement at this interval is recurrence until histology proves otherwise
This is expected scar enhancement at fourteen months; repeat the study in twelve months
This is fat necrosis, whose enhancement follows fat on every sequence and needs no action
This is radiotherapy oedema; report the skin thickening and continue annual mammography
quiz.explain: Granulation tissue in a healing surgical bed does enhance, but its enhancement is typically thin and linear along the cavity wall, and it fades over the first year to eighteen months. Nodular enhancement, particularly with washout kinetics, at more than a year from surgery, is the pattern of recurrence and warrants biopsy. Fat necrosis is the important mimic and is excluded here by the absence of internal fat signal: fat necrosis contains a central component that follows fat on every sequence and loses signal with fat suppression, usually with a smooth enhancing rim. Radiotherapy change causes diffuse skin thickening and oedema that settles over two to three years. Comparison with the earliest post-treatment baseline study is what makes this judgement reliable.

quiz.prompt: A woman presents with an axillary nodal deposit of adenocarcinoma consistent with a breast primary, but mammography and whole-breast ultrasound are both normal. What is the most useful next imaging step?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI, which finds the primary in most such patients and can spare mastectomy
choices: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI, which finds the primary in most such patients and can spare mastectomy
Whole-body PET-CT alone, reserving breast MRI for those with dense fibroglandular tissue
Bilateral mastectomy without further breast imaging, to clear the presumed occult primary
Six-monthly mammographic follow-up, until the primary tumour grows to a detectable size
quiz.explain: Occult primary presenting as axillary nodal metastasis is one of the strongest indications for breast MRI, because it locates a mammographically and sonographically invisible tumour in the majority of cases. That matters practically rather than academically: if MRI shows a small unifocal primary, the woman can have breast-conserving surgery and radiotherapy instead of the mastectomy that historically followed a negative work-up, and if MRI is genuinely negative, whole-breast radiotherapy with axillary treatment becomes a defensible alternative. PET-CT contributes to distant staging and may show the primary, but its spatial resolution is poor for small breast lesions. Delay while awaiting growth is not an option once nodal disease is established.

approach.detail: Check the finding across more than one sequence and phase before committing to a mass — flow artifact and trabeculation are common mimics.
Chamber, wall versus septum versus valve, pedunculated versus broad-based, and any relation to an indwelling line or catheter.
Thrombus shows no early or late gadolinium enhancement. Tumours, myxoma included, typically show heterogeneous enhancement.
Fat, calcification, necrosis and vascularity on the available sequences narrow the differential.
A cardiac mass is far more likely to be a secondary metastasis than a primary tumour.
Identify every lead, valve and support device present, its expected position, and any complication before reporting the mass in isolation.

classify.name: Cardiac masses and mimics
rows: Myxoma (around half of adult cardiac tumours), lipoma, rhabdomyoma, fibroma, papillary fibroelastoma

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old five months after an anterior infarct has a 2 cm mass sitting on the akinetic apical endocardium. First-pass perfusion shows no signal within it. Say which single sequence you would add and what result would let you report thrombus with confidence.
quiz.answer: Add a late enhancement acquisition with a long inversion time of about 600 ms: thrombus is avascular and takes up no gadolinium, so it stays uniformly black against grey myocardium and bright blood, whereas a tumour would enhance.
quiz.explain: Thrombus has no blood supply, so it does not perfuse on the first pass, does not enhance early, and retains nothing late. That is the whole discriminator, and the long inversion time sequence is simply the way to make it visible. At the standard inversion time of roughly 250 to 300 ms, chosen to null normal myocardium, thrombus is dark too and can hide or be mistaken for scar. Lengthening the inversion time to about 600 ms drives normal myocardium up to mid grey and leaves the avascular thrombus conspicuously black, and it also separates true thrombus from the slow-flow signal that collects in an apical aneurysm. Corroborate with context rather than relying on one sequence: thrombus sits on akinetic or aneurysmal wall or in a fibrillating appendage, is broad based, and does not invade. A mass that enhances is not thrombus, however apical it sits and however tempting the history.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old in sinus rhythm has recurrent syncope on standing and a 3 cm left atrial mass on a narrow stalk arising close to the fossa ovalis. It swings through the mitral orifice on the cines, is heterogeneously bright on T2 and enhances patchily. What should this study lead to?
quiz.answer: Refer for surgical excision, since this behaves as an atrial myxoma
choices: Refer for surgical excision, since this behaves as an atrial myxoma
Start anticoagulation and rescan in three months for resolution
Arrange a PET-CT, since a stalked atrial mass suggests a sarcoma
Leave it, as a prominent Chiari network needs no further action
quiz.explain: Every feature here points one way. Myxoma is the commonest primary cardiac tumour in adults, about three quarters of them in the left atrium, characteristically attached by a stalk to the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis, mobile enough to prolapse through the mitral valve and produce positional syncope or obstruction, bright on T2 because the matrix is myxoid, and enhancing because it has a blood supply. That last point is what excludes thrombus, which is avascular and would neither enhance nor sit on a stalk in a patient in sinus rhythm with a normal-sized atrium, so anticoagulating and waiting risks an embolic stroke or sudden death from valve obstruction while the diagnosis is on the screen. Sarcoma is typically right-sided, broad based, invasive, and comes with a haemorrhagic effusion. A Chiari network is a fine right atrial web. Excision is curative, and multiple or atypically sited myxomas should raise the Carney complex, which brings family screening with it.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with two embolic strokes and no atrial fibrillation has a 9 mm mobile mass with a frond-like surface on the aortic aspect of the aortic valve. She is afebrile and blood cultures are negative. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: Surgical referral, since a mobile left-sided valve tumour keeps embolising
choices: Surgical referral, since a mobile left-sided valve tumour keeps embolising
Six weeks of antibiotics on the assumption that this is endocarditis
Anticoagulation alone, since a mass on a valve is usually a thrombus
Discharge, since a lesion of this size carries a negligible embolic risk
quiz.explain: Papillary fibroelastoma is the commonest tumour of the cardiac valves, usually under 15 mm, pedunculated, with a shaggy frond-like surface that shimmers on cine imaging and often gives a stippled edge. Its danger is embolic rather than haemodynamic, and the risk tracks mobility and left-sided position far more than size, which is why a mobile aortic valve lesion in a patient who has already thrown two emboli is usually excised, often with the valve preserved. The mimic that matters is a vegetation, and it is separated clinically rather than by imaging: fever, positive cultures, valve destruction, regurgitation, and abscess or pseudoaneurysm formation. Treating this as endocarditis without an organism commits the patient to six weeks of antibiotics and leaves the source of embolism in place. Thrombus on a native valve in sinus rhythm is uncommon and would not have this frond-like surface, and Lambl's excrescences are much thinner filiform strands at the line of valve closure.

quiz.prompt: A staging FDG PET-CT in a woman with lymphoma reports a hypermetabolic interatrial septal lesion as suspicious for cardiac metastasis. On the CT component it measures fat attenuation, is 18 mm thick, spares the fossa ovalis and gives the septum a dumbbell shape. Say what you would tell the oncologist.
quiz.answer: This is benign lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum, unencapsulated fat sparing the fossa ovalis, and the FDG uptake is brown fat metabolism rather than tumour, so it needs no biopsy and should not alter the staging.
quiz.explain: Lipomatous hypertrophy is an accumulation of unencapsulated mature and brown adipose tissue in the interatrial septum that spares the fossa ovalis, and that sparing is what produces the dumbbell or hourglass profile. Thickness beyond about 2 cm is the usual descriptive threshold, but the shape and the spared fossa are the diagnosis, not the millimetres. Brown fat is metabolically active, so this lesion can be strikingly FDG-avid and it is a classic false positive on oncological staging; the correction is to look at the attenuation on the CT rather than at the standardised uptake value. Distinguish it from a true lipoma, which is encapsulated, homogeneous and non-enhancing and may arise anywhere in the heart. Both follow fat on every MRI sequence and lose signal with fat saturation, which settles the question in a minute if there is any doubt. Lipomatous hypertrophy is associated with age and obesity, is occasionally arrhythmogenic, and is not cancer.

quiz.prompt: A CT for suspected pulmonary embolus in a breathless, tachycardic patient shows a 2 cm circumferential pericardial effusion, reflux of contrast down the inferior vena cava into the hepatic veins, a distended cava and a compressed right atrium, with the interventricular septum bowed towards the left ventricle. What should you do with this study?
quiz.answer: Telephone the referrer now, as these appearances suggest tamponade physiology
choices: Telephone the referrer now, as these appearances suggest tamponade physiology
Report the effusion size and suggest a routine echocardiogram next week
Report a chronic effusion, since the pericardium is of normal thickness
Report constriction, since a bowed septum indicates a stiff pericardium
quiz.explain: Tamponade is physiology rather than volume. Two hundred millilitres accumulating over an hour can tamponade a patient while a chronic litre does not, so no measurement of depth makes or excludes the diagnosis. What CT offers are the surrogates of raised right-sided filling pressure: reflux of contrast into the cava and hepatic veins, a distended cava and azygos vein, compression or flattening of the right atrium and ventricle, a septum bowed towards the left, and periportal oedema. On real-time cine MRI you can watch the septum shift with inspiration, which is the same physiology seen directly. None of this replaces echocardiography and the patient in front of the clinician, but the radiologist who notices it and picks up the telephone changes the outcome, because the treatment is drainage and the window can be short. Normal pericardial thickness belongs to the constriction question and offers no reassurance here.

quiz.prompt: A patient with breathlessness, a raised jugular venous pressure and a dilated inferior vena cava has a pericardium measuring 2 mm, a septal bounce on the cines, and a septal shift towards the left on the first inspiratory beat of a free-breathing real-time acquisition. Myocardial late enhancement is normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: Constriction remains likely, since normal thickness does not exclude it
choices: Constriction remains likely, since normal thickness does not exclude it
Constriction is excluded by a pericardium under four millimetres thick
Restriction is the answer, given that late enhancement is normal here
The septal shift is a respiratory artefact of real-time cine imaging
quiz.explain: Interdependence is the physiology of constriction. A stiff pericardium fixes the total volume the heart may occupy, so the inspiratory increase in right-sided filling has to come at the left ventricle's expense, shoving the septum leftwards, and early diastolic filling stops abruptly against the shell, which is the septal bounce. Free-breathing real-time cine is how MRI demonstrates this, and it is more useful than any millimetre measurement, because up to about a fifth of surgically proven constriction has a pericardium of normal thickness. Thickening beyond 4 mm supports the diagnosis, calcification on CT supports it strongly, and tagged cine showing the pericardium moving with the myocardium instead of sliding over it is another good sign. Restriction is a myocardial disease: the pericardium is normal, interdependence is absent, the atria are usually large, and the myocardium generally declares itself with abnormal late enhancement, native T1 and extracellular volume, amyloid being the usual culprit. The distinction is pericardiectomy against treating the muscle.

quiz.prompt: A chest radiograph is performed to check a newly implanted cardiac resynchronisation defibrillator before discharge. How many separate leads should you be able to trace from the generator? Answer as a whole number of leads.
quiz.explain: A resynchronisation defibrillator carries three leads: a right atrial lead in the appendage, a right ventricular lead bearing shock coils in the apex or on the septum, and a left ventricular lead threaded through the coronary sinus into a lateral or posterolateral cardiac vein. Counting leads is the first step of every device radiograph, because the count tells you what the system is before you assess it. One lead with shock coils is a defibrillator, two fine leads a dual-chamber pacemaker, and a lead that runs leftwards and posteriorly around the atrioventricular groove rather than into the right ventricle is the coronary sinus lead, most easily confirmed on the lateral film where it heads backwards. Having counted, check each tip position, compare with the implant film for any lead that has moved, follow each lead through the costoclavicular space where fracture and insulation failure happen, and look for a new effusion or a tip that has passed beyond the cardiac contour.

quiz.prompt: Forty-five days after left atrial appendage occlusion a CT is done for a suspected device-related thrombus. The appendage distal to the device measures 40 HU on the early arterial phase while the left atrial cavity measures 350 HU on the same series. Report the appendage-to-atrium attenuation ratio, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Forty divided by three hundred and fifty is 0.11. Reading a filling defect beyond an occluder is a two-part job, and the ratio is only the first part: how dense is the appendage relative to the atrial blood pool, and then what happens on a delayed acquisition thirty to sixty seconds later. A low early ratio that fills in on the delayed series means contrast is arriving slowly, through an incompletely sealed device or simply through sluggish flow in a stagnant appendage, and that is a peri-device leak or circulatory stasis rather than clot. A defect that stays dark on the delayed phase is thrombus. Device-related thrombus proper looks different again, as a flat or slightly convex layer of soft tissue on the atrial face of the device, and it is the finding that reopens the anticoagulation decision. Acquire the delayed phase every time; without it stasis and thrombus are indistinguishable and the study will over-call clot.

quiz.prompt: Two days after pacemaker implantation a patient has pleuritic chest pain. CT shows the tip of the right ventricular lead lying beyond the epicardial fat within the pericardial space, with a new 8 mm effusion, and the pacing thresholds have risen since implant. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Urgent cardiology review for lead revision with surgical cover available
choices: Urgent cardiology review for lead revision with surgical cover available
Reassurance, since a tip within the fat is expected on thin sections
Watchful waiting, since the effusion measures under one centimetre
An increase in pacing output and a repeat radiograph in one month
quiz.explain: This is lead perforation, and the case assembles from the tip position beyond the myocardial contour, the new effusion, the rising capture threshold and the pleuritic pain. Other clues to look for are loss of capture altogether and diaphragmatic or intercostal muscle twitching from stimulation outside the heart. Thin-section CT with a sharp kernel reads tip position far better than a radiograph, though metal blooming exaggerates the tip, so the relationship to the wall, the presence of fluid and the clinical picture should carry the call rather than a single reformat. The reason it is done somewhere with pericardiocentesis and cardiac surgery available is that withdrawing the lead can unplug a sealed track and precipitate tamponade. Keep the other device complications in mind as you scroll: fracture or insulation failure at the costoclavicular crush point, twiddler's syndrome with the lead coiled about a rotated generator, subclavian vein stenosis or thrombosis, and lead-adherent vegetation.

quiz.prompt: A man with a renal cell carcinoma has a right atrial filling defect that is continuous with tumour filling the inferior vena cava, and it enhances on the arterial phase. Say what the enhancement tells the surgeon, and why the finding changes the operation being planned.
quiz.answer: Enhancement means this is vascularised tumour thrombus rather than bland clot, so the report must state its cephalad extent: tumour reaching the right atrium above the diaphragm makes this a level IV resection needing cardiopulmonary bypass rather than a straightforward nephrectomy.
quiz.explain: Cardiac masses are far more often secondary than primary. They arrive by direct invasion from lung, breast, oesophagus or mediastinal lymphoma, by haematogenous spread, melanoma being the notorious one and often bright on T1 because of melanin, or by growing up a vein, which is what renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma do through the inferior vena cava and what lung cancer does through the pulmonary veins. Enhancement is the discriminator against bland thrombus, supported by expansion of the vein and by unbroken continuity with the primary tumour. The staging that changes the operation is how high the thrombus reaches: renal vein only, infrahepatic, retrohepatic below the diaphragm, or into the right atrium above it. Only the last routinely requires cardiopulmonary bypass and a combined urological and cardiac team, so the level is the single most useful sentence the report can contain, and it should be measured against a fixed landmark such as the diaphragmatic hiatus.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a mechanical mitral prosthesis has rising transvalvular gradients and an INR that has been subtherapeutic for a month. Gated CT shows reduced opening of one leaflet and a soft, low-attenuation mass on the atrial side of the sewing ring, considerably larger than the ring is thick. What does this favour, and what follows?
quiz.answer: Thrombus; anticoagulate or thrombolyse and repeat the gated CT afterwards
choices: Thrombus; anticoagulate or thrombolyse and repeat the gated CT afterwards
Pannus; plan surgical exploration, since medical treatment will not shift it
Vegetation; start antibiotics and arrange transoesophageal echocardiography
Metal artefact; repeat the study with a sharper kernel and tighter gating
quiz.explain: On CT, prosthetic valve thrombus is softer than pannus, generally under about 90 Hounsfield units, tends to be bulkier, sits on the atrial side of a mitral prosthesis, and appears against a short history of inadequate anticoagulation. That combination matters because thrombus responds to anticoagulation or thrombolysis, which spares a redo sternotomy. Pannus is dense fibrous ingrowth around and beneath the sewing ring, smaller, adherent, developing over years in a patient whose INR has been fine, and only surgery removes it. The two coexist often enough that the honest answer is sometimes both, and the attenuation overlap is real, so report the reasoning rather than a bare label. Gated CT is doing two jobs here, characterising the mass and measuring leaflet opening angles, which is the functional evidence of obstruction and is what a repeat study will use to judge whether treatment worked. Blooming around metal is a genuine limitation, but it does not manufacture a discrete soft-tissue mass with a stuck leaflet and a rising gradient.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these structures in the order blood passes through them in a patient supported by a continuous-flow left ventricular assist device.
quiz.answer: left-ventricle inflow-cannula pump-housing outflow-graft ascending-aorta
quiz.explain: Following the blood is how these studies are read, because each station fails in its own way. The inflow cannula should sit at the apex pointing towards the mitral valve; angled into the septum or the free wall it obstructs intermittently and produces suction events and low flow alarms. The pump itself can thrombose, which shows clinically as rising power draw and haemolysis and on CT as a filling defect in or beside the housing, though metal artefact limits how much you can promise. The outflow graft is the classic surgical problem: kinked, twisted, compressed by thrombus in the sheath around it, or stenosed at the anastomosis, and it is where a careful multiplanar look pays off. At the aorta, remember that continuous flow may keep the aortic valve shut, which risks fusion and thrombosis of the cusps and root. One protocol note: flow is non-pulsatile, so standard bolus timing is unreliable and a test bolus with generous delayed imaging serves better, and scan widely when hunting a driveline infection.

curriculum_modules.title: Cardiac MRI: Function, Oedema and Late Enhancement

module_contract.goal: Read a cardiac MRI by its sequences, use the late enhancement pattern to separate ischaemic from non-ischaemic disease, and call viability, oedema and iron with the numbers that go with them.

approach.detail: Ejection fraction, chamber volumes and dimensions, regional wall motion — hypokinesis, akinesis, dyskinesis.
High signal marks acute injury; use it to date an infarct or flag active myocarditis.
The single most important discriminator: does it involve the subendocardium, and does it follow a coronary territory.
Subendocardial involvement is always present; enhancement follows a coronary distribution and progresses from subendocardial toward transmural with longer occlusion.
Enhancement is midwall or epicardial, never follows a coronary territory, and spares the subendocardium.

approach.step: Match the pattern to a diagnosis
approach.detail: Use the disease-specific pattern to name the cause rather than just describing it.
Transmural extent of enhancement in a hypocontractile segment predicts recovery after revascularisation.

measure.how: Cine-derived left ventricular ejection fraction.

measure.what: Transmural extent of LGE for viability
measure.how: Proportion of wall thickness enhanced in a hypocontractile segment on the 17-segment model.
measure.cutoff: < 50% transmural — likely to recover after revascularisation; > 50% — recovery unlikely; transmural — virtually no chance of recovery

classify.name: Late gadolinium enhancement pattern
rows: Subendocardial, always involved; follows a coronary territory; extends toward transmural with longer occlusion

Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy — midmyocardial fibrosis marks higher risk of sudden cardiac death

Does not respect a coronary territory
Subepicardial or midmyocardial, lateral free wall
Does not originate from the subendocardium
Segmental, with hypokinesis, dilatation, fatty infiltration
No late enhancement despite acute wall-motion abnormality
Tako-tsubo cardiomyopathy — distinguishes it from infarction
classify.note: Subendocardial involvement means ischaemic until proven otherwise; its absence points to a non-ischaemic cause.

pitfalls: Calling a pattern ischaemic without subendocardial involvement — non-ischaemic disease can still infarct-mimic on cine alone.
Missing midwall fibrosis in dilated cardiomyopathy because it is subtle and non-territorial — it carries prognostic weight for sudden death.
Misreading normal RV trabeculation or the moderator band bulge as pathology when working up suspected ARVC.
Diagnosing ARVC from MRI alone — MRI findings must be integrated with Task Force criteria, not used in isolation.
Struggling to null myocardium in amyloidosis and reading a poor inversion-time image as absent enhancement — the difficulty finding a null point is itself a clue to amyloid.
