quiz.prompt: A short-axis cine stack is contoured slice by slice and summed by the method of discs. End-diastolic volume is 210 mL and end-systolic volume is 130 mL. Report the left ventricular ejection fraction as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Stroke volume is 210 minus 130, which is 80 mL, and ejection fraction is 80 divided by 210, or 38.1 per cent. Cardiac MRI is the reference standard for this number because summing discs across the whole ventricle makes no assumption about its shape, which is exactly where echocardiographic estimates go wrong in a remodelled or aneurysmal heart. Two habits protect the figure. Choose the basal slice consistently, because including or dropping one basal slice moves the volumes more than any other decision, and it is the commonest source of disagreement between two readers of the same study. And state your convention for the papillary muscles and trabeculae, since counting them as blood pool rather than as myocardium raises the reported volumes and shifts the fraction by several points. That matters here: 38 per cent sits just above the 35 per cent band that drives primary-prevention defibrillator decisions, so a technical difference of three points has a real consequence for the patient.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with a dilated, globally hypokinetic left ventricle and unobstructed coronary arteries has a linear band of late enhancement running through the middle of the septal wall and sparing the subendocardium. Ejection fraction is 34 per cent. What does that band add to the decision in front of you?
quiz.answer: It marks non-ischaemic scar and raises the arrhythmic risk
choices: It marks non-ischaemic scar and raises the arrhythmic risk
It marks a small old infarct in the septal perforator bed
It marks acute oedema and calls for repeat imaging in weeks
It marks a nulling error and should be left out of the report
quiz.explain: The one rule that organises late enhancement is the layer it starts in. Ischaemic necrosis advances as a wavefront from the subendocardium outwards, so an infarct always takes the innermost layer and always sits inside a coronary artery territory; enhancement that spares the subendocardium cannot be an infarct, whatever the coronary anatomy suggests. That is why the septal perforator answer fails here. Mid-wall septal fibrosis is the characteristic non-ischaemic pattern in dilated cardiomyopathy, present in roughly a third of these patients, and it is not merely descriptive: it is associated with ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death independently of ejection fraction, so it belongs in the conversation about a defibrillator rather than in a list of incidental findings. Oedema is a T2 question, not a late enhancement one, and a nulling error is a diffuse grey wash across the whole myocardium rather than a discrete band with clean borders, which is what the inversion-time scout and a phase-sensitive reconstruction are there to settle.

quiz.prompt: On the inversion-time scout of a 74-year-old with concentric wall thickening and low voltages on the ECG, the myocardium darkens before the blood pool does, and the ten-minute images show diffuse enhancement of the subendocardial layer around both ventricles. Say what this gadolinium behaviour indicates and what you would ask the referring team to arrange.
quiz.answer: The reversed nulling and the diffuse subendocardial enhancement indicate cardiac amyloid, because amyloid expands the interstitium and holds gadolinium while clearing it fast from the blood; ask the team for bone scintigraphy with a DPD or PYP tracer and a serum and urine light chain screen.
quiz.explain: Amyloid deposition expands the extracellular space enormously, so the myocardium takes up and holds gadolinium while the blood clears it quickly. The result is the abnormal kinetics you have just seen: on the scout, myocardium nulls at a shorter inversion time than blood, which is the reverse of every normal study, and the late images show enhancement that is global and subendocardial rather than confined to one artery's territory, progressing to transmural in advanced disease. Native T1 and extracellular volume are raised strikingly, often above 40 per cent, and extracellular volume tracks amyloid burden well enough to follow treatment. The next step is not a biopsy but a fork: bone-avid tracer scintigraphy that is strongly positive with a negative light chain screen supports transthyretin amyloid without histology, whereas abnormal light chains mean AL amyloid, which is a haematological emergency and must be excluded first rather than assumed away.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old man has chest pain and a raised troponin ten days after a coryzal illness, with normal coronary arteries. The study shows enhancement in the subepicardial half of the basal inferolateral wall and regionally raised T2 in the same segments. What does the raised T2 add to the enhancement finding?
quiz.answer: It dates the injury as acute and meets an oedema criterion
choices: It dates the injury as acute and meets an oedema criterion
It confirms an infarct in the obtuse marginal territory instead
It indicates iron deposition and should prompt T2* mapping
It reflects fat within the wall and needs a fat-saturated repeat
quiz.explain: The 2018 revision of the Lake Louise criteria pairs the two kinds of evidence: one T2-based marker of oedema, either regional high signal on T2-weighted imaging or a raised T2 map value, together with one T1-based marker of injury, being raised native T1, raised extracellular volume, or non-ischaemic late enhancement. Both halves are present here, so this is acute myocardial inflammation rather than an old scar, and that distinction drives the advice on abstaining from competitive exercise for three to six months and on when to rescan. The distribution does the other half of the work: subepicardial and inferolateral is the classic myocarditis pattern, and its sparing of the subendocardium is what excludes infarction. Iron shortens T2 and T2* and makes myocardium dark, so it moves the signal the other way. Fat is bright on T1, drops out with fat saturation, and does not belong to this presentation.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and new second-degree heart block has patchy enhancement in the basal septum and in the epicardial half of the lateral wall, with a further focus in the right ventricular free wall. Stress perfusion is normal. What should follow from this study?
quiz.answer: Refer for FDG PET after a high-fat, low-carbohydrate preparation
choices: Refer for FDG PET after a high-fat, low-carbohydrate preparation
Refer for invasive angiography to exclude three-vessel disease
Repeat the scan in six weeks to look for resolution of oedema
Reassure and discharge, as insertion point scar is a benign finding
quiz.explain: Multifocal enhancement that ignores coronary territories, favours the basal septum and the epicardial layer, and crosses into the right ventricle, in a patient with hilar nodes and conduction disease, is cardiac sarcoidosis until proved otherwise; basal septal involvement is what interrupts the conduction system and produces the block. Late enhancement marks scar, and scar in sarcoid predicts ventricular arrhythmia and death, so this study has already changed the patient's risk category and opens the defibrillator conversation. What it cannot say is whether anything is still burning, and that is the question immunosuppression turns on. FDG PET with a preparation that starves normal myocardium of glucose, typically a prolonged fast on a high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet with heparin, separates active inflammation from inert scar. Angiography answers a question the normal perfusion study has already closed, and watchful waiting in a patient with heart block is not a safe plan.

quiz.prompt: In the mid-inferior segment of a patient being assessed before revascularisation, the late enhancement occupies 5.6 mm of a wall that measures 8.0 mm thick at end-diastole. Report the transmural extent of the scar as a percentage of wall thickness, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 5.6 divided by 8.0 is 0.70, so the scar occupies 70 per cent of the wall. The transmurality of enhancement, not the presence of it, is what predicts recovery: segments with scar through less than a quarter of the wall recover contraction after revascularisation in the large majority of cases, segments beyond half are unlikely to, and the band between is genuinely uncertain and best reported as such rather than dressed up as a decision. At 70 per cent this segment should be reported as unlikely to recover. Two cautions travel with the rule. Thin, chronically scarred walls make the denominator small and the percentage unstable, so measure at end-diastole and say if the wall is thinned below about 5.5 mm, which is itself a poor sign. And dysfunction without any enhancement is stunned or hibernating myocardium, which is viable and should recover, so a segment that contracts poorly with a clean late enhancement image is an argument for revascularisation rather than against it.

quiz.prompt: During adenosine stress first-pass perfusion a thin dark rim appears along the subendocardium of the whole left ventricle at the moment of peak myocardial enhancement, persists for two heartbeats and has gone by the time the myocardium is fully enhanced. Rest perfusion and late enhancement are normal. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: A dark rim artefact, so the perfusion study is reported as normal
choices: A dark rim artefact, so the perfusion study is reported as normal
Circumferential subendocardial ischaemia from three-vessel disease
An inadequate adenosine dose, so the stress should be repeated
A subendocardial infarct that the late enhancement has missed
quiz.explain: The dark rim artefact lives at the boundary between bright blood and dark myocardium, where truncation of the Fourier series and a little motion produce a ringing band. Its signature is timing and thickness: it appears at the instant of maximal contrast gradient, is one or two pixels thick, follows the phase-encode direction, and disappears within a few beats. True hypoperfusion behaves differently. It persists well beyond peak enhancement, is thicker, and either matches a coronary territory or, in the balanced case, is genuinely circumferential and accompanied by symptoms, ST change and splenic switch-off confirming that the vasodilator worked. Balanced ischaemia in three-vessel disease is a real trap, and quantitative perfusion mapping in millilitres per gram per minute is what defeats it, since relative comparison has nothing normal left to compare against. An infarct invisible on ten-minute enhancement is not a thing; late enhancement is the more sensitive test of the two.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old with transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia has a myocardial T2* of 8 ms and a heavily loaded liver. Ejection fraction is 61 per cent and the ventricle looks entirely unremarkable on the cines. What should this study drive?
quiz.answer: Intensified chelation now, because the myocardium is severely loaded
choices: Intensified chelation now, because the myocardium is severely loaded
No change to chelation, since ventricular function is preserved
A search for myocarditis, since a low T2* indicates active oedema
More transfusion, since a low T2* here indicates poor ventricular filling
quiz.explain: Iron is strongly paramagnetic and destroys signal quickly, so the more iron there is, the shorter T2* becomes. A myocardial T2* below 20 ms indicates myocardial iron loading, and below 10 ms indicates severe loading, a value that carries a substantial risk of heart failure and arrhythmia within the following year. The whole clinical value of the measurement is that it turns abnormal before the ventricle does, so a normal ejection fraction is not reassurance, it is the expected finding in the window where intervention still works. Note also that liver and heart load and unload on different timescales, so ferritin and liver iron cannot stand in for the cardiac measurement in either direction: a heavily loaded liver with a normal heart is common, and so is the reverse. Iron shortens T2 and T2* rather than lengthening them, which is what separates this from the bright, oedematous myocardium of inflammation.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old man with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, proteinuria and burning neuropathic pain in his hands has a native T1 well below the normal range for your scanner, with enhancement confined to the basal inferolateral epicardium. Explain why the native T1 value is the measurement that settles the differential here.
quiz.answer: Almost everything that thickens myocardium, including amyloid, hypertension and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, raises native T1, so a low value points to Fabry disease, where stored glycolipid shortens T1; confirm with alpha-galactosidase A activity and genetic testing.
quiz.explain: Native T1 is a mapped tissue property, and the direction it moves is more informative than its exact value. Oedema, fibrosis, infiltration by amyloid and the fibre disarray of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy all lengthen it, so almost every cause of a thick wall raises native T1. Very few things shorten it, and the ones that do are storage: the globotriaosylceramide of Fabry disease, iron, and fat. In a man with hypertrophy, proteinuria and acroparaesthesia, a low native T1 with basal inferolateral late enhancement is the picture of Fabry, and that matters because it is one of the few causes of left ventricular hypertrophy with a specific treatment, in enzyme replacement or chaperone therapy, which is wasted if the case is filed as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. One caveat to carry: once fibrosis and oedema supervene in that lateral wall they push T1 back up, so a pseudo-normal segmental value in advanced disease does not exclude it, and pairing the map with T2* keeps iron from being mistaken for it.

quiz.prompt: A 66-year-old diabetic has two separate areas of late enhancement: one subendocardial and confined to the inferior wall and inferior septum, and one running through the middle of the anteroseptal wall while sparing the subendocardium. Say what you conclude from having both, and what your report should say.
quiz.answer: The subendocardial inferior enhancement is an old right coronary territory infarct, while the anteroseptal mid-wall band is non-ischaemic fibrosis, so report both patterns separately rather than forcing one diagnosis, and state the transmural extent of the infarct.
quiz.explain: Readers are taught to sort a study into ischaemic or non-ischaemic, and most studies do sort. Some patients have both, and the mistake is to let the first pattern found suppress the second. Apply the rule segment by segment: enhancement that involves the subendocardium and sits within a single artery's territory is infarction, and the inferior wall with the inferior septum is the right coronary distribution. Enhancement that spares the subendocardium is not infarction whatever else it is, and a mid-wall anteroseptal band belongs to the non-ischaemic group, in this patient most likely a cardiomyopathic process alongside his coronary disease. Reporting both matters practically, because the ischaemic component with its transmural extent drives the revascularisation discussion while the non-ischaemic scar carries independent arrhythmic weight, and a report that averages them into one diagnosis loses both.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old with asymmetric septal hypertrophy of 19 mm has patchy mid-wall enhancement at both right ventricular insertion points and through the hypertrophied septum, quantified at 22 per cent of left ventricular mass. Conventional risk assessment leaves him in an intermediate band. How does the enhancement bear on the decision?
quiz.answer: Extensive scar is a risk modifier that favours a defibrillator discussion
choices: Extensive scar is a risk modifier that favours a defibrillator discussion
Insertion point scar is expected in hypertrophy and adds nothing here
Scar of this extent argues against hypertrophic disease altogether
Scar burden counts chiefly when it sits in a coronary artery territory
quiz.explain: The point is the burden, not the presence. Small foci at the right ventricular insertion points are common in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and in other causes of right ventricular pressure loading, and on their own they carry little weight. Extensive enhancement is different: in the 2020 American guideline on hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, late enhancement of roughly 15 per cent of left ventricular mass or more is one of the modifiers used to tip a decision when conventional risk assessment, built on family history of sudden death, unexplained syncope, maximal wall thickness, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, apical aneurysm and systolic impairment, has not settled it. At 22 per cent this study moves the discussion towards a defibrillator. That the scar ignores coronary territories is consistent with the diagnosis rather than against it, and cardiac MRI is also earning its place here by measuring the true maximal wall thickness that echocardiography often understates and by finding apical aneurysms that echocardiography misses.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these cardiac MRI sequences in the order a standard adult protocol acquires them, from patient setup to the last series.
quiz.answer: localisers cine-function native-T1-mapping stress-perfusion late-enhancement
quiz.explain: Everything that has to be free of gadolinium comes first, and the order is dictated by that one constraint rather than by convenience. Localisers set the cardiac axes, the cines then give volumes, mass and wall motion, and native T1 and T2 mapping follow while the tissue is still untouched, because a single dose of contrast makes native mapping uninterpretable for the rest of the day. Contrast enters the study at stress perfusion, and late enhancement is acquired roughly ten minutes after the last dose, once normal myocardium has washed out and scar has not; imaged at three minutes it is not late enhancement, and normal myocardium is still bright. If extracellular volume is wanted, the post-contrast T1 map sits at the end, around fifteen minutes, paired with a haematocrit drawn the same day, since the calculation converts the myocardium-to-blood ratio into a tissue fraction using it. Get the order wrong and the numbers cannot be salvaged by any amount of post-processing.

module_contract.goal: Read the pattern and distribution of a chest infection, place a COVID-19 CT on the CO-RADS scale, and separate active tuberculosis and the opportunistic infections of the immunocompromised from their mimics.

approach.detail: Ground-glass, consolidation, or a mix, and whether it is unifocal or multifocal, before you reach for a category.
COVID-19 pneumonia is typically bilateral, multifocal and peripheral or posterior, with a lower-lobe predominance.

approach.step: Score CO-RADS on the CT alone
approach.detail: The category reflects the level of suspicion for pulmonary COVID-19 involvement — it is independent of the PCR result.

approach.step: Separate TB and its mimics by distribution and immune status
approach.detail: Upper-lobe cavitating consolidation in the immunocompetent adult; lower-zone consolidation and adenopathy with a compromised immune system; adenopathy and lower-zone disease with effusion in the child.

approach.step: Look specifically for cavitation and tree-in-bud
approach.detail: Cavitation signals a high bacterial load and infectivity; tree-in-bud signals active endobronchial spread — both push toward active rather than healed disease.
Apical fibrosis, calcification and volume loss without new consolidation mean inactive, non-infectious disease.

classify.name: CO-RADS — level of suspicion for pulmonary COVID-19 on CT
rows: Normal CT, or findings entirely explained by another diagnosis (heart failure, fibrosis, malignancy)
Findings consistent with another infection (e.g. bronchiolitis, TB) — no typical COVID-19 features
CT abnormalities consistent with an infection, but findings are non-specific for COVID-19
Unilateral ground-glass, or multifocal consolidation without the typical COVID-19 pattern
Multifocal, bilateral ground-glass and/or consolidation, peripheral, with vascular thickening or subpleural bands
PCR-positive for COVID-19, with typical bilateral ground-glass on CT
classify.note: CO-RADS 1 has a high negative predictive value once the patient has been symptomatic for 4 or more days; CO-RADS 5 has a very high positive predictive value in an epidemic setting.

pitfalls: Scoring CO-RADS in the first 0–4 days of symptoms and treating a normal or near-normal CT as reassuring — CT sensitivity is low this early and roughly half of patients are still normal.
Assuming the classic radiographic split between primary and post-primary TB — that distinction is unreliable; immune status, not disease stage, drives the pattern.
Missing tree-in-bud on chest X-ray — it is far better seen on CT and signals active endobronchial spread.
Calling miliary nodules "probably infective" without registering how uncommon but specific the pattern is for haematogenous TB spread.
Reporting a CO-RADS category without a distribution description in the impression — the category alone does not tell the clinician where the disease is.

quiz.prompt: An unenhanced chest CT in a patient with four days of fever and cough shows multifocal bilateral ground-glass opacities of rounded shape in a peripheral and subpleural distribution, with areas of crazy paving, no effusion and no lymphadenopathy. No swab result is available. Give the CO-RADS category. Answer as a single whole number from 0 to 6.
quiz.explain: CO-RADS 5 is the very high level of suspicion and is reserved for the typical picture: bilateral, multifocal ground-glass, often rounded, peripheral and posterior in distribution, with crazy paving, subpleural bands, or an organising pneumonia pattern including the reversed halo. CO-RADS 4 covers findings that are suspicious but carry more overlap, such as unilateral or peribronchovascular disease, or ground-glass superimposed on severe pre-existing lung disease where the pattern cannot be read cleanly. CO-RADS 3 is genuinely equivocal, CO-RADS 2 fits another infection better, CO-RADS 1 is normal or clearly non-infectious, and CO-RADS 0 means the scan is technically uninterpretable. Note that CO-RADS 6 is not a radiological judgement at all: it is reserved for a patient with a positive RT-PCR, so a scan you would have called 5 becomes 6 the moment the swab returns.

quiz.prompt: A patient scanned for the same clinical question has centrilobular nodules with tree-in-bud opacities in the right lower lobe, a lobar consolidation containing air bronchograms, and a small parapneumonic effusion. Give the CO-RADS category. Answer as a single whole number from 0 to 6.
quiz.explain: CO-RADS 2 is the low-suspicion band, used when the findings are typical of an infection other than COVID-19. Tree-in-bud and centrilobular nodules are the signature of material filling terminal bronchioles, which is bacterial bronchopneumonia, aspiration or endobronchial tuberculosis, and they are conspicuously absent from the COVID-19 picture. Lobar consolidation with a parapneumonic effusion points the same way. In practice, effusion, lymphadenopathy, cavitation and tree-in-bud are the four findings that should push the category down rather than up. Two things are worth remembering about the scale. It grades suspicion of COVID-19, not severity, so a CO-RADS 2 patient may well be the sicker of the two. And it was designed for unenhanced CT in patients with moderate to severe symptoms, not as a screening tool for the asymptomatic.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these stages of tuberculous infection in the order they occur in one patient over a lifetime, from the first parenchymal lesion to disease reappearing years later.
quiz.answer: ghon-focus hilar-lymphadenopathy ranke-complex apical-reactivation
quiz.explain: Inhaled bacilli lodge in a well-ventilated part of the lung, typically the middle or lower zone, and produce the parenchymal Ghon focus. Lymphatic drainage carries them to the ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal nodes, and in children those nodes dominate the picture; on CT they characteristically show low-attenuation centres with rim enhancement, reflecting caseation. Healing calcifies both, and a calcified parenchymal focus with its calcified draining node is the Ranke complex, one of the commonest incidental findings on adult chest imaging. Reactivation, when it comes, favours the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, where oxygen tension is highest and lymphatic clearance poorest, and it cavitates. Cavitation is the moment the patient becomes infectious, which is why the distribution of disease on a CT carries an immediate infection-control consequence.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these pulmonary infections in the order they typically appear after solid-organ transplantation, from the first post-operative days through to beyond six months.
quiz.answer: aspiration-pneumonia cytomegalovirus-pneumonia community-acquired-pneumonia
quiz.explain: The first month after transplantation belongs to the operation rather than to the immunosuppression, which has not yet had time to take full effect: aspiration around intubation, nosocomial bacterial pneumonia, fluid overload and surgical complications dominate. From roughly one to six months the pharmacological effect is at its deepest and the opportunists arrive, cytomegalovirus above all, with Pneumocystis, Aspergillus and Nocardia sharing the same window. Beyond six months, most patients on maintenance doses resemble the general community again and acquire the community's pathogens, with continued opportunistic risk confined to those needing heavy immunosuppression for rejection. Knowing where in this timeline a patient sits narrows a non-specific chest CT more reliably than any single sign on the images, and it is the first question to ask before describing ground-glass in a transplant recipient.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient in intensive care develops a new fever and her chest CT shows new consolidation. Say where you expect aspirated material to have settled in this patient, and why.
quiz.answer: Because she has been lying supine, aspirated material settles in the segments that are dependent in that position: the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes, more often on the right because the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.
quiz.explain: Aspiration obeys gravity, so its distribution tells you the posture at the time it happened. Supine, as almost every ventilated patient is, the dependent segments are the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes. Upright or seated, it is the basal segments of the lower lobes. Lying on one side, it is that side. The right lung is favoured throughout because the right main bronchus leaves the trachea at a shallower angle and has the wider lumen. Recognising the pattern changes the report from a generic hospital-acquired pneumonia to aspiration, and with it the antibiotic choice, the question of a swallow assessment, and the review of sedation, feeding and head-up positioning. Chemical pneumonitis from acid appears within hours and may clear within days; bacterial superinfection follows later and consolidates.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old from a high-incidence country has apical fibronodular change on CT and the registrar has reported it as old healed tuberculosis. Say which findings would make you call the disease active instead, and what you would do about it.
quiz.answer: Cavitation, clustered centrilobular tree-in-bud nodules and new or ill-defined consolidation all indicate activity; if any are present, isolate the patient and send sputum for smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification rather than reporting the scan as inactive disease.
quiz.explain: Imaging cannot prove inactivity, which is a microbiological verdict, but it can make activity very likely. Cavitation and tree-in-bud opacities are the two most useful signs: tree-in-bud represents bacilli-laden secretions filling terminal bronchioles, and tree-in-bud in a lobe remote from the cavity is bronchogenic spread, meaning the patient is coughing organisms into the room. Ill-defined consolidation, new nodules and an enlarging pleural effusion count too. Against that, upper-zone fibronodular opacity with volume loss, traction bronchiectasis and calcified granulomas favours old disease. But a report that calls such a scan inactive has overreached; the safer wording describes the findings, states that activity cannot be excluded on imaging alone, and asks for sputum. Getting this wrong puts an infectious patient onto an open ward, which is the sort of error that is discovered weeks later.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old smoker with fever has a rounded, well-defined 4 cm opacity in the right lower lobe that behaves clinically like a round pneumonia. Say what your report should ask for and why.
quiz.answer: Treat as pneumonia, but ask explicitly for repeat imaging in about six to eight weeks to document complete resolution, because in an adult a rounded opacity may be a malignancy and must be followed until it has cleared.
quiz.explain: Round pneumonia is largely a paediatric phenomenon, most often pneumococcal, in children under about eight years, in whom the collateral pathways of Kohn and Lambert are not yet developed and infection stays spherical rather than spreading through a segment. In an adult the same shape carries a real chance of being a carcinoma, an organising pneumonia, or a lymphoma, and the cheapest way to separate them is to show that it disappears. Six to eight weeks after treatment is the conventional interval: early enough to act on, late enough for a genuine pneumonia to have cleared. If it has not resolved, the next step is a contrast CT with bronchoscopy or percutaneous biopsy, not another course of antibiotics. Writing the interval and the reason into the report is what makes it happen; a recommendation to correlate clinically usually does not.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient has patchy multifocal peribronchial nodular consolidation in both lower lobes, without air bronchograms and without confinement by any fissure. What does this pattern tell the team about the disease they are treating?
quiz.answer: Bronchiolar spread, so expect a patchy, slower resolution
choices: Bronchiolar spread, so expect a patchy, slower resolution
Alveolar spread from one focus, confined by the fissures
Interstitial spread, with reticulation and septal thickening
Lymphatic spread along the bronchovascular bundles
quiz.explain: The three classical patterns each describe a route through the lung. Lobar pneumonia begins peripherally in one lobe and spreads through alveoli and the pores of Kohn until a fissure stops it, giving homogeneous non-segmental consolidation with air bronchograms because the airways remain patent; pneumococcus is the model. Bronchopneumonia begins in the bronchioles and spreads centrifugally into the surrounding lobules, giving patchy, often bilateral nodular consolidation without air bronchograms because the airways themselves are full of exudate. Staphylococci, Haemophilus, Pseudomonas and anaerobes behave this way, resolution is slower, and cavitation and scarring are commoner. Interstitial pneumonia, the viral, Mycoplasma and Pneumocystis pattern, gives reticulation, ground-glass and bronchial wall thickening, classically with a patient who sounds worse than the film looks.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old smoker with weight loss but no fever has a 5 cm right upper lobe cavity with a thick, irregular, nodular inner wall and no surrounding consolidation. What is the most appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Contrast CT and bronchoscopy or biopsy for tissue
choices: Contrast CT and bronchoscopy or biopsy for tissue
A course of antibiotics with a repeat film in a month
Sputum for acid-fast bacilli and a period of isolation
Antifungal therapy for a suspected aspergilloma
quiz.explain: The wall does most of the diagnostic work. A cavity whose wall exceeds roughly 15 mm with an irregular, nodular inner margin, in a smoker with weight loss and without fever, is a squamous cell carcinoma until proved otherwise, and the priority is tissue. A thin, smooth wall favours an infected bulla, a healed abscess or a bleb. An acute pyogenic abscess is thick-walled too, but the patient is febrile, there is surrounding consolidation, and an air-fluid level sits dependently. Tuberculosis cavitates in the apical and posterior upper lobe segments with surrounding tree-in-bud, and sputum should indeed be sent in parallel here, since the two can coexist; what does harm is sending sputum and then waiting. An aspergilloma is a mobile fungus ball lying within a pre-existing cavity, not a nodular wall.

quiz.prompt: A 6-year-old recently arrived from a high-incidence country has right middle lobe consolidation and a bulky right hilar node whose centre is low in attenuation with an enhancing rim. What does this combination indicate?
quiz.answer: Primary tuberculosis, with necrotic nodal disease
choices: Primary tuberculosis, with necrotic nodal disease
Reactivation tuberculosis with endobronchial spread
Bacterial lobar pneumonia with reactive adenopathy
Lymphoma with post-obstructive consolidation
quiz.explain: In primary tuberculosis the nodes are the disease, particularly in children, and a low-attenuation centre with rim enhancement reflects caseous necrosis. That appearance is close to specific in the right clinical setting, shared mainly with non-tuberculous mycobacteria and some fungal infections. Reactive nodes accompanying a bacterial pneumonia are smaller and enhance homogeneously. Consolidation in primary disease has no zonal preference and often sits in the middle or lower lobes, unlike reactivation, which favours the apical and posterior upper lobe segments and cavitates. Lymphoma produces bulky, usually bilateral mediastinal masses without central necrosis before treatment. Two other faces of primary disease are worth holding on to: a pleural effusion, which is common in adolescents and young adults, and lobar collapse from a node compressing a bronchus.

quiz.prompt: A patient on long-term corticosteroids has three weeks of fever, and CT shows innumerable sharply defined 2 mm nodules of uniform size distributed evenly through both lungs, involving the subpleural surfaces and the fissures. What distribution should be reported, and what does it imply?
quiz.answer: Random: haematogenous seeding, so treat as miliary disease
choices: Random: haematogenous seeding, so treat as miliary disease
Centrilobular: airway spread, so seek an endobronchial source
Perilymphatic: sarcoidosis or lymphangitic spread of tumour
Upper-zone predominant: an inhaled organic dust exposure
quiz.explain: Distribution is the first question in any nodular pattern, and the secondary pulmonary lobule is the reference frame. Random nodules involve the subpleural surfaces and the fissures and ignore lobular architecture, which is what arrival through the bloodstream looks like: miliary tuberculosis, miliary fungal disease, or haematogenous metastases. Uniform size with weeks of fever in an immunosuppressed patient should prompt a telephone call before the report is typed, because untreated miliary tuberculosis is rapidly fatal and the workup, sputum, blood cultures and often bone marrow or liver biopsy, needs to start today. Centrilobular nodules spare the pleural surface and, with tree-in-bud, indicate airway spread. Perilymphatic nodules follow the fissures, the subpleural line and the bronchovascular bundles in a beaded fashion, which is sarcoidosis, silicosis or lymphangitis carcinomatosa.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 80 has a month of exertional breathlessness with a near-normal chest radiograph. CT shows symmetrical perihilar ground-glass sparing the immediate subpleural lung, a few thin-walled cysts, and no effusion or adenopathy. Which treatment should be started while confirmation is sought?
quiz.answer: Co-trimoxazole, with steroids added if hypoxaemic
choices: Co-trimoxazole, with steroids added if hypoxaemic
Intravenous ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus
Quadruple antituberculous therapy and isolation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia
quiz.explain: This is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: onset over weeks, marked hypoxaemia with a chest film that looks better than the patient, and a CT showing perihilar or diffuse ground-glass that is often geographical and often spares the immediate subpleural lung. Thin-walled cysts or pneumatoceles appear in roughly a third and carry a genuine risk of pneumothorax, which is worth flagging before any positive-pressure ventilation. Pleural effusion and lymphadenopathy argue against the diagnosis. Treatment is co-trimoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids where the arterial oxygen is low, and it is begun on suspicion because induced sputum or lavage takes time the patient may not have. Cytomegalovirus pneumonitis occurs at similarly low CD4 counts but adds nodules and consolidation; tuberculosis at this CD4 count often looks atypical, with adenopathy and lower-zone disease rather than upper-zone cavitation.

quiz.prompt: Twelve days into neutropenia following induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia, a patient has fever unresponsive to broad antibacterial cover, and CT shows three peripheral nodules each surrounded by a rim of ground-glass. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Start antifungal therapy for angioinvasive aspergillosis
choices: Start antifungal therapy for angioinvasive aspergillosis
Wait for a repeat CT in a week before treating anything
Start antituberculous therapy and isolate the patient
Escalate the antibacterial cover and repeat blood cultures
quiz.explain: The halo sign, a nodule or wedge of consolidation surrounded by ground-glass, is haemorrhage around an infarct caused by fungus invading a pulmonary artery branch, and in a profoundly neutropenic haematology patient it is invasive aspergillosis until proved otherwise. It appears early in the life of the lesion and fades within about a week, and treatment started while the halo is still visible does measurably better than treatment started later, so this is a finding to telephone rather than to report. Serum galactomannan and bronchoalveolar lavage support the diagnosis but should not delay the drug. As neutrophils recover, at roughly two to three weeks, the infarcted centre retracts and air dissects around it to give the air-crescent sign, which marks recovery rather than deterioration though it also signals a risk of haemoptysis. The halo is not unique to aspergillus: mucormycosis, other angioinvasive moulds, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and haemorrhagic metastases all produce it.

quiz.prompt: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes recovering from ketoacidosis has necrotic nasal turbinates on examination, and chest CT shows a large area of ground-glass surrounded by a complete thick ring of consolidation. What does this combination most urgently raise?
quiz.answer: Mucormycosis, needing urgent antifungals and surgery
choices: Mucormycosis, needing urgent antifungals and surgery
Organising pneumonia, needing a course of corticosteroids
Pulmonary tuberculosis, needing four-drug treatment
Pulmonary infarction from a segmental embolus
quiz.explain: The reversed halo, a central ground-glass core ringed by consolidation, was first described in cryptogenic organising pneumonia and remains commonest there, and it also belongs to the organising pneumonia phase of COVID-19, where it supports a CO-RADS 5. But context outranks the sign. In a diabetic patient emerging from ketoacidosis with necrotic sinonasal tissue, a reversed halo with a thick, nodular rim is invasive mucormycosis, which crosses tissue planes over hours to days and needs liposomal amphotericin and surgical debridement. Treating that as organising pneumonia with corticosteroids would accelerate it, which is what makes this differential worth knowing rather than merely interesting. Tuberculosis and sarcoidosis can also produce a reversed halo, in which case the ring tends to be composed of small nodules rather than solid consolidation.

module_contract.goal: Conduct, interpret and report imaging for suspected physical abuse to a standard that will hold up in a courtroom.

approach.detail: Required in every child under 2 years old suspected of abuse — a babygram is not an acceptable substitute for the dedicated view series.
The subtle injuries of abuse — metaphyseal lesions, rib fractures — are only visible on correctly positioned, well-collimated radiographs. Repeat a poor view rather than accept it.
State explicitly how specific each finding is for abuse rather than reporting a flat list of fractures.
Repeat the skeletal survey after two weeks — healing injuries invisible acutely often become apparent by then.
A fracture pattern inconsistent with the stated mechanism, or with the child's developmental stage, raises rather than lowers concern regardless of specificity.
Document dating of injuries, specificity, and the reasoning behind your conclusion in language that will stand up to cross-examination, not just clinical shorthand.

classify.name: Fracture specificity for non-accidental injury
rows: Classic metaphyseal lesion (corner/bucket-handle fracture); rib fractures in a child under 2; scapular, sternal and spinous process fractures
Classic metaphyseal lesion is virtually pathognomonic for abuse; rib fractures in this age group are highly specific
Complex skull fractures (multiple, bilateral, or with associated intracranial injury); multiple or growing skull fractures
Specificity is context-dependent on fracture pattern and clinical history
Simple linear skull fractures; diaphyseal (shaft) fractures of the long bones
Occur in both accidental and non-accidental injury and cannot be used alone to diagnose abuse
classify.note: Specificity ranking guides the weight given to a finding — it does not replace correlation with history, developmental stage and the pattern of injury as a whole.

pitfalls: Substituting a limited film or a babygram for the full skeletal survey — the dedicated view series is what the standard requires for children under 2.
Reporting a diaphyseal fracture as if it were as specific as a metaphyseal lesion — shaft fractures happen accidentally too and carry low specificity alone.
Skipping the two-week follow-up survey. Healing rib and metaphyseal injuries invisible on day one are often the findings that confirm the diagnosis.
Accepting a technically inadequate radiograph because the child was distressed. Poor positioning is exactly what hides the findings that matter most in this indication.
Writing a report that lists fractures without stating their specificity or reasoning — a report that will be read in court needs the inference made explicit, not left implicit.

quiz.prompt: A five-month-old is admitted with an unexplained spiral femoral fracture and no history of injury. The night radiographer offers a single anteroposterior film covering the whole infant to save handling. What do you insist on instead?
quiz.answer: A full survey of coned, dedicated views of every region, with oblique rib views
choices: A full survey of coned, dedicated views of every region, with oblique rib views
A limited survey of the long bones and chest, adding skull views if bruised
A whole-body low-dose CT, which resolves ribs and skull in one acquisition
A whole-body MRI, which shows marrow oedema at every fracture that is present
quiz.explain: The single whole-body film — the babygram — fails because it images most of the skeleton off-axis, at the wrong exposure, with the divergent beam obliquing the metaphyses and ribs it most needs to show. The standard survey is a set of individually collimated projections: two views of the skull, lateral cervical and thoracolumbar spine, frontal chest with left and right oblique rib views, abdomen and pelvis, and separate frontal views of humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae and feet. Coning and correct positioning are what make a classic metaphyseal lesion visible at all. CT delivers a dose that cannot be justified as a screening survey, though targeted CT of head and, with reformats, of skull and ribs has a role. Whole-body MRI complements the survey by finding marrow and soft-tissue injury, but it misses metaphyseal and rib fractures and does not replace it.

quiz.prompt: Below a certain age a full skeletal survey is performed in every child in whom physical abuse is suspected, without needing a specific bony complaint. State that age in months, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty-four months. Under two years the survey is mandatory in suspected physical abuse because occult fractures are common, the child cannot report pain or localise it, and the yield is high enough that a negative survey is itself informative. Between two and five years the survey is used selectively, guided by findings and by the clinical account, and above five it is rarely productive because a child of that age reports the injured part and occult fractures are unusual. Age also shapes the interpretation, not just the decision to image: any fracture in a child who is not yet independently mobile demands an explanation, and a femoral or humeral shaft fracture in a non-ambulant infant is a serious concern in a way that the same fracture in a running four-year-old is not.

quiz.prompt: The first skeletal survey on a seven-month-old with an unexplained subdural collection shows no fractures at all. The safeguarding team asks whether imaging of the skeleton is now finished. What do you tell them?
quiz.answer: Repeat a limited survey about two weeks later; healing changes disclose new injuries
choices: Repeat a limited survey about two weeks later; healing changes disclose new injuries
The survey is complete, and a repeat adds radiation dose without new information
Substitute a bone scintigram, which will detect every fracture the survey missed
Repeat the entire survey with skull views on the morning of hospital discharge
quiz.explain: A normal first survey does not exclude skeletal injury, because the two most specific fractures are the two hardest to see acutely. Undisplaced posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions frequently become visible only as subperiosteal new bone and callus appear, and the accepted interval for that is eleven to fourteen days. The repeat is limited: chest with obliques, long bones, and any region of concern. Skull films are generally omitted, since fractures of the skull heal without callus and a repeat film adds nothing. Scintigraphy is sensitive for rib and shaft injury but is poor at the skull and at symmetrical metaphyseal disease, and it cannot characterise what it detects. Repeating on the day of discharge, if that is day four, wastes the examination — timing is the whole point.

quiz.prompt: A four-month-old's survey shows, at the distal femur, a thin lucency parallel to and just beneath the growth plate, with a small triangular density at each margin; on the follow-up film the same lesion has a curved rim of bone around it. Describe what has fractured and what evidential weight it carries.
quiz.answer: This is a classic metaphyseal lesion, a planar fracture through the primary spongiosa of the metaphysis, projecting as a corner fragment or a bucket-handle depending on beam angulation, and in an infant it sits at the top of the specificity ranking for inflicted injury.
quiz.explain: The lesion is a disc-shaped fracture running across the metaphysis just below the zone of provisional calcification, undercutting a thin rim of bone that stays attached to the periphery. Tangential to the beam it looks like a corner fragment; en face, with a little obliquity, the same rim projects as a bucket handle. It is produced by shearing and torsion of the limb, the forces of gripping and wrenching a small limb, not by axial loading, which is why it is rare in accidental falls. It heals with little periosteal reaction, so it can be invisible acutely and obvious a fortnight later. Its differential is real and must be addressed: rickets frays, cups and splays the metaphysis and widens the physis; the classic metaphyseal lesion does neither, and the surrounding bone is normally mineralised.

quiz.prompt: A four-month-old resuscitated after an apnoeic episode has healing fractures of the left fifth to eighth ribs posteriorly, close to the costovertebral junctions. The parents ask, through the paediatric team, whether the chest compressions caused them. How do you frame the answer in your report?
quiz.answer: Posterior rib fractures arise from anteroposterior compression of the chest by encircling hands
choices: Posterior rib fractures arise from anteroposterior compression of the chest by encircling hands
Infant resuscitation frequently fractures posterior ribs and readily explains this pattern
Fractures at this site in an infant point to an underlying metabolic disorder of bone
Fractures here follow direct blows to the back and suggest a fall onto a hard edge
quiz.explain: The mechanism is levering. When an infant's chest is gripped front and back and squeezed, the posterior rib is forced over the fulcrum of the transverse process and snaps close to the costovertebral junction. That geometry is not reproduced by accidental trauma, and posterior rib fractures accordingly sit in the highest-specificity group alongside classic metaphyseal lesions and scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation in infants rarely fractures ribs at all, and when it does the fractures tend to be anterior or anterolateral, from two-thumb compression, rather than posterior. Say the mechanism plainly and in general terms; describe the fracture, state its specificity and state that resuscitation does not account for it, and leave the question of who did what to the investigation.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these features of a healing long bone fracture in the order in which they become visible on radiographs.
quiz.answer: soft-tissue-swelling subperiosteal-new-bone soft-callus hard-callus remodelling
quiz.explain: Soft-tissue swelling is there from the day of injury and fades within a week or so. Subperiosteal new bone, a fine line of mineralisation lifted off the shaft by the periosteal haematoma, appears from roughly four to fourteen days and is the first true sign of healing. Soft callus follows, becoming visible around the second week, then hard, well-mineralised bridging callus in the third to sixth weeks, and finally remodelling, which reshapes the cortex over months to years. Use these as overlapping bands rather than as dates. The bands are wide, they run faster in infants than in older children, and they differ between a rib, a metaphysis and a diaphysis. That imprecision is exactly why a report should describe the stage of healing and not name a day.

quiz.prompt: A solicitor asks you, from your report, to state the date on which each of an infant's four fractures was inflicted. Two show fine periosteal new bone, one shows dense bridging callus, and one is a parietal skull fracture with sharp margins. Set out what your imaging can and cannot support.
quiz.answer: Imaging can place each fracture in a broad range — acute, healing or old — and can state that fractures of differing ages are present, but it cannot date any of them to a particular day, and a skull fracture cannot be dated at all because it heals without callus.
quiz.explain: Fracture dating is one of the places where a radiologist can do real harm by overreaching. The evidence supports wide, overlapping windows: subperiosteal new bone from about four to fourteen days, soft callus around ten to fourteen days, hard callus from roughly two to six weeks, remodelling over months. Rates vary with the child's age, the bone involved and whether the fracture was immobilised. Classic metaphyseal lesions and rib fractures may heal with minimal periosteal reaction, blunting the usual markers. Skull fractures neither form callus nor reliably narrow, so a sharply marginated linear fracture may be hours or months old. What the imaging supports powerfully is multiplicity and difference: several fractures at demonstrably different stages of healing means several occasions, and that statement is defensible in court while a specific date is not.

quiz.prompt: A three-month-old has CT showing bilateral subdural collections, partly hyperdense and partly of near-water attenuation, with an interhemispheric component. The referring clinician asks you to confirm in writing that there were two separate assaults. What do you report?
quiz.answer: Mixed attenuation has several explanations and does not by itself establish two events
choices: Mixed attenuation has several explanations and does not by itself establish two events
Mixed attenuation dates these injuries as one recent and one several weeks older
Interhemispheric blood on its own establishes the diagnosis of inflicted head injury
Water-density collections are the benign subarachnoid spaces of infancy, so no injury
quiz.explain: Attenuation is a poor clock. Hyperacute, unclotted blood is not markedly dense; a torn arachnoid lets cerebrospinal fluid dilute a collection within hours; rebleeding into an established collection produces layered density; and severe anaemia lowers the attenuation of fresh blood towards that of brain. So a mixed-density subdural is compatible with repeated injury but does not prove it. MRI characterises blood products more finely and adds parenchymal information, yet it too gives ranges rather than dates. Interhemispheric and posterior falcine collections are strongly associated with inflicted injury but are not by themselves diagnostic. Benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces is a genuine mimic of chronic collections, but it does not explain a hyperdense component. Report the appearances, list what could produce them, and say what the imaging does and does not support.

quiz.prompt: A six-week-old with a parietal skull fracture and a thin subdural collection has already had a head CT. Before the strategy meeting the paediatricians ask what an MRI would add to what you already know.
quiz.answer: Parenchymal and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, small collections, and cervical spine damage
choices: Parenchymal and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, small collections, and cervical spine damage
A precise date for the subdural collection, reliable to within two or three days
Better depiction of the fracture line itself, which CT tends to under-represent
Confirmation that the fracture is linear rather than complex, altering specificity
quiz.explain: CT is the emergency test: fast, excellent for fracture and for acute blood, and with three-dimensional reformats it depicts the skull better than MRI does. MRI is added because it answers different questions. Diffusion-weighted imaging shows hypoxic-ischaemic injury, which is the strongest determinant of outcome in inflicted head trauma and is largely invisible acutely on CT. It resolves thin convexity and posterior fossa collections that CT loses against bone, characterises blood products, and can show bridging vein injury. Crucially it includes the whole spine, where ligamentous injury at the craniocervical junction and spinal subdural blood are found and are otherwise missed. Timing is usually two to five days from presentation, with a repeat at two to three months to assess established damage. What MRI cannot do is give the courtroom a precise date.

quiz.prompt: A two-year-old presents with vomiting and a bruised abdominal wall. ALT is 260 U/L and AST 190 U/L. Ultrasound shows a small volume of free fluid and no solid organ abnormality. What is the appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, because ultrasound under-reads bowel and pancreas
choices: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, because ultrasound under-reads bowel and pancreas
Repeat the ultrasound at 24 hours, which will disclose a duodenal haematoma
A fluoroscopic upper gastrointestinal series as the first test for visceral injury
No further imaging, since transaminases at this level reflect muscle bruising
quiz.explain: Raised transaminases in a young child with an unexplained abdominal injury are a recognised trigger for cross-sectional imaging, with a threshold around 80 U/L widely used in practice. Inflicted abdominal trauma is uncommon but carries high mortality, largely because it presents late and because the injuries are hollow-viscus and pancreatic rather than the splenic injuries of road trauma. The duodenum and proximal jejunum are crushed against the vertebral column at their fixed points, producing intramural haematoma or perforation; the pancreatic body is transected across the spine and may present later as a pseudocyst; liver injury favours the left lobe from a midline blow. Ultrasound is insensitive for all of these, and free fluid without solid organ injury should itself raise suspicion of bowel or mesenteric damage. Contrast-enhanced CT is the test, with solid organ injuries described using the AAST grades.

quiz.prompt: Before a strategy meeting on an infant with three fractures at different stages of healing, you are asked which medical conditions you have considered and excluded on the imaging. Name the main ones and say what you looked for.
quiz.answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets and the metabolic bone disease of prematurity must be excluded, along with birth injury, by assessing bone density and modelling, the metaphyses and physes, the skull for wormian bones, and the age and site of any healing fracture.
quiz.explain: The differential deserves to be addressed explicitly in the report, because it will be raised later whether or not you raise it. Osteogenesis imperfecta shows generalised osteopenia, gracile or bowed bones, wormian bones in the lambdoid region and often a family history and blue sclerae, though mild type I can look near-normal, which is why clinical and genetic assessment sits alongside the imaging. Rickets frays, cups and splays the metaphyses, widens the physes and softens the bone; it is the mimic that matters most for metaphyseal lesions. Metabolic bone disease of prematurity does the same in an ex-preterm infant. Birth injury accounts for clavicular and humeral fractures, but these callus by two to three weeks and remodel, so a fresh fracture in a six-week-old is not birth-related. Copper deficiency, Menkes disease and congenital syphilis are rarer but real.

quiz.prompt: Your department repeats the skeletal survey once healing changes have had time to declare themselves; the accepted interval is quoted as a window of eleven to fourteen days. State the upper limit of that window, in days, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Fourteen days is the upper limit of the conventional eleven to fourteen day window, and the reason for both ends is physiological rather than administrative. Repeat too early and subperiosteal new bone has not yet mineralised enough to be seen on a plain film; leave it too long and a child is exposed to continuing risk while the investigation waits, and some rib callus begins to remodel. The repeat typically finds fractures the first survey missed in a meaningful minority of cases, chiefly posterior ribs and classic metaphyseal lesions, and it also reclassifies apparent findings as normal variants, which protects families as much as it protects children. It is limited rather than full — chest with obliques, long bones, and any site of concern — and the skull is normally left out because skull fractures do not heal with callus.

quiz.prompt: You have described a healing posterior rib fracture and two classic metaphyseal lesions in a five-month-old with no offered explanation. The consultant paediatrician asks you to write in your report that the mother's partner inflicted them. How do you frame the report?
quiz.answer: Describe the findings, state their specificity, and leave causation to the investigation
choices: Describe the findings, state their specificity, and leave causation to the investigation
Name the mechanism and the likely perpetrator, since the imaging is unambiguous here
Omit any interpretation and simply list the fractures without further qualification
Record the findings as indeterminate until the follow-up survey has been completed
quiz.explain: The report is a legal document that you may be cross-examined on years later, so write it as one. Describe each finding precisely, with site, appearance and stage of healing. Then interpret within your expertise: these injuries are of high specificity for inflicted trauma in an infant, no medical condition on the imaging accounts for them, and the pattern is not explained by the history given. That is a defensible clinical opinion. Identifying who caused an injury is not a radiological finding and belongs to the investigation. Saying nothing at all is also a failure, because the clinicians and the court need the specificity ranking that only you can supply. Add the practical duties: escalate to the safeguarding team the same day rather than waiting for the report to be typed, date what you write, and have a second radiologist review the images.

module_contract.goal: Read enhancement as a statement about which barrier has failed in which compartment, and use diffusion, distribution and the clinical setting to separate abscess, encephalitis, parasitic cyst and the mass lesions of advanced HIV.

approach.detail: Dura, pineal gland, vessels, pituitary stalk and gland, choroid plexus and area postrema have no blood-brain barrier and enhance. Parenchymal enhancement is always abnormal.

approach.step: Place the enhancement in a compartment
approach.detail: Dural, leptomeningeal, ependymal, perivascular or parenchymal. The compartment names the barrier that has failed.
Diffuse dural, focal dural, leptomeningeal, gyral, periventricular, perivascular, nodular, smooth ring, irregular ring, open ring, cyst with nodule.

approach.step: Put DWI through the centre of any ring
approach.detail: Central restriction is pus. Necrotic tumour does not restrict centrally.
Grey-white interface and watershed means haematogenous; basal cisterns means TB or sarcoid; temporal and insular limbic means herpes; periventricular means lymphoma.

approach.step: Choose the sequence that shows it
approach.detail: Contrast-enhanced FLAIR beats T1 post-contrast for leptomeningeal disease and carcinomatosis. Use SWI for the abscess rim.

classify.name: Enhancement patterns and their differential
rows: Meningioma with dural tail and hyperostosis, metastasis, lymphoma
Bacterial meningitis, TB (basal cisterns), cryptococcus, Lyme, carcinomatosis (sugarcoating), neurosarcoidosis
Infarction with luxury perfusion, SMART, herpes encephalitis
Thin: ventriculitis. Thick: lymphoma, tumour spread
Pyogenic abscess — central restricted diffusion, double rim sign on T2
GBM, cystic metastasis, toxoplasmosis with the eccentric target sign
Tumefactive MS; abscess rupturing towards the ventricle

measure.what: Central diffusion in a ring lesion
measure.how: Restricted centre with low rCBV and a smooth rim is a pyogenic abscess; unrestricted centre with high rCBV and an irregular rim is necrotic tumour.
Low T2 signal rim around an abscess cavity.
Lymphoma gives little oedema for its bulk, is hyperdense on CT, dark on T2 and restricts. Metastasis gives more peripheral oedema.
Do not exclude metastasis because there is only one lesion.

pitfalls: Calling dural enhancement disease. Dura, pineal, choroid plexus, pituitary and area postrema have no barrier and enhance normally.
Reading a ring lesion without DWI through its centre. That one sequence separates abscess from necrotic tumour.
Missing herpes because the CT is normal. Early DWI restriction in the temporal and insular cortex is there before anything else.
Looking for leptomeningeal disease on T1 post-contrast alone. Contrast-enhanced FLAIR shows meningitis and carcinomatosis that T1 does not.
Toxoplasmosis over-called as a generic ring lesion. The eccentric target sign, low T2 signal and absent central restriction are the discriminators.
Forgetting the cranial nerves when leptomeningeal enhancement is present — bilateral facial nerve enhancement in Lyme, sugarcoating in carcinomatosis.
