quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has fever, headache and neck stiffness. Post-contrast T1 shows thin enhancement running down into the sulci over both convexities and coating the cerebellar folia; the falx and tentorium are of normal thickness and show no extra enhancement. What does this distribution tell you, and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: The pia-arachnoid and the CSF spaces are inflamed, so lumbar puncture will sample the disease itself
choices: The pia-arachnoid and the CSF spaces are inflamed, so lumbar puncture will sample the disease itself
The cortex itself has broken down, so add perfusion and spectroscopy before considering a biopsy
The dura alone is inflamed, so look instead for low CSF pressure and image the whole spine for a leak
A collection sits between dura and arachnoid, so measure its depth and refer it for surgical drainage
quiz.explain: Contrast enhances where there is no blood-brain barrier or where one has failed. Enhancement that dips into sulci and follows the folia is leptomeningeal: pia and arachnoid, the walls of the CSF space, so the CSF is where the organism will be found. Dural (pachymeningeal) enhancement is a different signature - thick, continuous, following falx and tentorium, never entering a sulcus - and points to intracranial hypotension, post-surgical change or dural infiltration. Note the limits of the sign: leptomeningeal enhancement is neither sensitive nor specific for bacterial meningitis. Plenty of proven pyogenic meningitis has a normal scan, and carcinomatous and granulomatous meningitis look identical. Imaging in suspected meningitis is done to find the complication and to check that lumbar puncture is safe, not to make or exclude the diagnosis, and it must never delay antibiotics.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old smoker with a new seizure has a 3 cm ring-enhancing lesion at the grey-white junction. The rim is thick, nodular and irregular, the rim is not dark on T2, and the cavity is dark on diffusion-weighted imaging with a high ADC. There is a second smaller ring lesion in the cerebellum. What is the most reasonable next step?
quiz.answer: Treat it as metastatic disease and stage the chest, abdomen and pelvis before any neurosurgical referral
choices: Treat it as subacute infarction and repeat the study in six weeks to watch the enhancement settle down
Treat it as metastatic disease and stage the chest, abdomen and pelvis before any neurosurgical referral
Treat it as a pyogenic abscess and arrange urgent aspiration with blood cultures and empirical antibiotics
Treat it as tumefactive demyelination and arrange spinal imaging with oligoclonal bands before any therapy
quiz.explain: The cavity is the discriminator. Pus is viscous and packed with inflammatory cells, so water is restricted: bright on diffusion, low ADC. Tumour necrosis is thin liquefied debris, so water moves freely: dark on diffusion, high ADC. The rim adds to the argument - abscess rims are thin, smooth, complete, often thinner on the ventricular side, and characteristically dark on T2 from free radicals in the inflammatory wall, while necrotic tumour rims are thick and nodular. Two lesions at the grey-white junction in a smoker complete the picture. Keep two traps in mind: a treated abscess loses its restriction, and some abscesses caused by fungi or by treated organisms behave atypically. Where doubt persists, aspiration answers the question and treats the patient at the same time.

quiz.prompt: On a diffusion study acquired at b = 0 and b = 1000 s/mm2, the centre of a ring-enhancing lesion measures 900 arbitrary signal units on the b = 0 image and 450 units on the b = 1000 image. Calculate the apparent diffusion coefficient of the cavity contents. Answer in units of 10^-3 mm2/s, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Signal decays exponentially with the b value, so ADC = ln(S0 / Sb) divided by b. Here the signal halves, ln(2) = 0.693, and dividing by 1000 s/mm2 gives 0.69 x 10^-3 mm2/s. That number does clinical work. The cavity of an untreated pyogenic abscess sits low, typically below about 1.0 x 10^-3 mm2/s and often nearer 0.5, because pus is cellular and viscous. Necrotic tumour usually sits above the value of normal white matter, commonly 1.5 and higher. Normal adult white matter is around 0.7 to 0.8, so a lesion reading like white matter or lower is behaving like pus. Always read the ADC map itself rather than the trace image: a very T2-bright lesion can look bright on diffusion with a perfectly normal ADC, which is T2 shine-through, not restriction.

quiz.prompt: On day four of treatment for pneumococcal meningitis a 30-year-old loses two points of GCS. CT shows a thin crescent of extra-axial fluid over the left convexity that had been read as a sterile effusion. Which MRI finding would separate an infected collection from a sterile one, and what does that change?
quiz.answer: A subdural empyema shows restricted diffusion within the collection with an enhancing membrane, unlike a sterile effusion which follows CSF freely, and it changes the plan to urgent neurosurgical drainage alongside antibiotics.
quiz.explain: Sterile subdural effusions are common in treated meningitis, particularly in children, and they resolve on their own. An empyema is a surgical emergency, and CT alone will not tell them apart because both are thin crescents of near-CSF density. Diffusion does: pus restricts, effusion does not, and the empyema usually shows a thin enhancing membrane along its inner border. Look for the company it keeps - cortical vein thrombosis, adjacent gyral swelling and early venous infarction, since an empyema inflames the veins running through the subdural space. The deteriorating patient on adequate antibiotics is the trigger for rescanning, and a scan without diffusion has not answered the question you were asked.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old is confused and febrile with complex partial seizures. FLAIR shows swelling and hyperintensity of both medial temporal lobes, asymmetrically, extending into the insula and the inferior frontal cortex; the lentiform nuclei are spared, there is gyral restricted diffusion and a few foci of petechial haemorrhage. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Start intravenous aciclovir immediately and send CSF for viral PCR, accepting that a negative early PCR does not stop it
choices: Start levetiracetam alone for peri-ictal change and repeat the imaging in one week once the seizures are controlled
Start high-dose steroids for autoimmune limbic encephalitis and screen for an underlying malignancy with body CT
Start intravenous aciclovir immediately and send CSF for viral PCR, accepting that a negative early PCR does not stop it
Start intravenous thrombolysis for a middle cerebral artery infarct once the time of onset is confirmed by a reliable witness
quiz.explain: This is the herpes simplex distribution: limbic and paralimbic cortex - medial temporal, insula, inferior frontal, cingulate - bilateral but asymmetric, with cortical swelling, early restricted diffusion and a tendency to bleed. The sparing of the lentiform nucleus is the classic separator from middle cerebral artery infarction, which takes the basal ganglia and stops at a vascular boundary; herpes crosses vascular territories because it spreads along trigeminal and olfactory routes. Autoimmune limbic encephalitis looks similar but is usually more symmetric, less haemorrhagic and without restricted diffusion. Treatment is the point of the item: aciclovir is started on suspicion. Untreated mortality is high, PCR can be falsely negative in the first 72 hours, and the drug is comparatively safe.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the four evolutionary stages of a parenchymal neurocysticercosis lesion in the sequence that serial imaging would show, from the newly established viable cyst to its end point.
quiz.answer: vesicular colloidal-vesicular granular-nodular nodular-calcified
quiz.explain: The larva is invisible to the host while alive. In the vesicular stage the cyst follows CSF signal, holds an eccentric mural scolex, and shows no oedema and little or no enhancement because the parasite is immunologically quiet. As it dies the fluid turns proteinaceous - colloidal vesicular - the wall enhances as a ring and surrounding oedema appears, and this is when the patient usually seizes. In the granular nodular stage the cyst retracts to a small enhancing nodule with less oedema, and finally it becomes a small calcified nodule with no enhancement. Reading the stage matters practically: antiparasitic drugs are aimed at viable vesicular cysts and can provoke a severe inflammatory reaction, so steroid cover and a search for intraventricular and subarachnoid disease come first, and a purely calcified burden needs no antiparasitic treatment at all.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old from a high-prevalence country has three weeks of headache, low fever and a new sixth nerve palsy. Which imaging pattern would you report as fitting tuberculous meningitis, and why does calling it early matter?
quiz.answer: Thick enhancing exudate filling the basal cisterns, communicating hydrocephalus, and infarcts in the basal ganglia and internal capsule from perforator vasculitis; calling it early matters because treatment starts on the pattern long before culture returns.
quiz.explain: Tuberculous meningitis is a disease of the basal cisterns. Sticky exudate fills the suprasellar and ambient cisterns, encases the cranial nerves - hence the sixth and third nerve palsies - and blocks CSF resorption, giving communicating hydrocephalus in most cases. The same exudate strangles the lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating vessels, so infarcts appear in the basal ganglia, internal capsule and thalami, a distribution that is a strong clue in a young patient with no vascular risk. Tuberculomas may coexist and can be T2-hypointense centrally. Culture takes weeks and CSF microscopy is often negative, so the triad on imaging, with the right epidemiology, is what starts anti-tuberculous therapy and steroids. Hydrocephalus that progresses may need diversion, so it must be reported and followed, not just mentioned.

quiz.prompt: A man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 80 has headache and a right hemiparesis. MRI shows four ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and at the grey-white junction, with marked oedema; the cavities show high ADC, and thallium-201 SPECT shows no uptake above background. What is the appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Give empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy and rescan at two weeks, reserving biopsy for lesions that fail to shrink
choices: Give antifungal therapy for cryptococcal disease and repeat imaging after the induction course has finished
Give whole-brain radiotherapy for presumed primary CNS lymphoma once staging of the body has been completed
Give supportive care alone for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy while antiretroviral therapy is being started
Give empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy and rescan at two weeks, reserving biopsy for lesions that fail to shrink
quiz.explain: Multiplicity, a basal ganglia and grey-white junction distribution, heavy oedema and facilitated diffusion all favour toxoplasmosis, and the negative thallium study is the clincher. Toxoplasma lesions are abscesses without viable cells to take up thallium or FDG; primary CNS lymphoma is densely cellular and takes up both avidly, tends to be solitary and periventricular, shows subependymal spread and typically restricts diffusion. The eccentric target sign - a small enhancing nodule on one wall of a ring - is specific for toxoplasmosis when present, though it is often absent. Standard practice is a therapeutic trial: clinical and radiological improvement within about two weeks confirms it, and failure to respond is the trigger for CSF EBV PCR and biopsy. Cryptococcus more often gives dilated perivascular spaces and gelatinous pseudocysts rather than florid ring enhancement.

quiz.prompt: A man with HIV and a CD4 count of 40 has a solitary periventricular enhancing mass with subependymal spread and a low ADC. Thallium-201 SPECT shows intense uptake. What does the thallium study add, and what must you advise before any biopsy is booked?
quiz.answer: Avid thallium uptake supports lymphoma rather than toxoplasmosis because the tissue is densely cellular, so ask for CSF EBV PCR and biopsy, and advise that corticosteroids be withheld until tissue is taken because they can shrink the lesion and make it non-diagnostic.
quiz.explain: Thallium-201 and FDG are read the same way here: they are cellularity and metabolism probes, and an infectious abscess is neither cellular nor metabolically active in the way a lymphoma is. Combined with a solitary periventricular mass, subependymal creep and restricted diffusion from a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, the study shifts the working diagnosis decisively. The practical warning is the steroid one. AIDS-related primary CNS lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive; a dose given for oedema before biopsy can dissolve the enhancing tissue and leave the neurosurgeon with gliosis. If intracranial pressure forces steroids, say so explicitly in the report so that the timing is understood. CSF EBV DNA is a useful adjunct in this population, since the tumour is EBV-driven.

quiz.prompt: A patient on natalizumab for multiple sclerosis develops slowly worsening speech and right-sided clumsiness. FLAIR shows a confluent asymmetric subcortical white matter abnormality in the left frontal lobe that reaches the cortex and involves the U-fibres, with no enhancement and almost no mass effect. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Stop the drug and send CSF for JC virus PCR, warning the team that enhancement may appear as immune reconstitution develops
choices: Stop the drug and send CSF for JC virus PCR, warning the team that enhancement may appear as immune reconstitution develops
Continue the drug and treat this as an active demyelinating relapse, giving a further course of high-dose intravenous steroids
Stop the drug and treat this as a septic embolic shower, adding echocardiography and empirical broad antibiotics
Continue the drug and treat this as small vessel ischaemia, adding blood pressure control and an antiplatelet agent
quiz.explain: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a lytic infection of oligodendrocytes by JC virus. It is asymmetric, confluent, spreads through subcortical white matter and characteristically involves the subcortical U-fibres, which small vessel ischaemia and HIV encephalopathy spare. It does not enhance and it does not push, because there is no intact immune response to generate inflammation and no mass to speak of. A leading edge of mildly restricted diffusion marks the advancing front. The management point is immune reconstitution: once natalizumab is withdrawn or antiretroviral therapy is started, the returning immune system attacks infected tissue and the lesion swells and enhances. That is expected, not treatment failure, and recognising it in the report prevents the drug being wrongly blamed or the patient being biopsied unnecessarily.

quiz.prompt: A shunted child has fever and irritability. Non-contrast CT shows slightly enlarged ventricles with a layered debris-fluid level in both occipital horns. MRI adds restricted diffusion in that dependent material and thin enhancement of the ependymal lining. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: Urgent shunt tap and CSF sampling for ventriculitis, since the intraventricular debris restricts and the ependyma is inflamed
choices: Expectant management for choroid plexus prominence, which commonly mimics debris in the dependent occipital horns
Urgent shunt tap and CSF sampling for ventriculitis, since the intraventricular debris restricts and the ependyma is inflamed
Routine outpatient review for layering blood products after a small intraventricular bleed, with repeat imaging in about a month
Elective shunt revision for gradual proximal catheter blockage, since the ventricles have enlarged since the last scan
quiz.explain: Ventriculitis is easy to under-call because the ventricles may be only mildly larger and the CT change is subtle. The two findings that make the case are debris that restricts diffusion, which is pus rather than blood or choroid plexus, and ependymal enhancement, which marks inflammation of the ventricular lining. Blood products layer too, but they follow the expected signal evolution and do not enhance the ependyma. The consequence is time-critical: infected shunt hardware usually has to be externalised or removed, and organisms are recovered from a shunt tap rather than from a lumbar puncture. Ventriculitis also loculates, so mention any developing septation or trapped horn, because that changes where the catheter has to go.

quiz.prompt: A trainee asks why an inflammatory demyelinating plaque enhances for a few weeks and then stops enhancing while the plaque itself remains visible on FLAIR for years. Answer in terms of what contrast enhancement actually reports.
quiz.answer: Enhancement reports a breached blood-brain barrier letting contrast leak into the interstitium, not the presence of disease itself, so it fades once the barrier is repaired even though the tissue damage persists.
quiz.explain: Gadolinium does not cross an intact blood-brain barrier, so enhancement is a map of where the barrier has failed or where it never existed - dura, choroid plexus, pituitary, pineal, the vessels themselves. That single idea explains most of the patterns in this module: a leptomeningeal pattern means the disease is in the CSF compartment, an abscess rim enhances because inflamed granulation tissue is leaky while the pus inside has no vessels at all, and an active plaque enhances only during the weeks in which inflammation is actively opening the barrier. It also explains the negatives. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy does not enhance in an untreated immunosuppressed patient because there is no inflammatory response to open anything. Absence of enhancement is a positive finding, not a normal study.

module_contract.goal: Analyse a congenital heart CT segment by segment and pick CT or MRI to fit.

approach.step: Follow the blood, right to left
approach.detail: Read the chambers and connections in the order blood actually flows: right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary valve and arteries, left atrium, left ventricle, aortic valve.

approach.step: Confirm ventricular morphology independently of position
approach.detail: Use internal features, not location, to call a ventricle right or left — the moderator band and coarse trabeculation mark the right ventricle, which matters in complex or discordant anatomy.
State the atrioventricular and ventriculo-arterial connections explicitly rather than assuming the normal arrangement.

approach.step: Screen for the aortic arch and great vessel anomalies
approach.detail: Check arch sidedness and branching pattern, and look for the vascular ring and sling patterns described on the vascular-anomalies page.

pitfalls: Assuming a ventricle's identity from its position rather than confirming it with internal morphology — this fails in discordant or complex connections.
Reporting 'normal situs and connections' as a default rather than a stated observation in a referral for suspected congenital disease.
Missing an arch-sidedness or branching anomaly because the arch was not specifically checked as its own step.

quiz.prompt: A newborn with dextrocardia has the stomach bubble on the right, and the referring team has recorded situs inversus on that basis alone. Working from the same CT, what would you look for at the atrial appendages and at the bronchi to settle atrial situs, and why does the abdominal arrangement not settle it for you?
quiz.answer: Atrial situs is settled by appendage morphology, and on CT the bronchi are the dependable surrogate for it. A morphologic right appendage is broad and triangular with a wide junction and pectinate muscles running around the vestibule; a morphologic left appendage is narrow and finger-like with a smooth vestibule. A short bronchus passing above its pulmonary artery is right-sided morphology, a long bronchus passing below its pulmonary artery is left-sided, and the systemic venous return helps too, since the inferior caval vein normally enters the morphologic right atrium. Abdominal and atrial arrangement usually agree, but they are separate determinations made on separate evidence, and dextrocardia is the setting in which the liver, stomach and spleen scatter independently. If bronchial and appendage morphology look the same on both sides, the diagnosis is isomerism (heterotaxy) rather than simple inversus.
quiz.explain: Sequential segmental analysis begins with atrial situs because everything downstream is described relative to it. The appendage defines situs, and bronchial morphology is the reliable imaging proxy because broncho-atrial concordance is high. Abdominal situs does agree with atrial situs in the great majority of hearts, which is why the shortcut is tempting - but agreement is not identity, and the hearts in which it fails are the ones that matter. In heterotaxy the viscera arrange themselves independently, so reading situs off the stomach bubble can start the whole segmental analysis from a false premise and mislabel an isomeric heart as mirror-image normal.

quiz.prompt: A CT in an infant with complex congenital heart disease shows two long bronchi, each passing below its pulmonary artery, with bilobed lungs on both sides. Which further finding would you expect on the same study?
quiz.answer: Interruption of the inferior vena cava with azygos continuation
quiz.explain: Bilateral hyparterial bronchi with bilateral bilobed lungs are left isomerism, in which the hepatic segment of the inferior caval vein usually fails to form and lower body blood returns through a dilated azygos vein. Finding that before anyone plans a cannulation or a cavopulmonary connection is the point of the observation. 'Aorta and inferior vena cava on the same side of the spine' is the tempting wrong answer, and 'Pulmonary venous drainage below the diaphragm to the portal vein' the other: both are genuine associations, but of right isomerism, whose bronchi are short and eparterial and whose lungs are trilobed on both sides.
choices: Aorta and inferior vena cava on the same side of the spine
Pulmonary venous drainage below the diaphragm to the portal vein
A right aortic arch with mirror-image branching of its vessels
Interruption of the inferior vena cava with azygos continuation

quiz.prompt: A 3 kg neonate is ventilated for stridor and recurrent desaturation, and a left pulmonary artery sling is suspected. The team needs the vessels and the trachea in one look. Which approach fits the problem?
quiz.answer: Non-gated CT angiography, showing vessel and airway together
quiz.explain: CT takes seconds, needs no transfer to an MR environment and no MR-compatible ventilator, and it resolves the tracheal lumen, the lung parenchyma and the anomalous left pulmonary artery in a single acquisition; the length of airway narrowed by complete tracheal rings, which is what decides the operation, is measured in the same dataset that shows the vessel. Rigid bronchoscopy sees the rings and the absent posterior membrane directly and remains the reference standard for the mucosal side of the airway, so it complements the CT rather than being displaced by it - and the report should state where the tube tip sits, since an endotracheal tube can splint or hide the narrowed segment. 'Cardiac MRI under anaesthesia, resolving airway and vessels' is the tempting wrong answer: it settles the vascular half without ionising radiation, but it demands a long anaesthetic in an unstable infant and depicts the airway poorly. Echocardiography can show the anomalous origin itself and still does not reach the trachea.
choices: Cardiac MRI under anaesthesia, resolving airway and vessels
Repeat echocardiography with suprasternal and subcostal views
Non-gated CT angiography, showing vessel and airway together
Fluoroscopic bronchography, then catheter pulmonary angiography

quiz.prompt: A 2-month-old with a heart rate of 140 needs the coronary origins shown before surgery, at the lowest dose that will answer the question. Which acquisition strategy would you use?
quiz.answer: Prospective triggering set to end-systole, the steadier rest
quiz.explain: As the rate rises the cardiac cycle shortens almost entirely at the expense of diastole, and diastasis is the first thing to vanish; a mid-diastolic target that is quiet at 60 beats per minute lands on a moving vessel at 140, which is what makes 'Prospective triggering at seventy percent of the R-R interval' - the standard adult setting - the tempting wrong answer here. End-systole shortens far less and stays predictable, so paediatric protocols trigger there. 'Retrospective gating across the cycle at full tube current' would freeze the vessel too, and that is precisely why it has to be excluded on dose rather than on motion: it irradiates the whole cycle to get there, which is the wrong trade in an infant. Beta blockade at this age is neither safe nor reliably effective, and the rate is not the thing to change.
choices: Prospective triggering at seventy percent of the R-R interval
Prospective triggering set to end-systole, the steadier rest
Retrospective gating across the cycle at full tube current
Oral beta blockade first, to bring the rate under sixty-five

quiz.prompt: A paediatric cardiac CT protocol is changed so that the tube current-time product is halved, with every other parameter held constant. By what factor does the image noise, the standard deviation of attenuation in a uniform region, increase? Give the factor to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Image noise varies inversely with the square root of the number of detected photons, and the photon count is proportional to mAs, so noise goes as one over the square root of mAs. Halving the mAs halves the dose and multiplies the noise by the square root of two, which is 1.41 to two decimal places. The trade is therefore cheap in dose and expensive in noise, and in a small patient it is usually worth taking, because the contrast those missing photons cost can be bought back with iodine at a low tube potential rather than with more photons - the effect this domain meets again in the TAVI protocol. Dose discipline counts for more here than in an adult: a small body absorbs a larger share of the beam, the tissues are dividing faster, and decades remain for a stochastic effect to appear.

quiz.prompt: A 15-year-old collapses while running. CT shows the left coronary artery arising from the right sinus and passing between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk, and the surgeon proposes unroofing the proximal vessel. Which CT feature has to be present for unroofing to be the operation that fits?
quiz.answer: A proximal segment running inside the aortic wall
quiz.explain: Unroofing is an incision of the wall the coronary shares with the aorta, so it presupposes an intramural segment: divide that wall and the intramural course ceases to exist, the slit-shaped orifice is laid open, and the neo-ostium comes to sit in its own sinus, because those three features are one lesion abolished in one cut. That segment is also the mechanism most consistently tied to ischaemia, since inside the aortic media the lumen is elliptical and is squeezed further as aortic pressure and diameter rise with exercise. Where the interarterial course lies outside the aortic wall there is nothing to unroof, and translocation with reimplantation is the operation instead - which is why the report has to say whether the proximal segment lies inside the aortic wall and for how far, not merely that the vessel passes between the great arteries. 'A myocardial bridge over the mid anterior descending' is the trap, since bridges are unroofed as well, but that is myocardium lifted off a mid-vessel and a different problem from the one that dropped this patient.
choices: A proximal segment running inside the aortic wall
A myocardial bridge over the mid anterior descending
A separate circumflex origin from the same sinus
A dominant right coronary reaching the cardiac crux

quiz.prompt: An adolescent repaired for tetralogy of Fallot is listed for percutaneous pulmonary valve implantation in the right ventricular outflow tract. Which CT finding would most change the plan?
quiz.answer: A coronary artery crossing the intended landing zone
quiz.explain: In a small but important minority of these patients the left anterior descending artery arises from the right coronary and crosses the outflow tract. The vessel that forbade a transannular incision at the first operation can be crushed by a stent or a valve expanded in the same place, which is why balloon testing with simultaneous coronary angiography is routine and why the CT is done beforehand. 'A right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian' is the tempting wrong answer, because a right arch is the commonest arch anomaly in repaired tetralogy - about a quarter of these patients - but the arch says nothing about what will happen in the outflow tract. Root dilatation and patch calcification belong in the report, and neither of them stops the procedure.
choices: A right aortic arch with an aberrant left subclavian
A coronary artery crossing the intended landing zone
Aortic root dilatation measured at the sinuses of Valsalva
Calcification within the old transannular patch

quiz.prompt: Before intervention on a native coarctation, the surgeon wants to know how much of the descending aortic flow is being delivered by collaterals rather than through the narrowing. Which measurement answers that question?
quiz.answer: Phase-contrast flow beyond the narrowing against flow at the diaphragm
quiz.explain: Blood that leaves the aorta above the coarctation and re-enters below it through internal mammary and intercostal channels makes the descending aorta carry more flow at the diaphragm than immediately beyond the stenosis, whereas a normal aorta steadily loses flow to its branches on the way down. Phase-contrast MRI measures those two volumes directly, and this is one of the questions CT has no way of answering: it gives exquisite anatomy and stent detail, but no velocity. Diameters and gradients describe the lesion rather than the collateral burden - and rib notching skips the upper two ribs, whose intercostal supply comes from the costocervical trunk.
choices: Aortic diameter at the narrowing against diameter at the diaphragm
The number of notched ribs graded against the intercostal calibre
Phase-contrast flow beyond the narrowing against flow at the diaphragm
Peak systolic gradient across the narrowing taken at echocardiography

quiz.prompt: In an adult repaired by arterial switch, the pulmonary bifurcation sits in front of the neo-aorta with the branches draped around it. Which late problem follows most directly from that geometry?
quiz.answer: Stenosis of the branch pulmonary arteries
quiz.explain: The LeCompte manoeuvre carries the pulmonary bifurcation anterior to the aorta, so the branches must stretch around it; supravalvar and branch pulmonary stenosis is the commonest reason these patients come back for reintervention, and echo tends to underestimate it. Neo-aortic regurgitation is frequent too, but it follows from the native pulmonary valve being asked to hold systemic pressure, not from where the branches sit. A systemic venous baffle belongs to the atrial switch operations, which this patient did not have.
choices: Stenosis of the branch pulmonary arteries
Obstruction within a systemic venous baffle
Regurgitation through the neo-aortic valve
Aneurysm at the ascending aortic suture

quiz.prompt: A Fontan patient is scanned after a single arm-vein injection at a short delay. The cavopulmonary confluence and the left pulmonary artery contain swirling low-attenuation material that sits in mid-lumen and touches no wall, while the extracardiac conduit is uniformly unopacified. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Rescan after a longer delay, letting the streams mix
quiz.explain: An arm injection opacifies the superior caval stream alone. Hepatic and lower body blood reaches the lungs through the extracardiac conduit having never seen contrast, which is why the conduit is uniformly dark rather than full of defects - itself a finding to recognise, so that nobody reports an occluded conduit. The two streams meet at the cavopulmonary confluence and run side by side into the branch arteries, throwing up swirling defects that float in mid-lumen and shift between phases. 'Report thrombus at the confluence and anticoagulate' is the dangerous wrong answer: a true thrombus is fixed, meets the wall and holds its shape across phases. The remedy is time or a second injection site - a delayed series, or simultaneous upper and lower limb injections, gives a uniformly opacified pathway. Driving the rate up through one arm widens the disparity instead of closing it.
choices: Report thrombus at the confluence and anticoagulate
Put the appearance down to sternal wire streaking
Raise the injection rate through the same arm cannula
Rescan after a longer delay, letting the streams mix

quiz.prompt: Phase-contrast MRI in a child with a suspected atrial septal defect measures a net forward flow of 7.4 litres per minute in the main pulmonary artery and 3.7 litres per minute in the ascending aorta. What shunt ratio, Qp:Qs, do those measurements give? Answer as a number to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Qp:Qs is pulmonary flow divided by systemic flow, so 7.4 / 3.7 = 2.0: the lungs are receiving twice what the body does, and the extra litres are the shunt. A ratio at or above about 1.5, in a patient whose right heart is dilated by the volume it is carrying, is the conventional trigger for closing a defect. Two habits make the number trustworthy. First, check it against something independent, since the systemic figure should agree roughly with the sum of the caval flows, and disagreement means a plane, a velocity encoding or a background phase offset needs revisiting rather than a shunt being large. Second, remember that this is a measurement CT cannot make: CT gives the anatomy of the defect and the veins beautifully and says nothing whatever about flow, which is the practical reason these patients meet both scanners.

quiz.prompt: A neonatal CT angiography protocol prescribes 600 mg of iodine per kilogram of body weight, using a contrast agent containing 300 mg of iodine per millilitre. The baby weighs 3.4 kg. What volume of contrast should be drawn up? Answer in millilitres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The iodine dose is 600 x 3.4 = 2040 mg, and at 300 mg/mL that is 6.8 mL. Dosing by iodine per kilogram rather than by a fixed volume is what keeps the protocol transferable between agents of different concentration. The consequences of such a small volume are the interesting part. Seven millilitres through a 24 gauge cannula makes a very short bolus, so timing has to be measured rather than assumed, and the saline chaser matters proportionately far more here than in an adult, since a comparable volume of contrast would otherwise be left sitting in the tubing and the arm vein. The injection is often given by hand for that reason. And because the bolus is brief, a scan that starts even a second or two late finds the peak already gone.

quiz.prompt: Put the determinations of sequential segmental analysis into the order in which a congenital heart study is worked through.
quiz.answer: atrial-situs atrioventricular-connections ventriculoarterial-connections associated-anomalies
quiz.explain: The order is not a convention but a dependency chain: each step is described relative to the one before it, so answering them out of sequence produces statements that cannot be interpreted. Situs comes first because atrial arrangement is what everything downstream is named against. The atrioventricular connections then say which atrium empties into which ventricle, and this requires that the ventricles have been identified by their own morphology rather than by position. The ventriculoarterial connections say which great artery leaves which ventricle. Only then do the associated lesions get listed, the septal defects, obstructions and vascular anomalies. Congenitally corrected transposition is the case that shows why the discipline pays: it is discordant at both connections, so the reader who jumps to the great arteries and stops there reports a transposition and misses that the circulation is, physiologically, corrected.

quiz.prompt: An adult repaired for tetralogy of Fallot in infancy attends annual review for progressive pulmonary regurgitation. Say which modality you would make the routine surveillance study and on what grounds, and give the circumstances that would send the same patient to CT instead.
quiz.answer: Cardiac MRI is the routine surveillance study. It measures right ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes reproducibly and quantifies the pulmonary regurgitant fraction by phase contrast, and it is those serial volumes and that fraction which decide the timing of pulmonary valve replacement, with no ionising radiation in someone who will be followed for decades. CT takes over when MRI cannot be done or cannot answer the question: a non-conditional pacemaker or defibrillator, metallic artefact obscuring the outflow tract, a stent lumen to be assessed, coronary anatomy needed before intervention, or a patient unable to lie still or hold a breath.
quiz.explain: The choice follows from what the decision needs. Nobody replaces a pulmonary valve because of how the outflow tract looks; they replace it because the right ventricle has dilated to the point where recovery after surgery becomes unlikely, and that is a volumetric measurement made repeatedly on the same patient over years. Reproducibility therefore matters more than spatial resolution, which is precisely MRI's advantage, and phase contrast supplies the regurgitant fraction in the same sitting. CT earns its place in this population by answering the questions MRI answers badly: the calibre of a stented conduit, the course of a coronary artery across the outflow tract before a percutaneous valve, and any patient whose device or breath-holding makes an MRI study uninterpretable.

quiz.prompt: A 5-month-old has noisy breathing and difficulty swallowing solids. CT shows a right-sided aortic arch, a left subclavian artery arising last from a bulbous origin on the proximal descending aorta, and tracheal narrowing just above the carina. Explain what completes the encircling structure and set out what the report must give the surgeon.
quiz.answer: The circle is completed by the left arterial ligament, which CT cannot show directly: the arch passes to the right of the trachea, the bulbous origin of the aberrant left subclavian artery, a Kommerell diverticulum, passes behind the oesophagus, and the ligament runs forward from it to the left pulmonary artery to close the ring on the left. The report should state the side and branching pattern of the arch, the size of the Kommerell diverticulum and its relation to the oesophagus, the level, length and minimum calibre of the tracheal narrowing, whether the airway is being compressed from outside or is intrinsically narrowed, and any associated intracardiac defect.
quiz.explain: This is the commonest complete vascular ring, and the trap in it is that the structure closing the ring is invisible. A reader who looks only for vessels sees a right arch with an aberrant subclavian artery, calls it a variant, and misses that the child is symptomatic because the circle is complete. Infer the ligament from the geometry and from the symptoms. The measurements listed are what change the operation: division of the ligament relieves most rings, but a large Kommerell diverticulum is often resected and the subclavian artery transferred, and an airway that stays narrow after the ring is divided is either malacic or has complete cartilage rings, which is a different operation and worth predicting beforehand rather than discovering afterwards.

source.title: Coronary Artery Disease-Reporting and Data System 2.0

approach.detail: Chambers and wall thickness, pericardium, valves and any calcification, aortic root and thoracic aorta, pulmonary arteries and veins.
Mediastinum, lungs, chest wall and breasts, upper abdomen, bones. The incidental nodule and the adrenal lesion are yours to report.
Dominance first. Then the origin of each vessel, an interarterial or retroaortic course, myocardial bridging, fistula, aneurysm.
Grade every vessel over 1.5 mm. The patient's category is the single worst lesion, not the sum.
Calcium score, segment involvement score, or a visual estimate — whichever your service uses. The most severe assessment wins.
High-risk plaque, stents, grafts, non-atherosclerotic exceptions, and CT-FFR or CT perfusion if you ran it.

measure.how: Minimal luminal diameter against the normal reference segment, judged on the cross-section rather than the curved reformat alone.
Per patient, on the clinically most relevant — usually the highest-grade — stenosis.
Agatston from the non-contrast series. Raise the P category if there is appreciable non-calcified plaque the score cannot see.

measure.what: Plaque burden by segment involvement score
measure.how: One point for each of the 16 segments carrying any plaque.
measure.cutoff: P1 1–2 · P2 3–4 · P3 5–7 · P4 ≥ 8 (SIS 0 is CAD-RADS 0, which carries no P)

classify.name: CAD-RADS 2.0 — stable chest pain
rows: Reassurance. Look elsewhere for the pain.
Risk-factor modification and preventive therapy, weighted by P.
Risk-factor modification; aggressive if P3 or P4.
Consider CT-FFR, CTP or stress testing
Aggressive prevention and anti-anginal therapy. Consider invasive angiography if I1.
Consider invasive angiography or functional assessment
Aggressive prevention; consider revascularisation per guideline care.
Consider invasive angiography, functional and viability assessment
Say which segments were uninterpretable and why.
classify.note: Applied per patient. P is not reported for CAD-RADS 0 — there is no plaque to grade.

modifiers.meaning: Overall plaque burden: mild, moderate, severe, extensive.
High-risk plaque — positive remodelling, low attenuation, spotty calcification, the napkin-ring sign. Raises acute-coronary-syndrome risk independently of the stenosis.
CT-FFR or CT perfusion was performed: I1 lesion-specific ischaemia present, I2 negative.
Stent present. Say whether it is assessable, and patent or not.
Graft present. Grade the graft and the native vessel it feeds.
Exception — a non-atherosclerotic coronary abnormality: dissection, anomalous origin, aneurysm, vasculitis, fistula, extrinsic compression.
Non-diagnostic study.

IMPRESSION

pitfalls: Grading off the curved reformat alone. Blooming from dense calcium and motion both overstate stenosis — confirm on the cross-section, in more than one phase if you have it.
Reporting the sum of disease rather than the worst lesion. CAD-RADS is a per-patient category taken from one lesion.
Omitting P because the calcium score is zero. Non-calcified plaque carries no calcium and still counts.
Calling the study diagnostic when a segment is not. If obstructive disease cannot be excluded in a segment that matters, the study is N — say which segment and why.
Leaving CAD-RADS to stand alone. It complements the impression; it does not replace the sentence that says what you actually think.

LIMA [ ] | RIMA [ ] | SVG [ ] | other conduit [ ].
For each graft: origin [ ]; course [ ]; body [ ]; distal anastomosis [ ]; distal runoff [ ].
Native vessels and ungrafted territories: [ ].

sections.body:
[Not performed / performed / non-diagnostic].
CT-FFR lesion-specific value: [__] measured 1–2 cm distal to [vessel/segment lesion].
CT-FFR lowest value: [__] in [vessel/segment]; distinguish this from the lesion-specific value.

Ischaemia modifier: [I+ / I− / I± / none].
CT-FFR guide: I+ ≤0.75; I− >0.80; I± 0.76–0.80. Use lesion-specific interpretation and anatomical correlation; the lowest distal value alone should not drive catheterisation referral.

Cardiac chambers: [normal / enlarged: specify].

Pericardium: [normal / effusion / thickening / calcification].

Other cardiac findings: [ ].

sections.body:
Mediastinum/hila: [unremarkable / abnormal].
Lungs/pleura: [unremarkable / nodule / consolidation / emphysema / effusion / other].
Upper abdomen/bones/chest wall: [unremarkable / abnormal].
Incidental follow-up finding: [none / specify finding, comparison and applicable follow-up rationale].

sections.heading: CAD-RADS 2.0
sections.body:
CAD-RADS category:
0: no plaque or stenosis.
1: 1–24% stenosis, or plaque with positive remodelling but no luminal narrowing.
2: 25–49%.
3: 50–69%.
4A: 70–99% in one or two vessels.
4B: LM ≥50% or severe three-vessel disease.
5: total occlusion.
N: non-diagnostic.
Final CAD-RADS: CAD-RADS [0/1/2/3/4A/4B/5/N] / [P1/P2/P3/P4 when applicable] / [N / HRP / I+ / I− / I± / S / G / E as applicable].
If a relevant segment >1.5 mm is non-evaluable and evaluable segments show only <50% stenosis, use category N. If ≥50% stenosis is demonstrated elsewhere, retain the stenosis category and append N. Report P only if reliable.

sections.heading: IMPRESSION
sections.body:
1. [Right / left / co-dominant] coronary circulation.
2. Coronary origins/course: [normal / anomaly described].
3. CAD: [none / minimal / mild / moderate / severe / obstructive]. Most significant lesion: [vessel/segment], [plaque type], [stenosis category/%].
4. Plaque burden: [no plaque / P1 / P2 / P3 / P4 / indeterminate]. HRP: [absent / present].
5. Stents/grafts: [none / findings].
6. CAD-RADS 2.0: CAD-RADS [ ] / [P category if applicable] / [modifiers]. Physiology, if performed: [ ].
7. Non-coronary findings: [none significant / specify].
8. Diagnostic limitation affecting interpretation, if any: [ ].

sections.heading: OPTIONAL MANAGEMENT LINE
sections.body:
Clinical setting: [stable / acute chest pain / other]. Suggested next step: [ ], considering symptoms, ECG/troponin where relevant, prior treatment, comorbidity and patient preference.
Stable chest pain prompts: [0: usually no additional CAD testing / 1–2: preventive risk discussion / 3: consider functional assessment / 4A: consider ICA or functional assessment / 4B: consider ICA / 5: consider ICA with viability/functional assessment where appropriate / N: additional evaluation if clinically indicated].
Acute chest pain prompt: [integrate stenosis and image quality with the ACS pathway; do not diagnose or exclude ACS from CAD-RADS alone].
Document the individualised recommendation and rationale; delete unused options.

notes: Complete bracketed fields and remove unused alternatives before issuing a report. Use the study’s own de-identified images in the final report; the gallery contains independent published teaching examples.
The user-supplied CCTA example provides the report foundation. Classification clarifications are referenced to CAD-RADS 2.0.
S and G record the presence of stents and bypass grafts. E identifies a relevant non-atherosclerotic coronary exception that requires a narrative description.
A fixed perfusion defect should be described separately from reversible ischaemia. Record failed or non-diagnostic physiology explicitly.

protocol: Review ECG phase quality, source images, curved MPR and orthogonal lumen cross-sections.
Use the comprehensive CCTA template below, keeping anatomical stenosis, plaque burden and physiology separate.

checklist.label: Quality
checklist.detail: Name each non-evaluable segment and its effect on excluding significant stenosis.

checklist.label: Anatomy
checklist.detail: Establish dominance, origins, proximal course and coronary anomalies.

checklist.label: Stenosis
checklist.detail: Record vessel/segment, plaque composition and highest confident stenosis.

checklist.label: Burden
checklist.detail: Assess CAC/SIS/visual burden with the method identified; no plaque is not P1.

checklist.label: Additional findings
checklist.detail: Assess stents/grafts, physiology when available and extracoronary findings.

measurements.name: Stenosis
measurements.method: Compare the minimum orthogonal lumen with an appropriate reference segment.
measurements.pitfall: Calcific blooming and motion can overestimate narrowing.

measurements.name: Plaque burden
measurements.method: Record CAC and/or plaque-containing segment count; use the most severe reliable burden method.
measurements.pitfall: Zero CAC does not exclude non-calcified plaque.

measurements.name: CT-FFR
measurements.method: Record lesion-specific value 1–2 cm beyond the lesion and distinguish the distal nadir.
measurements.pitfall: The lowest distal value alone should not drive lesion attribution.

classification.name: CAD-RADS
classification.applicability: Coronary CTA interpreted with the full diagnostic quality and clinical context.
classification.summary: Report stenosis category with plaque burden and applicable N, HRP, I, S, G or E modifiers. CAD-RADS 0 has no plaque burden category.

pitfalls: HRP requires at least two specified high-risk plaque features in a plaque.
When a relevant segment is non-diagnostic, apply the N category/modifier rules rather than treating it as normal.
impression_prompts: State the most important stenosis and its vessel/segment.
Summarise plaque burden and the complete applicable CAD-RADS 2.0 notation.
Describe anomaly, graft/stent, physiology and significant extracardiac findings.
escalation: Communicate a suspected acute coronary complication or critical unexpected coronary anatomy in the relevant clinical context.

quiz.prompt: A single-source scanner runs a gantry rotation time of 0.30 s and reconstructs each image from a half-scan segment. Taking that segment as half a turn, how long is the window during which the coronary must hold still? Answer in milliseconds, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: A half-scan reconstruction needs projections over 180 degrees plus the fan angle, so one image is built from a little over half a rotation; taking the segment as half a turn, 0.30 s halved is 0.15 s, which is 150 ms. Everything in the preparation of the patient follows from that number. A coronary that moves appreciably inside that window blurs, and the dependable way to buy a longer motionless interval is to slow the heart, since diastasis lengthens steeply as the rate falls. A dual-source scanner collects the same 180 degrees from two tubes a quarter-turn apart and so halves the requirement again, to about 75 ms here.

quiz.prompt: Despite oral and intravenous beta-blockade the heart rate stays at 96 bpm through a retrospectively gated helical acquisition. Reconstruction at 75 per cent of the R-R interval shows a doubled, blurred right coronary artery. Which reconstruction gives the best chance of a diagnostic study?
quiz.answer: End-systole, near 40% of the R-R interval
quiz.explain: Diastasis, the quiet interval in mid-to-late diastole, is what the standard 70 to 75 per cent reconstruction targets, and it shortens sharply as the rate rises until, past roughly 80 bpm, little of it is left. Systole shortens far less, so at fast rates the most reproducible still point is end-systole, near 40 to 45 per cent, which is why a retrospective study at this rate is reconstructed there. 'Mid-diastole, near 65% of the R-R interval' and 'Late diastole, near 90% of the R-R interval' both sit in a diastole that barely exists at 96 bpm, and 90 per cent lands on atrial contraction, which drags the atrioventricular groove and with it the right coronary, the fastest-moving of the three vessels: that is why the right coronary, not the left anterior descending, is the artery this study lost. 'Early systole, near 15% of the R-R interval' falls in isovolumic contraction, the other peak of cardiac motion.
choices: Mid-diastole, near 65% of the R-R interval
End-systole, near 40% of the R-R interval
Late diastole, near 90% of the R-R interval
Early systole, near 15% of the R-R interval

quiz.prompt: A step-and-shoot study is prospectively triggered at 75 per cent of the R-R interval with no padding. A ventricular ectopic falls during one slab and the left anterior descending artery is blurred at that level. The registrar asks for that slab to be reconstructed at 45 per cent instead. Why can that not be done?
quiz.answer: The tube was off at 45 per cent of the R-R interval
quiz.explain: Prospective triggering fires the tube inside the programmed window and nowhere else, so the projections a 45 per cent reconstruction would need were simply not collected, and no workstation effort conjures them. Padding, which widens the irradiated window by perhaps 100 ms on either side, buys a little freedom to shift the phase at a dose cost, but even generous padding does not reach from mid-diastole back to end-systole, which is why an ectopic on a single-phase study usually means a repeat rather than a re-reconstruction. 'Tube current modulation lowered the current there' describes retrospective helical scanning instead: modulation reduces the current outside the phase of interest but still leaves noisy, usable data across the cycle, and that is what makes a retrospective study rescuable and this one not. The vessel here is blurred by motion, not by a thin bolus or a soft kernel.
choices: The tube was off at 45 per cent of the R-R interval
Tube current modulation lowered the current there
The ectopic beat pushed the bolus past its peak
The kernel is too smooth to resolve a small vessel

quiz.prompt: On the curved reformat of the left anterior descending artery there is an abrupt sideways step in the vessel contour. Scrolling the axial images, the same step appears in the sternum and the anterior chest wall at that level. What does this appearance point to?
quiz.answer: Misregistration between adjacent acquisition slabs
quiz.explain: The discriminator is what else moved. A stair-step displaces the whole block of anatomy acquired in one heartbeat, so ribs and sternum step along with the artery; the heart simply sat in a slightly different place from one gated slab to the next. 'Coronary motion within the reconstruction window' blurs or doubles the coronary while the stationary chest wall stays crisp. Streak radiates from the dense structure that causes it and beam hardening tracks a calcified plaque, and neither respects a slab boundary. The remedy here is rhythm and coverage, not reconstruction: a slower, steadier rate, wider detector coverage, or a high-pitch acquisition that takes the heart in a single beat.
choices: Misregistration between adjacent acquisition slabs
Coronary motion within the reconstruction window
Streak from dense contrast in the superior vena cava
Beam hardening across a densely calcified segment

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old with typical exertional chest pain has a calcium score of 0. The referrer proposes stopping the workup there. What is the strongest objection?
quiz.answer: Non-calcified plaque can obstruct despite a zero score
quiz.explain: A zero score is a genuinely powerful negative in asymptomatic and low-risk people, where it reclassifies risk downward better than most risk factors. It is weakest in exactly this patient: young, symptomatic, and therefore in the group whose plaque is most likely to be lipid-rich and not yet calcified. Calcium marks the age of plaque rather than its presence, so a zero score does not settle a symptomatic presentation, and contrast CCTA remains the test that answers the question, which is also where the 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline sends this patient. 'A score of zero has poor reproducibility between studies' is the tempting alternative and is untrue: interscan variability bites at low non-zero scores, while zero is highly reproducible. The limitation is what calcium fails to see, not measurement noise.
choices: Non-calcified plaque can obstruct despite a zero score
The 130 HU threshold understates calcium on new scanners
A score of zero has poor reproducibility between studies
Calcium scoring underestimates burden in a small vessel

quiz.prompt: A 2.75 mm stent in the proximal left anterior descending artery appears to fill most of its own lumen on the routine reconstruction. Which change to the reconstruction most improves assessment of the in-stent lumen?
quiz.answer: A sharp kernel with thin slices
quiz.explain: Blooming is a partial-volume and point-spread effect: a dense strut spills into neighbouring voxels, and the smoother the kernel and the thicker the slice, the further it spills, so the lumen it hides grows. A sharp, high-resolution kernel with thin slices shrinks the apparent strut thickness and opens the visible lumen. The cost is noise, and that is precisely where iterative or deep-learning reconstruction earns its keep, restoring the noise the sharp kernel spent. 'A lower tube voltage, same mAs' raises iodine attenuation, which is why it flatters ordinary vessels, but it raises calcium and metal attenuation too, so blooming worsens rather than improves. One caution to carry away: even reconstructed well, stents of about 3 mm and under are often non-diagnostic inside, so a small stent whose lumen still looks filled is reported as unassessable rather than as occluded.
choices: A sharp kernel with thin slices
A smooth kernel with higher mAs
A lower tube voltage, same mAs
A thicker slice with less noise

quiz.prompt: Immediately before sublingual glyceryl trinitrate is given for a CCTA, the patient mentions taking tadalafil the previous evening. The list cannot be rearranged and the study is to go ahead today. What is the appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Withhold the nitrate and scan without it
quiz.explain: A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor and a nitrate act on the same cGMP pathway from opposite ends, and together they produce hypotension that is slow to reverse. 'Give the nitrate as over 12 hours have passed' is the trap, and it is where tadalafil differs from the rest: its half-life of around 17 hours is several times sildenafil's, so an overnight gap that would clear sildenafil leaves tadalafil active, and the published abstinence window for tadalafil is correspondingly the longer one. The previous evening sits inside every version of that window. Halving the dose halves neither the mechanism nor the risk, and a fluid preload is treatment for a complication rather than a licence to cause one. So the study goes ahead without nitrate: the distal vessels are smaller and harder to grade, which degrades the study rather than voiding it. Where distal grading is critical and the list allows, deferring the scan until the drug has cleared is the better answer, and that is why the drug question is asked before the spray is drawn up.
choices: Withhold the nitrate and scan without it
Give the nitrate as over 12 hours have passed
Give half the usual sublingual nitrate dose
Give the nitrate with intravenous fluids

quiz.prompt: A patient with severe biventricular failure is scanned at the department's fixed 22-second delay. The coronary arteries opacify weakly while the pulmonary arteries are dense. What change makes the next attempt most likely to succeed?
quiz.answer: Trigger acquisition from the descending aorta
quiz.explain: The image describes a bolus caught in transit: in a failing circulation contrast takes far longer to cross the lungs and left heart, so a delay calibrated on ordinary patients samples the pulmonary phase. The variable at fault is circulation time, and the fix is to measure it rather than assume it. Bolus tracking watches an aortic region of interest and fires when enhancement crosses threshold, so it adapts to this patient automatically; a test bolus answers the same question at the cost of an extra injection and a little more contrast. More contrast, faster or denser, delivered at a delay that is wrong for this circulation still arrives after the scan has finished.
choices: Trigger acquisition from the descending aorta
Increase the injected volume at the same delay
Raise the injection rate and keep the delay
Use a more concentrated contrast at that delay

quiz.prompt: A patient with typical angina still has limiting symptoms on optimal medical therapy. CCTA shows a smooth 60 per cent stenosis in the mid left anterior descending artery, in a well-opacified segment free of heavy calcium, and CT-derived fractional flow reserve 2 cm distal to the lesion is 0.71. How should this change the plan?
quiz.answer: Refer for invasive angiography with a view to stenting
quiz.explain: An intermediate stenosis is the one anatomical finding that settles nothing: in the FAME lesion analysis about a third of 50 to 70 per cent stenoses proved flow-limiting on invasive measurement, so two thirds of them were not, and the eye cannot tell which this is. CT-FFR applies computational fluid dynamics to the same dataset and answers the physiological question instead, and a value at or below 0.80 marks a lesion that restricts flow. Physiology by itself would not send a stable patient to the catheter laboratory, since ISCHEMIA found no reduction in death or infarction from an invasive strategy in stable disease; what earns the referral is angina that persists on optimal medical therapy, for which revascularisation is offered as symptom relief. 'Arrange stress perfusion imaging to confirm ischaemia' repeats a question CT-FFR has already answered. Two cautions travel with the number: CT-FFR inherits the quality of the images it is computed from, so heavy calcium or motion in the segment makes it unreliable, and its agreement with invasive FFR is loose enough that a value sitting near 0.80 deserves an invasive measurement rather than a stent, which is in any case how the lesion is confirmed in the laboratory.
choices: Continue medical therapy and repeat the CCTA in a year
Refer for invasive angiography with a view to stenting
Arrange stress perfusion imaging to confirm ischaemia
Rescan at a sharper kernel to grade the stenosis better

quiz.prompt: In one clinic a CCTA showing unobstructed arteries in a patient with low-to-intermediate pretest probability ends the workup, while a CCTA showing a 60 per cent stenosis is followed by a functional test rather than by a stent. Justify both decisions in terms of test performance.
quiz.answer: CCTA has very high sensitivity for obstructive stenosis, so where the pretest probability is low the normal study carries a negative predictive value close to certainty and effectively excludes obstructive coronary disease, which is why CCTA is used as a rule-out test. Its specificity is lower, and blooming from calcium, motion and partial volume make the eye overestimate visually graded stenoses, so the positive predictive value is only moderate; an intermediate stenosis is therefore a question rather than an answer, and a physiological measure such as CT-FFR, stress perfusion or invasive FFR must show ischaemia before revascularisation is justified.
quiz.explain: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test; predictive values also depend on how common disease is among the patients being scanned. CCTA's near-complete sensitivity is what makes a normal study powerful, and it is powerful precisely because the pretest probability was low, since the same normal study in a high-prevalence group leaves more residual risk behind. Running the argument the other way explains the second decision: a modest positive predictive value, inflated further by blooming, means the eye overcalls severity, and anatomy has never been the same thing as ischaemia. The corollary worth carrying into reporting is that a single non-diagnostic segment forfeits the rule-out argument for that vessel, so such a study is flagged as non-diagnostic rather than reported as normal.

quiz.prompt: Put these CAD-RADS 2.0 stenosis categories in order, from the least narrowing to the most.
quiz.answer: CAD-RADS-0 CAD-RADS-1 CAD-RADS-2 CAD-RADS-3 CAD-RADS-4A CAD-RADS-5
quiz.explain: 0 is no visible plaque or stenosis; 1 is 1-24%, minimal; 2 is 25-49%, mild; 3 is 50-69%, moderate — the band where a functional test earns its place; 4A is 70-99%, severe; 5 is total occlusion. The category is assigned per patient, from the clinically most relevant — usually the highest-grade — stenosis, and only in vessels 1.5 mm or larger.

quiz.prompt: A coronary CT angiogram is read to a checklist so that a subtle finding outside the coronaries is not lost. Put the review steps in the order the guide recommends.
quiz.answer: extracoronary extracardiac coronary-origins CAD-RADS modifiers
quiz.explain: Chambers, pericardium and great vessels first; then the non-cardiac chest, abdomen and bones — the incidental lung nodule is found here or not at all; then the origin, course and termination of the coronaries, with dominance, bridging and anomalies; only then the stenosis-and-plaque grade; and finally the modifiers. Grading first is how an anomalous origin gets missed on a study that was otherwise reported perfectly.

quiz.prompt: A CCTA is scored for total plaque burden using the segment involvement score: one point for each of the sixteen coronary segments containing any detectable plaque. Seven segments carry plaque. Which P category does that segment involvement score place the patient in? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: The segment involvement score bands onto plaque burden as SIS 1-2 for P1 (zero plaque has no P category), 3-4 for P2, 5-7 for P3 and >=8 for P4. Seven segments is the top of the P3 band — severe plaque burden — and P3 or P4 is what moves the management column from risk-factor modification to aggressive preventive therapy, whatever the stenosis grade happens to be.

quiz.prompt: Motion artefact renders the mid right coronary artery non-diagnostic. In the segments that can be interpreted, the mid left anterior descending artery has a 50-69 per cent stenosis and there is a moderate total plaque burden. How should the study be coded?
choices: CAD-RADS 3/P2/N
CAD-RADS N alone, as one segment is uninterpretable
CAD-RADS N/P2, with the stenosis described only in the text
CAD-RADS 3/P2, as a single non-diagnostic segment does not change the grade
quiz.answer: CAD-RADS 3/P2/N
quiz.explain: N is a modifier before it is a category. Where a diagnostic segment already shows a stenosis of 50 per cent or more, that stenosis is graded and N is appended — the finding stands and further evaluation is still flagged. N replaces the numeric category only when the interpretable segments show nothing above mild, because then the study genuinely cannot exclude obstructive disease.

quiz.prompt: Focal non-calcified plaque in the mid right coronary artery causes 25-49 per cent narrowing. It shows an attenuation below 30 HU and an outer-vessel-diameter ratio of 1.2 at the plaque compared with the reference segments. Which coding is correct?
choices: CAD-RADS 2/HRP, as two high-risk features are present
CAD-RADS 2, as high-risk features apply only from 50 per cent narrowing
CAD-RADS 2/HRP, as low attenuation alone is sufficient
CAD-RADS 4A/HRP, as high-risk plaque upgrades the category
quiz.answer: CAD-RADS 2/HRP, as two high-risk features are present
quiz.explain: Low attenuation below 30 HU and positive remodelling above 1.1 are two of the four high-risk features, alongside spotty calcification and the napkin-ring sign — and the modifier requires two or more, which is why one feature does not earn it. HRP never changes the stenosis category; it travels beside it, and it matters most exactly here, on non-obstructive disease, where it argues for more aggressive prevention than the narrowing alone would.

quiz.prompt: A patient has a patent left internal mammary artery graft to the left anterior descending artery. The native proximal left anterior descending artery, upstream of the anastomosis, is occluded. There is no other stenosis above 50 per cent anywhere. How is the study coded?
choices: By the grafts and the native segments distal to and including the anastomosis, so not CAD-RADS 5
CAD-RADS 5/G, because a native vessel is totally occluded
CAD-RADS 5, because occlusion is graded wherever it is found
CAD-RADS N/G, because a bypassed circulation cannot be graded
quiz.answer: By the grafts and the native segments distal to and including the anastomosis, so not CAD-RADS 5
quiz.explain: In a grafted patient the native segments proximal to an anastomosis are not evaluated for CAD-RADS: a stenosis that a patent graft has bypassed is no longer the thing determining flow, and grading it would report a severity the patient does not have. The graft, the anastomosis and everything distal are what carry the blood, and therefore what carry the category.

quiz.prompt: CT-derived fractional flow reserve is used to decide whether a moderate stenosis is haemodynamically significant. At or below which value is the result treated as abnormal, warranting the ischaemia modifier I+? Answer as a decimal.
quiz.explain: 0.75 or below is abnormal and earns I+; above 0.80 is negative and earns I-; the grey zone from 0.76 to 0.80 is borderline, I+/-, where the decision leans on symptoms, lesion location and the trans-lesional gradient. The value is read 1 to 2 cm distal to the stenosis rather than at its narrowest point, because it is the pressure downstream that tells you what the myocardium is actually receiving.

quiz.prompt: On the post-processing workstation the software extracts a volume of interest, computes a centreline through the vessel and then measures a cross-section at every point along it. It asks you to accept or reject the tracking. Why does this prompt exist rather than the software proceeding straight to the stenosis figures?
choices: Every diameter and area measurement is taken perpendicular to that centreline, so a centreline that has strayed reports a stenosis that is not there
Accepting confirms the correct patient and study have been loaded before measurement
Rejecting is required whenever calcified plaque is present anywhere in the vessel
The prompt records that a human performed the measurement, for medico-legal purposes
quiz.answer: Every diameter and area measurement is taken perpendicular to that centreline, so a centreline that has strayed reports a stenosis that is not there
quiz.explain: Identification and quantification are one chained operation: the centreline is computed first, then each cross-section is cut at right angles to it. Where the line clips a calcified plaque, jumps to an adjacent vein or cuts a corner at a bend, the cross-sections are taken through the wrong plane and the lumen is measured too small. Rejecting returns you to vessel identification to place new points; accepting an unverified centreline is how a confident percentage gets reported from a bad line.

quiz.prompt: A CCTA in a patient with prior stenting shows severe in-stent restenosis of 70-99 per cent in the proximal left anterior descending artery, and a severe total plaque burden. Give the full CAD-RADS 2.0 coding for this study and say what each part of it is doing.
quiz.answer: CAD-RADS 4A/P3/S — 4A for the 70-99 per cent severe stenosis, P3 for the severe plaque burden, and S to declare that a stent is present.
quiz.explain: In-stent restenosis is graded on the same stenosis scale as a native vessel, so 70-99 per cent is 4A. P records total plaque burden across native vessels and grafts together. S simply declares that a stent is somewhere in the coronary tree; it does not change the category, because what determines management is whether a severe stenosis is present, not whether the narrowed segment happens to be stented.

quiz.prompt: A left circumflex artery is found arising from the ostium of the right coronary artery and taking a course behind the aorta. The coronary tree shows no atherosclerotic narrowing at all. How does CAD-RADS 2.0 accommodate this?
choices: CAD-RADS 0/E, as the exception modifier carries non-atherosclerotic abnormalities
CAD-RADS 0, as the classification describes atherosclerosis only
CAD-RADS N, as an anomalous vessel cannot be graded normally
CAD-RADS 1/E, as an anomalous course counts as minimal disease
quiz.answer: CAD-RADS 0/E, as the exception modifier carries non-atherosclerotic abnormalities
quiz.explain: The stenosis category still says what it says — no atherosclerotic narrowing is CAD-RADS 0 — and E is appended so the report does not read as entirely normal when it is not. E covers anomalous origin, dissection, aneurysm, vasculitis, fistula, extrinsic compression and arteriovenous malformation. A retroaortic circumflex is generally benign, but the modifier is what stops a clinically important anatomical finding disappearing behind a reassuring number.

quiz.prompt: A prospectively triggered coronary CT angiogram is performed with a dose-length product of 320 mGy.cm. Using the conventional chest conversion coefficient of 0.014 mSv per mGy.cm, what effective dose does the acquisition deliver? Answer in millisieverts, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Effective dose is estimated as the dose-length product multiplied by a region-specific coefficient, so 320 x 0.014 = 4.48, which is 4.5 mSv to one decimal place. Two things are worth carrying away. The first is what the number is for: it lets you compare this acquisition with the retrospectively gated version of the same study, which commonly costs several times as much, and with the calcium score that may have preceded it, and it is comparison rather than absolute risk that the figure is good at. The second is what it is not. The coefficient is derived for a reference adult and a reference chest, so applying it to a small woman or a large man reports a dose neither of them received, and the cardiac coefficient differs a little from the general chest one. Quote it as an estimate, and record the dose-length product itself in the report, since that is the measured quantity.

quiz.prompt: Contrast containing 370 mg of iodine per millilitre is injected at 5 mL/s for a coronary CT angiogram. What iodine delivery rate does that combination give? Answer in grams of iodine per second, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Iodine delivery rate is concentration multiplied by flow rate: 370 mg/mL x 5 mL/s = 1850 mg/s, that is 1.85 g of iodine per second. It is the rate, not the total volume, that sets how bright the coronary lumen becomes, because arterial enhancement at any moment reflects how much iodine is arriving per second against how fast the circulation is diluting it; volume mostly sets how long that enhancement lasts. Most coronary protocols aim somewhere between about 1.5 and 2.0 g/s. The practical use of the arithmetic is substitution: if the department switches to a 350 mg/mL agent, the same delivery rate needs about 5.3 mL/s, and if the only cannula available is a 20 gauge in the forearm that will not take that rate, the honest options are a lower rate with a longer injection or a frankly less well opacified study, not a silent downgrade.

quiz.prompt: On a curved multiplanar reformat the narrowest lumen in the mid right coronary artery measures 1.2 mm across, and the mean of the normal reference segments immediately proximal and distal to it is 3.4 mm. What is the diameter stenosis at that point? Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Diameter stenosis is one minus the ratio of the narrowed lumen to the reference lumen: 1 - (1.2 / 3.4) = 0.647, so 65 per cent. That figure places the lesion in the 50 to 69 per cent band, CAD-RADS 3, the moderate category where anatomy alone settles nothing and a physiological measure decides. Notice how differently the same lesion reads if you look at the cross-section instead: area falls with the square of the diameter, so the area stenosis here is about 88 per cent. Both numbers are true and they describe the same vessel, which is why a percentage quoted without its convention is close to meaningless, and why CAD-RADS is explicit that grading is by diameter. The eye that reads an axial cross-section rather than the reformat is quietly working in the area convention and will overcall severity in every case.

quiz.prompt: A coronary CT angiogram in a patient with stable angina shows a 55 per cent stenosis of the distal left main stem. No other vessel exceeds 50 per cent, and plaque is present in five of the sixteen segments. Give the CAD-RADS 2.0 code for this study, say what should happen next, and explain why the left main is handled differently from any other vessel.
quiz.answer: The study codes as CAD-RADS 4B/P3. A stenosis of 50 per cent or more in the left main stem is category 4B whatever the rest of the tree looks like, and plaque in five of the sixteen segments is a segment involvement score of 5, which is P3. What follows is referral for invasive coronary angiography rather than a functional test, because the left main supplies most of the myocardium, so a stenosis there is prognostic and the question to be answered is about revascularisation, not about proving ischaemia.
quiz.explain: CAD-RADS 2.0 splits the severe band in two: 4A is a 70 to 99 per cent stenosis in one or two vessels, while 4B is reserved for a left main stenosis of 50 per cent or more, or for obstructive disease of 70 per cent or more in all three vessels. The split exists because those two patterns carry a weight the ordinary severity scale does not capture, and both are sent to the catheter laboratory. That is the exception to the habit this domain otherwise teaches, which is that an intermediate stenosis deserves a physiological test before anyone reaches for a stent. It is also where image quality has to be beyond argument: the left main is short, often calcified at its ostium, and a motion-degraded left main is a study to repeat rather than to grade.

quiz.prompt: Oral beta-blockade takes 45 to 60 minutes to work, an intravenous top-up acts within a few minutes, and sublingual nitrate acts within two to three minutes while causing a reflex rise in heart rate. Put the preparation steps for a coronary CT angiogram into the order those facts dictate.
quiz.answer: oral-beta-blocker rate-recheck intravenous-top-up sublingual-nitrate scan-acquisition
quiz.explain: The sequence falls out of the pharmacology. The oral dose goes in early, on arrival, because it needs the best part of an hour; the rate is then measured again on the table, because the dose that worked for the last patient may have done little for this one; an intravenous top-up is titrated against that measurement, since it acts fast enough to be steered. Nitrate comes last, as close to the acquisition as the workflow allows, for two separate reasons: its dilating effect on the coronary arteries is short-lived, and it provokes a reflex tachycardia that would undo rate control if it were given first. Give the spray before the beta-blocker and you spend the rest of the slot chasing a rate you had already achieved. And the drug history is checked before any of it, since a recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor removes the nitrate from the plan entirely.
