quiz.prompt: A patient coughs immediately when drinking after a stroke. Which examination most directly shows bolus timing and airway protection?
choices: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
Routine contrast-enhanced neck CT
Non-contrast chest CT
Static coronal sinus MRI
quiz.answer: Videofluoroscopic swallowing study
quiz.explain: A dynamic swallow examination samples bolus transit and airway protection. Protocol selection follows the oropharyngeal symptom, with speech and language expertise supporting interpretation.

quiz.prompt: During fluoroscopy, contrast enters the laryngeal vestibule but stays above the vocal folds. Which observation belongs in the report?
choices: Aspiration below the glottis
Laryngeal penetration
A pharyngeal perforation
Normal oesophageal clearance
quiz.answer: Laryngeal penetration
quiz.explain: Penetration stays above the true vocal folds; aspiration passes below them. Report when it occurs, clearance, and response to the tested bolus consistency.

quiz.prompt: An oesophagram shows a dilated oesophagus and smooth distal tapering. What prevents an overconfident diagnosis of primary achalasia?
choices: Smooth tapering excludes every tumour
A dilated oesophagus proves reflux
Clinical and endoscopic assessment for an obstructing mimic
Oesophageal motility cannot be assessed radiologically
quiz.answer: Clinical and endoscopic assessment for an obstructing mimic
quiz.explain: An achalasia pattern is a functional description, not proof of its cause. A distal tumour can imitate it, especially with an atypical history.

quiz.prompt: A contrast-filled posterior pouch arises above the cricopharyngeus and retains material after swallowing. Which diagnosis fits the location?
choices: Sliding hiatus hernia
Epiphrenic diverticulum
Oesophageal varices
Zenker diverticulum
quiz.answer: Zenker diverticulum
quiz.explain: The pouch arises at the pharyngoesophageal junction. Record retained material and associated swallowing dysfunction, because size alone does not describe its functional effect.

quiz.prompt: Severe chest pain follows forceful vomiting, and CT shows paraoesophageal gas and fluid. Which interpretation takes priority?
choices: Possible oesophageal perforation requiring urgent communication
An uncomplicated distal oesophageal ring
Physiological oesophageal contraction
A benign motility finding requiring no correlation
quiz.answer: Possible oesophageal perforation requiring urgent communication
quiz.explain: Extraluminal findings in this setting raise concern for a leak. State its suspected level and mediastinal or pleural consequences, and communicate promptly.

quiz.prompt: A referral says only “dysphagia”. The patient describes difficulty initiating a swallow, whereas the clinic letter describes food sticking behind the sternum. Explain what you would clarify before selecting the examination.
quiz.answer: Clarify the symptom location and timing, the effect of liquids versus solids, coughing or choking, and progression or other concerning symptoms. Difficulty initiating a swallow raises an oropharyngeal question suitable for dynamic swallowing assessment; retrosternal sticking raises an oesophageal structural or transit question. The two may coexist, so the referral may require more than one focused assessment.
quiz.explain: A symptom label is not a complete imaging question. Resolving the phase of difficulty avoids a technically successful examination that cannot explain the complaint.

quiz.prompt: During a swallow study, material passes below the vocal folds without a cough. A draft report says “no aspiration because the patient did not cough”. Correct the reasoning and describe what to record.
quiz.answer: This is aspiration despite the absent cough. Record that airway entry was observed below the vocal folds, whether it occurred before, during or after the swallow, the tested consistency, and whether material cleared. Document the absent protective response and communicate the result to the swallowing team for the patient-specific plan.
quiz.explain: The observed route of the bolus establishes aspiration. A clinical reaction is an additional observation and must not replace the imaging evidence.

quiz.prompt: Two studies show the same small pharyngeal pouch. On the first it empties completely; on the second it retains material that later spills toward the airway. Explain why reporting only its size loses information.
quiz.answer: The dynamic behaviour has changed even if the measured size has not. Report retention, emptying and any subsequent airway invasion, together with the bolus conditions and study limitations. The pouch provides an anatomical finding; the observed sequence helps explain symptoms and informs the swallowing assessment.
quiz.explain: Functional imaging describes events over time. A static dimension cannot capture delayed spillage or the effect of a manoeuvre.

quiz.prompt: A smooth distal oesophageal narrowing and delayed emptying suggest achalasia, but the patient has rapidly progressive symptoms. Write a cautious conclusion and name the unresolved question.
quiz.answer: The examination demonstrates impaired oesophageal emptying with distal tapering, compatible with an achalasia pattern. The cause remains unresolved: an obstructing lesion or other secondary process must be considered in the clinical context. Correlate with endoscopic and physiological assessment rather than declaring primary achalasia from the shape alone.
quiz.explain: Imaging can identify a pattern while leaving its mechanism uncertain. Preserving that distinction prevents the pattern name from prematurely closing the work-up.

quiz.prompt: A patient stops an oesophagram after two small swallows because of discomfort. No abnormality appears in the recorded segment. How should the final report distinguish the observation from the conclusion?
quiz.answer: State which segments and swallowing phases were actually assessed, why the examination stopped, and that no abnormality was demonstrated within that limited assessment. Do not label the entire oesophagus or swallowing mechanism normal. Relate the limitation to the clinical question and propose further evaluation if the question remains unanswered.
quiz.explain: A negative observation is bounded by the examination performed. Explicit coverage prevents a limited test from being interpreted as a complete exclusion.

quiz.prompt: CT shows an eccentric jejunal mass projecting mainly outside the bowel, with central necrosis. Which diagnosis belongs high in the differential?
choices: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
Simple intraluminal lipoma
Uncomplicated diverticulosis
Physiological jejunal contraction
quiz.answer: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
quiz.explain: An exophytic soft-tissue mass with necrosis suggests a mesenchymal tumour such as GIST. Describe its bowel attachment and complications; imaging does not supply histology.

quiz.prompt: A small enhancing ileal lesion accompanies a spiculated mesenteric mass that tethers adjacent loops. Which association is most useful?
choices: The mesenteric mass excludes a bowel primary
A small bowel neuroendocrine primary can produce a desmoplastic mesenteric mass
Every such appearance proves active Crohn disease
The lesion must be a benign lipoma
quiz.answer: A small bowel neuroendocrine primary can produce a desmoplastic mesenteric mass
quiz.explain: A small primary may be less conspicuous than its mesenteric manifestation. Examine adjacent bowel carefully and assess vessels, obstruction and metastatic disease.

quiz.prompt: An unexplained focal ileal inflammatory mass contains a thin linear hyperdensity extending through the wall. The patient recalls no ingestion. What is the next interpretive step?
choices: Discard the finding because the history is negative
Call it intravenous contrast without checking another plane
Trace it on multiplanar images as a possible perforating foreign body
Ignore it if there is no free intraperitoneal gas
quiz.answer: Trace it on multiplanar images as a possible perforating foreign body
quiz.explain: Patients may not recall ingestion, and a contained perforation may lack free gas. Define the object, bowel relationship, abscess and adjacent-organ involvement.

quiz.prompt: A bulky circumferential bowel lesion has a relatively expanded lumen rather than a tight obstructing stricture. Which statement is best?
choices: This proves the lesion is benign
Malignancy requires complete obstruction
This finding excludes lymphoma
The pattern can suggest lymphoma but still needs tissue diagnosis
quiz.answer: The pattern can suggest lymphoma but still needs tissue diagnosis
quiz.explain: Luminal behaviour helps prioritise the differential. It is not a reliable substitute for histology, and overlapping appearances occur among bowel malignancies.

quiz.prompt: A sharp object is found at the margin of a liver abscess next to an abnormal gastric antrum. What should the report connect?
choices: Possible migration from a gastrointestinal perforation into the abscess
A liver abscess cannot have an enteric source
The object is irrelevant after leaving the bowel
The object proves a primary liver tumour
quiz.answer: Possible migration from a gastrointestinal perforation into the abscess
quiz.explain: Map the potential route, remaining object and collection. This supplies an anatomical explanation for source control planning without assuming that antibiotics alone address the cause.

quiz.prompt: An enhancing bowel mass is visible, but the lumen is collapsed and it is unclear whether the lesion arises from bowel or adjacent mesentery. Outline a report that preserves the useful findings without inventing an origin.
quiz.answer: Give the location, dimensions, enhancement and relationship to the nearest bowel loops, vessels and mesentery. Describe obstruction, bleeding, perforation or metastases if present. State that the epicentre is uncertain because of limited luminal assessment, offer a focused differential, and identify what additional imaging or tissue assessment would resolve.
quiz.explain: An uncertain origin does not erase the demonstrable anatomy. Separate measured observations from the proposed diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: A patient has anaemia and a short irregular jejunal narrowing with upstream dilatation. A colleague labels it Crohn disease because the wall is thickened. What competing explanation and supporting observations should be considered?
quiz.answer: An obstructing neoplasm remains a competing explanation. Assess the length and symmetry of thickening, margins, enhancement, adjacent invasion, nodes and distant findings, and consider whether there are other segments supporting inflammatory disease. Report the obstructing lesion and differential rather than converting wall thickening into a definitive inflammatory diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Thickening is shared by several diseases. The distribution and consequences of the lesion should guide the differential and further investigation.

quiz.prompt: An abscess has recurred after drainage. Thin-section review reveals a linear object at its edge, but the initial report said there was no free gas. Explain why the earlier negative finding does not settle the current diagnosis.
quiz.answer: Absent free gas does not exclude a contained gastrointestinal perforation. Trace the object in multiple planes and describe its location, possible bowel entry site and relation to the collection or adjacent organs. Highlight the retained foreign body as a possible persistent source and communicate the finding to the treating team.
quiz.explain: A negative secondary sign cannot outweigh a directly visible potential cause. The report should make the object findable for the team planning source control.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a small ileal enhancing focus and a much larger mesenteric mass. How can the impression connect them while preserving diagnostic uncertainty?
quiz.answer: Describe both lesions and their anatomical relationship, noting that a small bowel primary with mesenteric involvement is a possibility. Include tethering, vascular relationships, obstruction and metastatic findings. A neuroendocrine tumour may be favoured by the pattern, but histological confirmation and the clinical work-up determine the final diagnosis.
quiz.explain: The largest abnormality need not be the primary lesion. Showing the possible relationship makes the differential clinically useful without claiming tissue certainty.

quiz.prompt: A large exophytic bowel lesion has a necrotic centre. The request asks whether it is a GIST. What can imaging contribute, and what should it leave unresolved?
quiz.answer: Imaging can establish the apparent bowel attachment, size, viable enhancing components, necrosis and local or distant extent. Describe complications and explain why a mesenchymal tumour such as GIST is considered. Imaging cannot by itself establish the histological subtype or biological risk classification; those require the appropriate tissue and clinical assessment.
quiz.explain: A useful tumour report maps extent and supports a differential. It should not substitute morphology for pathology.

quiz.prompt: A superficial ileal loop is poorly resolved with a low-frequency curved probe. Which adjustment is most useful?
choices: Increase image smoothing until the layers disappear
Use a higher-frequency linear probe if penetration remains adequate
Measure only the gas interface
Assume superficial bowel cannot be examined
quiz.answer: Use a higher-frequency linear probe if penetration remains adequate
quiz.explain: Probe frequency balances resolution against penetration. Select it for the depth of the target after compression, and optimise focus and gain before measurement.

quiz.prompt: Gas obscures a bowel segment. What is the purpose of controlled graded compression?
choices: To guarantee exclusion of perforation
To replace the need for another imaging modality in every case
To displace intervening gas and assess compressibility
To create a fixed normal wall-thickness value
quiz.answer: To displace intervening gas and assess compressibility
quiz.explain: Compression improves access to some loops and supplies dynamic information. It should be controlled and tolerable; persistent nonvisualisation is a limitation, not a normal finding.

quiz.prompt: A short segment appears thickened on one oblique image. What should be checked before calling disease?
choices: Only the colour of the transducer
Whether the saved image has a label
Whether the patient has eaten this week
Perpendicular wall measurement, distension, layering and adjacent findings
quiz.answer: Perpendicular wall measurement, distension, layering and adjacent findings
quiz.explain: Obliquity and contraction can simulate thickening. Assess the segment in more than one plane and integrate mural stratification, vascularity and surrounding tissues.

quiz.prompt: The appendix has not been identified despite a careful study. Which report statement is most accurate?
choices: Appendix not visualised; document secondary signs and study limitations
Normal appendix definitively demonstrated
Appendicitis excluded in all circumstances
The caecum must therefore be absent
quiz.answer: Appendix not visualised; document secondary signs and study limitations
quiz.explain: Nonvisualisation and demonstrated normality are different results. The clinical probability and secondary signs determine whether observation or further evaluation is needed.

quiz.prompt: A bowel-ultrasound report lists wall thickness alone. Which addition most improves its diagnostic value?
choices: Only the room number
Length and distribution, layering, Doppler signal, motility and extramural findings
Only the examination start time
Only the nominal probe frequency
quiz.answer: Length and distribution, layering, Doppler signal, motility and extramural findings
quiz.explain: Bowel disease has a spatial and dynamic pattern. A reproducible segmental report includes the lumen, wall and surrounding mesentery, with acquisition limitations stated.

quiz.prompt: A measured bowel wall is 5 mm on an oblique image and thinner when measured perpendicular to the wall. Explain which measurement should be trusted and what else belongs in the assessment.
quiz.answer: Use a reproducible perpendicular measurement on an adequately visualised segment, with its degree of distension and compression considered. Assess length, distribution, layering, Doppler signal and surrounding tissues. Do not infer disease from an oblique measurement that may exaggerate thickness or from a single numeric threshold in isolation.
quiz.explain: Geometry and acquisition affect measurement. A number should be interpreted within a documented segmental pattern.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up intestinal ultrasound reports improvement because Doppler signal is lower, but the gain and flow settings differ. How would you reassess the claim?
quiz.answer: Check whether settings, depth, compression and sampling conditions were comparable. Describe the observed signal but qualify the apparent change if technical differences could explain it. Correlate with wall morphology, extent and other findings rather than using an unstandardised Doppler comparison as sole evidence of improvement.
quiz.explain: Doppler appearance is partly a measurement of the acquisition. Longitudinal claims require comparable technique as well as biological plausibility.

quiz.prompt: The symptomatic right lower quadrant is examined, but neither appendix nor terminal ileum is confidently seen. No collection is identified. Write a conclusion that does not overstate the negative study.
quiz.answer: The appendix and terminal ileum were not confidently visualised. No collection was demonstrated within the assessed region, but the study does not exclude pathology in the unvisualised structures. Document limiting factors and any secondary signs, and relate further evaluation to the ongoing clinical probability and symptoms.
quiz.explain: Absence of a collection answers a narrower question than exclusion of appendiceal or ileal disease. The conclusion should retain that distinction.

quiz.prompt: A short bowel segment appears abnormal, but adjacent fat and lymph nodes have not been assessed. Why should the operator expand the examination beyond the bowel wall?
quiz.answer: Extramural tissues can help characterise the process and reveal complications or alternative causes. Assess mesenteric fat, nodes, collections, free fluid and relevant vessels, while documenting the segment and extent. Interpret these findings with mural layering, motility and vascularity rather than treating wall thickness as a standalone diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Bowel disease has relationships outside the lumen. A complete local survey can change both the differential and the urgency.

quiz.prompt: A superficial bowel loop is sharply depicted with a linear probe, but deeper loops are not adequately penetrated. What should an appropriate scanning and reporting strategy do?
quiz.answer: Use a suitable lower-frequency probe or adjusted settings to survey deeper targets, while retaining the higher-frequency assessment for accessible detail. Record which regions remain limited. Do not generalise a well-seen superficial segment into a normal examination of the whole bowel.
quiz.explain: The best probe for one depth may be inadequate for another. Coverage and detail are complementary requirements.

curriculum_modules.title: Hip: Impingement, Arthroplasty and the Painful Hip

module_contract.goal: Measure the impingement and coverage angles that decide hip surgery, stage osteonecrosis, find the fracture the radiograph hides, and work up a failing arthroplasty.

approach.step: Check the pelvic radiograph is not rotated or tilted
approach.detail: Every version sign — crossover, posterior wall, ischial spine — is invalidated by rotation, so judge the film before you judge the hip.

approach.step: Look at the femoral head-neck junction
approach.detail: Cam morphology is a benign bony prominence at the head-neck junction, an asphericity of the head that makes abnormal contact in flexion and rotation.
Pincer morphology is an abnormal orientation or shape of the acetabulum, giving excessive coverage through retroversion or protrusion.
On radial or oblique axial images at the position of the bump, not on a single default plane — the bump is often anterosuperior.
Lateral centre-edge angle to the lateral margin of the anterosuperior sourcil, the weight-bearing zone. Low means dysplasia, high means overcoverage.
Crossover, posterior wall and ischial spine signs are read as a set; one alone on a tilted film means nothing.

measure.how: Circle fitted to the femoral head; the angle from the centre of the femoral neck to the head centre, then out to where the head-neck junction leaves the circle.
On cross-sectional imaging, measured on the anterior femoral head parallel to the neck axis.
To the lateral margin of the anterosuperior sourcil — the weight-bearing zone.
measure.cutoff: < 20° dysplasia · 20–25° borderline dysplasia · ≥ 40° global pincer overcoverage

classify.name: Impingement and coverage — what each finding means
rows: Alpha angle on the plane through the bump
Aspherical head-neck junction; abnormal contact in flexion and rotation. Threshold was raised to 60° for greater specificity
Anterior femoral head offset parallel to the neck axis
Same lesion, measured on cross-sectional imaging
Anterior and posterior wall outlines on the AP pelvis
Anterior wall projects laterally beyond the posterior wall — focal acetabular retroversion
Posterior wall outline against the head centre
Posterior wall projects medial to the centre of the femoral head — deficient posterior coverage
Ischial spine relative to the pelvic brim
Ischial spine projects abnormally medially — supports true retroversion

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
AP pelvis and [lateral view]. [MR / MR arthrography of the [right/left] hip with radial reformats.]

FINDINGS
Film adequacy: [no rotation or tilt / rotated — version signs not assessable].
Alpha angle: [n]° at the [anterosuperior / superior] position.
Head-neck offset: [n] mm.
Lateral centre-edge angle: [n]°.
Version signs: crossover [present/absent], posterior wall [present/absent], ischial spine [present/absent].
Labrum: [intact / tear at [position] / paralabral cyst].
Cartilage: [intact / delamination or loss at the [position]].
Herniation pit or fibrocystic change at the head-neck junction: [absent / present].
Joint space and osteoarthritis: [ ].

IMPRESSION
1. [Cam / pincer / mixed] morphology of the [right/left] hip: alpha angle [n]°, L-CEA [n]°.
2. [Chondrolabral injury and its position.]
3. [Coverage: normal / borderline dysplasia / dysplasia / overcoverage.]
pitfalls: Measuring the alpha angle on one default plane. The cam bump is usually anterosuperior; a single oblique axial through the wrong clock position reads normal.
Reporting a crossover sign off a rotated or tilted pelvis. All three version signs depend on projection, and a rotated film manufactures retroversion.
Taking the centre-edge angle to the acetabular rim rather than to the lateral margin of the sourcil. The sourcil is the weight-bearing zone and it is what the threshold refers to.
Using the older alpha angle threshold. The cut-off is 60°, raised from the earlier figure for specificity — 50-something degrees is not cam morphology.
Calling morphology a diagnosis. Cam and pincer shapes occur in asymptomatic hips; the report names the morphology and the chondrolabral damage, and leaves the syndrome to the clinic.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old footballer has anterior groin pain on flexion and internal rotation. Oblique axial MR images show an aspherical anterolateral head-neck junction with an alpha angle of 72 degrees. The lateral centre-edge angle is 31 degrees and there is no crossover sign. Where do you expect the joint damage to be, and of what kind?
quiz.answer: Anterosuperior chondral delamination running from the rim inward, the labrum spared at first
choices: Anterosuperior chondral delamination running from the rim inward, the labrum spared at first
Anterosuperior labral crushing with a narrow rim of chondral loss and posteroinferior contrecoup injury
Posterior chondral loss with anterior capsular thickening and an otherwise normal acetabular labrum
Global cartilage thinning with medial joint space narrowing and central acetabular subchondral cysts
quiz.explain: The alpha angle of 72 degrees marks a cam bump, and the coverage numbers are normal: a lateral centre-edge angle of 31 degrees sits in the usual 25 to 39 degree range, and the absence of a crossover sign argues against focal retroversion. So this is cam impingement, where the aspherical junction is jammed into the joint on flexion and internal rotation and shears the cartilage off the subchondral plate from the acetabular rim inward. The delamination often runs well ahead of any labral tear, which is why the arthroscopist finds a carpet of loose cartilage under a labrum that still looks reasonable. The second option describes the pincer mechanism instead, where an over-covering rim pinches the labrum, chondral loss is confined to a thin rim strip, and the head levers into the posteroinferior socket to give the contrecoup lesion. Posterior chondral loss with capsular change is a pattern of trauma or instability, and global thinning with medial narrowing belongs to established or inflammatory arthritis, not to a young athlete with mechanical pain.

quiz.prompt: On a well-centred AP pelvis of a 24-year-old with lateral hip pain, the lateral centre-edge angle of Wiberg measures 18 degrees. Coverage of 25 degrees or more is taken as normal, 20 to 25 degrees as borderline and below 20 degrees as dysplastic. By how many degrees short of the normal range is this hip? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Twenty-five minus eighteen is seven, and the arithmetic matters less than what it puts the hip into. The lateral centre-edge angle is built from a vertical line through the centre of the femoral head and a second line from that centre to the lateral edge of the acetabular sourcil, so it measures how much roof sits over the head. Below 20 degrees the hip is dysplastic, 20 to 25 is a borderline zone that is argued over, 25 to 39 is normal, and 40 or more is over-coverage of the kind that produces global pincer impingement. The direction of travel is the point: a dysplastic hip is short of coverage, so it overloads the rim, hypertrophies its labrum and tears it, and it is treated by adding coverage with a periacetabular osteotomy. Trimming the rim, the operation for pincer morphology, would make it worse. Measure only on a properly centred film, because pelvic rotation and tilt shift the apparent rim.

quiz.prompt: An AP pelvis shows the anterior acetabular wall line crossing lateral to the posterior wall line in the upper third of the socket. The coccyx lies 2 cm off the midline of the symphysis and the obturator foramina are markedly asymmetric. What do you do with that crossover?
quiz.answer: Repeat the radiograph properly centred, because rotation and tilt both create and erase this sign
choices: Repeat the radiograph properly centred, because rotation and tilt both create and erase this sign
Report cranial acetabular retroversion and refer for arthroscopic trimming of the anterior rim
Report the sign as valid, because the wall lines are unaffected by the position of the pelvis
Disregard the wall lines and measure the alpha angle, which answers the same question about version
quiz.explain: The crossover sign is only as good as the film. On a valid AP pelvis the coccyx sits in the midline above the symphysis, roughly 1 to 3 cm from it, and the obturator foramina and iliac wings look symmetric. Rotation towards one side swings the anterior wall of the opposite acetabulum laterally and manufactures a crossover in a normally orientated socket; rotation the other way hides a real one. Increasing pelvic tilt does much the same. Here the coccyx is off midline and the foramina are asymmetric, so the film cannot support the call, and the correct move is a properly centred repeat before anyone discusses a rim trim. When the film is valid, look for the supporting features of true retroversion: a prominent ischial spine projecting into the pelvis and a posterior wall line running medial to the head centre. The alpha angle describes the femoral side and says nothing at all about acetabular version.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with mechanical groin pain has a non-contrast 3 T hip MRI reported as showing a possible anterosuperior labral abnormality. The surgeon asks whether direct MR arthrography would add anything before arthroscopy. What does the intra-articular injection actually do for you, and when is it worth it?
quiz.answer: Intra-articular dilute gadolinium contrast distends the capsule and drives fluid into the substance of the labrum, so a tear or a detachment is shown directly rather than inferred from a line of intermediate signal; it earns its place when the non-contrast study is equivocal and the answer will decide arthroscopy, and adds little when a dedicated small field-of-view study is already unambiguous.
quiz.explain: Distension is the whole mechanism. Without it, a partial detachment lies collapsed against the rim and reads as a vague grey line; with a few millilitres of dilute gadolinium the capsule is opened, the contrast is forced into the cleft, and the tear is outlined. Direct arthrography also lets the operator inject local anaesthetic, so a patient whose pain abates for an hour has told you the pain is intra-articular, which is diagnostic information no sequence provides. Against that, it is an invasive procedure, usually guided by fluoroscopy or ultrasound, and a good small field-of-view non-contrast study on a modern scanner is often enough. The commonest error either way is over-calling normal anatomy: a sublabral sulcus at the anterosuperior junction, the perilabral sulcus, and the labral base where the physis once ran can all mimic a cleft. A paralabral cyst next to the finding is the reassuring secondary sign that the tear is real.

quiz.prompt: A 42-year-old man has six weeks of hip pain and now limps. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema through the whole femoral head, the neck and the intertrochanteric region with a small effusion, no demarcated subchondral segment and no low signal line. Radiographs show mild osteopenia of the head and neck. What follows?
quiz.answer: Protected weight-bearing and repeat imaging, since this pattern usually settles over several months
choices: Protected weight-bearing and repeat imaging, since this pattern usually settles over several months
Urgent core decompression, since the oedema marks the necrotic segment before it can collapse
Immediate arthroplasty referral, since collapse of the femoral head is already under way here
CT-guided biopsy of the femoral neck, since diffuse oedema of this extent implies a tumour
quiz.explain: Transient osteoporosis of the hip, or bone marrow oedema syndrome, produces exactly this: oedema that fills the head, crosses the neck and reaches the intertrochanteric region without a demarcated lesion inside it, in a middle-aged man or a woman in the third trimester, and it resolves over six to twelve months. Osteonecrosis looks different even when oedematous, because there is a geographic subchondral segment bounded by a serpiginous line, and on T2 the double line sign, an inner bright band of granulation tissue with an outer dark sclerotic band. Core decompression is aimed at that demarcated lesion, so it has nothing to work on here. Nothing has collapsed, so arthroplasty is premature, and a biopsy would sample oedematous marrow and tell you nothing while risking a fracture. The one thing that does matter is protection: the bone is transiently weak, and subcapital fracture during the oedema phase is the known complication.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these findings of femoral head osteonecrosis in the order they appear as the disease progresses, earliest first.
quiz.answer: marrow-signal-change sclerotic-demarcation crescent-sign head-flattening joint-space-loss
quiz.explain: This is the ARCO 2019 sequence in imaging terms. Stage 1 is MRI-only disease: the radiograph is normal and the marrow signal has changed, with the reactive interface giving the double line on T2. Stage 2 adds radiographically visible sclerosis, osteolysis or focal osteoporosis, still with no subchondral fracture and no flattening. Stage 3 is the subchondral fracture, the crescent of gas or fluid immediately beneath the plate, with or without collapse of the contour; ARCO 2019 splits it by the depth of femoral head depression, 3A at 2 mm or less and 3B beyond that. Stage 4 is secondary arthritis, when the acetabular cartilage finally gives way and the joint space narrows. The clinically useful part of the order is that the joint space stays normal all the way through stage 3, which is what separates osteonecrosis from arthritis on a plain film, and the frog lateral view shows the crescent best because the anterosuperior segment is thrown into profile.

quiz.prompt: Two hips have osteonecrosis of similar volume, both involving the anterosuperior weight-bearing segment. In one the subchondral bone plate is intact; in the other a thin fluid-signal line lies immediately beneath it on the T2 images. Why does that line change what you recommend?
quiz.answer: The line is a subchondral fracture, so the head has already lost its mechanical support and will go on to collapse; core decompression and the other joint-preserving procedures are aimed at the pre-fracture hip and rarely rescue a head once the crescent is present, so this patient moves towards osteotomy or arthroplasty rather than decompression.
quiz.explain: The crescent is a fracture through dead trabecular bone under the articular plate, and it is the point at which the natural history stops being reversible. That is why ARCO 2019 makes it the boundary between stage 2 and stage 3 rather than treating collapse as a matter of degree. MRI and CT both find it earlier than the radiograph, and CT is particularly good at showing a subtle break in the subchondral plate when the MRI is equivocal. Size and site are the other predictors that belong in the report: a lesion occupying more than about a third of the head, or one that involves the lateral pillar under the weight-bearing dome, will collapse whatever is done, whereas a small medial lesion may be watched. So the report should state the stage, the proportion of head involved, whether the lateral pillar is included, and whether a subchondral fracture is present.

quiz.prompt: An uncemented total hip replacement is reviewed for pain. On the immediate post-operative AP radiograph the acetabular component inclination measures 42 degrees; on a film taken three years later, measured against the same landmarks, it is 49 degrees. By how many degrees has the inclination changed? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Seven degrees, and that is enough to matter. A change in cup inclination beyond about five degrees, or migration of the component by more than two or three millimetres, is taken as evidence of loosening whatever the lucent lines are doing, because a fixed implant does not move. The measurement is only meaningful if the two films are comparable, so use the same reference line each time, usually the inter-teardrop or inter-ischial line, and check that rotation and tilt are similar. The other half of the assessment is the interfaces: describe acetabular lucency by the three zones of DeLee and Charnley and femoral lucency by the seven Gruen zones, and treat a thin, non-progressive lucency of under 2 mm as acceptable while a wide or progressive one is not. Note also that the starting figure of 42 degrees sits inside the traditional Lewinnek target of 40 plus or minus 10 degrees of inclination, so this cup was well placed and has since moved.

quiz.prompt: An 82-year-old woman cannot weight-bear after a fall. An AP pelvis and a lateral of the hip show no fracture, but she has groin pain on any rotation of the leg and is unable to lift it from the trolley. What imaging do you arrange next?
quiz.answer: MRI of the hip with coronal T1 and STIR, which will show or exclude the fracture today
choices: MRI of the hip with coronal T1 and STIR, which will show or exclude the fracture today
Repeat radiographs in ten days, when resorption at the fracture line makes it visible
An isotope bone scan today, which is the most sensitive test in the first 24 hours
No further imaging, with full mobilisation, analgesia and physiotherapy review
quiz.explain: A normal radiograph does not exclude a hip fracture in an osteopenic patient, and a missed one that displaces converts a screw fixation into a hemiarthroplasty. MRI is the reference standard: a limited protocol of coronal T1 and STIR through the pelvis takes a few minutes, shows the fracture line as low signal on T1 within hours of the injury, and needs no contrast. It also answers the question when the hip is normal, because pubic rami fractures, greater trochanteric and abductor injuries, and occasionally a metastatic deposit are the alternative explanations, and they are all in the same field of view. CT is the fallback when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, but it does miss undisplaced trabecular fractures in porotic bone. A bone scan can stay negative for one to three days in the elderly, and repeating radiographs at ten days leaves an unprotected fracture to displace in the interval.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old on long-term corticosteroids has low back and buttock pain that came on without injury. Radiographs and MRI of the lumbar spine show only degenerative change. Pain is reproduced by pressure over the sacroiliac region. What is the most useful next step?
quiz.answer: Image the sacrum and pelvic ring, looking for vertical alar and pubic ramus fractures
choices: Image the sacrum and pelvic ring, looking for vertical alar and pubic ramus fractures
Inject the L4/5 and L5/S1 facet joints under fluoroscopic guidance to treat the pain
Arrange flexion and extension views of the lumbar spine for degenerative instability
Arrange a whole-body isotope scan to search for the primary tumour causing the pain
quiz.explain: The sacrum sits below the field of view of most lumbar spine studies, so a sacral insufficiency fracture is missed by a protocol aimed at the discs. Steroids, osteoporosis and previous pelvic radiotherapy are the classic settings. On STIR the fractures run vertically through the sacral ala parallel to the sacroiliac joints, often with a transverse component across the body, which is the H or Honda pattern that isotope imaging shows so memorably. CT confirms the line and the surrounding sclerosis. Because the pelvis is a ring, always look for the second break: pubic rami fractures accompany alar fractures in a large proportion of cases. The trap is calling the marrow change a metastasis, so look for a fracture line and an absent soft tissue mass; conversely, a lesion that destroys the cortex and has a mass is not an insufficiency fracture. Treatment is analgesia and mobilisation, sometimes sacroplasty, not a facet injection.

quiz.prompt: Four months after a cemented total hip replacement, radiographs show a 4 mm lucency around the whole cement-bone interface of the stem, new periosteal reaction along the proximal femur, and ultrasound shows a joint effusion. The patient has rest pain and a raised C-reactive protein. What is the leading explanation?
quiz.answer: Periprosthetic infection, given the speed of change, the periosteal reaction and the raised CRP
choices: Periprosthetic infection, given the speed of change, the periosteal reaction and the raised CRP
Aseptic loosening from polyethylene wear particles, which produces the same appearances
Stress shielding by a stiff stem that transfers load to the distal femur instead
Heterotopic ossification in the abductor mass, which often follows this surgical approach
quiz.explain: Timing carries most of the weight. Particle disease and aseptic loosening take years to produce a wide lucency, and they do not raise inflammatory markers; a wide, circumferential lucency at four months with rest pain and a raised CRP is infection until an aspirate says otherwise. Periosteal reaction is the other strong pointer, being uncommon in aseptic loosening and characteristic of infection, and the effusion supports it. The next step is aspiration before any antibiotic is given, so the culture is not sterilised, and the report should say so explicitly. Stress shielding produces the opposite appearance, proximal bone resorption and calcar rounding with a well-fixed distal stem, and no pain. Heterotopic ossification is new bone in the soft tissues around the joint, not a lucency at the interface. For reference, a thin, non-progressive lucency of under 2 mm at the cement-bone interface can be entirely normal.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing has groin pain and a rising blood cobalt level, and the clinician wants MRI for adverse reaction to metal debris. Say what you ask the radiographer to change from a standard protocol, and what each change buys.
quiz.answer: Scan at 1.5 T rather than 3 T; use turbo spin echo rather than gradient echo sequences, with a high receiver bandwidth, a short echo time and a short echo spacing; use thin slices with a fine matrix; and use STIR rather than spectral fat saturation. Each change either reduces the off-resonance frequency shift near the metal or spreads it across fewer millimetres, so the pseudotumour and the abductor muscles remain visible next to the implant.
quiz.explain: Metal distorts the local field, and the size of the resulting displacement is the frequency shift divided by the bandwidth per pixel, so raising the receiver bandwidth is the single most effective lever, at a cost in signal to noise. Gradient echo sequences have no refocusing pulse to recover dephasing and are the worst offenders, so they are dropped. Spectral fat saturation depends on a uniform field and fails precisely where you need it, whereas STIR nulls fat by inversion time and tolerates inhomogeneity. Lower field means a smaller shift, and orienting the long axis of the prosthesis along the main field reduces distortion further. Where they exist, the multispectral techniques MAVRIC and SEMAC do the job properly. What you are looking for is a periprosthetic fluid collection or solid mass with a thickened capsule, plus atrophy or frank necrosis of the abductors and osteolysis, since abductor destruction is what makes revision urgent.

quiz.prompt: An elderly man falls and breaks his femur around a cemented stem. CT shows a spiral fracture around the distal stem, a fractured cement mantle, and the stem sitting in a slightly different position from the film taken a year ago; the bone stock elsewhere looks good. What should the report emphasise, and what does it mean for the operation?
quiz.answer: The stem is loose, so this needs revision of the stem rather than fixation of the fracture alone
choices: The stem is loose, so this needs revision of the stem rather than fixation of the fracture alone
The stem is stable, so plate fixation around the retained implant is all that is required
The bone stock is inadequate, so this needs proximal femoral replacement rather than a stem
The fracture lies below the stem, so it can be managed as an isolated femoral shaft break
quiz.explain: The Vancouver classification divides periprosthetic femoral fractures into type A at the trochanters, type B around or just below the stem, and type C well distal to it, and type B is subdivided by exactly the two things the radiologist can report: B1 has a stable stem and is fixed, B2 has a loose stem with adequate bone and needs a revision stem, and B3 has a loose stem with deficient bone and needs proximal femoral reconstruction or replacement. Here a change in stem position against a previous film and a fractured cement mantle both say the implant is loose, while the bone stock is preserved, so this is B2. That is why the sentence the surgeon needs is not the shape of the fracture but whether the stem has moved and whether the bone will hold a new one. Always compare with the earliest post-operative film rather than the most recent one, since loosening is a slow drift.

curriculum_modules.title: Crohn Disease: MR Enterography and Ultrasound

module_contract.goal: Run and read an MR enterography, separate active inflammation from fibrotic stricture so the team can choose drug or knife, and use bowel ultrasound to follow the response.

approach.detail: A 2% mannitol in water solution gives the lumen contrast that works on both T1 and T2. An undistended loop mimics thickening and will be over-called.
Balanced FFE axial and coronal, breath-hold; T2 with fat saturation axial; T1 pre- and post-contrast axial and coronal. Add T2 without fat saturation, DWI and cine motility.

approach.step: Measure the wall and grade it
approach.detail: 3–5 mm mild, 5–7 mm moderate, over 7 mm marked. Measure on the loop at its least contracted.
High mural T2 signal, mucosal or homogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion and a comb sign mean active. Low mural T2 signal with fat deposition on the non-fat-saturated T2 means fibrosis.
Bowel wall thickening with lumen narrowing plus prestenotic dilatation. Use the motility sequence to prove it is not a transient contraction.
Sinus tracts and fistulae enhance markedly and may show a layered tram-track. An abscess has rim enhancement on post-contrast T1 with central high T2 signal.
Graded compression against the iliopsoas. Wall thickening and the inflamed fat mass both decrease as the patient responds to medical therapy.

measure.how: On the post-contrast T1 or balanced FFE, on a distended, non-contracted segment.
measure.cutoff: 3–5 mm mild · 5–7 mm moderate · > 7 mm marked

measure.how: Compare the segment with psoas muscle on the post-contrast T1.
High signal on DWI with low ADC in the involved segment.
From the outer contour of the muscular layer to the opposite side, then divided by 2.
measure.cutoff: Normal ileum ≈ 1.5 mm · Crohn typically ≥ 6.5 mm

classify.name: Active inflammation against fibrostenotic disease
rows: Low, with fat deposition on non-fat-saturated T2
Layered enhancement — also seen in severe activity
Enhancement alone does not settle it
Restricted: high DWI, low ADC at b = 600–1000
Moderate to deep ulceration with increased enhancement
Narrowed by oedema, may relax on cine
Drug for the first, knife for the second
classify.note: Overall activity is reported as none, mild, moderate or severe, from wall thickness, degree of enhancement and mural T2 signal together with any complication.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
MR enterography after oral 2% mannitol solution. Balanced FFE axial and coronal, T2 fat-saturated axial, T1 pre- and post-gadolinium axial and coronal[, DWI, cine motility]. [Buscopan.]

FINDINGS
Distension: [adequate / inadequate].
Involved segments: [site], length [n] cm. Wall thickness [n] mm — [mild / moderate / marked].
Mural T2 signal: [normal / minor / moderate / marked increase].
Enhancement: [homogeneous / mucosal / layered], relative to psoas [ ].
DWI: [no restriction / restricted].
Ulceration: [absent / moderate / deep]. Comb sign: [absent / present].
Stricture: [absent / present at (site)] — lumen narrowing with prestenotic dilatation to [n] mm; [fixed on cine / relaxes].
Penetrating disease: sinus [ ], fistula [ ] (to [bowel / bladder / skin / vagina]), abscess [absent / present, n mm at (site)].
Mesentery: creeping fat [absent / present]. Nodes: [ ].

IMPRESSION
1. Crohn disease of the [segment], [no / mild / moderate / severe] active inflammation.
2. [Fibrostenotic stricture at (site) with prestenotic dilatation / no stricture.]
3. [Penetrating complication.]
4. [Compared with (date): improved / stable / progressed.]
pitfalls: Reporting a contracted loop as thickened. Without adequate mannitol distension, and without a cine sequence to show it relaxing, a normal contraction becomes a stricture.
Using enhancement alone to call fibrosis. A layered enhancement pattern occurs in chronic disease and in severe activity — the mural T2 signal is what separates them.
Missing the fat on non-fat-saturated T2. Submucosal fat deposition is the sign of chronic fibrotic change, and it disappears on the fat-saturated series you probably read first.
Calling a stricture without prestenotic dilatation. The definition is wall thickening plus lumen narrowing plus upstream dilatation.
Measuring the bowel wall on ultrasound without halving. Outer contour to opposite outer contour must be divided by 2 to get the wall thickness.

radiology_reference.overview: Run and read an MR enterography, separate active inflammation from fibrotic stricture so the team can choose drug or knife, and use bowel ultrasound to follow the response.
learning_points: Hyperenhancement, oedema and comb-like vessels support activity.
Fixed narrowing may suggest fibrosis, but cross-sectional imaging cannot accurately quantify the fibrotic component.
Fistula, abscess and upstream dilatation alter management.
Review bowel preparation, distension and motion.
Review involved segments, length and mural thickness.
Review oedema, enhancement, ulcers and diffusion.
Review stricture length and prestenotic dilation.
Review fistula, abscess, mesentery and extraintestinal findings.
Imaging features of inflammation and fibrosis overlap; avoid claiming an exact tissue fraction from routine images.

measurements.name: Wall and length
measurements.method: Measure maximum wall thickness perpendicular to adequately distended bowel and affected length.
measurements.pitfall: Collapsed bowel can mimic mural thickening.

measurements.name: Prestenotic dilatation
measurements.method: Measure maximum upstream calibre and stricture length.
measurements.pitfall: Inflammation and fibrosis often coexist and cannot be cleanly separated by one sign.

quiz.prompt: A patient managed only 400 mL of the oral agent before MR enterography. Several ileal loops are collapsed; their walls measure 5 mm and enhance briskly. There is no mural T2 signal, no comb sign, no restricted diffusion and no mesenteric fat change. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Those loops are non-diagnostic, since collapsed bowel mimics mural thickening
choices: Those loops are non-diagnostic, since collapsed bowel mimics mural thickening
There is active ileal inflammation, since thickening with enhancement suffices
There is a fibrotic stricture, since the loops are narrowed and fail to distend
The bowel is normal, since the mesenteric and diffusion findings are absent
quiz.explain: Distension is the examination. A contracted loop has a genuinely thick, avidly enhancing wall, and the appearance is indistinguishable from disease if you look at the wall alone, which is why 1 to 1.5 litres of a biphasic agent over 45 to 60 minutes is a technical requirement rather than a courtesy. Two habits protect you. First, require corroboration before calling inflammation: mural T2 hyperintensity on fat-saturated images, restricted diffusion, ulcers, engorged vasa recta, creeping fat, upstream dilatation. Second, require persistence, since a peristaltic contraction changes between sequences while disease does not. Reporting the loops as normal is the mirror-image error and is just as unsafe, because you cannot exclude disease in bowel you have not seen. If the patient cannot drink, say so and offer bowel ultrasound instead.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the oral agent used for MR enterography is chosen to be bright on T2 and dark on T1, and say what the mannitol in it is doing.
quiz.answer: A bright lumen on T2 outlines the wall against fluid so thickening and ulcers stand out, while a dark lumen on T1 lets the wall show its intravenous contrast enhancement without competition; the mannitol is an osmotic agent that holds water in the bowel so the loops stay distended for the whole examination.
quiz.explain: The two signal requirements come from the two questions the study asks. On T2 you want the wall silhouetted, so bright luminal fluid is ideal and mural oedema shows as high signal within a dark wall. On post-contrast T1 you want mural enhancement to be the brightest thing in the field, so the lumen must stay dark; a positive luminal agent would swamp it. An agent that satisfies both is biphasic. Mannitol, sorbitol and polyethylene glycol are poorly absorbed solutes that keep water in the lumen by osmosis, which is what maintains distension over the 45 minutes of drinking and the 30 minutes of scanning, and also why they cause the cramping and diarrhoea patients complain about. Intravenous hyoscine butylbromide is added to stop peristalsis before the motion-sensitive sequences.

quiz.prompt: Post-contrast images are obtained at about 45 seconds and again at about 7 minutes. A terminal ileal segment enhances less than adjacent normal bowel at 45 seconds, but more than it at 7 minutes. What does that pattern favour?
quiz.answer: Fibrosis, where contrast accumulates late in a collagen-rich wall
choices: Fibrosis, where contrast accumulates late in a collagen-rich wall
Active inflammation, which peaks early and then washes out fast
A timing artefact, since two phases are not comparable this way
Ischaemia, since the wall enhances less than the neighbouring loops
quiz.explain: The enteric phase at roughly 45 seconds is when actively inflamed bowel is most conspicuous, because hyperaemic mucosa and submucosa take up contrast quickly and stratify. Fibrotic wall behaves in the opposite direction: contrast diffuses slowly into an expanded extracellular collagen matrix and leaves slowly, so a segment that looked unimpressive early is brighter than its neighbours on delayed imaging. Reading the two phases as a pair therefore separates the two processes better than either alone, and it is why a delayed acquisition earns its place in the protocol. Two cautions belong with it. Most strictures contain both processes, so this pattern shifts the balance rather than settling it; and the comparison must be made against normal bowel in the same acquisition, not against a remembered brightness.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old has a 6 cm terminal ileal stricture with 4.5 cm of upstream dilatation. The wall is 8 mm thick, dark on fat-saturated T2, shows no restricted diffusion, has no ulcers and no comb sign, and enhances progressively on the 7-minute images. The team asks whether to escalate the biologic.
quiz.answer: Predominantly fibrotic; escalating the biologic will not open this stricture
choices: Predominantly fibrotic; escalating the biologic will not open this stricture
Predominantly inflammatory; escalate the biologic before considering surgery
Indeterminate, since T2 signal and diffusion have no bearing on this question
Predominantly fibrotic, but a biologic is still the first line before surgery
quiz.explain: Every feature here points the same way. A wall dark on fat-saturated T2 holds no free water, absent restricted diffusion argues against a dense inflammatory infiltrate, there are no ulcers and no hyperaemic vasa recta, and enhancement is late and progressive rather than early and layered. That is scar, and no anti-inflammatory drug dissolves scar; the options are endoscopic balloon dilatation for a short stricture, strictureplasty, or resection. The upstream dilatation matters too, because the 2018 Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Gastroenterological Association consensus defines a stricture as luminal narrowing with unequivocal upstream dilatation, taken as greater than 3 cm, so 4.5 cm qualifies and the narrowing is doing real mechanical work. Where inflammation coexists, a drug trial is entirely reasonable; this scan is simply too clean to justify one.

quiz.prompt: At the next scan the same stricture is bright on fat-saturated T2, restricts diffusion and shows a deep ulcer, while still enhancing progressively on the delayed images. What should you tell the multidisciplinary meeting?
quiz.answer: This is now a mixed stricture, with active inflammation superimposed on the fibrosis, so a trial of medical therapy is justified first and dilatation or resection is held in reserve for the fibrotic component if the obstruction persists.
quiz.explain: Most Crohn strictures are mixed, and the honest report says so rather than forcing a binary. What the meeting needs is the proportion and its consequence: an inflammatory component can be treated medically and may relieve enough of the narrowing to defer an operation, whereas the fibrotic component sets a floor below which no drug will take the calibre. So the sequence is a defined trial of therapy with a stated endpoint and a planned reassessment, and an agreed intervention if symptoms of obstruction continue. Two practical points support this. Deep ulceration is a marker of severity and of poorer medical response, so it argues for close follow-up rather than complacency; and length matters to the surgeon, since a short stricture is a candidate for balloon dilatation while a long one is not.

quiz.prompt: On bowel ultrasound the terminal ileal wall measures 6.4 mm at its thickest, against the accepted upper limit of normal of 3 mm in adults. By how much does it exceed that limit? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Wall thickness is the workhorse of bowel ultrasound because it is the most reproducible thing the probe measures, and above 3 mm in an adult it is abnormal, with normal bowel usually under 2 mm. Technique decides whether the number means anything: use a high-frequency linear probe, measure perpendicular to the wall from the luminal interface to the serosa, exclude luminal content, and take the thickest point of the diseased segment rather than an average. The figure then feeds the composite activity scores such as the International Bowel Ultrasound Segmental Activity Score, alongside colour Doppler hyperaemia, loss of the layered pattern and mesenteric fat changes. MR enterography uses the same 3 mm threshold for adequately distended small bowel, which is why the two examinations can be used in series without recalibrating.

quiz.prompt: Coronal MR enterography shows the vasa recta on the mesenteric border of a thickened ileal segment splayed apart and engorged, with proliferation of the adjacent mesenteric fat and several small reactive nodes. What does this add to the assessment?
quiz.answer: It supports active transmural disease and helps localise the diseased segment
choices: It supports active transmural disease and helps localise the diseased segment
It indicates chronic burnt-out disease with no current inflammatory activity
It suggests mesenteric venous thrombosis rather than Crohn inflammation here
It is expected in well distended bowel and carries no diagnostic significance
quiz.explain: Engorged vasa recta standing perpendicular to the bowel are the vascular expression of active disease: flow to the segment has increased and the feeding vessels dilate to carry it. Fibrofatty proliferation around the same segment is the more chronic partner, a mesenteric response that tends to accumulate with disease duration but also tracks with activity. Both sit on the mesenteric border, which is where Crohn disease characteristically concentrates, sparing the antimesenteric side and producing the pseudosacculations seen there. Their practical value is twofold: they raise confidence that a thickened loop is truly diseased rather than contracted, and they mark the extent of involvement when the loops themselves are hard to follow. Be careful with the nodes, though; small reactive nodes belong here, whereas nodes over a centimetre deserve a separate thought.

quiz.prompt: MR enterography shows a blind-ending tract leaving the mesenteric border of a diseased ileal loop and ending in a 4 cm rim-enhancing collection that contains gas and restricts diffusion. The gastroenterologist would like to start infliximab this week.
quiz.answer: Drain the collection and treat the sepsis before any anti-TNF agent is started
choices: Drain the collection and treat the sepsis before any anti-TNF agent is started
Start the anti-TNF agent now, since it will close both the tract and the cavity
Resect the segment immediately, since any sinus tract mandates a resection
Repeat the enterography in three months before committing to an intervention
quiz.explain: Penetrating disease has a vocabulary worth keeping straight because it maps onto different actions. A sinus tract ends blind in the mesentery; a fistula reaches another epithelialised surface, whether bowel, bladder, vagina or skin; an abscess is a rim-enhancing collection, and restricted diffusion with gas is what distinguishes it from a fluid-filled loop. Starting potent immunosuppression into undrained sepsis is the one clearly wrong move, since it removes the containment the patient is relying on. So the order is drainage, percutaneous where the collection is accessible, with antibiotics, and then the biologic once the sepsis is controlled, which is also when the drug has the best chance of closing the tract. Immediate resection is not mandatory; many tracts settle once the cavity is drained and the inflammation treated.

quiz.prompt: Perineal MRI shows a primary tract crossing the external anal sphincter into the ischioanal fossa, with a secondary ramification and a 2 cm collection within that fossa. Using the St James's University Hospital MRI grading of perianal fistulas, which grade is this? Answer as a whole number from 1 to 5.
quiz.explain: The St James's grading runs from 1 to 5 and combines the anatomical course with whether there is a secondary tract or abscess. Grade 1 is a simple linear intersphincteric tract; grade 2 is intersphincteric with a secondary tract or abscess; grade 3 is a simple transsphincteric tract; grade 4 is transsphincteric with an abscess or secondary tract in the ischioanal or ischiorectal fossa; grade 5 is supralevator or translevator disease. Crossing the external sphincter makes it transsphincteric, and the ischioanal collection takes it to grade 4. This matters because grades 3 and above are complex disease: fistulotomy would divide sphincter and risk continence, so management moves to seton drainage plus medical therapy, and the report must state the relationship to the sphincter complex, the presence of collections and any secondary tracts.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the five sonographic layers of the bowel wall from the lumen outwards.
quiz.answer: lumen-interface mucosa submucosa muscularis-propria serosa
quiz.explain: High-frequency ultrasound resolves the wall into five alternating bands: a bright interface where the lumen meets the mucosa, dark mucosa, bright submucosa, dark muscularis propria and a bright serosal line. Reading them is the point rather than reciting them. In Crohn disease the thickening concentrates in the submucosa, so the bright band widens while the layering is preserved, and that preserved pattern is the reassuring finding. Loss of stratification, where the layers blur into a single hypoechoic mass, indicates severe transmural inflammation or deep ulceration and is associated with a poorer response to medical therapy and a higher chance of penetrating disease. Adding colour Doppler to a stratified thickened wall gives the hyperaemia score, and the two together are what a follow-up scan is really comparing.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old with terminal ileal Crohn disease needs assessment three times over the coming year to judge treatment response. Give the properties of bowel ultrasound that make it the right tool, and name the limitation that would send you back to MR enterography.
quiz.answer: It involves no ionising radiation, needs no oral preparation or sedation, is cheap and can be repeated at the bedside, giving wall thickness and Doppler hyperaemia at every visit; its limitation is poor access to the deep pelvis, the proximal jejunum and perianal disease, which need MR enterography or perineal MRI.
quiz.explain: Serial imaging has different requirements from diagnostic imaging. What matters over a year is that the test can be done often, quickly and identically, and bowel ultrasound wins on all three: no radiation, no drinking a litre of mannitol, no cannula, a few minutes in clinic, and quantitative outputs in wall thickness and Doppler signal that can be tracked visit to visit. That is why it has become a standard tool for monitoring response and for detecting relapse early. Its weaknesses are anatomical and operator-dependent rather than conceptual. Deep pelvic loops, the proximal jejunum, and anything perianal are beyond it, obesity degrades it, and reproducibility depends on training. So the usual arrangement is MR enterography to map the disease and ultrasound to follow it.

quiz.prompt: Another patient has continuous mucosal disease from the rectum to the splenic flexure, with symmetrical mildly thickened bowel, loss of haustration, no mesenteric fat proliferation, no deep ulcers and no fistulas. What does that combination favour, and what changes as a result?
quiz.answer: Ulcerative colitis; medical therapy and surveillance, with no hunt for fistulas
choices: Ulcerative colitis; medical therapy and surveillance, with no hunt for fistulas
Crohn colitis; the rectal involvement makes penetrating disease more likely
Infective colitis; a continuous distribution argues against a chronic process
Ischaemic colitis; the splenic flexure limit marks a watershed territory here
quiz.explain: Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum proximally, confined to mucosa and submucosa, and it does not penetrate: no creeping fat, no sinus tracts, no fistulas, and thickening that is usually modest compared with Crohn disease. Chronic change gives the smooth, foreshortened, haustra-free colon. Crohn colitis is the opposite in every respect that matters here, being discontinuous, asymmetric, mesenteric-border predominant, and prone to penetrating complications, which is why the distinction changes what you look for as well as what you call it. Two caveats keep you honest. Treated ulcerative colitis can become patchy and can spare the rectum after topical therapy, so distribution alone is unreliable in a patient already on treatment; and backwash ileitis gives a short, patulous, thin-walled terminal ileum, quite unlike the narrowed thickened ileum of Crohn disease.

module_contract.goal: Argue from the shape, compartment, distribution and density of intracranial blood to the vessel and the cause, and state the imaging or intervention that should follow.

approach.detail: Subarachnoid blood between arachnoid and pia is a different problem from intracerebral blood; they get different next investigations.

approach.step: For intracerebral blood, ask central or lobar
approach.detail: Putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum are hypertensive. Lobar and peripheral in an elderly patient is amyloid angiopathy.
Multiple peripheral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis following gyral contours make the case for amyloid angiopathy.

approach.step: For SAH, decide aneurysmal or perimesencephalic
approach.detail: Blood centred anterior to the pons and midbrain, with a negative CTA, is the perimesencephalic pattern and needs no further angiography.

approach.step: Ask whether the haemorrhage is hiding a lesion
approach.detail: Tumour, cavernoma, AVM, dural fistula, haemorrhagic infarction and pituitary apoplexy all present as blood. Plan the follow-up study that would show them.
Non-enhanced CT, then CTA as first-line for aneurysm, then DSA where CTA is negative and suspicion remains.

classify.name: Non-traumatic haemorrhage by site
rows: Lenticulostriate arteries — high internal pressure, perpendicular origin from the parent vessel
Blood pressure history; CTA if the patient is young or the site is atypical
Multiple peripheral microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis following the gyri
SWI or T2* to document the microbleed burden
Subarachnoid, around the circle of Willis
Multiple in 20%; over 2.5 cm are giant aneurysms, seen in 5%
CTA first-line; DSA if CTA negative
Subarachnoid, centred anterior to pons and midbrain
Suggested venous or capillary rupture at the tentorial hiatus; no rebleeding risk in the initial years, normal life expectancy
No further angiography if CTA is negative and the pattern fits
Intra-axial with a nidus or flow voids
Spetzler-Martin grade 1–5, 6 is inoperable; eloquent locations score higher
Intra-axial, popcorn lesion with haemosiderin rim
CT detects only the large, the recently bled or the calcified
Melanoma 50%, then renal cell, lung, breast
classify.note: 85% of non-traumatic haemorrhages occur in patients with hypertension or cerebral amyloid angiopathy. AVM bleeding risk is 1–2% per year.

measure.how: A negative CT with a convincing history still needs a lumbar puncture.
Maximum diameter of the sac.
Having found one, keep looking at the other bifurcations of the circle of Willis.
Spetzler-Martin, weighted towards eloquent brain.
T2* gradient echo and FLAIR are the most sensitive sequences once the CT has gone negative.

FINDINGS
Compartment: [intracerebral / subarachnoid / intraventricular / combined].
Site and volume: [ ], [n] mL.
Pattern: [central — putamen/thalamus/pons/cerebellum] or [lobar / peripheral].
Microbleeds on SWI: [none / n, lobar or deep]. Cortical superficial siderosis: [absent / present].
SAH distribution: [diffuse around the circle of Willis / centred anterior to pons and midbrain].

Mass effect: midline shift [n] mm, ventricles [normal / hydrocephalus], cisterns [ ].

IMPRESSION

pitfalls: Excluding subarachnoid haemorrhage on a CT done late. Sensitivity is 98% within 12 hours and falls after that — a convincing history still gets a lumbar puncture.
Stopping at the first aneurysm. One in five patients has more than one.

Sending every negative-CTA subarachnoid haemorrhage for DSA. If the blood is centred anterior to the pons and midbrain and the CTA is negative, the perimesencephalic pattern needs no further angiography.
Calling a lobar haemorrhage in an elderly patient hypertensive. Central is hypertensive, lobar is amyloid — and the microbleeds on SWI settle it.
Forgetting that a haematoma can hide its cause. Tumour, cavernoma and vascular malformation all need a delayed study once the blood has resolved.

checklist.label: Compartment
checklist.detail: Map intraparenchymal, subarachnoid, intraventricular and extra-axial blood separately.

checklist.label: Distribution
checklist.detail: Distinguish deep, lobar, posterior fossa and convexity patterns.

checklist.label: Complications
checklist.detail: Look for expansion, active contrast extravasation if acquired, shift and hydrocephalus.

checklist.label: Cause
checklist.detail: Inspect vascular lesions, venous thrombosis, underlying mass and infarction.

checklist.label: Background
checklist.detail: Record microbleed distribution and superficial siderosis when susceptibility imaging is available.

measurements.name: Haematoma size/volume
measurements.method: Record three diameters; if using ABC/2, label volume approximate and specify cm units for mL output.
measurements.pitfall: ABC/2 is less reliable for irregular, multilobulated or multifocal haemorrhage.

measurements.name: Mass effect
measurements.method: Measure shift in mm and describe ventricular obstruction and cisterns.
measurements.pitfall: Posterior fossa compression can be critical without supratentorial shift.
