quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old struck on the side of the head has a lucid interval and is now drowsy. CT shows a biconvex right temporal extra-axial collection 18 mm thick with an overlying undisplaced squamous temporal bone fracture. Within the dense collection are irregular low-attenuation swirls. What do those swirls tell you?
quiz.answer: Active arterial extravasation into unclotted haematoma, predicting rapid expansion and urgent evacuation
choices: Layering of cerebrospinal fluid within a chronic collection, indicating a long-standing previous injury
Beam-hardening artefact from the adjacent temporal bone fracture, carrying no clinical consequence here
Active arterial extravasation into unclotted haematoma, predicting rapid expansion and urgent evacuation
Mixed-age subdural blood from repeated minor injury, favouring conservative management and repeat CT
quiz.explain: The swirl sign is fresh, unretracted blood — still liquid and therefore lower in attenuation than the clotted blood around it — and it means the bleeding has not stopped. In an extradural haematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery, that is a surgical emergency: the collection can double in an hour, and the lucid interval described here is the classical prelude to rapid decompensation. The shape and the fracture together make the compartment clear. Extradural blood is biconvex because it has to strip the dura off the inner table against its firm attachment at the sutures, so it does not cross a suture, though it can cross the midline and the tentorium because it is not bounded by dural reflections. Subdural blood is the reverse: crescentic, crossing sutures freely, but halted at the falx and tentorium. Chronic collections are uniformly low in attenuation without the irregular internal swirls, and artefact from bone runs as linear streaks across the whole slice rather than sitting inside the clot.

quiz.prompt: A crescentic hyperdense extra-axial collection extends along the right frontal convexity, continues across the coronal suture onto the parietal region, and stops abruptly at the midline. Say which compartment the blood is in and give the anatomical reason that lets you be certain.
quiz.answer: It is subdural. The periosteal layer of the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, so extradural blood cannot cross a suture, whereas subdural blood can; but the falx is a dural reflection in the subdural space's midline boundary, so subdural blood stops at the midline. Crossing a suture while respecting the midline is therefore subdural.
quiz.explain: Two anatomical rules do almost all the work in the extra-axial compartment, and they are complementary rather than competing. The dura is two layers: an outer periosteal layer fused to the inner table and adherent at the sutures, and an inner meningeal layer that folds inwards to form the falx and tentorium. Blood in the extradural space lifts the periosteal layer off the bone and is arrested where that layer is tethered, at the sutures; nothing stops it crossing the falx or tentorium, because those structures lie deep to it. Blood in the subdural space slides under the sutures without difficulty but meets the falx and tentorium head on. So crossing a suture argues subdural; crossing the midline argues extradural. Neither rule is absolute — a fracture that runs through a suture and diastases it lets extradural blood across — which is why shape, the presence of a fracture and the clinical story are read together. Look for interhemispheric or tentorial layering, which is subdural blood in profile and easily mistaken for subarachnoid.

quiz.prompt: On axial CT a spontaneous right basal ganglia haematoma measures 5.0 cm in its longest axial diameter and 3.0 cm perpendicular to that on the same slice, and it is visible on 8 contiguous slices of 5 mm each. Estimate its volume with the ABC/2 method. Answer in millilitres to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: ABC/2 approximates the ellipsoid: A is the largest diameter on the slice where the clot is biggest, B is the diameter perpendicular to A on that same slice, and C is the craniocaudal extent, obtained here as 8 slices times 0.5 cm, giving 4 cm. So 5.0 times 3.0 times 4.0, divided by 2, is 30.0 mL. It takes a few seconds and it is the number the medical and surgical teams actually use, because volume is one of the strongest predictors of 30-day mortality in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, along with the Glasgow Coma Scale score and intraventricular extension. Two caveats keep you honest. ABC/2 systematically overestimates irregular or lobar haematomas, so a segmented volume is better when the shape is complex, and for the C measurement count only slices where the clot occupies a reasonable fraction of the largest area rather than every slice with a trace of blood. Record the baseline volume clearly, because the definition of significant expansion is relative to it.

quiz.prompt: A 66-year-old presents 2 hours after sudden left hemiparesis. CT shows a 22 mL right putaminal haematoma. On the arterial phase CT angiogram there is a 3 mm rounded focus of 150 Hounsfield units lying within the clot, not continuous with any adjacent vessel, which enlarges on the delayed acquisition. What does this predict?
quiz.answer: A high risk of haematoma expansion, warranting monitored care and early repeat imaging
choices: A high risk of haematoma expansion, warranting monitored care and early repeat imaging
An underlying ruptured aneurysm, warranting immediate catheter angiography and coiling
Calcification in a long-standing cavernous malformation, warranting outpatient MRI only
Contrast within a normal lenticulostriate branch, warranting no change to the current plan
quiz.explain: This is the spot sign: a focus of contrast extravasation within the haematoma, conventionally at least 1.5 mm, with attenuation clearly above the surrounding clot, discontinuous from any normal or abnormal vessel, and growing on delayed phases. It marks bleeding that is still happening and is one of the better predictors of haematoma expansion in the first few hours, with more and larger foci predicting more growth. Expansion itself is conventionally defined as growth of at least 33% relative or at least 6 mL absolute on repeat CT, and it is strongly associated with deterioration. The consequence is practical rather than glamorous: a monitored bed, prompt blood pressure control, urgent reversal of any anticoagulant, and a repeat scan rather than waiting for the patient to declare themselves. Trials of haemostatic therapy targeted at spot-positive patients have not shown a clear outcome benefit, so the sign informs vigilance, not a specific drug. Unenhanced markers point the same way: the blend sign, black hole sign, island sign and an irregular heterogeneous clot.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these MRI stages of an intraparenchymal haematoma in the order they occur from the moment of bleeding onwards.
quiz.answer: hyperacute acute early-subacute late-subacute chronic
quiz.explain: The sequence is driven by what happens to the haemoglobin iron and by whether it is inside or outside intact red cells. Hyperacute, within the first day, the clot is oxyhaemoglobin and diamagnetic: isointense to slightly hypointense on T1 and bright on T2, essentially looking like water with a rim. Acute, roughly days one to three, oxygen is stripped to deoxyhaemoglobin, which is paramagnetic but sequestered inside cells, so T2 goes dark while T1 stays middling. Early subacute, from about day three, deoxyhaemoglobin oxidises to intracellular methaemoglobin: T1 becomes bright, T2 stays dark. Late subacute, from about a week to a month, the cells lyse and methaemoglobin becomes extracellular, so both T1 and T2 are bright — the easiest stage to recognise. Chronic, beyond a month, iron is stored as haemosiderin and ferritin in macrophages at the rim, dark on T1 and T2 and blooming heavily on gradient echo and susceptibility imaging. The practical use is dating: a haematoma that does not follow this progression, or that has non-haemorrhagic enhancing tissue within it, should raise the question of an underlying tumour or malformation.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old has thunderclap headache. CT shows blood centred in the interpeduncular and prepontine cisterns with a little in the ambient cisterns, no extension into the anterior interhemispheric fissure or the lateral sylvian fissures, and no intraventricular blood. A good quality thin-section CT angiogram is negative. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
quiz.answer: Manage as non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage; the yield of further angiography is very low
choices: Treat as aneurysmal regardless and repeat catheter angiography at one week and again at three months
Assume a missed posterior inferior cerebellar aneurysm and proceed directly to surgical exploration
Attribute the blood to a spinal arteriovenous fistula and image the whole spinal cord urgently instead
Manage as non-aneurysmal perimesencephalic haemorrhage; the yield of further angiography is very low
quiz.explain: The perimesencephalic pattern is defined by distribution, and the definition is strict: blood centred immediately anterior to the midbrain or pons, with no more than a trace in the proximal sylvian or anterior interhemispheric fissures, and no frank intraventricular blood. Held to that standard, with a technically good CT angiogram that clearly demonstrates the basilar tip and both posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, the probability of an aneurysm is very low, the course is benign, and vasospasm and rebleeding are rare. Many units therefore stop there, although practice still varies and some perform one catheter angiogram; what almost nobody now does is a repeated cycle of angiography. The reason to be strict is the mirror image: a diffuse basal pattern with a negative angiogram deserves repeat imaging, because a small or thrombosed aneurysm is genuinely missed in a few percent. The presumed source in perimesencephalic bleeding is venous or from a small perforator, which is consistent with its confinement and its benign natural history.

quiz.prompt: A CT after thunderclap headache shows the densest blood filling the anterior interhemispheric fissure, a small haematoma in the left gyrus rectus, and blood layering in both lateral ventricles. State which aneurysm you would look for first on the angiogram and one complication you should specifically warn the team about.
quiz.answer: Look first at the anterior communicating artery complex, because interhemispheric and gyrus rectus blood points there. Warn about acute obstructive hydrocephalus from the intraventricular blood, which may need an external ventricular drain urgently.
quiz.explain: The clot points at the hole. Blood centred in the anterior interhemispheric fissure, especially with a haematoma in the gyrus rectus or blood tracking into the septum pellucidum and lateral ventricles, indicates the anterior communicating complex. Blood filling one sylvian fissure with a temporal haematoma indicates a middle cerebral bifurcation aneurysm. Blood in the suprasellar and ambient cisterns on one side, particularly with a third nerve palsy, indicates a posterior communicating origin aneurysm. Blood predominantly in the fourth ventricle and around the foramen magnum indicates a posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm. Saying which one you favour makes the angiogram faster and the interventional plan sharper. The complication to flag with intraventricular extension is acute hydrocephalus, which can develop within hours and is reversible with a drain — so look every time at the temporal horns and the third ventricle. Beyond that, warn about rebleeding before securing, and delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm from about day four to day fourteen.

quiz.prompt: An 81-year-old on no anticoagulant has a spontaneous right occipital lobar haematoma. Susceptibility-weighted imaging shows numerous cortical and subcortical microbleeds with sparing of the basal ganglia, thalami and pons, plus curvilinear low signal over two convexity sulci. What should you conclude and convey?
quiz.answer: Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy on the Boston criteria version 2.0, which argues against anticoagulation
choices: Hypertensive small vessel disease, whose microbleeds concentrate in the basal ganglia, thalami and pons
Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy on the Boston criteria version 2.0, which argues against anticoagulation
Haemorrhagic metastases, which would show enhancing nodules and disproportionate surrounding vasogenic oedema
Multiple cavernous malformations, which would show complete haemosiderin rims around popcorn-like cores
quiz.explain: The location argument is the strongest tool you have in spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage. Hypertensive bleeds arise from lipohyalinotic deep perforators and sit in the putamen and external capsule, the thalamus, the pons and the cerebellar dentate; their chronic microbleeds sit in the same deep places. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy affects leptomeningeal and cortical vessels, so its bleeds are lobar and corticosubcortical, with an occipital predilection, and its microbleeds spare the deep grey. The curvilinear sulcal low signal is cortical superficial siderosis, and the Boston criteria version 2.0 of 2022 incorporate it explicitly: in a patient aged 50 or over with lobar haemorrhage and no other cause, probable amyloid angiopathy can be reached with two or more haemorrhagic lesions, or with one haemorrhagic lesion plus a white matter feature such as severe centrum semiovale perivascular spaces or a multispot white matter pattern. The consequence is a conversation about anticoagulation, since amyloid angiopathy carries a high annual recurrence risk. Metastases and cavernomas look different, and the stem's distribution excludes both.

quiz.prompt: An arteriovenous malformation has a nidus measuring 4.2 cm in maximum diameter, lies within the left precentral gyrus, and drains through a subependymal vein into the internal cerebral vein. Give its Spetzler–Martin grade. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Spetzler–Martin scale sums three components. Size scores 1 for a nidus under 3 cm, 2 for 3 to 6 cm and 3 for over 6 cm, so 4.2 cm scores 2. Eloquence of adjacent brain scores 1 if present and 0 if not; the precentral gyrus is eloquent, along with sensory cortex, language cortex, visual cortex, the internal capsule, thalamus, hypothalamus, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles and deep cerebellar nuclei, so that adds 1. Venous drainage scores 1 if any component is deep and 0 if it is entirely superficial; drainage into the internal cerebral vein is deep, so that adds 1 more. Total 4. The scale predicts surgical morbidity, and grades 4 and 5 are usually managed conservatively or with staged embolisation and radiosurgery rather than primary resection. Your report should therefore state each component explicitly rather than only the total, and add the features that carry independent bleeding risk: prior haemorrhage, an intranidal or flow-related aneurysm, venous stenosis and exclusively deep drainage.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with a small cerebellar haemorrhage has MRI showing a 12 mm lesion with a mixed-signal core and a complete low-signal rim on susceptibility imaging, immediately adjacent to a tuft of small veins converging on a single enlarged transcortical draining vein. How should this be managed?
quiz.answer: Leave the venous anomaly alone and direct treatment at the cavernous malformation beside it
choices: Embolise the venous anomaly, since it is the arteriovenous shunt responsible for this bleed
Resect both lesions together, since the anomaly recruits arterial supply once it has bled
Leave the venous anomaly alone and direct treatment at the cavernous malformation beside it
Report an arteriovenous malformation and grade it for radiosurgery on the Spetzler–Martin scale
quiz.explain: Two lesions, only one of which bleeds. The caput medusae of small medullary veins draining into a single large collecting vein is a developmental venous anomaly, an anatomical variant of normal venous drainage rather than a malformation with a shunt. It carries essentially no bleeding risk of its own, and crucially it drains normal brain, so occluding or resecting it causes venous infarction — which is why the correct action is to leave it and to say so plainly in the report. The lesion with the mixed-signal popcorn core and the complete haemosiderin rim is a cavernous malformation, and cavernomas are the things that bleed. They are associated with venous anomalies often enough that finding one should prompt a careful search for the other. If surgery is contemplated, the surgeon must preserve the draining vein. An arteriovenous malformation would show enlarged feeding arteries, a compact nidus and early venous filling on angiography, none of which is described here.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old fell three weeks ago and the CT is reported as normal. Looking again, the sulci over the left convexity are effaced, the grey–white junction is displaced inwards, and the left hemisphere looks subtly compressed. State what is most likely happening and give one manoeuvre at the workstation that will confirm it.
quiz.answer: This is most likely an isodense subacute subdural haematoma, at the stage where its attenuation matches cortex. Confirm it by widening the display to subdural windows, around 150 to 200 units wide, which separates the collection from the underlying cortex, and compare the two sides at identical slices.
quiz.explain: Acute extravasated blood measures around 50 to 70 Hounsfield units and then loses roughly 1.5 units a day as the clot breaks down, so somewhere between about one and three weeks it passes through the attenuation of cortex and becomes invisible on standard brain windows. The trap is real: the scan looks unremarkable until you notice the secondary signs — effaced sulci on one side, inward displacement of the grey–white interface, a cortex that appears abnormally thick, midline shift out of keeping with any visible lesion. Widening the window compresses the greyscale of the brain and lets the collection separate from cortex; comparing the two hemispheres on the same slice is the other half of the trick. If doubt persists, MRI is definitive because subacute blood is bright on T1, and a contrast-enhanced CT shows the enhancing displaced cortical veins. Bilateral isodense collections are the hardest of all, since there is no shift and no asymmetry to alert you — look for the absent sulci at the vertex.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old with haemoglobin 68 g/L after a gastrointestinal bleed falls and strikes their head. CT shows a 9 mm crescentic collection over the right convexity measuring 38 Hounsfield units, without internal septation, and the injury is definitely recent. How should you interpret the density?
quiz.answer: Acute blood becomes isodense to cortex at very low haemoglobin, so an acute subdural remains possible
choices: The density proves a chronic collection at least three weeks old, so this trauma cannot be the cause
The density indicates a subdural hygroma, so the collection is cerebrospinal fluid rather than any blood
The density indicates an early empyema, so contrast and inflammatory markers should be the next step
Acute blood becomes isodense to cortex at very low haemoglobin, so an acute subdural remains possible
quiz.explain: The attenuation of blood on CT is driven mostly by the protein in haemoglobin, so it falls with the haemoglobin concentration. At a haemoglobin of around 80 to 100 g/L, fresh blood can measure close to grey matter, and below that it can look frankly hypodense, meaning an acute subdural haematoma in a profoundly anaemic patient can be reported as chronic or missed altogether. Density alone therefore never dates a collection; you read it alongside the history, the shape, and the presence of a fluid–fluid level or a mixed-density clot, which suggests active bleeding or rebleeding into an older collection. A hygroma is genuinely cerebrospinal fluid density, near zero, typically after trauma or shunting, and it lacks the internal complexity of chronic haematoma. An empyema is usually loculated with an enhancing membrane and restricted diffusion, with a septic patient attached. Coagulopathy is the other setting that changes appearance, producing unclotted low-density blood layered against denser clot.

quiz.prompt: A clinician asks whether adding a susceptibility-weighted sequence changes anything when the CT has already shown a lobar haematoma in a 78-year-old. Give the strongest reason to acquire it and one caveat about interpreting what it shows.
quiz.answer: The strongest reason is that susceptibility imaging detects lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis, which support cerebral amyloid angiopathy and directly influence whether anticoagulation is restarted. The caveat is that blooming exaggerates lesion size, and calcification, cavernomas and small vessels can mimic microbleeds, so phase images and a second sequence are needed before counting them.
quiz.explain: Susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the phase difference between paramagnetic blood products and surrounding tissue and is substantially more sensitive to microbleeds than conventional gradient echo, which is itself far more sensitive than CT. In an elderly patient with a lobar haemorrhage, that sensitivity is what turns a single event into a pattern: strictly lobar microbleeds with deep sparing and cortical superficial siderosis fulfil elements of the Boston criteria version 2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and cortical superficial siderosis in particular predicts recurrent lobar haemorrhage. That is exactly the evidence a cardiologist needs when weighing atrial fibrillation against bleeding risk. The interpretive caveats are worth stating in the report. Blooming makes every lesion look larger than it is and the apparent size varies with echo time and field strength, so counts are not comparable between scanners. Calcification also blooms, and phase imaging distinguishes it from haemorrhage. Finally, do not count microbleeds within or immediately around the acute haematoma — they are part of the index bleed.

curriculum_modules.title: Interventional Radiology: Access, Embolisation and Drainage

module_contract.goal: Gain and close vascular access safely, choose the embolic agent and the level of occlusion the target demands, plan a drainage route, and recognise the common complications early enough to act on them.

approach.step: Fix the bleeding-risk category before the drapes go on
approach.detail: Angiography, chemoembolisation, uterine fibroid embolisation and venous intervention are moderate risk — INR routinely, target INR < 1.5, aPTT < 1.5 × control, platelets ≥ 50,000/μL. TIPS, biliary intervention through a new tract, complex ablation, renal biopsy and nephrostomy are high risk, and need INR, aPTT, platelets and haematocrit.

approach.step: Get access under image guidance, by Seldinger
approach.detail: Hollow needle into the lumen, soft curved-tip wire advanced through it, needle removed over the held wire, sheath passed over the wire, wire withdrawn. Everything afterwards goes through the sheath. Modified Seldinger advances a catheter over the needle instead, then uses it as the conduit for the wire.

approach.step: Never let go of the wire
approach.detail: The complication list of vascular access is short and mostly mechanical: failed access, haemorrhage, infection, visceral perforation, guidewire embolus and pseudoaneurysm. Wire discipline prevents two of the six.

Double-wall puncture — through the anterior and posterior wall, then withdrawing into the lumen — is obsolete under image guidance and causes haematoma, arteriovenous fistula and retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

approach.step: Decide the level of occlusion before you choose the agent
approach.detail: Proximal occlusion with coils or a plug preserves distal tissue and permits collateral supply. Distal occlusion with particles or a liquid devascularises the bed and is what you want for a tumour — and what you must avoid where non-target tissue shares the supply.
Gelfoam and autologous clot are temporary and appropriate where the bleeding will stop and the organ should recover. PVA, microspheres, coils, glue and EVOH copolymers are permanent.

approach.step: Name the non-target territory out loud before you inject
approach.detail: Run the angiogram from the position you will embolise from, at the flow rate you will use, and identify every branch the agent could reflux into.
Set the observation period, the parameters that trigger escalation, and the restart time for anticoagulation before the patient leaves the room.

measure.what: Coagulation before a moderate-risk vascular intervention
measure.how: Angiography, chemoembolisation, uterine fibroid embolisation, venous intervention. INR checked routinely.
TIPS, biliary intervention through a new tract, complex radiofrequency ablation, nephrostomy. Full screen: INR, aPTT, platelets, haematocrit.
Held before the procedure, aPTT checked, protamine available for rapid reversal.
measure.cutoff: Hold 4 h · aPTT < 1.5 × control · restart 6–48 h

measure.what: Dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary stenting
measure.how: Do not interrupt inside the window without a cardiology opinion.
measure.cutoff: Bare metal: ≥ 6 weeks, ideally 3 months · drug-eluting: 6–12 months

classify.name: Embolic agents by permanence and class
rows: Autologous blood clot; gelfoam sponge or powder; starch microspheres; microfibrillar collagen haemostat (Avitene); thrombin phase-change nanoparticles
Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA); trisacryl gelatin microspheres; drug-eluting beads
EVOH copolymers (Onyx, Squid, Menox, LAVA); PHIL; EasyX; OBSIDIO
Absolute alcohol; sodium tetradecyl sulfate; polidocanol; ethanolamine oleate; bleomycin; doxycycline
Amplatz plug; caterpillar device; LOBO braided occluder; IMPEDE cross-polymer plug; EMBA Hourglass; balloons
classify.note: PVA works by adhering to the vessel wall and provoking thrombus rather than by plugging the lumen mechanically. The first embolic agent used was autologous clot, in 1974.

pitfalls: Choosing the agent before choosing the level. Particles and liquids travel distally and devascularise the bed; coils and plugs occlude proximally and leave collaterals to fill. The wrong level either fails to stop the bleeding or infarcts an organ.
Using a permanent agent where the organ has to recover. Gelfoam and autologous clot exist for exactly that case.
Blind double-wall puncture. It belongs to the pre-imaging era and causes haematoma, arteriovenous fistula and retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

Losing wire control during an exchange. Guidewire embolus is on the standard complication list of the Seldinger technique, alongside failed access, haemorrhage, infection, visceral perforation and pseudoaneurysm.
Embolising from a position you have not angiographically cleared. The completion run is not the place to discover a branch you should have protected.

Treating an embolisation as low risk because it is percutaneous. Chemoembolisation and fibroid embolisation are moderate-risk procedures for coagulation purposes; TIPS and new-tract biliary work are high risk.
Discharging without a restart plan. The omitted resumption of anticoagulation causes as much harm as the omitted hold.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of the Seldinger technique for arterial access in the order they are performed.
quiz.answer: puncture-vessel confirm-pulsatile-return advance-guidewire withdraw-needle railroad-sheath remove-wire-and-dilator
quiz.explain: The whole logic of Seldinger's method is that nothing wide ever passes through tissue unless a wire is already sitting in the lumen for it to follow. Puncture the anterior wall, confirm pulsatile return, then feed the guidewire until it advances without resistance. If it does not advance freely, stop and look rather than push, because a wire forced into a subintimal plane is where most access complications begin. Only then does the needle come out over the wire, with the wire held. The sheath and its dilator follow as a single unit and are withdrawn together, leaving the sheath behind. Keep a hand on the wire at every exchange: a wire lost into the vessel, or dragged out with the dilator, is the most avoidable event in the room.

quiz.prompt: A 6 French angiographic catheter is being selected for a case. What is its outer diameter? Answer in millimetres to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: One French is a third of a millimetre, so dividing the French size by three gives the outer diameter: 6 Fr is 2.0 mm, 5 Fr is about 1.7 mm, 9 Fr is 3.0 mm. The convention that catches people is that catheters are sized by their outer diameter while sheaths are sized by their inner diameter, so a 6 Fr sheath will take a 6 Fr catheter but its own outer diameter is roughly 2 Fr larger, making an arteriotomy nearer 8 Fr, about 2.7 mm. That difference drives the closure strategy and the access site complication rate, because those complications scale with the hole in the artery rather than with the catheter inside it. Microcatheters are quoted in French too, typically 2.0 to 2.8 Fr, and their usability is set by the inner lumen of the guide and the wire they will accept.

quiz.prompt: Forty minutes after sheath removal from a right common femoral puncture, a patient becomes tachycardic and hypotensive with lower abdominal and back pain. The groin looks unremarkable, with no palpable swelling and no bruit, and both feet are warm. What has most likely happened?
quiz.answer: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a puncture above the inguinal ligament
choices: Retroperitoneal haemorrhage from a puncture above the inguinal ligament
A pseudoaneurysm arising from a puncture of the superficial femoral artery
An arteriovenous fistula between the femoral artery and the adjacent vein
Acute limb ischaemia from thrombus at the site of the arteriotomy closure
quiz.explain: A puncture above the inguinal ligament enters the external iliac artery, where there is no femoral head behind the vessel to compress against, so blood tracks freely into the retroperitoneum while the groin stays deceptively normal. Hypotension with flank, back or lower abdominal pain after femoral access is retroperitoneal haemorrhage until proven otherwise: resuscitate, cross-match, and get a CT, or take the unstable patient straight to angiography for balloon occlusion or a covered stent. The alternatives look different. A pseudoaneurysm from a low puncture presents hours to days later as a painful pulsatile swelling with a bruit; an arteriovenous fistula gives a continuous bruit and rarely destabilises anyone; limb ischaemia gives a cold, pulseless leg rather than shock. Prevention is the real lesson: puncture over the lower half of the femoral head with fluoroscopy or ultrasound, never by palpation of the skin crease.

quiz.prompt: Two days after a 6 French femoral procedure a patient returns with a tender pulsatile groin swelling. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm sac with a 1 cm neck and to-and-fro flow within the neck. The overlying skin is intact and the leg is well perfused. What is the appropriate first treatment?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac, away from the neck
choices: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac, away from the neck
Immediate surgical exploration with direct repair of the arteriotomy
A covered stent placed across the neck from a contralateral approach
Observation alone, with repeat ultrasound at six weeks to show closure
quiz.explain: A post-catheterisation pseudoaneurysm with a narrow neck and intact skin is treated by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, which thromboses the sac in the great majority of patients at one sitting. The needle tip goes into the body of the sac well away from the neck, and injection stops the instant flow ceases, so that thrombin cannot track into the femoral artery and embolise distally. Small pseudoaneurysms under about 2 cm often thrombose on their own and can reasonably be watched, but a symptomatic 3 cm sac is not one of them. Surgery is reserved for rapid expansion, threatened or broken skin, infection, distal ischaemia, or failure of thrombin. A covered stent in the common femoral artery is poor practice, since it lies across a flexion point and a future access site. Look for an accompanying arteriovenous fistula before treating, because that changes the plan.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with bronchiectasis has massive haemoptysis. Angiography shows a hypertrophied, tortuous right bronchial artery and no spinal branch is seen. Say which embolic agent you would deliver, and explain why coils and very small particles are both poor choices here.
quiz.answer: Deliver calibrated particles of roughly 300 to 500 micrometres through a microcatheter positioned distally in the bronchial artery. Coils occlude the vessel proximally, which stops today's bleeding but blocks catheter access when haemoptysis recurs, and recurrence is common because collaterals refill the bed beyond the coil. Particles much smaller than 300 micrometres, and liquid agents, can pass through a spinal or bronchopulmonary anastomosis and cause spinal cord infarction or bronchial wall necrosis.
quiz.explain: The choice of embolic follows what the target needs. A vascular bed to be devascularised takes particles; a single high-flow vessel to be shut takes coils or a vascular plug; an arteriovenous malformation, or a bleed in a coagulopathic patient, takes a liquid agent such as glue or an ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer, because it polymerises without needing the patient to clot. Bronchial arteries are a bed, and one that is very likely to be worked on again, since recurrent haemoptysis after bronchial artery embolisation is frequent over the following years, so preserving the route back in matters as much as today's haemostasis. The specific hazard is the anterior spinal artery, which can arise from an intercostobronchial trunk: look for it before you embolise, and size the particles so that they lodge before reaching anything you could not see. Gelatin sponge is temporary and is reserved for situations where recanalisation is actually wanted.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a bleeding posterior duodenal ulcer has failed two endoscopic attempts and remains transfusion-dependent. Catheter angiography shows no active extravasation and no pseudoaneurysm. What is the appropriate course?
quiz.answer: Empirical embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery, on both sides of the ulcer
choices: Empirical embolisation of the gastroduodenal artery, on both sides of the ulcer
Stop, and repeat angiography only once further bleeding is clinically documented
Embolisation of the left gastric artery, which supplies the posterior duodenal wall
A covered stent in the common hepatic artery, across the origin of the ulcer supply
quiz.explain: A duodenal ulcer that has defeated endoscopy is embolised whether or not extravasation is visible, because angiography sees only bleeding that is active during the run, and a negative study in a transfusion-dependent patient does not mean the vessel is safe. The gastroduodenal artery is occluded on both sides of the bleeding point, front door and back door, because the pancreaticoduodenal arcades reconstitute it retrogradely from the superior mesenteric artery: a proximal coil alone leaves the ulcer perfused from below while removing the route you would need to get back to it. The duodenum tolerates the occlusion thanks to that same dual supply. The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curve of the stomach rather than the duodenum, and a covered hepatic artery stent treats a hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm, a different problem. Waiting for documented rebleeding squanders the safest window to intervene.

quiz.prompt: CT angiography localises acute bleeding to a branch of the right colic artery in a patient with diverticular disease, and catheter angiography confirms the bleeding branch. Which technique keeps the risk of bowel infarction lowest?
quiz.answer: Advance a microcatheter to the vasa recta and deploy microcoils at that level
choices: Advance a microcatheter to the vasa recta and deploy microcoils at that level
Deliver 100 to 300 micrometre particles from within the right colic artery
Occlude the ileocolic artery proximally with a gelatin sponge slurry instead
Deploy a vascular plug in the superior mesenteric artery branch that supplies it
quiz.explain: The colon has little useful collateral once you are beyond the marginal artery, so lower gastrointestinal embolisation is always a trade between stopping the bleeding and infarcting bowel. Superselective microcoils in the vasa recta or the terminal branch closest to the bleeding point occlude the smallest territory available, usually one or two vasa recta, and ischaemic complications with that technique are uncommon and mostly self-limiting. Small particles do the opposite: they travel beyond the level you can see and lodge in the mucosal capillary bed, which is precisely the tissue that infarcts. Proximal occlusion with gelatin sponge or a plug lowers perfusion pressure across a wide segment while leaving collateral inflow to the bleeding point, so it risks ischaemia and may not achieve haemostasis. If you cannot reach the target vessel, stop and hand over rather than embolise from wherever the catheter happens to sit.

quiz.prompt: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is being created for recurrent variceal bleeding, and the portosystemic pressure gradient before the shunt is 21 mmHg. To what value must the gradient be brought down, at most, for the shunt to be considered adequate for variceal bleeding? Answer in mmHg as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Variceal bleeding does not occur below a portosystemic gradient of about 12 mmHg, and that figure is the target after a shunt created for variceal haemorrhage: dilate until the measured gradient is 12 or less, and measure rather than assume, since the pressures often do not follow the angiographic appearance. Lower is not better. The more portal flow that bypasses the liver, the greater the risk of hepatic encephalopathy, which affects a substantial minority of patients after the procedure and is the commonest reason a shunt has to be reduced or occluded later. Refractory ascites is often managed with a slightly less aggressive reduction for that reason. Patient selection carries as much weight as technique: heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension and uncontrolled sepsis are the standing contraindications, because a shunt delivers a sudden rise in preload to a right ventricle that may not tolerate it.

quiz.prompt: Four patients with hepatocellular carcinoma are discussed at the multidisciplinary meeting. Which one is the appropriate candidate for transarterial chemoembolisation?
quiz.answer: Multifocal tumour confined to the liver, Child-Pugh A, with a patent portal vein
choices: Multifocal tumour confined to the liver, Child-Pugh A, with a patent portal vein
A single 2 cm tumour in a Child-Pugh A patient who is fit for surgical resection
Tumour thrombus filling the main portal vein, Child-Pugh B7, performance status 0
Diffuse tumour with refractory ascites and encephalopathy, Child-Pugh C, ten points
quiz.explain: Chemoembolisation is the standard treatment for intermediate-stage disease: multinodular tumour still confined to the liver, preserved liver function and good performance status, with no macrovascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread, which is BCLC stage B. The reason the other three fail is the same in each case, that the procedure deliberately infarcts liver tissue and the liver must be able to absorb that insult. A patient fit for resection or ablation should have the curative treatment rather than a palliative one. Main portal vein occlusion means the hepatic artery is now supplying tissue that has lost its other inflow, so embolising it risks hepatic infarction, although selective treatment is sometimes used with segmental thrombus in experienced hands. Decompensated Child-Pugh C disease belongs to transplant assessment or supportive care. Expect post-embolisation syndrome afterwards in most patients: that is the treatment working.

quiz.prompt: A woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease needs six months of intermittent adjuvant chemotherapy. The ward has requested a PICC. Say what device you would place instead, and give two reasons for the change.
quiz.answer: Place a totally implantable chest port. First, a PICC would consume the arm veins she is likely to need for an arteriovenous fistula if her kidney disease progresses to dialysis, and it can stenose the subclavian or brachiocephalic vein and make the whole limb unusable for access. Second, a port suits intermittent treatment over months: it sits under intact skin between cycles, carries a lower infection rate per catheter-day than a PICC, and interferes far less with washing, working and sleeping.
quiz.explain: Choosing venous access is a question of how long, how often, how fast, and what the patient will need next. Under two weeks in hospital calls for a non-tunnelled line; weeks to a few months of continuous or daily therapy suits a PICC; months to years of intermittent treatment suits a port; high-flow or frequent access, apheresis or dialysis needs a tunnelled cuffed catheter. Vein preservation cuts across all of it, and in advanced chronic kidney disease the cephalic and basilic veins are a future fistula rather than a convenient route today. Ask about the dialysis plan before you puncture anything, and where a PICC is unavoidable in such a patient, discuss it with the renal team and use the non-dominant arm they nominate. Choose the smallest catheter with enough lumens, since infection and thrombosis both track with size and with the number of lumens.

quiz.prompt: Thirty-six hours after transarterial chemoembolisation for hepatocellular carcinoma a patient has a temperature of 38.4 degrees, right upper quadrant pain, nausea and a white cell count of 14. Ultrasound shows no collection, a normal gallbladder and normal bile ducts. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.answer: Post-embolisation syndrome from the infarcted tumour, needing supportive care
choices: Post-embolisation syndrome from the infarcted tumour, needing supportive care
A developing hepatic abscess within the treated segment, needing drainage
Non-target embolisation of the cystic artery, causing ischaemic cholecystitis
Catheter-related bloodstream infection seeded from the femoral access site
quiz.explain: Fever, pain, nausea and a raised white cell count in the first two to three days after embolisation are the expected inflammatory response to infarcted tissue. Most patients have some of it after chemoembolisation, and after uterine artery embolisation too. Treat with fluids, analgesia and antiemetics, warn the patient beforehand so that they are not frightened by it, and expect it to settle within a few days. Time course and trajectory separate it from the alternatives: an abscess declares itself later, with a collection and often gas, and is far likelier in a patient with a bilioenteric anastomosis or an incompetent sphincter of Oddi; ischaemic cholecystitis follows non-target embolisation and shows a distended, thick-walled gallbladder; a line infection has no reason to localise to the right upper quadrant. The fever that matters is the one still climbing on day five rather than falling, and that one gets re-imaged.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm presacral abscess after anterior resection cannot be reached from the front because of bowel and bladder, so a transgluteal approach is planned. Where should the needle cross the greater sciatic notch?
quiz.answer: Medially and inferiorly, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
choices: Medially and inferiorly, close to the sacrum and below the piriformis muscle
Laterally through the notch, keeping well clear of the adjacent sacral cortex
Superiorly through the notch, passing immediately above the piriformis muscle
Through the sacrospinous ligament, angled forwards towards the ischial spine
quiz.explain: The sciatic nerve and the gluteal vessels occupy the lateral part of the greater sciatic notch, so a transgluteal puncture is taken as close to the sacrum as the anatomy permits and inferior to the piriformis, where the corridor is relatively bare. Crossing laterally is the error that produces a lasting sciatic neuropathy or serious gluteal bleeding, and passing above the piriformis threatens the superior gluteal artery, which is hard to compress and awkward to catheterise if it bleeds. Transgluteal drains hurt, because the catheter crosses muscle that moves with every step, so exclude the shorter routes first: transrectal or transvaginal drainage is well tolerated for a collection abutting either wall, and endoscopic transrectal drainage may be available. Where no safe window genuinely exists, say so in writing rather than accept a marginal one.

quiz.prompt: During prostatic artery embolisation, cone-beam CT from the left prostatic artery opacifies a small branch running to the rectal wall. Say what you do before delivering any particles, and what you are preventing.
quiz.answer: Reposition the microcatheter distal to the origin of that branch and repeat the cone-beam CT to confirm the rectum no longer opacifies. If the branch cannot be bypassed, occlude it with a coil to protect it before embolising. This prevents non-target embolisation causing rectal ischaemia and ulceration, and the same manoeuvre protects branches running to the bladder, the seminal vesicles and the penis.
quiz.explain: Prostatic arterial anatomy is highly variable and richly anastomotic, and the pelvic branches it communicates with, middle rectal, vesical and internal pudendal, supply tissue that does not forgive infarction. Cone-beam CT before embolisation is what makes the procedure safe, because a two-dimensional angiographic run cannot tell you which organ a small branch is heading for. There are two responses and they are both simple: get distal to the anastomosis, which a microcatheter usually manages, or coil the branch so that particles cannot enter it. Particle size helps as well, since larger microspheres are less likely to traverse a small anastomosis. Non-target embolisation announces itself afterwards as rectal pain and bleeding, dysuria and haematuria, or penile ulceration, and avoiding it is most of what separates a good service from a bad one.

quiz.prompt: A haemodynamically stable 24-year-old has a grade IV splenic laceration with a contrast blush on the arterial phase and a moderate haemoperitoneum. Say what you would offer, and explain why occluding the proximal splenic artery does not infarct the spleen.
quiz.answer: Offer splenic artery embolisation to support non-operative management and preserve the spleen. A coil or plug placed in the proximal splenic artery, beyond the dorsal pancreatic branch, lowers the perfusion pressure reaching the injured parenchyma so that it can clot, while the spleen stays perfused through collateral supply from the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries. A single focal injury can instead be embolised selectively; multiple or diffuse bleeding points favour the proximal approach.
quiz.explain: Non-operative management succeeds in the great majority of haemodynamically stable patients with splenic injury, and embolisation extends it to the high AAST grades that once went straight to splenectomy. A contrast blush, a pseudoaneurysm or an arteriovenous fistula on the arterial phase is the finding that predicts failure of observation alone and identifies the patient who gains from the angiography suite. The mechanism worth holding on to is perfusion pressure rather than occlusion: the collateral network through the short gastrics and the gastroepiploic arcade keeps the organ alive while pressure at the tear falls far enough for haemostasis, which is also why splenic immune function is largely retained, though local policy on vaccination after proximal embolisation varies. Keep the coil beyond the dorsal pancreatic artery to avoid pancreatic ischaemia. The unstable patient still goes to theatre; embolisation is for the patient whose physiology grants you the time.

module_contract.goal: Report a knee MRI so that you name the meniscal tear pattern and its mechanical consequence, recognise ligament injury from direct and secondary signs, and grade cartilage and patellofemoral injury in terms that change management.

approach.detail: Two criteria make a tear: abnormal meniscal shape, and high signal unequivocally contacting the meniscal surface on proton density images.

approach.step: Insist the signal reaches the surface
approach.detail: Only when the high signal unequivocally reaches the surface of the meniscus can you call a tear. Menisci do not have to be homogeneously dark on PD.

approach.step: Name the plane of the tear
approach.detail: Longitudinal runs parallel to the long axis at a constant distance from the outer margin. Horizontal splits the meniscus into superior and inferior halves. Radial runs perpendicular to the long axis.

approach.step: Recognise the radial tear by its two signs
approach.detail: A triangle missing its tip on one plane, and a disrupted bow tie on the perpendicular plane. Both come from the same lesion.
Bucket-handle, flap and parrot-beak tears all displace. If part of the meniscus is missing from where it should be, find where it has gone before you finish.
Root tears are radial tears at the meniscal attachment — an absent meniscus or empty meniscus sign next to the PCL insertion.

approach.step: Then the rest of the knee
approach.detail: Cruciates, collaterals, cartilage, bone bruise pattern. The bruise pattern names the mechanism.

measure.how: High signal traced to the meniscal surface, confirmed on a second plane.
Proportion of fibres not traceable from tibia to femur. MRI separates high from low grade, not complete from partial.
Avulsion of the lateral collateral band, visible on radiographs.

classify.name: Meniscal tear patterns and what they mean mechanically
rows: Parallel to the long axis, staying the same distance from the outer margin
Stable unless it displaces; the peripheral vascular zone may be repairable
Displaced longitudinal tear — the inner fragment flips into the notch
Locking. Find the displaced handle before reporting
Divides the meniscus into superior and inferior components
May decompress into a parameniscal cyst
Perpendicular to the long axis: triangle missing the tip on one plane, disrupted bow tie on the perpendicular plane
Interrupts the circumferential collagen — hoop stress is lost
Displaced fragment arising from a horizontal or radial tear
Mechanical symptoms; the fragment may sit in a recess
Radial tear at the attachment — absent meniscus or empty meniscus sign adjacent to the PCL insertion
Functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy; extrusion follows
classify.note: After meniscal surgery, abnormal signal and shape stop being reliable. MR arthrography with dilute gadolinium separates a healed tear from a re-tear.

pitfalls: Calling a tear on intrameniscal signal that never reaches the surface. A meniscus need not be homogeneously dark on proton density, and internal signal alone is degeneration.
Missing the radial tear because you only looked at one plane. The triangle missing its tip and the disrupted bow tie are the same lesion seen on perpendicular planes — you need both.
Reporting a bucket-handle tear without finding the handle. If the meniscus is short, the fragment is somewhere, and the surgeon needs to know where.
Reading the postoperative meniscus by the same rules. Abnormal signal and abnormal shape lose their reliability after repair; use arthrography if the question is a re-tear.

Reporting an ACL as partially torn on MRI. MRI separates high grade from low grade by fibre loss; it does not separate complete from partial — and a Segond fracture on the radiograph carries a 75–100% association with an ACL tear.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old footballer has a locked knee. On the sagittal images through the intercondylar notch there is a low-signal band lying anterior and roughly parallel to the posterior cruciate ligament. On the same 4 mm sagittal series the body of the medial meniscus produces a bow tie on only one slice. What do you report?
quiz.answer: A displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus, fragment lying in the notch
choices: A displaced bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus, fragment lying in the notch
A prominent meniscofemoral ligament of Wrisberg passing behind the posterior cruciate
A torn anterior cruciate bundle displaced forwards to form a cyclops lesion
A normal transverse geniculate ligament crossing the anterior intercondylar area
quiz.explain: Three findings converge. The double PCL sign is a displaced meniscal fragment sitting in the notch beneath the true PCL, and because the medial meniscus is longer and more tethered it accounts for the great majority of these. The absent bow-tie sign is its companion: with 4 to 5 mm sagittal slices a normal meniscal body should produce a bow tie on at least two consecutive images, so a single bow tie means tissue has left the periphery. A locked knee ties it together clinically. Wrisberg runs posterior to the PCL, not anterior, and is a thin band that can be traced to the lateral meniscal posterior horn. A cyclops lesion is a nodule of arthrofibrosis anterior to a reconstructed graft. The transverse geniculate ligament lies anteriorly, between the anterior horns, well away from the notch.

quiz.prompt: Describe the signs you would systematically look for before committing to a diagnosis of a displaced bucket-handle meniscal tear.
quiz.answer: I look for the double PCL sign in the notch, the flipped fragment or double anterior horn sign, an absent bow-tie on fewer than two consecutive sagittal slices, and a truncated or diminutive parent meniscus at the donor site.
quiz.explain: A bucket-handle tear is a longitudinal vertical tear whose inner fragment has hinged into the joint, and every reliable sign is really the same observation made twice: tissue is missing from where it should be and present where it should not. The double PCL sign shows the fragment in the notch. The flipped fragment, or double anterior horn sign, shows it folded forwards on top of the anterior horn, which is the pattern to expect when the handle displaces anteriorly rather than centrally. The absent bow tie quantifies the loss at the donor site. Always confirm that the parent meniscus is truncated, because the displaced fragment has to have come from somewhere; if the meniscus looks intact, reconsider the diagnosis. Reporting it is urgent in a locked knee, since early repair of a peripheral vascular tear preserves the meniscus.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old felt a pop while squatting. The coronal images show a vertical cleft at the posterior attachment of the medial meniscus with no meniscal tissue visible on the slice through the root, the meniscal body lies 5 mm beyond the tibial margin, and there is marrow oedema in the medial femoral condyle. What is the mechanical significance?
quiz.answer: A posterior medial root tear; the extruded meniscus no longer carries hoop stress
choices: A posterior medial root tear; the extruded meniscus no longer carries hoop stress
A degenerative horizontal cleavage tear with a parameniscal cyst at the root
Chondrocalcinosis producing linear meniscal signal that stops short of the surface
A ramp lesion at the meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn medially
quiz.explain: The meniscal roots anchor the circumferential collagen bundles to bone. Cut the root, or make a full radial tear near it, and the meniscus can no longer convert axial load into hoop tension: it simply squeezes outwards. That is why root tears and extrusion travel together, and why a root tear is biomechanically close to a total meniscectomy. The signs are a ghost meniscus on the slice through the root, a vertical cleft on coronal images and extrusion of the body of 3 mm or more measured at the level of the medial collateral ligament. Marrow oedema signals the load now going straight into bone, and subchondral insufficiency fracture is the feared sequel. Report it explicitly, because root repair in the right patient is a different operation from a meniscectomy. A horizontal cleavage tear splits the meniscus into upper and lower leaves and does not abolish hoop stress. Chondrocalcinosis gives linear intrameniscal signal without a surface-reaching cleft.

quiz.prompt: On the coronal image at the level of the medial collateral ligament, the outer margin of the medial meniscal body lies 8.2 mm beyond the mid-coronal tibial plateau margin, but a marginal osteophyte projects 3.4 mm beyond that true plateau margin and must be excluded from the measurement. Report the true meniscal extrusion in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 8.2 minus 3.4 leaves 4.8 mm. Extrusion is measured on the mid-coronal image at the level of the medial collateral ligament, from the outermost meniscal edge to the peripheral tibial cortex, and osteophytes are deliberately excluded because they push the reference line outwards and inflate the figure. Anything at or beyond about 3 mm counts as significant extrusion, and 4.8 mm is well past that. The finding matters because extrusion is a marker of lost hoop-stress function rather than a diagnosis in itself: look immediately for a posterior root tear or a large radial tear, and check the cartilage and subchondral bone of the same compartment, which is where the consequence shows up. Extrusion also increases with weight bearing, so a borderline value on a supine scan may understate the problem.

quiz.prompt: A single sagittal image shows a thin line of high signal reaching the inferior articular surface of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. The images either side of it are normal, the coronal series is normal, and there is no marrow oedema or joint effusion. How should you handle this?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a single-slice finding and do not yet call a tear; specificity is poor
choices: Treat it as a single-slice finding and do not yet call a tear; specificity is poor
Call a definite tear, since one surface-contacting slice is sufficient evidence
Call a bucket-handle tear whose fragment has displaced out of the imaging plane
Attribute it to magic angle effect, expected on short echo time sequences at 55 degrees
quiz.explain: The two-slice-touch rule says a meniscal tear should be called when abnormal signal contacts an articular surface on two or more consecutive images, in either plane. A single contacting slice has a positive predictive value barely better than chance, because volume averaging, vascular remnants, the concave meniscal undersurface and normal insertional signal all generate one-slice findings. Applying the rule lifts specificity substantially at very little cost in sensitivity, and it stops a stream of unnecessary arthroscopies. Say what you saw and say you are not calling it: a one-line comment protects the next reader. Magic angle is a real phenomenon at 55 degrees to the main field on short echo time sequences, but it affects the popliteus and the patellar tendon rather than producing a surface-reaching line in the meniscus. A displaced bucket-handle fragment would leave a truncated parent meniscus, which is absent here.

quiz.prompt: List the normal anatomical structures that most often produce a false-positive meniscal tear, and say where each of them sits.
quiz.answer: The transverse geniculate ligament at the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus, the popliteus tendon and popliteomeniscal fascicles at the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, and the meniscofemoral ligaments of Humphrey and Wrisberg near the lateral posterior root.
quiz.explain: Almost every classic meniscal pseudo-tear is on the lateral side, and each is a normal structure creating a fat or fluid cleft where it meets the meniscus. The transverse geniculate ligament crosses the anterior intercondylar fat and inserts on the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus, producing an oblique line at that junction. The popliteus tendon passes through its hiatus beside the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus, and the superior and inferior popliteomeniscal fascicles create two further clefts. The meniscofemoral ligaments, Humphrey in front of the posterior cruciate and Wrisberg behind it, insert near the posterior root and can mimic a tear or a fragment. The defence is anatomical rather than statistical: follow the suspect line onto adjacent slices and into the orthogonal plane, and if it can be traced to a named structure, it is not a tear.

quiz.prompt: A knee with an acute anterior cruciate rupture is being reported. Say what a ramp lesion is and why it is easy to miss.
quiz.answer: A ramp lesion is a tear at the meniscocapsular junction of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus; it is missed because it lies at the posteromedial corner, shows only as a thin fluid line between meniscus and capsule, and attention is usually on the ACL itself.
quiz.explain: The posteromedial meniscocapsular attachment is a secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation, so it fails alongside the anterior cruciate ligament in a meaningful minority of acute ruptures. The MRI sign is subtle: fluid or high signal interposed between the peripheral edge of the posterior horn and the capsule on fluid-sensitive sagittal and coronal images, sometimes with posteromedial tibial marrow oedema as the only clue. It is also hard to see arthroscopically from the standard anterior portals, which is why the finding is valued. It matters because an unrepaired ramp lesion leaves residual rotational laxity and is associated with graft failure after reconstruction. Make a habit of looking specifically at the posteromedial corner on every acute ACL study rather than trusting incidental detection.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old had a non-contact twisting injury. The knee is too swollen for the cruciate to be traced with confidence, but there is marrow oedema in the sulcus terminalis of the lateral femoral condyle and in the posterolateral tibial plateau, together with a thin vertical cortical avulsion at the lateral tibial rim. What do you conclude?
quiz.answer: A pivot-shift contusion pattern with a Segond fracture: the anterior cruciate is torn
choices: A pivot-shift contusion pattern with a Segond fracture: the anterior cruciate is torn
A dashboard contusion pattern with a reverse Segond, so the posterior cruciate is torn
A hyperextension kissing contusion pattern of the anterior tibia and anterior femur
A lateral patellar dislocation pattern with medial patellar and lateral condylar oedema
quiz.explain: Secondary signs rescue the study when the ligament itself cannot be judged. The pivot shift drives the posterolateral tibial plateau against the lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis, so that pair of contusions is close to diagnostic of an anterior cruciate rupture even when the ligament is obscured. The Segond fracture is a vertical avulsion from the lateral tibial rim at the attachment of the anterolateral capsular structures, and its association with ACL rupture is around ninety per cent, with a high rate of meniscal injury alongside. Other useful secondaries are anterior tibial translation beyond about 5 to 7 mm, an uncovered lateral meniscus and a deep lateral femoral notch. A reverse Segond is a medial tibial rim avulsion and points to the posterior cruciate. The dashboard pattern bruises the anterior tibia. Patellar dislocation bruises the inferomedial patella and the anterolateral condyle, not the posterolateral plateau.

quiz.prompt: Eight months after a hamstring anterior cruciate reconstruction, a patient with a clinically stable knee has an MRI for anterior ache. The graft is continuous, correctly angled along Blumensaat line, with well-placed tunnels, but shows diffuse intermediate signal through its substance and no fluid-filled cleft. What should you say?
quiz.answer: Expected graft remodelling signal at this interval; report the graft as intact
choices: Expected graft remodelling signal at this interval; report the graft as intact
Graft rupture; the raised intrasubstance signal indicates fibre discontinuity
Roof impingement from an anterior tibial tunnel producing the abnormal signal
A cyclops lesion of arthrofibrosis lying in front of the graft and limiting extension
quiz.explain: A new graft is low signal throughout, but between roughly four and twelve months it undergoes revascularisation and remodelling, and diffuse intermediate signal during that window is normal and should not be read as failure. What signals a genuine problem is fluid-signal discontinuity, an abnormally horizontal graft that no longer parallels Blumensaat line, anterior tibial translation, or the graft draping over the intercondylar roof. Tunnel position is worth checking on every post-operative study: an anteriorly placed tibial tunnel causes roof impingement with signal concentrated at the distal graft and a fluid-filled ganglion, while an anteriorly placed femoral tunnel makes the graft tighten in flexion. A cyclops lesion is a discrete nodule of scar anterior to the graft in a patient who cannot fully straighten the knee, which is a different clinical picture from a dull ache.

quiz.prompt: A patient sustained a varus blow. The radiograph shows a small avulsed fragment off the tip of the fibular styloid. On MRI there is fluid around the popliteus tendon at its femoral origin and the lateral collateral ligament is lax and thickened. What must the report emphasise?
quiz.answer: A posterolateral corner injury; missing it is a recognised cause of graft failure
choices: A posterolateral corner injury; missing it is a recognised cause of graft failure
An isolated Segond fracture of the lateral tibial plateau with an intact corner
An avulsion of biceps femoris from the fibular head without ligamentous injury
A normal fabella lying posterolateral to the lateral femoral condyle in the capsule
quiz.explain: The arcuate sign is an avulsion at the fibular styloid, where the arcuate ligament complex and the popliteofibular ligament insert, and it is a flag for injury to the whole posterolateral corner: lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament and the posterolateral capsule. It is rarely isolated, so search deliberately for cruciate injury alongside it. The reason to be emphatic is surgical: an unrecognised posterolateral corner injury leaves persistent varus and external rotation laxity that stretches out a cruciate reconstruction, and it is one of the commonest causes of graft failure. Check the common peroneal nerve too, since it is injured in a significant minority. A Segond avulsion comes off the tibia, not the fibula, and points anterolaterally. A fabella is a corticated sesamoid within the lateral head of gastrocnemius, well away from the styloid.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these articular cartilage appearances in order of increasing Outerbridge grade.
quiz.answer: softening shallow-fissuring deep-fissuring exposed-subchondral-bone
quiz.explain: Outerbridge was written for what the surgeon sees through the arthroscope and has been adapted for MRI, so the language crosses over usefully. Grade 1 is softening and swelling with an intact surface, which on MRI appears as focal signal change without contour loss. Grade 2 is fissuring or fragmentation through less than half the cartilage thickness. Grade 3 is fissuring deeper than half thickness with the subchondral plate still covered. Grade 4 is full-thickness loss with subchondral bone exposed, usually accompanied by marrow oedema and often by a subchondral cyst. The step that changes management is the one from 3 to 4: full-thickness loss over a defined area in a young patient opens the conversation about resurfacing, whereas partial-thickness change is managed conservatively. Always state the size and location of the defect as well as the grade, because a 5 mm and a 25 mm grade 4 lesion are different problems.

quiz.prompt: A 16-year-old netball player felt the knee give way with the leg planted, and it swelled immediately. MRI shows oedema in the inferomedial patella and the anterolateral aspect of the lateral femoral condyle, disruption of the medial patellofemoral ligament at its femoral attachment, and a 10 mm osteochondral fragment lying in the lateral gutter. What most changes management?
quiz.answer: A transient lateral patellar dislocation with a loose osteochondral fragment to retrieve
choices: A transient lateral patellar dislocation with a loose osteochondral fragment to retrieve
An osteochondritis dissecans of the medial femoral condyle with a stable in-situ fragment
A direct blow to the front of the knee with avulsion of the quadriceps tendon insertion
A bucket-handle meniscal fragment that has displaced laterally into the lateral gutter
quiz.explain: The bone bruise pair is diagnostic even after the patella has relocated: the medial facet of the patella strikes the anterolateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle as it reduces, so oedema appears in both. The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary restraint and usually fails at the femoral attachment near the adductor tubercle. What alters the immediate plan is the loose fragment: an osteochondral body of that size in a young patient is taken to theatre for removal or fixation, whereas the ligament injury and the predisposing features are managed afterwards. Look for and report those predisposing features too, since they drive the decision about stabilisation: trochlear dysplasia, patella alta and a raised tibial tuberosity to trochlear groove distance. Osteochondritis dissecans classically involves the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle, without this bruise pattern or a torn ligament.

quiz.prompt: On the sagittal image of the same knee, the patellar tendon measures 57 mm from the inferior pole of the patella to its tibial insertion, and the greatest diagonal length of the patella is 38 mm. Calculate the Insall-Salvati ratio, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 57 divided by 38 is 1.5. The Insall-Salvati ratio compares patellar tendon length with the greatest diagonal length of the patella; the normal range is about 0.8 to 1.2, so 1.5 is patella alta. That is a meaningful finding in a dislocator, because a high-riding patella engages the trochlear groove later in flexion and is therefore less constrained in the range where the knee is most vulnerable. Report it alongside the other structural risk factors, since together they decide whether the patient is offered a soft-tissue reconstruction alone or a bony procedure. A ratio below 0.8 is patella baja, seen after tibial tuberosity transfer, in chronic arthrofibrosis, or acutely with a quadriceps tendon rupture. Note that the ratio is measured on a lateral radiograph or a sagittal image with the knee in modest flexion, since it is insensitive to knee position compared with some alternatives.

curriculum_modules.title: Bone Marrow, Stress Injury, Muscle and the Diabetic Foot

module_contract.goal: Separate normal marrow and reactive oedema from disease, grade stress and muscle injury by what changes management, and decide osteomyelitis in a neuropathic foot.

approach.step: Mark the ulcer before the patient goes in
approach.detail: Place a marker on the ulcer or sinus tract, track it down to the bone, and read the marrow signal at the end of that track. If there is marrow oedema along the tract, osteomyelitis is very likely.
Confluent low T1 marrow signal in the bone under the ulcer is the finding that makes osteomyelitis. STIR oedema alone does not.
Osteomyelitis lives in the forefoot at the metatarsal heads and interphalangeal joints, and in the hindfoot at the posterior calcaneus. Charcot lives in the midfoot at the tarsometatarsal joints.

approach.step: Ask whether the soft tissues are involved
approach.detail: Osteomyelitis in this foot spreads contiguously from a skin ulcer, so the soft tissues carry an ulcer or sinus tract. Charcot leaves the soft tissues relatively uninvolved.

approach.step: If it is Charcot, look for the ghost sign
approach.detail: Bone margins that are poorly defined on native T1 and become sharp after contrast, enhancing to the brightness of normal marrow, mean neuro-osteoarthropathy with superimposed osteomyelitis.
Abscess, sinus tract, septic arthritis, joint effusion, ligamentous laxity, loose bodies.

measure.how: Physical marker on the ulcer or sinus tract, traced to bone; assess marrow signal at the contact point.
measure.cutoff: Marrow oedema along the tract → osteomyelitis very likely

measure.how: High STIR signal, low to intermediate T1, with ring enhancement after contrast.
Graded 1–4 on periosteal oedema, then marrow signal, then a visible line.
Initial radiographs, then follow-up.

measure.what: MRI versus scintigraphy for stress fracture
measure.how: Both detect the injury; specificity separates them.

classify.name: Osteomyelitis against Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy
rows: Forefoot — metatarsal heads and interphalangeal joints; hindfoot — posterior calcaneus
Contiguous spread from a skin ulcer
Involved — ulcer or sinus tract present
Warm red foot, normal or slightly elevated CRP
classify.note: Both together is the commonest hard problem. The ghost sign settles it: poorly defined bone margins on native T1 that sharpen after contrast, the osteomyelitic bone enhancing to the brightness of normal marrow.

modifiers.meaning: Mild to moderate periosteal oedema on STIR, no marrow changes.
Moderate to severe periosteal oedema on STIR plus marrow changes on T2.
Grade 2 plus marrow changes on T1.
Fracture line visible.
Femoral neck tension side, transverse patella, anterior tibial shaft, medial malleolus, talus, tarsal navicular, fifth metatarsal, sesamoid of the great toe.
Femoral neck compression side, longitudinal patella, posteromedial tibia, fibula, calcaneus, second and third metatarsals.
Partial thickness muscle injuries, suffixed a myofascial, b musculotendinous, c intratendinous.
Full thickness tear, with or without retraction.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
MRI of the [right/left] foot. T1, STIR [preferred over T2 fat-sat — fat suppression is more uniform across the curve of the foot], and post-contrast fat-suppressed T1. Sagittal for the midfoot, plantar surface and posterior calcaneus; axial parallel to the toes for the MTP and IP joints. Skin marker placed on the [ulcer / sinus tract].

FINDINGS
Skin marker sits over the [site]. Tract extends to [bone / stops in soft tissue].
Marrow T1 at the contact point: [normal fatty / confluent low signal].
Marrow STIR: [normal / oedema, confined to [site]].
Post-contrast: [no abnormal enhancement / marrow enhancement / ghost sign present].
Distribution: [forefoot / midfoot / hindfoot].
Soft tissues: [ulcer [n] cm / sinus tract / cellulitis / abscess — high STIR, low-intermediate T1, ring enhancement, [n] cm].
Joints: [effusion / septic arthritis / ligamentous laxity / loose bodies].

IMPRESSION
1. [Osteomyelitis of the [bone] / Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy / both, with the ghost sign].
2. [Soft tissue complications requiring drainage.]
3. [Extent for surgical planning: the proximal limit of marrow involvement is at [level].]
pitfalls: Calling osteomyelitis on STIR oedema alone. Reactive oedema is everywhere in this foot; it is confluent low T1 marrow signal under an ulcer that makes the diagnosis.
Reading the midfoot as infection. Tarsometatarsal disease with uninvolved soft tissues is Charcot, and the clinical picture — warm red foot, near-normal CRP — usually agrees.
Scanning without a marker on the ulcer. The whole method is tracing the ulcer to the bone; without the marker you are guessing which bone.
Combining STIR with contrast. STIR cannot be used post-contrast — the post-contrast series has to be fat-suppressed T1.

Grading a muscle injury by signal intensity alone. Chronic injuries can show only mild signal change and still be high grade clinically; the length of the strain is the best predictor of the duration of disability.

Treating all stress fractures the same. The high-risk sites — femoral neck tension side, anterior tibial shaft, tarsal navicular, fifth metatarsal — heal badly and need naming as high risk in the impression.

learning_points: Signal follows load or nearby inflammation without destructive replacement.
Fracture line or fibre disruption helps grade injury and informs activity modification with clinical findings.
Track ulcer to bone while separating neuropathic joint change.
Review clinical pathway: infection, stress, muscle or marrow disease.
Review signal abnormality: site, length and compartment.
Review fracture line, cortical disruption or muscle/tendon tear.
Review ulcer, sinus tract, collection and enhancement.
Review joint, neurovascular and adjacent tissue involvement.
Oedema is a response pattern, not a specific diagnosis; use the anatomic route and clinical context to narrow its cause.

measurements.name: Stress lesion
measurements.method: Record fracture length/extent, cortical side and displacement where present.
measurements.pitfall: Marrow oedema extent alone is not fracture severity.

measurements.name: Muscle/tendon injury

measurements.pitfall: Oedema can overstate structural disruption.

measurements.pitfall: Fluid signal without supporting features does not prove abscess.

pitfalls: Neuropathic arthropathy and infection can coexist.
Reactive marrow oedema adjacent to an ulcer is not automatically osteomyelitis.
Diffuse muscle oedema has traumatic, denervation, inflammatory and vascular causes.
