quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old woman who smokes twenty a day and runs marathons has a knee MRI for pain. Both the distal femoral and proximal tibial metaphyses contain patchy, symmetric, ill-defined intermediate T1 signal that stays brighter than adjacent skeletal muscle. The epiphyses and subchondral bone are entirely fatty, the cortex is intact and there is no soft-tissue mass. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Normal marrow reconversion; no further marrow imaging is required
choices: Normal marrow reconversion; no further marrow imaging is required
Diffuse marrow infiltration; recommend haematology referral and biopsy
Multifocal marrow oedema; recommend a repeat examination in three months
Marrow replacement by tumour; stage with whole-body imaging next
quiz.explain: Conversion from red to yellow marrow runs from the periphery inwards and from distal to proximal within a limb, with epiphyses and apophyses turning fatty within months of their ossification centre appearing; the adult pattern — red marrow confined to the axial skeleton and the proximal femoral and humeral metaphyses — is settled by the mid-twenties. Reconversion simply runs the film backwards: axial skeleton first, then proximal to distal, and it spares epiphyses. Its drivers are smoking, obesity, altitude, chronic anaemia, endurance training and marrow-stimulating drugs, and this patient has two of them. The rules that protect you are on the T1 image: normal red marrow is brighter than muscle and than a normal disc, is symmetric and ill-defined, and does not touch cortex. Signal at or below muscle, epiphyseal involvement, or a focal well-defined lesion moves you the other way.

quiz.prompt: A focal marrow lesion is interrogated with in-phase and opposed-phase gradient-echo imaging. A region of interest gives a signal intensity of 612 on the in-phase images and 401 on the opposed-phase images. Calculate the opposed-phase signal drop as a percentage of the in-phase signal, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The arithmetic is (612 minus 401) divided by 612, which is 0.345, or 34.5 per cent. The interpretation rests on one idea: fat and water protons in the same voxel cancel on the opposed-phase image, so any tissue containing both loses signal. Normal red marrow is a mixture of haematopoietic cells and fat and typically drops by more than about 20 per cent, whereas a lesion that has replaced the marrow has pushed the fat out and holds its signal or gains a little. A drop of this size therefore favours red marrow or a benign process. Know the failure modes: sclerotic and treated lesions, diffusely infiltrated marrow that still retains some fat early on, and haemorrhagic or iron-laden marrow. At 1.5 T the echo times sit near 2.3 ms opposed and 4.6 ms in phase; at 3 T both halve.

quiz.prompt: You are handed a lumbar spine MRI and asked whether the marrow is normal. Using the sagittal T1 images alone, state the internal comparisons you make and what would make you call the marrow abnormal.
quiz.answer: Compare the marrow with adjacent skeletal muscle and with a normal intervertebral disc on the same T1 image. Normal marrow, red or yellow, is brighter than both. Marrow that is equal to or darker than muscle or disc, whether diffuse or as a focal well-defined lesion, is abnormal and should be characterised further with fluid-sensitive, chemical-shift or diffusion imaging.
quiz.explain: Window and level settings vary, monitors vary, and absolute signal on MRI means nothing, so every marrow judgement is a comparison made inside the same image. Muscle and disc are convenient internal standards because both are reliably present and neither is usually altered by marrow disease. The comparison has real teeth: diffuse marrow signal below that of muscle on T1 in an adult is one of the more reliable signs of infiltration, whether from myeloma, leukaemia or widespread metastasis, and it can be the first clue in a patient scanned for back pain. Two traps: in young children red marrow is normally darker, so the rule is an adult rule; and in a marrow packed with fat by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, an ordinary red marrow island can look startlingly dark against its background.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old man has six weeks of worsening left hip pain and can barely weight-bear. MRI shows diffuse low T1 and high STIR signal through the left femoral head and neck, extending to the intertrochanteric line, with a small effusion, no subchondral low-signal line, no double-line sign and an intact subchondral plate. What is the appropriate report?
quiz.answer: Bone marrow oedema syndrome; protect weight-bearing and reimage later
choices: Bone marrow oedema syndrome; protect weight-bearing and reimage later
Avascular necrosis with collapse; refer for core decompression now
Septic arthritis of the hip; arrange aspiration of the joint today
Subchondral insufficiency fracture; the pattern here is diagnostic
quiz.explain: Marrow oedema is a sign, not a diagnosis, and it is the company it keeps that tells you which one. Here the oedema is diffuse and undemarcated, crossing from head into neck without a boundary, and the subchondral bone is clean — the picture of transient osteoporosis of the hip, or bone marrow oedema syndrome, which affects middle-aged men and women in late pregnancy and settles over six to twelve months with protected loading. Avascular necrosis is defined by its border: a geographic serpiginous low-signal line on T1 and the double line on T2, with oedema appearing late as pain and collapse approach. A subchondral insufficiency fracture shows a low-signal line running parallel to and abutting the subchondral plate. Sepsis is worth a thought with an effusion, but that decision is driven by fever and inflammatory markers, and if they are up you aspirate regardless of the marrow pattern.

quiz.prompt: A distance runner has anteromedial shin pain. MRI shows periosteal oedema and marrow oedema in the posteromedial tibial diaphysis, the marrow abnormality being visible both on the fluid-sensitive images and as low signal on T1, with no discernible fracture line. Using the Fredericson grading of tibial stress injury, what grade is this? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Fredericson scale escalates with what the marrow does: grade 1 is periosteal oedema with normal marrow, grade 2 adds marrow oedema seen only on fluid-sensitive sequences, grade 3 is marrow oedema also visible as low signal on T1, and grade 4 is a visible fracture line — commonly subdivided into 4a, intracortical signal, and 4b, a discrete line. Higher grades take longer to return to running, which is the grading's real use. But the site outranks the grade. This injury is on the posteromedial cortex, the compression side, and it heals with load modification. The same grade on the anterior cortex, which is loaded in tension, is a high-risk lesion prone to non-union. Report the grade if the referrer uses it, but report the surface without fail.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old basketball player has four months of anterior shin pain, worse on landing. Radiographs show fusiform thickening of the anterior tibial cortex at the mid-diaphysis with a transverse lucency crossing the outer cortex. What should the report advise?
quiz.answer: A tension-side high-risk lesion; stop loading and refer for surgical review
choices: A tension-side high-risk lesion; stop loading and refer for surgical review
A benign compression-side injury; a graded return to running is safe
An osteoid osteoma is likely; arrange thin-section CT to find a nidus
A chronic osteomyelitis; arrange MRI to look for a sequestrum
quiz.explain: The anterior tibial cortex is loaded in tension, and a stress fracture there tends not to heal: the lucency persists for months, may go on to complete fracture across the bone, and often needs intramedullary nailing rather than rest. That is what earns it high-risk status. The wider list of tension-side or poorly vascularised sites is worth carrying: the superolateral femoral neck, the medial malleolus, the tarsal navicular, the base of the fifth metatarsal at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction, the great toe sesamoids, the patella and the talus. Low-risk sites — posteromedial tibia, fibula, calcaneus, metatarsal shafts, femoral shaft, the compression side of the femoral neck — heal with rest. Osteoid osteoma is a fair differential, since it too thickens cortex, but its nidus is round and centred rather than a transverse line, and CT settles it.

quiz.prompt: Two patients have sacral fractures with no history of a fall: a 24-year-old army recruit six weeks into basic training, and a 79-year-old woman on long-term corticosteroids. Explain what separates the two mechanisms, and what each obliges you to do beyond reporting the fracture.
quiz.answer: The recruit has a fatigue fracture: abnormal repetitive loading of normal bone, so the action is load modification and a look at training error. The older woman has an insufficiency fracture: normal loading of abnormal, osteoporotic bone, so the report should prompt bone density assessment and treatment of the osteoporosis, and should also raise metastasis or myeloma if the marrow signal or the bone elsewhere does not fit a simple fracture.
quiz.explain: The two words are not interchangeable, and the distinction changes who gets referred where. Sacral insufficiency fractures run vertically through one or both alae, often with a horizontal component across the body, giving the H or Honda configuration classically seen on bone scintigraphy and equally visible as oedema on MRI; they are easy to miss on radiographs and are a common cause of sudden immobility in an older patient. Steroids, radiotherapy, osteomalacia, renal disease and long-term bisphosphonates are the usual soil. The trap is the middle ground: a sacral or pelvic fracture in an older patient may be the presenting feature of myeloma or a metastasis, so look at whether the marrow signal outside the fracture line is normal, and whether there is a soft-tissue mass or cortical destruction that a fracture would not explain.

quiz.prompt: A 76-year-old woman who has taken alendronate for nine years has six weeks of dull right thigh pain. Radiographs show focal thickening of the lateral cortex of the right femoral diaphysis with a transverse lucency in the outer cortex and no comminution. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Image the opposite femur too, since these lesions are often bilateral
choices: Image the opposite femur too, since these lesions are often bilateral
Reassure; lateral cortical thickening is a normal variant at this age
Treat as a metastasis and stage with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
Continue the bisphosphonate; the appearance is unrelated to treatment
quiz.explain: This is an atypical femoral fracture: subtrochanteric or diaphyseal, originating at the lateral cortex, transverse or short oblique, non-comminuted, with localised periosteal or endosteal beaking, and following minimal or no trauma. Prodromal thigh pain of weeks to months is characteristic, and the contralateral femur is involved often enough that imaging both is standard practice, whether by radiographs, a dedicated MRI or the femora already included on a dual-energy absorptiometry study. The referral is for orthopaedic assessment with a view to prophylactic fixation and for a review of the drug. Two balances to hold: a metastasis is the differential but is usually permeative rather than confined to the lateral cortex, and the absolute risk of this complication remains small against the hip and vertebral fractures that bisphosphonates prevent.

quiz.prompt: A sprinter pulls up mid-race. MRI shows a proximal biceps femoris injury with high signal disrupting the intramuscular tendon over 3 cm, oedema extending 10 cm craniocaudally, and no retraction. A team-mate with the same symptom has feathery oedema at the musculotendinous junction with an intact tendon. What separates their prognoses?
quiz.answer: Tendon involvement predicts a longer absence and a higher reinjury rate
choices: Tendon involvement predicts a longer absence and a higher reinjury rate
The length of the oedema is the single predictor of time to return
They are equivalent, since neither tendon has retracted from its origin
The second is worse, because junctional oedema implies an avulsion
quiz.explain: Muscle fails at the myotendinous junction under eccentric load, and the long head of biceps femoris is the classic casualty in sprinting. What the report has to establish is whether tendon is involved. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grades 0 to 4 and adds a letter for the site: a for myofascial, b for musculotendinous, c for intratendinous. The c lesions, where the intramuscular or free tendon is disrupted, keep athletes out longest and re-tear most often, which is exactly the first case here. Oedema length and cross-sectional area correlate with time lost but far more loosely, so they are descriptors rather than the decider. Proximity to the ischial tuberosity also lengthens recovery, and frank retraction or a tuberosity avulsion moves the patient to a surgeon. Describe the structures; the grade is a summary, not the finding.

quiz.prompt: Order the imaging appearances of post-traumatic heterotopic ossification in a thigh haematoma, from earliest to latest.
quiz.answer: ill-defined-oedema faint-peripheral-calcification mature-cortical-rim shrinkage-and-remodelling
quiz.explain: In the first fortnight there is a cellular, oedematous, enhancing mass with extensive surrounding oedema, and it can look exactly like a sarcoma on MRI — which is the whole danger of this lesion, because the early histology mimics sarcoma too, and an ill-timed biopsy has cost patients limbs. At around three to six weeks faint peripheral floccular calcification appears, and this zonal pattern is the diagnostic key: mature at the rim, immature in the centre, the reverse of an extraskeletal osteosarcoma, which mineralises most densely centrally and is most aggressive at its edge. Over a few months the rim corticates and a lucent cleft usually separates it from adjacent bone, and thereafter it commonly shrinks. The practical rule: when the appearance is early and worrying, repeat radiographs or CT in a few weeks rather than reaching for a needle. CT shows the rim before MRI does.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old swimmer has a weak, aching shoulder. MRI shows uniformly increased STIR signal throughout infraspinatus with normal muscle bulk and normal T1 signal, while supraspinatus, teres minor and deltoid are normal. There is no rotator cuff tear. What should be looked for and reported?
quiz.answer: A cyst at the spinoglenoid notch and a posterior labral tear
choices: A cyst at the spinoglenoid notch and a posterior labral tear
A mass at the suprascapular notch compressing the whole nerve
An inflammatory myositis confined to a single rotator cuff muscle
A quadrilateral space lesion affecting the axillary nerve branches
quiz.explain: Denervation oedema respects a nerve territory rather than a compartment or a vascular territory, and that is what makes it recognisable. Isolated infraspinatus signal places the lesion distal to the branch supplying supraspinatus, at the spinoglenoid notch, where a paralabral cyst is the usual culprit — and the cyst is usually fed by a posterior labral tear through a one-way valve. That tear is the finding that changes the operation, so search for it deliberately. A lesion at the suprascapular notch, higher up, would denervate supraspinatus as well. Teres minor with or without deltoid is the axillary nerve and the quadrilateral space. Multiple territories that fit no single nerve suggest Parsonage-Turner syndrome. Timing matters as much as location: acute denervation keeps normal bulk and normal T1, whereas chronic disease brings fatty T1 signal and volume loss, which does not reverse.

quiz.prompt: A diabetic patient has an ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head, and the fluid-sensitive images show extensive oedema throughout the forefoot. State the sequence and the finding you rely on to call osteomyelitis, and say why the oedema by itself will not do.
quiz.answer: Rely on the T1 images: confluent, geographic low signal replacing the medullary fat of the bone subjacent to the ulcer, in a marrow rather than a periarticular distribution. Oedema on STIR is reactive and surrounds any inflamed, fractured or overloaded bone, so it is sensitive but not specific; confluent T1 marrow replacement makes the diagnosis, supported by cortical erosion, a sinus tract, an adjacent ulcer, abscess or loss of the soft-tissue fat planes.
quiz.explain: Almost every painful diabetic forefoot lights up on STIR, so a report built on fluid-sensitive images alone will over-call infection and cost patients bone. The T1 image is the discriminator because osteomyelitis physically replaces marrow fat, and replacement is confluent and geographic rather than hazy and subcortical. Anatomy helps too: infection reaches bone by contiguous spread from the skin, so it sits directly beneath an ulcer at a pressure point — metatarsal heads, malleoli, the calcaneus — and a tract or a rim-enhancing collection joining ulcer to bone effectively closes the case. Two refinements. Post-contrast fat-suppressed sequences are for tracts and abscesses, not for making the marrow diagnosis. And say which bones are involved and how far the marrow signal extends, because that determines the level of resection.

quiz.prompt: A diabetic with a rocker-bottom midfoot deformity has an ulcer over the plantar prominence. MRI shows tarsometatarsal subluxation with periarticular cysts and debris and, separately, the plantar aspect of the cuboid is indistinct on T1 but its outline reappears on the post-contrast fat-suppressed images, with a tract running from the ulcer to that surface. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: Neuropathic arthropathy with superimposed osteomyelitis of the cuboid
choices: Neuropathic arthropathy with superimposed osteomyelitis of the cuboid
Neuropathic arthropathy alone; the cuboid change is reactive oedema
Osteomyelitis alone; the midfoot changes are infective in origin too
Neither process; the appearances are those of an acute Charcot foot
quiz.explain: Distribution normally separates the two conditions. Neuropathic arthropathy is a midfoot, periarticular disease — tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform subluxation, subchondral cysts, fragmentation, debris and deformity — while osteomyelitis is medullary and lies beneath an ulcer at a pressure point. The difficulty is that a rocker-bottom deformity manufactures a new pressure point, an ulcer forms over it, and the two then coexist, which is the situation described. The ghost sign is the useful pointer in that setting: a bone whose margins disappear on T1 within the surrounding oedema and then reappear after contrast or on T2 indicates infection rather than the ill-defined T1 loss of neuropathic marrow change. The tract from ulcer to cortex seals it. Name the infected bones explicitly, because that, not the diagnosis alone, is what the surgeon operates on.

curriculum_modules.title: Mediastinal Masses and the Nodal Map

module_contract.goal: Localise a mediastinal mass to its ITMIG compartment, narrow it with tissue characteristics and serum markers, and report the nodal map in the terms the surgeon needs.

approach.step: Localise the mass to a compartment
approach.detail: Anterior, middle or posterior, using the lines drawn on the lateral radiograph rather than a true anatomic plane.

Hilum overlay sign for an anterior mass in front of the hilar vessels; displaced azygo-oesophageal recess for a middle-compartment mass; cervicothoracic sign for a posterior mass extending above the clavicle.
Fat, fluid, calcification or enhancement each shortlist a different differential — do this before reaching for a biopsy.

Anterior — the four T's (thymus, teratoma/germ cell, thyroid, "terrible" lymphoma). Middle — foregut duplication cyst, lymphadenopathy, vascular anomaly. Posterior — neurogenic tumour, arising from the sympathetic chain or nerve roots, by far the most common.

approach.step: Report the nodal map in station terms
approach.detail: Use the IASLC station numbers, not "paratracheal" or "subcarinal" alone, so the surgeon can locate what you found without re-reading the images.

classify.name: Mediastinal compartments and their differential
rows: Obliterated retrosternal clear space; hilum overlay sign
Thymoma, teratoma / germ cell tumour, thyroid mass, lymphoma
Fat (thymolipoma, teratoma, lipoma); fluid (thymic cyst, teratoma)
Foregut duplication cyst, lymphadenopathy, aortic arch anomaly
Fluid-filled cyst; enhancing nodes or vascular structure
Cervicothoracic sign — mass visible above the clavicle
Neurogenic tumour (sympathetic ganglia or nerve roots)

modifiers.meaning: Supraclavicular and upper paratracheal nodes, from the cricoid/manubrium down to the innominate vein (2R) or aortic arch (2L).
Prevascular (anterior to the great vessels) and prevertebral (behind the oesophagus) — not reachable by mediastinoscopy.
Lower paratracheal nodes, down to the azygos vein (right) or upper margin of the left pulmonary artery (left).
Subaortic (aortopulmonary window, lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum) and para-aortic (anterolateral to the ascending aorta/arch).
Subcarinal — below the carina, to the azygos vein (right) and upper lobe bronchus (left).
Paraoesophageal, below the subcarinal nodes; pulmonary ligament nodes.
Hilar and lobar nodes — classified as N1, not mediastinal.

pitfalls: Naming a compartment by "where it looks like it is" on the frontal film alone — the lateral view and the hilum overlay/cervicothoracic signs are what actually localise it.
Reporting "mediastinal lymphadenopathy" without a station number — the surgeon cannot plan a nodal dissection from that sentence.
Forgetting the thymus as a normal anterior structure in a young adult and calling it a mass.
Missing fat or fluid content on a routine window — narrow windows over the mass before concluding it is solid.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old has a 5 cm soft-tissue mass on CT lying behind the pericardium, in front of a coronal plane drawn 1 cm posterior to the anterior margin of the vertebral bodies, and pushing the oesophagus to the left. Which reading of the case follows from where it sits?
quiz.answer: Visceral compartment, so nodal disease and foregut cysts lead
choices: Visceral compartment, so nodal disease and foregut cysts lead
Prevascular compartment, so thymic epithelial tumours lead
Paravertebral compartment, so nerve sheath tumours lead
Visceral compartment, so a retrosternal goitre is likeliest
quiz.explain: The ITMIG compartments are drawn on axial CT, and their boundaries are lines you can actually find. The prevascular compartment runs from the sternum back to the anterior surface of the pericardium; the visceral compartment runs from there back to a coronal plane 1 cm behind the anterior margin of the vertebral bodies; everything behind that plane, out to the posterior margin of the transverse processes, is paravertebral. This mass is behind the pericardium and ahead of the vertebral line, so it is visceral, and the visceral differential is dominated by lymph nodes, foregut duplication cysts and oesophageal disease. Thymic tumours belong to the prevascular compartment and nerve sheath tumours to the paravertebral, so neither fits the position given. A retrosternal goitre can descend into the visceral compartment, but it is only a goitre if the images show it continuous with the cervical thyroid, and that was not described. The odd-looking 1 cm offset exists because paravertebral tumours are commonly centred a little anterior to the vertebral body; drawing the line on the body itself would misassign them.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old woman who has just finished chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma has a diffusely enlarged thymus that keeps its arrowhead shape. On chemical-shift MRI a region of interest over the thymus measures 384 signal units on the in-phase image and 246 on the opposed-phase image. Calculate the signal intensity index, ((in-phase minus opposed-phase) divided by in-phase) times 100. Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: (384 - 246) / 384 = 0.3594, so 35.9 per cent. What the number means is more useful than the arithmetic. Opposed-phase imaging cancels signal wherever fat and water protons share a voxel, so a tissue that is lymphoid cells interspersed with fat loses signal, while a tissue that is solid tumour does not. Normal and hyperplastic thymus keep that fatty interspersion, so they drop; thymoma, thymic carcinoma and lymphoma are cellular masses without microscopic fat and stay bright. A substantial drop like this one, in a gland that is diffusely enlarged and has kept its bipyramidal shape, says rebound hyperplasia after chemotherapy rather than relapse - and rebound hyperplasia is FDG-avid, which is exactly why the PET alone will not settle it. Two limits are worth carrying: below about sixteen years of age the normal thymus is fat-poor and the test loses its footing, and beyond about forty the gland is usually fat-replaced anyway, so a soft-tissue prevascular mass in that age group is abnormal whatever the chemical shift shows.

quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old has an incidental smoothly marginated 3 cm prevascular lesion measuring 42 HU on unenhanced CT with no measurable enhancement afterwards. MRI shows uniform very high T2 signal throughout and no internal enhancement. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: A thymic cyst: no tissue diagnosis or surgery is needed
choices: A thymic cyst: no tissue diagnosis or surgery is needed
A thymoma: refer for surgical resection of the lesion
A lymphoma: arrange PET-CT and an image-guided biopsy
Indeterminate: repeat the CT in three months to compare
quiz.explain: Attenuation is the trap. Cyst fluid that is proteinaceous or has bled measures well above water, and 40-something Hounsfield units in a small lesion is also inflated by partial volume from the surrounding fat, so a cyst can look convincingly solid on CT. The pair of findings that settles it is uniform very high T2 signal with absent enhancement; no thymic epithelial tumour and no lymphoma looks like that. Thymoma enhances and is intermediate on T2. Lymphoma is homogeneous soft tissue, usually with nodal disease elsewhere, and is intensely FDG-avid. Waiting three months is not neutral - it commits the patient to another scan and to months of not knowing, for a lesion already characterised. Two caveats before you sign it off benign: a multilocular cyst, unlike the simple unilocular thymopharyngeal remnant, arises in inflammation and can harbour tumour in its walls, so a solid enhancing nodule within a multilocular lesion is resected; and a cyst that grows on interval imaging deserves the same suspicion.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old man has a 9 cm heterogeneous prevascular mass with central necrosis. Serum AFP is 1,850 kU/L and beta-hCG is normal. The multidisciplinary meeting asks whether to biopsy before starting treatment. What do you advise, and on what reasoning?
quiz.answer: No biopsy is needed: a markedly raised AFP means a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour whatever a core would show, so chemotherapy can start on the markers, and biopsy only adds delay and sampling error.
quiz.explain: Pure seminoma does not make alpha-fetoprotein. A markedly raised AFP therefore proves non-seminomatous elements are present, and it does so more reliably than a core from one part of a heterogeneous 9 cm mass, which may sample only necrosis or only the seminomatous component. Treatment is platinum-based combination chemotherapy started on the markers, with resection of any residual mass afterwards; a mediastinal non-seminomatous germ cell tumour is poor-prognosis by site alone, so the delay a biopsy buys is a real cost. Two habits follow. First, request testicular ultrasound - a mediastinal germ cell tumour is usually primary, but a burnt-out testicular primary changes the picture, and there is a recognised association with Klinefelter syndrome. Second, be careful with the alternatives: mature teratoma contains fat and calcium with normal markers and is a surgical problem, not a chemotherapy one; seminoma is a homogeneous lobulated mass with a normal AFP and at most a modest hCG rise, and it is exquisitely chemo- and radiosensitive.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old woman treated for stage II nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma has an end-of-treatment PET-CT. The residual prevascular mass measures 3.4 cm, down from 9 cm, and its FDG uptake is above mediastinal blood pool but below liver. How should this be reported and what follows?
quiz.answer: Deauville 3, complete metabolic response: stop and survey
choices: Deauville 3, complete metabolic response: stop and survey
Deauville 4, partial metabolic response: give more therapy
Deauville 5, progressive disease: change the chemotherapy
Deauville 2, but the residual size still means partial response
quiz.explain: The Deauville five-point scale reads uptake against two internal reference organs and nothing else. Score 1 is no uptake, 2 is uptake at or below mediastinal blood pool, 3 is above blood pool but at or below liver, 4 is moderately above liver, and 5 is markedly above liver or any new disease. Uptake above blood pool but below liver is score 3, and in standard practice scores 1 to 3 at the end of treatment are a complete metabolic response. Size does not enter the scale, which is the point of the fourth option: nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically leaves a bulky sterile fibrotic mass in the prevascular compartment that never shrinks to nothing, and calling that partial response by CT criteria led to years of unnecessary radiotherapy. One nuance worth knowing: in response-adapted trials that de-escalate treatment on an interim scan, score 3 is sometimes handled cautiously rather than as a clean pass, so state the score itself and let the clinical protocol decide what it means.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old with stridor has a 7 cm mass in the visceral compartment displacing the trachea to the right. Unenhanced attenuation is 96 HU, there are coarse calcifications, and contiguous images show the mass to be continuous with the right thyroid lobe. Which feature is doing the most diagnostic work here?
quiz.answer: Continuity with the cervical thyroid on contiguous slices
choices: Continuity with the cervical thyroid on contiguous slices
High unenhanced attenuation from intrinsic iodine content
The coarse calcification within the solid part of the mass
Displacement of the trachea towards the opposite side
quiz.explain: High baseline attenuation is thyroid tissue's most characteristic feature, because the gland concentrates iodine, and intense prolonged enhancement supports it - but haemorrhagic nodes, dense treated lymphoma and some vascular masses can also measure high, so the finding is suggestive rather than decisive. Coarse calcification appears in thymoma, teratoma, treated lymphoma and old granulomatous nodes. Tracheal displacement is mass effect and says nothing about tissue. Continuity with the cervical thyroid on unbroken contiguous images is the one observation only a goitre produces, and it is the reason you scroll up rather than reason about numbers. What the surgeon then needs from you is different again: the inferior extent relative to the arch and brachiocephalic vessels, the minimum tracheal calibre and the length of narrowing, whether the mass reaches behind the trachea or oesophagus, and whether it crosses to the contralateral side - retrotracheal or posterior mediastinal extension is what turns a collar incision into a sternotomy.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old has an incidental 4 cm rounded paravertebral mass at T7 with splaying of the adjacent ribs and widening of the neural foramen. The thoracic surgeon plans a thoracoscopic resection. What further imaging information must your report supply, and why does it change the operation?
quiz.answer: Whether the tumour extends through the foramen into the spinal canal, which needs MRI of the thoracic spine, because a dumbbell tumour requires a combined neurosurgical approach rather than thoracoscopic resection alone.
quiz.explain: A widened neural foramen is a warning, not a diagnosis, and CT is poor at showing what lies within the canal. Peripheral nerve sheath tumours arise on intercostal nerves and grow along them, so a proportion are dumbbell lesions with an intraspinal component. Resecting the thoracic half first can avulse the intraspinal half, bleed into the canal and leave a cord injury, so the operation becomes a staged or combined neurosurgical and thoracic procedure - which is why MRI of the spine belongs in your recommendation before anyone books a list. Two other habits round this out. Look at the shape: a rounded mass centred on a single interspace suggests a nerve sheath tumour, whereas an elongated, vertically oriented mass spanning several vertebral levels suggests a sympathetic chain tumour such as ganglioneuroma or, in a child with calcification and vascular encasement, neuroblastoma. And exclude the impostors before calling anything a tumour: extramedullary haematopoiesis, a paravertebral abscess with disc and endplate destruction, and a lateral meningocoele all sit in the same place.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a right upper lobe adenocarcinoma shows a 14 mm short-axis node anterior to the trachea, lying to the left of the sagittal midline but to the right of the left lateral tracheal border, at the level of the aortic arch. How should this node be assigned and what follows?
quiz.answer: Station 4R, making it ipsilateral N2 and possibly operable
choices: Station 4R, making it ipsilateral N2 and possibly operable
Station 4L, making it contralateral N3 and inoperable
Station 3a, prevascular, and therefore ipsilateral N2
Station 10R, a hilar node, and therefore N1 disease
quiz.explain: In the IASLC map the border between the right and left paratracheal stations is the left lateral wall of the trachea, not the sagittal midline. A node anterior to the trachea and left of the midline is still 4R provided it does not cross that tracheal border - which matters enormously here, because 4R for a right-sided tumour is ipsilateral N2 and potentially resectable after multidisciplinary discussion, while 4L would be contralateral N3 and takes surgery off the table. Station 3a is prevascular, anterior to the great vessels and not against the trachea; station 10 lies distal to the mediastinal pleural reflection, in the hilum. One more thing the report must not imply: 14 mm short axis is enlarged, but size is a poor discriminator, with roughly a quarter to a third of enlarged nodes reactive and a meaningful minority of normal-sized nodes harbouring tumour. Enlargement earns the node a needle, not a stage.

quiz.prompt: Staging CT for a left lower lobe primary shows enlarged nodes at stations 5 and 7, an enlarged node at station 10L, and a 12 mm short-axis node at station 4R. Using the IASLC map, how many separate mediastinal nodal stations - that is, stations counted as N2 or N3 rather than N1 - are involved? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Stations 5 (subaortic), 7 (subcarinal) and 4R are mediastinal; station 10L is hilar and therefore N1, not mediastinal. That gives three. The more important lesson is what the count does and does not decide. Stations 5 and 7 are ipsilateral or midline for a left-sided tumour and so are N2; station 4R is contralateral and so is N3, and the presence of any N3 station supersedes the N2 count entirely - this patient is N3 whatever the tally, and that is a non-surgical stage. The count matters when disease is confined to ipsilateral N2, because the ninth edition of the lung cancer TNM classification, in use since 2025, splits N2 into N2a for a single involved station and N2b for multiple stations, on evidence that single-station disease carries a distinctly better prognosis. That is why a modern report lists the stations individually by number rather than saying mediastinal nodes are enlarged: the count is now part of the stage.

quiz.prompt: The multidisciplinary team wants tissue from an enlarged subaortic (station 5) node before deciding on surgery for a left upper lobe tumour. The bronchoscopist has already sampled stations 4R and 7 by endobronchial ultrasound. What should you advise about station 5?
quiz.answer: It lies outside EBUS reach: VATS or anterior mediastinotomy
choices: It lies outside EBUS reach: VATS or anterior mediastinotomy
It is reachable at EBUS from within the left main bronchus
It is reachable at standard cervical mediastinoscopy instead
It is reachable at EUS from within the oesophageal lumen
quiz.explain: Sampling routes follow anatomy, and every route needs a window without a great vessel in it. Endobronchial ultrasound reaches what abuts the airway - stations 2, 4, 7, 10 and 11. Endoscopic ultrasound from the oesophagus reaches the posterior and inferior stations, 4L, 7, 8 and 9, and the left adrenal gland. Cervical mediastinoscopy covers 2R, 2L, 4R, 4L and the anterior part of 7. Stations 5 and 6 sit lateral to the aortic arch with the aorta and pulmonary artery interposed, so they are the classic blind spot of every needle technique and are sampled at left video-assisted thoracoscopy or anterior mediastinotomy. This matters most in exactly this tumour: the subaortic node is the first-echelon mediastinal station for a left upper lobe primary, so it is the one that decides the operation. Say in the report which stations are involved and which route can reach them - it saves the team a procedure that was never going to answer the question.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these steps in the assessment of a newly discovered bulky prevascular mass in a young man, earliest first.
quiz.answer: chest-radiograph contrast-CT serum-tumour-markers image-guided-biopsy
quiz.explain: The radiograph is usually how the mass announces itself; contrast CT characterises it, defines the compartment and plans access; serum markers come before any needle; biopsy is last and sometimes unnecessary. The order is not bureaucratic. A markedly raised AFP or beta-hCG makes the diagnosis of a non-seminomatous germ cell tumour on its own, so drawing markers first can spare the patient a procedure and start chemotherapy days earlier. When a biopsy is still needed, the CT is what makes it a good one: an anterior approach that avoids the internal mammary vessels, and enough core tissue for immunophenotyping, because fine-needle cytology will not subtype a lymphoma and a repeat is another week lost. There is one recognised exception to biopsying at all - a well-circumscribed prevascular mass with the appearances of an encapsulated thymoma in a patient fit for surgery is often resected without preoperative sampling, to avoid seeding the pleura along a transpleural tract.

quiz.prompt: A 31-year-old woman has facial swelling and distended chest wall veins. CT shows a 12 cm infiltrative prevascular mass encasing an occluded superior vena cava, with dense collaterals and mild tracheal narrowing. The team asks whether to start high-dose steroids overnight and biopsy tomorrow. What is your advice?
quiz.answer: Get tissue first if she is safe to lie flat, because steroids can lyse a lymphoma within hours and leave a non-diagnostic biopsy; flag the tracheal narrowing so the biopsy is planned with anaesthetic support.
quiz.explain: This is almost certainly primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or Hodgkin lymphoma, and both are steroid-sensitive enough that a night of dexamethasone can render a core non-diagnostic or, worse, leave a partially treated lymphoma that cannot be subtyped or staged. Superior vena cava obstruction itself is rarely the emergency it looks like; the collaterals that make the chest wall veins so striking are also what keep the patient alive, and the genuinely time-critical problem is the airway. So the report should describe the tracheal calibre and the length of narrowing, whether the patient can lie supine, the level and length of the caval occlusion, and the collateral pathways - azygos, internal mammary, lateral thoracic - which the interventional team will want if a stent is needed. Endovascular stenting relieves symptoms quickly and can be done before or after sampling. If the airway genuinely will not permit a procedure, steroids are the right call, but that should be a decision made openly, not a default.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old presenting with new myasthenia gravis has a 4.5 cm prevascular mass on CT. Which additional feature would most change the surgical plan?
quiz.answer: Nodular soft tissue on the pleural surface beyond the mass
choices: Nodular soft tissue on the pleural surface beyond the mass
Punctate calcification within the capsule of the mass
A lobulated contour with a smooth fat plane preserved
Cystic change occupying about a third of the mass
quiz.explain: Thymoma spreads by contiguity and by dropping implants along the pleura rather than by nodal or haematogenous routes, so discontinuous pleural nodules are metastatic disease - Masaoka-Koga stage IVa - and they convert a straightforward total thymectomy into a case for induction chemotherapy and possibly extended pleurectomy. That is why every slice of the pleural surface, including the diaphragmatic and paravertebral reflections, is worth a deliberate look on a thymoma staging CT. The other options are noise: calcification and cystic change occur in encapsulated and invasive thymomas alike, and a lobulated contour with preserved fat planes is common in tumours that turn out to be entirely encapsulated. The CT features that genuinely suggest invasion are vascular or pericardial encasement, an irregular interface with adjacent lung, and pleural or pericardial nodularity; microscopic capsular invasion is simply not visible, which is why staging is ultimately surgical. Note too that in myasthenia the whole thymus is removed regardless of tumour size.

curriculum_modules.title: Multiple Sclerosis and the White Matter Differential

module_contract.goal: Apply the McDonald 2024 imaging criteria to a real study, use the central vein sign and the paramagnetic rim to argue for demyelination, and separate multiple sclerosis from the mimics that carry different treatment.

source.title: Multiple Sclerosis — Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis 3.0

approach.step: Count the anatomical regions, not the lesions
approach.detail: Periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve. Dissemination in space is about how many of the five are involved.

approach.step: Ask whether space alone is enough
approach.detail: Under the 2024 criteria, lesions in 4 of the 5 regions establish the diagnosis without further evidence.

approach.step: Then look for dissemination in time
approach.detail: A new T2 or enhancing lesion against a baseline, or enhancing and non-enhancing lesions present together on one study.

approach.step: Use susceptibility imaging to argue the case
approach.detail: Central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions on SWI at 3 T, acquired with contrast immediately before or during the sequence.

approach.step: Read the cord as part of the same study
approach.detail: MS cord lesions are small, peripheral and usually span fewer than 2 vertebral segments.

approach.step: Work the red flags before you commit
approach.detail: Longitudinally extensive cord disease, bilateral or long-segment optic neuritis, area postrema involvement, symmetrical monophasic change — each points elsewhere.

classify.name: McDonald 2024 — what satisfies the criteria
rows: Typical lesions in ≥ 2 of 5 regions: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve
≥ 4 of the 5 regions in relapsing or progressive-onset MS — diagnosis without additional evidence
≥ 2 spinal cord lesions are sufficient for dissemination in space
A new T2 or gadolinium-enhancing lesion on follow-up, or enhancing and non-enhancing lesions simultaneously at any time
≥ 6 lesions with a central vein; in patients with ≤ 10 white matter lesions, the sign in the majority is sufficient
Highly MS-specific and a marker of poor prognosis; detectable on susceptibility-weighted imaging at 3 T
CSF alternative to dissemination in time
Kappa free light chain index or oligoclonal bands
With sufficient MRI evidence, can now be diagnosed and treated as MS without clinical symptoms
classify.note: The 2024 criteria prioritise dissemination in space over dissemination in time, and the optic nerve now counts as the fifth region — optic neuritis can establish space without a clinical history.

measure.how: 3D acquisition, whole brain, orientated to the subcallosal plane, with gadolinium given at the start of the examination.

measure.what: Susceptibility sequence for CVS and PRL
measure.how: SWI or SWAN, with contrast immediately before or during acquisition.
Measure in vertebral segments on sagittal images; MS lesions are small and peripheral.
Two different sagittal sequences plus axial T2. Exclude FLAIR and myelographic sequences — they do not work in the cord.
Coronal fat-suppressed T2 or STIR as a minimum; add post-contrast coronal fat-suppressed T1 in acute neuritis.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
MRI brain at [1.5 / 3] T, 3D 1 mm isotropic T1 and FLAIR, susceptibility-weighted imaging, gadolinium[; spinal cord: two sagittal sequences and axial T2][; optic nerves: coronal fat-suppressed T2].

FINDINGS
Regions involved: periventricular [y/n], cortical/juxtacortical [y/n], infratentorial [y/n], spinal cord [y/n], optic nerve [y/n] — [n] of 5.
Lesion count: [n]. New since [date]: [n / no prior].
Enhancement: [none / n enhancing lesions, with non-enhancing lesions also present].
Central vein sign: [n] lesions.
Paramagnetic rim lesions: [none / n].
Cord: [none / n lesions, site, length in segments, peripheral or central].
Red flags: [none / longitudinally extensive cord lesion / area postrema / bilateral long-segment optic neuritis / symmetrical central brainstem].

IMPRESSION
1. Dissemination in space: [n] of 5 regions — [satisfied / not satisfied].
2. Dissemination in time: [satisfied by — / not demonstrated].
3. [Consistent with MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria / alternative diagnosis to consider — ].
4. [Follow-up interval or further sequence.]
pitfalls: Counting lesions instead of regions. Dissemination in space is 2 of 5 anatomical regions — twenty periventricular lesions are still one region.
Leaving the optic nerve out of the count. Since 2024 it is the fifth region, and optic neuritis can establish space with no clinical history.
Running FLAIR or a myelographic sequence in the cord. The criteria exclude them; use two sagittal sequences and axial T2.

Calling small vessel disease MS. Small vessel disease spares the temporal lobes, U-fibres and cord and sits symmetrically in the central brainstem; MS goes for the corpus callosum, U-fibres, temporal lobes, brainstem, cerebellum and cord.
Missing a longitudinally extensive cord lesion of 3 or more segments with central grey matter involvement. That is AQP4+ NMOSD until the antibody says otherwise.
Reporting a central vein sign from too few lesions. The threshold is 6 lesions with a central vein, or the majority when there are 10 or fewer white matter lesions.

radiology_reference.overview: Apply the McDonald 2024 imaging criteria to a real study, use the central vein sign and the paramagnetic rim to argue for demyelination, and separate multiple sclerosis from the mimics that carry different treatment.
learning_points: Periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, and infratentorial lesions are separate characteristic regions.
Short-segment cord lesions and typical optic-nerve involvement add dissemination in space.
A central-vein sign supports perivenular origin; enhancement and a paramagnetic rim answer different activity and chronicity questions.
Review lesion number and periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or cord location.
Review lesion morphology and orientation.
Review new or enlarging T2 lesions against dated comparison.
Review enhancing lesions and sequence timing.
Review mimics, vascular burden and atypical features.
Apply the explicitly named diagnostic criteria in clinical context; nonspecific white-matter foci are not equivalent to multiple sclerosis.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old presents with painful loss of vision in the right eye. MRI shows an enhancing lesion in the right intraorbital optic nerve and two ovoid periventricular T2 lesions lying perpendicular to the callosal margin. The cord is clear and the cortex looks normal. What can you say about dissemination in space?
quiz.answer: It is satisfied: the optic nerve is a topographical region in its own right under McDonald 2024
choices: It is satisfied: the optic nerve is a topographical region in its own right under McDonald 2024
It is not satisfied: the optic nerve is excluded from the regions that may be counted
It is satisfied by the periventricular lesions alone, with no need to invoke the optic nerve
It cannot be assessed at all until a dedicated spinal cord study is added to the protocol
quiz.explain: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria recognises five typical topographies rather than four: periventricular, cortical or juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, and the optic nerve, which may be demonstrated by MRI, optical coherence tomography or visual evoked potentials. Dissemination in space requires involvement of at least two of them, and this patient has periventricular disease plus an optic nerve lesion, so it is met. The third option is the common trap: several lesions in one region remain one region, however convincing their morphology. Cord imaging is genuinely useful here for prognosis and for flushing out mimics, but the criteria do not require it once two regions are already shown. Note also that the symptomatic lesion counts toward dissemination in space, which was not always the case in earlier versions.

quiz.prompt: A patient has three ovoid periventricular lesions, one lesion abutting the cortex in subcortical white matter, one lesion in the left middle cerebellar peduncle, a normal whole-spine study and normal dedicated optic nerve imaging. How many of the five McDonald 2024 topographical regions are demonstrated? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Periventricular counts once no matter how many lesions sit there, the juxtacortical lesion counts as the cortical or juxtacortical region, and the middle cerebellar peduncle lesion counts as infratentorial. The cord and the optic nerve are clear, so three of five regions are demonstrated. Counting regions rather than lesions is the discipline the criteria demand, and it is where reports most often go astray by implying that a heavy periventricular burden alone is enough. Two regions satisfy dissemination in space, so this study clears that bar comfortably. What it does not do by itself is establish dissemination in time, and it does not exclude the mimics: the same region count could be produced by small vessel disease or migraine, which is exactly why the supportive biomarkers such as the central vein sign have been brought into the diagnostic conversation.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old with hypertension and long-standing migraine has multiple T2 hyperintense white matter lesions and is being assessed for possible multiple sclerosis. A high-resolution susceptibility-weighted acquisition shows a single small vein running through the centre of most of the lesions. How do you interpret this?
quiz.answer: These lesions carry the central vein sign, which favours demyelination over small vessel disease
choices: These lesions carry the central vein sign, which favours demyelination over small vessel disease
These lesions carry the central vein sign, which is the expected finding in small vessel disease
The veins are incidental, since a perivenular arrangement is as common in migraine lesions
The finding is a paramagnetic rim, which marks chronic active lesions rather than vein position
quiz.explain: Demyelinating plaques form around a central venule, so on susceptibility-based imaging, or on a combined FLAIR and T2-star acquisition, a thin vein is seen traversing the lesion and emerging from it in at least one plane. Ischaemic small vessel lesions, migraine-associated lesions and most other mimics arise from arteriolar territory and lack that central vessel, which is why the sign carries real discriminating power in exactly this middle-aged, vascular-risk-factor patient. Practical caveats belong in the report: assess only lesions above about 3 mm, exclude confluent lesions where the vein cannot be assigned to one plaque, and confirm the vein runs centrally on two planes. A paramagnetic rim is a different sign entirely, describing a dark iron-laden edge to a chronic active lesion, and the two may be present in the same patient.

quiz.prompt: A neurologist asks what a paramagnetic rim lesion is and why you have highlighted one in your report. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: It is a chronic active lesion whose iron-rich edge produces a paramagnetic rim: usually dark on susceptibility-weighted imaging, with increased susceptibility on QSM. The chronic rim lesion is non-enhancing and supports multiple sclerosis in the appropriate clinical setting.
quiz.explain: Chronic active, or smouldering, lesions have a quiescent demyelinated core surrounded by a ring of iron-laden microglia and macrophages that continue to expand the plaque slowly. That iron is paramagnetic, so it appears as a dark ring on susceptibility-weighted imaging and as a bright ring on quantitative susceptibility mapping. Two things make the sign useful. First, specificity: a paramagnetic rim is rarely produced by vascular, migrainous or other mimicking lesions, so even one strengthens a demyelinating interpretation, and the 2024 criteria bring it in as a supportive biomarker alongside the central vein sign. Second, prognosis: a higher rim lesion burden tracks with more severe disability and greater progression. Do not confuse it with an enhancing acute lesion; a rim lesion has an intact blood-brain barrier and takes no gadolinium.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old woman develops severe paraparesis over three days. Sagittal T2 shows a swollen, centrally placed cord lesion extending from C2 to C7, and the brain shows a lesion in the dorsal medulla at the area postrema with no ovoid periventricular lesions. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Test for AQP4 antibodies and manage as NMOSD, because several MS drugs make this disease worse
choices: Test for AQP4 antibodies and manage as NMOSD, because several MS drugs make this disease worse
Start a multiple sclerosis disease-modifying drug, as this cord pattern lies within its spectrum
Call it idiopathic transverse myelitis, since a long cord lesion carries no antibody association
Call it cord infarction, since the central grey matter pattern and the length are typical of that
quiz.explain: Two findings define this study. A longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, conventionally three or more vertebral segments, sitting centrally within the cord and involving grey matter, is characteristic of aquaporin-4 antibody disease; multiple sclerosis produces short, peripherally placed, often dorsolateral cord lesions spanning fewer than two segments. The area postrema lesion is the second: it explains intractable hiccups and vomiting and is close to specific for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which also favours periependymal surfaces around the third and fourth ventricles and the optic chiasm. Getting this right is urgent because it is not merely a labelling exercise. Several multiple sclerosis therapies, including interferon beta and natalizumab, can worsen NMOSD, and treatment moves instead to complement, IL-6 or CD19 targeted agents. Cord infarction is hyperacute and usually anterior in distribution.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old develops simultaneous painful visual loss in both eyes. MRI shows long segments of both optic nerves enhancing, most marked anteriorly, with enhancement extending into the nerve sheath and adjacent orbital fat. The brain is otherwise normal. What do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Send MOG antibodies: bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement fits MOGAD
choices: Send MOG antibodies: bilateral anterior optic neuritis with perineural enhancement fits MOGAD
Send AQP4 antibodies only: this appearance represents posterior chiasmal disease in a child
Diagnose multiple sclerosis: bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis is its usual first presentation
Diagnose orbital inflammatory disease: sheath and fat enhancement place the process outside the nerve
quiz.explain: Antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein produce a recognisable optic neuritis: bilateral, longitudinally extensive along the nerve, anteriorly predominant with disc swelling, and characteristically spilling beyond the nerve into the sheath and surrounding orbital fat as perineural enhancement. Aquaporin-4 disease tends to hit the posterior nerve and chiasm and is rarer in children. Multiple sclerosis optic neuritis is usually unilateral and short-segment, with brain lesions to accompany it. Orbital inflammatory disease is a reasonable thought given the fat enhancement, but the intrinsic long-segment nerve enhancement makes it secondary here. Elsewhere MOGAD may look ADEM-like in a child, produce fluffy poorly marginated brainstem and deep grey lesions, or involve the conus. It matters clinically because MOGAD lesions often resolve completely and relapse risk and treatment differ from both multiple sclerosis and NMOSD.

quiz.prompt: A registrar asks how acute disseminated encephalomyelitis differs on imaging and clinically from a first attack of multiple sclerosis. Answer in one or two sentences.
quiz.answer: ADEM is monophasic and usually follows an infection or vaccination in a child, with large, poorly demarcated, bilateral but asymmetric white matter lesions of similar age that commonly involve the deep grey matter of the thalami and basal ganglia.
quiz.explain: The strongest discriminator is that the lesions all look the same age, because they arose in one wave: they tend to enhance, or not enhance, together, whereas multiple sclerosis is defined by lesions of different vintages coexisting. Morphology helps too. ADEM lesions are large, fluffy and ill-defined rather than ovoid and sharply marginated, they are bilateral though asymmetric, and involvement of thalami and basal ganglia is common while it is unusual in multiple sclerosis. Clinically, encephalopathy is required for the diagnosis and the illness is monophasic. Many paediatric cases are MOG antibody positive, so testing is worthwhile, and it also identifies the minority who will relapse. Follow-up imaging is informative: ADEM lesions often resolve substantially, whereas new lesions appearing later should prompt reconsideration of a chronic demyelinating disease.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these deep white matter appearances in order from Fazekas grade 0 to Fazekas grade 3.
quiz.answer: absent punctate-foci early-confluence large-confluent-areas
quiz.explain: The Fazekas scale is scored in two compartments. In the deep white matter, grade 0 is no lesion, grade 1 punctate foci, grade 2 the beginning of confluence between those foci, and grade 3 large confluent areas. The periventricular compartment is scored separately: caps or a pencil-thin lining is grade 1, a smooth halo grade 2, and irregular hyperintensity extending into the deep white matter grade 3. Two cautions apply in a demyelination service. First, Fazekas describes presumed small vessel disease and is not a way to quantify multiple sclerosis burden, so do not use it to grade plaques. Second, in a middle-aged patient the two processes coexist, and disentangling them rests on morphology and on the central vein sign rather than on a severity score. Grading well still matters, because it anchors follow-up comparison.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has been on natalizumab for three years and is JC virus antibody positive with a high index. New subtle cognitive slowing prompts an MRI, which shows an asymmetric confluent subcortical lesion in the left frontal lobe involving the U-fibres, T1 hypointense, without mass effect or enhancement, with punctate T2 foci at its advancing margin. What do you do?
quiz.answer: Raise PML, recommend stopping the drug and arrange cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR today
choices: Raise PML, recommend stopping the drug and arrange cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR today
Call it a new demyelinating plaque, continue the drug and repeat the MRI in three months
Call it immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which swells and enhances at this stage
Call it a tumefactive plaque, which shows an incomplete ring opening toward the adjacent cortex
quiz.explain: Every described feature belongs to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: asymmetric subcortical white matter involvement that reaches the U-fibres, marked T1 hypointensity, no mass effect out of proportion to size, absent enhancement while the patient remains immunosuppressed, and punctate T2 or diffusion-hyperintense foci at the leading edge, sometimes described as a milky-way appearance. Multiple sclerosis plaques are usually periventricular, ovoid and U-fibre sparing, and a new plaque does not creep. The risk profile fits too, since JC virus seropositivity with a high index, natalizumab beyond two years and prior immunosuppression together define the high-risk group who need short-interval surveillance MRI. Enhancement and swelling appear later, once the drug is withdrawn and immune reconstitution begins, and that phase can be clinically worse than the infection. Confirmation is cerebrospinal fluid JC virus PCR, and delay costs brain.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old develops subacute right hemiparesis. MRI shows a 35 mm left frontal white matter lesion with incomplete ring enhancement whose open edge faces the cortex, mass effect that is modest for the size of the lesion, and relative cerebral blood volume lower than in normal white matter. What do you favour and advise?
quiz.answer: Tumefactive demyelination: the open ring and the low perfusion argue against a high grade glioma
choices: Tumefactive demyelination: the open ring and the low perfusion argue against a high grade glioma
A high grade glioma: the incomplete ring and the low perfusion are characteristic of that tumour
A pyogenic abscess: the ring thins medially and the centre restricts diffusion markedly in that entity
A solitary metastasis: a ring lesion with modest oedema is the usual appearance of that diagnosis
quiz.explain: Three findings converge. The incomplete or open ring, with the deficient segment facing the cortical grey matter, reflects the inflammatory front advancing through white matter and is far more typical of demyelination than of tumour. Mass effect and oedema that look too mild for a lesion of this size point the same way, as neoplasms of 35 mm generally behave more aggressively. Perfusion is the clincher, since a high grade glioma raises relative cerebral blood volume while a demyelinating lesion does not, its enhancement reflecting a permeable barrier rather than neovascularity. An abscess would show a thin ring that is thinner on its ventricular side and a centre with striking diffusion restriction. The practical consequence is large: recognising this can avoid a biopsy, whose demyelinating hypercellularity is itself readily misread as tumour, and short-interval follow-up after steroids usually settles the question.

quiz.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences how the distribution of small vessel disease differs from that of multiple sclerosis on brain MRI.
quiz.answer: Small vessel disease spares the U-fibres, the corpus callosum and the cord, and comes with lacunes, basal ganglia perivascular spaces and deep microbleeds, whereas its lesions rarely carry a central vein.
quiz.explain: This is the everyday reporting problem, because after the fifth decade almost everyone has some white matter signal change. The distributions differ in a way that is reliable when applied carefully. Multiple sclerosis lesions sit against the callososeptal interface, are ovoid and oriented perpendicular to the ventricle, reach the juxtacortical U-fibres and the cortex itself, and are frequently accompanied by short dorsolateral cord lesions. Small vessel disease favours deep and subcortical white matter with periventricular caps and haloes, spares the callosum and the cord, and travels with lacunes, enlarged basal ganglia perivascular spaces and deep microbleeds. When the pattern is genuinely ambiguous, susceptibility-based imaging settles it more often than any distribution rule, since demyelinating plaques are perivenular and vascular lesions are not.

quiz.prompt: State in one or two sentences what imaging must show for dissemination in time, including how a single scan can achieve it.
quiz.answer: Dissemination in time needs either a new T2 or enhancing lesion on a follow-up scan, or, on a single scan, the simultaneous presence of an enhancing lesion and a non-enhancing lesion.
quiz.explain: The idea is simply that the disease has been active at more than one point in time, and imaging can demonstrate that in two ways. Comparing with a prior study, any new T2 lesion or any new enhancing lesion counts, regardless of when the baseline was performed. On a single study, an enhancing lesion sitting alongside a non-enhancing one implies lesions of different ages, because gadolinium enhancement in a plaque generally persists for only a few weeks. This is the practical reason a first study in suspected demyelination should be performed with contrast: without it a diagnosis that could be made today may take another six months. Cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands, or kappa free light chains, can substitute for dissemination in time in patients who satisfy dissemination in space, which is why the lumbar puncture is not merely confirmatory.

module_contract.goal: Choose the MRI sequence a joint question needs, and tell artefact from disease.

approach.detail: Axial, coronal and sagittal, on both 1.5T and 3T. Add obliques only when the question needs them.

approach.step: Add an oblique when a tendon runs obliquely
approach.detail: Scans perpendicular to the peroneal and tibialis posterior tendons show subtle tendinopathy and small tears that the orthogonal planes cut at an angle.

approach.step: Pick fat suppression by the question
approach.detail: Fat-saturated sequences for screening bone marrow oedema and for ligamentous injury, where the oedema is the finding.
Non-fat-sat T2 or T1 for capsular thickening and fibrotic soft tissue abnormality, where suppressing the fat removes the contrast you need.

approach.step: Check the tendon's angle before you call tendinosis
approach.detail: If the tendon lies near 55° to B0 on a short TE sequence, suspect magic angle and go to a long TE image before committing.

approach.step: Read a bright rim at a ligament for what it is
approach.detail: Chemical shift, from subcortical fatty marrow exposed to joint fluid at a full-thickness tear.

measure.how: Tendon orientation relative to the main magnetic field. Hyperintensity appears on short TE sequences such as proton density and is less pronounced on long TE images such as T2.
Standard axial, coronal and sagittal planes are used at both.

classify.name: Choosing the sequence by the question
rows: Oedema patterns are far more apparent once the fat is suppressed
Same — the finding is the oedema around the ligament
Fat suppression removes the contrast that makes thickened fibrous tissue visible
Subtle tendinopathy or a small tendon tear
Oblique planes perpendicular to the tendon
Orthogonal planes cut an obliquely running tendon at an angle
A tendon that looks bright but normal in shape
Long TE (T2) rather than short TE (PD)
Magic angle hyperintensity at 55° to B0 is less pronounced on long TE

pitfalls: Calling tendinosis on a short TE sequence alone. A morphologically normal tendon at 55° to B0 is bright from magic angle; check the shape, and check a long TE image.
Reading a bright rim at a full-thickness ligament tear as a second lesion. It is chemical shift artefact from subcortical fatty marrow meeting joint fluid.
Suppressing fat for a question that needs the fat. Capsular thickening and fibrosis are best seen on non-fat-sat T2 or T1.
Relying on three orthogonal planes for an obliquely running tendon. The peroneal and tibialis posterior tendons need planes perpendicular to their own course.
Assuming 3T changes the protocol. The same standard axial, coronal and sagittal planes are used at 1.5T and 3T — field strength is not a substitute for the right plane.
