quiz.prompt: On a shoulder study the distal supraspinatus shows intermediate signal on the short-TE proton-density images, in the segment where the tendon curves over the humeral head. That same segment is normal in thickness and contour, and uniformly dark on the long-TE T2 images. What follows?
quiz.answer: The signal is an orientation effect and the tendon is intact
quiz.explain: Tendon collagen is dark because tightly bound water dephases fast, and the dipolar term that does the dephasing scales as 3cos-squared(theta) minus 1, which vanishes near 55 degrees to B0. Where the fibres pass through that angle T2 lengthens, so signal appears on sequences whose TE is short compared with the lengthened T2 and fades once TE is long. A tear holds fluid and stays bright as TE lengthens; tendinosis keeps at least intermediate signal at long TE and usually thickens the tendon. A segment that returns to uniform low signal at normal calibre does neither, so 'The finding is tendinosis that needs an arthrogram to grade' fails on both counts, and calling a tear here treats a geometry effect as disease.
choices: An interstitial tear is present and hidden on T2 imaging
The finding is tendinosis that needs an arthrogram to grade
The signal is an orientation effect and the tendon is intact
A partial-thickness bursal-side tear should be reported

quiz.prompt: Take the proton resonant frequency at 1.5 T as exactly 64 MHz, with fat precessing 3.5 ppm below water. A knee sequence is read out at a bandwidth of 100 Hz per pixel. By how many pixels is fat displaced along the frequency-encoding direction? Give the number of pixels to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Convert the chemical shift to hertz, then hertz to pixels. 64 MHz times 3.5 ppm is 224 Hz, and frequency encoding turns that offset into a position offset of 224 divided by 100, which is 2.24 pixels, or 2.2 to one decimal place. Using the true 1.5 T frequency of 63.87 MHz gives 2.235 and rounds to the same figure. The same arithmetic governs metal, whose induced off-resonance is far larger, which is why raising the receiver bandwidth is the first move next to a prosthesis; the price is signal-to-noise falling as one over the square root of bandwidth. At 3 T the offset doubles to about 447 Hz, so the same bandwidth buys half as much protection.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a cobalt-chrome hip arthroplasty needs MRI for suspected periprosthetic infection, and both a 1.5 T and a 3 T scanner are free. Give three protocol decisions that shrink the metal artefact, with the physical reason each one works.
quiz.answer: Scan at 1.5 T rather than 3 T, because the off-resonance spread the metal induces scales with field strength. Raise the receiver bandwidth, because the displacement produced by a given off-resonance equals that offset divided by the bandwidth per pixel. Suppress fat with STIR rather than a spectral pulse, because inversion recovery nulls by T1 and does not need the fat resonance to sit where the scanner expects it. Beyond the three asked for, thin slices, view-angle tilting and SEMAC or MAVRIC correct the residual in-plane and through-plane distortion.
quiz.explain: Each decision follows from one fact: metal warps B0, so protons near it precess at the wrong frequency and the scanner mislocates them. Lower field means a smaller absolute frequency spread; higher bandwidth means each hertz of error buys less displacement; STIR nulls by T1 recovery rather than by resonant frequency, so it tolerates a fat peak shifted out of the saturation band. Spin echo with its refocusing pulses is essential and gradient echo is the wrong family here, since gradient echo lets exactly this off-resonance dephasing accumulate.

quiz.prompt: Sagittal proton-density images show a linear high-signal line separating a small triangular structure from the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus on two adjacent slices. Coronal images show a band running transversely across the front of the joint into that point. What is the appropriate action?
quiz.answer: Report the meniscus intact; the band explains the cleft
quiz.explain: The transverse intermeniscal ligament crosses the front of the joint to the anterior horns, and the fat between ligament and meniscus makes a pseudotear line that can be traced onto contiguous coronal or axial images as a discrete band. The two-slice rule bites only on signal that reaches an articular surface; this line lies along the interface between ligament and meniscus and stops there, which is why persisting on adjacent slices does not make it a tear. So 'Report a tear of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus' misapplies a criterion whose premise is missing, and ordering an arthrogram to confirm a structure the plain study already resolves adds a needle for nothing.
choices: Report the meniscus intact; the band explains the cleft
Report a tear of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Recommend MR arthrography to confirm an anterior horn tear
Report a displaced flap in the anterior joint recess

quiz.prompt: Sagittal images through the lateral compartment show fluid signal separating the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus from the capsule, at the level where the popliteus tendon runs obliquely behind it. The meniscal substance is uniformly dark, both popliteomeniscal fascicles are continuous, and the meniscus sits in normal position. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Call it the normal popliteal hiatus and report no tear
quiz.explain: Over roughly a centimetre the lateral meniscus has no capsular attachment, because the popliteus tendon passes through the hiatus, and fluid or fat there imitates a peripheral detachment. What settles it is that the meniscal substance carries no signal reaching an articular surface, and that the gap follows the tendon's course rather than continuing along the meniscal margin beyond the hiatus. 'Attribute the appearance to a torn popliteomeniscal fascicle' is the real differential and the tempting one, but that diagnosis rests on disrupted fascicles and a hypermobile or displaced meniscus, and this study reports both fascicles continuous and the meniscus sited normally.
choices: Report a peripheral tear detaching the posterior horn
Describe a bucket-handle tear with the fragment displaced
Attribute the appearance to a torn popliteomeniscal fascicle
Call it the normal popliteal hiatus and report no tear

quiz.prompt: After a non-contact twisting injury a knee MRI shows marrow oedema in the lateral femoral condyle at the sulcus terminalis and in the posterior lateral tibial plateau. The cruciate images are degraded by motion. What does the oedema pattern support?
quiz.answer: Pivot-shift impaction, which places the ACL at high risk
quiz.explain: In the pivot shift a valgus load with rotation carries the tibia forward, and the lateral femoral condyle strikes the posterior lateral tibial plateau; the paired contusions record that collision and carry a strong association with a torn ACL. The motion-degraded cruciate images should therefore be repeated, or the ACL reported as suspect, rather than passed over. 'Dashboard impaction, which points to a posterior cruciate tear' is the closest rival, but dashboard loading drives the tibia backwards and bruises the anterior tibia instead, which is a different pattern in a different place.
choices: Dashboard impaction, which points to a posterior cruciate tear
Pivot-shift impaction, which places the ACL at high risk
Clip injury, which points to a medial collateral tear
Hyperextension impaction, which spares both cruciate ligaments

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after partial medial meniscectomy a patient has recurrent locking, and conventional MRI shows intermediate signal touching the tibial surface of the small remnant. Why is direct MR arthrography preferred here to an intravenous gadolinium study?
quiz.answer: Contrast placed in the joint fills a re-tear cleft directly
quiz.explain: In an operated meniscus the usual criterion fails, because the cut surface and its granulation tissue produce surface-reaching intermediate signal for years; the question becomes whether a cleft is open to the joint. Dilute gadolinium injected into the joint tracks into an open cleft, which answers exactly that. 'Intravenous gadolinium fails to reach the joint space itself' is the tempting distractor and its premise is false: indirect arthrography does opacify the joint by diffusion from synovium, given a delay and some exercise. What it shows, though, is enhancement rather than filling, and enhancing granulation tissue is read as a sign of re-tear by some authors and as a confounder by others, so it settles the question less directly than contrast running into a cleft.
choices: Intravenous gadolinium fails to reach the joint space itself
Distension of the capsule is what displays the remnant
Contrast placed in the joint fills a re-tear cleft directly
Intra-articular injection carries a lower contrast dose

quiz.prompt: In-phase and opposed-phase gradient-echo images of the lumbar spine show a focus that loses more than a fifth of its signal on the opposed-phase image, and on T1 the focus is a little brighter than the adjacent disc. What does the signal drop indicate about the focus?
quiz.answer: Fat and water share the voxels, favouring a benign focus
quiz.explain: At the opposed-phase echo time fat and water magnetisation point in opposite directions, so a voxel loses signal in proportion to how much of each it holds, and a drop therefore requires both to be present. Haematopoietic marrow keeps interspersed adipocytes and drops; a marrow-replacing lesion has pushed the fat out and holds its signal, so 'The focus is cellular, so marrow replacement is likely' reads the drop backwards. The T1 comparison with disc and muscle is the independent check. Sclerosis and blood products act through T2-star, which attenuates the longer in-phase echo more than the shorter opposed-phase one, so they shrink or even reverse an apparent drop rather than creating one.
choices: The focus is cellular, so marrow replacement is likely
Blood products are present and dephase the gradient echo
The focus is sclerotic, which shortens T2* and darkens it
Fat and water share the voxels, favouring a benign focus

quiz.prompt: One distance runner with shin pain has periosteal and marrow oedema in the posteromedial tibia on fluid-sensitive images, with normal T1. A second runner has the same oedema plus a dark line crossing the cortex on T1. What separates the two?
quiz.answer: The second shows a fracture line, so a longer time unloaded
quiz.explain: Stress injury runs a continuum, and the established MRI grading climbs from periosteal oedema, through marrow oedema visible on fluid-sensitive images alone, to marrow signal change seen on T1, and finally a discrete fracture line, with return to sport lengthening at each step. T1 does the discriminating work because marrow fat, and its displacement, is what T1 shows. 'The two grade alike, because marrow oedema settles the grade' is the trap: fluid-sensitive sequences are sensitive but unspecific, and oedema by itself can follow a change in training load. MRI outperforms radiographs and CT at the early end, so sending the first runner for CT loses information rather than adding it.
choices: The second shows a fracture line, so a longer time unloaded
The first has the higher grade, since oedema outweighs a line
The two grade alike, because marrow oedema settles the grade
The first needs a CT, since MRI misses periosteal reaction

quiz.prompt: A suspected soft-tissue sarcoma of the thigh is imaged, and the radiographer, worried that spectral fat saturation will fail at the edge of the field, acquires the post-gadolinium sequence as a STIR. Why is that the wrong choice?
quiz.answer: STIR nulls by T1, and enhancement drives tumour T1 toward fat
quiz.explain: Inversion recovery suppresses whatever has recovered to the null point at the chosen inversion time, and that is a statement about T1 rather than about frequency. Gadolinium shortens the T1 of enhancing tissue, so enhancing tumour or granulation can be driven into the nulled band and erased, which defeats the purpose of giving contrast at all. Use spectral fat suppression on the post-contrast T1, or a Dixon water-only reconstruction, which separates fat from water by phase evolution and tolerates far more field inhomogeneity than a single saturation pulse. 'Gadolinium shifts the fat resonance, so the inversion mistimes' is the plausible-sounding rival, but gadolinium at clinical doses does not move the fat resonance, and inversion recovery would not care where that resonance sat even if it did.
choices: Gadolinium shifts the fat resonance, so the inversion mistimes
STIR nulls by T1, and enhancement drives tumour T1 toward fat
Inversion recovery images the tumour rim but not its centre
The inversion pulse breaks down the chelate in the contrast

quiz.prompt: Taking the T1 of fat at 1.5 T as 260 ms, at what inversion time does an inversion-recovery sequence cross zero for fat and so null its signal? Answer in milliseconds, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Longitudinal magnetisation recovers as 1 - 2exp(-TI/T1) after a 180 degree pulse, and it passes through zero when TI = T1 x ln2 = 0.693 x 260 = 180 ms. Two consequences follow. The first is why STIR survives conditions that defeat spectral fat saturation: nulling by T1 needs no assumption about where the fat resonance sits, so a poor shim, a large field of view or a lump of metal does not break it. The second is the price. Anything else whose T1 approaches that of fat is nulled too, which is why STIR after gadolinium is a mistake and why some subacute blood disappears. In practice scanners use a shorter time than the ideal figure, often around 150 to 170 ms at 1.5 T, because the repetition time is finite and the magnetisation never fully recovers between pulses.

quiz.prompt: A two-dimensional fast spin-echo protocol acquires 0.4 mm by 0.5 mm in plane at a slice thickness of 3.0 mm. An isotropic three-dimensional sequence on the same scanner acquires 0.6 mm in all three directions. By what factor is the two-dimensional voxel larger in volume than the three-dimensional one? Answer to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The 2D voxel is 0.4 x 0.5 x 3.0 = 0.6 cubic millimetres and the isotropic voxel is 0.6 cubed = 0.216, so the ratio is 2.8. That single number explains most of the trade. Signal-to-noise scales with voxel volume, so the isotropic acquisition starts with well under half the signal per voxel and has to buy it back with long echo trains and acceleration, which costs edge sharpness. What it buys is the loss of partial volume in the slice direction and the freedom to reformat along any plane the anatomy asks for, which is why isotropic 3D suits obliquely oriented structures and post-operative anatomy. The 2D protocol keeps better tissue contrast per unit time, which is why most joint protocols still hang on 2D sequences and add a 3D acquisition to answer a particular question.

quiz.prompt: Put these parts of a long bone into the order in which their red marrow converts to yellow marrow during normal childhood.
quiz.answer: epiphysis diaphysis distal-metaphysis proximal-metaphysis
quiz.explain: Conversion begins in the epiphysis within months of its ossification centre appearing, then takes the diaphysis, then the distal metaphysis, and reaches the proximal metaphysis last, so that in an adolescent or young adult the residual red marrow is exactly where it looks most alarming: the proximal humeral and proximal femoral metaphyses. Reconversion under demand, from anaemia, smoking, obesity or endurance training, runs the sequence backwards and repopulates the same regions in reverse. Knowing the order is what keeps a normal variant out of the report. Red marrow follows the rules: it stays higher in signal than skeletal muscle and than the intervertebral disc on T1, it is symmetrical and it has no mass effect, and it drops signal on opposed-phase imaging because fat still shares the voxels. Marrow that is darker than muscle on T1 is not red marrow.

quiz.prompt: On a large field-of-view coronal study of both thighs the fat is well suppressed centrally, but bright at both lateral edges of the image, and a fluid-sensitive series is being read there for muscle oedema. Explain what has gone wrong and give two ways to obtain a dependable fat-suppressed image.
quiz.answer: Spectral fat saturation assumes the fat and water resonances sit where the scanner expects them, which requires a uniform main field. At the edges of a large field of view the field is least uniform and the shim is poorest, so the saturation pulse misses fat there, and it may partly saturate water instead, which can also produce artefactual signal loss. The remedies are to shim over a smaller volume and bring the region of interest to isocentre, imaging one thigh at a time if necessary, or to change technique: STIR nulls by T1 and is indifferent to where the resonance sits, and a Dixon acquisition separates fat from water using the phase difference between echoes and tolerates inhomogeneity far better.
quiz.explain: The failure is regional, and that is the clue: an artefact of field uniformity gets worse with distance from isocentre, while a true absence of fat suppression would be uniform across the image. It matters clinically because both errors it produces are dangerous in opposite directions. Unsuppressed fat at the edge of the field hides oedema, so a myositis or an infected collection is missed at the very periphery. Partially suppressed water in the same region mimics oedema where there is none. Dixon has largely become the pragmatic answer for big fields and awkward geometry, since it yields fat-only, water-only, in-phase and opposed-phase images from one acquisition, and its water image is robust where a spectral pulse is not.

quiz.prompt: On an axial fluid-sensitive series of the knee, a row of evenly spaced bright and dark smudges runs across the image from the popliteal artery, and one of them lies over the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Explain the appearance and say what you would change so that it stops obscuring the meniscus.
quiz.answer: Pulsatile flow in the popliteal artery changes signal from one repetition to the next, and since the phase-encoding direction is sampled one line per repetition, that inconsistency is mismapped along the phase-encode axis as a train of evenly spaced ghosts of the vessel. It is an artefact and not a lesion: the smudges repeat at a regular interval, they trace back to the artery, and they cross tissue planes. The first fix is to swap the phase-encoding direction so the ghosts run away from the structure being assessed; a saturation band placed over the vessel outside the slice, gradient moment nulling, and more signal averages all reduce them further.
quiz.explain: Ghosting is the classic artefact that reads as disease because it lands somewhere plausible. The discriminators are all geometric rather than anatomical: the repeats are regular, they run along one axis of the image, and that axis is the phase-encode direction rather than any plane in the knee. Swapping the phase-encode direction is worth understanding as more than a trick, since it moves the artefact without removing it, so the choice is really about where you are willing for the ghosts to fall. It also costs something in most protocols, because the field of view usually has to grow in the new phase direction to avoid wrap. When the same smudge persists in the same anatomical place after the direction is swapped, it was never a ghost.

curriculum_modules.title: Cervical Node Levels and the Malignant Node

module_contract.goal: Place a cervical node in its level from the anatomy on the image, decide whether it is malignant, and say what your call changes about the stage, the operation and the search for a primary.

source.title: Cervical Lymph Node Mapping — Cervical Node Map

approach.detail: Place the node against bony and vascular landmarks — hyoid, cricoid, posterior edge of the internal jugular vein, sternocleidomastoid, sternoclavicular joint — before you describe it.

approach.step: Split II, IV and VI where it changes management
approach.detail: Level II splits into IIa/IIb at the posterior edge of the internal jugular vein; IV splits into IVa/IVb 2 cm above the sternoclavicular joint; VI splits into anterior jugular (VIa) and pre-laryngeal/pre-tracheal/paratracheal (VIb).

Retropharyngeal (VIIa, skull base to hyoid) and retrostyloid (VIIb, around the jugulo-carotid vessels to skull base) nodes sit outside the standard neck dissection levels and are easy to miss on axial-only review.

approach.step: Match the level to the primary site
approach.detail: Each level drains a predictable set of primaries — use the level to direct the search for an occult primary, or to say whether a known primary's drainage pattern fits.
Report each involved level by side; the level pattern changes the N category and the extent of neck dissection more than the node count does.

classify.note: This is an anatomic level map. The Radiology Assistant page gives no imaging criteria (size, necrosis, shape, extracapsular spread) for calling a node malignant — do not report a threshold that isn't on this page.

pitfalls: Calling a level by eye instead of by landmark — IIa/IIb, IVa/IVb and VIa/VIb hinge on the jugular vein and a point 2 cm above the sternoclavicular joint, not on a guess.
Missing level VII because it sits above and behind the standard axial slab most people scroll through quickly.
Reporting 'enlarged node' without a level — the level is what tells the clinician which primary to hunt for.
Treating retropharyngeal nodes as untouchable by neck dissection — they still need reporting because they change the radiotherapy field even when surgery can't reach them.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old smoker with a supraglottic laryngeal carcinoma has a 15 mm necrotic node on the right. On the sagittal reformat its centre lies below the lower border of the cricoid arch and above the clavicle; on the axial images it sits anteromedial to a line drawn along the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid, just lateral to the common carotid artery. Which level does it belong in, and what follows from that?
quiz.answer: Level IV, so the dissection reaches the clavicle
choices: Level IV, so the dissection reaches the clavicle
Level III, so the dissection stops at cricoid
Level VB, so the accessory nerve is at risk
Level VI, so the central compartment is opened
quiz.explain: The jugular chain is cut into three by two horizontal landmarks: the lower body of the hyoid divides level II from III, and the lower border of the cricoid arch divides III from IV. A node below cricoid and above the clavicle is therefore level IV, provided it lies anteromedial to the oblique line joining the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid to the posterolateral edge of the anterior scalene; behind that line the same node would be level VB, which matters because the spinal accessory nerve runs there and its dissection carries a shoulder cost. Level VI is the central compartment between the carotid arteries, the territory of thyroid and subglottic disease, not of a lateral jugular node. Supraglottic larynx drains to levels II, III and IV, so this node is entirely in keeping with the primary; the practical consequence is that the neck dissection and the radiotherapy volume must extend down to the clavicle.

quiz.prompt: On axial CT a level II node measures 16 mm in its longest axis and 10 mm in its shortest. Divide the long axis by the short axis and give the ratio. Answer as a number, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Sixteen divided by ten is 1.6. A reactive node is ovoid and stretched along the chain, with a long-to-short ratio of about 2 or more; as tumour fills a node it becomes spherical and the ratio falls, so a value under 2 is the shape criterion for suspicion. Note what the size criterion alone would have done here. Using the widely applied minimal-axial-diameter thresholds, a node needs 11 mm short axis at level II and 10 mm elsewhere before size alone calls it involved, so at 10 mm this node would have passed. Shape, loss of the fatty hilum, central necrosis and irregular margins all carry more weight than a millimetre either side of a size cut-off, and necrosis carries the most of all. Measure the ratio in the axial plane, on the same image, and record the short axis in your report so that the next reader can compare.

quiz.prompt: Staging MRI for a nasopharyngeal carcinoma shows a lateral retropharyngeal node with a short axis of 7 mm and no necrosis. State whether you would report it as involved, and give the short-axis figure above which a retropharyngeal node in an adult is treated as malignant.
quiz.answer: Report it as involved: in an adult a lateral retropharyngeal node of 5 mm or more in short axis is treated as malignant, and this one at 7 mm is beyond that.
quiz.explain: The lateral retropharyngeal nodes sit between the prevertebral muscles and the pharyngeal wall, above the hyoid, and they are the first echelon for the nasopharynx, the posterior pharyngeal wall and the sinonasal cavities. In adults they are ordinarily involuted and invisible, which is why the threshold is so much lower than in the neck proper: 5 mm short axis is the figure in common use, and some readers reserve a confident call for 8 mm or a node with necrosis. Children are different — reactive retropharyngeal nodes are a normal finding. The reason to hunt for these nodes is that a standard neck dissection does not reach them, so they are covered by the radiotherapy volume rather than by the surgeon. In the AJCC 8th edition staging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, retropharyngeal nodal involvement counts within N1, so calling it changes the stage as well as the plan.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old who has never smoked has a painless 3 cm cystic mass at level IIA. Ultrasound shows a thin wall with a 6 mm solid mural nodule, and there is no preceding infective illness. What is the appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with p16 testing
choices: Ultrasound-guided aspiration with p16 testing
A course of antibiotics and repeat ultrasound
Excision, assuming a branchial cleft cyst
Aspiration to dryness for symptom relief
quiz.explain: A cystic level II node in an adult is a metastasis from a human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma until proved otherwise, and the primary in the tonsil or tongue base is often tiny and impalpable. These nodes are famously mistaken for second branchial cleft cysts, which sit in the same place; the discriminators are a thicker or irregular wall, a mural nodule, and the patient's age, and the safe rule is that a first branchial cleft cyst presenting in adult life is a node until the cytology says otherwise. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration with p16 immunostaining or HPV testing on the aspirate answers the question with the least harm. Antibiotics simply delay. Simple aspiration decompresses the cyst, loses the specimen and lets it refill. Proceeding straight to excision performs an open biopsy on an undiagnosed squamous carcinoma, which spills tumour into a neck that has not yet been staged or planned.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the work-up of an adult with a cystic level II node and no visible mucosal primary, from the first step to the last.
quiz.answer: contrast-CT ultrasound-guided-FNA PET-CT panendoscopy-with-biopsies open-excision
quiz.explain: The sequence is driven by one principle: every step should be taken before the step that would spoil it. Cross-sectional imaging comes first, while the mucosa is undisturbed, because post-biopsy oedema and haemorrhage mimic a primary. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is the least invasive way to prove malignancy and to run p16 or HPV testing. PET-CT then goes before instrumentation, since biopsy sites and a recently traumatised tonsil take up tracer avidly and a false-positive there sends the surgeon to the wrong place; PET is also the step most likely to find the occult primary or a synchronous tumour. Panendoscopy with directed biopsies, guided by the PET, and usually with ipsilateral tonsillectomy, comes next. Open excision of the node is last and is a confession that everything else failed: it violates an unstaged neck, and in a patient with squamous carcinoma it is the step you most want to avoid having taken.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old smoker has a p16-negative tonsillar carcinoma and a single ipsilateral level II node of 2.5 cm. Its margin is spiculated, the perinodal fat is infiltrated and the sternocleidomastoid is invaded; the node is fixed on palpation. Using the AJCC 8th edition, what does the clinical nodal category become?
quiz.answer: N3b, which brings adjuvant chemoradiotherapy
choices: N3b, which brings adjuvant chemoradiotherapy
N1, unchanged by the perinodal appearances
N2a, taken from the 2.5 cm nodal diameter
N2b, because two compartments are involved
quiz.explain: The 8th edition, which is the edition head and neck staging still runs on, brought extranodal extension into the N category for the first time. For a p16-negative tumour, clinically overt extranodal extension makes the neck N3b whatever the size or number of nodes, so a 2.5 cm node that would otherwise be N1 leaps to the top of the N ladder. That is not bureaucracy: extranodal extension roughly halves survival, and its presence on the specimen is one of the two classic indications, with a positive margin, for concurrent chemotherapy alongside post-operative radiotherapy. Two cautions. Pathological staging is graded differently — a single ipsilateral node of 3 cm or less with extranodal extension is pN2a — and for p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer extranodal extension is deliberately excluded from the clinical N categories. On imaging, reserve the call for unequivocal signs: matted nodes and irradiated fat both mimic it.

quiz.prompt: A staging CT for an oral tongue carcinoma shows a level IB node of 8 mm short axis containing a rounded low-attenuation centre with an enhancing rim. Give the call you would make and the reason it outranks the measurement.
quiz.answer: Call it a metastatic node: central necrosis is the most specific sign of nodal metastasis and holds at any size, so a node under the 10 mm short-axis threshold is still reported as malignant.
quiz.explain: Size is the weakest of the nodal criteria; it is simply the one that is easiest to measure. A node enlarges for a fortnight of tonsillitis, and a node harbouring a 2 mm deposit may be entirely normal in calibre, so thresholds of 10 mm short axis in general and 11 mm at level II buy sensitivity at a heavy cost in specificity. Central necrosis is the opposite: an ovoid or round low-attenuation centre with an enhancing rim, in a node draining a known squamous primary, is close to diagnostic, and it is reported as involved at any size. The mimics worth holding in mind are a suppurative node in acute infection and a caseating node in tuberculosis, which is why the clinical setting is part of the reading. On ultrasound the same finding appears as an anechoic or heterogeneous centre; on MRI as a high-T2, non-enhancing core.

quiz.prompt: A 70-year-old has a firm 2 cm node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Flexible nasendoscopy, a dedicated contrast-enhanced neck CT and an ultrasound of the thyroid are all unremarkable. Where should the search for a primary now be directed?
quiz.answer: Below the clavicles, to chest, abdomen and pelvis
choices: Below the clavicles, to chest, abdomen and pelvis
To the nasopharynx, with blind directed biopsies
To the ipsilateral tonsil and the tongue base
To the thyroid bed, with a repeat ultrasound scan
quiz.explain: The level of the node is a map of where to look. The left supraclavicular fossa receives the thoracic duct, so a node there commonly reflects an infraclavicular primary — lung, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, kidney, ovary, testis or breast — and the appropriate next test is a CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, often followed by PET-CT. The other options each describe a real pattern that does not fit this case. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma announces itself with retropharyngeal nodes and level V disease, usually in a younger patient, and the neck CT would rarely be clean. An HPV-associated oropharyngeal primary drains to a cystic level II node, not to the supraclavicular fossa. Thyroid carcinoma spreads to levels VI, III and IV and would be sought on ultrasound of a gland that is here normal. Learning the drainage territories is what turns an unexpected level from a curiosity into a direction of travel.

quiz.prompt: A node is measured three ways on the same CT: 14 mm transverse and 9 mm anteroposterior on the axial image, and 22 mm craniocaudal on the coronal reformat. Give the figure you would enter in the report as the short axis. Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The short axis is the smallest diameter in the axial plane, so it is 9 mm here. The craniocaudal measurement is not part of the criterion at all, and quoting it is the commonest way a normal node is reported as enlarged: nodes are cigar-shaped along the chain, so their long axis in the coronal plane is routinely twice the short axis. Measuring in the axial plane also keeps the number reproducible between readers and between studies, which is what makes follow-up comparisons mean anything. At 9 mm this node falls below the 10 mm threshold used outside level II and the 11 mm used at level II, so size alone does not call it. That is precisely the moment to look at everything else: is it round rather than ovoid, has it lost its fatty hilum, is there a necrotic centre, is the margin irregular?

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has bilateral rubbery non-tender nodes up to 3 cm at levels II and V with preserved fatty hila, and CT shows mediastinal nodes as well. Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration returns atypical lymphoid cells. State the sampling you would arrange next and why aspiration was the wrong tool here.
quiz.answer: Arrange a core biopsy, and an excision if the core is not diagnostic: lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture and immunophenotype, and an aspirate of dispersed cells cannot show architecture.
quiz.explain: Fine-needle aspiration is superb where the question is whether malignant epithelial cells are present — squamous carcinoma in a neck node, a thyroid nodule — because a cytological diagnosis needs only the cells. Lymphoma is diagnosed on how the cells are arranged as well as on what they are, and it is subclassified with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry on tissue, so an aspirate yields the unhelpful answer this patient received. A core biopsy under ultrasound usually suffices and is the sensible next step; excisional biopsy of a whole node remains the reference standard when cores are equivocal. Note that the general warning against open biopsy of a neck node applies to suspected squamous carcinoma, not to suspected lymphoma, where excision is the right operation. When sampling, choose the node with the most abnormal cortex and vascularity rather than the largest, and avoid a node that is largely necrotic.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound of the right neck in a patient with a 12 mm thyroid nodule shows two level III nodes. The first is oval, 6 mm in short axis, with an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar flow on Doppler. The second is round, 9 mm in short axis, with no hilum, punctate echogenic foci within it and peripheral subcapsular flow. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Sample the second node; its features outweigh size
choices: Sample the second node; its features outweigh size
Sample the first node, being the more accessible
Sample neither, as both are under 10 mm short axis
Rescan in six months to see which node grows
quiz.explain: Every feature of the second node argues for malignancy except its size, and size is the criterion to abandon first. Loss of the fatty hilum, a rounded contour, and vascularity that enters through the capsule instead of the hilum together carry far more weight than a millimetre of short axis, and punctate echogenic foci in a lateral neck node alongside a thyroid nodule point hard at metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; cystic change in such a node points the same way. Waiting six months in a patient with a thyroid nodule and an abnormal node forfeits the chance to plan a single operation that clears the lateral compartment. Sampling the first node would return reactive tissue and falsely reassure. When a papillary carcinoma is suspected, the aspirate can be supplemented with a thyroglobulin washout from the needle, which is more sensitive than cytology alone in a cystic node.

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after resection of an oral tongue carcinoma, surveillance CT shows a new 12 mm node at level IV with a necrotic centre. Levels I to III are clear and the primary site looks normal. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Metastasis; tongue can drain straight to level IV
choices: Metastasis; tongue can drain straight to level IV
Reactive node, given the clear upper levels
Post-radiation change in a treated nodal bed
A thyroid primary presenting in its first echelon
quiz.explain: Two things settle this. Necrosis in a node draining a treated squamous primary is a metastasis whatever its size, and the oral tongue is the classic site for a skip deposit: lymphatic channels from the tongue can run directly to levels III and IV, bypassing the submandibular and upper jugular nodes altogether. That is why an elective dissection for an oral tongue primary is often extended beyond the levels I to III of the supraomohyoid operation, and why a clean upper neck is no reassurance about the lower neck. Reactive nodes do not develop necrotic centres in this setting. Radiotherapy change is diffuse, involves fat and skin, and does not produce a discrete new node. A thyroid primary would drain first to level VI and would be visible in the gland. The report should state the level, the size, the necrosis and whether the node abuts the carotid or the scalene muscles.

quiz.prompt: A young infant is referred with an atypical sacral skin marker. Why can ultrasound depict the spinal canal particularly well at this age?
choices: The posterior elements are incompletely ossified
The spinal cord is outside the canal
Ultrasound penetrates fully ossified adult bone equally well
The infant has no cauda equina
quiz.answer: The posterior elements are incompletely ossified
quiz.explain: The immature posterior elements provide an acoustic window. The window becomes more limited with ossification, so age and image quality affect confidence.

quiz.prompt: The conus seems low, but the lumbosacral junction is uncertain. What should be resolved before assigning a vertebral level?
choices: The ultrasound machine brand
Vertebral numbering and the landmark used to count
Only the infant's weight
Only the skin-marker colour
quiz.answer: Vertebral numbering and the landmark used to count
quiz.explain: An incorrect count can produce a false low-conus diagnosis. Document the numbering method and use correlation or further imaging when the landmarks remain uncertain.

quiz.prompt: Only a midline sagittal still image has been saved. What important part of a neonatal spinal examination is missing?
choices: A routine oral contrast study
A chest radiograph in every infant
Transverse assessment and evaluation of cord or root movement
An obligatory contrast-enhanced sequence
quiz.answer: Transverse assessment and evaluation of cord or root movement
quiz.explain: Multiple planes and dynamic assessment add information about filum, roots and canal contents. A single still image cannot represent the complete examination.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound suggests an abnormal filum and limited root motion, but the acoustic window is poor. What is the appropriate conclusion?
choices: Definite normality because ultrasound has no radiation
Tethering is excluded without further assessment
A precise operative recommendation from the incomplete study
State suspicion and limitations, with further specialist-directed evaluation
quiz.answer: State suspicion and limitations, with further specialist-directed evaluation
quiz.explain: The report should distinguish a concerning observation from a complete anatomical diagnosis. MRI can characterise suspected dysraphism when ultrasound is abnormal or incomplete.

quiz.prompt: An infant has an exposed open spinal lesion. Which safety principle applies?
choices: Do not place a routine ultrasound probe directly on the exposed lesion
Compress the lesion to improve resolution
Apply nonsterile gel to confirm the defect
Delay clinical referral until after repeated compression views
quiz.answer: Do not place a routine ultrasound probe directly on the exposed lesion
quiz.explain: Direct scanning of an open defect risks contamination and adds little to the obvious lesion. Follow the specialist pathway and appropriate infection precautions.

quiz.prompt: A neonatal ultrasound labels the conus “L3” after counting from an uncertain sacral landmark. The conclusion says tethered cord. Explain the steps needed before accepting that conclusion.
quiz.answer: Confirm vertebral numbering using reliable landmarks and document the method, age and any segmentation uncertainty. Reassess conus position alongside the filum, cord and root movement and associated abnormalities. If ultrasound remains indeterminate or concerning, further specialist-directed imaging is needed; an uncertain number alone should not establish tethering.
quiz.explain: A precise-looking vertebral label can conceal an uncertain count. The diagnosis requires concordant anatomy rather than a solitary unsupported level.

quiz.prompt: Only sagittal still images were recorded in an infant with an atypical skin marker. The conus looks normal on one image. Explain why this does not document a complete normal examination.
quiz.answer: The study lacks transverse and dynamic documentation needed to assess canal contents, filum and root movement adequately. State what is visible and what has not been evaluated, including vertebral numbering and the relationship to the skin marker. Completion or further evaluation depends on the clinical question and technical window.
quiz.explain: A normal-looking structure in one projection does not establish normality of the whole examination. Documentation should support each conclusion.

quiz.prompt: An older infant has a limited ultrasound acoustic window, with the distal cord poorly seen. The referral is for suspected dysraphism. Write an appropriate conclusion and next-step rationale.
quiz.answer: The distal cord and relevant canal anatomy are incompletely assessed because of the limited window, so dysraphism is not excluded. Describe any observed abnormalities and recommend specialist-directed further assessment, commonly MRI when detailed anatomy is required. The limitation, rather than a presumed normal result, determines what remains to be answered.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound's usefulness depends on the window. A modality without radiation can still be nondiagnostic for the specific patient and question.

quiz.prompt: A small cystic focus near the distal cord is seen, but conus position, filum and nerve-root motion are otherwise reassuring. How would you avoid turning an isolated observation into an unsupported diagnosis?
quiz.answer: Localise and describe the cystic focus, assess its relationship to the cord and filum, and evaluate for associated abnormalities. Consider a recognised developmental variant in the appropriate context, but state any uncertainty. Do not diagnose clinically significant dysraphism or tethering from a small isolated cystic appearance alone.
quiz.explain: The significance of a focal finding depends on its location and accompanying anatomy. Pattern assessment protects against both dismissal and overdiagnosis.

quiz.prompt: An infant with an exposed spinal defect is sent for “ultrasound confirmation”. Explain how you would handle the request without applying a routine probe directly to the lesion.
quiz.answer: Clarify the question with the neonatal or specialist team and avoid direct routine scanning of the open defect because of contamination risk and limited added value. Follow the clinical pathway and infection precautions. If another covered region or associated finding requires ultrasound, define that separate question and appropriate technique.
quiz.explain: The requested test should add information safely. An already visible open abnormality does not justify a routine examination across exposed tissue.

curriculum_modules.title: Bone Scan, V/Q, Thyroid and Sentinel Node

module_contract.goal: Choose between the common single-photon studies and read their patterns against the clinical question, from the three-phase bone scan to lymphoscintigraphy.

approach.step: Ask which phase answers the question before you book the scan
approach.detail: A single delayed bone scan answers "are there metastases". Only the three-phase study separates cellulitis from osteomyelitis, because you need flow and blood pool as well as the delayed image.

approach.step: Check the preparation for the study you are reading
approach.detail: Bone scan: hydration, metal removed, bladder emptied immediately before imaging. Thyroid: four hours fasted, amiodarone, potassium iodide and iodinated contrast excluded. V/Q: a chest radiograph within 12–24 hours, reviewed first.

approach.step: Read the bone scan by phase, in order
approach.detail: Flow — is there hyperaemia. Blood pool — is there capillary dilatation and inflammation. Delayed — is there new bone formation. Only the pattern across all three is diagnostic.

approach.step: Look at the kidneys on a bone scan
approach.detail: Faint or absent renal uptake is usually renal insufficiency; in a patient with normal renal function it is most often widespread metastatic disease — the superscan.

approach.step: On V/Q, decide matched or mismatched, not just abnormal
approach.detail: Reflex vasoconstriction produces a perfusion defect wherever the airway is obstructed, so a matched defect is airway disease. Mismatch is the finding — acute or chronic pulmonary embolism, tumour obstructing an artery, or previous radiotherapy.

approach.step: Check for a right-to-left shunt on the perfusion study
approach.detail: Renal or cerebral activity from Tc-99m MAA that has bypassed the pulmonary capillary bed.

approach.step: On thyroid scintigraphy, take the uptake value and the pattern together
approach.detail: High uptake homogeneous is Graves; high and heterogeneous is toxic multinodular goitre; a single focus with the rest of the gland suppressed is a toxic adenoma.

approach.step: For lymphoscintigraphy, image until the drainage is complete, then hand it over
approach.detail: Dynamic or static acquisition out to 45–60 minutes, a cobalt-57 flood source to outline the body, and SPECT-CT where the anatomy is complex, as in the head and neck. The surgeon then uses a handheld gamma probe on the highest-activity node.

measure.how: Tc-99m diphosphonate (usually MDP) intravenously in an adult.
Why the delayed phase is timed where it is.
measure.cutoff: About 50% of the injected dose in bone by 2–6 hours

measure.how: Flow, blood pool, delayed, and optionally delayed/delayed.
measure.cutoff: Flow 2–5 s frames over 60 s · blood pool 5 min · delayed 2–4 h · delayed/delayed 24 h

measure.what: V/Q performance against CTPA or DSA
measure.how: For the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism.
Oral capsule; scan at one of the two standard time points.
measure.cutoff: 3.7–14.8 MBq (100–400 μCi); scan at 4–6 h or 24 h

measure.how: Percentage of administered activity in the gland at the stated time.
Pinhole collimator, gland filling about two-thirds of the field, anterior plus 45° LAO and RAO.
measure.cutoff: 3–6 mm pinhole · 20% window at 159 keV · 100–250,000 counts per view

measure.how: Intradermal, 25- or 27-gauge needle nearly tangential to the skin, 5–10 mm from the lesion margin, two to four sites.
measure.cutoff: 0.1–0.2 mL per site · total 7.4–37 MBq (200–1000 μCi)

measure.how: Intraparenchymal, around the lesion.

classify.name: Choosing among the common single-photon studies
rows: Skeletal metastases and their follow-up; radiographically occult stress or insufficiency fracture; Paget disease
Flow over 60 s, blood pool at 5 min, delayed at 2–4 h
Osteomyelitis; complex regional pain syndrome; infection versus loosening around a hip prosthesis
Tc-99m DTPA aerosol by non-rebreathing mask, supine, imaged upright
Regional ventilation — the denominator against which perfusion is judged
Tc-99m MAA intravenously, supine, lodging in pre-capillary arterioles
Pulmonary embolism where CTPA is contraindicated; lung function before pneumonectomy; graft function after lung transplant
I-123 orally, 3.7–14.8 MBq (or Tc-99m pertechnetate intravenously)
4–6 h or 24 h (pertechnetate peaks at about 20 min)
Functional status of a nodule; the cause of thyrotoxicosis; residual tissue or recurrence after thyroidectomy
Tc-99m colloid — sulfur colloid, nanocolloid albumin, antimony trisulfide or tilmanocept, by region
Which node the tumour drains to, for sentinel node surgery
classify.note: Tc-99m pertechnetate is trapped by follicular cells but not organified, which is why it must be imaged early and why it is not interchangeable with iodine.

pitfalls: Reading a bone scan against a poor renal excretion pattern. Tc-99m MDP is renally excreted, so impaired function leaves tracer in the soft tissues and degrades every image — hydrate and check the kidneys before you blame the technique.
Missing the superscan. Faint or absent renal activity in a patient without renal disease usually means widespread skeletal metastases, not a good scan.
Forgetting iron. Thalassaemia major and haemochromatosis raise renal and hepatic uptake and lower skeletal uptake, and the scan reads as falsely reassuring.
Reading a V/Q without the chest radiograph. Atelectasis and consolidation produce perfusion defects of their own; the film should be within 12–24 hours and looked at first.

Calling every perfusion defect embolic. Airway obstruction causes reflex vasoconstriction and a matched defect; only mismatch supports embolism, and even mismatch includes tumour and prior radiotherapy.

Sending a patient for thyroid scintigraphy after iodinated contrast. CT or angiographic contrast, amiodarone, potassium iodide and some supplements all block uptake, and inadequate preparation falsely lowers the I-123 uptake into the hypofunctioning range.

Injecting lymphoscintigraphy tracer too far from the lesion. For a cutaneous primary the needle goes intradermally, nearly tangential, 5–10 mm from the lesion margin — deeper or further out maps the wrong basin.

quiz.prompt: A man with diabetes has a red, swollen forefoot and an equivocal radiograph. His three-phase bone scan shows increased flow and increased blood pool activity over the forefoot, but no corresponding focal uptake on the three-hour delayed images.
quiz.answer: Report soft tissue infection with no scintigraphic evidence of underlying osteomyelitis
choices: Report soft tissue infection with no scintigraphic evidence of underlying osteomyelitis
Report osteomyelitis of the metatarsal heads and recommend six weeks of antibiotics
Report a metatarsal stress fracture, which produces exactly this three-phase pattern
Report Charcot neuroarthropathy, which produces no delayed uptake in the mid foot
quiz.explain: The three phases answer three different questions. Flow and blood pool reflect regional hyperaemia and extracellular tracer, so cellulitis lights both; only osteomyelitis adds focal bone uptake on the delayed images, where soft tissue has cleared and the diphosphonate is bound to bone. A stress fracture is positive on all three phases early, with a focal delayed abnormality that is the whole point of the study. The genuinely difficult case is the neuropathic Charcot foot, which is hyperaemic and osteoblastically busy and so is positive on all phases too — which is why a bone scan alone cannot separate Charcot from superimposed osteomyelitis, and labelled white cell imaging with SPECT/CT, or MRI, is used instead. A negative delayed phase, as here, is the reassuring result: sensitivity for osteomyelitis is high, so its absence carries weight.

quiz.prompt: A bone scan in a man with prostate cancer shows uniformly intense skeletal uptake, faint kidneys and almost no soft tissue background. The radiographer wonders whether the injection went well and asks whether to repeat it.
quiz.answer: Report a superscan from diffuse skeletal metastases and correlate with his PSA
choices: Report a superscan from diffuse skeletal metastases and correlate with his PSA
Report a technically excellent normal study, since the skeleton is evenly labelled
Report a failed injection, since faint kidneys indicate poor tracer delivery here
Report free pertechnetate, which produces high skeletal and low renal activity
quiz.explain: A superscan is defined by the ratio, not the absolute counts: bone-to-soft-tissue contrast is so high that the kidneys become faint or invisible, the so-called absent kidney sign, because almost all the tracer has been extracted by bone. Its two families look subtly different. Diffuse osteoblastic metastasis, typically prostate or breast, is usually axial-predominant and slightly irregular on close inspection, with ribs and skull patchy. Metabolic bone disease — renal osteodystrophy, primary hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, myelofibrosis — gives a smoother pattern with prominent calvarium, mandible and costochondral junctions. Free pertechnetate from a poor radiolabel does the opposite: thyroid, salivary glands and stomach light up and the skeleton is faint. The trap this item guards against is dismissing a superscan as a beautiful normal study.

quiz.prompt: A woman with bone metastases from breast cancer starts endocrine therapy. Ten weeks later her repeat bone scan shows more intense uptake at known sites plus two apparently new foci, yet her pain has improved and her tumour markers have fallen.
quiz.answer: Suggest a flare response and repeat the imaging in about three months before changing treatment
choices: Suggest a flare response and repeat the imaging in about three months before changing treatment
Report progression and recommend an immediate change of systemic therapy for her
Report progression and recommend urgent palliative radiotherapy to the two new foci
Suggest a flare response and stop the endocrine therapy pending a bone biopsy
quiz.explain: The flare phenomenon is osteoblastic healing misread as disease. Lesions that are responding lay down new bone, which is exactly what a diphosphonate tracer measures, so uptake at known sites intensifies and deposits that were previously lytic and photopenic become visible for the first time. It appears roughly two to three months after starting effective therapy and settles thereafter. The discriminator is discordance: the images look worse while the patient and the biochemistry look better. Repeat imaging at around three to six months resolves it — genuine progression keeps progressing, flare fades. The same trap appears on radiographs, where lytic deposits becoming sclerotic is healing, and on PSMA imaging early after starting treatment. Calling flare progression costs the patient a drug that is working.

quiz.prompt: A woman with breast cancer has a single focus of increased uptake in a lower lumbar vertebra on planar bone scan. SPECT/CT localises the activity to the right facet joint, and the CT component shows facet osteophytes with joint space narrowing.
quiz.answer: Report degenerative facet disease with no scintigraphic evidence of skeletal metastasis
choices: Report degenerative facet disease with no scintigraphic evidence of skeletal metastasis
Report a probable metastasis, since solitary vertebral uptake is usually malignant
Report an indeterminate lesion and request whole spine MRI within the same week
Report a pars interarticularis defect, which gives this pattern in the vertebral body
quiz.explain: A solitary hot spot in a patient with cancer is benign roughly half the time, so the planar image alone leaves you stranded. What SPECT/CT adds is precisely this: anatomical localisation within the vertebra, plus attenuation correction and better lesion contrast. Location decides the report. Uptake in a pedicle or in the vertebral body away from the endplate favours metastasis; uptake centred on a facet joint, an endplate with a Schmorl node, or an osteophyte is degenerative; a pars defect sits in the posterior elements, not the body. Ribs follow the same logic — several foci aligned in a vertical row are almost always traumatic. Correlating with the CT component turns an equivocal study into a definite answer and spares the patient an MRI, a delay and an anxious week.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Her chest radiograph is normal and her renal function is normal. The medical team asks which imaging test you would recommend for suspected pulmonary embolism.
quiz.answer: Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy, since her chest radiograph is normal and breast dose is lower
choices: Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy, since her chest radiograph is normal and breast dose is lower
CT pulmonary angiography, since it delivers less radiation to the maternal breast tissue
D-dimer measurement alone, since a negative result in pregnancy excludes embolism safely
Echocardiography alone, since right heart strain is a dependable screen for embolism
quiz.explain: In pregnancy with a normal chest radiograph, perfusion or ventilation-perfusion imaging is generally preferred because CT pulmonary angiography delivers a considerably higher dose to radiosensitive breast tissue in a young woman, and because the hyperdynamic circulation of pregnancy frequently produces transient interruption of the contrast bolus and a non-diagnostic study. Fetal dose is low with either technique and is not the deciding factor. The other classic indications for scintigraphy are severe iodinated contrast allergy and renal impairment, and young patients likely to need repeated studies. The precondition is a normal or near-normal chest radiograph: parenchymal disease creates matched defects that cannot be interpreted, and pushes you back to CT. D-dimer rises physiologically through pregnancy, and echocardiography is neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule out embolism.

quiz.prompt: A ventilation-perfusion study shows two wedge-shaped, pleural-based perfusion defects in the right lower zone with preserved ventilation in those segments, and a third defect at the left base that is matched and corresponds to consolidation on the chest radiograph.
quiz.answer: Report the two mismatched right basal defects as pulmonary embolism, and the left base separately
choices: Report the two mismatched right basal defects as pulmonary embolism, and the left base separately
Report all three of the defects as pulmonary embolism, including the matched left basal one
Report the whole study as non-diagnostic, because one defect is matched to consolidation
Report the matched left basal defect as the embolus and the right sided defects as artefact
quiz.explain: Mismatch is the diagnostic unit: a perfusion defect with preserved ventilation, segmental or subsegmental in shape, wedge-shaped and pleural-based. Two such defects are convincing evidence of embolism. The left base here is a triple match — perfusion defect, ventilation defect and radiographic opacity — which is not evidence of embolus, since pneumonia, atelectasis and infarct all produce it; conventionally it is reported as indeterminate for that region, particularly in the lower zones. Crucially, an indeterminate region does not contaminate an unequivocal mismatch elsewhere; you report both, and the patient is anticoagulated. Modern practice, especially with V/Q SPECT, has moved away from PIOPED probability language towards a three-way report of embolism present, absent, or study non-diagnostic.

quiz.prompt: A woman is thyrotoxic with a fully suppressed TSH, a tender neck and a raised CRP. Her technetium-99m pertechnetate thyroid scan shows almost no tracer anywhere in the gland.
quiz.answer: Report suppressed uptake consistent with a destructive thyroiditis rather than Graves disease
choices: Report suppressed uptake consistent with a destructive thyroiditis rather than Graves disease
Report Graves disease, since thyrotoxicosis with a suppressed TSH establishes that diagnosis
Report a toxic multinodular goitre whose nodules are too small to resolve on this study
Report a technical failure, since pertechnetate is not trapped by normal thyroid tissue
quiz.explain: The thyroid scan separates the two mechanisms of thyrotoxicosis, and the treatments diverge completely. Overproduction shows increased uptake: Graves disease diffusely and homogeneously, a toxic adenoma as one hot nodule with the remaining gland suppressed, a toxic multinodular goitre as patchy areas of activity. Destruction shows low or absent uptake, because preformed hormone is leaking from a gland that is not making any — subacute de Quervain thyroiditis, silent and postpartum thyroiditis, amiodarone type 2, and exogenous thyroxine. Antithyroid drugs and radioiodine work in the first group and are useless in the second, which needs analgesia, sometimes steroids, and time. Separately, in a euthyroid patient with a nodule, a hot nodule is almost never malignant and does not need aspiration, while a cold nodule is assessed on ultrasound and aspirated on its sonographic features.

quiz.prompt: A man with right upper quadrant pain has an equivocal ultrasound. Technetium-99m HIDA imaging shows prompt hepatic uptake with tracer in the duodenum by 40 minutes, but the gallbladder is not visualised at 60 minutes nor after morphine augmentation.
quiz.answer: Report findings consistent with acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
choices: Report findings consistent with acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
Report common bile duct obstruction, since tracer reached the duodenum slowly
Report a normal study, since biliary excretion into the duodenum is preserved
Report chronic cholecystitis, which characteristically shows early gallbladder filling
quiz.explain: Hepatobiliary agents are extracted by hepatocytes and excreted into bile along the same pathway as bilirubin, so the study is a map of bile flow. Duodenal activity proves the common duct is patent, which excludes distal obstruction. Non-visualisation of the gallbladder in that setting means the cystic duct is blocked, and cystic duct obstruction is the functional definition of acute cholecystitis. Morphine raises sphincter of Oddi tone and diverts bile towards the gallbladder, so persistent non-visualisation after morphine, or on four-hour delayed images, gives the diagnosis a high specificity — useful precisely when ultrasound is equivocal. Delayed but eventual filling suggests chronic cholecystitis. False positives arise with prolonged fasting, parenteral nutrition, severe intercurrent illness and opiates, all of which leave the gallbladder full of viscous bile.

quiz.prompt: A technetium-99m DMSA study gives background-corrected renal counts of 18,400 for the left kidney and 27,600 for the right. Report the left kidney's relative function. Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Total counts are 46,000, and the left kidney contributes 18,400 of them, so its relative function is 18,400 divided by 46,000, which is 40.0 per cent. DMSA binds to proximal tubular cells and stays there, which makes it the reference study for cortical scarring and for split function; MAG3, which is secreted and cleared, is the study for drainage. Normal split is close to 50:50, with roughly 45 to 55 per cent regarded as within normal limits, so 40 per cent is a real reduction and would prompt a search for scarring or a structural cause. The word to keep hold of is relative: this is a share of the whole, not a measure of glomerular filtration, so symmetrical bilateral disease produces a perfectly normal 50:50 split alongside a dreadful total function.

quiz.prompt: Explain what a technetium-99m diphosphonate bone scan is physically measuring, and why a purely lytic myeloma deposit can be invisible on it.
quiz.answer: The diphosphonate is chemisorbed onto hydroxyapatite in newly formed bone, so the scan maps osteoblastic activity and regional blood flow rather than tumour cells; a purely lytic myeloma deposit provokes little osteoblastic response and can therefore be photopenic.
quiz.explain: This single mechanistic fact explains most of what the study does and does not do. Because uptake requires an osteoblastic reaction and adequate perfusion, the scan is exquisitely sensitive to healing bone — fractures, degenerative change, Paget disease, osteoblastic metastases — and blind to disease that destroys bone without provoking repair. Myeloma is the classic example, which is why myeloma is staged with whole-body low-dose CT or MRI rather than scintigraphy. Very aggressive or highly anaplastic metastases can also appear photopenic. In the other direction, the mechanism explains the flare phenomenon, where successful treatment increases uptake because healing is osteoblastic. Around half the injected tracer is excreted renally, so the kidneys, bladder and any urinary contamination are part of every normal study.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a 1.4 mm melanoma on the upper back is listed for sentinel node biopsy. Say what preoperative lymphoscintigraphy contributes beyond the surgeon's intraoperative blue dye.
quiz.answer: Lymphoscintigraphy maps the true drainage basin before surgery and SPECT/CT localises the sentinel node anatomically, which matters on the trunk where drainage is unpredictable and may cross the midline or stop at an interval node.
quiz.explain: Blue dye tells the surgeon where a node is once the incision is open; it does not tell them which incision to make. Truncal melanoma drains unpredictably — bilaterally, across the midline, to axilla and groin simultaneously, or to an interval node sitting in the subcutaneous fat between the primary and the basin, which will simply be missed if nobody knows to look. Dynamic imaging immediately after intradermal injection of technetium-99m nanocolloid catches the first-order node before second-tier nodes label, and SPECT/CT then gives depth and the relation to vessels and muscle, allowing the skin to be marked accurately. Intraoperatively the gamma probe leads and the dye confirms. Previous wide local excision or prior nodal surgery can divert or obstruct lymphatics, and is worth knowing before you start.

quiz.prompt: A hydronephrotic kidney with a dilated pelvicalyceal system is being assessed for obstruction. Say what a MAG3 diuretic renogram gives you that ultrasound cannot.
quiz.answer: The diuretic renogram shows whether the dilated system actually drains under a furosemide challenge and measures relative function, so a prolonged clearance half-time indicates true obstruction rather than a capacious unobstructed system.
quiz.explain: Dilatation is anatomy; obstruction is physiology, and ultrasound can only see the first. MAG3 is secreted by the proximal tubule with high extraction, giving good images even in impaired kidneys. Furosemide, given either 20 minutes after the tracer or 15 minutes before it, generates a high urine flow to stress the system: clearance half-time under 10 minutes is normal drainage, over 20 minutes suggests obstruction and 10 to 20 minutes is equivocal. The curve shape matters as much as the number, and a rising curve that falls when the patient stands or empties the bladder was never obstructed. The study is invalid if the patient is dehydrated, the bladder is full, or renal function is too poor to respond to diuretic, all of which produce a falsely obstructed appearance.

quiz.prompt: Put the acquisitions of a three-phase bone scan, together with its optional late acquisition, into the order in which they are performed.
quiz.answer: dynamic-flow-images blood-pool-images delayed-three-hour-images twenty-four-hour-images
quiz.explain: The sequence is dictated by where the tracer is at each moment. Flow images are rapid frames acquired from the moment of injection over the first minute, showing regional arterial perfusion. Blood pool images follow within about five to ten minutes, while tracer is still largely in the extracellular space, and show hyperaemia and soft tissue inflammation. Delayed images at two to four hours, conventionally three, are acquired once soft tissue has cleared and the diphosphonate is bound to bone, and these are the only phase that reports osteoblastic activity. An optional 24-hour set improves bone-to-background contrast where perfusion is poor, classically in the dysvascular diabetic foot. Interpretation depends on which phases are positive, so a single delayed acquisition answers a narrower question than the full study.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these three investigations for gastrointestinal bleeding by the rate of blood loss each can detect, starting with the one that detects the slowest bleeding.
quiz.answer: labelled-red-cell-scintigraphy CT-angiography catheter-angiography
quiz.explain: Technetium-99m labelled red cells detect bleeding of roughly 0.1 to 0.2 mL per minute, CT angiography around 0.3 to 0.5, and catheter angiography needs approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mL per minute before contrast extravasation is visible. Scintigraphy has a second advantage that matters more than the threshold: the labelled cells circulate for hours, so delayed imaging can catch intermittent bleeding that was quiescent when the patient was first imaged. Its weakness is localisation — the finding you are looking for is a focus that appears where there was none, increases in intensity, and moves both antegrade and retrograde along a bowel loop, and it is that movement rather than the initial position that names the segment. A static focus is usually a vascular structure or renal activity. Its practical role is to tell the interventional radiologist whether catheter angiography is worth attempting.

approach.detail: Globe, intraconal space (within the muscle cone: optic nerve, vessels, cranial nerves III/IV/VI), conal space (the extraocular muscles and their fascial envelope) or extraconal space (lacrimal gland, orbital walls, periosteum) — the compartment narrows the differential before you name a lesion.

approach.step: Check the extraocular muscles for tapering
approach.detail: Thyroid eye disease spares the tendinous insertion (the muscle belly is enlarged but tapers normally at the tendon); pseudotumour involves the tendon as well as the muscle.

The retina is fixed at the ora serrata anteriorly and at the optic disc posteriorly, so a retinal detachment cannot extend past the ora serrata; a choroidal detachment can cross the optic nerve and is not bound by the ora serrata.

approach.step: Use the orbital septum to grade cellulitis
approach.detail: Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis is superficial to the septum and treated with oral antibiotics; postseptal (orbital) cellulitis is deep to it and needs IV antibiotics — say which side of the septum the infection sits on.

approach.step: In trauma, look specifically for globe rupture
approach.detail: Shallow anterior chamber, increased anterior chamber density (haemorrhage), decreased lens density (traumatic cataract), vitreous haemorrhage and posterior globe flattening together indicate rupture.
Vascular, Infectious, Traumatic, Acquired (thyroid eye disease), Neoplastic, Congenital — go through each before closing the report.

pitfalls: Calling thyroid eye disease when the tendon itself is thickened — that pattern is pseudotumour.
Missing a small anterior chamber or subtle lens density change that is the only sign of an open globe on CT.
Reporting a choroidal process as retinal because it has crossed the ora serrata or the optic nerve.
Blurring preseptal and postseptal cellulitis in the report when the orbital septum is identifiable and the distinction changes the antibiotic route.
