quiz.prompt: Ethmoid sinusitis in a child spreads laterally across the lamina papyracea. Arrange these five orbital complications into the classical staging sequence of increasing severity.
quiz.answer: preseptal-cellulitis orbital-cellulitis subperiosteal-abscess orbital-abscess cavernous-sinus-thrombosis
quiz.explain: The classical five stages track the infection across one anatomical barrier at a time. It begins in the lid soft tissues in front of the orbital septum, where the eye itself is untouched. Once it crosses the septum the orbital fat is inflamed and the eye becomes proptosed, painful on movement and at risk. Pus then collects first between the periorbita and the medial wall, lifting the periosteum off the bone as a lentiform collection, before breaking through it into the orbital fat as a true intraorbital abscess. Finally it travels back along the valveless ophthalmic veins into the cavernous sinus. Two practical consequences: the septum is the line your report must comment on, because it separates an oral-antibiotic problem from an admission, and the direction of travel is medial and posterior, so it is the medial wall and the apex you scrutinise. In real children the stages blur and can be skipped, so the staging is a way of describing severity rather than a timetable.

quiz.prompt: A 6-year-old has a hot, swollen right upper lid. Eye movements are full and painless, acuity and colour vision are normal, and there is no proptosis. Contrast CT shows swelling of the lid soft tissues in front of an intact orbital septum, clean retroseptal fat, and an opacified ipsilateral ethmoid cell. Which additional finding on the same scan would most change what happens that day?
quiz.answer: A thin lentiform rim-enhancing collection along the lamina papyracea
choices: A thin lentiform rim-enhancing collection along the lamina papyracea
Mucosal thickening in the ipsilateral maxillary antrum as well
Reactive enlargement of the ipsilateral submandibular lymph nodes
A small quantity of fluid within the ipsilateral middle ear cavity
quiz.explain: A rim-enhancing lens-shaped collection hugging the medial wall is a subperiosteal abscess, and it moves the child from oral antibiotics and review to admission, intravenous antibiotics and a surgical conversation, with drainage if there is any visual compromise, a large collection, or failure to improve within about 48 hours. It is the one finding here that crosses the septum. Look for it deliberately on the coronal images, because a thin collection is easy to mistake for thickened periorbita on axial slices alone, and measure the medial rectus displacement. The other three findings are all common travelling companions of paediatric sinonasal infection and change nothing on the day: maxillary mucosal thickening simply confirms that the sinuses are inflamed, reactive nodes are expected, and middle ear fluid is incidental. None of them tells you where the eye stands.

quiz.prompt: Coronal and sagittal reformats after a blunt orbital injury show a floor defect measuring 18 mm anteroposteriorly by 14 mm transversely. The intact floor of the opposite orbit measures 30 mm by 24 mm. Treating both as rectangles, what proportion of the floor is defective? Answer as a percentage to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The defect is 18 x 14 = 252 square millimetres against an intact floor of 30 x 24 = 720, so 252/720 = 35 per cent. The reason to do this arithmetic rather than eyeball it is that defect size is one of the few reproducible things imaging contributes to the repair decision. The widely used surgical rule of thumb is that a defect of roughly half the floor or more tends to produce late enophthalmos and is offered repair, while smaller defects are often watched for one to two weeks and repaired only if enophthalmos of about 2 mm or more, or persistent diplopia in the functional field of gaze, declares itself. Note that this is a rule of thumb and not a graded classification, so give the surgeon the measurements rather than a verdict. And it never overrides true muscle entrapment, which is repaired on its own merits and urgently, however small the crack.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old is struck in the eye by a football. He cannot elevate the left eye, is retching, and his pulse is 46. CT shows a hairline linear crack in the orbital floor with a small tag of soft tissue in the antral roof and almost no herniated fat. The on-call team plan to see him in fracture clinic in two weeks. Say what is going on and what should happen instead.
quiz.answer: This is a paediatric trapdoor fracture with genuine entrapment of the inferior rectus, and the bradycardia and vomiting are the oculocardiac reflex. The child's elastic bone has sprung back on the muscle, so the CT looks unimpressive while the muscle is being strangled. He needs urgent ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral for release within hours, not a clinic appointment in two weeks.
quiz.explain: This is the orbital fracture that punishes a proportionate CT report. In children the floor is greenstick rather than comminuted: it hinges open, the inferior rectus or its surrounding fat slips through, and the bone recoils and grips it. Because almost nothing herniates, the scan shows only a hairline defect and perhaps a small soft-tissue tag in the antrum, so the imaging looks trivial while the clinical picture is severe. The tell is the mismatch: marked restriction of upgaze, pain on movement, and the oculocardiac reflex of bradycardia, nausea and vomiting from traction on the extraocular muscles. Ischaemic muscle necroses, so this is repaired within hours to a day, not after the usual two-week wait for swelling to settle. Adults get the comminuted version and rarely the entrapment, which is why the same CT in a 40-year-old would not be urgent. When your scan looks mild and the referrer describes a fixed eye and a slow pulse, believe the referrer.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT through the lenses, a line is drawn between the two zygomatic frontal processes. The right globe measures 24.0 mm in anteroposterior diameter, and 9.0 mm of it projects anterior to that line. What proportion of the globe lies behind the line? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Fifteen of the 24 millimetres lie behind the line, which is 62.5 per cent. The convention worth carrying is that at least two-thirds, about 66.7 per cent, of a normal globe sits posterior to the interzygomatic line, so this eye is proptosed. The other common cut-off measures from the line to the anterior corneal surface, with more than about 21 to 23 millimetres taken as abnormal; both are rules of thumb rather than a graded system, and both are worth stating with the raw numbers so the clinician can follow them over time. Two cautions. First, the measurement is only valid on a straight axial slice through both lenses, because head tilt fakes asymmetry. Second, proptosis is a sign, not a diagnosis: what matters next is why. Bilateral and painless suggests thyroid eye disease, painful and unilateral suggests inflammation or infection, and pulsatile with an enlarged superior ophthalmic vein suggests a carotid-cavernous fistula.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old woman has bilateral proptosis and lid retraction. Coronal CT shows fusiform enlargement of both inferior and medial recti with tendinous insertions of normal calibre, and an increased volume of orbital fat. She has no orbital pain. Which finding on that same study would most urgently alter her management?
quiz.answer: Crowding of the orbital apex effacing the perineural fat
choices: Crowding of the orbital apex effacing the perineural fat
Enlargement of the superior ophthalmic vein bilaterally
Bowing of the medial orbital wall into the ethmoid cells
Increased retrobulbar fat displacing the globes forwards
quiz.explain: The muscle bellies enlarged with the tendons spared, bilaterally and painlessly, is thyroid eye disease, and the classical order of recruitment is inferior, then medial, then superior, then lateral rectus. The complication that threatens sight is dysthyroid optic neuropathy, produced not by the proptosis but by the swollen muscles crowding the optic nerve at the apex, and its imaging surrogate is loss of the fat plane around the nerve on posterior coronal slices. That finding triggers visual field testing, high-dose steroids and consideration of urgent decompression. Medial wall bowing is the opposite of a worry: it is spontaneous decompression, and orbits that bow tend to be the ones that spare the nerve. An enlarged superior ophthalmic vein is common in congested thyroid orbitopathy and is only alarming if it is thrombosed or if the picture suggests a fistula. Increased fat drives proptosis and exposure keratopathy, which is a corneal problem treated with lubricants and taping, not an emergency for the nerve.

quiz.prompt: A 58-year-old man has painless bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement and mildly enlarged lateral recti. The glands are hypointense on T2 and enhance homogeneously. A colleague has called it idiopathic orbital inflammation. What additional imaging finding would push you towards IgG4-related disease instead, and what would you ask the physicians to send?
quiz.answer: Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve in the orbital floor, together with disease elsewhere such as the pancreas, kidneys or salivary glands, favours IgG4-related disease over idiopathic orbital inflammation. Ask for a serum IgG4 level, and where the diagnosis will change treatment, tissue showing IgG4-positive plasma cells and storiform fibrosis.
quiz.explain: Both conditions are fibro-inflammatory, both are T2 dark because of that fibrosis, and both enhance, so signal alone will not separate them. Three things tilt the balance towards IgG4-related disease: bilateral and painless involvement, enlargement of the infraorbital nerve as it runs in the floor of the orbit, which is unusual enough in other orbital disease to be worth hunting for on coronal fat-saturated images, and extra-orbital sites, so widen your review to any prior chest or abdominal imaging for autoimmune pancreatitis, a sclerosing kidney lesion, retroperitoneal fibrosis or an enlarged submandibular gland. Idiopathic orbital inflammation is more often unilateral, painful, acute and steroid-responsive, and when it involves a muscle it involves the tendon insertion too, which is the point of difference from thyroid eye disease. The distinction matters because IgG4 disease relapses on steroid withdrawal and is increasingly managed with rituximab, and because a small number of orbital lymphomas hide in exactly this appearance, so a persistent or atypical case earns a biopsy.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old woman has slowly progressive visual loss in the right eye. Post-contrast fat-saturated T1 shows enhancing tubular thickening surrounding the right optic nerve with a non-enhancing linear structure running through its centre, and CT shows fine calcification along it. What follows from these appearances?
quiz.answer: A sheath lesion: the nerve is spared but endangered by resection
choices: A sheath lesion: the nerve is spared but endangered by resection
A nerve lesion: the nerve is expanded and buckles within the orbit
A perineuritis: the enhancement should resolve on corticosteroids
Perineural spread: search the face and sinuses for a primary tumour
quiz.explain: Enhancement surrounding a dark central nerve is the optic nerve sheath meningioma, seen as tram-track thickening on axial images and as a doughnut on coronals, in a middle-aged woman, and calcification on CT is close to confirmatory. The reason the distinction is worth making is surgical: the tumour is in the sheath, so the nerve itself is anatomically intact but takes its blood supply through the very tissue that would have to be removed. Resection therefore blinds the eye, and management is observation while vision holds and fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy when it does not. An optic nerve glioma expands the nerve itself, kinking and buckling it, occurs in children, does not calcify, and is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, bilateral involvement being effectively diagnostic of it. Optic perineuritis enhances the sheath too but is painful, acute and steroid-responsive without calcification. Perineural tumour spread reaches the orbit along the trigeminal branches, not along the optic nerve, which is a central nervous system tract.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old has two years of slowly progressive painless proptosis. MRI shows a well-defined encapsulated ovoid intraconal mass lateral to the optic nerve, bright on T2, enhancing patchily in the early phase and filling in progressively on delayed images. The referrer has suggested an orbital varix. Which observation would settle the question at the scanner?
quiz.answer: Whether the lesion swells when the patient performs a Valsalva manoeuvre
choices: Whether the lesion swells when the patient performs a Valsalva manoeuvre
Whether the lesion contains fluid-fluid levels on the T2 sequence
Whether the lesion contains internal flow voids on the T2 sequence
Whether the lesion abuts the periosteum of the lateral orbital wall
quiz.explain: A varix is a distensible venous channel in continuity with the orbital venous system, so it enlarges with Valsalva, with jugular compression or in the prone position, and collapses when the patient sits up. That single manoeuvre, added to the end of the study, answers the question. What is described here is a cavernous venous malformation, the commonest intraconal mass in adults: encapsulated, slow-growing, and characterised by patchy early enhancement that fills in centripetally on delayed imaging because contrast seeps slowly through its low-flow spaces. Its capsule is what makes it resectable when it becomes symptomatic. Fluid-fluid levels would point instead to a lymphatic malformation, which is transspatial, unencapsulated, presents in childhood and can enlarge abruptly after haemorrhage. Internal flow voids would suggest a high-flow lesion such as an arteriovenous malformation or a carotid-cavernous fistula, where you would also expect an enlarged superior ophthalmic vein and swollen extraocular muscles. Contact with the periosteum discriminates nothing.

quiz.prompt: A 7-year-old has developed proptosis and downward displacement of the left globe over three weeks. He is afebrile with a normal white cell count. MRI shows a superomedial extraconal soft-tissue mass, intermediate on T2, enhancing avidly, with erosion of the adjacent bone. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Urgent tissue biopsy and staging: this behaves like a malignant lesion
choices: Urgent tissue biopsy and staging: this behaves like a malignant lesion
Intravenous antibiotics and review: this behaves like an orbital abscess
A course of corticosteroids: this behaves like orbital inflammation
Interval imaging at six months: this behaves like a slow malformation
quiz.explain: Rapid painless proptosis in a well child with a bone-eroding extraconal mass is rhabdomyosarcoma until proved otherwise: it is the commonest orbital malignancy of childhood, arises from undifferentiated mesenchyme rather than from the extraocular muscles themselves despite the name, favours the superior and superomedial extraconal compartment, and grows over weeks. It is treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy after biopsy, with orbital preservation the norm, so the job of imaging is to get tissue and stage rather than to plan an exenteration. An abscess would come with fever, sinus disease and a rim-enhancing collection, and it displaces bone rather than destroying it. Idiopathic orbital inflammation is painful and steroid-responsive, and giving steroids blind here obscures the histology, which is the classic way to lose weeks. A lymphatic malformation is long-standing and shows fluid-fluid levels. The other paediatric bone-destroying orbital lesion to hold in mind is metastatic neuroblastoma, typically bilateral, centred on the sphenoid wing, with periorbital bruising.

quiz.prompt: An 18-month-old is referred with a white pupillary reflex on the right. Ultrasound shows an echogenic mass arising from the posterior retina containing foci that shadow, and the globe is of normal size. What imaging should follow, and for what reason?
quiz.answer: MRI of orbits and brain, to seek nerve, choroidal and pineal disease
choices: MRI of orbits and brain, to seek nerve, choroidal and pineal disease
CT of the orbits, to confirm the calcification within the retinal mass
Ultrasound of the opposite eye alone, repeated again in three months
Catheter angiography, to map the ophthalmic arterial supply first
quiz.explain: Shadowing foci in a retinal mass in a toddler with leukocoria are the calcification of retinoblastoma, and ultrasound has already shown them, so CT would add ionising radiation without adding information to a child who may carry a germline RB1 mutation and is therefore at raised lifetime risk of second malignancies. MRI answers the questions that change treatment: post-laminar optic nerve invasion, choroidal and extrascleral extension, the state of the fellow eye, and a pineal or suprasellar primitive neuroectodermal tumour, which makes the disease trilateral. The differential for leukocoria is worth carrying alongside. Coats disease gives exudative subretinal fluid that is bright on T1, in an older boy, without calcification. Persistent fetal vasculature gives a small globe with a stalk running from disc to lens and no calcification. Toxocariasis gives a granuloma with vitreous inflammation. Scanning only the good eye abandons the diseased one, and angiography belongs later, if intra-arterial chemotherapy is chosen.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old was grinding steel without eye protection and now has a painful watering right eye with reduced acuity. The eye clinic has requested an MRI of the orbits to look for a foreign body. What do you do with that request, and why?
quiz.answer: Do not send him to MRI yet. Get orbital CT first, or at least orbital radiographs, to exclude a metallic intraocular foreign body, because a ferromagnetic fragment can be torqued or displaced by the magnet and blind him. CT also shows an open globe and localises the fragment; MRI can follow if the fragment proves non-metallic or none is present.
quiz.explain: The history is the whole item: grinding, striking or hammering metal without protection is the classic mechanism for a small, fast, sometimes painless intraocular foreign body, and it is the standard screening question before any orbital MRI. A ferromagnetic fragment sitting against the retina can rotate or migrate in the static field and cause irreversible damage, so the sequence is imaging that cannot move it first. Thin-section CT is the workhorse: it detects metal and glass reliably, shows globe contour, lens position and intraocular gas, and localises the fragment relative to the sclera for the surgeon. Plain radiographs are an acceptable screen where CT is not available but miss small fragments. Wood and some plastics are poorly seen on CT and are the situation where MRI genuinely helps, but only once metal has been excluded. Do not let the urgency of the visual loss reverse the order; the eye that needs MRI today will still need it in an hour.

quiz.prompt: A patient struck in the eye by a bungee hook has a right globe of reduced volume with an irregular posterior contour, a few tiny locules of gas within the vitreous, and the lens lying dependently in the posterior segment. What does this combination require?
quiz.answer: Urgent surgical exploration, with a rigid shield and no pressure on the eye
choices: Urgent surgical exploration, with a rigid shield and no pressure on the eye
Topical antibiotics, a firm pad over the eye and clinic review tomorrow
Immediate lateral canthotomy to relieve raised intra-orbital pressure
Digital and applanation tonometry to establish the intraocular pressure
quiz.explain: A collapsed, irregular globe, intraocular gas and a dislocated lens are the CT signature of an open globe, and each of the three would raise the question on its own. The management consequence is immediate and mostly about what not to do: nothing may press on the eye, because pressure expresses vitreous, uvea and retina through the wound. So no pad, no tonometry, no forced lid retraction; a rigid shield instead, systemic antibiotics, tetanus cover, antiemetics, nil by mouth and theatre. Reviewing tomorrow risks endophthalmitis, which is the reason repair is measured in hours. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis is the right answer to a different emergency, the orbital compartment syndrome of retrobulbar haemorrhage, where the globe is tense and tented posteriorly with a hard, proptosed eye. Performing it on an open globe would be actively harmful. Finish the read by looking for an intraocular foreign body and by checking the optic canal and orbital walls.

curriculum_modules.title: Ovarian Lesions: O-RADS on Ultrasound and MRI

module_contract.goal: Categorise an adnexal lesion with O-RADS on ultrasound and MRI, decide when to escalate and when to say nothing, and recognise the classic benign lesions, torsion and peritoneal spread.

approach.detail: Step 1 of the roadmap: decide whether the lesion is ovarian or non-ovarian before anything else.

approach.step: Look for a classic benign pattern
approach.detail: Step 2: try to place the lesion into one of four benign categories — simple cyst, haemorrhagic cyst, endometrioma or mature cystic teratoma — before calling it indeterminate.
Cysts up to 3 cm in reproductive-age women need no description or follow-up. Up to 7 cm, in both pre- and postmenopausal women, is almost certainly benign.
Step 3: place the patient as low-risk (premenopausal, no additional risk factors) or high-risk, which changes the threshold for action.
Ascites, lymphadenopathy or peritoneal implants change the assessment regardless of the lesion's own appearance.
Combine morphology, risk group and symptom status into an explicit plan — ignore, follow, or refer for excision.

measure.how: Longest diameter on ultrasound.
measure.cutoff: ≤ 3 cm — no description or follow-up needed

measure.how: Longest diameter on ultrasound.
measure.cutoff: ≤ 7 cm — almost certainly benign · > 7 cm — consider MRI or surgical evaluation

classify.name: Roadmap to evaluate ovarian cysts (not O-RADS)
rows: Is the lesion ovarian or non-ovarian in origin?
Confirm two normal ovaries elsewhere; reconsider a non-ovarian differential if the lesion cannot be separated from the ovary
Does it fit a classic benign pattern (simple cyst, haemorrhagic cyst, endometrioma, mature cystic teratoma) or is it indeterminate?
Classic benign patterns need no further work-up; indeterminate lesions move to risk stratification
Is the patient low-risk (premenopausal, no added risk factors) or high-risk?
Weigh morphology, risk group, symptoms and ascites/nodes/implants to decide: ignore, follow, or refer for excision
classify.note: This is the Radiology Assistant's own three-step roadmap, not the O-RADS lexicon and score. O-RADS is not published on this site under that name; use this roadmap for triage and cite an O-RADS reference separately if a formal O-RADS category is required.

pitfalls: Presenting this roadmap as O-RADS. It is a related but distinct triage tool from the same authors' site — do not quote an O-RADS category number from it.
Measuring and describing every incidental small cyst. Cysts ≤3 cm in reproductive-age women need no mention.

Calling a haemorrhagic cyst indeterminate on a single study. Its classic reticular or lace-like internal pattern and lack of internal flow are diagnostic; recommend short-interval follow-up rather than escalation.
Ignoring peritoneal and nodal findings because the ovarian lesion itself looks simple. Ascites, lymphadenopathy or peritoneal implants override a reassuring ovarian appearance.
Treating postmenopausal status alone as high-risk. The great majority of cystic ovarian lesions remain benign even after menopause — risk factors and morphology drive the category, not age alone.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old woman has pelvic ultrasound for right iliac fossa pain. The appendix is normal. The right ovary contains a 2.4 cm anechoic thin-walled avascular cyst with posterior acoustic enhancement, and the left ovary is unremarkable. What should the report say about the cyst?
quiz.answer: Call it a normal follicle and give no follow-up, since a simple cyst of this size in a premenopausal ovary is a physiological structure
choices: Call it a normal follicle and give no follow-up, since a simple cyst of this size in a premenopausal ovary is a physiological structure
Call it a simple cyst and arrange repeat ultrasound in six to twelve weeks to document that it has resolved as would be expected
Call it an O-RADS 3 lesion and recommend pelvic MRI, since a discrete cyst warrants characterisation before it is dismissed as benign
Call it an O-RADS 2 lesion and recommend a serum CA-125, since simple cysts in this age group carry a low but genuine risk
quiz.explain: O-RADS US 1 is the normal premenopausal ovary, and it includes a follicle up to 3 cm and a corpus luteum up to 3 cm. These are physiology, not findings; describing them, following them and measuring them generates anxiety and repeat scans for nothing. Above 3 cm and up to 10 cm a simple cyst becomes O-RADS 2 — almost certainly benign, under 1% risk — and even then most need no imaging follow-up. The postmenopausal ovary is different: category 1 does not apply to it, because it should not be making follicles, so a simple cyst there is scored 2 rather than 1. Even so, the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus regards a simple cyst of 1 cm or less in a postmenopausal woman as clinically inconsequential and not worth describing. Knowing what to leave out is part of the skill.

quiz.prompt: A premenopausal woman has a unilocular, entirely anechoic ovarian cyst with a smooth thin wall, no septation and no solid tissue, measuring 12.3 cm in maximum diameter. Give the O-RADS US category as a single whole number.
quiz.explain: Morphology alone would keep this in O-RADS 2: a simple cyst has anechoic contents, a smooth thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement, and there is no solid tissue anywhere. But O-RADS US applies a size rule on top of morphology. A simple cyst above 3 cm and below 10 cm is category 2, almost certainly benign. At 10 cm or more it becomes category 3 — low risk, in the 1% to under 10% band — because very large cysts carry a small but real chance of a cystadenoma or a borderline tumour, and because their size itself raises the risk of torsion or rupture. The same 10 cm rule pushes the other classic benign lesions, such as a haemorrhagic cyst, an endometrioma or a dermoid, from category 2 into category 3. The practical consequence is that this woman needs gynaecological assessment, with MRI or specialist ultrasound as an option, not simple discharge.

quiz.prompt: A 6 cm multilocular ovarian cyst has smooth inner walls, thin septations, no solid tissue and no papillary projections. On Doppler interrogation there is very strong flow within the septations, corresponding to colour score 4. What category applies and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: O-RADS 4: very strong flow lifts a smooth multilocular cyst into the intermediate-risk band, so MRI or gynaecological oncology assessment follows
choices: O-RADS 4: very strong flow lifts a smooth multilocular cyst into the intermediate-risk band, so MRI or gynaecological oncology assessment follows
O-RADS 3: a multilocular cyst under 10 cm with smooth walls stays in the low-risk band, and Doppler findings within septations are disregarded
O-RADS 5: a colour score of 4 anywhere within an adnexal lesion places it in the high-risk band and mandates gynaecological oncology referral
O-RADS 2: septations without solid tissue are benign, so neither imaging follow-up nor any specialist referral is required for this woman
quiz.explain: The O-RADS US colour score comes from the IOTA lexicon: 1 is no flow, 2 minimal, 3 moderate and 4 very strong. For a multilocular cyst with no solid tissue, the category depends on three things — size, the smoothness of the inner wall, and the colour score. Smooth, under 10 cm, colour score 1 to 3 gives category 3. Reaching 10 cm, or having an irregular inner wall, or a colour score of 4, moves it to category 4, the 10% to under 50% band. Colour score 4 does not by itself produce a category 5; that requires solid tissue behaviour, four or more papillary projections, an irregular solid lesion, or ascites with peritoneal nodularity. Category 4 is the band where MRI earns its place, because most category 4 lesions are reclassified downwards once the tissue is characterised.

quiz.prompt: A 7 cm unilocular adnexal cyst in a 58-year-old contains four discrete papillary projections, each more than 3 mm high, with detectable internal flow. There is no ascites and no peritoneal nodularity. How should this be reported and referred?
quiz.answer: O-RADS 5, the high-risk band: four or more papillary projections put the lesion there, and referral to gynaecological oncology is the next step
choices: O-RADS 5, the high-risk band: four or more papillary projections put the lesion there, and referral to gynaecological oncology is the next step
O-RADS 4, the intermediate band: papillary projections in a unilocular cyst stay there whatever their number, so pelvic MRI is the next step
O-RADS 3, the low-risk band: without ascites or peritoneal nodules the lesion cannot climb higher, so interval ultrasound is the next step
O-RADS 4, the intermediate band: internal vascularity must be absent before the high-risk band applies, so pelvic MRI is the next step
quiz.explain: A papillary projection in the O-RADS lexicon is solid tissue at least 3 mm high protruding into the cyst lumen, and it is counted whether or not it shows flow — vascularity raises suspicion but is not required for it to count. The number is what moves the category: a cystic lesion with one to three projections is O-RADS 4, and four or more takes it to O-RADS 5, the band at 50% risk or above. Other routes into category 5 are a solid lesion with an irregular outer contour and any colour score, a smooth solid lesion with colour score 4, and the presence of ascites with peritoneal nodules regardless of the lesion itself. Category 5 means the referral is to gynaecological oncology, because outcomes in ovarian cancer depend heavily on who performs the primary surgery.

quiz.prompt: Your ultrasound report ends at O-RADS 4 for a 5 cm adnexal lesion with an enhancing solid component in a 42-year-old. Say what O-RADS MRI is expected to add here, and describe the situation in which MRI would not be the right next step.
quiz.answer: MRI restratifies the lesion by characterising the solid tissue — fat, dark T2 and dark diffusion fibrous tissue, or genuinely enhancing tumour with a time-intensity curve — and most intermediate-risk lesions are moved down to a lower risk band. MRI is not the next step when there is already ascites with peritoneal nodularity or unambiguous high-risk morphology, where the referral goes straight to gynaecological oncology.
quiz.explain: The purpose of O-RADS MRI is to rescue lesions from the indeterminate middle. Ultrasound can see that there is solid tissue but often cannot say what kind, and the intermediate-risk band spans 10% to just under 50% — too high to ignore and too low to justify oncological surgery. MRI answers the tissue question three ways: fat suppression identifies a dermoid, uniformly dark tissue on T2 and on high b-value diffusion identifies benign fibrous tissue, and dynamic contrast gives a time-intensity curve that separates low, intermediate and high risk. In practice a large share of O-RADS US 4 lesions come down to MRI 2 or 3. What MRI cannot do is add value when the diagnosis is already made: ascites with peritoneal nodularity is O-RADS 5 on ultrasound alone, and the delay of a further scan costs the patient time.

quiz.prompt: On O-RADS MRI a 6 cm adnexal lesion contains enhancing solid tissue. On the dynamic series that tissue begins to enhance earlier than the outer myometrium, rises steeply and then plateaus above it. What does the curve mean for the score and the referral?
quiz.answer: It is the high-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 5, and referral to a gynaecological oncology service should be made
choices: It is the high-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 5, and referral to a gynaecological oncology service should be made
It is the intermediate-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 4, and surgery under a general gynaecologist is appropriate
It is the low-risk curve: the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 3, and imaging follow-up rather than surgery is the proportionate step
The curve shape is not scored: the presence of enhancing solid tissue is what matters, so the lesion scores O-RADS MRI 4
quiz.explain: O-RADS MRI uses the outer myometrium as an internal reference standard, which neatly removes the effect of injection rate and cardiac output. Three curve types are recognised. The low-risk curve rises gradually without an early shoulder and stays below the myometrium; it gives a score of 3, roughly a 5% risk. The intermediate curve has a shoulder and then a plateau but enhances later and less than the myometrium; that is a score of 4, around 50%. The high-risk curve enhances earlier than the myometrium and plateaus above it, reflecting neovascular shunting; that is a score of 5, around 90%. If dynamic imaging is unavailable, the fallback is a single comparison with the outer myometrium at 30 to 40 seconds. Note that the curve is only needed for solid tissue that is not uniformly dark on T2 and diffusion — that tissue is already benign.

quiz.prompt: A 4 cm solid adnexal mass is uniformly very low signal on T2 and low signal on high b-value diffusion imaging, with only mild enhancement. There is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and no peritoneal nodularity. How should it be scored and managed?
quiz.answer: O-RADS MRI 2: uniformly dark solid tissue on T2 and on diffusion is benign fibrous tissue, so no oncological referral is required here
choices: O-RADS MRI 2: uniformly dark solid tissue on T2 and on diffusion is benign fibrous tissue, so no oncological referral is required here
O-RADS MRI 4: enhancing solid tissue within an adnexal mass reaches the intermediate band, so surgical assessment should be arranged
O-RADS MRI 5: free pelvic fluid alongside a solid adnexal mass counts as ascites and places the lesion in the high-risk band
O-RADS MRI 3: dark solid tissue sits in the low-risk band but still needs a time-intensity curve before a category can be given
quiz.explain: Solid tissue that is homogeneously dark on T2 and dark on high b-value diffusion is the signature of dense fibrous stroma, and O-RADS MRI treats it as almost certainly benign — category 2, under 0.5% risk — without requiring a time-intensity curve at all. The lesions in this group are ovarian fibroma and fibrothecoma, Brenner tumours, and pedunculated subserosal fibroids masquerading as adnexal masses. A small volume of physiological free fluid in the pouch of Douglas is not ascites; ascites in the O-RADS sense means fluid beyond the pelvis or fluid with peritoneal nodularity. This item is also the argument for MRI: on ultrasound a fibroma is a hypoechoic shadowing solid mass with colour score 1, which scores O-RADS US 3 and generates a referral. Remember Meigs syndrome, where a benign fibroma is accompanied by ascites and a pleural effusion that both resolve after removal.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has a 5 cm ovarian cyst containing fine lacy internal strands and an avascular retracting clot with straight margins. State the conclusion you would report, the features that exclude a solid neoplastic nodule, and the follow-up you would advise.
quiz.answer: Report a haemorrhagic cyst. The strands are thin and fishnet-like and the clot is avascular with straight or concave margins, unlike a papillary projection, which has convex margins and detectable internal flow. Under 10 cm in a premenopausal woman this is O-RADS 2 and needs no follow-up; if there is any doubt, repeat the scan in six to twelve weeks, by which time it should have resolved.
quiz.explain: The haemorrhagic cyst is the commonest cause of an anxious adnexal report, and it has a reliable signature. Early on, fibrin strands make a fine reticular or fishnet pattern with no flow. As the clot organises it retracts from the wall, producing a solid-looking element that is nonetheless avascular and has straight or concave margins where it has pulled away — the opposite of the convex bulging outline of a true papillary projection. Nothing inside a haemorrhagic cyst should show Doppler flow, although flow in the surrounding ovarian tissue is normal. The lesion evolves and disappears, usually within about eight weeks, which is why the classic safety net is a repeat scan in the six to twelve week window, timed just after a period. On MRI it is bright on T1 and on fat-suppressed T1, variable on T2, and it does not enhance.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these peritoneal spaces in the order that ascitic fluid, and the ovarian tumour cells carried within it, normally reaches them.
quiz.answer: pouch-of-Douglas right-paracolic-gutter Morison-pouch right-subphrenic-space
quiz.explain: Ovarian cancer spreads chiefly by shedding cells into peritoneal fluid, and that fluid follows a predictable circulation. Gravity takes it first to the most dependent recess, the pouch of Douglas. From there the flow generated by respiration and bowel movement carries it up the right paracolic gutter, which is the wider and less obstructed of the two; the left gutter is partly barred by the phrenicocolic ligament and the spleen. It then reaches the subhepatic recess, Morison's pouch, and finally the right subphrenic space beneath the diaphragm, where absorptive lymphatics draw fluid in and implants take hold. Those four sites, together with the omentum and small bowel serosa, are where you should look first on a staging study. Right diaphragmatic disease matters disproportionately at the multidisciplinary meeting, because stripping the diaphragm is what often stands between the surgeon and complete cytoreduction.

quiz.prompt: A 3.5 cm adnexal cyst is homogeneously hyperintense on fat-suppressed T1 imaging and loses signal centrally on T2, leaving a dependent very dark focus. There is no enhancing solid tissue and no fat. What score applies and what should the report add?
quiz.answer: O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of an endometrioma, and the report should flag the likelihood of deep endometriosis elsewhere in the pelvis
choices: O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of an endometrioma, and the report should flag the likelihood of deep endometriosis elsewhere in the pelvis
O-RADS MRI 2: the signal behaviour is that of a mature teratoma, and the report should confirm macroscopic fat on the fat-suppressed sequence
O-RADS MRI 4: loss of T2 signal within a cyst indicates solid tissue, and the report should recommend prompt surgical assessment of the lesion
O-RADS MRI 3: haemorrhagic cysts and endometriomas cannot be separated on MRI, so the report should recommend short interval repeat imaging
quiz.explain: Two signal facts do the work here. Staying bright on fat-suppressed T1 means the content is blood, not fat — a dermoid loses its signal the moment fat saturation is applied. Losing signal on T2 is shading, caused by chronically degraded blood products with high protein and iron concentration, and it is characteristic of the endometrioma rather than the acute haemorrhagic cyst. The very dark dependent focus, the T2 dark spot, is more specific still. That combination is O-RADS MRI 2, almost certainly benign. Two things belong in the report nonetheless. First, endometriomas travel with deep infiltrating disease, so the uterosacral ligaments, torus, rectovaginal septum and bowel deserve a look. Second, malignant transformation, although uncommon, is announced by an enhancing mural nodule, loss of the usual shading, or interval growth, most often in women over 45.

quiz.prompt: A 19-year-old has sudden severe right iliac fossa pain with vomiting. The right ovary measures 6 cm and looks oedematous with follicles displaced to the periphery, there is a twisted vascular pedicle at the hilum, and colour Doppler shows preserved arterial flow within the ovary. What should you do?
quiz.answer: Report torsion as very likely and escalate for urgent surgical assessment, since preserved arterial flow does not exclude the diagnosis
choices: Report torsion as very likely and escalate for urgent surgical assessment, since preserved arterial flow does not exclude the diagnosis
Report torsion as excluded by the preserved arterial flow, and look instead for a haemorrhagic cyst or pelvic inflammatory disease
Report an oedematous ovarian mass and arrange contrast-enhanced MRI to confirm torsion before making any surgical referral
Report a physiological polycystic appearance, since peripherally arranged follicles are the expected pattern in this age group
quiz.explain: The commonest error in suspected torsion is trusting the Doppler. The ovary has a dual arterial supply, from the ovarian artery and from the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, and torsion is often intermittent or incomplete, so arterial flow may persist in an ovary that is nonetheless twisted and dying. Venous and lymphatic drainage fails first, which is exactly why the grey-scale findings — a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, a whirlpool of twisted vessels at the pedicle, the ovary sitting in an abnormal midline or superior position, and free fluid — carry more weight than the colour box. In adults a lead mass is usually present, most often a dermoid. Torsion is a surgical emergency in which detorsion salvages ovarian function, so the report should escalate rather than defer to further imaging.

quiz.prompt: In FIGO staging of ovarian, fallopian tube and primary peritoneal carcinoma, macroscopic peritoneal deposits beyond the pelvis are divided into two substages by the greatest dimension of the largest deposit. Give that threshold in centimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Stage III of the FIGO system is subdivided by how much extrapelvic peritoneal disease there is. IIIA1 is retroperitoneal nodal disease alone, further split by whether the largest node is at or below 10 mm. IIIA2 is microscopic extrapelvic peritoneal involvement. IIIB is macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal deposits measuring 2 cm or less, and IIIC is deposits larger than 2 cm — a category that also captures tumour on the capsule of the liver or spleen without invasion of the parenchyma. That capsule-versus-parenchyma distinction is the one radiologists are asked to make most often, because parenchymal liver metastasis is stage IVB. Stage IVA is a malignant pleural effusion with positive cytology, and IVB covers parenchymal metastases, transmural bowel involvement and disease outside the abdomen, including inguinal nodes. Measure the largest deposit, and say plainly whether liver disease is on the surface or within it.

quiz.prompt: You are reporting a staging CT for newly diagnosed advanced ovarian carcinoma ahead of the multidisciplinary meeting. Set out the sites of disease you must comment on specifically, because they are the ones that predict that complete debulking will not be achieved.
quiz.answer: Comment specifically on the porta hepatis and gastrohepatic ligament, the lesser sac, the root of the small bowel mesentery, the diaphragmatic surfaces, suprarenal retroperitoneal nodes, any liver or splenic parenchymal disease as distinct from capsular deposits, and the volume of ascites.
quiz.explain: The surgeon's question is not what stage the disease is, but whether residual disease of zero is achievable, because that is what drives survival. A handful of sites make that unlikely, and they are hard to see unless you go looking. Disease at the porta hepatis or in the gastrohepatic ligament threatens vascular and biliary structures; lesser sac disease is easily overlooked behind the stomach; a retracted, thickened small bowel mesenteric root implies disease that cannot be excised without catastrophic bowel loss; extensive diaphragmatic plaques require stripping and sometimes resection; suprarenal nodal disease lies outside the standard field. Distinguish surface deposits on liver or spleen, which remain stage III and are resectable, from parenchymal metastases, which are stage IV. Large-volume ascites tends to accompany all of the above. Reporting these explicitly is what lets the meeting choose between primary surgery and neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

module_contract.goal: Work the child with an acute abdomen up in the right order — serial film, ultrasound, contrast study — and recognise the findings that mean theatre now.

approach.detail: It is the first study in every neonate with a suspected acute abdomen, before any contrast study or ultrasound.
Bowel dilatation, the number of dilated loops, small bowel versus colon, rectal air, pneumatosis, and free air or ascites.

approach.step: Use the vomiting colour to localise a high obstruction
approach.detail: Non-bilious vomiting suggests an obstruction proximal to the ampulla of Vater; bilious (green) vomiting suggests obstruction distal to it.

approach.step: Use meconium timing to localise a low obstruction
approach.detail: Meconium should pass within 48 hours of birth — delayed or absent passage points to a low obstruction.
Upper GI study for an equivocal high obstruction (avoid it in a typical complete obstruction); colon enema for a suspected low obstruction, to assess microcolon and the transition point.

approach.step: Reach for ultrasound for specific questions
approach.detail: Malrotation with volvulus and hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are the two diagnoses ultrasound is specifically good for in this setting.

measure.how: Ratio of rectal to sigmoid diameter on a lateral view or contrast enema.

measure.what: Pyloric muscle wall thickness (hypertrophic pyloric stenosis)
measure.how: Ultrasound measurement of a single muscle wall in long axis.
Ultrasound measurement of the total pyloric transverse diameter.

classify.name: Neonatal acute abdomen — classic signs by diagnosis
rows: High, non-bilious or bilious obstruction depending on level relative to the ampulla
Double bubble sign — dilated stomach and duodenum
Triple bubble sign, without distal bowel gas
Bilious vomiting, may be a surgical emergency
Corkscrew or reversed-3 sign on upper GI study
Delayed or absent meconium passage, low obstruction
Recto-sigmoid index < 1 with a disproportionately small rectum
Acquired causes, presenting after the immediate neonatal period
Pneumatosis intestinalis (NEC); muscle wall > 3 mm and transverse diameter > 14 mm (pyloric stenosis)
classify.note: Vomiting colour and meconium timing split the differential into high versus low obstruction before any imaging sign is even sought.

pitfalls: Ordering an upper GI study in a typical complete high obstruction — the source advises against this; the diagnosis is usually clear from the plain film and contrast risks aspiration.

Missing malrotation with volvulus because the plain film looked unremarkable. Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation until proven otherwise, and the plain film can be normal or non-specific — go to the upper GI study or ultrasound.
Confusing the double bubble of duodenal atresia with the triple bubble of jejunal atresia — the absence of distal bowel gas and a third dilated loop is the distinguishing feature.
Diagnosing Hirschsprung disease from the recto-sigmoid index alone on a single early contrast enema — the classic transition zone can be absent in the neonatal period.

Treating pyloric stenosis measurements as fixed absolutes in a very small or premature infant — use them as the standard threshold but correlate with clinical findings (a palpable olive, projectile vomiting) when the measurements are borderline.

quiz.prompt: A 28-week infant, now nine days old and fed for four days, has bilious aspirates and blood in the stool. The film shows separated dilated loops, a bubbly and curvilinear lucency within the wall of loops in the right lower quadrant, and fine branching lucencies reaching the outer edge of the liver. There is no free gas. What does this add up to, and what follows?
quiz.answer: Necrotising enterocolitis with portal venous gas; medical treatment and serial films
choices: Necrotising enterocolitis with portal venous gas; medical treatment and serial films
Necrotising enterocolitis with perforation; take the infant to theatre on this film
Gas in the biliary tree from a duodenal fistula; a contrast study will find it
Meconium plug syndrome with normal wall gas; a contrast enema comes next
quiz.explain: Two intramural findings and one vascular one. Gas within the bowel wall is pneumatosis, bubbly where it is submucosal and curvilinear where it dissects subserosally, and in a preterm infant of this age with these symptoms it is diagnostic of necrotising enterocolitis. The branching lucencies over the liver are portal venous gas, and the direction of flow tells them apart from gas in the biliary tree: portal blood flows towards the periphery, so portal gas reaches within a couple of centimetres of the capsule, while bile drains centrally, so biliary gas sits around the hilum. Portal gas marks more extensive disease — stage IIB in the modified Bell system — and predicts a worse course, but it is not by itself a reason to operate. Free intraperitoneal gas is. So the plan is medical: stop feeds, decompress the stomach, antibiotics, cultures, and frequent films while the child is unstable, with ultrasound adding wall thickness, wall perfusion, free fluid and bubbles seen moving in the portal vein.

quiz.prompt: That infant is filmed six-hourly. Overnight the abdomen becomes more distended and one dilated loop keeps the same position and shape on three consecutive films. State what the fixed loop suggests, the single finding that would take the child to theatre, and the extra film view you would add to look for it.
quiz.answer: A loop that does not change over serial films suggests a segment that has lost peristalsis and may be necrotic or about to perforate. The finding that mandates surgery is free intraperitoneal gas, that is pneumoperitoneum. Add a left lateral decubitus view, in which free gas rises to lie over the lateral edge of the liver, where it is visible against solid organ instead of being lost among gas-filled loops.
quiz.explain: The value of serial films is comparison rather than any single appearance. Normal bowel is restless; a loop that holds its shape and position through several films has stopped moving, and a segment that has stopped moving is usually ischaemic. Persistent asymmetric dilatation and increasing separation of loops by fluid carry the same warning. Pneumoperitoneum remains the one agreed absolute indication for surgery in necrotising enterocolitis, and it is easy to miss on a supine film in a distended abdomen — look also for Rigler's sign, where both sides of the bowel wall are outlined, for the falciform ligament drawn as a line, and for a triangle of gas between loops. The left lateral decubitus is preferred over an erect film because a sick preterm infant tolerates the position and the liver gives a reliable background; a cross-table lateral with the infant left supine is the fallback when turning is impossible.

quiz.prompt: A previously well 4-day-old has two bilious vomits. The abdomen is soft and not distended, and the supine film shows gas in the stomach and duodenal bulb with a modest amount scattered distally. The surgical team asks what imaging to arrange. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: An upper gastrointestinal contrast study now, to site the duodenojejunal flexure
choices: An upper gastrointestinal contrast study now, to site the duodenojejunal flexure
An abdominal ultrasound alone, since a normal vessel relationship excludes it
A contrast enema first, to establish the position of the caecal pole
Repeat the film in six hours and act if the appearance progresses
quiz.explain: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until a study says otherwise, and the reason for the urgency is anatomical: a narrow mesenteric base lets the whole midgut twist about the superior mesenteric vessels, and once it does, the entire small bowel can infarct within hours. The plain film is the trap here, because in early volvulus it is commonly normal or nearly so — a soft abdomen and some distal gas exclude nothing. The upper gastrointestinal series remains the reference standard because it shows the position of the duodenojejunal flexure directly. Ultrasound is a useful adjunct and can show the whirlpool of the mesenteric vein wrapping the artery, but a normal vein-to-artery relationship does not exclude malrotation and an abnormal one does not prove volvulus. The enema is unreliable, since a mobile caecum is common in normal neonates and a normally sited caecum does not exclude a narrow mesentery. Waiting six hours is the one option that can cost the bowel.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising that upper gastrointestinal study. Describe where the duodenojejunal flexure must lie on a correctly positioned frontal film for you to call the study normal, and state the appearance that tells you the midgut has already twisted.
quiz.answer: On a true frontal film with the infant supine, the duodenojejunal flexure should lie to the left of the left-hand pedicle of the vertebral body and at the height of the duodenal bulb, that is at the level of the pylorus. A flexure that lies low, or to the right of the midline, is abnormal. Volvulus itself appears as a corkscrew, with the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum spiralling downwards to the right, or as an abrupt beak-like cut-off of the third part.
quiz.explain: Two coordinates define the flexure and both must be satisfied: left of the left-sided pedicle, and as high as the bulb. The commonest cause of a wrong answer is not anatomy but positioning, because any rotation of the infant swings the duodenum across the spine and manufactures both false positives and false negatives — so check that the film is truly frontal before calling anything abnormal, and repeat it if it is not. Technique matters as much: give a small volume of contrast and watch the first swallow under fluoroscopy, because once the stomach is full it overlies and hides the duodenum. A lateral run then confirms that the third part passes posteriorly and retroperitoneally as it should. The corkscrew and the beak are the signs of an established twist, and they turn an urgent study into an immediate call to theatre for a Ladd procedure.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the segments through which the contrast column is followed during an upper gastrointestinal study for malrotation, from the swallow to the point of assessment.
quiz.answer: oesophagus stomach duodenal-cap descending-duodenum transverse-duodenum duodenojejunal-flexure
quiz.explain: The study is a piece of real-time observation rather than a set of pictures, and the sequence is the study. Contrast passes the oesophagus, fills the stomach, enters the cap, descends as the second part along the right of the spine, crosses the midline behind the stomach as the third part, and rises to the flexure on the left. Everything hinges on that last transition, so the first swallow is the important one — after that, contrast pooled in the stomach projects over the duodenum and obscures exactly what you came to see. Practical consequences follow: use a small volume, have the infant supine and square to the table, and be ready to turn to a lateral immediately afterwards to confirm the retroperitoneal course of the third part. If the flexure cannot be seen because of overlying stomach, the honest report says the study was not diagnostic and repeats it, rather than reassuring a surgeon about a landmark nobody saw.

quiz.prompt: A 1-day-old with trisomy 21 vomits, at first milk and then bile. The film shows a distended stomach and a distended duodenal bulb, each with an air-fluid level, and a modest amount of gas in loops in the lower abdomen. What is the right next move?
quiz.answer: An urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because gas beyond the block matters
choices: An urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because gas beyond the block matters
Await theatre for duodenal atresia; the two bubbles have settled the question
An urgent contrast enema, because distal gas suggests Hirschsprung disease
Ultrasound of the pylorus, because a hypertrophied muscle explains this picture
quiz.explain: The two bubbles say the obstruction is duodenal; the distal gas says it is incomplete, and that changes everything. Complete duodenal atresia gives a double bubble with a gasless abdomen beyond it, and it can wait for a planned operation after the infant is resuscitated. Gas distal to the block means the lumen is still partly open — a stenosis, a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas — or, and this is the possibility that cannot wait, malrotation with midgut volvulus obstructing the third part. So the presence of distal gas converts an elective operation into an urgent contrast study to site the duodenojejunal flexure. Trisomy 21 accompanies roughly a third of duodenal atresias and makes atresia more likely, but it confers no protection against volvulus. A more distal atresia, such as jejunal, gives three or four dilated loops with levels and no gas beyond; Hirschsprung disease obstructs at the other end of the bowel; and pyloric stenosis gives non-bilious vomiting at several weeks with a single bubble.

quiz.prompt: A 5-week-old boy has forceful non-bilious vomiting. On the first pass the pyloric muscle measures 2.6 mm with a channel of 13 mm and nothing crosses. Over the next ten minutes of scanning, peristaltic waves carry fluid through into the duodenum and the wall thins. What should the report say?
quiz.answer: The appearances are of spasm rather than hypertrophy; the pylorus opened and emptied
choices: The appearances are of spasm rather than hypertrophy; the pylorus opened and emptied
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is confirmed; refer for pyloromyotomy today
The study is non-diagnostic; proceed to an upper gastrointestinal contrast study
A gastric outlet mass is likely; arrange contrast-enhanced abdominal CT next
quiz.explain: Pylorospasm is the great imitator, and time is what separates it from hypertrophy. The cut-offs in common use are a single-wall muscle thickness of 3 mm or more and a channel length of about 15 to 17 mm or more, with thickness the more reliable of the two — and these measurements fall below both. More telling than any number is behaviour: a spastic pylorus eventually relaxes and lets fluid through, whereas a hypertrophied one does not open however long you watch. Technique protects you from both errors. Use a high-frequency linear probe, turn the infant into a right posterior oblique so gastric fluid falls into the antrum and outlines the channel, find the true long axis, and measure the anterior muscle wall perpendicular to it, since an obliquely cut or contracted antrum manufactures thickness. If the infant is the right age with the right history and the numbers sit just under the threshold, the correct report asks for a repeat scan in a day or two rather than declaring the study normal.

quiz.prompt: Your scan on a different 5-week-old shows a muscle thickness of 4.1 mm and a channel of 19 mm with no gastric emptying over ten minutes of observation. The surgeon asks whether the infant should go straight from the department to theatre. What do you say, and why?
quiz.answer: The diagnosis is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, but the operation is not an emergency. Prolonged vomiting of gastric contents produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with dehydration, and anaesthetising an alkalotic infant risks postoperative apnoea. The child needs intravenous fluid with chloride and potassium replacement until the alkalosis has corrected, and pyloromyotomy after that.
quiz.explain: This is the point where imaging hands over to physiology. Losing gastric contents means losing hydrogen ions and chloride; the kidney defends volume by retaining sodium and, running short of chloride, excretes potassium and hydrogen in exchange, which deepens the alkalosis and produces the paradoxical aciduria of a late presentation. An infant in that state is dehydrated and hypoventilating to compensate, and general anaesthesia on top of it is associated with apnoea in recovery. Pyloromyotomy relieves an obstruction that has been building for weeks; a few more hours of correction cost nothing and remove the main anaesthetic risk. Saying this in the report — or on the phone — is part of the radiologist's job, because the enthusiasm to operate on a confirmed diagnosis is exactly what the finding tends to generate.

quiz.prompt: A 9-month-old has intermittent screaming with drawing up of the legs and one redcurrant stool. Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant shows a concentric layered mass 3.4 cm across, a pseudokidney appearance along its length, and a little trapped fluid between the layers. He is alert and well perfused. What follows?
quiz.answer: Resuscitate, tell the surgical team, and attempt pneumatic reduction now
choices: Resuscitate, tell the surgical team, and attempt pneumatic reduction now
Rescan in four hours, since a lesion of this size usually reduces itself
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT to seek a lead point before any reduction
Take the child straight to laparotomy; enema reduction has no role here
quiz.explain: Measure the doughnut, because size decides what it is and what you do. An ileocolic intussusception is bulky, typically well over 2.5 cm in diameter, sits under the right ribs or across the upper abdomen, persists while you watch, and needs treatment. A small-bowel intussusception is small, usually under 2 cm, short, central, transient, and is left alone — the layered target and the pseudokidney look identical, so the diameter and the location do the work. Trapped peritoneal fluid between the layers, absent Doppler flow in the walls and a long history all predict a harder reduction and a higher chance of needing surgery, but none of them forbids an attempt. Preparation is the substance of the answer: intravenous access, a resuscitated child, an informed surgical team, and the enema done in the department by someone who does them. CT contributes nothing before the attempt, and a lead point is uncommon below the age of two.

quiz.prompt: A 2-year-old with a proven ileocolic intussusception has a tense tender abdomen, a heart rate of 190 and capillary refill of five seconds, and the supine film shows gas outlining the falciform ligament. What is the correct course?
quiz.answer: Resuscitate and go to theatre; enema reduction is contraindicated here
choices: Resuscitate and go to theatre; enema reduction is contraindicated here
Attempt pneumatic reduction at a lower pressure with the surgeons present
Attempt hydrostatic reduction under ultrasound, which is gentler than air
Repeat the film erect first, then reduce if the gas has cleared by then
quiz.explain: Gas drawn along the falciform ligament on a supine film is free intraperitoneal gas, and free gas means the bowel is already open. Insufflating a perforated colon pushes air into the peritoneum under pressure and can produce a tension pneumoperitoneum that splints the diaphragm and obstructs venous return within seconds. Perforation, peritonitis and haemodynamic instability are the accepted contraindications to attempted reduction, and this child has all three; a lower pressure does not make an open bowel safe, and hydrostatic reduction has the same objection. By contrast, a long history, small-bowel obstruction, a known lead point and the extremes of age are relative factors: they lower the success rate and shape the conversation with the surgeon, but they do not forbid an attempt in a stable child. The enema is never the resuscitation — fluid, analgesia and a surgical team come first in every case, and here they come instead.

quiz.prompt: Your department's pneumatic reduction protocol permits up to three attempts, each lasting up to three minutes, with a two-minute pause between attempts for reassessment. If a reduction runs the full protocol, for how many minutes in total is the colon insufflated? Answer in minutes, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Three attempts of three minutes gives nine minutes of insufflation; the pauses between them are not insufflation time, and they exist so that the child is reassessed and the images reviewed before pressing on. The clock is only half the protocol — the pressure ceiling is the other half, commonly quoted as up to about 120 mmHg in an older child and lower in a small infant, and the operator watches the manometer as closely as the screen. Success is not air reaching the caecum: it is the mass disappearing with free flooding of air into the terminal ileum, which is why a post-reduction check and a period of observation belong to the procedure. Before starting, have intravenous access, a resuscitated child, the surgical team informed, and a wide-bore needle in the room in case a perforation produces a tension pneumoperitoneum. Recurrence runs at roughly one in ten, and most recurrences can be reduced again.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old has twenty hours of periumbilical pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, with fever and focal tenderness. Ultrasound does not show the appendix, and there is no free fluid, no echogenic fat and no collection. State what your report should conclude and what you would advise next.
quiz.answer: Report the study as non-diagnostic rather than normal: a non-visualised appendix with no secondary signs lowers the probability but does not exclude appendicitis, and the retrocaecal or deep pelvic appendix is the one ultrasound misses. Advise either active clinical observation with re-examination and a repeat scan, or cross-sectional imaging — MRI first in a child because it avoids ionising radiation and performs comparably to CT, with CT reserved for where MRI is unavailable or the child is unstable.
quiz.explain: The wording of the conclusion is the clinical act here. Ultrasound is the right first test in a child — no radiation, no sedation, and a positive study is a positive study: a blind-ending non-compressible tube over 6 mm in diameter, often with an appendicolith, surrounding echogenic inflamed fat, hyperaemia and free fluid. Its weakness is negative work. Visualisation rates vary with body habitus, bowel gas and operator, and the appendix hiding behind the caecum or down in the pelvis is precisely the one that fails to appear. If a report of that study reads 'normal appendix not seen — no appendicitis', a surgeon may be reassured about a child who has it. Say instead that the appendix was not visualised, list the secondary signs that were absent, and set out the two acceptable paths, so that the decision returns to the clinical assessment where it belongs.

quiz.prompt: A 13-year-old boy woke with sudden severe left scrotal pain at 23:00 and arrives in the ultrasound room at 04:00. Salvage rates are highest when detorsion is achieved within six hours of onset. How many hours of that window remain when he arrives? Answer in hours, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Five hours have gone, so one remains — which is the whole argument for arranging the scan around the operation rather than in front of it. Where the history and examination are convincing, sudden pain with a high-riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, the boy goes to theatre and imaging must not delay him; a normal scan does not overrule that picture. When ultrasound is done, compare with the normal side, turn the Doppler settings right down for slow flow, and look for two things: reduced or absent intratesticular flow, and the twisted cord above the testis, seen as a whirlpool of vessels. The cord sign is the more specific, and it is the one that still holds when torsion is incomplete and some arterial flow persists. A focal tender nodule at the upper pole with preserved testicular flow is torsion of an appendix testis, which is treated with analgesia and does not need an operation.

quiz.prompt: A 12-year-old girl has twelve hours of severe right iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm right ovary, far larger than the left, with follicles pushed out to the periphery, a little free fluid, and demonstrable arterial flow within the ovarian stroma. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: Torsion is likely despite the flow; the surgical team should be called now
choices: Torsion is likely despite the flow; the surgical team should be called now
Torsion is excluded by the arterial flow; look for another cause of pain
A haemorrhagic cyst explains the size; rescan in six weeks to confirm
Appendicitis with reactive ovarian change; image the appendix next
quiz.explain: Doppler is the trap in ovarian torsion, and it fails in a predictable direction. The ovary has a dual arterial supply, from the ovarian artery and from the uterine artery, and a twisted pedicle occludes the thin-walled veins before the arteries, so the ovary becomes congested and oedematous while arterial flow is still demonstrable. Absent flow is therefore a late and specific sign whose presence proves nothing and whose absence you cannot wait for. The grey-scale carries the diagnosis: an ovary markedly enlarged compared with its neighbour, stroma swollen so that the follicles are displaced to the periphery in a ring, free fluid, often a lead mass such as a mature teratoma, and sometimes the twisted vascular pedicle itself. A torted ovary recovers surprisingly well after untwisting even when it looks infarcted, so the ovary-conserving operation is worth doing quickly, and the report should say plainly that flow does not exclude torsion.

module_contract.goal: Read the neonatal and paediatric chest film for lines, air leak and the cause of respiratory distress, and choose the next study without over-irradiating a child.

approach.detail: Gestational age, postnatal age and current respiratory support change the differential more than the film itself does.
Normal, hypo-inflated or hyper-inflated volume narrows the differential before you look at the parenchyma in detail.
Decide whether the opacity is fine and granular, coarse and patchy, or linear, and whether it is symmetric or asymmetric.

approach.step: Match the pattern to gestational age and timing
approach.detail: Respiratory distress syndrome occurs in preterm infants; transient tachypnoea and meconium aspiration occur in term or post-term infants — the same pattern means different things at different ages.
Look specifically for pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum and pulmonary interstitial emphysema, which change management urgently.

approach.step: Do not call pneumonia from the film alone
approach.detail: A consolidation without clinical signs of infection is unlikely to represent pneumonia — correlate before committing to that diagnosis.

classify.name: Neonatal respiratory distress — pattern by diagnosis
rows: Low lung volume, air bronchograms, symmetric fine granular opacities; four grades of severity from mild ground-glass to complete white-out
Subtle increased lung volume, parahilar linear densities, pleural effusions
Coarse, bilateral, often asymmetric densities with areas of atelectasis and air-trapping
Radiographic pattern overlaps the others; a consolidation without clinical signs of infection is unlikely to be pneumonia
classify.note: Pattern alone rarely gives a confident diagnosis without gestational age and clinical context — state both explicitly in the report.

pitfalls: Diagnosing RDS in a term infant. RDS occurs almost exclusively in preterm infants — the same granular pattern at term should prompt a different differential.
Calling pneumonia from an isolated consolidation. The source is explicit that a consolidation without clinical signs of infection is unlikely to represent pneumonia.
Missing an air leak because attention was fixed on the parenchymal pattern. Pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum and pulmonary interstitial emphysema need a specific, separate check.

Ignoring postnatal age and respiratory support. The same film can represent a different stage of disease, or a superimposed complication of ventilation, depending on how long the infant has been supported.
Treating TTN and mild RDS as radiographically distinguishable with confidence when the pattern is subtle — gestational age and clinical trajectory often settle it, not the film alone.
