quiz.prompt: A 48-year-old man is scanned on day 6 of acute alcohol-associated pancreatitis. Contrast-enhanced CT shows the pancreatic body failing to enhance over roughly 40% of the gland, and a heterogeneous collection containing both fluid and fat density tracking into the lesser sac, with no discernible wall. How should this be reported, and what follows from it?
quiz.answer: An acute necrotic collection; describe its immature wall and extent, with intervention decisions requiring multidisciplinary assessment
choices: An acute peripancreatic fluid collection; homogeneous fluid without necrosis, and most of these resolve with supportive care alone
A pancreatic pseudocyst; a mature wall has formed around simple fluid, so an endoscopic cyst-gastrostomy can be planned now
An acute necrotic collection; describe its immature wall and extent, with intervention decisions requiring multidisciplinary assessment
Walled-off necrosis; the necrosis has matured inside a defined capsule, so transmural necrosectomy can be undertaken safely
quiz.explain: Necrotic content and incomplete encapsulation in this early episode support an acute necrotic collection. Imaging describes the anatomy and maturity; symptoms, infection, complications and clinical stability determine intervention needs. A fixed wait based only on the calendar is insufficient.

quiz.prompt: A day-4 contrast-enhanced CT in acute pancreatitis shows an enlarged gland with peripancreatic fat inflammatory change but no collection, roughly 40% of the parenchyma failing to enhance, and a left pleural effusion. Score this using the modified CT severity index. Answer in points, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The modified CT severity index scores three things out of ten. Pancreatic inflammation: normal 0, intrinsic pancreatic abnormality with or without peripancreatic fat change 2, a pancreatic or peripancreatic collection or peripancreatic fat necrosis 4. Necrosis: none 0, 30% or less 2, more than 30% 4. Extrapancreatic complications (pleural effusion, ascites, vascular or gastrointestinal involvement) 2. Here that is 2 plus 4 plus 2, so 8 out of 10. The modified index differs from the original Balthazar-based CTSI by collapsing the grades and by adding the extrapancreatic component, which is why it correlates better with length of stay and organ failure. Do not let the score replace the clinical picture: the revised Atlanta severity categories are driven by organ failure, not by a CT number.

quiz.prompt: A patient presents 10 hours after the onset of epigastric pain with a lipase five times the upper limit of normal. The admitting team asks for a contrast-enhanced CT tonight to see how bad it is. What do you tell them, and why?
quiz.answer: Necrosis takes up to 72 hours to declare itself, so a scan this early will underestimate or miss it; unless the diagnosis itself is in doubt or a complication is suspected, delay the contrast CT to 72 to 96 hours after onset.
quiz.explain: Pancreatic necrosis is a perfusion phenomenon that evolves. In the first day the gland can enhance almost normally even when large territories are destined to infarct, so an early scan gives false reassurance and then has to be repeated. The revised Atlanta classification (2012) explicitly ties its collection terminology to time from onset for the same reason. Early CT still has proper indications: genuine diagnostic uncertainty where a perforated ulcer or ischaemic bowel is in the differential, or a patient deteriorating in a way that suggests haemorrhage or a hollow viscus problem. Otherwise the useful scan is at 72 to 96 hours, and severity in the first 48 hours is a clinical and biochemical judgement, not a radiological one.

quiz.prompt: A woman with gallstone pancreatitis has hypotension that responds to fluids and resolves within 30 hours. No qualifying respiratory or renal organ failure is documented. CT on day 5 shows a peripancreatic collection. How should the episode be graded from the stated findings?
quiz.answer: Moderately severe because a local complication is present without documented persistent organ failure
choices: Severe: any documented organ dysfunction defines severe disease, whatever the duration, because it marks a systemic inflammatory response
Moderately severe because a local complication is present without documented persistent organ failure
Mild: dysfunction that corrects with fluid does not count as organ failure, and a collection on its own does not raise the grade
Severe: the peripancreatic collection is a local complication and it upgrades the episode independently of the organ failure course
quiz.explain: The collection is a local complication and supports moderately severe acute pancreatitis without documented persistent organ failure. Fluid-responsive hypotension alone does not establish modified Marshall organ failure; qualifying clinical measurements and duration must be assessed. CT morphology cannot supply missing clinical severity data.

quiz.prompt: Symptoms began on day 0. CT on day 26 shows a necrotic collection with an incomplete wall. What should the report say about maturity?
quiz.answer: Describe the incomplete encapsulation; reaching day 28 alone will not establish walled-off necrosis.
choices: Describe the incomplete encapsulation; reaching day 28 alone will not establish walled-off necrosis.
Call walled-off necrosis now because any visible wall is sufficient.
Wait exactly two days and call walled-off necrosis without reassessing the wall.
Call a pseudocyst because a partially formed wall excludes necrotic debris.
quiz.explain: Document onset, necrotic content and actual encapsulation. Calendar age alone cannot establish a mature enclosing wall. Collection classification and intervention planning require the observed morphology and clinical context.

quiz.prompt: Three weeks into necrotising pancreatitis a patient drops his haemoglobin by 30 g/L and his known peripancreatic collection has enlarged and become denser. What scan do you ask for, what are you looking for, and what is the treatment?
quiz.answer: An arterial-phase CT angiogram, looking for a pseudoaneurysm, most often of the splenic artery, bleeding into the collection; the treatment is catheter angiography with embolisation.
quiz.explain: Enzyme-rich fluid digests the wall of an adjacent artery and a pseudoaneurysm forms; the splenic artery is the classic culprit, with the gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries next. Bleeding into a collection or into the gut through the duct produces exactly this picture: falling haemoglobin, a collection that grows and becomes hyperdense. A portal venous phase alone can miss it or make it look like a mural nodule, so the request must specify an arterial phase; a small pseudoaneurysm follows the aortic attenuation on arterial images and fades on delayed ones. Treatment is endovascular embolisation, which is both quicker and safer than operating in an inflamed field. Do not drain such a collection percutaneously until the vessel has been dealt with.

quiz.prompt: Six weeks after necrotising pancreatitis, CT shows a non-opacified splenic vein, a patent portal vein, and prominent gastric fundal and short gastric collaterals. The patient is well and has never bled. What should you advise?
quiz.answer: Report sinistral portal hypertension with gastric varices, note the bleeding risk, and reserve splenectomy for those who actually bleed
choices: Report the finding and recommend immediate splenectomy, since gastric varices from this cause bleed in the great majority of patients
Report the finding and recommend lifelong anticoagulation, which reliably recanalises the vein and makes the collaterals regress
Report sinistral portal hypertension with gastric varices, note the bleeding risk, and reserve splenectomy for those who actually bleed
Regard the collaterals as an incidental finding, since portal vein patency means that gastric varices in this setting carry no bleeding risk
quiz.explain: Peripancreatic inflammation thromboses the splenic vein, and splenic outflow reroutes through the short gastric and gastroepiploic veins into the gastric fundus. That produces isolated gastric varices with a normal portal pressure, which is why it is called left-sided or sinistral portal hypertension. Most patients never bleed, so prophylactic splenectomy is not justified; the operation is curative in the minority who do bleed, because removing the spleen removes the inflow. Anticoagulation is a debated option in acute, extensive splenic or portal vein thrombosis, particularly where the mesenteric axis is threatened, but it does not dependably recanalise a chronically occluded splenic vein. The one thing you must not do is stay silent: the endoscopist needs to know why the fundal varices are there.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a large walled-off necrosis at week 5 has new fever and rising inflammatory markers. CT shows several small gas locules within the collection. There has been no drain, no endoscopy and no gastrointestinal instrumentation. What do you conclude and recommend?
quiz.answer: Strong concern for infected necrosis; prompt multidisciplinary review, with instrumentation and possible enteric fistula considered
choices: Gas is expected within maturing necrosis; recommend supportive care alone, with a repeat scan in a fortnight to reassess the collection
Gas indicates a fistula to the stomach or duodenum; recommend an urgent water-soluble contrast study before anything else
Gas mandates immediate open necrosectomy; recommend theatre today because delay in this setting is what drives mortality
Strong concern for infected necrosis; prompt multidisciplinary review, with instrumentation and possible enteric fistula considered
quiz.explain: Gas with clinical deterioration raises strong concern for infection, while instrumentation and enteric fistula can also introduce gas. Prompt specialist assessment is appropriate. Routine CT-guided needle aspiration is unnecessary in most cases; sampling and drainage decisions depend on clinical uncertainty and the planned management pathway.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the step-up management of infected walled-off necrosis from the first measure to the last resort.
quiz.answer: culture-directed-antibiotics catheter-drainage minimally-invasive-necrosectomy open-necrosectomy
quiz.explain: The step-up approach exists because primary open necrosectomy carried a punishing rate of organ failure, fistula and death. Antibiotics directed by culture come first and buy time for the collection to wall off. If the patient does not improve, the next step is drainage: percutaneous, ideally by a left retroperitoneal route that can later be upsized, or endoscopic transmural drainage through the stomach or duodenum. Roughly a third of patients need nothing further. If sepsis persists after several days, the existing tract is used for minimally invasive necrosectomy, either video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement or endoscopic necrosectomy through the stent. Open surgery is reserved for failure of that pathway or for abdominal catastrophe such as perforation or uncontrolled bleeding. The other principle is patience: delay intervention beyond four weeks where the patient allows it.

quiz.prompt: A woman admitted with pancreatitis has gallstones on ultrasound, a common bile duct of 9 mm, and a bilirubin that has risen over 24 hours. She is afebrile with no rigors and is otherwise improving. What is the right next imaging or intervention step?
quiz.answer: MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound to look for a retained duct stone, with ERCP reserved for cholangitis or persisting obstruction
choices: Urgent ERCP tonight with sphincterotomy, because a dilated duct after gallstone pancreatitis is an indication in its own right
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen tonight, which is the most sensitive test available for a stone in the distal bile duct
MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound to look for a retained duct stone, with ERCP reserved for cholangitis or persisting obstruction
No further duct imaging, and list her for cholecystectomy in three months once the pancreatic inflammation has fully settled
quiz.explain: Imaging in gallstone pancreatitis has to answer three questions: is the cause biliary, is a stone still obstructing, and is the gallbladder coming out. Ultrasound answers the first. For the second, MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are the accurate non-invasive tests; CT is poor at distal duct stones because many are not calcified. ERCP is a treatment, not a screening test, and its clear indications are cholangitis and persistent biliary obstruction, where early ERCP improves outcome. A rising bilirubin without fever or rigors is an equivocal picture that deserves MRCP or EUS first. The third question is the one juniors forget: in mild gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy on the index admission markedly reduces recurrence, and deferring it for months invites a second, worse attack.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising the first ultrasound in a patient admitted overnight with acute pancreatitis of unknown cause. What must that scan answer, and what decision hangs on each answer?
quiz.answer: Whether there are gallstones in the gallbladder, and whether the common bile duct is dilated or contains a stone; the first decides index-admission cholecystectomy, the second decides whether MRCP, EUS or ERCP is needed.
quiz.explain: Ultrasound in acute pancreatitis is not there to look at the pancreas, which is usually obscured by bowel gas and unhelpful in the first day anyway. It is there to settle aetiology and biliary obstruction, because those are the two findings that change what happens next. Stones in the gallbladder mean the patient needs cholecystectomy, ideally on the same admission for a mild attack. A dilated common bile duct, or a visible duct stone, moves the patient towards MRCP, endoscopic ultrasound, or straight to ERCP if there is cholangitis. Note the trap of the normal-calibre duct: a stone can pass and leave the duct entirely normal, so a normal ultrasound never excludes a biliary cause when the alanine transaminase is high.

quiz.prompt: Seven weeks after an episode of interstitial oedematous pancreatitis, a well patient has a 6 cm round collection anterior to the pancreatic body with homogeneous fluid content, a thin enhancing wall and no debris. She eats normally and is not jaundiced. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Describe a pseudocyst and recommend observation, since an asymptomatic collection of this kind needs no drainage on size alone
choices: Describe walled-off necrosis and recommend endoscopic drainage, since encapsulated collections at this stage should be evacuated
Describe a pseudocyst and recommend observation, since an asymptomatic collection of this kind needs no drainage on size alone
Describe a mucinous cystic neoplasm and recommend resection, since a thin-walled unilocular cyst in a woman is neoplastic
Describe a pseudocyst and recommend drainage, since a collection above 5 cm at six weeks will rarely resolve on its own
quiz.explain: Homogeneous fluid, a defined wall and a preceding episode of interstitial rather than necrotising pancreatitis give a pseudocyst under the revised Atlanta classification (2012); by contrast walled-off necrosis contains heterogeneous solid debris, best appreciated on MRI or endoscopic ultrasound when CT looks deceptively simple. The old teaching that pseudocysts above 6 cm or older than 6 weeks must be drained has not survived; the indications now are symptoms, gastric or biliary obstruction, infection or growth. The differential worth pausing over is a mucinous cystic neoplasm or a branch-duct IPMN that caused the pancreatitis in the first place, so if the history of a genuine attack is thin, or there are septations, mural nodularity or peripheral calcification, do not label it a pseudocyst by assumption.

curriculum_modules.title: Pancreatic Cancer Staging and Cystic Lesions

module_contract.goal: Report a pancreatic protocol CT in the surgeon's language of vascular contact and resectability, and triage cystic and hypervascular pancreatic lesions to surveillance, sampling or resection.

approach.detail: Late arterial phase shows the hypodense tumour at greatest conspicuity and maps the arteries. Portal venous phase is for venous involvement and for liver metastases.

approach.step: Find the tumour, or the sign of it
approach.detail: If there is no mass, look for the double duct sign — combined biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction — and for an interrupted duct.
Coeliac axis, common hepatic artery, superior mesenteric artery. Report the arc of circumferential contact, not 'abutment' alone.

Describe SMV/PV contact angle, longitudinal extent, contour, filling defects and patent proximal/distal segments. Deformity or thrombosis raises concern for involvement but does not alone prove microscopic invasion or exclude a treatment-related change.
A replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA changes the operation. Say where it arises and whether the tumour touches it. Note coeliac stenosis.

approach.step: Then the rest of the staging
approach.detail: Mesentery and mesocolon, perineural spread, regional against extra-regional nodes, liver, peritoneum and lungs.

measure.how: On reconstructions perpendicular to the vessel at maximal contact, document the circumferential arc and longitudinal extent; oblique axial cuts can misrepresent contact.
Contact of less than 180° with an intact vessel wall.
Circumferential involvement of more than half the vessel.
Maximal axial diameter, and head, body or tail.

classify.name: Resectability categories — framework-dependent anatomical overview
rows: Assess absence of critical arterial involvement and the exact SMV/PV contact, contour and patency under the stated framework.
Report local/distant disease, diagnosis and treatment time point; operative suitability requires multidisciplinary review.
Borderline anatomical pattern requiring framework review
Assess potentially addressable arterial/venous contact, tumour site, variants and source vessel segments that may permit reconstruction.
Use the named current guideline/version and complete clinical context; do not select treatment from contact angle alone.
Locally advanced anatomical pattern requiring framework review
Assess extensive critical arterial/aortic involvement or venous occlusion considered unreconstructable under the stated framework.
Document all source findings and treatment context; persistent post-treatment contact alone does not establish viable tumour or preclude reassessment.
classify.note: This is an anatomical overview, not a complete current NCCN/DPCG algorithm or treatment directive. Tumour-site-specific criteria, exact vessel/branch anatomy, distant disease, treatment status, biology and multidisciplinary assessment remain required. Venous morphology raises suspicion rather than proving invasion.

modifiers.meaning: Combined biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction — look for a small head tumour you have not yet seen.
An abrupt cut-off of the pancreatic duct without a visible mass. Treat as tumour until proven otherwise.
Arising from the SMA. State its origin and whether the tumour contacts it — it alters the resection.
Report it: the hepatic supply may depend on the gastroduodenal collateral that the operation divides.
Report actual duct calibre and clinical context; dilatation alone does not distinguish cystic neoplasm from inflammatory or obstructive causes.

For presumed IPMN under Kyoto 2024, main duct 5 to under 10 mm is a worrisome feature and at least 10 mm is a high-risk stigma. Assess obstruction, other criteria and clinical context; calibre alone does not prove malignancy or surgical suitability.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Pancreatic protocol CT: late arterial and portal venous phases, [water as neutral oral contrast], thin-section reformats.

FINDINGS
Tumour: [head / uncinate / body / tail], [n] mm, [hypodense / isodense with secondary signs].
Ducts: main pancreatic duct [n] mm, common bile duct [n] mm — [double duct sign / interrupted duct / normal].
Arteries: coeliac axis [n]° contact; common hepatic artery [n]°; superior mesenteric artery [n]°. Contour [normal / irregular].
Veins: superior mesenteric vein [n]°; portal vein [n]°. Contour [normal / teardrop deformity / occluded / thrombosed].
Arterial variants: [none / replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA / other]. Coeliac stenosis: [absent / present].
Pathway-region soft tissue concerning for perineural spread: [ ]. Microscopic invasion is not established by CT. Mesentery and mesocolon: [ ].
Nodes: regional [ ]; extra-regional [ ].
Metastases: liver [ ], peritoneum [ ], lungs [ ].

IMPRESSION
1. Pancreatic [head / body / tail] mass, [n] mm, [suspicious for adenocarcinoma / known source diagnosis / differential].
2. Vascular summary: [artery/vein] [n]° with [length/contour/patency]. Framework/version and treatment time point: [ ]. Multidisciplinary resectability assessment: [ ].
3. [Arterial variant that changes the operation.]
4. [Metastatic disease.]
pitfalls: Using abutment without degrees, length and contour, or assigning resectability from an isolated contact angle without the framework, tumour site and full clinical context.
Reading only the portal venous phase. The late arterial phase is where a small hypodense head tumour is conspicuous and where the arterial anatomy is legible.
Missing a replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA. It runs straight through the operative field and must be named whether or not it is involved.
Calling a vein uninvolved solely because contact is under 180°, or declaring microscopic invasion from deformity/thrombus alone. Describe source morphology and treatment-related uncertainty.
Failing to chase a double duct sign or an interrupted duct when no mass is visible. Those signs are often the only evidence of a small carcinoma.

measurements.name: Tumour size
measurements.method: Measure the best-defined solid tumour or cyst dimensions and sequence/phase.
measurements.pitfall: Isoattenuating tumour may be inferred from duct cutoff but should not receive an invented size.

measurements.method: Record circumferential angle and longitudinal extent for each relevant vessel.
measurements.pitfall: Post-treatment soft tissue may not represent viable tumour.

measurements.method: Measure enhancing mural nodule and main duct separately.
measurements.pitfall: Dependent debris should not be labelled an enhancing nodule.

quiz.prompt: A registrar wants to cancel the late arterial acquisition on a pancreatic protocol CT for a suspected head mass, arguing that the portal venous phase shows the liver and the veins perfectly well. What is the strongest argument against, in terms of what the study would lose?
quiz.answer: Tumour-to-parenchyma contrast peaks in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, and arterial mapping for coeliac and hepatic variants is lost
choices: Liver metastases from pancreatic cancer are hypervascular, and they are seen far better in the arterial phase than in the venous phase
Tumour-to-parenchyma contrast peaks in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, and arterial mapping for coeliac and hepatic variants is lost
The main pancreatic duct opacifies during the arterial phase, and its calibre cannot otherwise be assessed with reliability on a CT study
Portal and superior mesenteric vein contact is graded on arterial images alone, since venous walls are indistinct at 70 seconds
quiz.explain: Ductal adenocarcinoma is desmoplastic and hypovascular, so it shows up as a low-attenuation defect against enhancing parenchyma. That difference is greatest in the pancreatic parenchymal phase, roughly 40 to 50 seconds after injection or about 20 to 25 seconds after bolus tracking triggers, which is later than a pure angiographic arterial phase. The same acquisition maps the coeliac axis, the superior mesenteric artery and variants such as a replaced right hepatic artery, which the surgeon must know before opening. The portal venous phase at about 65 to 70 seconds is kept because it is better for the veins and for liver metastases, which in adenocarcinoma are typically hypovascular and most conspicuous then. The two phases answer different questions; dropping either degrades the report.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old has an incidental branch-duct IPMN. MRI shows a 3.4 cm cyst in the uncinate process, a main pancreatic duct of 6 mm, a thickened enhancing cyst wall, no mural nodule, no lymphadenopathy, a normal bilirubin and a normal CA 19-9. Count the worrisome features present under the 2017 international consensus (Fukuoka) criteria. Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Under the stated Fukuoka 2017 framework, the three findings are cyst size at least 3 cm, main duct 5 to under 10 mm, and thickened/enhancing wall. Report each finding. Do not present this as the complete Kyoto 2024 criteria set or as a stand-alone surgical decision.

quiz.prompt: Before treatment, a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma contacts the SMA over about 90° and the SMV over roughly 200°, with a narrowed patent lumen and no other local vascular involvement or distant metastases. The multidisciplinary team considers the proximal/distal vein technically suitable for reconstruction. Under an NCCN-style anatomical assessment at diagnosis, which category best describes these vascular findings?
quiz.answer: Borderline resectable: arterial contact is 180 degrees or less and the vein is reconstructible with normal vein above and below the segment
choices: Locally advanced: venous contact beyond 180 degrees with luminal narrowing places the tumour past the limit of surgical reconstruction
Resectable: the artery is not encased and venous involvement of any degree is dealt with routinely at operation without changing the plan
Borderline resectable: arterial contact is 180 degrees or less and the vein is reconstructible with normal vein above and below the segment
Locally advanced: contact with the superior mesenteric artery of any degree at all excludes an operation and commits to chemotherapy
quiz.explain: In this explicitly untreated head-tumour scenario, limited SMA contact and potentially reconstructible SMV involvement fit a borderline anatomical pattern under the stated framework. Report the actual angle, longitudinal extent, contour, variants and proximal/distal segments. This example is not a complete current guideline or an operative recommendation: tumour site, other local/distant disease, biology and treatment time point must be reviewed, and the multidisciplinary team determines the applicable classification and plan.

quiz.prompt: A jaundiced 70-year-old has a pancreatic protocol CT in which no mass is visible on any phase, yet the surgeon is convinced there is a tumour. What secondary signs would you go back and hunt for, and what would you do next?
quiz.answer: Look for an abrupt cut-off of the main pancreatic duct with upstream dilatation, distal parenchymal atrophy, a subtle contour bulge of the gland and loss of the fatty cleft around vessels, then proceed to endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling.
quiz.explain: Around one in ten ductal adenocarcinomas is isoattenuating on every phase, more often when the tumour is small, and this is precisely the group where a confident negative report does harm. The secondary signs carry the diagnosis: an abrupt interruption of the main pancreatic duct, dilatation and parenchymal atrophy upstream, a focal convexity of the pancreatic contour, and effacement of the fat plane around the superior mesenteric vessels. The double duct sign, with both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct dilated and cut off at the same level, is the classic presentation in the head. When the CT is negative and suspicion persists, endoscopic ultrasound is the next test: it detects small isoattenuating lesions and it gives tissue in the same sitting.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old with painless jaundice has CT showing a dilated common bile duct to 14 mm and a dilated main pancreatic duct to 6 mm, both terminating abruptly in the pancreatic head, with no discrete mass and no metastases. What is the most appropriate next step?
quiz.answer: Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling of the head at the level of the duct cut-off, since a mass is present until proven otherwise
choices: Endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle sampling of the head at the level of the duct cut-off, since a mass is present until proven otherwise
Repeat the pancreatic protocol CT in three months, since a lesion invisible on a dedicated study is very unlikely to be a carcinoma
Proceed directly to pancreaticoduodenectomy without tissue, since this pattern is diagnostic and sampling only delays the operation
Perform a FDG PET-CT as the next test, since it is the most sensitive available means of demonstrating a small primary pancreatic adenocarcinoma
quiz.explain: Simultaneous obstruction of both ducts at the same point in the head is a periampullary mass until disproved, whether or not you can see it. Endoscopic ultrasound is the right next test because it resolves small isoattenuating lesions and yields tissue, and because it may instead show an ampullary tumour, a duodenal lesion or focal autoimmune pancreatitis, each of which is managed differently. Waiting three months on a jaundiced patient risks losing a resectable window. Operating without any tissue does happen, in a fit patient with a convincing mass and a clear plan, but with no visible lesion it is indefensible. PET-CT has a role in occult metastatic disease at some centres, not in finding a small primary; and a benign stricture from chronic or autoimmune disease can reproduce this picture.

quiz.prompt: On a CT reformat perpendicular to the SMA, tumour contact extends continuously from the 10 o’clock to the 2 o’clock position on the vessel circumference. Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number: what is the circumferential contact?
quiz.explain: Each clock hour is 30°, so four hours of continuous contact span 120°. The perpendicular measurement plane matters: an oblique axial section can distort the apparent arc. Report the exact vessel, angle, longitudinal extent and contour. This numeric measurement alone does not establish histological invasion, complete resectability or treatment; apply the stated current framework to the full source anatomy and clinical/treatment context.

quiz.prompt: The hepatobiliary surgeon asks what your report needs to state about the superior mesenteric vein in a pancreatic head cancer. Give the three things.
quiz.answer: The degree of circumferential contact in degrees, whether the vein contour is deformed or thrombosed rather than merely touched, and the craniocaudal length of involvement with whether there is normal vein above and below for reconstruction.
quiz.explain: Describe the actual circumferential contact, contour/filling defect or thrombosis, and longitudinal extent with patent proximal/distal segments. Include the confluence, relevant tributaries and collateral routes. These findings help a surgeon assess possible reconstruction but do not alone prove technical feasibility or microscopic invasion. A resectability category requires the current framework, tumour site, complete local/distant findings and treatment time point; persistent post-treatment tissue or narrowing may remain viability-uncertain.

quiz.prompt: A 71-year-old woman has an incidental 4 cm pancreatic body lesion made of many small cysts each under 2 cm, with a central stellate scar containing calcification, no communication with the main pancreatic duct and no mural nodule. She is asymptomatic. What should you advise?
quiz.answer: A serous cystic neoplasm pattern is favoured; avoid automatic resection and base further assessment/follow-up on diagnostic confidence, symptoms and the named guideline.
choices: The features indicate a mucinous cystic neoplasm; advise distal pancreatectomy given the malignant potential of every mucinous lesion
The features indicate a branch-duct IPMN; advise endoscopic ultrasound and then annual MRI surveillance, given a size above the 3 cm threshold
The features suggest a walled-off collection after silent pancreatitis; advise a repeat scan at three months to confirm resolution
A serous cystic neoplasm pattern is favoured; avoid automatic resection and base further assessment/follow-up on diagnostic confidence, symptoms and the named guideline.
quiz.explain: The honeycomb/central-scar pattern favours a serous cystic neoplasm, but morphology is not histology. A confident diagnosis and symptoms matter; different named guidelines use different follow-up approaches. An equivocal or macrocystic lesion requires appropriate further assessment rather than a blanket benign/no-follow-up label.

quiz.prompt: Give the features on cross-sectional imaging that let you separate a mucinous cystic neoplasm from a branch-duct IPMN, and say why the distinction changes what you recommend.
quiz.answer: Duct communication favours branch-duct IPMN in the appropriate setting; a body/tail macrocystic lesion without demonstrated communication may favour MCN. Neither imaging pattern alone establishes histology. Recommend assessment under a named guideline using size, nodules, symptoms and patient fitness, rather than automatic resection of every presumed MCN.
quiz.explain: Assess actual MRCP duct communication, cyst architecture, wall/nodule enhancement and clinical context. Absence of visible communication may reflect limited imaging. European 2018 guidance permits surveillance of selected presumed MCN below 40 mm without symptoms or suspicious mural nodules; type alone is not an operative directive.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the acquisitions of a pancreatic protocol CT in the order the scanner performs them.
quiz.answer: unenhanced-series bolus-tracking-monitoring pancreatic-parenchymal-phase portal-venous-phase
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series comes first and is useful for duct calculi, for a baseline against which faint enhancement is judged, and for calcification in a cystic lesion. Bolus tracking then monitors the abdominal aorta and triggers when a threshold, commonly around 100 Hounsfield units, is reached. The pancreatic parenchymal phase follows after a diagnostic delay of roughly 20 to 25 seconds, that is about 40 to 50 seconds after the start of injection, giving maximal difference between hypovascular tumour and enhancing gland along with the arterial map. The portal venous phase at about 65 to 70 seconds finishes the study for the veins and the liver. Thin collimation, a rate of 3 to 5 millilitres per second, and water as neutral oral contrast are the other ingredients; positive oral contrast obscures vessels on reformats.

quiz.prompt: A fit 66-year-old man has a main pancreatic duct dilated to 12 mm throughout the body and tail with no obstructing stone or stricture, diffuse parenchymal atrophy, and a 7 mm enhancing mural nodule within the duct. There is no jaundice and no mass. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: Refer for surgical assessment: duct dilatation of 10 mm or more and a nodule of 5 mm or more are both high-risk stigmata
choices: Arrange MRI surveillance at six months: without jaundice or a mass, duct dilatation alone does not warrant an operation
Refer for surgical assessment: duct dilatation of 10 mm or more and a nodule of 5 mm or more are both high-risk stigmata
Arrange ERCP with duct brushings first: cytology is required before any patient can be offered pancreatic resection
Attribute the appearances to chronic pancreatitis: duct dilatation with atrophy in this age group is usually a burnt-out gland
quiz.explain: This is main-duct IPMN, and it behaves quite differently from the branch-duct form. Under the international consensus criteria (2017 revision, carried into the 2024 Kyoto update), a main pancreatic duct of 10 mm or more and an enhancing mural nodule of 5 mm or more are each high-risk stigmata, which in a fit patient means resection rather than surveillance; the rate of high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma in main-duct disease is high. Chronic pancreatitis can dilate the duct, but it usually brings calcification and a history to match, and it does not produce an enhancing intraductal nodule. Brush cytology has poor sensitivity and a negative result would not change the plan. Report the duct calibre, the nodule size and its enhancement explicitly.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with mild obstructive jaundice has a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with a featureless border, a thin hypoenhancing rim around the gland, delayed homogeneous enhancement, a long narrowed main pancreatic duct without upstream dilatation, and bilateral renal cortical lesions. What should you suggest?
quiz.answer: Raise autoimmune pancreatitis, check the serum IgG4 level and look for other organ involvement before anyone commits to a resection
choices: Raise diffusely infiltrating adenocarcinoma and refer directly for staging laparoscopy, since the gland is expanded throughout
Raise acute interstitial pancreatitis and treat supportively, since gland enlargement with a peripheral rim is the usual pattern
Raise pancreatic lymphoma and arrange PET-CT, since diffuse enlargement with renal lesions is the characteristic combination
Raise autoimmune pancreatitis, check the serum IgG4 level and look for other organ involvement before anyone commits to a resection
quiz.explain: Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis is the great mimic and its treatment is steroids, so the cost of missing it is an unnecessary Whipple. The features to hold on to are diffuse sausage-like enlargement with loss of the normal lobulated contour, a capsule-like rim that is hypoenhancing early and enhances late, delayed homogeneous parenchymal enhancement, and a duct that is narrowed over a long segment rather than cut off with upstream dilatation and atrophy. IgG4-related disease elsewhere clinches it: renal cortical lesions, retroperitoneal fibrosis, sclerosing cholangitis, salivary gland involvement. The harder problem is the focal form presenting as a mass, where the duct penetrating sign, the absence of marked upstream atrophy and a raised IgG4 tilt the balance; even then a mass that does not resolve on steroids must be treated as cancer.

quiz.prompt: An asymptomatic 60-year-old has a 1.2 cm solid lesion in the pancreatic tail that enhances avidly in the arterial phase and becomes nearly isoattenuating in the portal venous phase, with a normal duct and a normal liver. What is the most appropriate management recommendation?
quiz.answer: Probable neuroendocrine tumour: confirm with endoscopic ultrasound and somatostatin receptor imaging, then consider surveillance for a small grade 1 lesion
choices: Probable neuroendocrine tumour: confirm with endoscopic ultrasound and somatostatin receptor imaging, then consider surveillance for a small grade 1 lesion
Probable small ductal adenocarcinoma: refer for urgent distal pancreatectomy, since a solid tail lesion at this age is malignant until disproved
Probable hypervascular metastasis: search for a renal primary, since an isolated hypervascular pancreatic deposit nearly always arises from the kidney
Probable intrapancreatic accessory spleen: take no further action, since arterial hyperenhancement in the pancreatic tail has no other explanation
quiz.explain: Arterial hyperenhancement with venous washout towards the parenchyma is the signature of a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, which is why the arterial phase must be preserved when these are suspected, and why their liver metastases are missed on portal venous imaging alone. Grade follows Ki-67: grade 1 below 3 per cent, grade 2 from 3 to 20, grade 3 above 20. Small non-functioning grade 1 lesions, conventionally 2 cm or less, are increasingly watched rather than resected, whereas functioning tumours are removed regardless of size and gastrinomas in particular are often malignant. Two mimics deserve respect: an intrapancreatic accessory spleen, which follows splenic attenuation on every phase and can be confirmed with heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy, and a hypervascular metastasis, classically from renal cell carcinoma, sometimes many years after nephrectomy.

module_contract.goal: Acquire and read a CTPA, tell true embolus from artefact, grade right heart strain, and set what you find against the pretest probability the clinician started with.

approach.detail: Central, low-attenuation, surrounded by contrast — distinguish from flow artefact and from a partial volume effect at a vessel bifurcation.

Acute clot forms acute angles with the vessel wall in a normal or slightly enlarged vessel; chronic clot is eccentric, forms obtuse angles, and the vessel is tapered, sometimes with intraluminal webs or bands.
Dilated bronchial collaterals point to longstanding, not acute, thromboembolic disease.
RV/LV ratio on the axial image, plus right atrial and right ventricular chamber size, as the marker of haemodynamic significance.
Main pulmonary artery diameter and the MPA:aorta ratio as CT surrogates for pulmonary hypertension.
A sign of chronic thromboembolic disease from redistributed perfusion, not of acute PE.

measure.how: Right ventricle to left ventricle diameter ratio on axial images.
Diameter of the main pulmonary artery, and its ratio to the ascending aorta.
Maximum transverse diameter.
Maximum transverse diameter.
Right heart catheterisation, not CT, is the reference standard.

classify.name: Acute versus chronic pulmonary thromboembolic disease on CTPA
rows: Webs and bands from partial recanalisation
classify.note: Anatomical location of chronic clot determines treatment: pulmonary endarterectomy for central disease to the segmental level, balloon pulmonary angioplasty for more distal disease.

pitfalls: Calling a bifurcation partial-volume artefact a filling defect — confirm on more than one plane.
Grading right heart strain from a poorly ECG-gated or motion-degraded axial slice.
Missing chronic thromboembolic disease because there is no discrete filling defect — vessel tapering, webs and mosaic attenuation are the clues, not a clot.
Diagnosing pulmonary hypertension from CT alone — the CT signs (MPA size, RV/LV ratio) are surrogates; the diagnosis is haemodynamic, made at catheterisation.
Missing the anatomical detail (central versus distal) that decides whether the patient is an endarterectomy or angioplasty candidate.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA on a breathless 34-year-old shows dense contrast in the superior vena cava, poor opacification of the main and lobar pulmonary arteries at about 90 HU, and low-attenuation unopacified blood filling the inferior vena cava and right atrium. The patient took a deep breath in on command. What has happened and what do you do?
quiz.answer: Transient interruption of contrast; repeat with quiet breathing
choices: Transient interruption of contrast; repeat with quiet breathing
Extensive central embolus; report a saddle pulmonary embolism
Bolus timed too late; repeat with a longer scan delay set
Poor cardiac output; repeat with a slower injection rate
quiz.explain: A deep inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure and draws a slug of unopacified blood up the inferior vena cava into the right atrium, where it dilutes the contrast arriving from the arm. The signature is a well-opacified superior vena cava alongside a poorly opacified pulmonary trunk, with unopacified blood visible in the inferior vena cava and right atrium. This is an artefact of the breathing instruction, not of the timing or the injection, which is why lengthening the delay makes matters worse by letting the interruption reach the lungs, and why the remedy is a shallow breath or quiet breathing with bolus tracking in the pulmonary trunk. It matters because the mixing interface throws up pseudo-defects that get reported as emboli, and because a genuinely occlusive central clot would show intraluminal filling defects rather than uniformly dilute opacification. As a working rule, a pulmonary trunk far below about 200 HU should be called technically inadequate rather than negative.

quiz.prompt: In a lower lobe a rounded soft-tissue-attenuation structure sits beside a segmental artery on one axial image and appears to occupy its lumen. On the adjacent images the structure is separate from the vessel and lies alongside a bronchus, and the artery opacifies normally above and below. How should this be reported?
quiz.answer: Not an embolus: a perivascular structure mimicking a defect
choices: Not an embolus: a perivascular structure mimicking a defect
A segmental embolus; start therapeutic anticoagulation now
An indeterminate defect; repeat the CTPA in twenty-four hours
A chronic web; refer for assessment for endarterectomy
quiz.explain: Three questions separate a clot from an impostor. Does the defect persist across consecutive images, or does it come and go with one slice? Is it intraluminal - surrounded by contrast in cross-section, the polo-mint appearance, or tracked as a longitudinal filling defect with contrast either side? And does the artery it sits in look right above and below? Here the answers are no, no and yes, so it is not an embolus. The commonest mimics are exactly this: a small lymph node or a mucus-filled or fluid-filled bronchus lying against the artery, given away by the fact that every pulmonary artery travels with a companion bronchus, so finding the bronchus identifies the intruder. Others include partial volume at a branch point, respiratory motion blurring a vessel, and flow-related mixing where poorly opacified blood streams into dependent lower lobe arteries. Reporting an equivocal subsegmental defect as definite embolus commits a patient to months of anticoagulation, so say what you actually saw.

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old woman is assessed for possible pulmonary embolism. Her Wells score is 3, placing her in the 'PE unlikely' group on the two-level scale, and your department uses an age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off of age multiplied by ten, in micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units. What cut-off applies to her? Answer in micrograms per litre, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: 78 x 10 = 780 micrograms per litre. The adjustment applies only above the age of 50; below that the conventional 500 threshold stands. Its justification is that D-dimer rises with age, so a fixed threshold is exceeded by nearly every elderly patient and the test stops discriminating; raising the bar with age substantially improves specificity, with the ADJUST-PE study showing no meaningful loss of sensitivity. Two conditions have to hold before you use it. The patient must already have been placed in a low or 'unlikely' pretest probability group by a formal rule - the adjustment rescues specificity, not a misapplied test. And the units must match the assay, because D-dimer units and fibrinogen-equivalent units differ by roughly a factor of two, and a laboratory reporting in the other convention needs a correspondingly different threshold. Applying an age-adjusted cut-off to a 'PE likely' patient is the error the rule cannot fix, because a negative result there still leaves too much probability behind.

quiz.prompt: A 40-year-old with pleuritic pain has no clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis and no haemoptysis, and you judge an alternative diagnosis more likely than pulmonary embolism. Her D-dimer is 780 micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units. Applying the YEARS algorithm, what follows?
quiz.answer: No YEARS items, so the threshold is 1000: no imaging needed
choices: No YEARS items, so the threshold is 1000: no imaging needed
One YEARS item, so the threshold is 500: proceed to CTPA
No YEARS items, but 780 exceeds 500: proceed to CTPA now
YEARS is not valid outside pregnancy: proceed to CTPA now
quiz.explain: YEARS has three clinical items - clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis, haemoptysis, and pulmonary embolism as the most likely diagnosis - and a single D-dimer whose threshold depends on how many are present. None present raises the cut-off to 1000; one or more keeps it at 500. With no items and a D-dimer of 780 the diagnosis is excluded without imaging, which is the whole purpose of the algorithm: it cut CTPA use by around a seventh in the original study while leaving a very low three-month failure rate. It is not a pregnancy-only tool; the pregnancy-adapted version is a separate validated pathway that adds compression ultrasound of the leg when there are symptoms of deep vein thrombosis. The one rule that must not be broken is mixing pathways within a single patient - a Wells score used to select a threshold from YEARS, or vice versa, has no validation behind it and the failure rates simply do not transfer.

quiz.prompt: On axial CTPA images the maximal right ventricular short-axis internal diameter is 47 mm and the left ventricular short-axis internal diameter at the same level is 38 mm. Calculate the right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: 47 / 38 = 1.24. A ratio of 1.0 or above marks right ventricular dilatation, and the 2019 European Society of Cardiology acute pulmonary embolism guideline accepts it as CT evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. It is a prognostic marker, not by itself a treatment trigger. In a normotensive patient, a raised ratio together with a raised troponin defines intermediate-high risk, which means a monitored bed and reperfusion held in reserve rather than given immediately; haemodynamic instability is what mandates immediate reperfusion, and that is a clinical, not a radiological, judgement. Two practical points: the measurement is more reproducible on a reformatted four-chamber plane than on axial images, which overestimate when the heart is rotated, and it should be made from inner wall to inner wall. Look also for the supporting signs - leftward bowing of the interventricular septum, reflux of contrast into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins, and a dilated pulmonary trunk - and state them, because they are what the receiving team stratifies on.

quiz.prompt: Two normotensive patients on the same list have pulmonary embolism. The first has a saddle embolus with a right-to-left ventricular ratio of 0.8 and a normal troponin. The second has segmental clot only, a ratio of 1.3, septal bowing and a raised troponin. Which report should carry more urgency, and why?
quiz.answer: The second: risk in acute pulmonary embolism follows right ventricular function rather than clot bulk, so a ratio above 1 with septal bowing and a positive troponin puts that patient at intermediate-high risk, while a saddle embolus with a normal right ventricle is not itself high risk.
quiz.explain: Clot burden scores such as Qanadli and Mastora correlate only weakly with outcome once right ventricular function is accounted for, and the reason is physiological rather than statistical: what kills in acute pulmonary embolism is a right ventricle that cannot generate the pressure the obstructed vascular bed now demands. A young patient with a healthy right ventricle can accommodate a saddle embolus and look remarkably well, while a patient with limited cardiopulmonary reserve can decompensate on a segmental clot. That asymmetry has a practical consequence for the report: describe the distribution because it matters for the interventional options, but always state the ratio, the septal position and any caval contrast reflux, because those are what feed the risk stratification and determine where the patient is nursed. It also explains why the phrase 'massive pulmonary embolism' has been retired in favour of high-risk - the adjective described the clot when the point was the circulation.

quiz.prompt: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks' gestation has pleuritic pain and a normal chest radiograph. She is anxious about radiation reaching the baby. Which pathway best fits, and how do you frame the dose conversation?
quiz.answer: Perfusion imaging first; fetal dose is tiny, breast dose lower
choices: Perfusion imaging first; fetal dose is tiny, breast dose lower
CTPA first; fetal dose is tiny and breast dose is lower too
No imaging; treat empirically to avoid radiation exposure
MR pulmonary angiography; it avoids ionising radiation here
quiz.explain: With a normal chest radiograph, a perfusion or ventilation-perfusion study is a reasonable first test in pregnancy and is the one many guidelines favour, because the discriminator is not fetal dose but maternal breast dose: CTPA delivers tens of milligray to breast tissue that is proliferating and radiosensitive in pregnancy, while a perfusion study delivers a small fraction of a milligray there. Fetal dose from both sits in the fraction-of-a-milligray range, orders of magnitude below the roughly 100 mGy at which deterministic fetal effects are considered, so the honest sentence to the patient is that neither test poses a measurable risk to her baby and the choice is being made largely on her own breast dose and on which test is likelier to answer the question. Where the radiograph is abnormal, a perfusion study will often be uninterpretable and CTPA is preferred. Note also that CTPA is technically harder in pregnancy - the hyperdynamic circulation dilutes the bolus and transient interruption of contrast is commoner - so raise the flow rate, track in the pulmonary trunk and ask for a shallow breath-hold. MR angiography is not validated to exclude pulmonary embolism.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA in a large patient scanned at 120 kV has a pulmonary trunk attenuation of 160 HU with marked image noise, and there are indistinct low-attenuation areas in several segmental arteries. Which single change is most likely to make the repeat diagnostic?
quiz.answer: Lower the tube voltage and reconstruct iteratively
choices: Lower the tube voltage and reconstruct iteratively
Raise the tube voltage and lengthen the scan delay
Halve the injection rate and double the contrast volume
Widen the collimation and thicken the reconstructed slices
quiz.explain: Iodine attenuates far more strongly at lower photon energies, because the mean beam energy moves towards iodine's K-edge at about 33 keV, so dropping from 120 kV to 80 or 90 kV raises vessel attenuation substantially for the same iodine delivered. The price is noise, and that is exactly what iterative or deep-learning reconstruction, or a compensating rise in tube current, is for. Raising the tube voltage does the opposite and flattens the contrast you are trying to see. A longer delay does not concentrate a bolus that is simply too dilute, and halving the injection rate reduces the rate of iodine delivery, which is the quantity that governs peak arterial attenuation - volume without flow does not fix opacification. Thicker slices reduce noise but blur the subsegmental arteries the study exists to show, trading one non-diagnostic result for another. When the repeat is still inadequate, say so: 'no embolus demonstrated on a technically limited study' is a different report from 'no embolus'.

quiz.prompt: On CT the main pulmonary artery measures 34 mm at the level of its bifurcation and the ascending aorta measures 31 mm at the same level. Calculate the pulmonary artery to ascending aorta diameter ratio. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: 34 / 31 = 1.10. A ratio above 1 raises suspicion of pulmonary hypertension and is more specific in patients under about 50, in whom the aorta has not yet dilated with age; the corresponding absolute threshold is a main pulmonary artery of 29 mm or more, measured at the bifurcation perpendicular to the vessel's long axis. Both are supportive rather than diagnostic - sensitivity is only moderate, and a normal-calibre artery does not exclude the disease - because CT measures calibre, not pressure. The diagnosis belongs to right heart catheterisation, and under the 2022 ESC/ERS definition pulmonary hypertension is a mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg at rest, lowered from the previous 25 mmHg, with pre-capillary disease additionally requiring a wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less and pulmonary vascular resistance above 2 Wood units. What CT genuinely contributes is the cause: mosaic perfusion with webs pointing to chronic thromboembolic disease, fibrosis or emphysema to lung disease, a dilated left atrium to left heart disease.

quiz.prompt: A 52-year-old remains breathless two years after a large pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography estimates a raised pulmonary artery systolic pressure. A CTPA has already been reported as showing no acute embolus. What is the right next test?
quiz.answer: A ventilation-perfusion scan, which is the sensitive screen
choices: A ventilation-perfusion scan, which is the sensitive screen
A repeat CTPA with a dedicated late arterial phase acquired
Right heart catheterisation before any further lung imaging
Cardiac MRI to quantify right ventricular volumes and mass
quiz.explain: Ventilation-perfusion scintigraphy remains the screening test for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension because a normal perfusion scan effectively excludes it, and its sensitivity exceeds that of CTPA, which is read for acute clot and readily passes over webs, bands, eccentric wall-adherent thrombus and subtle abrupt narrowing. The defects of chronic thromboembolic disease are typically large, wedge-shaped and mismatched, in contrast with the patchy, non-segmental defects of other pulmonary hypertension groups. Catheterisation is needed eventually to confirm pre-capillary haemodynamics, but it comes after the perfusion question is settled rather than instead of it. Once the diagnosis is suspected, the road map for the surgeon comes from a dedicated CT pulmonary angiogram or digital subtraction pulmonary angiography, which decides whether disease is proximal enough for pulmonary endarterectomy - potentially curative - or whether balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy are the route. Missing this diagnosis condemns a treatable patient to progressive right heart failure.

quiz.prompt: A CTPA shows a crescent of soft tissue lying against the wall of the right lower lobe artery and making obtuse angles with it; the vessel is narrower than its neighbours rather than expanded, and the lung shows mosaic attenuation with reduced vessel calibre within the darker regions. What do you conclude, and what should the report ask for?
quiz.answer: This is chronic rather than acute thromboembolic disease, given eccentric wall-adherent thrombus with obtuse angles, a narrowed rather than expanded vessel and mosaic perfusion, so the report should raise chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and request a ventilation-perfusion scan and referral to a pulmonary hypertension centre.
quiz.explain: Acute clot sits centrally in the lumen with contrast around it, makes acute angles with the wall, and distends the artery. Chronic material is organised and incorporated into the wall, so it is eccentric and crescentic, makes obtuse angles, and leaves the vessel narrowed or abruptly cut off rather than expanded; look also for intraluminal webs and bands, mural calcification, post-stenotic dilatation and hypertrophied tortuous bronchial arteries. The lung supplies the corroboration: mosaic attenuation in which the darker regions contain smaller, sparser vessels is perfusion mosaic and points to vascular obstruction, whereas mosaic from small airways disease shows unchanged vessel calibre and accentuates on expiratory imaging. Getting this right is the difference between anticoagulating a patient indefinitely and referring them for pulmonary endarterectomy, which can be curative. Note also that a proportion of patients with chronic thromboembolic disease have no history of acute embolism at all.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old with active cancer, unilateral leg swelling and tachycardia has a Wells score of 7. The junior doctor sends a D-dimer, which returns at 380 micrograms per litre of fibrinogen-equivalent units, and proposes discharge. What is wrong with that reasoning?
quiz.answer: With a high pretest probability a negative D-dimer cannot lower the posterior probability enough to exclude pulmonary embolism, because the test is only validated in the low-risk or 'unlikely' groups, so she needs a CTPA whatever the result.
quiz.explain: This is Bayes at the workstation. A test result moves a probability by its likelihood ratio; it does not set one. D-dimer earns its place through high sensitivity and therefore a very low negative likelihood ratio, which turns a small prior into a negligible posterior - but with a Wells score of 7 the prior sits somewhere around a half, and the same negative result still leaves a posterior in the region of five to fifteen per cent, far above the roughly two per cent failure rate accepted for sending someone home untreated. The same logic sets the boundary for the PERC rule: eight negative criteria are only meaningful when the clinician's gestalt probability is already below about fifteen per cent, because PERC lowers a small probability below the testing threshold rather than making a large one disappear. And when the prior is high and the CTPA is negative, the right reflex is to look at the leg veins and to reconsider the alternatives, not simply to reassure.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stages of a bolus-tracked CTPA acquisition in the order they occur, from first to last.
quiz.answer: scout-topogram monitoring-slice contrast-injection threshold-trigger helical-acquisition
quiz.explain: The scout defines the coverage - lung apices to below the costophrenic angles - and lets you set the range before any contrast is committed. The monitoring image is then acquired and the region of interest placed within the pulmonary trunk, not the aorta, because it is pulmonary arterial opacification the study depends on. Injection follows, typically 4 to 5 mL per second of high-concentration contrast with a saline chaser that pushes the tail of the bolus out of the arm veins and reduces the dense streak artefact from the superior vena cava that ruins the right upper lobe arteries. Low-dose monitoring images then repeat until attenuation in the trunk crosses the trigger threshold, and the helical acquisition begins after the shortest diagnostic delay the scanner allows. Two refinements worth carrying: scanning caudocranially gets the lower lobes, where most emboli land, before respiratory motion sets in, and a lower tube voltage raises iodine attenuation so that contrast volume can come down.

quiz.prompt: An MR defecography study includes rest and strain images but no evacuation because the patient could not empty. What belongs in the conclusion?
choices: A definite normal functional study
A limitation that may conceal prolapse or intussusception
Proof that the patient has no symptoms
Automatic diagnosis of severe anismus
quiz.answer: A limitation that may conceal prolapse or intussusception
quiz.explain: Evacuation can reveal abnormalities absent on strain images. Document performance and its diagnostic consequence; an unsuccessful attempt alone does not establish a specific functional diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: An anterior rectal wall bulge fills during evacuation and retains gel after the rectum empties. What is the relevant description?
choices: Only the resting rectal diameter
An enterocele because it is anterior
A rectocele with size and retained contents documented
A normal study if the bulge is small on rest images
quiz.answer: A rectocele with size and retained contents documented
quiz.explain: A rectocele is a rectal-wall outpouching. Dynamic size and trapping help explain symptoms and are more informative than naming the finding alone.

quiz.prompt: Small bowel loops descend into the space between vagina and rectum during straining. Which term identifies the contents?
choices: Cystocele
Rectal intussusception
Urethral diverticulum
Enterocele
quiz.answer: Enterocele
quiz.explain: The herniating contents determine the name. Identify the compartment and bowel-containing sac, and distinguish it from an anterior bulge of the rectal wall.

quiz.prompt: Two serial MR reports use different reference lines for organ descent. What should be standardised before declaring interval worsening?
choices: Reference line, landmark, measurement direction and manoeuvre
Only the scanner vendor
Only the rectal filling volume
The patients' surname spelling
quiz.answer: Reference line, landmark, measurement direction and manoeuvre
quiz.explain: Measurements require a reproducible anatomical reference and comparable functional phase. The pubococcygeal line is commonly used, with distances measured perpendicular to it.

quiz.prompt: A patient with obstructed defecation has pelvic organ descent in more than one compartment. What is the most useful reporting approach?
choices: Describe only the compartment named in the referral
Report each compartment and the adequacy of evacuation
Assign surgery from the most dramatic still image
Ignore dynamic cine images after obtaining measurements
quiz.answer: Report each compartment and the adequacy of evacuation
quiz.explain: Pelvic-floor disorders often coexist. Combine compartmental anatomy with the dynamic sequence, rectal emptying and study limitations to support multidisciplinary interpretation.

quiz.prompt: A patient strains well but cannot evacuate rectal gel during MR defecography. The anterior compartment descends, while no intussusception is seen. Write the key limitation that should accompany the findings.
quiz.answer: Report the observed anterior descent during the achieved manoeuvre and document absent evacuation. State that posterior-compartment assessment, including exclusion of an evacuation-dependent intussusception, is limited. Do not equate failure to demonstrate a finding during an incomplete functional phase with proof of its absence.
quiz.explain: The completed manoeuvre defines the scope of a negative finding. Performance is part of the result, not merely a technical footnote.

quiz.prompt: The bladder base lies 12 mm above a named reference line at rest and 18 mm below it during strain. Explain the observed movement and the information needed to compare this with another study.
quiz.answer: The bladder base moves 30 mm downward between those phases. Record the reference line, the bladder landmark, perpendicular measurement convention and which manoeuvre produced the lower position. Comparison also needs similar effort and acquisition conditions; the arithmetic alone does not supply a clinical severity category.
quiz.explain: Signed positions and displacement answer different questions. Preserve the measurement method before inferring progression or severity.

quiz.prompt: A rectocele appears large during strain but empties completely. Another smaller rectocele traps gel. Why should the report describe both size and evacuation behaviour?
quiz.answer: Size maps the anatomical bulge, while retention describes its behaviour during the test. Record the maximum dimension, emptying or trapping, coexisting descent and whether the patient reproduced their usual difficulty. Neither size alone nor one evacuation attempt automatically proves that the rectocele causes all symptoms.
quiz.explain: The most conspicuous still image may not identify the principal functional problem. Anatomy and observed function should be reported together.

quiz.prompt: A study shows rectal-wall infolding and descent of a separate small-bowel-containing sac. A draft calls both findings “rectal prolapse”. Explain how to make the description anatomically precise.
quiz.answer: Describe the rectal infolding as intussusception, stating how far it extends and whether it reaches or passes the anal canal. Separately describe the small-bowel-containing sac as an enterocele with its compartment and dynamic extent. Specify any external prolapse rather than using one broad term for different structures.
quiz.explain: Structural names should identify what moves and where it goes. This prevents two distinct mechanisms from being merged into an ambiguous label.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up report claims improved prolapse because the lowest measured position is smaller, but the patient barely strained. How would you reassess that comparison?
quiz.answer: Check the cine images and report reduced manoeuvre adequacy. Describe the positions actually observed, but qualify the apparent improvement because the functional challenge was weaker. Compare technique, reference line, landmarks and evacuation phase, and avoid declaring true anatomical improvement from noncomparable examinations.
quiz.explain: A measurement can be precise yet answer the wrong comparison. Functional effort is a confounder that must remain visible in the conclusion.

curriculum_modules.title: Peripheral, Carotid and Mesenteric Vascular Imaging

module_contract.goal: Plan and report CT and MR angiography of the peripheral, carotid, mesenteric and visceral circulations in the terms a vascular surgeon acts on, and recognise the traps in measurement and timing.

approach.step: Match protocol to the clinical question
approach.detail: Intermittent claudication: a single one-step run from aorta to lower leg is usually enough, and venous filling is rarely a problem. Chronic critical ischaemia: image the lower leg and foot first, at maximal resolution, then the iliac and femoral levels separately.
Iliac vessels tolerate lower resolution; the femoral station needs a small field of view; the crural and pedal vessels need the highest resolution the protocol allows.

approach.step: Time the bolus to the station
approach.detail: Use centric k-space filling so the arterial phase fills the centre of k-space; for critical ischaemia consider a separate bolus for the lower leg before the aorto-iliac-femoral run.
A thigh compression cuff at 50–60 mmHg delays venous return and buys a longer clean arterial window, especially at the crural station.
State patency and stenosis at each named segment the surgeon will want — inflow, femoropopliteal, and the crural/pedal runoff.

approach.step: Confirm carotid or mesenteric stenosis by NASCET-style measurement
approach.detail: Measure perpendicular to the vessel's long axis against a normal reference segment, not on a single axial slice.

measure.what: Spatial resolution needed to grade 50% stenosis
measure.how: At least three pixels across the vessel diameter are needed to reliably differentiate a 50% stenosis.
Mid-thigh pneumatic cuff applied before the peripheral run to delay venous filling.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
Contrast-enhanced MRA, [one-step aorta-to-foot / biphasic lower-leg-first] protocol. Centric k-space filling. Thigh compression cuff [applied at 50-60 mmHg / not used]. [n] mL gadolinium contrast.

FINDINGS
Aorto-iliac segment: [patent / stenosis, % and location].
Femoropopliteal segment: [patent / stenosis, % and location].
Crural / pedal runoff: [vessels patent, occluded, or reconstituted distally — name each].
Venous contamination: [none / present, affected station].

IMPRESSION
1. [Summary of the most proximal flow-limiting lesion].
2. Distal runoff: [n] of 3 crural vessels patent to the foot.
3. [Suitability comment for planned intervention, if relevant].
pitfalls: Running one uniform resolution across all stations — under-resolving the crural vessels is the commonest reason for an unreliable pedal read.
Skipping venous compression in a critical-ischaemia protocol and losing the distal arterial phase to venous enhancement.
Accepting a higher-resolution scan degraded by breathing over a lower-resolution scan without motion — the motion-free image reads better.
Grading carotid or mesenteric stenosis on a single axial slice rather than perpendicular to the vessel's long axis, which underestimates severity.
Ignoring linear k-space filling limitations distally — acceptable at the iliac level but unreliable for arterial contrast at the crural level.
