quiz.prompt: A CT run-off is performed in a man with a 6.5 cm aortic aneurysm and poor cardiac output. The aorta and iliacs opacify densely, the thighs less so, and the calf arteries show no contrast at all, with no venous opacification either. What happened, and what do you do?
quiz.answer: The table outran the bolus; repeat the calf stations with a delayed acquisition
choices: The table outran the bolus; repeat the calf stations with a delayed acquisition
The tibial arteries are occluded; report a hostile run-off and end the examination
Venous contamination has obscured the arteries; re-inject using a longer scan delay
Motion has degraded the calves; repeat those stations with immobilisation and thin slices
quiz.explain: The giveaway is that the calves contain no contrast in any compartment. Real tibial occlusion still opacifies collaterals and, given time, the veins; an empty calf means the contrast column has not arrived. Aneurysmal reservoirs and low cardiac output both slow the bolus, so a table speed set for a normal circulation overtakes it. The fix costs one short acquisition: rescan the calves after a delay, which is diagnostic in almost every case. Preventing it next time means slowing the table, lengthening the injection duration rather than simply raising the rate, using a biphasic injection, and adding a trigger delay after the threshold in the suprarenal aorta is reached. Never report absent distal vessels from a study you suspect of outrunning its bolus.

quiz.prompt: On CT angiography the narrowest residual lumen of the internal carotid artery measures 1.8 mm, and the normal artery distal to the bulb measures 5.4 mm. Calculate the degree of stenosis by the NASCET method. Answer as a whole-number percentage.
quiz.explain: NASCET compares the residual lumen with the normal distal internal carotid, well beyond the bulb where the walls have become parallel: one minus 1.8 divided by 5.4, which is one minus 0.333, giving 67 per cent. ECST instead compares the residual lumen with the estimated original outer diameter at the site of the plaque, which is a larger denominator and therefore always yields a higher figure; roughly, a 70 per cent NASCET stenosis corresponds to about 85 per cent by ECST. Because the surgical trial thresholds that guide practice are NASCET thresholds, state which method you have used in the report. The same plaque reported by the two conventions can look like the difference between operating and not.

quiz.prompt: Using the 2003 Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus criteria, above what internal carotid peak systolic velocity does a stenosis of 70 per cent or greater become likely? Answer in centimetres per second, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The 2003 Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus set a peak systolic velocity above 230 cm/s, with an internal-to-common carotid peak systolic ratio above 4 and an end-diastolic velocity above 100 cm/s, as the combination indicating 70 per cent or more stenosis by NASCET criteria. Below that, 125 to 230 cm/s with a ratio of 2 to 4 indicates 50 to 69 per cent. Use the ratio as well as the absolute velocity, because velocity alone misleads when cardiac output is low, when there is contralateral occlusion driving compensatory flow, or when the vessel is tortuous. Velocities also fall paradoxically in very tight or near-occlusive disease, which is exactly where the criteria stop working.

quiz.prompt: A CT angiogram shows a threadlike internal carotid lumen beyond a bulky plaque, with the vessel beyond it narrower than the external carotid and narrower than the opposite side. In one or two sentences, say why applying the NASCET ratio here misleads you, and what you should report instead.
quiz.answer: The distal internal carotid has collapsed from low flow, so the NASCET denominator shrinks and the calculated percentage falls, understating the disease; report near-occlusion with distal collapse rather than a percentage, since the treatment benefit differs.
quiz.explain: NASCET assumes the distal internal carotid is a normal reference vessel. In near-occlusion, pressure beyond the stenosis is so low that the artery collapses, and a shrinking denominator drags the computed stenosis down; in extreme cases the ratio approaches zero or turns negative, so the tightest lesions can be reported as the mildest. Look for the supporting signs rather than the number: reduced calibre of the distal internal carotid compared with the contralateral side or with the ipsilateral external carotid, delayed contrast filling on a timed study, and a threadlike or string lumen. This is not a semantic point, because the benefit of endarterectomy in near-occlusion is much less clear than in conventional severe stenosis, and the surgeon needs to know which one they are looking at.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old presents with sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination. In one or two sentences, give the CT feature that separates an embolus in the superior mesenteric artery from thrombosis on pre-existing atherosclerotic plaque, and explain why the distinction changes management.
quiz.answer: An embolus typically lodges a few centimetres beyond the superior mesenteric artery origin and spares the proximal jejunal branches, whereas thrombosis occludes calcified plaque at the origin itself; the embolus suits embolectomy or aspiration, while origin thrombosis needs stenting or bypass.
quiz.explain: The superior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta at an acute angle, so emboli travel a short distance before wedging, usually just distal to the middle colic origin, which is why the proximal jejunal branches keep filling and the very proximal small bowel is often spared. Thrombosis occurs where the disease is, at the ostium, in a patient who frequently has a history of postprandial pain and weight loss and who has developed collaterals. Scan biphasically: an arterial phase to see the vessel and a portal venous phase to judge the bowel, where loss of mural enhancement, paper-thin walls, pneumatosis and portal venous gas indicate infarction. Non-occlusive ischaemia and mesenteric venous thrombosis complete the differential and are managed differently again.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these arterial segments in the order a bolus of contrast reaches them during a lower limb run-off study, from proximal to distal.
quiz.answer: aorto-iliac common-femoral superficial-femoral popliteal tibioperoneal-trunk posterior-tibial
quiz.explain: Knowing the chain in order is what lets you convert a list of stenoses into the three headings a vascular surgeon thinks in. Inflow is the aorto-iliac segment down to the common femoral: disease here must be corrected first, because no distal reconstruction survives a poor inflow. Outflow is the femoropopliteal segment, the commonest site of claudicating disease and the usual target for bypass or endovascular treatment. Run-off is what lies below the knee, where the popliteal divides into the anterior tibial and then the tibioperoneal trunk, which gives the posterior tibial and peroneal. The critical question below the knee is how many of the three crural vessels remain continuous to the ankle, and whether the pedal arch is complete, because that determines where a graft can land.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the acquisitions of a CT protocol for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia in the order they are obtained.
quiz.answer: non-contrast arterial-phase portal-venous-phase delayed-phase
quiz.explain: The unenhanced series is not padding: it is what lets you recognise intramural haemorrhage, spontaneously hyperdense thrombus in the mesenteric veins, and mural hyperattenuation that would otherwise be mistaken for enhancement once contrast is on board. The arterial phase, triggered on the aorta, defines the occlusion and its level and shows the calibre changes of non-occlusive ischaemia. The portal venous phase is the one that answers the clinical question, because bowel viability is judged on mural enhancement, and it also shows mesenteric venous thrombosis, bowel wall thickening, mesenteric oedema and ascites. A delayed phase is added selectively, for example when reduced or delayed mural enhancement is equivocal. Reconstruct thin sagittal images: the mesenteric origins are best judged in that plane.

quiz.prompt: A diabetic man with a heel ulcer has a run-off showing patent iliacs, occlusion of the superficial femoral artery from the adductor canal with reconstitution of the popliteal, and only the peroneal artery continuous to the ankle with an incomplete pedal arch. What conclusion does the surgeon need?
quiz.answer: Patent inflow, occluded outflow, and single-vessel peroneal run-off to an incomplete arch
choices: Patent inflow, occluded outflow, and single-vessel peroneal run-off to an incomplete arch
Diffuse three-vessel crural disease with no identifiable target for a distal anastomosis
Aorto-iliac inflow disease that requires iliac stenting before any infrainguinal bypass
Isolated tibial vessel disease with a normal femoropopliteal segment and complete arch
quiz.explain: The surgeon is planning an operation, so the report has to answer their three questions in their language. Inflow is patent, so no iliac work is needed first. The outflow lesion is a superficial femoral occlusion beginning at the adductor canal, with a reconstituted popliteal that gives a proximal anastomotic target. Run-off is the limiting factor: one continuous crural vessel, the peroneal, and an incomplete pedal arch, which matters for a heel ulcer because the peroneal supplies the hindfoot through its calcaneal branches but connects to the foot only through collaterals. State the length of the occlusion, the quality of the reconstituted segment, the calcification burden, and whether a vein is available on any venous mapping, because those determine bypass versus endovascular treatment.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old woman with postprandial epigastric pain and weight loss has CT angiography showing focal narrowing of the proximal coeliac axis with a hooked indentation on its superior surface, more marked on the expiratory series. The superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries are normal. What do you conclude, and what do you do next?
quiz.answer: Median arcuate ligament compression: repeat the imaging in deep inspiration before referral
choices: Median arcuate ligament compression: repeat the imaging in deep inspiration before referral
Atherosclerotic chronic mesenteric ischaemia: proceed to coeliac angioplasty and stenting
Takayasu arteritis: request inflammatory markers and PET imaging before any treatment
Segmental arterial mediolysis: arrange urgent embolisation of the affected arterial segment
quiz.explain: Two features settle this. The indentation is on the superior aspect of the coeliac origin, producing the hooked configuration, because the compressing structure is the median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm lying above it, whereas atherosclerotic ostial disease is concentric and usually calcified. And it varies with respiration, worsening in expiration as the diaphragm rises and the coeliac axis is drawn cranially, improving in deep inspiration. Isolated coeliac disease rarely causes chronic mesenteric ischaemia anyway, because the pancreaticoduodenal arcades collateralise so effectively from the superior mesenteric artery; genuine chronic mesenteric ischaemia usually requires significant disease in the superior mesenteric artery, commonly with two of the three vessels involved. Always acquire both inspiratory and expiratory phases when this diagnosis is suspected.

quiz.prompt: A 42-year-old woman who is planning a pregnancy has an incidental 2.4 cm saccular aneurysm of the mid splenic artery on CT performed for another reason. There is no pancreatitis, and the wall is partly calcified. What do you recommend?
quiz.answer: Refer for elective treatment: both the size and the planned pregnancy argue for repair
choices: Refer for elective treatment: both the size and the planned pregnancy argue for repair
Repeat the CT in twelve months, as visceral aneurysms under three centimetres seldom grow
Discharge without follow-up, since splenic aneurysms in women of this age rarely enlarge
Treat once she becomes symptomatic, because elective intervention carries the higher risk
quiz.explain: The splenic artery is the commonest site of visceral arterial aneurysm, accounting for roughly 60 per cent, with the hepatic artery next. Most are found incidentally and many are left alone, but the widely applied thresholds for elective repair are a diameter of about 2 cm, symptoms, rapid growth, and a woman who is pregnant or planning pregnancy, because rupture in pregnancy carries a very high maternal and fetal mortality. Portal hypertension and liver transplantation are further reasons to treat. Distinguish a true aneurysm from a pseudoaneurysm, which is treated regardless of size because it is contained only by clot and adventitia and has no natural history of stability; pseudoaneurysms follow pancreatitis, trauma and intervention, and most often involve the gastroduodenal or splenic arteries.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old woman has left arm claudication and a 30 mmHg blood pressure difference between arms. CT angiography shows long smooth circumferential wall thickening of the left subclavian artery and thickened aortic wall with mural enhancement on delayed images, without calcification. What is your interpretation, and how should it steer treatment?
quiz.answer: Takayasu arteritis: assess disease activity and treat medically before any revascularisation
choices: Takayasu arteritis: assess disease activity and treat medically before any revascularisation
Atherosclerosis: modify the risk factors and consider subclavian angioplasty and stenting
Fibromuscular dysplasia: look for a string-of-beads appearance in the renal arteries too
Aortic dissection: obtain an ECG-gated study to define the entry tear and its full extent
quiz.explain: Age, sex and morphology all point one way. Takayasu arteritis affects the aorta and its primary branches in women typically under 40, and the subclavian is the commonest branch involved. The wall change is long, smooth and circumferential rather than the eccentric, calcified, ostial plaque of atherosclerosis, and on delayed phase imaging the thickened wall enhances, giving the double ring appearance. Giant cell arteritis produces very similar large-vessel appearances but in patients over 50. The reason this distinction changes management is that angioplasty or stenting performed during active inflammation restenoses at a high rate, so activity should be assessed, with inflammatory markers and often FDG PET or vessel-wall MRI, and suppressed with steroids before mechanical treatment is considered.

quiz.prompt: A 74-year-old with new temporal headache, jaw claudication and an ESR of 88 has temporal artery ultrasound showing hypoechoic circumferential wall thickening around the lumen that does not disappear when the probe compresses the vessel. What follows?
quiz.answer: The halo and compression signs support giant cell arteritis: start steroids without awaiting biopsy
choices: The halo and compression signs support giant cell arteritis: start steroids without awaiting biopsy
The appearance is within normal limits, as the wall is commonly thickened at this age
This is atherosclerotic plaque: report the eccentric calcified disease and modify risk factors
A vein has been mistaken for the artery: repeat the scan with a lower frequency probe
quiz.explain: The halo sign is a hypoechoic, homogeneous, circumferential rim of oedematous inflamed wall around the lumen, and the compression sign is its persistence when the probe compresses the vessel, which distinguishes it from an incompressible lumen. Cut-offs of roughly 0.4 mm for the temporal artery and 1.0 mm for the axillary artery are widely used, and both temporal and axillary arteries should be examined because large-vessel involvement is common and can be the only finding. Atherosclerotic disease is eccentric, echogenic or calcified, not a uniform hypoechoic ring. Do not delay steroids for imaging or biopsy in a patient with visual symptoms or classic features, but do image early, because the halo can resolve within days of starting treatment.

quiz.prompt: Three years after endovascular aneurysm repair, surveillance CT shows the sac has grown by 8 mm. The arterial phase shows no contrast outside the graft, but the delayed phase shows a focus of contrast at the posterior sac periphery continuous with a lumbar artery. How do you report it, and what should happen next?
quiz.answer: Type II endoleak from a lumbar artery, and the documented sac growth makes it treatable
choices: Type II endoleak from a lumbar artery, and the documented sac growth makes it treatable
Type I endoleak at the proximal attachment site, requiring urgent placement of a cuff
Type III endoleak through a fabric or junctional defect, needing urgent relining of the graft
Endotension with no demonstrable leak, so continue with routine annual surveillance imaging
quiz.explain: The delayed phase is what makes this diagnosis, which is why a single arterial acquisition is not adequate surveillance: retrograde filling through lumbar or inferior mesenteric branches is slow and frequently invisible early. Type II endoleaks are the commonest and most are benign, so the trigger for treatment is not the leak itself but sac behaviour, conventionally growth of 5 mm or more, at which point the branch is embolised. Type I leaks arise at the proximal or distal attachment zones and type III at a fabric tear or component junction; both pressurise the sac directly and are treated promptly. Endotension is sac expansion with no visible leak, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion reached only after a properly delayed study has been reviewed.

curriculum_modules.title: Peritoneum, Mesentery and the Abdominal Wall

module_contract.goal: Track disease through the peritoneal recesses, distinguish carcinomatosis from its mimics in the peritoneum and mesentery, and read the abdominal wall for the hernia that needs an operation tonight.

approach.step: Follow the fluid, not the organs
approach.detail: Peritoneal fluid circulates on diaphragmatic movement and bowel peristalsis, predominantly up the right paracolic gutter, which is deeper than the left. Around 90% is cleared at the subphrenic space through lymphatics. Disease deposits where the fluid slows.

approach.step: Go to the watershed areas first
approach.detail: The ileocaecal region, the root of the sigmoid mesentery, and the pouch of Douglas — the deepest recess in women. These are where disease pools and hides.

approach.step: Then the paracolic gutters and Morison's pouch
approach.detail: Right and left gutters, the subphrenic spaces, and the hepatorenal recess.

approach.step: Read the diaphragm on coronal and sagittal
approach.detail: Diaphragmatic deposits are usually underestimated or overlooked on axial images alone.
Nodular and heterogeneous omentum — omental cake — is a confluent mass floating in fluid.

approach.step: Treat ascites as a finding, not a background
approach.detail: Ascites is nonspecific. Review fluid distribution, actual visible implants and alternative causes; new ascites alone does not establish peritoneal metastasis.

approach.step: Score it if cytoreduction is on the table
approach.detail: If requested, report a CT-estimated PCI with each regional contribution and limitations. Imaging burden is not surgical PCI or a stand-alone eligibility decision.

measure.how: Thirteen abdominopelvic regions, each scored 0–3 according to lesion size, then summed.

State imaging versus surgical assessment, regional burden, primary diagnosis, treatment context and limitations. Selection for cytoreduction requires the applicable framework and multidisciplinary assessment.

quiz.prompt: CT in severe pancreatitis shows a large collection filling the space behind the stomach and in front of the pancreas, while the paracolic gutters and pelvis are almost dry. The team asks how this can be so localised, and how it might be drained.
quiz.answer: It lies in the lesser sac, a compartment draining through one narrow foramen
choices: It lies in the lesser sac, a compartment draining through one narrow foramen
It lies in the greater sac, so it will redistribute along the paracolic gutters
It lies in the retroperitoneum, so a transperitoneal route would be safest
It lies in the right subphrenic space, which is continuous with the gutter
quiz.explain: The peritoneal cavity is a set of communicating recesses rather than one bag, and the lesser sac is the most sequestered of them. It sits behind the stomach and lesser omentum and in front of the pancreas, and it communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen alone, a slit bounded in front by the free edge of the lesser omentum carrying the portal triad and behind by the inferior vena cava. That single narrow communication is why a pancreatic collection can fill it while the rest of the abdomen stays dry, and it is also why such collections are so often approached transgastrically at endoscopic ultrasound, since the stomach is the wall in front of them. Fluid in the greater sac behaves quite differently, obeying gravity into the gutters and the pelvis.

quiz.prompt: Two CTs each show about 500 mL of intraperitoneal fluid: one is simple ascites, the other a loculated collection. Give the features that separate them, and say why the distinction matters before a drain is placed.
quiz.answer: Ascites conforms to the shape of the recesses, has thin margins, shifts when the patient is repositioned and displaces nothing; a loculated collection is rounded or lentiform, exerts mass effect on adjacent bowel, may have an enhancing rim and stays put, so the drain must be sited into that specific cavity rather than into the free cavity.
quiz.explain: The question a drain asks is whether the fluid is one connected space or several. Free ascites fills the recesses passively, takes their outline, has no wall, and redistributes when the patient rolls, so a single catheter anywhere dependent will empty it. A loculated collection has been walled off by fibrin and adhesions, so it has convex margins, pushes bowel away rather than insinuating between loops, often has an enhancing rim if infected, and does not move. Drain the free fluid beside it and you will report a technically successful procedure while the abscess stays where it is. So the report should state the number of collections, the safest window to each, and whether any of them communicate, and the patient may need repositioned imaging or a repeat scan to answer that.

quiz.prompt: CT shows a thick nodular sheet of soft tissue replacing the greater omentum, with smooth concave indentations of the surface of the liver and spleen, while the hepatic parenchyma itself is normal. What do the indentations tell you?
quiz.answer: Extrinsic serosal deposits pressing on the capsule, not parenchymal disease
choices: Extrinsic serosal deposits pressing on the capsule, not parenchymal disease
Subcapsular hepatic metastases eroding the surface from within the liver
Chronic hepatic fibrosis remodelling the outline of the liver and spleen
Compression by tense ascites distributed around the whole upper abdomen
quiz.explain: Scalloping is a mechanical sign: material sitting on the outside of a solid organ, firm enough to indent a capsule, which means it belongs to the peritoneal surface rather than to the organ. It is the fingerprint of bulky serosal disease, most characteristically gelatinous mucin in pseudomyxoma peritonei but also mucinous carcinomatosis from the colon, appendix, stomach or ovary. Parenchymal metastases do the opposite, bulging the contour outwards from within and enhancing as discrete lesions, and simple ascites indents nothing because a liquid cannot deform a capsule. The finding changes the referral pathway rather than just the wording, since extensive surface disease with an omental cake is the territory of cytoreductive surgery with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy in a specialist centre.

quiz.prompt: Using the Sugarbaker peritoneal cancer index, a staging laparotomy records lesion size 2 in region 0, lesion size 3 in region 1, lesion size 1 in region 3, lesion size 3 in region 6, lesion size 2 in region 9, and no disease in any other region. What is the peritoneal cancer index? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The index is the sum of the regional lesion size scores, so 2 plus 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 2 gives 11. The abdomen is divided into thirteen regions, nine abdominopelvic regions numbered 0 to 8 and four small bowel regions numbered 9 to 12 covering upper and lower jejunum and upper and lower ileum. Each region scores 0 for no disease, 1 for deposits up to 0.5 cm, 2 for deposits up to 5 cm and 3 for deposits over 5 cm or confluent disease, giving a maximum of 39. The number carries prognostic weight and helps select patients for cytoreduction, with thresholds that depend on the primary tumour, and it is worth saying in the report that CT systematically underestimates it, particularly for deposits under 5 mm and for small bowel serosal disease.

quiz.prompt: Before planned cytoreductive surgery, CT shows moderate ascites, an omental cake, and multiple small nodules along the small bowel serosa with tethering and angulation of the mesentery at its root. What is the most important thing to convey to the surgeon?
quiz.answer: Small bowel and mesenteric root disease, which threatens complete cytoreduction
choices: Small bowel and mesenteric root disease, which threatens complete cytoreduction
The volume of ascites, which is the strongest predictor of the operative result
The omental cake, which is removed at omentectomy and rarely alters the plan
That CT overstates disease burden, so the index will fall at the laparotomy
quiz.explain: Small-bowel serosal and mesenteric-root disease are important technical findings to communicate, together with exact extent, vessel relations and obstruction. They may limit complete cytoreduction but do not make imaging alone an operative verdict. CT can miss small deposits; primary-specific specialist assessment and additional evaluation when appropriate remain necessary.

quiz.prompt: A man has a slowly distending abdomen. CT shows loculated low-attenuation material with fine septa and curvilinear calcification, scalloping the liver and spleen, with small bowel loops held centrally and posteriorly rather than floating. The appendix is expanded and filled with mucin.
quiz.answer: Mucinous spread from an appendiceal neoplasm; refer for peritonectomy
choices: Mucinous spread from an appendiceal neoplasm; refer for peritonectomy
Simple ascites from portal hypertension; look for cirrhosis and varices
Tuberculous peritonitis; send fluid for culture and start antituberculous drugs
Ovarian carcinomatosis; the appendiceal finding is an incidental mucocele
quiz.explain: Mucin does not behave like fluid, and the CT says so in three ways. It loculates and septates instead of layering; it is viscous enough to indent the liver and spleen; and it displaces bowel rather than letting it float, so the loops sit centrally and posteriorly instead of drifting anteriorly as they do in true ascites. Add a distended mucin-filled appendix and the source is announced, since most pseudomyxoma arises from a ruptured low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. Calcification within the material supports it further. Treatment is complete cytoreduction with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy in a specialist centre, and long survival is possible, so the referral matters. In a woman the ovaries are often involved secondarily, so an ovarian mass in this setting does not settle where the disease began.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old from a country with a high incidence of tuberculosis has ascites, peritoneal thickening and omental infiltration, and a raised CA-125. Give the CT features that would move you towards tuberculosis rather than peritoneal carcinomatosis.
quiz.answer: Smooth, regular, thin peritoneal enhancement rather than discrete nodular implants, ascites of higher attenuation than water because of its protein and cell content, and lymph nodes with low-attenuation necrotic centres and rim enhancement; ileocaecal thickening and splenic lesions support it further.
quiz.explain: These two diseases overlap almost completely in their clinical presentation, and CA-125 is raised in both, so the imaging has to carry the discrimination. Tuberculous peritonitis tends to thicken the peritoneum smoothly and uniformly with avid thin enhancement, produce ascites denser than water because it is proteinaceous and cellular, and give nodes with caseous low-attenuation centres and enhancing rims, particularly in the mesenteric and peripancreatic stations. Carcinomatosis favours discrete nodules and plaques, irregular thickening, scalloping of solid organ surfaces and nodes that enhance homogeneously. Neither pattern is diagnostic, and the omental caking of the fibrotic form of tuberculosis is a well-known trap. The safe report names the features on both sides and asks for tissue or fluid, because the treatments could hardly be further apart.

quiz.prompt: The same appearance of increased mesenteric fat attenuation is reported twice in one clinic: once in a patient with decompensated cirrhosis and hypoalbuminaemia, and once in a patient with weight loss and 2 cm mesenteric nodes. How should it be handled in each?
quiz.answer: Attribute it to oedema in the first; pursue lymphoma or deposits in the second
choices: Attribute it to oedema in the first; pursue lymphoma or deposits in the second
Attribute it to panniculitis in both; a follow-up scan at one year will suffice
Attribute it to oedema in both; the nodes are reacting to the fat inflammation
Biopsy the mesentery in the first; observe the second, since nodes are common
quiz.explain: Hazy mesenteric fat is a finding with a wide differential and almost no specificity on its own, so it must be read against the patient. The causes group into oedema from cirrhosis, cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia or venous and lymphatic obstruction; inflammation from pancreatitis, diverticulitis or mesenteric panniculitis; haemorrhage after trauma or in an anticoagulated patient; and tumour, particularly lymphoma, carcinoid with its desmoplastic reaction, and carcinomatosis. The nodes are the most useful modifier. Small nodes with surrounding preserved fat fit an inflammatory or oedematous cause, whereas nodes above about a centimetre in short axis, a discrete mass, or vascular encasement should not be dismissed as panniculitis. A calcified spiculated mesenteric mass with tethering of adjacent bowel is a different pattern again and points at carcinoid.

quiz.prompt: A well 60-year-old has an incidental fat-attenuation mass at the root of the small bowel mesentery containing several 4 mm nodes, with preserved fat immediately around the vessels and nodes and a thin hyperattenuating rim around the whole lesion. The mesenteric vessels are patent and undisplaced.
quiz.answer: Sclerosing mesenteritis; interval imaging rather than biopsy at this stage
choices: Sclerosing mesenteritis; interval imaging rather than biopsy at this stage
Mesenteric lymphoma; arrange a core biopsy of the mesenteric mass promptly
Carcinoid deposit; arrange somatostatin receptor imaging and small bowel MR
Peritoneal carcinomatosis; search for a gastrointestinal or ovarian primary
quiz.explain: Two features do the work here. The fat ring sign, where a halo of normal fat is preserved immediately around the vessels and nodes within the mass, and the pseudocapsule, a thin dense rim demarcating the lesion from surrounding fat, together favour sclerosing mesenteritis strongly. Lymphoma behaves differently: it encases and displaces vessels, obliterates perivascular fat, and gives nodes larger than a centimetre. Carcinoid produces a spiculated, frequently calcified soft tissue mass with retraction and tethering of adjacent loops, and it is a soft tissue mass rather than a fat-attenuation one. Most cases of sclerosing mesenteritis are incidental and stable, which is why interval imaging is a reasonable first move in a well patient, but a minority accompany lymphoma or IgG4-related disease, so a lesion that grows or changes character earns tissue.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the peritoneal spaces a leak from a perforated appendix passes through as it ascends on the right.
quiz.answer: right-iliac-fossa right-paracolic-gutter hepatorenal-recess right-subphrenic-space
quiz.explain: The right paracolic gutter is deeper than the left and runs uninterrupted from the iliac fossa to the subhepatic region, so fluid arising on the right ascends freely with respiratory and postural movement and reaches the hepatorenal recess, which is the most dependent part of the upper abdomen in a supine patient, and then the subphrenic space. On the left the phrenicocolic ligament interrupts the gutter and blunts that ascent, which is one reason left-sided collections behave less predictably. Knowing this path tells you where to hunt for an abscess after appendicitis, and the same anatomy explains the classic sites of peritoneal deposit in carcinomatosis: the pouch of Douglas, the right subphrenic space and paracolic gutter, the sigmoid mesocolon and the ileocaecal region at the end of the small bowel mesentery.

quiz.prompt: An 80-year-old woman with vomiting has a small bowel loop passing below the inguinal ligament and medial to a flattened femoral vein. The neck of the defect measures 8 mm, the herniated loop is thick-walled and there is fluid in the sac. What follows from the site and the neck?
quiz.answer: A femoral hernia with a tight neck; the strangulation risk demands urgent repair
choices: A femoral hernia with a tight neck; the strangulation risk demands urgent repair
A direct inguinal hernia; attempted reduction in the department is appropriate
An indirect inguinal hernia; elective repair on a routine operating list is fine
An obturator hernia; the loop lies between pectineus and obturator externus here
quiz.explain: Site is decided by relations, not by where the lump appears. A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein, which it commonly flattens, through a ring bounded medially by the lacunar ligament, and that rigid narrow neck is why femoral hernias strangulate so often and why they should be repaired promptly rather than listed routinely. Inguinal hernias emerge above and medial to the pubic tubercle: direct ones through the posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, indirect ones through the deep ring lateral to those vessels. An obturator hernia takes a different route through the obturator canal and lies between pectineus and obturator externus; it too strangulates readily, and it should be looked for specifically in a thin elderly woman with unexplained obstruction.

quiz.prompt: A hernia contains a loop of small bowel that cannot be reduced, with dilated bowel proximal to it. Give the single CT observation that separates incarceration from strangulation, and two further findings that support the latter.
quiz.answer: Reduced or absent enhancement of the herniated bowel wall is the observation that marks strangulation, since incarceration is only mechanical irreducibility; supporting findings include fluid within the sac with fat stranding around the neck, mural thickening, mesenteric vascular engorgement and pneumatosis.
quiz.explain: Incarceration is a mechanical statement, meaning the contents will not go back, and an incarcerated hernia can sit unchanged for years. Strangulation is a vascular statement, and the wall is where you read it: enhancement that is reduced compared with non-herniated loops on the same acquisition, judged against a neighbouring loop rather than against a remembered attenuation, is the finding that changes the timing of the operation. Everything else is supportive. Fluid in the sac and haziness of the fat at the neck indicate venous congestion, mural thickening and mesenteric vascular engorgement follow it, and pneumatosis in the herniated loop is late and grave. A narrow neck raises the risk, which is why femoral and obturator hernias declare themselves this way more often than wide-necked incisional ones.

quiz.prompt: An anticoagulated 75-year-old with a week of violent coughing has a tender abdominal wall mass. Unenhanced CT shows a 9 cm haematoma in the right rectus muscle extending across the midline into the space in front of the bladder. Explain the anatomy that permits that spread, and say what you would do next.
quiz.answer: Below the arcuate line the posterior rectus sheath is absent, so blood is no longer confined by it or by the linea alba and tracks across the midline into the preperitoneal and prevesical space; the next step is an arterial phase acquisition to look for active extravasation from the inferior epigastric artery, which would be treated by embolisation.
quiz.explain: A rectus sheath haematoma usually comes from tearing of the inferior epigastric artery or its perforators, in an anticoagulated patient, after coughing, straining or an injection. Above the arcuate line the intact posterior sheath and the linea alba hold the blood on one side, so the collection is spindle-shaped and confined to the muscle. Below the arcuate line there is no posterior sheath, and blood spreads into the preperitoneal and prevesical space, crosses the midline, and can become very large, which is why the haemoglobin can fall dramatically and the appearance can be mistaken for intraperitoneal haemorrhage. A fluid-fluid level within the haematoma reflects an anticoagulated patient still bleeding. Most cases are managed with reversal and support; contrast extravasation on the arterial phase is what selects the patient for embolisation.

module_contract.goal: Read an oncological FDG PET/CT with its preparation, its physiological traps and its treatment timing in mind, and act proportionately on incidental uptake.

approach.step: Check the preparation before you read a single voxel
approach.detail: Fasted 4–6 hours (diabetic patients overnight, 12 hours), blood glucose below 150 mg/dL, no strenuous activity for 24 hours, no speech for 20 minutes before injection, imaging at 60 minutes post-injection. A failure in any of these changes what the study can exclude.

approach.step: Read the CT first, then the PET, then the fusion
approach.detail: The whole-body CT is acquired first and supplies the attenuation map. Anything you find on PET must be placed on an anatomical structure you can name on the CT.

approach.step: Set your two internal reference points
approach.detail: Mediastinal blood pool and liver. Both hold relatively constant uptake on serial imaging, and every visual judgement in lymphoma is made against them rather than against an absolute number.

approach.step: Walk the sites of physiological uptake deliberately
approach.detail: Brain (basal ganglia, posterior cingulate, visual cortex), myocardium, kidneys and bladder, liver, Waldeyer ring, thymus, spleen and marrow, salivary glands, brown fat in neck and mediastinum, bowel wall on metformin, muscle after exertion, larynx after speech, breast in lactation, spinal cord at T11–L1 and C4.

approach.step: Interrogate anything focal against the attenuation-correction artefacts
approach.detail: The respiratory 'mushroom effect' at the lung bases, prosthesis artefact where the correction cannot handle high density, and truncation when arms are down and the CT field of view is narrower than the PET.

approach.step: Score each FDG-avid lesion independently in lymphoma
approach.detail: Deauville is applied lesion by lesion, not as a single global impression, and then translated into a response category.

approach.step: Judge incidental uptake by size and by plausible cause
approach.detail: Sensitivity and specificity both fall below 7 mm. Granulomatous disease, abscess, surgical change, foreign-body reaction including talc pleurodesis, fat necrosis and inflammation all light up — say which is more likely before you generate a cancer pathway.

measure.how: Tissue radioactivity concentration in the ROI divided by injected dose per kilogram of body weight. Report which flavour you used — max, mean or peak — and keep to one.
measure.cutoff: Benign/malignant cut-off falls in the range SUV 2.0–2.5

measure.how: Below this, absence of uptake does not exclude disease.
measure.cutoff: Sensitivity and specificity fall for lesions < 7 mm

measure.how: Measured before the tracer goes in; competitive inhibition by glucose degrades the study.
Before injection.
Injection to acquisition. Keep it constant if the SUV is going to be compared.
Markedly increased uptake, defined against the liver.
measure.cutoff: 2–3× the maximum SUV in the liver, or any new lesion

measure.what: Residual mass after complete metabolic response in DLBCL
measure.how: Measure the residual mass on CT even when the PET is Deauville 1.
measure.cutoff: > 2 cm carries increased risk of recurrence

measure.how: Governs scheduling and the dose that actually arrives.

classify.name: Deauville five-point scale
rows: No uptake, or no residual uptake when used at interim
Slight uptake, at or below mediastinal blood pool
Uptake above mediastinum but at or below liver
Partial response if uptake is down from baseline with no structural progression on CT; stable disease if unchanged; progressive disease if rising
Markedly increased uptake (2–3× maximum liver SUV), or any new lesion on response evaluation

Partial response if uptake is down from baseline with no structural progression on CT; stable disease if unchanged; progressive disease if rising or if a new FDG-avid focus consistent with lymphoma appears
Any new area of uptake not overtly attributable to lymphoma
Reported separately, not a response category
classify.note: Complete metabolic response requires scores 1–3 together with the absence of FDG-avid bone marrow lesions, and holds irrespective of a persistent mass on CT. The scale is recommended for Hodgkin lymphoma of any type, DLBCL, marginal zone NHL with aggressive transformation, and FDG-avid nodal lymphomas generally — but not CLL, small lymphocytic lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenström, or mycosis fungoides. It is incorporated into the Lugano criteria.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
FDG PET/CT from [skull base to mid-thigh / vertex to toes]. Fasted [n] hours. Blood glucose [n] mg/dL. [n] MBq F-18 FDG intravenously; uptake time [n] minutes. [Diagnostic / low-dose] CT [with / without] intravenous contrast. Comparison: [date and type].

FINDINGS
Quality: [adequate / limited by (hyperglycaemia, motion, truncation, brown fat, prosthesis artefact)].
Reference organs: mediastinal blood pool SUVmax [n]; liver SUVmax [n].
Index lesion: [site], [size] mm, SUVmax [n] (previously [n]).
Nodal disease: [stations involved, above and below the diaphragm], most avid SUVmax [n].
Extranodal: [organ], [size], SUVmax [n].
Bone marrow: [no FDG-avid marrow lesion / focal lesions at ...].
Physiological and non-malignant uptake accounted for: [brown fat / bowel on metformin / muscle / larynx / post-surgical / other].
CT-only findings of note: [ ].

IMPRESSION
1. [Lymphoma: Deauville score (1-5) — (complete metabolic response / partial response / stable disease / progressive disease).] [Other tumours: metabolic response in plain words with the SUVmax then and now.]
2. [Sites of active disease, named.]
3. [Incidental uptake: what it probably is, and whether it needs anything.]
4. [Recommendation and the interval.]
pitfalls: Comparing SUVs across scanners or across methods. SUV moves with blood glucose, noise, resolution and ROI placement — serial comparison is only reliable on the same scanner with the same method and the same uptake time.

Calling a Deauville 4 or 5 progressive disease on the score alone. Both scores are compatible with partial response if uptake has fallen from baseline and CT shows no structural progression; it is the direction of change that decides.

Reading a persistent mass on CT as residual disease. Scores 1–3 with no FDG-avid marrow lesion are a complete metabolic response whatever the mass looks like — though in DLBCL a residual mass over 2 cm still carries an increased risk of recurrence.

Applying Deauville where it does not apply. CLL, small lymphocytic lymphoma, lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma/Waldenström and mycosis fungoides are outside the scale, and primary extranodal and cutaneous lymphomas have separate proposed criteria.
Chasing sub-centimetre uptake. Both sensitivity and specificity deteriorate below 7 mm, so a small hot focus is a weak finding in both directions.
Missing the preparation failure that explains the study. Diffuse symmetrical muscle uptake, brown fat in the neck, laryngeal activity and bowel uptake on metformin are all preparation, not disease.
Trusting fused position over an artefact. The mushroom effect at the lung bases, prosthesis artefact and truncation with arms down all come from attenuation correction, not from the patient.

radiology_reference.overview: Read an oncological FDG PET/CT with its preparation, its physiological traps and its treatment timing in mind, and act proportionately on incidental uptake.
learning_points: Confirm fasting and serum glucose before FDG, standardise uptake time, and record recent treatment.
Every focus is located and compared with expected physiology.
Stage-changing disease differs from incidental uptake needing context.
Review indication, tumour type and treatment timing.
Review tracer, activity, uptake time and glucose.
Review pET and CT acquisition quality.
Review disease sites, size and uptake measurements.
Review response criteria if applicable and incidental findings.
Inflammation and treatment effects can be FDG-avid; standardise comparisons and identify limitations of the CT component.

quiz.prompt: A lung primary measured SUVmax 8.4 on a staging PET/CT performed at another hospital and SUVmax 5.9 on your restaging scan six weeks later. No treatment was given in between and both studies were technically satisfactory. How should you handle the comparison in your report?
quiz.answer: Describe the appearances qualitatively and avoid a numerical comparison across the two scanners
choices: Describe the appearances qualitatively and avoid a numerical comparison across the two scanners
Report a 30% metabolic response, treating SUVmax as an absolute calibrated measurement
Report metabolic progression, since a lower SUV reflects a shorter uptake time
Report a partial response under RECIST 1.1, which grades response using SUVmax
quiz.explain: SUV is not a measurement of the tumour so much as a ratio: activity concentration in the region divided by injected activity per unit body weight. Everything in that chain travels badly between departments — uptake time, plasma glucose, any dose extravasation, scanner calibration, and reconstruction (point spread function and time-of-flight modelling both push small-lesion SUVmax up). Harmonisation programmes such as EARL exist precisely because raw numbers are not portable. Quantitative response assessment (PERCIST) therefore demands the same scanner, protocol and uptake time. RECIST 1.1 is an anatomical system; it uses FDG PET only in a limited way, to confirm that a new lesion is genuinely new, and it never grades response by SUV. A falling SUV would need a longer, not shorter, uptake time to be an artefact, since tumour uptake rises for the first hour or more.

quiz.prompt: A thin 22-year-old woman scanned in January for lymphoma staging has symmetrical intense uptake in both supraclavicular fossae, along the paravertebral gutters and around the aortic arch. The CT component shows only fat at these sites.
quiz.answer: Report brown adipose tissue and warm the patient thoroughly before any repeat study
choices: Report brown adipose tissue and warm the patient thoroughly before any repeat study
Report bilateral nodal disease and stage her as having supradiaphragmatic involvement
Report a paraneoplastic myositis and recommend creatine kinase and a muscle biopsy
Report probable sarcoidosis and recommend mediastinoscopy before treatment begins
quiz.explain: Brown fat is metabolically active, sympathetically driven and richest in young, thin, female patients scanned in cold weather. Its signature is symmetry and distribution: supraclavicular and lower neck, paravertebral, perirenal, around the aortic arch and in the mediastinal fat, always with fat attenuation on the co-registered CT rather than a soft tissue node. That co-registration is the whole reason PET is fused with CT. The clinical problem is not misdiagnosis so much as concealment — brown fat sits exactly where supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes sit and can mask them. Prevention is practical: a warm waiting room and blankets, avoiding cold exposure before injection, and in some departments a benzodiazepine or a beta blocker. If the neck genuinely has to be assessed, rescan the patient warm rather than argue with the images you have.

quiz.prompt: A patient with type 2 diabetes arrives for a staging PET/CT. His capillary glucose is 15 mmol/L (270 mg/dL) two hours after breakfast and his usual short-acting insulin.
quiz.answer: Rebook the study after better glycaemic control rather than inject the tracer today
choices: Rebook the study after better glycaemic control rather than inject the tracer today
Inject now and give short-acting insulin at the same time to bring the glucose down
Inject now and correct the reported SUV values afterwards for the measured glucose
Inject a doubled activity of tracer to overcome the competing plasma glucose load
quiz.explain: FDG and glucose compete for the same GLUT transporters and for hexokinase, so hyperglycaemia lowers tumour uptake while raising muscle and background activity: sensitivity falls and lesion contrast falls with it. Simple arithmetic correction of SUV for glucose is not reliable enough to rescue the study. Giving insulin at the time of injection is worse than doing nothing, because insulin drives FDG into skeletal muscle and produces a diagnostically useless scan; if short-acting insulin has been given, most departments wait at least four hours. Doubling the activity increases dose without improving the competitive block. Standard preparation is a four to six hour fast with water allowed, glucose checked at the door, and a working threshold around 11 mmol/L (200 mg/dL), above which the patient is better rescheduled with the diabetes team's help.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old smoker has a 3 cm right upper lobe adenocarcinoma. Staging PET/CT shows an avid 9 mm right lower paratracheal node (SUVmax 4.8) and no distant uptake. He is otherwise fit for lobectomy.
quiz.answer: Recommend endobronchial ultrasound sampling of the node before the stage is settled
choices: Recommend endobronchial ultrasound sampling of the node before the stage is settled
Report confirmed N2 disease and refer him directly for chemoradiotherapy instead
Report the node as reactive on size criteria and proceed straight to lobectomy
Recommend a repeat PET/CT in three months to see whether the node grows further
quiz.explain: PET is far better than CT at finding mediastinal disease, but a positive node is a probability, not a diagnosis. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis, reactive nodes draining a post-obstructive pneumonia and sarcoidosis all take up FDG happily, and in a population with any burden of tuberculosis or histoplasmosis the false positive rate is high enough to matter. The decision hanging on this node is enormous — single-station N2 disease moves a resectable patient into multimodality treatment — so guidelines require pathological confirmation of PET-positive mediastinal nodes, usually by endobronchial ultrasound with mediastinoscopy in reserve. Note also that lung cancer is staged by TNM 9th edition, which subdivides N2 by single versus multiple station involvement, making accurate nodal mapping more consequential than it used to be. Waiting three months simply lets a curable cancer grow.

quiz.prompt: A man with HPV-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma and a bulky ipsilateral level II node completes chemoradiotherapy. The head and neck multidisciplinary team asks when to image the neck and what the imaging will decide.
quiz.answer: PET/CT at around 12 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
choices: PET/CT at around 12 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
PET/CT at around 3 weeks, reserving neck dissection for residual nodal uptake
Planned neck dissection at 6 weeks, with PET/CT used afterwards for surveillance
Contrast-enhanced CT at 6 weeks, with neck dissection decided on node size alone
quiz.explain: The PET-NECK randomised trial established the modern pathway: PET/CT-guided surveillance after chemoradiotherapy gave survival equivalent to planned neck dissection while sparing most patients an operation, and cost less. The timing is the substance of the item. Scan too early and radiation mucositis, dermatitis and reactive nodal uptake generate false positives, while incompletely regressed but sterilised nodes look like residual disease; around 12 weeks the inflammation has settled and residual uptake means something. Size criteria on CT are unreliable after chemoradiotherapy because necrotic sterilised nodes stay large for months. The same principle governs the rest of the body: allow roughly six weeks after surgery and around three months after radiotherapy before treating uptake as tumour.

quiz.prompt: Staging PET/CT for a biopsy-proven mucinous adenocarcinoma of the rectum shows only faint uptake in the primary (SUVmax 2.6) and nothing elsewhere. CT shows a 5 cm annular tumour and two 9 mm low-attenuation liver lesions, neither of which is FDG-avid.
quiz.answer: Treat the PET as insensitive in this histology and characterise the liver with MRI
choices: Treat the PET as insensitive in this histology and characterise the liver with MRI
Report the liver lesions as benign, since neither of them shows any FDG uptake
Report a complete metabolic response and defer any further staging investigation
Report the primary as a low-grade tumour that needs no further local staging
quiz.explain: Mucinous and signet ring adenocarcinomas have low cellular density and abundant extracellular mucin, so there are simply fewer glycolytic cells per voxel and uptake is modest even in large tumours. The same trap recurs across the false negative list: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, lepidic-predominant lung adenocarcinoma, indolent lymphomas such as marginal zone and MALT, renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, and prostate adenocarcinoma. Lesion size compounds it — below roughly 8 to 10 mm partial volume averaging dilutes true uptake towards background, so two 9 mm liver lesions could not be called benign on PET even in an avid tumour. Liver MRI with a hepatobiliary or diffusion-weighted protocol is the sensitive test here, and rectal MRI still does the local staging that PET cannot.

quiz.prompt: A patient with resected stage IIIC melanoma has a staging FDG PET/CT reported as negative from vertex to thigh. Three weeks later he presents with a first generalised seizure.
quiz.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced brain MRI, which PET cannot replace because of cortical background
choices: Arrange contrast-enhanced brain MRI, which PET cannot replace because of cortical background
Repeat the PET/CT with a delayed brain acquisition, which resolves the cortical background
Arrange non-contrast CT of the head, which matches MRI for small parenchymal metastases
Reassure him, since a negative whole-body PET makes intracranial metastasis unlikely
quiz.explain: Normal grey matter is intensely glycolytic, so a small cortical metastasis sits inside a bright background and is easily invisible; delayed imaging does not fix this because the background is physiological, not a clearance problem. PET is likewise weak for sub-centimetre pulmonary nodules, where respiratory motion and partial volume averaging both work against it, which is why the CT component is read in its own right rather than as a map for the PET. Melanoma staging therefore pairs whole-body PET/CT with dedicated contrast-enhanced brain MRI in higher-stage disease, and non-contrast CT is a poor substitute for either. Where PET does earn its place in melanoma is in stage III and IV disease, finding unsuspected nodal, subcutaneous and visceral deposits that alter systemic treatment.

quiz.prompt: A restaging PET/CT in a woman taking metformin shows intense uptake continuously throughout the colon and, separately, one discrete intense focus in the sigmoid that is brighter than the surrounding bowel.
quiz.answer: Attribute the diffuse activity to metformin and refer the focal sigmoid uptake for colonoscopy
choices: Attribute the diffuse activity to metformin and refer the focal sigmoid uptake for colonoscopy
Attribute both the diffuse activity and the focal sigmoid uptake to metformin and stop there
Refer her for colonoscopy on the basis of the diffuse pattern and disregard the sigmoid focus
Attribute both patterns to an infective colitis and recommend stool culture with review
quiz.explain: Metformin produces striking, continuous FDG uptake through small bowel and colon, thought to reflect increased enterocyte glucose handling; where the bowel is the question, stopping it for around 48 hours before the scan clears the picture. That diffuse pattern is not itself an indication for colonoscopy. Focal colonic uptake is a different finding entirely and is the incidental most worth chasing: it appears in something like one or two per cent of oncological PET studies, and in pooled colonoscopy series a large minority — of the order of a third — prove to be an adenoma or a carcinoma. A polyp found this way is a cure. Report it explicitly and name the segment, because the endoscopist will otherwise not know where to look.

quiz.prompt: Fluorine-18 has a half-life of 110 minutes. A syringe is calibrated to contain 370 MBq of FDG at 08:00, but the patient is delayed and is not injected until 11:40 the same morning. What activity remains in the syringe at 11:40? Answer in MBq to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: From 08:00 to 11:40 is 220 minutes, exactly two half-lives, so the activity halves twice: 370 to 185 to 92.5 MBq. The arithmetic is trivial but the working day depends on it. Fluorine-18 is cyclotron-produced and shipped, so a department's schedule is written around decay: a delivery calibrated for a mid-morning slot is worth a quarter of that by early afternoon, which is why late-running lists get abandoned rather than rescued. It is also why administered activity must be recorded as the dose actually given, corrected for residual activity left in the syringe and line, since SUV divides by that number and an over-recorded dose falsely lowers every SUV on the study. Compare gallium-68, with a 68 minute half-life, which is eluted on site from a generator rather than delivered.

quiz.prompt: Two PET studies of the same patient on the same scanner give different SUVmax for the same node. Give three technical variables that could account for this, and say briefly why SUV is so sensitive to them.
quiz.answer: Uptake time before acquisition, the patient's blood glucose and the reconstruction algorithm can all change SUVmax, because SUV is only a ratio of measured activity concentration to injected dose per unit body weight.
quiz.explain: SUV = tissue activity concentration divided by (injected activity / body weight). Nothing in that expression is a property of the tumour alone. Tumour uptake continues to rise for 60 to 90 minutes, so a delayed acquisition raises the number; hyperglycaemia competitively lowers it; extravasated dose inflates it because the denominator overstates what actually circulated; body weight normalisation over-reads in obese patients, which is why PERCIST uses lean body mass (SUL) instead; and iterative reconstruction with point spread function or time-of-flight modelling raises small-lesion SUVmax substantially. Region-of-interest method matters too, SUVpeak being more reproducible than the single hottest voxel. The practical rule is unglamorous: compare like with like, and when you cannot, say so and read the images.

quiz.prompt: A staging PET/CT for lymphoma shows a single focus of intense uptake in the right thyroid lobe, with the rest of the gland quiet. State the proportionate next step and the reason for it.
quiz.answer: Recommend thyroid ultrasound, with fine needle aspiration if the nodule looks suspicious, because focal thyroid uptake carries a malignancy risk of roughly a quarter to a third.
quiz.explain: Focal thyroid incidentalomas appear on around one to two per cent of FDG studies, and pooled series put the malignancy rate at roughly 25 to 35 per cent — high enough that ignoring it is indefensible, low enough that most are benign. The proportionate response is ultrasound first, then risk-stratify by sonographic features using ACR TI-RADS or the local equivalent, and aspirate on that basis rather than on the PET alone. Diffuse thyroid uptake is a different finding, usually chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, and needs only thyroid function tests if there is a clinical reason. The same graded logic applies to incidental focal prostate uptake: check the PSA and refer for urological assessment rather than either ignoring it or launching straight into biopsy. Always weigh it against the prognosis of the cancer being staged.

quiz.prompt: A patient with oesophageal carcinoma finishes neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and the surgeon requests a PET/CT before oesophagectomy. Say when you would perform it and what the study is chiefly looking for.
quiz.answer: Scan at least six weeks after chemoradiotherapy, chiefly to find interval distant metastases that would make oesophagectomy futile, since earlier imaging is confounded by treatment inflammation.
quiz.explain: The honest purpose of restaging PET before oesophagectomy is not to grade the primary but to spare a patient a major operation they cannot benefit from, by detecting metastases that declared themselves during the months of neoadjuvant treatment. Grading the primary is unreliable, because radiotherapy leaves a band of intense oesophagitis exactly where the tumour was. Timing is the same family of judgements throughout oncological PET: allow around six weeks after surgery for the wound bed to quieten, roughly three months after radiotherapy, and for lymphoma end-of-treatment studies at least three weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle, since marrow rebound and growth factor support make the marrow and spleen light up diffusely, and thymic rebound produces an arrowhead of anterior mediastinal uptake in younger patients.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these reference levels of uptake in the order the Deauville five-point scale ranks them, from score 1 through to score 5.
quiz.answer: no-uptake-above-background at-or-below-mediastinal-blood-pool above-blood-pool-up-to-liver moderately-above-liver markedly-above-liver
quiz.explain: The Deauville scale, embedded in the Lugano criteria for Hodgkin and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, scores residual uptake visually against two internal reference organs: the mediastinal blood pool and the liver. Scores 1 to 3 are generally taken as a complete metabolic response in patients on standard therapy, and 4 to 5 mean residual metabolic disease, driving escalation, biopsy or a change of plan; score 5 also covers new lesions attributable to lymphoma. An additional score X is used for new uptake unlikely to be lymphoma at all. Two cautions: it is a visual comparison, not an SUV threshold, so the reference organs must be assessed on the same study; and it was validated in lymphoma, so importing it into solid tumour reporting is a category error.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of a standard oncological FDG PET/CT into the order in which they happen on the day of the scan.
quiz.answer: fast-four-hours check-capillary-glucose inject-FDG rest-quietly-60-minutes void-bladder acquire-PET-CT
quiz.explain: Each step exists to remove a specific artefact. A four to six hour fast with water allowed lowers circulating insulin, which keeps FDG out of skeletal muscle and shifts the myocardium towards fatty acid metabolism. Glucose is checked before injection, not after, because a high reading changes the plan rather than the report. The uptake phase is roughly 60 minutes in a warm, quiet room: talking loads the vocal cords and larynx, chewing loads the muscles of mastication, exercise loads the limbs, and cold recruits brown fat. Voiding immediately before acquisition reduces bladder activity and the streak-like artefact around it, and matters most in pelvic malignancy. The low-dose CT then provides attenuation correction and anatomical localisation, which is what turns a blob of activity into a diagnosis.

module_contract.goal: Detect and quantify pleural fluid and air across modalities, separate empyema and malignant disease from simple effusion, and get a drain into the right space.

approach.step: Establish the patient's position before you judge the volume
approach.detail: Erect, supine and decubitus each hide fluid differently. A supine film can carry a large effusion as nothing more than a veil-like density over the hemithorax, and bilateral equal effusions are the hardest of all because both sides match.

approach.step: Follow the fluid where it goes first
approach.detail: Costophrenic then cardiophrenic angle blunting, fluid tracking in the horizontal or oblique fissure, then the meniscus sloping down and medially. On the lateral, the posterior costophrenic angles are deepest and show fluid earliest.

approach.step: Ask which way the mediastinum has moved
approach.detail: A large effusion shifts the mediastinum away. Shift towards the effusion means collapse is dominating, and that changes the diagnosis, not just the size.
Ultrasound resolves loculated fluid from thickened pleura, shows the spine sign where fluid conducts sound above the diaphragm, and finds the intercostal vessels before you puncture.

approach.step: For air, name the convention before you name the size
approach.detail: BTS measures chest wall to lung edge at the level of the hilum, ACCP measures thoracic cupola to lung apex. The two thresholds are different numbers for different lines — say which you used.

approach.step: On CT, look at the pleura in the portal-venous phase
approach.detail: The pleura enhances maximally in the portal-venous (pleural) phase. That is the series on which nodularity, circumferential thickening and mediastinal involvement declare themselves.

Skin fold, scapular border, clothing, monitoring leads and giant bullous emphysema all imitate a pneumothorax. A skin fold is a band of increased attenuation sharply outlined laterally, often running beyond the chest cavity.

measure.how: Your baseline for what counts as an effusion at all.

measure.what: Fluid detectable on an erect chest radiograph
measure.how: Costophrenic blunting on PA or AP erect.
Coronal view, mid to posterior axillary line.
measure.cutoff: 3–5 mL, against > 50 mL for a lateral decubitus radiograph

measure.how: Chest wall to lung edge, measured at the level of the hilum.
Thoracic cupola to lung apex.
Largest air pocket between parietal and visceral pleura, measured perpendicular to the chest wall on axial CT, in a stable non-intubated patient.
measure.cutoff: < 35 mm — about 10% need a drain in the first week

measure.how: Perpendicular to the chest wall, portal-venous phase.

classify.name: Benign versus malignant pleural thickening on CT
rows: Diffuse pleural calcification overlying the thickening
classify.note: CT is highly specific — close to 100% in reported series — but insensitive. A normal-looking pleura does not exclude malignancy. Malignant pleural disease is metastatic carcinoma in 58%, mesothelioma in 28%, non-Hodgkin lymphoma in 8%.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
[Erect PA / supine AP / lateral decubitus, side down] chest radiograph. [CT chest, portal-venous phase.] [Thoracic ultrasound, curvilinear probe.]

FINDINGS
Side and character: [right / left / bilateral] pleural [fluid / gas / both].
Volume or size: [effusion — blunting of the costophrenic angle / meniscus to the level of the (n)th rib]. [Pneumothorax — (n) cm chest wall to lung edge at the hilum (BTS), or (n) cm cupola to apex (ACCP); state which.]
Mediastinum: [central / shifted away — mass effect / shifted towards — collapse dominant].
Fluid character on ultrasound: [anechoic / septated / echogenic swirling]; [loculated / free].
Pleura: [smooth / nodular / circumferential]; maximum parietal thickness [n] mm; [mediastinal pleura involved / spared]; [calcification present].
Lung and elsewhere: [underlying consolidation, mass, collapse]; [chest wall invasion]; [nodal or bone disease].

IMPRESSION
1. [Effusion / pneumothorax], [size by named convention].
2. [Simple versus complicated or malignant — cite the features you are relying on.]
3. [Recommendation: observation, aspiration, intercostal drain, image-guided pleural biopsy.]
4. [If drainage is planned: proposed site, with a safe window and the intercostal vessels identified on ultrasound.]
pitfalls: Quoting a pneumothorax size without saying which convention you used. BTS at the hilum and ACCP at the apex are different lines with different cut-offs, and the choice moves patients across the small/large boundary.
Excluding a large effusion on a supine film. Fluid layers posteriorly with no meniscus; bilateral equal effusions cancel each other out entirely.
Missing a subpulmonic effusion. Look for the peak of the right hemidiaphragm displaced laterally, or an increased gap between lower lobe air and the gastric bubble on the left.
Calling a hydropneumothorax an effusion because you looked for a meniscus. There is no meniscus once there is air above the fluid — there is a flat air-fluid level.
Trusting Light's criteria to exclude malignancy. They misclassify 5–10% of malignant pleural effusions as transudates.
Reading FDG uptake in the pleura as proof of tumour. It is falsely positive in inflammatory disease and after pleurodesis.
Reporting a skin fold as a pneumothorax. The fold is a band of increased attenuation with a sharp lateral edge, often extending outside the chest, with lung markings still visible beyond it.

radiology_reference.overview: Detect and quantify pleural fluid and air across modalities, separate empyema and malignant disease from simple effusion, and get a drain into the right space.
learning_points: A pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings shows pneumothorax.
Dependent fluid layers unless loculation fixes its shape.
Enhancing thick pleura or nodularity changes management.
Review laterality and extent of effusion or pneumothorax.
Review pleural thickness, nodularity and enhancement.
Review loculation, gas and drain position.
Review adjacent lung expansion and parenchymal disease.
Review chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinal involvement.
Imaging may suggest pleural infection or malignancy but does not replace appropriate fluid or tissue sampling.
