quiz.prompt: A ventilated patient lies supine. On ultrasound at the lung base, the maximal separation between the visceral and parietal pleura at end-expiration is 34 mm. Using the bedside estimate that volume in millilitres is twenty times the interpleural distance in millimetres, what volume does this predict? Answer in millilitres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: 34 x 20 = 680 mL. The estimate was derived in supine ventilated patients with the probe at the posterior axillary line at the lung base, and it is a working figure rather than a measurement - expect it to be right to within a couple of hundred millilitres, and do not use it in a seated patient or with loculated fluid. The reason it is worth knowing is the contrast with radiography. A frontal erect film needs roughly 200 mL before the lateral costophrenic angle blunts, a lateral film about 50 mL in the posterior sulcus, and a supine film can hide well over half a litre behind a veil of increased density. Ultrasound sees a few millilitres. So a supine intensive care film reported as showing no significant effusion is a statement about the projection, not about the chest, and the volume you quote should almost always come from ultrasound or CT. Volume alone never decides drainage: whether the fluid is infected, and whether the patient is breathless because of it, do.

quiz.prompt: An intubated patient has a supine anteroposterior film showing uniformly increased density across the whole right hemithorax, with pulmonary vessels still visible through it and no mediastinal shift. What is happening and what should you do next?
quiz.answer: Layering pleural fluid; confirm and quantify by ultrasound
choices: Layering pleural fluid; confirm and quantify by ultrasound
Complete lobar collapse; request an urgent bronchoscopy
Diffuse consolidation; start antibiotics and repeat film
A large haemothorax; call for immediate tube drainage
quiz.explain: Supine fluid layers along the posterior pleural space and is therefore spread across the whole hemithorax as a thin sheet the beam passes through. That produces a graded veil of increased density with the lung markings still visible through it, which neither consolidation nor collapse permits: consolidation fills the alveoli and obscures the vessels, and collapse takes volume with it and pulls the mediastinum towards the opacity. The other supine clues are worth collecting - an apical cap, loss of the hemidiaphragm outline, thickening of the paraspinal line, and blunting that never appears because there is no dependent costophrenic angle to blunt. Ultrasound answers the question in under a minute and does more than confirm: it measures the depth, shows whether the fluid is anechoic or complex, and marks the safe puncture site. Haemothorax is a statement about what the fluid is, which the density pattern cannot supply.

quiz.prompt: Ultrasound of a moderate effusion in a febrile patient shows freely mobile internal echoes swirling with the heartbeat, several fine septations, and parietal pleural thickening of 4 mm. What do these features tell you?
quiz.answer: An exudate is certain; anechoic fluid would not exclude one
choices: An exudate is certain; anechoic fluid would not exclude one
A transudate is likeliest; the echoes reflect cell debris
A chylothorax is likeliest given the swirling echo pattern
Little: these appearances are seen in transudates as well
quiz.explain: The test is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the whole teaching point. Echogenic fluid, septations, loculation, parietal pleural thickening beyond about 3 mm and pleural nodularity are close to specific for an exudate - a transudate essentially does not produce them. But anechoic fluid tells you nothing, because most exudates are anechoic too, so the absence of these features cannot be used to call an effusion transudative. Swirling echoes appear in empyema, haemothorax and chylothorax alike, so they mark protein and cells rather than a particular fluid. Finding septations before you aspirate changes what you expect: septated fluid will not come out through a small catheter placed and forgotten. The biochemical arbiter remains Light's criteria - an exudate if the pleural-to-serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, or the pleural-to-serum LDH ratio exceeds 0.6, or the pleural LDH exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

quiz.prompt: Contrast CT in a septic patient shows a lentiform right pleural collection making obtuse angles with the chest wall, with thickened enhancing visceral and parietal pleura separated by the fluid, increased attenuation of the extrapleural fat, and internal loculation. What does this appearance commit you to, and how should it change the drainage plan?
quiz.answer: This is an empyema rather than a simple parapneumonic effusion, so a single small catheter is likely to fail: it needs a drain plus intrapleural fibrinolysis with alteplase and dornase alfa, and early surgical referral if it does not clear.
quiz.explain: The split pleura sign - two enhancing pleural layers with fluid between them - means the pleural surfaces are inflamed and thickened, not merely wet, and together with lentiform shape, obtuse angles, extrapleural fat stranding and loculation it says organising empyema. That changes the drain in two ways. First, a loculated collection is a set of compartments, and one catheter drains one of them; the fluid that will not come out is not a suction problem. Second, fibrinous septations respond to intrapleural alteplase with dornase alfa given together, the combination tested in the MIST2 trial, which improved drainage and reduced surgical referral where either agent alone did not. Bore size matters less than most people assume - small-bore catheters do as well as large ones for empyema provided they are flushed regularly - so the real decisions are fibrinolysis and a timely surgical opinion, since a collection that fails to clear needs video-assisted thoracoscopic decortication before the visceral peel becomes fixed.

quiz.prompt: A cavity with an air-fluid level abuts the chest wall. On CT it is round with a thick irregular wall, makes acute angles with the pleura, and destroyed lung and vessels can be traced right up to its edge. The air-fluid level measures the same width on the frontal and lateral projections. How should this be managed?
quiz.answer: Lung abscess: antibiotics, with drainage only if it fails
choices: Lung abscess: antibiotics, with drainage only if it fails
Empyema: place a chest drain and start fibrinolytic therapy
Empyema: refer directly for surgical decortication instead
Necrotic tumour: arrange biopsy of the wall before treating
quiz.explain: An abscess forms within lung and expands equally in all directions, so it is spherical: the air-fluid level is the same width whichever way you look at it, the angles with the pleura are acute, the wall is thick and irregular, and the vessels and airways of the lung it destroyed run up to it and stop. An empyema is confined to a potential space, so it is lentiform, makes obtuse angles, its air-fluid level is longer in one projection than the other, and it compresses and displaces lung rather than destroying it, with the vessels swept around the collection. The distinction earns its keep because the management diverges sharply: most lung abscesses drain through the bronchial tree and resolve on antibiotics, whereas passing a drain through aerated lung into an abscess risks a bronchopleural fistula and turns a treatable pneumonia into an empyema. Percutaneous drainage of an abscess is reserved for failure of medical treatment, and preferably where the cavity abuts the pleura without intervening lung.

quiz.prompt: On a frontal chest radiograph the average diameter of the collapsed lung is 8 cm and the average diameter of the hemithorax is 10 cm. Using Light's index, in which pneumothorax size as a percentage of the hemithorax is (1 minus lung diameter cubed divided by hemithorax diameter cubed) times 100, what is the size of the pneumothorax? Answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 8 cubed is 512 and 10 cubed is 1000, so the lung occupies 51.2 per cent of the hemithorax and the pneumothorax is 48.8 per cent. The cube is why the eye is such a poor judge: a rim of air that looks like a fifth of the width is nearly half the volume, which is the reasoning behind the old rule that a 2 cm interpleural distance at the level of the hilum corresponds to roughly half the hemithorax. The rule itself has moved on. Where the 2010 British Thoracic Society guidance used that 2 cm measurement as the trigger for intervention, the 2023 BTS pleural disease guideline directs management by symptoms and by the presence of high-risk characteristics instead, after randomised evidence that conservative management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax is non-inferior to intervention with fewer adverse events. Size still belongs in your report, because it informs the discussion and the follow-up; it simply no longer decides it on its own.

quiz.prompt: A ventilated trauma patient becomes hypotensive with rising airway pressures. The registrar asks you to fit in a CT to look for a tension pneumothorax before decompressing. What is your answer, and what is the reasoning?
quiz.answer: Decline the scan and decompress at once: tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and imaging only adds delay while obstructed venous return is what is killing him.
quiz.explain: The physiology explains the urgency. Air entering the pleural space under positive pressure with no way out raises intrapleural pressure above atmospheric, and the great veins - thin-walled and low-pressure - are compressed and kinked where they enter the mediastinum, so venous return and therefore cardiac output collapse. The patient dies of obstructed filling, not of hypoxia alone. A ventilated patient reaches that point in minutes, so a trip to the scanner is exactly the wrong direction. Needle decompression, followed by a chest drain, is the treatment, and a needle alone is temporary and often too short to reach the pleura in an adult chest. Two corollaries for the reporting radiologist. Radiographic signs - mediastinal shift away, a depressed or inverted hemidiaphragm, a splayed rib cage - are confirmation after the fact, not permission before it. And mediastinal shift on a film in a comfortable, haemodynamically stable patient is a large pneumothorax, not a tension pneumothorax.

quiz.prompt: A supine trauma film shows an abnormally lucent, deep left costophrenic sulcus with a sharply outlined left hemidiaphragm and cardiac border, but no visible pleural line. The patient is about to go to theatre for laparotomy under positive-pressure ventilation. What should happen next?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a pneumothorax and drain before positive pressure
choices: Treat it as a pneumothorax and drain before positive pressure
Disregard it: a pneumothorax needs a visible pleural line
Repeat the film erect after theatre to see if it enlarges
Request a CT of the chest before allowing any anaesthesia
quiz.explain: In a supine patient pleural air rises to the anterior and basal pleural space rather than the apex, so the visceral pleural line is often projected en face and invisible. The signs are indirect: a deep, lucent lateral costophrenic sulcus, unusually crisp outlines of the hemidiaphragm, cardiac border or pericardial fat pad because air rather than lung now abuts them, and a lucent upper abdominal quadrant. Recognising them matters most in exactly this scenario, because positive-pressure ventilation forces more air across the visceral pleural defect with each breath and a small pneumothorax can tension quickly under anaesthesia. The observational data supporting watchful waiting for occult pneumothorax come from patients who are not being ventilated, so they do not apply here. CT would confirm the finding, but the finding is already actionable, and the transfer costs time the patient has better uses for.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old former boilermaker has a unilateral effusion. CT after drainage shows circumferential pleural thickening, nodularity along the mediastinal pleura, and thickening measuring 14 mm posteriorly. Calcified plaques are present on the contralateral diaphragm. What does this combination mean?
quiz.answer: Malignant pleural disease; the plaques are exposure alone
choices: Malignant pleural disease; the plaques are exposure alone
Benign asbestos pleural disease with a reactive effusion
The plaques have undergone malignant transformation here
Chronic empyema with fibrothorax and pleural calcification
quiz.explain: Four CT features carry high specificity for malignant pleural disease: circumferential pleural thickening, nodular thickening, parietal pleural thickening greater than 1 cm, and mediastinal pleural involvement. Three of them are present, and any one of them should send the patient for tissue. They are specific but not sensitive, so their absence does not reassure - a malignant effusion may show no pleural abnormality at all on CT. Note what the imaging cannot do: mesothelioma and metastatic pleural disease share these appearances, and histology decides. Ipsilateral volume loss with a contracted hemithorax that does not pull the mediastinum across, and involvement of the interlobar fissures, lean towards mesothelioma; a known primary with discrete pleural nodules leans towards metastasis. Pleural plaques are markers of asbestos exposure and do not themselves become malignant; they raise your suspicion only because they prove the exposure that mesothelioma shares. Report the extent - chest wall, diaphragm, pericardium - since that is what drives staging.

quiz.prompt: A retired dockworker is breathless with a restrictive spirometry pattern. CT shows a continuous sheet of pleural thickening on the left, 6 mm thick, extending over 10 cm craniocaudally and involving the costophrenic angle. There are discrete calcified plaques on the right. Which finding explains his physiology, and how do you tell the two apart?
quiz.answer: The continuous left-sided sheet is diffuse pleural thickening, which restricts the lung; it is continuous, involves the costophrenic angle and exceeds the conventional 5 cm width, 8 cm craniocaudal and 3 mm thickness, whereas discrete plaques spare the costophrenic angle and do not restrict.
quiz.explain: Plaques are discrete, well-circumscribed islands of parietal pleural collagen, typically posterolateral over the mid and lower ribs and on the diaphragmatic domes, often calcified, and characteristically sparing the costophrenic angles and the apices. They are a marker of exposure and, on their own, cause no symptoms and no measurable restriction. Diffuse pleural thickening is a different entity: a continuous sheet, conventionally at least 5 cm wide, 8 cm in craniocaudal extent and 3 mm thick, that involves the costophrenic angle and frequently follows a benign asbestos-related pleural effusion. It tethers the lung, so it does restrict, and in many jurisdictions it is compensable where plaques are not - which is a reason to be precise in the report rather than writing pleural thickening and leaving it there. One caution: diffuse thickening and early mesothelioma overlap, so nodularity, mediastinal involvement or progression on interval CT should prompt PET-CT and biopsy rather than reassurance.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the steps of inserting a large-bore surgical chest drain by blunt dissection in a spontaneously breathing patient, from first to last.
quiz.answer: ultrasound-marking local-anaesthetic blunt-dissection tube-insertion underwater-seal check-radiograph
quiz.explain: Each step guards against a specific disaster. Ultrasound marking must happen immediately before the procedure and with the patient in the position they will stay in - a mark made on a ward round and used an hour later after the patient has been sat up is a well-documented route to a drain in the liver or spleen. The site itself should sit within the safe triangle, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the anterior border of latissimus dorsi and a horizontal line at the level of the nipple, and the tract should pass over the top of the rib to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle in the subcostal groove. Local anaesthetic goes down to the pleura, and drawing back fluid or air with it confirms you are aimed at the right space. Blunt dissection with forceps, then a finger sweep, replaces the trocar that used to spear organs. The tube goes to an underwater seal so that air can leave and cannot return, and only then does the check radiograph confirm position and re-expansion.

quiz.prompt: A drain placed for a pneumothorax has stopped bubbling, the pneumothorax persists, and the patient has developed extensive surgical emphysema. The film shows the tube tip in the upper hemithorax, and the radiopaque line along the tube is interrupted 2 cm outside the skin surface. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: A side hole lies outside the pleura; the drain must be replaced
choices: A side hole lies outside the pleura; the drain must be replaced
The drain is kinked in the soft tissues and should be flushed
The drain sits within a fissure, which explains poor drainage
The lung is stuck against the tip, so suction should be raised
quiz.explain: The interruption in the radiopaque stripe marks the most proximal side hole, sometimes called the sentinel eye, and every side hole must lie inside the pleural space. An interruption seen outside the chest wall means air is being vented straight into the subcutaneous tissues, which is precisely the picture here: bubbling stops because the drain is no longer connected to the pleural space, the pneumothorax persists, and surgical emphysema spreads. The fix is a new drain through a fresh site, because advancing a tube that has already been in situ pushes a contaminated length inwards and invites empyema. Worth knowing about the alternatives: a drain in a fissure is a common finding and usually works acceptably, so it is not by itself a reason to replace; a kinked drain would not usually produce this stripe appearance; and raising suction on a malpositioned drain simply pumps more air into the chest wall. The other placements that must be corrected are intraparenchymal and intra-abdominal.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising drainage of a 3-litre malignant effusion that has been present for six weeks. The team plans to run it all off in one sitting. What limit do you set and why, and what symptom should stop them earlier?
quiz.answer: Drain no more than about 1.5 litres at a sitting and then clamp for a few hours, because rapid re-expansion of chronically collapsed lung risks re-expansion pulmonary oedema; chest tightness or persistent coughing should stop the drainage immediately.
quiz.explain: Lung that has been compressed for weeks has lost surfactant and has a leaky, remodelled microvasculature, and pulling it open quickly against a large negative intrapleural pressure floods the interstitium. Re-expansion pulmonary oedema is uncommon but can be severe and occasionally fatal, and the two risk factors that recur are a large volume removed rapidly and a long-standing collapse. Hence the convention of stopping at roughly 1.5 litres and clamping for several hours before continuing, and hence the instruction to stop for chest tightness or a persistent cough, which are the symptoms of the pleural pressure falling too far - manometry, where available, makes the same point numerically. Two further habits: never apply suction to a large chronic effusion at the outset, and expect a proportion of malignant effusions to be trapped lung, where the visceral pleura is encased and cannot re-expand at all. Recognising trapped lung on the post-drainage film matters, because pleurodesis will fail and an indwelling pleural catheter is the better answer.

module_contract.goal: Score a prostate MRI by PI-RADS v2.1 and tell real lesions from benign mimics.

approach.detail: Locate the lesion in the peripheral zone (70-75% of cancers), transition zone (~25%), central zone or anterior fibromuscular stroma before you score anything.
DWI/ADC drives the peripheral zone; T2W drives the transition zone. Assign the category on that sequence alone first.

In the PZ, a DWI/ADC score of 3 is upgraded to 4 if DCE shows early focal enhancement, otherwise it stays 3. In the TZ, a T2W score of 2 becomes 3 if DWI/ADC ≥ 4, and a T2W score of 3 becomes 4 if DWI/ADC = 5.
Greatest dimension on the sequence that best shows the lesion decides PI-RADS 4 vs 5 in both zones.
Definite capsular breach or seminal vesicle invasion makes the lesion a 5 regardless of size.
Record the lesion on the standardised 39-sector map (base, mid, apex, seminal vesicles, urethral sphincter) so biopsy can find it.
Document family history, DRE, PSA, prior biopsies, prostate volume and the index (highest-category) lesion when there is more than one.

measure.how: Focal marked hypointensity on ADC with marked hyperintensity on high b-value DWI.
measure.cutoff: <1.5 cm = PI-RADS 4 · ≥1.5 cm or definite extraprostatic extension = PI-RADS 5

measure.how: Lenticular, non-circumscribed, homogeneous, moderately hypointense lesion.
measure.cutoff: <1.5 cm = PI-RADS 4 · ≥1.5 cm or definite extraprostatic extension = PI-RADS 5

measure.how: DCE positive (early focal enhancement corresponding to the DWI/ADC finding) upgrades a PZ 3 to a 4.
T2W score 2 stays 2 if DWI/ADC ≤ 3, becomes 3 if DWI/ADC ≥ 4. T2W score 3 stays 3 if DWI/ADC < 5, becomes 4 if DWI/ADC = 5.

As score 4 but ≥1.5 cm, or definite extraprostatic extension
classify.note: PZ is scored primarily on DWI/ADC and can be upgraded by DCE. TZ is scored primarily on T2W and can be upgraded by DWI/ADC. Report the index lesion as the highest category when there is more than one.

pitfalls: Scoring the PZ on T2W or the TZ on DWI/ADC. Each zone has its own dominant sequence — do not let the wrong sequence drive the category.
Forgetting the DCE upgrade rule in the PZ. A DWI/ADC score of 3 with a genuinely early, focal enhancement corresponding to the lesion becomes a 4.
Measuring the lesion on the sequence that overestimates it. Use the sequence that best defines the true margin for the 1.5 cm cut, not the one that looks most dramatic.
Missing definite extraprostatic extension because it looks subtle. Any definite capsular breach makes the lesion a 5 regardless of size.
Calling post-biopsy haemorrhage on T2W a lesion. Check the corresponding T1 for haemorrhage before scoring a hyperintense area on DWI as pathology.

learning_points: Identify the lesion's zone of origin before scoring and correlate the same location across T2, ADC, high-b-value DWI and DCE.
Describe BPH, inflammation and haemorrhage when they explain an apparent lesion or reduce confidence.
Keep PI-RADS suspicion separate from extension/staging findings, PSA density and subsequent management.
Use consistent lesion numbers, sector labels and image references so that comparison and biopsy targeting remain reproducible.

sections.heading: SCORING CHECK
sections.body:
PZ: DWI determines the category; DWI 3 becomes PI-RADS 4 only with positive DCE. Positive DCE requires focal early enhancement corresponding to the suspicious finding.
TZ: T2 determines the category, except T2 2 with DWI ≥4 becomes PI-RADS 3, and T2 3 with DWI 5 becomes PI-RADS 4. DCE does not upgrade TZ lesions.
A score-4-pattern lesion is score 5 on the relevant sequence at ≥1.5 cm or with definite extraprostatic extension/invasion.
No DCE means no DCE-based upgrade. If DWI is inadequate, consult the PI-RADS alternative-assessment table and state the limitation.

5. Individualised next-step discussion, if appropriate [ ].

notes: PI-RADS categories express imaging suspicion: 1 very low; 2 low; 3 equivocal; 4 high; 5 very high likelihood of clinically significant cancer. They do not independently prescribe biopsy or treatment.
Choose the index lesion by highest PI-RADS category; resolve ties by extraprostatic extension, then size. Map up to four principal suspicious lesions and identify all sectors involved.
Measure AP and longitudinal gland dimensions on mid-sagittal T2, transverse on axial T2. Avoid mixing millimetres and centimetres in the ellipsoid formula.
PI-RADS diagnostic scoring is not a post-treatment recurrence system. A negative MRI does not exclude clinically significant cancer; interpret with clinical risk.
If both DWI and DCE are unavailable or inadequate, do not imply a complete PI-RADS assessment; the formal guidance limits assessment to staging for extraprostatic extension.
Use actual study images in the image slots and retain matching series/image references in the report.

quiz.prompt: A 1.2 cm anterior mid-gland lesion has its epicentre in the transition zone, with one edge abutting the anterior horn of the peripheral zone. It is lens-shaped, its margin fading into the surrounding gland rather than being sharply drawn, and it is uniformly and moderately dark on T2W. On diffusion it is focally hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500. How should it be assessed?
quiz.answer: Assess it in the transition zone; T2 governs, giving PI-RADS 4
quiz.explain: PI-RADS v2.1 assigns a lesion straddling the zones to the zone it appears most likely to have arisen from, and the epicentre is the practical guide to that; the choice then fixes which sequence dominates, T2W in the transition zone and DWI in the peripheral zone. Lenticular or non-circumscribed, homogeneous, moderately hypointense and under 1.5 cm is a transition zone T2W score of 4, which is exactly what the described lens shape, fading margin and uniform moderate darkness amount to, and a transition zone T2W score of 4 is PI-RADS 4 whatever diffusion shows. Diffusion moves a transition zone lesion at two points and no others: a T2W score of 2 with DWI 4 or 5 becomes PI-RADS 3, and a T2W score of 3 with DWI 5 becomes PI-RADS 4. Neither applies here. 'Let DCE break the tie between T2 and DWI, giving PI-RADS 4' arrives at the right number down a road that does not exist, since DCE plays no part in the transition zone whatever it shows.
choices: Assess it in the peripheral zone; DWI governs, giving PI-RADS 3
Assess it in the transition zone; T2 governs, giving PI-RADS 4
Take the lower of the two sequence scores, giving PI-RADS 3
Let DCE break the tie between T2 and DWI, giving PI-RADS 4

quiz.prompt: A 9 mm posterolateral peripheral zone focus is discretely but not markedly hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500, giving a DWI score of 3. On DCE there is focal enhancement at that site, appearing before the surrounding normal peripheral zone. What follows for the report?
quiz.answer: The category becomes 4, so biopsy usually follows
quiz.explain: DCE has exactly one job in PI-RADS v2.1: a peripheral zone lesion scored 3 on DWI becomes PI-RADS 4 if DCE is positive, meaning focal enhancement that is earlier than or contemporaneous with adjacent normal prostate and corresponds to the T2W or DWI finding. It is a binary read, so 'The category stays 3 unless washout appears later on' fails twice over: v2.1 abandoned curve typing, and the upgrade has already been earned. What DCE cannot buy is a higher ceiling, so 'The category becomes 5, as two sequences are positive' is wrong too; a DWI 4 lesion stays 4 however it enhances, since only a size of 1.5 cm or more, or definite extraprostatic extension, makes 5. The move from 3 to 4 is the one that matters clinically, because 3 is equivocal and may be watched, while v2.1 says biopsy should be considered for 4 or 5.
choices: The category stays 3, since DCE does not alter DWI
The category becomes 5, as two sequences are positive
The category becomes 4, so biopsy usually follows
The category stays 3 unless washout appears later on

quiz.prompt: A 65-year-old man has a transition zone nodule that is homogeneous and circumscribed but not encapsulated. On diffusion the nodule is discretely, though only mildly, hypointense on ADC and mildly hyperintense at b=1500. A colleague wants to call it PI-RADS 3 on the diffusion finding. Why should you resist?
quiz.answer: Mild restriction is expected in stromal hyperplasia nodules
quiz.explain: Score it first. A homogeneous circumscribed nodule without encapsulation is the atypical nodule, a T2W score of 2; a discrete focus that restricts only mildly on both ADC and high b-value is a DWI score of 3. PI-RADS v2.1 blocks precisely that upgrade: mildly or moderately restricted diffusion is common in mostly encapsulated and unencapsulated transition zone lesions, much of it stromal hyperplasia, so a T2W score of 1 or 2 is not raised on a DWI score of 3. The nodule stays PI-RADS 2. 'Diffusion has no bearing whatever on transition zone scores' overshoots: diffusion does count there, but only above that threshold, and v2.1 added exactly that step, a T2W score of 2 with DWI 4 or 5 becoming PI-RADS 3, and a T2W score of 3 with DWI 5 becoming PI-RADS 4.
choices: The nodule must exceed 1.5 cm before diffusion is counted
Mild restriction is expected in stromal hyperplasia nodules
Diffusion has no bearing whatever on transition zone scores
Restriction counts here if the nodule also enhances early on

quiz.prompt: Three weeks after systematic TRUS biopsy, T1W images show diffuse hyperintensity through much of both peripheral zones. Within it, a 14 mm right posterolateral area is conspicuously T1 hypointense, and that same area is T2 hypointense with markedly reduced ADC and marked b=1500 signal. What does the T1-dark area most likely represent?
quiz.answer: Tumour, spared by the blood and standing out as a T1 defect
quiz.explain: This is the haemorrhage exclusion sign. The explanation usually offered is that tumour has markedly reduced citrate, and that citrate is anticoagulant, so blood collects in the benign peripheral zone and spares the cancer; that mechanism is a published hypothesis rather than a measured fact, but the pattern it predicts is reliable. Read the T1W series as a map of where cancer is not, and a dark hole in a bright field is the suspicious finding; reading T1 brightness itself as tumour inverts the sign. 'Older blood whose signal has decayed back towards low T1' is the tempting answer, since v2.1 grants that chronic blood products may appear hypointense on all sequences, but the surrounding blood is the same three weeks old and still bright, so blood of that age has no reason to be dark in one 14 mm patch, and marked b=1500 signal with a low ADC indicates restricted diffusion rather than the signal loss susceptibility from old blood would produce. PI-RADS v2.1 does suggest considering a gap of six weeks or more when the study is for staging, but here the haemorrhage has made the lesion more conspicuous, not less.
choices: Older blood whose signal has decayed back towards low T1
Prostatitis, which tends to bleed less than the normal gland
Tumour, spared by the blood and standing out as a T1 defect
Artefact from a needle track running across the posterior zone

quiz.prompt: At the prostatic base, bands of low T2W and low ADC signal encircle both ejaculatory ducts and converge towards the verumontanum. Bulky transition zone hyperplasia has displaced the left band so that it is visibly larger than the right, but signal is equal on the two sides on T2W, ADC and b=1500, and neither side enhances early. How should this be handled in the report?
quiz.answer: Report it as the normal central zone, with no lesion score
quiz.explain: Separate the two asymmetries. What PI-RADS v2.1 treats as suspicious in the central zone is asymmetry of signal between the two sides on T2W, ADC or high b-value images, or focal early enhancement; here the signal is equal on all three and neither side enhances. What is present is asymmetry of size, and v2.1 names that a normal variant, particularly when transition zone hyperplasia deforms or displaces the central zone at the base, which is the described mechanism exactly. Everything else fits the normal central zone as v2.1 describes it: low T2W and ADC signal wrapping the ejaculatory ducts from base to verumontanum, mildly hyperintense at high b-value. 'Score it PI-RADS 4 on the strength of the low ADC signal' is the trap, because it scores a normal structure on one sequence read in isolation and turns it into a biopsy target.
choices: Score it PI-RADS 4 on the strength of the low ADC signal
Call it bilateral tumour arising at the base, PI-RADS 5
Score it PI-RADS 3, because the appearance is equivocal
Report it as the normal central zone, with no lesion score

quiz.prompt: A prostate DWI acquires b = 100 and b = 1000 s/mm^2. In a peripheral zone lesion the mean signal falls from 800 to 400 arbitrary units between those two b-values. Fitting a mono-exponential decay through the two points only, what ADC does this give, in units of 10^-3 mm^2/s? Give it to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Mono-exponential decay is S(b) = S0 exp(-b x ADC), so ADC = ln(S1/S2) / (b2 - b1) = ln 2 / 900 = 7.70 x 10^-4 mm^2/s, that is 0.77 x 10^-3. Now resist the obvious next step. PI-RADS v2.1 offers 750-900 micrometre^2/s as the range within which a threshold may be set, and says that values below the chosen threshold correlate with clinically significant cancer. 770 sits inside that range, which makes it indeterminate rather than positive: suspicious if your unit has settled on 900, unremarkable if it has settled on 750. That is not a fault in the arithmetic but the reason the number is not a verdict, since ADC depends on which b-values were used and varies between vendors, and it is why v2.1 keeps visual assessment of the ADC map as the primary method rather than a numerical cut-off.

quiz.prompt: Your protocol acquires b = 50 and b = 800 s/mm^2, and the scanner then synthesises a b = 1500 image by extrapolation. A trainee asks why the b = 1500 data is not simply acquired directly and folded into the mono-exponential ADC fit as a third point. Give the two separate reasons, and state the b-values PI-RADS v2.1 requires for the high b-value image set and permits for the ADC calculation.
quiz.answer: Two reasons of different kinds. The first is practical: a directly acquired b = 1500 series needs strong diffusion gradients and so a longer echo time, and the signal-to-noise ratio falls as b rises, so it costs scan time and image quality and is more prone to artefact, which is why an image calculated from the acquired low and intermediate data is often the cleaner one. The second is about the model: prostate signal decay stops behaving in a mono-exponential way above roughly b = 1000 because of diffusion kurtosis, so folding a b = 1500 point into the fit would bias the calculated ADC and break comparability between studies. PI-RADS v2.1 requires a high b-value image set of at least 1400 s/mm^2, obtained either from a separate acquisition or calculated from the low and intermediate b-value images, and recommends that the maximum b-value used to calculate ADC be no greater than 1000 s/mm^2.
quiz.explain: The two reasons are of different kinds, and conflating them is the usual error. One is practical: strong diffusion gradients force a long echo time and the signal-to-noise ratio falls as b rises, so a directly acquired b = 1500 series costs time and quality. PI-RADS v2.1 accepts either route for the high b-value set, acquired separately or calculated, and notes only that calculating it avoids the longer echo times the strong gradient pulses would need. The other reason is about the model: the mono-exponential fit that defines ADC holds to roughly b = 1000 and then departs from the data, because kurtosis flattens the decay curve. A point at b = 1500 sits above the fitted line, drags the fitted slope shallower, and so lowers the reported ADC for reasons that have nothing to do with cellularity, which is why v2.1 recommends 1000 s/mm^2 as the maximum b-value used in the calculation while requiring at least 1400 s/mm^2 for the high b-value images. Those images earn their keep by suppressing signal from benign tissue with high diffusivity, lifting conspicuity at the apex, the base, subcapsular sites and beside the anterior fibromuscular stroma.

quiz.prompt: A 1.1 cm posterolateral peripheral zone lesion is markedly hypointense on ADC and markedly hyperintense at b=1500. It contacts the capsule over 16 mm, the rectoprostatic angle is obliterated, and a small tongue of tumour signal is measurable outside the gland beside the neurovascular bundle. Which category follows, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: PI-RADS 5, since definite extraprostatic extension overrides size
quiz.explain: A DWI score of 4 and a DWI score of 5 are separated by two things, not one: a size of 1.5 cm or more, or definite extraprostatic extension or invasive behaviour. Tumour measurably outside the gland is the second of those, so an 11 mm lesion is PI-RADS 5 and its size never comes into it. The grounds matter as much as the number. PI-RADS v2.1 lists several features used to assess extraprostatic extension, among them a bulging contour, an irregular or spiculated margin, obliteration of the rectoprostatic angle, neurovascular bundle asymmetry or invasion, a tumour-capsule interface over 1 cm, and breach of the capsule with direct tumour extension; it ranks none of them, and only the last is demonstrable extraglandular tumour. 'PI-RADS 5, since the lost rectoprostatic angle settles the point' therefore reaches the right category on the wrong ground: a lost angle, like a long contact length, raises suspicion but occurs in organ-confined disease too, and on its own supports an indeterminate margin rather than a definite one.
choices: PI-RADS 4, since the lesion measures well under 1.5 cm across
PI-RADS 5, since definite extraprostatic extension overrides size
PI-RADS 4, with the extraprostatic disease called indeterminate
PI-RADS 5, since the lost rectoprostatic angle settles the point

quiz.prompt: A 78-year-old man's seminal vesicles are diffusely low in T2W signal on both sides. There is no restricted diffusion and no abnormal enhancement in the walls, the angles with the prostatic base are preserved, and the sole prostatic finding is a small apical PI-RADS 3 focus. How do you report the vesicles, what benign process most likely accounts for the appearance, and what would have changed your mind?
quiz.answer: Report them as uninvolved. Bilateral symmetric T2W hypointensity with no restricted diffusion, no abnormal enhancement, preserved angles at the base and no contiguous tumour is the picture of senile seminal vesicle amyloidosis, or of age-related atrophy, rather than invasion. Invasion would show some combination of focal or diffuse low T2W signal with restricted diffusion or abnormal enhancement within or along the vesicle, obliteration of the angle between the prostatic base and the vesicle, and tumour continuous with the gland extending along the ejaculatory duct; no single one of those is strictly required, but low T2W signal is the weakest of them and is the only one present here. Geography argues the same way, since an apical lesion is at the wrong end of the gland to reach the vesicles.
quiz.explain: Low T2W signal is the least specific of the seminal vesicle invasion features, and in an elderly man amyloid deposition in the vesicle walls is the commoner cause. The features that carry weight are the ones invasion cannot easily avoid: a diffusion or enhancement abnormality in the vesicle itself, loss of the angle at the base, and physical continuity with tumour extending from the prostate. PI-RADS v2.1 gives these as features of invasion rather than as a checklist every case must complete, so the call is a weighing and not a tally, and real invasion can be diagnosed on two of them. Here bilateral symmetry argues against tumour, three of the four are absent, and a small apical focus is at the wrong end of the gland to reach the vesicles at all.

quiz.prompt: A staging study at 3T uses an endorectal coil whose balloon has been inflated with air. The T2W images are high in resolution and diagnostic, but DWI shows marked geometric distortion and signal dropout across the posterior gland. What is the most appropriate correction?
quiz.answer: Re-inflate the balloon with a liquid such as barium suspension
quiz.explain: Air in the balloon sits in a steep susceptibility gradient right against the posterior peripheral zone, and echo-planar DWI is the sequence least able to tolerate field inhomogeneity, which is why the T2W images survive and the diffusion images do not. The distortion grows with field strength, so 3T is where it bites hardest. PI-RADS v2.1 answers this directly: expel the air and distend the balloon with a liquid such as perfluorocarbon or barium suspension, or use a rigid coil that needs no balloon. 'Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble' would indeed shrink the distortion, and dropping field strength is the right move when the source of inhomogeneity cannot be removed, as with a metal prosthesis; here it can be removed, so 1.5T surrenders the signal-to-noise and resolution a staging study was booked for in order to solve a problem a syringe of barium solves. Raising the b-value lowers signal-to-noise without touching the inhomogeneity, and dropping the coil throws away the resolution the staging question depends on.
choices: Repeat the diffusion sequence after raising the b-value further
Re-inflate the balloon with a liquid such as barium suspension
Remove the coil and accept the lower-resolution T2W images
Rescan at 1.5T, where the same balloon causes less trouble

quiz.prompt: A 1.8 cm transition zone nodule is heterogeneous with obscured margins on T2W imaging, which scores 3. On diffusion it is markedly hypointense on the ADC map and markedly hyperintense at b=1500, which scores 5. Which PI-RADS v2.1 assessment category does the lesion take? Answer with the number alone.
quiz.explain: In the transition zone T2W is the dominant sequence, and diffusion acts only as an upgrade in one specific place: a T2W score of 3 becomes an assessment of 4 when the DWI score is 5, and only then. A T2W score of 3 with any DWI score of 4 or below stays at 3. The neighbouring rule runs the other way for a T2W score of 2, which is upgraded to 3 when DWI is 4 or 5. Note what does not happen here. Dynamic contrast enhancement has no role at all in the transition zone; its single defined job in v2.1 is to lift a peripheral zone DWI score of 3 to an assessment of 4. The 1.8 cm size and marked diffusion restriction establish DWI 5 here. Below 1.5 cm without definite extension, this diffusion pattern would score 4 and would not upgrade a T2W 3 lesion.

quiz.prompt: The prostate measures 4.8 cm by 3.6 cm by 4.2 cm on T2W imaging, and the volume is derived with the ellipsoid formula, multiplying the three dimensions by 0.52. The serum PSA is 8.4 ng/mL. What PSA density does that give? Answer in nanograms per millilitre per millilitre, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The gland volume is 4.8 x 3.6 x 4.2 x 0.52 = 37.7 mL, and 8.4 / 37.7 = 0.22 ng/mL/mL. The point of the calculation is that PSA alone cannot distinguish a large benign gland making a lot of protein from a small gland harbouring cancer, and dividing by volume does much of that work. A density of 0.15 or above is the threshold in common use to support proceeding to biopsy, and it earns its keep in exactly the situation this domain keeps returning to: a PI-RADS 3 lesion, where the imaging is equivocal and something else has to break the tie. Measure the three dimensions carefully and say which they were, since the ellipsoid figure is an approximation and a sloppy anteroposterior measurement moves the density more than anything else in the sum.

quiz.prompt: Put these local staging findings on prostate MRI into the order of increasing tumour stage.
quiz.answer: organ-confined extraprostatic-extension seminal-vesicle-invasion rectal-wall-invasion
quiz.explain: Disease confined within the capsule is T2 however large it is; extraprostatic extension is T3a; invasion of a seminal vesicle is T3b; and tumour fixed to or invading an adjacent structure such as the rectum, the external sphincter, the levator or the pelvic wall is T4. The ladder is worth holding because each rung changes a different decision. Extraprostatic extension at a particular site is what a surgeon needs in order to decide whether the neurovascular bundle on that side can be spared, so the report should say where along the gland the extension lies and how confident you are. Seminal vesicle involvement carries a distinctly worse prognosis and usually moves the conversation towards radiotherapy with androgen deprivation. T4 is uncommon at presentation and is often visible before anyone thinks about scoring.

quiz.prompt: You are reporting a study containing three lesions that score 3, 4 and 5, together with two further areas scoring 2. Say which sequence you measure each lesion on and how, how many lesions the report should carry, and which lesion is designated the index lesion.
quiz.answer: Measure each lesion on the sequence on which it was scored: the ADC map or high b-value images for a peripheral zone lesion, the T2W images for a transition zone lesion, taking the longest diameter on the axial image and using another plane only where the lesion is genuinely better seen there. PI-RADS v2.1 asks for up to four lesions of category 3 or above, so the three suspicious lesions are described individually and the two areas scoring 2 need no separate entry. The index lesion is the one with the highest category, here the lesion scoring 5; where two lesions share the highest category, the index is the one showing extraprostatic extension.
quiz.explain: These conventions exist so that two reports of the same gland can be compared, and so that a urologist reading yours can find the target again on the biopsy platform. Measuring on the sequence that generated the score keeps the size and the category describing the same thing, and the axial default keeps serial studies comparable. The cap of four lesions is a deliberate limit on clutter, since a report listing nine areas of low suspicion is harder to act on than one naming three. The index lesion is the one that will drive treatment, which is why the tie is broken by extraprostatic extension rather than by size: the lesion breaching the capsule is the one that changes the operation.

quiz.prompt: A 61-year-old man's peripheral zone shows several thin bands of low T2W signal radiating towards the capsule with indistinct margins. The ADC map is mildly and diffusely low across the same regions, there is no focal mass, and the high b-value images show nothing focal. How is this scored and reported, and what is the likely explanation?
quiz.answer: Linear or wedge-shaped hypointensity with indistinct margins in the peripheral zone is a T2W score of 2, and with nothing focal on the high b-value images and no focal defect on the ADC map the non-focal linear diffusion abnormality is DWI 2, so the assessment is PI-RADS 2 and no target is offered for biopsy. The likely explanation is chronic prostatitis with post-inflammatory fibrosis and atrophy, which is common at this age. Cancer is the exception here rather than the rule, because it usually forms a focal rounded or ill-defined mass with markedly restricted diffusion, not a thin band running along the course of the ducts.
quiz.explain: The peripheral zone is normally bright on T2W, so any darkening draws the eye, and the commonest cause of a dark peripheral zone in a man of this age is not cancer at all. Shape and margin do most of the discrimination: benign post-inflammatory change is linear, wedge-shaped or diffuse and fades into the surrounding gland, while tumour is focal and mass-like. Diffusion then decides, since a genuine lesion is focally and markedly restricted rather than mildly and diffusely so. The important discipline is not to be pushed by a rising PSA into scoring bands as a lesion; prostatitis raises PSA too. If the clinical suspicion stays high, PSA density and follow-up carry the argument, not an inflated category.

curriculum_modules.title: Rectal Cancer: MR Staging, Restaging and Perianal Fistula

module_contract.goal: Stage and restage a rectal cancer on high-resolution MR, report the circumferential resection margin and extramural venous invasion in terms that change treatment, and map a perianal fistula for the surgeon.

approach.detail: Lower border relative to the anorectal junction: low rectum is ≤ 5 cm from it, high rectum is > 5 cm up to the sigmoid take-off. The split decides whether the sphincter complex is part of your report.

approach.step: Read the muscularis propria on all three planes
approach.detail: An intact dark muscularis on every plane keeps the tumour T1–T2. Do not call T3 off one plane.
From the outer edge of the muscularis propria to the deepest tumour front, on the plane perpendicular to the bowel wall. That millimetre value gives the T3 sub-band.
Shortest distance from tumour, tumour deposit or EMVI to the MRF. ≤ 1 mm or direct invasion is MRF involved.
Follow the extramural vessels out of the tumour. Tumour signal inside a vessel with expanded or disrupted contour is EMVI positive.
Mesorectal nodes, then lateral compartments — internal iliac and obturator separately. Report tumour deposits apart from nodes.

approach.step: In the low rectum, the sphincter complex
approach.detail: Internal sphincter, intersphincteric plane, external sphincter, puborectalis and levator ani. Say which layers the tumour reaches.

measure.how: Perpendicular to the bowel wall, from the outer muscularis propria to the deepest tumour edge.
measure.cutoff: T3a < 1 mm · T3b 1–5 mm · T3c 5–15 mm · T3d > 15 mm

measure.how: Shortest distance on the high-resolution axial-oblique T2, including deposits and EMVI, not only the primary.
Lower tumour border to the anorectal junction, on sagittal T2.
measure.cutoff: Low ≤ 5 cm · High > 5 cm to sigmoid take-off

measure.how: Short axis, with signal and border morphology.
measure.cutoff: ≥ 9 mm short axis suspicious regardless of morphology · 5–8 mm if ≥ 2 of round, irregular border, heterogeneous signal · < 5 mm only if all 3 · any mucinous node at any size

measure.how: Short axis in each compartment, reported separately from mesorectal nodes.
measure.cutoff: Internal iliac ≥ 7 mm short axis · obturator ≥ 9 mm — the compartments carry different thresholds

classify.name: mrT category and what it drives
rows: Muscularis propria intact on all three planes
Surgery alone, unless organ preservation is the goal
Low risk if MRF− and EMVI−: surgery alone
Low risk if MRF− and EMVI−: surgery alone
Counts as high risk in several guidelines — neoadjuvant treatment
High risk — long-course chemoradiotherapy or total neoadjuvant treatment
Invasion of the peritoneum or peritoneal reflection
Invasion of adjacent organs or structures outside the mesorectum
Includes external sphincter, puborectalis and levator ani (skeletal muscle)
High risk — neoadjuvant treatment, extended resection planning
classify.note: Internal sphincter involvement alone does not upstage the T category. MRF and the peritoneum are not 'adjacent organs' for T4b.

modifiers.meaning: No nodular extension beyond the muscularis propria and no adjacent vessels. Negative.
Minimal nodular extension or stranding, not near a vessel. Negative.
Stranding near extramural vessels, vessel calibre normal. Negative.
Tumour signal within the vessel, contour normal or slightly expanded. Positive.
Tumour signal within the vessel with clear disruption of the vessel contour and/or nodular expansion. Positive.
Tumour, deposit or EMVI within 1 mm of the mesorectal fascia, or invading it.
MRI nodal accuracy is limited, so the category is collapsed to absent or present. State lateral nodes separately.

modifiers.code: Prefixes c / i / mr / y / p
modifiers.meaning: Clinical, imaging-unspecified, MR-derived, post-neoadjuvant, pathological. Use mr for your own staging and ymr after treatment.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
High-resolution T2 without fat saturation: sagittal, axial-oblique perpendicular to the tumour axis, coronal. [DWI. No / IV contrast.] [No / Buscopan.]

FINDINGS
Morphology: [polypoid / annular / semi-annular / mucinous].
Location: lower border [n] cm from the anorectal junction — [low / high] rectum; [anterior / posterior / left / right] quadrants, [n] o'clock to [n] o'clock.
Length: [n] cm.
mrT: [T1–2 / T3a / T3b / T3c / T3d / T4a / T4b]; maximal extramural depth [n] mm.
MRF: shortest distance [n] mm at [clock position / level], caused by [primary tumour / node / deposit / EMVI] — [involved / clear].
Sphincter complex (low tumours): internal sphincter [ ], intersphincteric plane [ ], external sphincter / puborectalis / levator [ ].
EMVI: grade [0–4] — [positive / negative]; vessel [ ].
Mesorectal nodes: [n] node(s), largest [n] mm short axis, [morphology].
Lateral nodes: internal iliac [ ], obturator [ ] — largest [n] mm.
Tumour deposits: [absent / present, n].
M: [no / describe] distant disease on the available imaging.

IMPRESSION
mrT[ ] N[0/+] MRF[+/−] EMVI[+/−], [low / high] rectal [adenocarcinoma / mucinous adenocarcinoma].
[Low-risk — surgery alone / high-risk — neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy or total neoadjuvant treatment.]
pitfalls: Measuring extramural depth on a plane that is not perpendicular to the bowel wall. An oblique cut lengthens the tumour front and pushes T3b into T3c.
Calling the MRF clear on the primary alone. A tumour deposit or an EMVI-positive vessel within 1 mm of the fascia makes it MRF positive.
Over-calling T3 from desmoplastic stranding. Spiculation without nodular tumour signal is not measurable extramural spread.
Upstaging for internal sphincter involvement. It does not change the T category; only external sphincter, puborectalis or levator does, as T4b.
Forgetting the lateral compartments. Internal iliac and obturator nodes lie outside the total mesorectal excision plane and are reported separately, at ≥ 7 mm.
Missing mucin. Mucinous tumours are high T2 signal, carry a poorer prognosis, and biopsy misses them — say so explicitly.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal tumour arrives for staging. The axial T2 stack was planned straight through the pelvis, in the same plane as the rest of the abdominal series, but the tumour-bearing segment runs obliquely. The outer border of the muscularis propria looks blurred and indistinct all the way round the tumour. What should happen before you commit to a T stage?
quiz.answer: Re-plan the high-resolution T2 stack perpendicular to the long axis of the tumour-bearing segment and repeat it
choices: Re-plan the high-resolution T2 stack perpendicular to the long axis of the tumour-bearing segment and repeat it
Give intravenous gadolinium and stage the tumour from fat-suppressed post-contrast images through the same block
Add fat suppression to the existing axial T2 stack so the mesorectal fat is darkened around the outer muscle border
Accept the images as acquired and take the measurements from the sagittal T2 sequence, which crosses the wall twice
quiz.explain: Obliquity is the commonest avoidable cause of overstaging. When the slice cuts the wall at an angle, the muscularis propria is partial-volumed with the mesorectal fat and its outer border smudges, so a T2 tumour reads as T3 and a shallow T3 reads as deep. The fix is geometric, not chemical: plan a small field-of-view T2 turbo spin echo, about 3 mm thick, perpendicular to the long axis of the bowel at the tumour, using the sagittal image to set the angle. Fat suppression is deliberately avoided here, because the contrast between intermediate-signal tumour, dark muscle and bright mesorectal fat is exactly what you are reading. Gadolinium adds nothing to T staging in the MERCURY-style protocol. For a low tumour, add an oblique coronal plane parallel to the anal canal to see the sphincters.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal cancer extends 4 mm beyond the muscularis propria. The deepest tumour edge lies 0.9 mm from the mesorectal fascia. There is no venous invasion and no node meets malignant criteria. How should the margin be reported, and what does it drive?
quiz.answer: Predicted CRM involved at 0.9 mm, which moves the patient towards neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before surgery
choices: Predicted CRM involved at 0.9 mm, which moves the patient towards neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before surgery
Predicted CRM clear at 0.9 mm, since involvement is called when tumour actually reaches and touches the fascia
Predicted CRM clear, because it is the T category that selects neoadjuvant therapy and this tumour is still T3
Predicted CRM indeterminate, so the decision should be deferred until the resected specimen has been reported
quiz.explain: The mesorectal fascia is the plane the surgeon dissects in a total mesorectal excision, so the shortest distance from any tumour-bearing structure to that fascia predicts whether the specimen will have a positive margin. One millimetre or less is reported as involved; many multidisciplinary teams treat 1 to 2 mm as threatened and manage it the same way. The MERCURY study established that this MR measurement matches the pathological margin closely enough to select treatment before an operation is done, which is why margin, not T category alone, drives neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Waiting for histology defeats the purpose: once the specimen is out, the chance to downstage the margin has gone. Note that the measurement is taken to the nearest tumour-bearing structure of any kind, which is the point of the next item.

quiz.prompt: On T2 images, tumour signal of the same intermediate intensity as the primary tracks along a vessel running out of the tumour into the mesorectal fat. The vessel has lost its flow void, its contour is nodular and its calibre exceeds that of the matching vein on the other side. The primary is otherwise mrT3b with a margin of 6 mm. What does this add to the report?
quiz.answer: Extramural venous invasion, which independently predicts distant relapse and strengthens the case for systemic therapy
choices: Extramural venous invasion, which independently predicts distant relapse and strengthens the case for systemic therapy
Peritumoural desmoplastic reaction, a common finding at the invasive edge that does not change the risk category
Direct invasion of a mesorectal structure, which upgrades the tumour from mrT3b to mrT4b and alters the operation
A mesorectal tumour deposit, which should be counted and reported within the nodal category rather than separately
quiz.explain: The MR signature of extramural venous invasion is tumour-signal material inside a vein that the tumour has reached, with expansion of the calibre, loss of the flow void and an irregular or nodular contour. It is an independent adverse prognostic factor, associated with synchronous and metachronous distant metastases and with worse disease-free survival, and it is often what tips a borderline case towards neoadjuvant and adjuvant systemic treatment. It does not change the T category, which is a measure of depth. It is also not a tumour deposit, which is a discrete nodule of tumour in the mesorectum without a nodal or vascular structure. One practical trap: a tumour-filled vein counts as tumour for margin purposes, so if it approaches within a millimetre of the mesorectal fascia the predicted margin is involved even when the primary itself is nowhere near it.

quiz.prompt: A mid-rectal cancer has three mesorectal nodes: one measures 4 mm in short axis and is round with a smooth border and uniform signal; one measures 6 mm with an irregular border and mottled internal signal; one measures 10 mm and is smooth-bordered and homogeneous. Applying the 2016 ESGAR consensus criteria, how should these be reported?
quiz.answer: The 6 mm and the 10 mm nodes are malignant; the 4 mm node would need all three morphological features
choices: The 6 mm and the 10 mm nodes are malignant; the 4 mm node would need all three morphological features
Only the 10 mm node is malignant, because below 9 mm a mesorectal node is reported as reactive
Only the 6 mm node is malignant, because a smooth homogeneous node is benign whatever its size
All three are malignant, because a round mesorectal node is sufficient evidence of tumour spread
quiz.explain: The 2016 ESGAR consensus grades a mesorectal node on short axis plus three morphological features: round shape, irregular border and heterogeneous internal signal. At 9 mm or more the node is called malignant regardless of morphology. Between 5 and 8 mm it needs at least two of the three features. Below 5 mm it needs all three. So the 6 mm node with an irregular border and mottled signal qualifies on two features, the 10 mm node qualifies on size alone, and the small round but otherwise bland node does not. Be honest about the accuracy of nodal MR: it is the weakest part of rectal staging, which is one reason the field shifted towards the circumferential margin and extramural venous invasion as the decision drivers. Report node counts and location, but do not let a borderline node override a clear margin.

quiz.prompt: An upper rectal cancer on the anterior wall extends beyond the muscularis propria, and on sagittal and oblique axial T2 images tumour signal reaches and thickens the anterior peritoneal reflection at its insertion onto the bowel. The bladder and seminal vesicles remain separated by preserved fat. What stage do you report, and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: mrT4a: the visceral peritoneum is breached, which carries an added risk of peritoneal relapse
choices: mrT4a: the visceral peritoneum is breached, which carries an added risk of peritoneal relapse
mrT3d: the extramural spread is deep, but the peritoneum is not a structure counted in T staging
mrT4b: contact with the peritoneal reflection counts as invasion of an adjacent pelvic organ
mrT2: the peritoneal reflection lies outside the bowel wall, so the muscularis propria is intact
quiz.explain: Anterior upper rectal tumours are the ones where the peritoneal reflection matters, because above the reflection the rectum has a serosal surface and below it the mesorectum is the only barrier. Tumour that reaches, thickens or nodularly elevates the reflection is mrT4a, invasion of the visceral peritoneum, and it changes the conversation: peritoneal breach adds a route of spread that the mesorectal envelope does not contain, and these patients are watched for peritoneal disease. T4b is reserved for invasion of an adjacent organ or structure, such as prostate, vagina, bladder or pelvic sidewall, and here the fat planes are preserved. The measurement of extramural depth still belongs in the report, but depth cannot substitute for the peritoneal finding. Note also that above the reflection there is no mesorectal fascia anteriorly, so the margin concept is applied differently at that level.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after long-course chemoradiotherapy, a patient is being considered for organ preservation. The tumour bed is mostly low-signal fibrosis, but a 9 mm focus of intermediate T2 signal sits within the scar, bright on high b-value diffusion images with a correspondingly dark ADC. Endoscopy shows a small persistent ulcer. What follows?
quiz.answer: This is residual tumour: the case fails clinical complete response and resection should be planned
choices: This is residual tumour: the case fails clinical complete response and resection should be planned
This is post-radiation inflammation: it is compatible with complete response and can be rescanned at 3 months
This is T2 shine-through on the diffusion images, so the surrounding fibrosis should settle the decision
This ambiguity cannot be resolved, so the pre-treatment stage should determine the operation offered
quiz.explain: A clinical complete response has three legs and needs all of them: a flat white scar with telangiectasia and no ulcer or nodule at endoscopy, no palpable abnormality on digital examination, and MRI showing only low-signal fibrosis without restricted diffusion. A discrete intermediate-signal focus that restricts diffusion, with a low ADC rather than shine-through, alongside a persistent ulcer, is residual disease until proved otherwise. Watch and wait is a legitimate pathway, but only for the complete responders and only inside a programme with intensive surveillance, typically three-monthly for the first two years, since most regrowth appears in that window and is usually still salvageable by surgery. Offering it to a partial responder converts a curable cancer into a missed one. When the scan and the endoscopy disagree, the more suspicious finding wins.

quiz.prompt: On the oblique axial T2 images of a mid-rectal cancer, the deepest edge of the primary tumour lies 4.2 mm from the mesorectal fascia. A tumour-filled vein tracks laterally and comes within 0.8 mm of the fascia, and a node meeting malignant criteria sits 6.0 mm from it. State the distance you should report as the predicted circumferential resection margin, in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The predicted circumferential resection margin is the shortest distance from the mesorectal fascia to any tumour-bearing structure, and that means the primary, a tumour-filled vein, a malignant node or a tumour deposit, whichever is closest. Here the vein is nearest at 0.8 mm, so the margin is reported as 0.8 mm and, being 1 mm or less, as involved. Radiologists most often go wrong by measuring only from the primary and reporting a comfortable margin while an extramural venous invasion track quietly abuts the fascia. Say in the report which structure the measurement came from and where on the clock face it lies, because that tells the surgeon whether the plane is threatened where it can be worked around or where it cannot. A margin of 1 to 2 mm is widely treated as threatened and managed as if involved.

quiz.prompt: Beyond the outer border of the muscularis propria, tumour signal extends 3 mm anteriorly, 8 mm laterally and 11 mm posteriorly on the oblique axial images. State the extramural depth of invasion you should report, in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Extramural depth is a single number: the greatest perpendicular distance from the outer border of the muscularis propria to the deepest edge of tumour, so you take the deepest point rather than an average. Eleven millimetres puts this tumour in the mrT3c band, using the widely applied subdivision of T3a under 1 mm, T3b 1 to 5 mm, T3c 5 to 15 mm and T3d over 15 mm. The subdivision earns its place because depth beyond about 5 mm carries prognostic weight comparable to nodal status and feeds the risk stratification that selects neoadjuvant treatment. The measurement trap is desmoplasia: fine low-signal spicules radiating into the fat are fibrous reaction and should not be measured, while a broad nodular intermediate-signal front is tumour and should. When you cannot separate the two, say so and let the margin do the work.

quiz.prompt: MRI of a perianal fistula shows a track leaving the anal canal at the 6 o'clock position, crossing both the internal and external sphincters into the right ischioanal fossa. In that fossa there is a 2 cm collection with an enhancing rim, and a secondary track runs anteriorly from it. Give the St James University Hospital MRI grade as a whole number from 1 to 5.
quiz.explain: The St James grading maps MR findings onto surgical difficulty in five steps. Grade 1 is a simple linear intersphincteric track; grade 2 is intersphincteric with an abscess or a secondary track; grade 3 is an uncomplicated transsphincteric track; grade 4 is transsphincteric with an abscess or secondary track in the ischioanal or ischiorectal fossa; grade 5 is supralevator or translevator disease. Crossing the external sphincter makes this transsphincteric, and the fossa collection with its secondary extension takes it to grade 4. The grade is useful because grades 1 and 3 can usually be laid open or treated with a simple sphincter-sparing repair, while an undrained collection or an unrecognised secondary track is the standard reason a fistula recurs after apparently successful surgery. Always state the level of the internal opening on the clock face too.

quiz.prompt: Eight weeks after chemoradiotherapy the tumour bed is mostly low-signal fibrosis but contains a 12 mm area of very high T2 signal with the glassy quality of mucin. The patient is being considered for organ preservation. State what you should report about that area and what has to happen next.
quiz.answer: Report it as a mucinous area within the treated tumour bed and say that MRI cannot separate acellular mucin, which is a good response, from mucin containing viable tumour cells, so it must not be called a complete response on imaging alone; endoscopy with biopsy and digital examination has to decide.
quiz.explain: Pools of acellular mucin are a recognised and generally favourable consequence of chemoradiotherapy, and they are very bright on T2. The difficulty is that mucin containing scattered viable cells looks the same, and diffusion imaging does not rescue you because mucin itself can be bright on high b-value images. The tumour regression grade scale was built for fibrosis versus residual tumour signal and applies poorly to a mucinous bed, so grading it mrTRG1 because there is no intermediate signal would be a false reassurance. Report the mucin, state the uncertainty explicitly, and hand the decision to clinical assessment. Remember also that mucinous rectal cancers respond less well overall, so a mucinous appearance before treatment should already have lowered your expectation of a complete response.

quiz.prompt: A tumour whose lower edge is 2 cm from the anal verge extends through the internal sphincter, while the intersphincteric fat plane and the external sphincter remain intact on the oblique coronal images. State what you should report about the sphincter complex and how it shapes the operation offered.
quiz.answer: Report that the tumour breaches the internal sphincter but stops at the intersphincteric plane, with the external sphincter and levators uninvolved, so a sphincter-preserving intersphincteric resection is feasible rather than an extralevator abdominoperineal excision.
quiz.explain: In the low rectum the mesorectum tapers to nothing, so the mesorectal fascia stops being the relevant margin and the sphincter complex takes over. What the surgeon needs is a statement of how far outwards the tumour has gone: confined to the wall, through the internal sphincter but not across the intersphincteric plane, into the external sphincter or puborectalis, or beyond into the ischioanal fat or levator. The first two allow an intersphincteric resection with a coloanal anastomosis; the last two mean an extralevator abdominoperineal excision with a permanent stoma. This is only assessable on an oblique coronal plane aligned parallel to the anal canal, which is why that sequence is added for every low tumour. Give the distance from the anal verge and the internal opening of the plane you think is threatened.

quiz.prompt: A fistula track leaves the intersphincteric space, arches upward over the top of the puborectalis sling, then turns down through the levator plate into the ischioanal fossa to reach the skin. State which Parks category this fits and why laying the track open would be the wrong operation.
quiz.answer: It is a suprasphincteric fistula, and because the track passes above the puborectalis, laying it open would divide the entire external sphincter and the puborectalis and leave the patient incontinent, so it is managed with a seton or a sphincter-sparing repair instead.
quiz.explain: Parks divides perianal fistulas by their relation to the sphincter complex: intersphincteric tracks stay between internal and external sphincters; transsphincteric tracks cross the external sphincter into the ischioanal fossa; suprasphincteric tracks run up over the puborectalis before descending through the levator; extrasphincteric tracks begin above the levator, from pelvic sepsis, Crohn disease or an iatrogenic injury, and enter the anal canal from outside the sphincters altogether. The classification is not academic, because how much sphincter would have to be divided determines whether the track can be laid open at all. The radiologist's job is to state the internal opening, the course relative to both sphincters and the levator, and every secondary track or collection, since undrained sepsis is the usual reason a repair fails.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these post-chemoradiotherapy appearances of the treated tumour bed from the most complete response to the least, as the mrTRG scale runs from grade 1 to grade 5.
quiz.answer: fibrosis-only dense-fibrosis-with-minimal-residual-signal over-half-fibrosis-with-visible-tumour-signal little-fibrosis-mostly-tumour-signal tumour-signal-unchanged-or-larger
quiz.explain: The MR tumour regression grade, adapted from the pathological Mandard scale and validated in the MERCURY work, reads the treated bed as a proportion of dark fibrosis to intermediate tumour signal. Grade 1 is fibrosis only with no tumour signal; grade 2 is dense fibrosis with a barely perceptible residual focus; grade 3 is more than half fibrosis with clearly visible tumour signal; grade 4 is scant fibrosis with mostly tumour; grade 5 is no change or growth. Grades 1 and 2 constitute a good response and carry better disease-free survival, and they are the group in which organ preservation is even discussed. Two caveats to carry: interobserver agreement is only moderate, so read it with diffusion imaging and with the endoscopic findings, and scan at around eight weeks, since fibrosis is still maturing before that.

module_contract.goal: Work the acute scrotum to a decision about theatre within the salvage window, and use the intratesticular-extratesticular split, the sonographic pattern and the tumour markers to steer a testicular mass down the right pathway.

approach.step: Ask first whether this can be torsion
approach.detail: Torsion is the only diagnosis on this differential that is time-critical — work every acute scrotum as a possible torsion until excluded, even though appendage torsion and epididymitis are more common.
In the first 4-6 hours the testis looks normal on grey-scale. Heterogeneity and enlargement develop from 4-24 hours as infarction sets in.

approach.step: Colour Doppler, compared side to side
approach.detail: Complete absence of intratesticular flow with normal flow in the contralateral, asymptomatic testis is diagnostic of torsion.

approach.step: Do not be reassured by some flow
approach.detail: Preserved flow does not exclude torsion — incomplete or intermittent vascular obstruction can still be present.

A swollen, heterogeneous epididymis with increased flow and hydrocele points to epididymitis. A small hypoechoic nodule adjacent to the epididymal head, often with a normal testis, points to torsion of an appendage.

approach.step: Grade echogenicity if torsion is confirmed
approach.detail: Any asymmetric change in testicular echogenicity correlates with reduced salvageability and should be stated explicitly to the surgical team.

measure.how: Time from onset of pain to surgical detorsion.
measure.cutoff: Ischaemia progressing to necrosis by 5-6 hours untreated

measure.how: Compare flow in the symptomatic testis with the asymptomatic contralateral side.
measure.cutoff: Complete absence of intratesticular flow with normal contralateral flow = diagnostic of torsion

pitfalls: Waiting for grey-scale changes before calling torsion. In the first 4-6 hours the testis can look entirely normal — Doppler flow, not morphology, makes the call early.
Treating any detectable flow as exclusion of torsion. Incomplete vascular obstruction can preserve some flow while the testis is still torsed.
Not scanning the contralateral testis. Torsion is a comparative diagnosis on Doppler — you need the normal side as your reference.
Delaying the call to phone the surgeon while the salvage window (5-6 hours) runs. This is one of the few paediatric ultrasound findings that should interrupt the list.

Mistaking a torsed appendage for a small, indolent finding. It is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in children but still needs a confident Doppler exclusion of true testicular torsion first.
