quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old man has a painless firm scrotal lump. Ultrasound shows a 15 mm well-defined solid nodule with some vascularity lying in the epididymal head, clearly separate from a normal homogeneous testis that has an intact tunica and normal flow. How should this be reported?
quiz.answer: As an extratesticular nodule, where the great majority are benign, so specialist review with interval ultrasound is reasonable
choices: As an extratesticular nodule, where the great majority are benign, so specialist review with interval ultrasound is reasonable
As an intratesticular nodule, which carries a high risk of malignancy, so urgent tumour markers and inguinal orchidectomy follow
As a probable metastatic deposit needing staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis before any local assessment
As an indeterminate nodule needing percutaneous transscrotal biopsy to obtain tissue before any surgical decision is made
quiz.explain: The first question in scrotal ultrasound is not what the lesion is but where it sits, because that alone shifts the prior probability enormously. A solid intratesticular mass in an adult is malignant until proven otherwise and goes down the marker-and-orchidectomy pathway. A solid extratesticular mass is far more often benign - adenomatoid tumour of the epididymis, lipoma of the cord, fibrous pseudotumour, a papillary cystadenoma in von Hippel-Lindau disease - and is managed with far less alarm, though sarcomas do occur and growth or heterogeneity warrants excision. Note the second rule embedded in the wrong options: never take a transscrotal biopsy of a possible germ cell tumour. It violates the scrotal lymphatic barrier and diverts drainage to inguinal nodes that would otherwise not be at risk. Access is via a high inguinal approach.

quiz.prompt: A 15-year-old has four hours of severe left testicular pain. Colour Doppler shows flow within the symptomatic testis, and the on-call team wants to send him home. Explain why detectable flow does not settle the question, and what you would do at the machine.
quiz.answer: Preserved intratesticular flow does not exclude torsion, because in incomplete or intermittent torsion the venous flow is obstructed first while arterial signal persists; scan both sides with identical settings and interrogate the spermatic cord above the testis for the whirlpool of twisted vessels.
quiz.explain: The classic teaching that torsion means absent flow describes complete torsion of 360 degrees or more. Below that the cord is only partly wound, and because veins are thin-walled and low-pressure they close before arteries do: the testis is congested and dying while a systolic arterial signal is still detectable. Two habits protect the patient. First, standardise the machine - the same colour scale, wall filter and gain for both sides, imaged in one transverse split-screen view, so a genuine asymmetry is obvious and a low-flow setting failure is not mistaken for pathology. Second, look at the cord itself. A spiral twist of cord vessels above the testis, the whirlpool sign, is the most reliable finding, is present in incomplete torsion, and can be seen before the parenchyma has changed at all. A convincing history outweighs any scan.

quiz.prompt: Give the duration of complete testicular torsion, measured from the onset of pain, within which detorsion salvages the great majority of testes and beyond which salvage rates fall steeply. Answer in hours, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Within about six hours of complete torsion, salvage exceeds ninety per cent. By around twelve hours it is roughly half, and beyond twenty-four hours it falls into the low single figures, with most such testes removed at exploration. That timeline is the reason the acute scrotum is a surgical rather than a radiological problem: if the clinical suspicion is high, the patient goes to theatre and ultrasound must not delay him. Where ultrasound helps is in the equivocal presentation, in confirming an alternative such as epididymo-orchitis or a torted appendix, and in the late presenter where establishing non-viability changes the consent conversation. Remember that time is measured from the onset of the current episode - intermittent torsion produces recurrent short-lived episodes with spontaneous detorsion, and those patients still need elective fixation because the next twist may not undo itself.

quiz.prompt: A 16-year-old presents 20 hours after the sudden onset of pain. The left testis is enlarged, markedly heterogeneous with hypoechoic and hyperechoic areas, there is no detectable intratesticular flow, the surrounding soft tissues are hyperaemic and there is a reactive hydrocele. What should the report convey to the surgical team?
quiz.answer: Heterogeneous parenchyma with absent flow indicates haemorrhagic infarction and probable non-viability, though surgery is still urgent
choices: Heterogeneous parenchyma with absent flow indicates an underlying germ cell tumour, so markers and a staging CT should precede any surgery
Heterogeneous parenchyma with absent flow indicates haemorrhagic infarction and probable non-viability, though surgery is still urgent
Heterogeneous parenchyma with absent flow indicates severe epididymo-orchitis, so intravenous antibiotics and analgesia should be started
Heterogeneous parenchyma with absent flow indicates an old missed torsion, so elective review in the outpatient clinic is appropriate
quiz.explain: Grey-scale change lags behind ischaemia in a useful way. In the first few hours the testis can look entirely normal, which is exactly why a normal grey-scale study never excludes torsion. By six to twenty-four hours the testis swells and becomes diffusely hypoechoic from oedema. Once it turns coarsely heterogeneous, haemorrhagic infarction has occurred and the organ is usually not salvageable. That prediction matters for consent rather than for urgency: the patient still goes to theatre, because the necrotic testis is removed and, crucially, the contralateral side is fixed at the same operation. Do not confuse this with severe epididymo-orchitis, in which the testis is hyperaemic rather than avascular, although late infective venous congestion can itself infarct a testis and produce a confusingly similar avascular picture.

quiz.prompt: The parents of that 16-year-old ask why the surgeon intends to operate on the unaffected right side as well. Which explanation is correct?
quiz.answer: The high tunical attachment that allowed the twist is usually present on both sides, so the remaining testis is also at risk
choices: Antisperm antibodies formed after infarction damage the other testis, and fixation interrupts that immune process directly
The blood supply to the other side runs through the affected cord, so fixation is required to protect its arterial inflow
The high tunical attachment that allowed the twist is usually present on both sides, so the remaining testis is also at risk
The remaining testis enlarges after the loss of its partner, and fixation prevents that compensatory growth from causing pain
quiz.explain: Intravaginal torsion happens when the tunica vaginalis invests the testis and epididymis too highly, leaving the testis suspended within it like a clapper in a bell, free to rotate on the cord and often lying transversely rather than vertically. That anatomy is developmental and is usually bilateral, which is why the accepted operation is exploration with fixation of both testes, whether the affected one is saved or removed. The other options are wrong on mechanism: compensatory hypertrophy is real but is not a reason for fixation, the antisperm antibody story is not the basis of the operation, and each testicular artery arises separately from the aorta so one cord's fate does not determine the other's inflow. Extravaginal torsion is a different entity, occurring perinatally when the whole cord and tunica twist.

quiz.prompt: Spectral Doppler of an intratesticular artery in a symptomatic testis records a peak systolic velocity of 15 cm/s and an end-diastolic velocity of 3 cm/s. Calculate the resistive index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The resistive index is peak systolic velocity minus end-diastolic velocity, divided by peak systolic velocity, so (15 - 3) / 15 = 0.80. Normal adult intratesticular arteries feed a low-resistance vascular bed and generally sit around 0.5 to 0.7, with continuous forward diastolic flow. A raised index on the symptomatic side, and particularly absent or reversed diastolic flow, indicates that outflow is obstructed while inflow continues - the haemodynamic signature of incomplete torsion, and a red flag even when colour flow appears present. Always sample the asymptomatic testis for comparison in the same sitting, because the index is age-dependent and is unreliable in prepubertal boys, in whom diastolic flow is often not detectable at all in a perfectly normal testis. Waveform asymmetry between the two sides carries more weight than any single absolute value.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old on day five of oral antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis is worse, with swinging fever. Ultrasound now shows an enlarged hyperaemic epididymis, a hypoechoic avascular collection with low-level internal echoes within the testis, and a hydrocele containing septations and moving debris. What should be arranged?
quiz.answer: Urgent urological referral, because an intratesticular abscess with an infected hydrocele usually needs drainage or orchidectomy
choices: A further two weeks of the same oral antibiotic, because complicated epididymitis routinely resolves with prolonged therapy
Immediate staging CT, because an avascular intratesticular lesion in this age group most often represents an underlying germ cell tumour
Reassurance and discharge, because a septated hydrocele is a normal reactive finding in the setting of acute epididymitis
Urgent urological referral, because an intratesticular abscess with an infected hydrocele usually needs drainage or orchidectomy
quiz.explain: Epididymo-orchitis becomes a surgical problem when it collects. A rounded avascular hypoechoic area with internal echoes inside the testis is an abscess, and a hydrocele filled with septations and mobile debris is a pyocele; neither reliably clears on oral antibiotics. Other complications worth naming in the report are venous congestion causing testicular ischaemia or frank infarction, which is why an avascular testis in a septic patient does not exclude infection, and extension into the scrotal wall with gas, which is Fournier gangrene and a true emergency. The tumour distractor is a real trap in reverse: a focal inflammatory mass can mimic a tumour, so any residual focal lesion should be rescanned after treatment, since a tumour will persist while an inflammatory focus resolves.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old is kicked in the scrotum during a football match and has a tense, exquisitely tender hemiscrotum. What must your ultrasound report answer for the surgeon, and within what timescale does it matter?
quiz.answer: State whether the tunica albuginea is disrupted, whether the parenchyma is heterogeneous with extruded seminiferous tubules and loss of contour, and whether there is a haematocele, because a ruptured testis explored within about 72 hours is usually salvaged whereas later surgery is not.
quiz.explain: Testicular trauma is a report with a short answer list. Rupture is a breach of the tunica albuginea, and although the tear itself is directly visible in only a minority of cases, the surrogate signs are reliable: an abnormal testicular contour, heterogeneous parenchyma from extruded tubules, and loss of the smooth echogenic tunical line. Add the state of the vascularity, since a devascularised testis behaves like rupture surgically, and describe the surrounding fluid, distinguishing a simple hydrocele from a haematocele with internal echoes and septations. Timing drives the urgency: exploration within about three days salvages the large majority of ruptured testes, and delay drops that sharply. A normal-looking testis in a very painful scrotum with a large haematocele still deserves a low threshold for exploration.

quiz.prompt: A 32-year-old man has a firm painless right testicular swelling. Ultrasound shows a 4 cm homogeneous markedly hypoechoic intratesticular mass with a lobulated margin and internal vascularity, confined within an intact tunica. Alpha-fetoprotein is normal, beta-hCG is mildly raised and LDH is raised. How should this be interpreted?
quiz.answer: The appearances and the normal alpha-fetoprotein are consistent with seminoma, since a raised level would indicate a non-seminomatous element
choices: The appearances and the normal alpha-fetoprotein are consistent with seminoma, since a raised level would indicate a non-seminomatous element
The appearances and the normal alpha-fetoprotein exclude germ cell tumour entirely, so lymphoma is the most likely diagnosis here
The appearances and the raised LDH indicate metastatic disease, so orchidectomy should be deferred until chemotherapy is given
The appearances and the raised beta-hCG together exclude a pure seminoma, since that marker is produced by non-seminomatous germ cell tumours alone
quiz.explain: Sonographic pattern and markers point the same way here. Seminomas are typically homogeneous, uniformly hypoechoic, lobulated or multinodular, and remain confined by the tunica albuginea. Non-seminomatous tumours are heterogeneous, with cystic spaces, calcification and coarse irregular architecture, and are more likely to breach the tunica. The marker rule is the one to hold firmly: alpha-fetoprotein is never produced by pure seminoma, so any elevation means a non-seminomatous element is present and the patient is treated as non-seminomatous whatever the histology says. Beta-hCG can be modestly raised by syncytiotrophoblastic cells within a pure seminoma, so it does not exclude the diagnosis. LDH is a bulk marker rather than a lineage marker. Markers are drawn before orchidectomy and repeated afterwards, since their half-life-adjusted decline is itself prognostic.

quiz.prompt: A 26-year-old man is found on CT to have a bulky para-aortic nodal mass and no obvious primary. His testes are clinically normal. What should you request, and what specific appearance are you asking the sonographer to look for?
quiz.answer: Request a scrotal ultrasound, looking for a burnt-out germ cell tumour: a small echogenic focus or cluster of calcification, often with an atrophic or shadowing area of scarring, which reclassifies the retroperitoneal mass as a metastasis rather than a primary tumour.
quiz.explain: Germ cell tumours can regress spontaneously in the testis while their metastases keep growing, so a young man with a retroperitoneal nodal mass and normal-feeling testes still needs his testes imaged. The regressed primary is small and easy to overlook: an echogenic focus, a cluster of coarse calcifications with shadowing, or an ill-defined hypoechoic scar, often with local atrophy and sometimes with no residual viable tumour at all. Finding it changes both the diagnosis and the operation, since the testis is removed by the inguinal route. The anatomy explains why the nodes come first: testicular lymphatics travel with the gonadal vessels to nodes at the level of the renal hila, left-sided tumours to the left para-aortic group and right-sided ones to the interaortocaval group, bypassing the pelvis and the groin altogether.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the lymphatic stations through which an untreated testicular germ cell tumour spreads, beginning with the first draining group.
quiz.answer: retroperitoneal-nodes thoracic-duct mediastinal-nodes left-supraclavicular-node
quiz.explain: The testis descends from the retroperitoneum and drags its lymphatic drainage with it, so the first station is retroperitoneal, at the level of the renal hila, and not inguinal. From there lymph travels up the thoracic duct to the mediastinum and, classically, to the left supraclavicular fossa. Two practical consequences follow. First, a staging CT must cover the chest as well as the abdomen and pelvis, and the retroperitoneum is where the disease is measured and followed. Second, the inguinal and pelvic nodes are involved only when the normal drainage has been disturbed - after a transscrotal operation or biopsy, with scrotal skin invasion, or after previous inguinal or scrotal surgery - which is precisely why the scrotum is never violated to obtain tissue. Haematogenous spread to the lungs is a separate route.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old has a scrotal ultrasound for a minor trauma. The testes are normal in size, echotexture and vascularity, but both contain numerous 1-2 mm non-shadowing echogenic foci scattered throughout, with more than five in a single field of view. He has no cryptorchidism, no previous tumour, no atrophy and no infertility. What advice should the report give?
quiz.answer: No surveillance imaging is needed for microlithiasis alone in a man without risk factors, but advise testicular self-examination
choices: Immediate tumour markers and a staging CT are required because this pattern indicates occult germ cell neoplasia in situ
No surveillance imaging is needed for microlithiasis alone in a man without risk factors, but advise testicular self-examination
Annual ultrasound surveillance is required until the age of fifty because microlithiasis is a premalignant condition in its own right
Bilateral testicular biopsy should be discussed because histology is the sole way to exclude germ cell neoplasia in situ here
quiz.explain: Testicular microlithiasis is common, found in a few per cent of asymptomatic men, and in isolation it does not justify surveillance imaging. Current European guidance is that microlithiasis in an otherwise normal testis, in a man with no additional risk factor, needs no follow-up ultrasound; the man is told to examine himself and to return if he feels a lump. The association with germ cell tumour is real but is carried almost entirely by the company it keeps: a history of cryptorchidism, a previous germ cell tumour, testicular atrophy, infertility or subfertility, or a first-degree family history. In those men, or when microlithiasis accompanies a focal lesion, follow-up ultrasound is offered. The older habit of routinely rescanning every man with microliths caused anxiety and biopsies without demonstrable benefit.

quiz.prompt: A 9-year-old boy has 12 hours of scrotal pain with a tender point at the upper pole and a small bluish discolouration through the skin. Ultrasound shows a 6 mm avascular ovoid nodule between the upper pole and the epididymal head, surrounded by hyperaemic tissue, with normal symmetrical flow in both testes and a small hydrocele. What is the right course?
quiz.answer: Manage conservatively with analgesia and rest, since a torted appendix testis settles over about a fortnight without surgery
choices: Start a course of antibiotics for bacterial epididymitis, since the hyperaemia and the hydrocele indicate an ascending infection
Arrange tumour markers and repeat imaging, since a discrete avascular nodule of this kind may represent a small neoplasm
Manage conservatively with analgesia and rest, since a torted appendix testis settles over about a fortnight without surgery
Arrange emergency exploration with bilateral fixation, since this appearance indicates an incomplete torsion of the testis
quiz.explain: Torsion of the appendix testis is the commonest cause of the acute scrotum in the prepubertal boy, and its whole value lies in being distinguished confidently from torsion of the testis so that the child is spared an operation. The findings are characteristic: a small avascular ovoid or rounded nodule at the upper pole or in the groove between testis and epididymal head, sometimes enlarged and echogenic, surrounded by reactive hyperaemia in the adjacent epididymis and scrotal wall, with a reactive hydrocele and, crucially, normal and symmetrical intratesticular flow. The blue dot seen through thin scrotal skin is specific but often absent. It resolves with simple analgesia over one to two weeks as the appendage infarcts and calcifies. If testicular flow is in any doubt, the child is explored.

quiz.prompt: A mass lies above the sella, and a normal pituitary gland is visible separately below it. Which first step improves the differential?
choices: Localise the epicentre before assuming a pituitary adenoma
Label every suprasellar mass an adenoma
Ignore the gland because the lesion is large
Classify the lesion only by its longest dimension
quiz.answer: Localise the epicentre before assuming a pituitary adenoma
quiz.explain: Identifying the normal gland and lesion epicentre narrows the possible tissue of origin. Signal and enhancement are interpreted after localisation.

quiz.prompt: A sellar mass extends superiorly in a patient with visual symptoms. Which relationship must be reported explicitly?
choices: Its distance from the frontal sinus only
Contact, displacement or compression of the optic apparatus
The number of visible scalp veins
The side of the nasal septal deviation
quiz.answer: Contact, displacement or compression of the optic apparatus
quiz.explain: Optic-apparatus involvement is clinically consequential. Describe its relationship to the lesion and integrate formal visual assessment rather than inferring visual function from MRI.

quiz.prompt: A parasellar lesion contains flow-related signal and is contiguous with the internal carotid artery. What should happen before tissue sampling is contemplated?
choices: Assume all enhancement represents meningioma
Ignore the vascular relationship
Evaluate for an aneurysm or other vascular lesion
Call it a cyst because it is rounded
quiz.answer: Evaluate for an aneurysm or other vascular lesion
quiz.explain: A vascular mimic must be recognised before intervention. Angiographic imaging can clarify vessel continuity and lumen; a rounded parasellar shape is not a tissue diagnosis.

quiz.prompt: Biochemistry suggests pituitary hypersecretion, but a routine thick-slice brain MRI is negative. Which study may better address the question?
choices: A chest radiograph
A lumbar CT
A repeat identical localiser
Dedicated thin-section pituitary MRI tailored to the endocrine question
quiz.answer: Dedicated thin-section pituitary MRI tailored to the endocrine question
quiz.explain: A small sellar lesion may be missed by a general brain protocol. Targeted imaging improves assessment, while interpretation still depends on the endocrine evidence.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a pituitary mass develops sudden severe headache and visual decline. MRI shows new intralesional haemorrhage. What is the reporting priority?
choices: Urgent communication of suspected pituitary apoplexy
Routine annual comparison only
Assuming haemorrhage proves malignant transformation
Waiting for lesion growth before reporting the change
quiz.answer: Urgent communication of suspected pituitary apoplexy
quiz.explain: The acute syndrome can threaten vision and endocrine function. Communicate the finding promptly and describe optic-apparatus compression and relevant extension.

quiz.prompt: A rounded suprasellar lesion is found, but the pituitary gland is not identified separately on a routine brain study. Explain how you would organise the differential and the next imaging question.
quiz.answer: First establish the epicentre and relationship to the gland, stalk, optic apparatus, cavernous sinuses and vessels. Describe cystic, solid, haemorrhagic or flow-related features without assuming pituitary origin. A dedicated sellar study or vascular assessment may be needed to resolve the uncertain origin and anatomy.
quiz.explain: Localisation constrains the differential. Naming a familiar sellar lesion before finding the normal structures risks anchoring on the wrong tissue of origin.

quiz.prompt: A pituitary lesion is visible in a patient with abnormal hormone tests. The draft calls it “definitely hormone-secreting” based only on enhancement. Explain the limitation.
quiz.answer: MRI describes the lesion's presence, size and anatomical effects but does not establish its secretory behaviour from enhancement alone. Correlate with the specific endocrine findings and relevant clinical assessment. Report whether the imaging and laboratory question are anatomically compatible without replacing biochemical diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Morphology and hormonal function are different types of evidence. A plausible relationship still needs clinical confirmation.

quiz.prompt: A sellar mass contacts the optic chiasm without obvious compression. The patient reports worsening vision. What should the report communicate?
quiz.answer: State the contact and any displacement or signal abnormality that is actually visible, and preserve the distinction between contact and compression. Highlight the visual symptoms as requiring prompt clinical and formal visual assessment. The absence of dramatic compression on MRI does not establish normal visual function.
quiz.explain: The image cannot substitute for examination of the patient's vision. Anatomical precision and clinical urgency should both remain clear.

quiz.prompt: A parasellar mass has an apparent connection to the carotid artery, but slow flow or thrombus makes the appearance unclear. What is the key unresolved issue before proposing a biopsy?
quiz.answer: A vascular lesion, including an aneurysm, must be assessed before tissue sampling is proposed. Describe the suspected arterial continuity and uncertain components, and obtain appropriate vascular characterisation through the clinical team. Do not use a solid-appearing or partially thrombosed component to exclude a vascular origin.
quiz.explain: The consequence of mistaking a vascular lesion for a tissue mass makes the anatomical uncertainty decisive for planning.

quiz.prompt: A follow-up scan shows haemorrhage within a known pituitary mass. The requisition mentions a sudden severe headache and new visual loss. Explain why a routine “interval signal change” conclusion is inadequate.
quiz.answer: The acute symptoms and haemorrhage raise concern for pituitary apoplexy. State and urgently communicate that concern, describe the optic-apparatus relationship and extension, and record communication. The clinical team must assess visual and endocrine consequences rather than treating the finding as an incidental change on surveillance.
quiz.explain: The same imaging change has different importance in an acute syndrome. The report should connect the finding to the time-sensitive clinical presentation.

module_contract.goal: Read a shoulder MRI or ultrasound so that you separate normal labral variants from real lesions, grade a cuff tear in the terms the surgeon plans by, and say whether an unstable shoulder needs bony treatment.

approach.step: Decide the tear is real, then decide its depth
approach.detail: Partial thickness or full thickness. Partial tears are articular-sided at the undersurface, bursal-sided at the bursal surface, or intrasubstance within the tendon.

approach.step: For a partial tear, state the proportion of tendon thickness
approach.detail: More or less than 50% of the tendon thickness is the split that matters to the surgeon.

approach.step: For a full thickness tear, take it through four stages
approach.detail: Incomplete (part of the tendon width), complete (the whole tendon ruptured), complete with retraction, then complete with retraction plus atrophy and fatty infiltration.

approach.step: Measure retraction and say where the stump sits
approach.detail: Retraction is the finding that converts a repairable tear into a difficult one.

approach.step: Assess the muscle on the oblique sagittal
approach.detail: Warner's tangent sign: a line across the supraspinatus fossa. Muscle convex above the line means no atrophy; muscle just below it means moderate atrophy.

approach.step: Then read the radiograph for arthropathy
approach.detail: Acromiohumeral distance, acetabularisation of the coracoacromial arch, glenohumeral narrowing, humeral head necrosis — the Hamada sequence.

measure.how: Proportion of tendon thickness involved, on the plane that shows the tendon in cross-section.
measure.cutoff: More or less than 50% of thickness

measure.how: On the AP radiograph, between the undersurface of the acromion and the humeral head.
measure.cutoff: Hamada 1 is ≥ 6 mm · Hamada 2 is ≤ 5 mm

measure.how: Oblique sagittal image at the level of the scapular spine; a line drawn across the supraspinatus fossa.
measure.cutoff: Convex above the line = no atrophy · just below = moderate atrophy

measure.how: Proportion of the cuff muscles replaced by fat on the oblique sagittal.
At the 12 o'clock biceps anchor, on coronal oblique images.
measure.cutoff: > 3–5 mm is always abnormal — regard it as a SLAP tear

classify.name: Hamada — rotator cuff arthropathy on the radiograph
rows: Acromiohumeral distance < 5 mm and acetabularisation of the coracoacromial arch
Narrowing of the glenohumeral joint, without acetabularisation
Narrowing of the glenohumeral joint, with acetabularisation
Humeral head necrosis, sometimes with humeral head collapse
classify.note: Signs of irreparability and an indication for reverse total shoulder arthroplasty are static superior migration, a narrowed or absent acromiohumeral interval, and fatty infiltration of more than 50% of the cuff muscles.

modifiers.meaning: Detachment of the anteroinferior labrum at 3–6 o'clock with complete tearing of the anterior scapular periosteum, with or without an osseous fragment.
Labral detachment with the periosteum medially stripped but intact. May need ABER positioning to be seen at all.
Medially displaced labroligamentous complex, with the labrum absent from the glenoid rim.
Partial tear of the anteroinferior labrum with adjacent cartilage damage.
Avulsion of the inferior glenohumeral ligament from its humeral insertion.
Posteroinferior labral injury at 6–9 o'clock, from posterior dislocation.
Posterolateral humeral head depression at or above the level of the coracoid. Present in 75–100% of anterior instability.

TECHNIQUE

FINDINGS
Supraspinatus: [normal / tendinosis / partial thickness — articular-sided, bursal-sided or intrasubstance, involving more or less than 50% of thickness / full thickness — incomplete or complete, [n] mm in AP width].
Retraction: [none / to the [humeral head apex / glenoid]].
Infraspinatus, subscapularis, teres minor: [ ].
Long head of biceps: [normal / tendinosis / subluxed / ruptured].
Muscle: tangent sign [negative / positive]; fatty infiltration [absent / < 50% / > 50%].
Labrum: [intact / tear at [o'clock positions]] — [Bankart / bony Bankart / Perthes / ALPSA / GLAD / reverse Bankart].
Normal variants present: [sublabral recess / sublabral foramen at 1–3 o'clock / Buford complex].
Humeral head: [Hill-Sachs present / absent].
Glenohumeral ligaments: [intact / HAGL].
Acromiohumeral distance: [n] mm.

IMPRESSION
1. [Cuff diagnosis with depth, width and retraction.]
2. Muscle quality: [ ] — [repairable / features of irreparability].
3. [Instability lesion named, with the labral clock positions.]
4. [Hamada grade if arthropathy present.]
pitfalls: Calling a sublabral foramen a tear. An unattached anterosuperior labrum at 1–3 o'clock occurs in about 11% of people; at 1–3 o'clock, absence plus a thickened middle glenohumeral ligament is a Buford complex, in about 1.5%.
Treating any superior recess as normal. A recess deeper than 3–5 mm at the biceps anchor is always abnormal and should be read as a SLAP tear.
Magic angle in a morphologically normal tendon. Increased signal on short TE sequences is artefact unless the tendon is also abnormal in shape.
Reporting the tear and not the muscle. Retraction, tangent sign and fatty infiltration over 50% are what decide between repair and reverse arthroplasty.
Missing a Perthes lesion on standard planes. The periosteum is stripped but intact, so the labrum can look attached — ABER positioning is what shows it.

radiology_reference.overview: Read a shoulder MRI or ultrasound so that you separate normal labral variants from real lesions, grade a cuff tear in the terms the surgeon plans by, and say whether an unstable shoulder needs bony treatment.
learning_points: Tendon, retraction, muscle and atrophy determine repairability.
Separate normal variants from tears by attachment and associated signs.
Quantify glenoid and humeral bone loss before choosing treatment.
Review rotator cuff tendon involvement, tear dimensions and retraction.
Review muscle atrophy and fatty change.
Review long head of biceps and pulley.
Review labrum, capsule and instability-related bone injury.
Review cartilage, AC joint and bursae.
Report both tendon failure and muscle condition; a tear measurement alone is insufficient for operative planning.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old swimmer has an MR arthrogram for anterior pain. There is no labral tissue at all between roughly the one and three o'clock positions, and the middle glenohumeral ligament is thickened into a cord that runs across the front of the glenoid neck. The rest of the labrum is smooth, there is no paralabral cyst, and she has never dislocated. What should your report conclude?
quiz.answer: A Buford complex, a normal anterosuperior variant that should not be repaired
choices: A Buford complex, a normal anterosuperior variant that should not be repaired
An anterosuperior labral tear that needs arthroscopic repair to restore stability
An anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion of the anterior labrum
A sublabral recess extending posteriorly behind the long head of biceps anchor
quiz.explain: An absent anterosuperior labrum combined with a cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament is the Buford complex, found in roughly one to two per cent of shoulders. On axial images the cord is easily read as a detached labral fragment floating in contrast. Saying so matters in both directions: suturing a Buford cord down to the glenoid tethers the joint and leaves a stiff, painful shoulder, while omitting it invites the arthroscopist to make the same error. A genuine anterosuperior tear has irregular margins, often a paralabral cyst, and a history to match. An ALPSA lies anteroinferiorly, where the shoulder actually dislocates. A sublabral recess belongs at the biceps anchor superiorly, not at two o'clock.

quiz.prompt: A registrar asks you how you decide, on a superior labral image, whether the fluid line at the biceps anchor is a normal recess or a tear. Give the features you use.
quiz.answer: A sublabral recess is a smooth, thin cleft under 2 mm wide that follows the glenoid contour medially and stops at the biceps anchor, whereas a SLAP tear is irregular, wider, and extends laterally into the labral substance or posterior to the anchor, often with a paralabral cyst.
quiz.explain: The superior labrum is the single most over-called structure in the shoulder. A sublabral recess is a developmental cleft between the labrum and the glenoid rim: it hugs the glenoid contour, points medially, is thin and smooth-walled, and dies out at the biceps anchor. A type II SLAP tear runs the other way, extending laterally into the substance of the labrum or tracking posteriorly behind the anchor, with irregular walls and often a paralabral cyst tracking into the spinoglenoid notch. Width helps but is not decisive on its own. Age helps too: a smooth superior cleft in a 60-year-old is usually degenerative fraying, and reporting it as a repairable SLAP in that group has driven a good deal of unnecessary surgery.

quiz.prompt: A 46-year-old decorator has a painful arc. On the MR arthrogram, contrast tracks from the joint into the deep surface of the supraspinatus at the footprint and extends 4 mm into a tendon that measures 11 mm thick. The bursal surface fibres are continuous and no contrast reaches the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa. What do you report?
quiz.answer: An articular-sided partial tear involving less than half of the tendon thickness
choices: An articular-sided partial tear involving less than half of the tendon thickness
A full-thickness tear with contrast tracking into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa
A bursal-sided partial tear of the kind that responds poorly to conservative care
Tendinosis alone, with intrasubstance signal that stops short of either surface
quiz.explain: Contrast entering the deep surface but stopping before the bursa is a partial articular-sided tear, the PASTA pattern, and articular-sided tears outnumber bursal-sided ones roughly three to one because the deep fibres are thinner and more highly stressed. Depth is what the surgeon acts on: Ellman grade 1 is under 3 mm, grade 2 is 3 to 6 mm and grade 3 is over 6 mm, which for a 10 to 12 mm tendon corresponds to more than half thickness and is where takedown and repair start to be considered. Here 4 mm of an 11 mm tendon is a grade 2 lesion, under half depth. Fluid in the bursa would have made it full thickness. Bursal-sided tears sit on the superficial surface and often accompany impingement. Tendinosis raises signal without a fluid-filled cleft reaching a surface.

quiz.prompt: The same tendon is re-measured on the arthrogram: the supraspinatus is 10.0 mm thick at the footprint and the articular-sided defect extends 6.5 mm from the deep surface. Report the depth of the tear as a percentage of tendon thickness. Answer as a percentage, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: 6.5 of 10.0 mm is 65 per cent. The arithmetic is trivial; the point is that surgeons think in proportions, not millimetres, because the decision threshold sits near half thickness. Below about 50 per cent, most partial tears are managed with debridement and rehabilitation; above it, takedown and repair or a transtendon repair come into play, since the remaining fibres carry a load they were not built for and the tear tends to propagate. State both the absolute depth and the tendon thickness in your report, because a 5 mm defect means something quite different in a 12 mm tendon than in an 8 mm one. Measure on the coronal oblique image perpendicular to the tendon, at the point of maximum depth, and note whether the defect reaches the bursa.

quiz.prompt: A 68-year-old has a full-thickness supraspinatus tear whose free edge lies at the level of the glenoid. On the sagittal oblique image at the scapular Y, the supraspinatus belly contains more fat than muscle and lies below a line drawn from the coracoid to the scapular spine. What does this add to the report?
quiz.answer: Patte 3 retraction with Goutallier 4 atrophy, which predicts poor healing after repair
choices: Patte 3 retraction with Goutallier 4 atrophy, which predicts poor healing after repair
Patte 1 retraction with Goutallier 1 change, a combination that repairs very reliably
Denervation change from suprascapular nerve entrapment rather than tear-related atrophy
Reversible disuse change that recovers once the subacromial space has been decompressed
quiz.explain: Two separate scales are being applied. Patte grades retraction in the coronal plane: stage 1 near the footprint, stage 2 at the level of the humeral head, stage 3 back at the glenoid. Goutallier grades fatty infiltration of the muscle belly on the sagittal oblique Y view: 0 none, 1 fatty streaks, 2 more muscle than fat, 3 equal fat and muscle, 4 more fat than muscle. The muscle failing to cross the coracoid-to-spine line is the tangent sign, an independent marker of atrophy. Goutallier 3 or 4 does not reverse after repair and carries a high retear rate, so this combination usually steers the surgeon away from repair towards debridement, tendon transfer or reverse arthroplasty. Nerve entrapment produces oedema or atrophy in a nerve territory, typically infraspinatus with or without supraspinatus, without a retracted tendon.

quiz.prompt: The referring surgeon asks why you always state the Goutallier grade rather than just describing the tear itself. Explain what the grade changes.
quiz.answer: Goutallier grade 3 or 4 fatty infiltration is irreversible: the muscle does not recover after repair, the retear rate is high, and so a high grade pushes the surgeon away from cuff repair towards debridement, tendon transfer or reverse arthroplasty.
quiz.explain: Tear size tells the surgeon what has to be reached; muscle quality tells them whether it is worth reaching. Fatty infiltration is the muscle's response to chronic retraction and denervation, and once fat has replaced muscle it does not convert back, whatever is done to the tendon. That is why Goutallier grade, measured on the sagittal oblique image at the level of the scapular spine, sits alongside Patte retraction in every good cuff report. Grades 0 to 2 are compatible with a durable repair; 3 and 4 predict failure of the construct and, in a low-demand patient, may push the plan to a reverse arthroplasty that does not depend on the cuff at all. The tangent sign is a quick sanity check on the same image.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these stages of degenerative rotator cuff disease in the order in which they typically develop.
quiz.answer: tendinosis articular-sided-partial-tear full-thickness-tear tendon-retraction fatty-atrophy
quiz.explain: Degenerative cuff disease follows a fairly orderly course, and knowing it tells you what to look for next once you have found one step. Intrasubstance signal without a surface-reaching cleft is tendinosis. The deep fibres fail first, giving an articular-sided partial tear, because they are thinner and bear more strain than the bursal fibres. Propagation through the remaining thickness produces a full-thickness defect and fluid then reaches the subacromial bursa. Once the tendon is discontinuous the muscle unloads and the free edge retracts medially, which Patte grades. Chronic retraction and the associated denervation then convert muscle to fat, which Goutallier grades and which does not reverse. Traumatic tears in young patients can skip the early steps, but in the degenerative shoulder this is the sequence, and the last two steps are the ones that decide reparability.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old rugby player has axial MR images after a first anterior dislocation. There is a shallow concavity on the posterolateral humeral head, but on the slices passing through the coracoid process the head is perfectly round; the concavity appears only well below the coracoid. There is no marrow oedema. What is the correct interpretation?
quiz.answer: The normal bare area of the humeral head, rather than a Hill-Sachs impaction
choices: The normal bare area of the humeral head, rather than a Hill-Sachs impaction
An acute Hill-Sachs impaction that will engage the glenoid rim in abduction
A reverse Hill-Sachs impaction, indicating a posterior rather than anterior dislocation
An osteochondral defect of the humeral head following previous septic arthritis
quiz.explain: The posterolateral humeral head has a normal flattening and a bare area below the level of the coracoid, where the articular cartilage thins and small vascular channels sit. A Hill-Sachs impaction happens when the head strikes the anteroinferior glenoid rim, which is why a real one is found on axial slices at or above the level of the coracoid tip. Depth below that level, with no marrow oedema and no cortical irregularity, is anatomy. The distinction matters because calling a Hill-Sachs in a first-time dislocator invites a discussion about bony augmentation. A reverse Hill-Sachs sits anteromedially and accompanies posterior dislocation, often after a seizure or electric shock. Post-infective defects are irregular, cross the articular surface and come with cartilage loss and effusion.

quiz.prompt: A 24-year-old has recurrent anterior dislocations. On the en face sagittal CT reconstruction the glenoid diameter measures 26.0 mm and the anterior glenoid bone defect measures 4.0 mm. The glenoid track is 0.83 times the glenoid diameter, minus the width of the anterior defect. Calculate the glenoid track width in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 0.83 times 26.0 is 21.58 mm, and subtracting the 4.0 mm anterior defect leaves 17.6 mm. The track is the zone of the humeral head that stays in contact with the glenoid through abduction and external rotation. You then measure the Hill-Sachs interval, which is the width of the Hill-Sachs defect plus the width of the intact bone bridge between it and the rotator cuff footprint. If that interval is wider than the track, the lesion is off-track and will engage the glenoid rim, so a soft-tissue Bankart repair alone is likely to fail and a bone procedure such as a Latarjet or a remplissage is considered. If it is narrower, the lesion is on-track. This concept has largely replaced the older habit of quoting a single percentage of glenoid bone loss, and it is worth reporting both numbers so the surgeon can do the comparison.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old has recurrent instability after non-operative treatment of a first dislocation. The MR arthrogram shows the anteroinferior labrum displaced medially along the scapular neck and rolled up beneath an intact, stripped periosteum, with no free fragment and no glenoid rim fracture. What is the significance of this appearance?
quiz.answer: An ALPSA lesion, which heals in a medialised position and leaves the capsule lax
choices: An ALPSA lesion, which heals in a medialised position and leaves the capsule lax
A classic Bankart lesion, with the periosteum torn and the labral fragment free
A Perthes lesion, with the labrum in anatomical position and the periosteum intact
A GLAD lesion, with a labral tear and adjacent glenoid cartilage loss but stability
quiz.explain: The anteroinferior labroligamentous complex fails in several patterns and the periosteum decides which. In a classic Bankart the periosteum tears and the labrum sits free at the rim. In a Perthes lesion the periosteum stays intact and the labrum remains anatomically placed, so it can be almost invisible without abduction and external rotation positioning. An ALPSA is the intermediate: the periosteum is stripped rather than torn, and the labroligamentous sleeve slides medially down the scapular neck and scars there. It matters because a medialised, healed labrum still fails mechanically, the capsule remains lax, recurrence rates are higher, and the surgeon has to mobilise the scarred tissue off the neck before reattaching it. A GLAD lesion adds a cartilage defect but is usually a stable, painful shoulder rather than a dislocating one.

quiz.prompt: A 54-year-old with type 2 diabetes has a shoulder stiff in every direction. MRI shows capsule and inferior glenohumeral ligament thickened to 5 mm at the axillary recess, soft tissue thickening in the rotator interval with obliteration of the subcoracoid fat, and an intact cuff with no effusion. What should you report and recommend?
quiz.answer: Adhesive capsulitis; report it so hydrodilatation or injection can be arranged
choices: Adhesive capsulitis; report it so hydrodilatation or injection can be arranged
An occult full-thickness cuff tear; arrange arthrography before any surgery
Calcific tendinitis; arrange ultrasound-guided barbotage of the supraspinatus deposit
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis; report the joint space loss and inferior osteophyte
quiz.explain: Adhesive capsulitis is diagnosed clinically, but MRI has reasonably specific signs and they are worth knowing because the request usually asks about the cuff. Thickening of the capsule and inferior glenohumeral ligament at the axillary recess beyond about 4 mm, oedematous soft tissue in the rotator interval replacing the normal subcoracoid fat triangle, and avid enhancement of those tissues after contrast are the constellation. It is commoner in diabetes and in thyroid disease. Naming it changes the pathway: the patient goes to physiotherapy with an intra-articular steroid injection or hydrodilatation rather than to arthroscopy for a cuff that is intact. A cuff tear gives a fluid-filled defect, not global capsular thickening. A calcific deposit is low signal on all sequences and visible on the radiograph. Osteoarthritis narrows the joint and builds an inferior humeral osteophyte.

quiz.prompt: A clinician reports that a patient has a hooked acromion on their radiograph and asks you to confirm subacromial impingement on that basis. Explain how you would answer.
quiz.answer: Impingement is a clinical diagnosis, and acromion shape alone does not make it: I would look for supporting findings such as a subacromial spur, bursal-sided cuff tendinosis or tearing, and fluid in the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa, and report the shape only as one part of that picture.
quiz.explain: The Bigliani description of acromial shape, flat, curved or hooked, is easy to quote and poorly reproducible: the apparent shape shifts with the obliquity of the sagittal slice or the radiographic projection, and interobserver agreement is modest. Hooked acromia are common in asymptomatic shoulders. What earns a place in the report is mechanical evidence: a spur projecting from the anterior acromial undersurface or the acromioclavicular joint, narrowing of the subacromial space, reactive change or tearing on the bursal surface of supraspinatus, and fluid in the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa. Even then the diagnosis is made by the examining clinician, since a painful arc relieved by local anaesthetic is the actual test. Describing shape without the mechanical findings can send a patient to acromioplasty for pain that came from somewhere else.

quiz.prompt: The MRI waiting list is three months. A 60-year-old presents with weakness after lifting and the team wants an answer this week. What is the honest account of what shoulder ultrasound will give them?
quiz.answer: It detects full-thickness tears accurately and allows dynamic side-to-side comparison
choices: It detects full-thickness tears accurately and allows dynamic side-to-side comparison
It shows labral tears and marrow oedema about as reliably as MR arthrography does
It grades fatty atrophy of the cuff bellies more accurately than sagittal oblique MRI
It reliably excludes the occult proximal humeral fracture that radiographs have missed
quiz.explain: In experienced hands ultrasound matches MRI for full-thickness cuff tears, with sensitivity and specificity in the ninety per cent range, and it does several things MRI cannot: it moves the shoulder while looking, so subluxation of the long head of biceps or dynamic bursal bunching is visible; it compares directly with the asymptomatic side; it is cheap and repeatable; and the same probe guides the injection afterwards. Its limits are equally clear. The labrum is largely hidden by bone, marrow oedema is invisible, and an undisplaced fracture will be missed. Fatty atrophy can be judged crudely by echogenicity but is graded far better on the sagittal oblique MRI. The classic pitfall is anisotropy: a normal tendon looks hypoechoic and torn when the beam is not perpendicular to it, so rock the probe before calling a defect.

curriculum_modules.title: Paranasal Sinuses: Anatomy, Variants and Disease

module_contract.goal: Read a sinus CT the way the endoscopic surgeon needs it read: work out which drainage pathway is blocked, flag the variants that put the skull base, optic nerve, carotid and orbit at risk, and separate inflammatory from neoplastic disease.

approach.step: Use CT for the anatomy the surgeon needs
approach.detail: CT is the modality of value for anatomic landmarks and variants — this is what the ENT surgeon is asking for before an endoscopic case.

approach.step: Use MRI to separate secretions from a mass
approach.detail: MRI can discern secretions and mucosal thickening from a true mass; CT density alone can't reliably make that call.

approach.step: Read the T2 signal and density of opacified sinus contents
approach.detail: A hyperdense, T2-bright content is usually benign, inspissated secretion; tumour is not hyperdense and does not show the bright T2 signal of retained mucus.

approach.step: Give contrast before you call something benign
approach.detail: Secretions do not enhance. If there is solid enhancement within an opacified sinus, you must rule out tumour rather than sign it out as retained secretions.

Unilateral sinus disease should raise suspicion for an obstructing lesion (inverted papilloma at the middle meatus/middle turbinate, silent sinus syndrome from infundibular occlusion) rather than routine sinusitis.

approach.step: Check the sphenoethmoidal recess in the right clinical setting
approach.detail: Allergic fungal sinusitis characteristically involves the sphenoethmoidal recesses — look here specifically when the clinical picture fits.

classify.name: Inflammatory disease versus tumour
rows: Intermediate/solid signal, no bright T2 component

pitfalls: Signing out an opacified sinus as chronic sinusitis on CT density alone without checking for solid enhancement on a contrast series.
Missing an inverted papilloma because the middle-meatus origin was not specifically sought.
Treating unilateral sinus disease as routine sinusitis — true unilateral sinusitis alone is uncommon and should prompt a search for an obstructing lesion.
Forgetting the sphenoethmoidal recess in suspected allergic fungal sinusitis.

quiz.prompt: Coronal CT shows complete opacification of the right maxillary sinus, the right anterior ethmoid cells and the right frontal sinus, with a clear right sphenoid and clear right posterior ethmoid cells. The left side is clear throughout. Where is the obstruction, and what does that imply for treatment?
quiz.answer: The right ostiomeatal complex, which drains those three sinuses
choices: The right ostiomeatal complex, which drains those three sinuses
The right sphenoethmoidal recess, which drains those three sinuses
The right inferior meatus, which drains those three sinuses
The right superior meatus, which drains those three sinuses
quiz.explain: The ostiomeatal complex, meaning the maxillary ostium, the ethmoid infundibulum, the uncinate process, the hiatus semilunaris, the ethmoid bulla and the middle meatus, is the shared final pathway for the maxillary, anterior ethmoid and frontal sinuses. Block it and exactly this triad opacifies while the posterior ethmoid cells and the sphenoid, which drain to the superior meatus and the sphenoethmoidal recess, stay clear. That is why the pattern of opacification is diagnostic of the level of the obstruction and why the report should describe it as a pathway rather than a list of sinuses. The mirror image, an opaque sphenoid and posterior ethmoid with clear anterior sinuses, sends you to the sphenoethmoidal recess. The inferior meatus receives no sinus at all, only the nasolacrimal duct, so its obstruction causes a watering eye rather than sinusitis. The surgical consequence is that clearing the middle meatus treats three sinuses at once, which is the whole logic of functional endoscopic surgery.

quiz.prompt: A sinus CT shows complete opacification of the left posterior ethmoid cells and the left sphenoid sinus, while the maxillary, frontal and anterior ethmoid sinuses are clear on both sides. Which drainage pathway should you inspect, and where does it lie?
quiz.answer: The left sphenoethmoidal recess. It lies between the superior turbinate and the nasal septum, above and behind the superior meatus, and it receives the sphenoid ostium; the posterior ethmoid cells drain into the adjacent superior meatus, which is why the two opacify together while the ostiomeatal complex sinuses stay clear.
quiz.explain: This is the posterior counterpart of the ostiomeatal pattern, and it is the one most often missed because the sphenoid sits at the edge of the field on coronal images and gets skipped. The recess is a narrow cleft medial to the superior turbinate, and the sphenoid ostium opens into it high on the anterior sinus wall, which is why sphenoid secretions drain badly when the patient is upright and why isolated sphenoid opacification can persist for months. Two things follow. First, isolated sphenoid disease in an adult is never quite routine: it causes vertex or retro-orbital headache rather than facial pain, it sits against the cavernous sinus, the optic nerves and the carotids, and the differential includes fungal disease and neoplasm as well as bacterial sinusitis. Second, the surgical route to the recess passes close to the skull base and the sphenopalatine artery, so your report should describe the recess itself, not just record that the sphenoid is opaque.

quiz.prompt: A pre-operative coronal CT shows the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate measuring 10 mm on the right and 5 mm on the left. By how much does the right measurement exceed the upper limit of Keros type II? Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: The Keros classification grades the depth of the olfactory fossa by the height of the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate: type I is 1 to 3 mm, type II is 4 to 7 mm, and type III is 8 to 16 mm. Ten millimetres exceeds the type II ceiling of 7 mm by 3, and puts the right side in type III. This matters because the lateral lamella is the thinnest bone of the entire anterior skull base, and the deeper the fossa the longer and more exposed that lamella is to an instrument working in the ethmoid roof. Type III therefore carries the highest risk of iatrogenic penetration, cerebrospinal fluid leak and, rarely, intracranial injury. Two further points belong in the report: state the depth on each side separately, because marked asymmetry is itself a hazard and the surgeon may not expect it, and note any asymmetry of the ethmoid roof height, which is a related and equally dangerous variant.

quiz.prompt: On a pre-operative sinus CT the most posterior ethmoid air cell extends above and lateral to the sphenoid sinus, and coronal images show a horizontal septation dividing the two. Which structure is now at particular risk, and what must the report say?
quiz.answer: The optic nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
choices: The optic nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The internal carotid, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The infraorbital nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
The vidian nerve, which may run bare in the wall of that cell
quiz.explain: A posterior ethmoid cell pneumatising superolaterally over the sphenoid is the Onodi or sphenoethmoidal cell, and its significance is entirely about the optic nerve. The nerve, normally safely tucked in the lateral wall of the sphenoid, ends up indenting or crossing the wall of this ethmoid cell, sometimes with dehiscent bone over it. A surgeon who believes he is in the last ethmoid cell and is working laterally is then working alongside the optic nerve, and the classic sign on coronal images is exactly the one described: a horizontal septation above the sphenoid, where the sphenoid septation would be vertical. Say it explicitly in the report and say which side. The internal carotid is the structure endangered by the lateral wall of a well-pneumatised sphenoid itself and by a septum inserting on its canal. The infraorbital nerve is put at risk by a Haller cell along the orbital floor, and the vidian nerve runs in the pterygoid canal below the sphenoid floor.

quiz.prompt: The sphenoid sinus is well pneumatised and its intersinus septum runs obliquely to insert on the bony canal of the left internal carotid artery, where the bone appears thinned. A transsphenoidal approach is planned. What should the report emphasise?
quiz.answer: Do not avulse the septum: it is anchored on the carotid canal
choices: Do not avulse the septum: it is anchored on the carotid canal
Do not resect the floor: it is anchored on the vidian canal
Do not open the recess: it is anchored on the optic canal
Do not drill the rostrum: it is anchored on the ethmoid roof
quiz.explain: The sphenoid intersinus septum is very often off-midline and oblique, and when its posterolateral end lands on the carotid canal, twisting or avulsing it during surgery can strip or fracture the thin bone and tear the artery. That is one of the few genuinely lethal complications of endoscopic sinus and pituitary surgery, so the finding earns an explicit sentence rather than a mention among variants. Describe which septum, which side it inserts on, and whether the bone over the carotid looks dehiscent, which on CT means no perceptible cortex over the vessel. Two related observations belong in the same paragraph: how far laterally the sphenoid pneumatises, since pneumatisation into the pterygoid process or greater wing brings the carotid and the maxillary nerve into the operative field, and whether the optic nerve canal is similarly dehiscent. None of the other three combinations described is an anatomical relationship that exists.

quiz.prompt: On a pre-operative CT the right uncinate process attaches superiorly to the lamina papyracea. What does that mean for the drainage of the right frontal sinus, and what does the surgeon need to be told?
quiz.answer: When the uncinate attaches laterally to the lamina papyracea, the ethmoid infundibulum ends blindly above as a terminal recess, so the frontal sinus cannot drain into it; the frontal recess instead drains medial to the uncinate, directly into the middle meatus. Tell the surgeon the frontal outflow is medial to the uncinate, so frontal disease can coexist with a clear infundibulum.
quiz.explain: The superior attachment of the uncinate process decides where the frontal sinus empties, and it varies from patient to patient and sometimes side to side. If the uncinate runs up to the lamina papyracea, the top of the infundibulum is closed off as a blind terminal recess and the frontal recess drains medial to the uncinate straight into the middle meatus. If it attaches instead to the skull base or to the middle turbinate, the frontal recess drains laterally into the infundibulum, and then infundibular disease and frontal disease travel together. The practical consequences are two. Reading: a patient can have an opaque frontal sinus with an entirely clear infundibulum, which is not a contradiction. Operating: the surgeon needs to know which side of the uncinate to look for the frontal outflow, and removing the uncinate blindly in the lateral-attachment pattern risks entering the orbit through the lamina papyracea.

quiz.prompt: Trace the path taken by mucus leaving the maxillary sinus, from its own ostium outwards into the nasal cavity.
quiz.answer: maxillary-ostium ethmoid-infundibulum hiatus-semilunaris middle-meatus
quiz.explain: Mucus leaves the antrum through its ostium high on the medial wall, which is why gravity is no help and mucociliary clearance does all the work. It then travels up the ethmoid infundibulum, the narrow three-dimensional channel bounded medially by the uncinate process and laterally by the lamina papyracea, escapes through the hiatus semilunaris, the crescentic gap between the free edge of the uncinate and the ethmoid bulla, and enters the middle meatus. Every step is a place where a few millimetres of mucosal swelling closes the pathway, which is why maxillary sinusitis is so often a middle meatal problem rather than an antral one. Two variants narrow the route further: a Haller cell hanging from the orbital floor into the roof of the antrum, and a large ethmoid bulla or concha bullosa crowding the hiatus. And an accessory ostium, when present, opens directly into the middle meatus and bypasses the infundibulum altogether, which is the route an antrochoanal polyp usually takes.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has had four months of nasal obstruction and facial pressure. CT shows circumferential mucosal thickening in both maxillary antra, thickened sclerotic bony walls, and no air-fluid levels anywhere. Which conclusion does the study support?
quiz.answer: Long-standing inflammation: sclerotic walls take months to develop
choices: Long-standing inflammation: sclerotic walls take months to develop
Acute bacterial infection: the mucosal thickening is a recent change
Aggressive infiltration: the bone reaction indicates tumour involvement
Post-surgical change: the antral walls remodel after previous surgery
quiz.explain: Reactive thickening and sclerosis of the sinus walls, sometimes called osteitis, is a marker of chronicity: it takes months of persistent inflammation to lay down, and it is the finding that lets you date the disease from a single scan. Acute rhinosinusitis looks different, with air-fluid levels, froth and oedematous mucosa over a normal-calibre bony wall, and in any case is a clinical diagnosis that rarely needs imaging at all; CT in chronic disease is done to map the anatomy for surgery, not to make the diagnosis. Tumour destroys or remodels bone rather than sclerosing it symmetrically and bilaterally, and would produce a unilateral soft-tissue mass, so unilateral is the word that should always slow you down on a sinus CT. Previous Caldwell-Luc surgery does thicken and sclerose an antral wall, but it is unilateral and comes with a defect in the anterior wall or a surgical antrostomy, neither of which is present here.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has a persistently blocked left nostril. An MRI performed for headache is reported as showing clear sinuses. On review, the left maxillary sinus is markedly dark on T2 and intermediate on T1, with a thin rim of enhancing mucosa around it. What should be done?
quiz.answer: Obtain a CT: markedly T2-dark contents can mimic an aerated sinus
choices: Obtain a CT: markedly T2-dark contents can mimic an aerated sinus
Accept the report: a dark sinus on T2 indicates normal aeration
Obtain a CT: the darkness suggests an aggressive marrow-based tumour
Repeat the MRI with contrast: the enhancing rim needs characterising
quiz.explain: This is the trap that MRI sets in the sinuses. A fungus ball is a dense mat of hyphae with concentrated manganese, iron and magnesium and almost no free water, so it is profoundly hypointense on T2 and can be a true signal void; read alone, the sinus looks aerated, and the only clue is the enhancing mucosal rim that air would not have. CT rescues it immediately, showing hyperattenuating material with punctate or amorphous calcification in a sclerotic, occasionally expanded sinus, usually a single maxillary or sphenoid sinus in an immunocompetent adult. Treatment is endoscopic removal and ventilation, not antifungal drugs. The same physics explains the dark central material of allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, which differs by being multi-sinus, expansile and bone-remodelling in an atopic patient with polyposis and a raised IgE. Very inspissated bacterial secretions can also be T2 dark. The habit to build is simple: never call a sinus clear on MRI alone.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old with acute myeloid leukaemia is neutropenic and has facial pain with a numb right cheek. CT shows only mild mucosal thickening in the right nasal cavity and a little stranding in the fat behind the maxillary sinus; the bone appears intact. What are you worried about, what MRI finding would support it, and what has to happen today?
quiz.answer: Acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis. Infiltration of the periantral fat before any bone destruction is the earliest sign, and on MRI a turbinate that fails to enhance after contrast, the black turbinate of mucosal necrosis, supports it. He needs same-day ENT endoscopy with biopsy, urgent surgical debridement and systemic antifungal treatment, alongside correction of the neutropenia.
quiz.explain: In a neutropenic, transplanted or ketoacidotic patient, facial pain with a numb cheek is an emergency and the CT is characteristically underwhelming. The disease is angioinvasive, so it crosses tissue planes through vessels long before it destroys bone: the first sign is infiltration of the periantral fat, in front of the maxilla or behind it in the retroantral fat, with an intact sinus wall, together with unilateral nasal mucosal thickening. Waiting for bone destruction means waiting for orbital, cavernous sinus and intracranial spread. MRI adds the loss of contrast enhancement in necrotic turbinate mucosa, the so-called black turbinate, and shows perineural and intracranial extension. Mortality is high and falls with hours, not days, so the report should reach the clinician by telephone. Treatment is surgical debridement plus a systemic antifungal, commonly liposomal amphotericin B, together with reversal of the underlying immunosuppression or ketoacidosis; imaging alone never excludes it, and endoscopy with biopsy is the arbiter.

quiz.prompt: A pre-operative sinus CT shows: a right lateral lamella of 9 mm; a posterior ethmoid cell extending superolateral to the sphenoid on the right; the sphenoid intersinus septum inserting on the left carotid canal; a 4 mm dehiscence of the left lamina papyracea with fat bulging medially; a right concha bullosa; and a Haller cell along the right orbital floor. How many of these six findings place the skull base, optic nerve, carotid artery or orbit directly at risk? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Four of the six are hazards that belong in a highlighted paragraph. A 9 mm lateral lamella is Keros type III and exposes the thinnest bone of the anterior skull base. A posterior ethmoid cell reaching superolateral to the sphenoid is an Onodi cell and endangers the optic nerve. A septum landing on the carotid canal endangers the artery if it is twisted out. A dehiscent lamina papyracea with herniating fat endangers the orbit and the medial rectus, and is the variant behind the classic complication of a surgeon following what looks like polyp into orbital fat. The other two are worth reporting but are not in that category: a concha bullosa is a pneumatised middle turbinate that can narrow the middle meatus and may be resected, and a Haller cell narrows the infundibulum and sits near the infraorbital nerve, but neither threatens the four structures named. The discipline this builds is separating the checklist that changes the operation from the anatomy that merely describes it.

quiz.prompt: A 15-year-old boy has recurrent heavy epistaxis and progressive nasal blockage. Contrast CT shows an avidly enhancing mass centred on the right sphenopalatine foramen, widening the pterygopalatine fossa and bowing the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus forwards. What is the correct next step?
quiz.answer: Cross-sectional angiography and embolisation planning, without biopsy
choices: Cross-sectional angiography and embolisation planning, without biopsy
Endoscopic biopsy in clinic to establish the histology before surgery
A trial of intranasal corticosteroids with repeat imaging at 3 months
Simple polypectomy through the nose under local anaesthetic in clinic
quiz.explain: Adolescent male, epistaxis, and a vascular mass at the sphenopalatine foramen that widens the pterygopalatine fossa and bows the posterior maxillary wall forwards, is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. The imaging is characteristic enough that biopsy is avoided: the lesion is fed mainly by the internal maxillary artery, often with ascending pharyngeal and sometimes internal carotid contributions, and a clinic biopsy can produce torrential bleeding. The pathway is cross-sectional angiography to map supply and intracranial extension, pre-operative embolisation, then endoscopic or open resection. Two things to report: how far the tumour reaches into the pterygopalatine fossa and beyond it into the infratemporal fossa or the cavernous sinus region, and any internal carotid supply, which limits how completely it can be embolised. The two lesions this sits between are the antrochoanal polyp, which arises in the antrum, passes through a widened ostium to the choana and enhances only at its rim, and the inverted papilloma, which arises on the lateral nasal wall in middle age.

quiz.prompt: An adenoid cystic carcinoma fills the right nasal cavity. On fat-saturated post-contrast T1 the right pterygopalatine fossa is filled with enhancing tissue and its normal fat has gone. Which structure should you follow next, and what would its involvement mean for the plan?
quiz.answer: Foramen rotundum and the cavernous sinus, along the maxillary nerve
choices: Foramen rotundum and the cavernous sinus, along the maxillary nerve
Stylomastoid foramen and the mastoid, along the facial nerve trunk
Jugular foramen and the cerebellopontine angle, along the vagus nerve
Hypoglossal canal and the tongue base, along the hypoglossal nerve
quiz.explain: The pterygopalatine fossa is the crossroads of the face, and loss of its fat on fat-saturated T1 is the sign that tumour has reached it. Five routes leave it: the foramen rotundum, carrying the maxillary nerve back to Meckel's cave and the cavernous sinus; the pterygoid canal, carrying the vidian nerve towards the petrous carotid; the inferior orbital fissure into the orbit; the pterygomaxillary fissure into the infratemporal fossa; and the palatovaginal canal into the nasopharynx. Adenoid cystic carcinoma has the highest perineural propensity of the sinonasal tumours, and its spread is often discontinuous, so a skip lesion can sit well behind an apparently clean margin. Intracranial extension usually moves the patient out of curative resection and into radiotherapy planning, and it changes the fields. Look for nerve enlargement, enhancement, and foraminal widening on thin coronals. The other three nerves listed have no anatomical connection to this fossa.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
ECG-gated CT, systolic phase (20-40%) reconstructed for annular sizing. Non-contrast series for calcium scoring. Full aorto-ilio-femoral run for access assessment.

FINDINGS
Annulus: diameter [n] mm, area [n] mm2, perimeter [n] mm, measured at [n]% phase.
Bicuspid valve: [absent / present — supra-annular measurement n mm].
Coronary height: left [n] mm, right [n] mm — [adequate / low, at risk of obstruction].
Aortic valve calcium score: [n] Agatston ([male/female threshold context]).
LVOT calcification: [absent / present, extent].
Access vessels: right common femoral [n] mm, left common femoral [n] mm, calcification/tortuosity [ ].
C-arm angulation for coplanar view: [n] degrees.

IMPRESSION
1. Annulus [n] mm / [n] mm2 / [n] mm perimeter — suggest valve size per manufacturer sizing chart.
2. Coronary obstruction risk: [low / elevated].
3. Access route: [transfemoral suitable / alternative route recommended, specify].
4. [LVOT calcium or other risk factors for annular rupture].
pitfalls: Sizing off a non-systolic phase — the annulus is smaller outside 20–40% of the cycle and this undersizes the valve.
Measuring a bicuspid annulus the same way as a tricuspid one — the functional restriction is often supra-annular at the leaflet tips, 4-5 mm above the ring.
Missing a low coronary ostium — under 10-12 mm height carries a real risk of coronary occlusion at deployment.
Reporting calcium score without noting sex — the severe-stenosis threshold differs for men and women.
Recommending transfemoral access without measuring the whole ilio-femoral route — a heavily calcified or tortuous segment proximal to an adequate common femoral artery still defeats the sheath.
