quiz.prompt: Two readers measure the same aortic annulus. One takes a 22 mm diameter off a single long-axis view of the root; the other reconstructs the plane through the three leaflet nadirs and reports an area-derived diameter of 25 mm. A valve chosen on the 22 mm figure leaks around its rim afterwards. What went wrong?
quiz.answer: A single linear diameter is just one chord across an oval ring
quiz.explain: The annulus is a virtual basal ring - a plane joining the three cusp nadirs, with no anatomical structure lying in it - and it is habitually oval, with a major-to-minor ratio of roughly 1.2 to 1.3. Any single long-axis view cuts that ring along one chord, and which chord it catches depends on how the plane happens to fall through a structure tilted in two directions, so the figure it yields is not the ring's size. Deriving a diameter from the traced area or perimeter uses the whole contour instead of one chord, which is why sizing charts are built on those figures and not on a caliper measurement. Note the direction of the error in 'Area-derived diameter overstates a ring that is not circular': by the isoperimetric inequality the area-derived diameter is the smallest of the conventions, not the largest.
choices: A single linear diameter is just one chord across an oval ring
An oblique long-axis cut stretches the ring along its long axis
Area-derived diameter overstates a ring that is not circular
The annulus shrinks once a stiff wire has crossed the valve

quiz.prompt: A planning dataset is reconstructed only in mid-diastole, where the coronary arteries are sharpest, and the annulus is traced there. What does sizing from that phase invite?
quiz.answer: Undersizing, with a leak around the frame or embolisation
quiz.explain: The basal ring is distensible and reaches its largest, roundest configuration in systole, when the outflow tract is pressurised; in diastole it is smaller and more oval. Measuring in diastole therefore biases the operator towards a smaller prosthesis, and a frame that fails to seal against the ring leaks around its outside or, if grossly small, embolises. The systolic-to-diastolic difference in annular area averages some 5 to 8%, so it need not cross a size boundary - but it is a one-way bias, and it runs towards the error that leaks. 'Oversizing, with rupture of the annulus during expansion' is the hazard of the opposite mistake, as is conduction block.
choices: Oversizing, with rupture of the annulus during expansion
Accurate sizing, since the fibrous annulus holds its shape
Undersizing, with a leak around the frame or embolisation
Oversizing, with new left bundle branch block after release

quiz.prompt: Planning CT shows a bulky shelf of calcium in the outflow tract just below the annulus. The operator intends a balloon-expandable valve at more than 20% area oversizing. What is the particular hazard of that combination, and what does it argue for?
quiz.answer: Annular rupture; cut the oversizing or use a self-expanding frame
quiz.explain: A balloon-expandable frame reaches its nominal size whatever is in the way, so the force of expansion is taken by whatever will not move. Rigid subannular calcium does not move: it is levered outward into the aortic root or the anterior mitral leaflet, and rupture there is frequently fatal. The two factors multiply - it was heavy outflow-tract calcification together with area oversizing beyond about a fifth that marked out the ruptures in Barbanti et al. (Circulation 2013), not either feature alone, which is why a modestly oversized frame in the same calcified root is a different proposition. A self-expanding frame applies gentler, sustained radial force and conforms around the calcium instead of displacing it, so it is the usual answer alongside restraint about oversizing and post-dilatation. 'Device migration; raise the oversizing and post-dilate the frame' inverts the remedy: more radial force against immovable calcium is the mechanism of the injury, not the escape from it.
choices: Coronary occlusion; place a protective wire in the left main stem
Annular rupture; cut the oversizing or use a self-expanding frame
Device migration; raise the oversizing and post-dilate the frame
Leaflet thrombosis; extend anticoagulation beyond the usual course

quiz.prompt: The left coronary ostium sits 8 mm above the annular plane, the left sinus measures 27 mm across, and the left cusp is 11 mm long and densely calcified. By what mechanism is that coronary threatened?
quiz.answer: The swept-aside cusp is longer than the ostium is high, in a sinus too small to hold it
quiz.explain: TAVI does not remove the native valve; it pins the diseased cusp against the sinus wall. The cusp is a hinged flap, so it sweeps up to a height set by its own length. If that length exceeds the ostial height and the sinus is too shallow to accommodate the displaced tissue, the cusp lies over the ostium like a lid, and a rigid calcified cusp holds that position. Open frame cells are not themselves obstructive, which is why strut position is a much weaker concern than cusp length, ostial height and sinus width taken together.
choices: The metal struts of the frame lie across the ostium and obstruct flow through the cells
The prosthetic leaflets swing out into the sinus and press on the ostium during systole
Calcium showers into the coronary as the balloon crushes the native cusp against the wall
The swept-aside cusp is longer than the ostium is high, in a sinus too small to hold it

quiz.prompt: A systolic annular contour is planimetered at 430 square millimetres. Treating that contour as a circle of the same area, what diameter in millimetres does it give? Give it to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The area-derived diameter is the diameter of the circle of equal area: d = 2 x sqrt(A / pi) = 2 x sqrt(430 / 3.1416) = 23.3986, so 23.4 mm to one decimal place. For any contour that is not a perfect circle this figure is smaller than the perimeter-derived diameter, and the gap widens as the ring becomes more oval - which is why stating which convention a number came from matters as much as the number itself.

quiz.prompt: Planning CT before TAVI shows a membranous septum only 3 mm long. Identify the structure that measurement locates, say what it predicts about the patient's course, and explain how it should shape the implantation plan.
quiz.answer: The His bundle penetrates at the inferior border of the membranous septum, so a short septum places the conduction tissue high in the outflow tract, immediately beneath where the frame will sit. If implantation depth exceeds the membranous septal length, the frame presses on the bundle and left bundle branch block or complete heart block may follow, making a permanent pacemaker likely. The plan should therefore aim for a shallow implant, avoid unnecessary oversizing, and provide for prolonged rhythm monitoring afterwards.
quiz.explain: The membranous septum is the roof of the conduction system's course: the bundle of His emerges at its inferior margin, beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Its length is therefore a direct measure of how much room lies between the annular plane and the conduction tissue. The quantity that matters in practice is the difference between septal length and implantation depth (Hamdan et al., JACC Cardiovascular Interventions 2015) - a depth greater than the septum is the geometry that predicts pacing, and it is one of the few TAVI risks the operator can still change on the table. Block is a strong risk here rather than a certainty, so the honest plan is a shallow implant plus rhythm monitoring, not a pre-emptive pacemaker.

quiz.prompt: The right external iliac artery has a minimum luminal diameter of 5.0 mm with an unbroken ring of calcium in its wall; the left measures 7.5 mm, is soft-walled, but loops through two tight bends. The delivery sheath is 6.0 mm across. Which route should be taken?
quiz.answer: The left, since a stiff wire straightens bends that hard calcium would not yield to
quiz.explain: Two things decide a transfemoral route: the narrowest luminal diameter along the whole path relative to the sheath, and whether the wall can give. A 6.0 mm sheath in a 5.0 mm lumen is a ratio well above the value at which vascular complications climb, and circumferential calcium removes the vessel's capacity to stretch, so the wall dissects or ruptures rather than dilating. Tortuosity in a soft, adequately sized vessel is the far weaker constraint: a stiff wire straightens it. Alternative access is for cases where neither side offers calibre or compliance.
choices: The left, since a stiff wire straightens bends that hard calcium would not yield to
The right, since a short narrowed segment stretches once the sheath is pushed through
The left, once the two tight bends have been stented open at an earlier sitting
Both sides fail here, so the case should go to a transcaval or axillary route

quiz.prompt: An eGFR of 28 forces a reduced-contrast protocol, and the radiographer proposes dropping the aortic run from 120 kVp to 80 kVp. Why does that allow less iodine for the same luminal opacification?
quiz.answer: Photon energies sit nearer iodine's K-edge, so each gram attenuates more
quiz.explain: Iodine's K-edge sits at about 33 keV. Lowering the tube potential shifts the spectrum down towards it, photoelectric absorption per gram of iodine rises steeply, and the same milligram of iodine yields a higher CT number - so the injected load can be cut for equal opacification. The price is noise: fewer and softer photons reach the detector, so tube current must rise to compensate, and the trade works best in slimmer patients. 'Beam hardening disappears at low kV, so calcium stops masking the lumen' is the trap and is backwards - beam hardening from calcium is worse at low kVp, not better. 'Low-energy photons slip past iodine, so the lumen is left looking brighter' is self-contradictory: photons that pass through would leave the lumen darker, not brighter.
choices: Fewer photons reach the detector, so the reconstruction lifts image contrast
Low-energy photons slip past iodine, so the lumen is left looking brighter
Photon energies sit nearer iodine's K-edge, so each gram attenuates more
Beam hardening disappears at low kV, so calcium stops masking the lumen

quiz.prompt: The planning CT is used to compute the fluoroscopic angulation that shows the annulus edge-on. The report gives not one gantry position but a curve of paired LAO/RAO and cranial/caudal values. Why is there a curve rather than a single angle, and what does that let the operator do?
quiz.answer: Any beam lying in the annular plane qualifies, so overlap can be dodged
quiz.explain: The three cusp nadirs define a plane, and a plane contains not one direction but a whole family of them: any X-ray beam lying in that plane sees the annulus edge-on and projects the three nadirs onto a single line. The angulations that satisfy this therefore trace a continuous curve of paired LAO/RAO and cranial/caudal values rather than one gantry position, and that freedom is the useful part - the operator slides along the curve to a projection that also keeps the spine, the pacing wire and overlapping structures out of the way. Cardiac phase and respiration are separate variables and generate no such curve, and the curve is a property of the patient's root, not of the device. Hunting for the same view in the laboratory instead means repeated aortic root injections, spending contrast and dose on a patient who often has little renal reserve to spare.
choices: Any beam lying in the annular plane qualifies, so overlap can be dodged
The curve allows for cardiac motion, so a phase can be picked to suit
Each point on it suits one valve size, so the chart follows the device
The curve spans the respiratory range, so a breath-hold can be avoided

quiz.prompt: A Sievers type 1 bicuspid valve has a heavily calcified raphe between the fused cusps. The annular area points to a 26 mm balloon-expandable valve, but the intercommissural distance a few millimetres above the annulus is appreciably smaller. What follows if the annular figure alone is used?
quiz.answer: The frame is held at the raphe above the annulus and expands unevenly there
quiz.explain: In a tricuspid valve the basal ring is the narrowest point the frame must pass, so annular sizing works. In bicuspid disease the constraining level is often supra-annular, at the calcified raphe between the fused cusps, and it can be several millimetres narrower than the annulus. Size to the annulus alone and the frame is effectively oversized where it is actually gripped: it deforms into an ellipse, seals poorly and leaks, and the load falls on a rigid calcified raphe with rupture as the extreme. Note that 'The frame is undersized throughout and drifts up into the ascending aorta' has the geometry backwards - the frame is over-, not undersized at the level that grips it. This is why bicuspid planning adds a measurement at the supra-annular level rather than trusting the basal ring.
choices: The frame seats too low, so that the basal ring carries the whole radial load
The frame is undersized throughout and drifts up into the ascending aorta
The frame expands fully but the native raphe covers a coronary ostium
The frame is held at the raphe above the annulus and expands unevenly there

quiz.prompt: A systolic annular contour is planimetered at 470 square millimetres. The operator is considering a balloon-expandable valve whose fully expanded frame is a circle 26 mm in diameter. By what percentage would that frame oversize the annulus by area? Answer as a percentage, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: The expanded frame has an area of pi x 13 squared = 530.9 square millimetres, and the oversizing is (530.9 - 470) / 470 = 0.1296, that is 13.0 per cent. Read that against the two failure modes on either side of it. Too little oversizing and the frame does not seal, so blood runs around its outside or the device embolises; balloon-expandable sizing charts therefore aim at a modest positive figure rather than a neutral one. Too much, and the expansion force is taken by whatever will not move, which is why oversizing beyond roughly a fifth in an outflow tract loaded with calcium is the combination associated with annular rupture. Note also that the number is only as good as the phase it came from: measure the same annulus in diastole and it will look smaller, so the calculated oversizing will read falsely high and tempt you into a valve that is actually too small.

quiz.prompt: Planning CT shows both iliofemoral routes to be unusable: the right external iliac artery is 4.5 mm with an unbroken ring of calcium and the left common iliac artery is occluded. The dataset already covers chest, abdomen and pelvis. Which alternative access routes would you assess on it, and for each, what decides whether it is usable?
quiz.answer: The subclavian or axillary artery is judged on its minimum luminal diameter along the whole course, on calcium and tortuosity, and on whether a patent internal mammary graft arises from it that the sheath would jail. The transcaval route needs a segment of infrarenal aorta lying close to the inferior vena cava with a calcium-free window on the aortic wall to cross, and the distance between the two vessels measured. Transapical access is judged on the left ventricular apex and the rib space overlying it, and transaortic or carotid access on a calcium-free ascending aorta or a patent carotid artery.
quiz.explain: The planning dataset already contains every one of these answers, which is why a report that stops at the femoral arteries wastes the scan. Each route has one dominant constraint. For the axillary and subclavian it is calibre and the internal mammary graft, since covering the origin of a graft that is feeding the heart is a serious matter. For transcaval it is the window: the crossing point must be aortic wall free of calcium, and the plan depends on knowing exactly where along the aorta that window sits. For transapical and transaortic it is the chest, and both are more invasive routes that have become uncommon as the others have improved. Say which route the anatomy supports and give the numbers behind it, rather than reporting only that the femoral route has failed.

quiz.prompt: Eighteen months after TAVI a patient is well and the echocardiographic gradients across the valve are unchanged from discharge. A CT performed for an unrelated reason shows crescentic hypoattenuated thickening on two of the three prosthetic leaflets. What does this represent, what acquisition would characterise it properly, and what should be done about it?
quiz.answer: This is hypoattenuated leaflet thickening, subclinical thrombus laid down on the aortic aspect of the cusps. Characterising it properly needs a retrospectively gated four-dimensional acquisition, because what matters is whether leaflet motion is restricted as well as thickened. With an unchanged gradient and no symptoms, the finding is followed rather than treated: most such thickening is subclinical and much of it resolves. Anticoagulation reliably clears it, but routine anticoagulation after TAVI produced more bleeding and death than an antiplatelet strategy in trial, so it is reserved for a rising gradient, restricted motion, or a thromboembolic event.
quiz.explain: Two words do the work here. Thickening is a static finding on a single phase; restricted motion is a dynamic one and needs images across the cardiac cycle, which is the whole reason a four-dimensional study is asked for rather than a single systolic phase. The distinction matters because the two carry different weight: thickening alone, with normal gradients, is common and mostly of no consequence, whereas reduced leaflet excursion with a climbing gradient is the beginning of valve failure. The GALILEO trial settled the management question in the unhelpful direction radiologists must nonetheless respect: a routine anticoagulant strategy after TAVI was worse, not better, than antiplatelet therapy. So the report describes what is seen, states whether motion was assessable, and stops short of prescribing.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a degenerated surgical bioprosthesis is being considered for a valve-in-valve TAVI. Working from the planning CT, explain why coronary obstruction is a greater danger here than in a native valve, and what you would measure to quantify that danger.
quiz.answer: In a native valve the displaced cusp is a short hinged flap and the sinus usually has room to hold it. In a valve-in-valve the failed bioprosthetic leaflets are pinned open by the new frame as a rigid cylinder at the level of the surgical stent posts, so the barrier sits higher, is fixed, and cannot be pushed aside. What is measured is the height of each coronary ostium above the surgical valve ring, the width of the sinus of Valsalva, the height and diameter of the sinotubular junction, and the distance from the projected new frame out to each ostium, together with the design of the failed valve, since externally mounted leaflets sit further out and obstruct more readily.
quiz.explain: The geometry to hold in mind is a cylinder inside a cone. Once the old leaflets are splayed vertically against the new frame, blood can only reach a coronary by passing between that cylinder and the aortic wall, or over the top of it through the sinotubular junction. So three measurements decide the risk together: how high the ostium sits, how much room lies between the projected frame and the ostium, and whether the sinotubular junction is high and wide enough to let flow come over the top. A narrow, low sinotubular junction converts an otherwise acceptable ostial height into a sealed sinus. Where the risk is real, the answer is planned in advance rather than improvised: leaflet laceration before implantation, a protective wire, or a decision that the patient belongs in theatre.

quiz.prompt: Put these vessels into the order a transfemoral delivery system meets them on its way from the groin puncture to the aortic valve.
quiz.answer: common-femoral-artery external-iliac-artery common-iliac-artery abdominal-aorta aortic-arch ascending-aorta
quiz.explain: The route is read retrograde, and the reason to walk it segment by segment is that the narrowest point anywhere along it governs the whole path: a generous common femoral artery is no comfort if the external iliac artery above it is 4 mm. Each segment also has its own question. At the puncture, where the common femoral artery crosses the femoral head and whether its anterior wall is calcified decides whether a closure device will work. The iliac segments give the minimum diameter and the calcium pattern. The abdominal aorta and the arch add atheroma and tortuosity, and a shaggy, ulcerated arch is a stroke risk to be flagged even when the calibre is ample. The ascending aorta and root then hand over to the valve measurements themselves.

curriculum_modules.title: Temporal Bone: Anatomy, Trauma and Pathology

module_contract.goal: Report a temporal bone study from the anatomy that surgery depends on: separate cholesteatoma from chronic inflammation, grade otosclerosis and fractures by what they predict, work up a cerebellopontine angle mass, and answer the questions a cochlear implant team asks.

approach.detail: A non-dependent soft-tissue mass in the middle ear, particularly in Prussak's space, points to cholesteatoma rather than the dependent, mucosa-thickening pattern of chronic otitis media.

approach.step: Check the predilection sites for erosion
approach.detail: Scutum, lateral semicircular canal, tegmen tympani and the long process of the incus are the sites cholesteatoma erodes; erosion here happens in a minority of chronic otitis media.
Erosion of the ossicular chain occurs in around 75% of cholesteatoma and is uncommon (under 10%) in chronic otitis media; displacement without erosion is not a cholesteatoma feature.

approach.step: Grade otosclerosis by where the lucency is
approach.detail: A small lucency at the fissula ante fenestram is fenestral disease; lucency around the cochlea as well marks combined disease; circumferential otospongiotic foci around the whole otic capsule form the 'fourth ring of Valvassori'.

approach.step: Trace the fracture rather than naming it longitudinal or transverse
approach.detail: Longitudinal fractures generally spare the inner ear and transverse fractures more often breach it, but many fractures are neither — describe every structure the fracture line actually crosses.

approach.step: Answer the cochlear implant team's specific questions
approach.detail: State mastoid pneumatisation, presence or absence of middle-ear inflammation, cochlear calcification or fibrous obliteration, and confirm the 8th nerve is present — its absence precludes implantation.

classify.name: Cholesteatoma versus chronic otitis media
rows: Discrete non-dependent mass, e.g. in Prussak's space
Thickened mucosal lining, not a discrete mass
Bony erosion at predilection sites (scutum, lateral semicircular canal, tegmen tympani, long process of incus)

pitfalls: Calling any middle-ear soft tissue cholesteatoma without checking whether it is a discrete non-dependent mass at a predilection site.
Missing early fenestral otosclerosis because the fissula ante fenestram lucency is subtle and easy to scroll past.
Forcing every temporal bone fracture into 'longitudinal' or 'transverse' when many fractures cross both patterns — describe the structures actually crossed instead.
Signing off a cochlear implant work-up without explicitly stating mastoid pneumatisation, middle-ear inflammation status, cochlear patency and 8th nerve presence.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old with a foul-smelling discharging ear has a retraction of the pars flaccida on otoscopy. CT shows non-dependent soft tissue filling the lateral epitympanic recess, blunting of the scutum, and erosion of the long process of the incus, with the mastoid opacified. What should the report say, and what must it exclude?
quiz.answer: Cholesteatoma; check lateral canal, tegmen and VII
choices: Cholesteatoma; check lateral canal, tegmen and VII
Granulation tissue; the ossicles would be spared
Tympanosclerosis; expect dense calcified plaques
Congenital cholesteatoma behind an intact drum
quiz.explain: Soft tissue in the middle ear is soft tissue on CT whatever it is made of, so the diagnosis rests on where it sits and what it has destroyed. A mass in the lateral epitympanic recess, medial to the pars flaccida and lateral to the malleus neck, with a blunted scutum, is an acquired pars flaccida cholesteatoma; the long process of the incus, with its precarious blood supply, is usually the first ossicle to go. Granulation tissue and chronic inflammation opacify without eroding bone, and tympanosclerosis appears as dense calcification. The report earns its keep with the complications: erosion of the lateral semicircular canal, which is the commonest labyrinthine fistula and threatens hearing and balance; the tegmen tympani, opening the way to meningitis, temporal lobe abscess or an encephalocele; the tympanic segment of the facial canal; and the sigmoid plate. Say whether the antrum and aditus are involved, as that shapes the operation.

quiz.prompt: Three years after a canal-wall-up mastoidectomy for cholesteatoma, a patient has soft tissue in the mastoid antrum on CT and no way to tell scar from recurrence. Which examination answers the question best?
quiz.answer: Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
choices: Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
Echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI
Immediate post-contrast T1-weighted MRI
Repeat high-resolution CT in twelve months
quiz.explain: Keratin restricts diffusion; granulation tissue, fluid and fibrous scar do not. That single fact turned second-look surgery from routine into the exception. The technique has to be non-echo-planar, however: echo-planar diffusion suffers badly from susceptibility artefact at the skull base, where bone, air and soft tissue meet, and it misses the small residual pearls that matter. Non-echo-planar sequences give thin sections with far less distortion and reliably show lesions of only a few millimetres, with the caveat that a very small or very early recurrence can still be missed and that bone dust, cholesterol granuloma and wax can occasionally mimic restriction. Delayed post-contrast imaging at around forty-five minutes, where granulation enhances and cholesteatoma does not, is the older approach and is now reserved for problem cases. Repeating CT gains nothing: both tissues have the same attenuation, which is why the question arose.

quiz.prompt: A child with progressive sensorineural hearing loss has a vestibular aqueduct measuring 1.9 mm at its midpoint on axial CT. Using the Valvassori criterion of 1.5 mm at the midpoint, by how much does this exceed the threshold? Answer in millimetres, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: One point nine minus one point five is 0.4 mm, which sounds trivial and is not: an enlarged vestibular aqueduct is the commonest imaging finding in a child with sensorineural hearing loss. The Valvassori criterion measures the midpoint against 1.5 mm; the later Cincinnati criteria are more sensitive, taking more than 0.9 mm at the midpoint or more than 1.9 mm at the operculum as abnormal, so quote which you have used. The association to look for is incomplete partition type II, where a normal basal turn accompanies a cystic apex and a dilated vestibule, and the syndromic link is Pendred syndrome with its SLC26A4 mutations, so a thyroid history is relevant. Two practical consequences follow: the hearing loss is characteristically stepwise and provoked by minor head injury, so contact sport is discouraged, and there is a raised risk of a perilymphatic gusher if the ear is implanted.

quiz.prompt: A temporal bone CT after a road collision shows a fracture crossing the vestibule and the basal turn of the cochlea, with a few bubbles of air within the labyrinth. State the two complications you would place first in the report, and why this fracture pattern predicts them.
quiz.answer: Profound sensorineural hearing loss and facial nerve injury come first: a fracture violating the otic capsule tears the membranous labyrinth and commonly runs through the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion, and cerebrospinal fluid leak with meningitis follows close behind.
quiz.explain: The old longitudinal-versus-transverse division described the fracture line; the otic-capsule-sparing versus otic-capsule-violating division describes what the patient loses, which is why it has replaced it in reporting. Violating fractures are much the rarer of the two but carry several times the rate of profound sensorineural deafness, facial palsy, cerebrospinal fluid leak, perilymphatic fistula and meningitis. Pneumolabyrinth, as here, is a direct sign that the labyrinth has been opened. The facial nerve is most often injured at the geniculate ganglion and the labyrinthine segment, so inspect them specifically and say whether the canal is displaced or transected, since immediate complete palsy with a transected nerve may go to exploration while a delayed partial palsy is managed conservatively. Then look at the carotid canal, which if breached demands angiographic assessment, and at the tegmen for an encephalocele.

quiz.prompt: After a lateral blow to the head, a patient has a conductive hearing loss and haemotympanum. CT shows a fracture running along the long axis of the petrous bone, sparing the otic capsule, and on the axial image through the epitympanum the rounded malleus head has separated from the body of the incus. What should the report state?
quiz.answer: Incudomalleolar dislocation causing conductive loss
choices: Incudomalleolar dislocation causing conductive loss
Stapes footplate fixation causing conductive loss
Perilymphatic fistula causing sensorineural loss
Cochlear ossification causing sensorineural loss
quiz.explain: On an axial section through the epitympanum the malleus head and the body of the incus make a shape like a scoop of ice cream on a cone; when the joint separates, the ice cream falls off, and that is what has happened here. Otic-capsule-sparing fractures typically produce conductive loss from haemotympanum, tympanic membrane injury and ossicular disruption, and the incudostapedial joint is the commonest to separate because the incus is anchored least securely of the three ossicles. Say which joint, since it determines the reconstruction. Timing matters as much as the finding: much early conductive loss is blood in the middle ear and resolves, so ossicular surgery waits until the effusion has cleared and the loss has proved persistent. Footplate fixation belongs to otosclerosis, not trauma, and the two sensorineural options require the otic capsule to have been breached, which it has not.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the segments of the facial nerve in the order the nerve passes through them, from the brainstem to the stylomastoid foramen.
quiz.answer: cisternal meatal labyrinthine tympanic mastoid
quiz.explain: The nerve leaves the pontomedullary junction, crosses the cerebellopontine angle as the cisternal segment, runs in the anterosuperior quadrant of the internal auditory canal as the meatal segment, then turns anterolaterally as the labyrinthine segment to the geniculate ganglion, where it gives the greater superficial petrosal nerve and makes its anterior genu. It then runs backwards as the tympanic segment beneath the lateral semicircular canal and above the oval window, turns at the posterior genu into the vertical mastoid segment, gives the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani, and exits at the stylomastoid foramen. Two things follow. The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest and lacks an epineural sheath, which is where a swollen nerve is trapped in Bell's palsy. And mild enhancement of the geniculate, tympanic and mastoid segments is normal, from the perineural venous plexus, so it is enhancement of the cisternal, meatal or labyrinthine segments that should worry you.

quiz.prompt: A 35-year-old woman has progressive conductive hearing loss with a normal tympanic membrane and intact ossicles. High-resolution CT shows a small focus of lucency in the bone immediately anterior to the oval window, with a normal pericochlear capsule. What should be reported, and what does it open the way to?
quiz.answer: Fenestral otosclerosis; stapedotomy becomes an option
choices: Fenestral otosclerosis; stapedotomy becomes an option
Retrofenestral disease with a pericochlear halo
Congenital stapes fixation with a normal capsule
Paget disease of the skull base in its early phase
quiz.explain: The fissula ante fenestram is a narrow cleft of cartilage just anterior to the oval window and is where otosclerosis almost always begins, so a lucent focus there in a young adult with conductive loss and a normal drum is the finding to name. Lucency reflects the active, resorptive otospongiotic phase; later disease sclerose and can become hard to see, which is why a normal CT does not exclude the diagnosis. Retrofenestral disease is the same process spreading around the cochlea to give a lucent halo and a sensorineural component, and the report should state whether it is present because it affects the counselling. Describe the footplate thickness, the patency of the round window, any facial nerve overhanging the oval window and any persistent stapedial artery, since each of these can obstruct or complicate a stapedotomy. Paget disease and osteogenesis imperfecta produce more diffuse skull base change.

quiz.prompt: A 3-year-old deafened by pneumococcal meningitis is being assessed for cochlear implantation. State the single finding on the CT and MRI that would make you telephone the implant surgeon the same day, and why it cannot wait.
quiz.answer: New ossification, or loss of the normal fluid signal, in the basal turn of the cochlea: labyrinthitis ossificans after meningitis obliterates the scala tympani, so implantation becomes urgent before the cochlea closes.
quiz.explain: Post-meningitic labyrinthitis ossificans begins with fibrosis and proceeds to new bone, typically starting in the basal turn near the round window, which is exactly where the electrode array must go. MRI is the more sensitive test early, because loss of the bright fluid signal on high-resolution T2 precedes anything visible on CT; CT then shows the ossification once it is established. Because the window for a straightforward full insertion may close within months, this is one of the few findings in a paediatric hearing assessment that carries genuine urgency, and it can justify implanting sooner or implanting the less affected ear first. The rest of the assessment can proceed at its own pace: cochlear nerve calibre, malformations, facial nerve course, jugular bulb position, mastoid pneumatisation and the state of the middle ear.

quiz.prompt: A child with unilateral profound sensorineural hearing loss has a cochlear nerve canal measuring 0.8 mm on CT, and on the oblique sagittal T2 through the internal auditory canal only three nerves are visible, the anteroinferior quadrant being empty. What does this mean for implantation?
quiz.answer: Cochlear nerve deficiency; implantation may not help
choices: Cochlear nerve deficiency; implantation may not help
A normal variant; proceed to implant that side
Labyrinthitis ossificans; implant the other side
An enlarged vestibular aqueduct; expect a gusher
quiz.explain: The parasagittal T2 through the internal auditory canal is the image the implant team most wants, because it shows the four nerves in cross-section: facial anterosuperiorly, cochlear anteroinferiorly, and the two vestibular nerves behind, separated from the facial nerve by Bill's bar and from the superior compartment by the falciform crest. The cochlear nerve should be at least as thick as the facial nerve; an empty anteroinferior quadrant means it is absent or hypoplastic. The bony cochlear nerve canal corroborates it, with a width below about 1.4 mm widely taken as stenotic. An implant stimulates the cochlear nerve, so without one the result is poor and the discussion turns to an auditory brainstem implant instead. Report both the nerve and the canal, and check the internal auditory canal itself, since a narrow canal often accompanies the deficiency.

quiz.prompt: On CT of a child with sensorineural hearing loss the basal turn of the cochlea is normal but the middle and apical turns are replaced by a single cystic cavity. Taking a normal cochlea as 2.5 turns and the fused cavity as occupying the outer one, how many turns are identifiable? Answer as a number of turns, to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: A normal cochlea makes two and a half turns around the modiolus; when the middle and apical turns fail to separate and merge into a single cystic cavity, one turn is lost and one and a half remain. That appearance, with a normal basal turn, is incomplete partition type II, the malformation long known by the eponym Mondini, and it usually travels with a dilated vestibule and an enlarged vestibular aqueduct. It is worth distinguishing from its neighbours. Incomplete partition type I gives a cystic cochlea with no modiolus at all alongside a dilated vestibule, and type III, the X-linked form, has a modiolus that is absent with an otherwise normal outer contour and a markedly widened fundus. Both type I and type III carry a high risk of a perilymphatic gusher at implantation, and type III often needs a specific electrode; type II is generally implanted with good results.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus has a 14 mm avidly enhancing extra-axial mass at the left cerebellopontine angle. It has a component filling and flaring the porus acusticus, makes acute angles with the petrous bone, and has no dural tail; the labyrinthine segment of the facial canal is normal. What is the most likely lesion, and on what grounds?
quiz.answer: Vestibular schwannoma, from the flared porus
choices: Vestibular schwannoma, from the flared porus
Meningioma, from a broad dural attachment
Epidermoid, which would restrict diffusion
Facial schwannoma, tracking to the geniculate
quiz.explain: The centre of gravity is the internal auditory canal and the porus is widened, which is what a vestibular schwannoma does as it grows out of the canal into the angle; the angles with the petrous bone are acute, and there is no dural tail. A meningioma sits eccentric to the canal on a broad dural base with obtuse angles, often with a tail, hyperostosis or calcification, and it may cap the porus without flaring it. An epidermoid does not enhance, insinuates around vessels and nerves, and restricts diffusion, while an arachnoid cyst follows cerebrospinal fluid on every sequence. The lesion always worth excluding before signing off is a facial nerve schwannoma, which is why the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion were inspected: extension there gives it away. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean NF2-related schwannomatosis. Record the maximal extrameatal diameter, since surveillance is judged on growth.

quiz.prompt: A CT shows complete opacification of the epitympanum, aditus, antrum and mastoid air cells, while the mesotympanum and protympanum are well aerated and the tympanic membrane is intact. State where the block must be, and the route air normally takes to reach the mastoid.
quiz.answer: The tympanic isthmus is blocked: air normally passes from the eustachian tube through the protympanum and mesotympanum, through the isthmus between the incus body and the tympanic facial nerve into the epitympanum, and then through the aditus into the antrum and mastoid cells.
quiz.explain: Middle ear ventilation is not one cavity filling uniformly; it is a series of narrow doors, and the pattern of opacification tells you which door has shut. Air enters the protympanum from the eustachian tube, crosses the mesotympanum, and reaches the epitympanum through the tympanic isthmus, the slot bounded by the incus body and malleus head laterally and the tympanic segment of the facial nerve medially. From the epitympanum the aditus ad antrum leads to the antrum and thence to the mastoid cells. Selective opacification of everything beyond the isthmus, with an aerated mesotympanum, therefore localises the obstruction precisely, and it is a recognised route to retraction of the pars flaccida and to cholesteatoma in Prussak's space. A blocked eustachian tube, by contrast, opacifies the whole middle ear from the protympanum outwards.

module_contract.goal: Select and follow patients for radioligand therapy using PSMA and DOTATATE imaging, and give sound radiation protection advice to the treated patient and their household.

source.title: Krenning score of neuroendocrine tumour uptake

approach.step: Establish what the scan is for — selection, localisation or follow-up
approach.detail: The imaging arm of a theranostic pair exists to decide whether the therapeutic arm will bind. Say explicitly whether the study supports treatment, and on what evidence.

approach.step: On somatostatin-receptor imaging, find the lesion with the highest uptake
approach.detail: The Krenning score is assigned to that single lesion, compared against liver and spleen — or the kidney where the spleen is not available.

approach.step: Learn the normal DOTATATE biodistribution before you call a lesion
approach.detail: High-intensity uptake in the spleen physiologically. Moderate in liver, uncinate process of the pancreas, pituitary, adrenals and bowel. Mild in salivary and thyroid glands. Almost none in the brain apart from focal pituitary activity. Urinary excretion.

approach.step: Name the ligand, not just "a PSMA scan"
approach.detail: 68Ga-PSMA-11 (Illuccix), 68Ga gozetotide (Locametz), 18F piflufolastat (Pylarify), 18F flotufolastat (Posluma) — VISION selected patients on 68Ga PSMA-11. The therapeutic agent is 177Lu-PSMA-617.

approach.step: Confirm PSMA expression before therapy is offered
approach.detail: PSMA is upregulated on about 95% of prostate cancer cells, but selection for radioligand therapy requires demonstrated expression on an approved PET agent, not an assumption.

approach.step: Follow up on the same axis you selected on
approach.detail: Response is monitored with PSMA PET/CT, or with SPECT/CT using the 208 keV gamma emission of Lu-177 after each administration.

approach.step: Say where the dose lands in normal tissue
approach.detail: For 177Lu-PSMA the highest absorbed doses go to salivary glands, lacrimal glands, kidneys and bladder wall. That is where xerostomia, dry eyes and renal toxicity come from, and it is what the patient should be warned about.

approach.step: Give protection advice grounded in the physics of the isotope you used
approach.detail: Lu-177 has a 6.65-day half-life, emits a 208 keV gamma, and is excreted renally. Household precautions and their duration are set by your local radiation protection adviser — quote theirs, not a remembered number.

measure.how: Governs the interval between doses and the duration of any protection advice.
Determines how much normal tissue around a deposit is irradiated.
Set the SPECT window to it.
Intravenous, with dose modification, interruption or discontinuation graded by CTCAE and the prescribing information.
measure.cutoff: 7.4 GBq (200 mCi) every 6 weeks, up to 6 doses

measure.how: The biological reason the target works at all.
measure.cutoff: Upregulated on about 95% of prostate cancer cells

measure.how: Binds somatostatin receptor subtype 2. DOTATOC targets subtype 3; DOTANOC subtypes 3 and 5.
The number to quote when a patient asks what the treatment buys.
measure.cutoff: Median survival 11.3 → 15.3 months; PFS 3.4 → 8.7 months (831 patients)

classify.name: Krenning score — somatostatin-receptor uptake
columns: Uptake in the most avid lesion
rows: Uptake less than or equal to liver
classify.note: Scored against liver and spleen — or kidney where the spleen is unavailable — on the single lesion with the highest uptake. Designed for indium-111 DTPA planar or SPECT imaging and carried over unchanged to SSTR PET as the modified Krenning score; the determination is identical. Its commonest present use is assessing candidacy for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Scores run higher on PET than on planar or SPECT imaging, particularly for lesions under 2 cm.

reference.template:
TECHNIQUE
[Ga-68 DOTATATE / Ga-68 PSMA-11 / F-18 piflufolastat] PET/CT, [n] MBq intravenously, uptake time [n] minutes, [skull base to mid-thigh / vertex to toes]. [Low-dose / diagnostic] CT. Comparison: [date and agent — state if the agent differs].

FINDINGS
Physiological biodistribution: [as expected / altered by ...].
Most avid lesion: [site], [size] mm, SUVmax [n].
SSTR studies — Krenning score of the most avid lesion: [0-4], referenced to [liver / spleen / kidney].
PSMA studies — sites of PSMA-expressing disease: [prostate bed / nodal stations / bone / visceral], most avid SUVmax [n].
Disease not expressing the target: [none / describe — this is what the therapy will not treat].
Organs at risk: [salivary and lacrimal glands, kidneys, bladder wall — note any abnormality].

IMPRESSION
1. [Target-expressing disease: extent, in plain words.]
2. [SSTR: Krenning (0-4).] [PSMA: expression present and sufficient / insufficient / discordant.]
3. Suitability for [PRRT / 177Lu-PSMA-617]: [supported / not supported], because [reason].
4. [Baseline for response assessment; recommended interval and modality.]
pitfalls: Scoring Krenning off an average or a summed impression. It is assigned to the single most avid lesion, against liver and spleen.
Comparing a Krenning score from planar or SPECT imaging with one from PET. PET scores run higher, especially for lesions under 2 cm, and a patient can appear to have progressed on modality alone.
Calling splenic uptake abnormal on DOTATATE. High-intensity splenic activity is physiological, as is moderate uptake in the uncinate process, pituitary, adrenals and bowel.
Reporting "a PSMA scan" without the agent. Selection evidence differs by ligand — VISION used 68Ga-PSMA-11 — and serial comparison across agents is not like for like.
Ignoring disease that does not express the target. Non-expressing lesions are precisely the ones radioligand therapy will not touch, and they belong in the impression.
Treating actinium-225 PSMA therapy as established. It emits alpha particles and remains under research; it is not approved by the FDA or EMA.
Quoting a household restriction period from memory. Take the interval from your radiation protection adviser; the isotope's 6.65-day half-life and 208 keV gamma are the physics, not the policy.

learning_points: Target uptake is one criterion alongside whole-body distribution, disease status, organ function, prior therapy and treatment-specific criteria.
The therapeutic ligand binds the same target distribution and carries a therapeutic radionuclide to expressing tissue.
Dosimetry, blood counts, renal or salivary toxicity, response and radiation-safety advice complete the pathway.

Review lesion distribution and target expression.
Review discordant lesions and anatomic correlation.
Review physiological uptake, pitfalls and relevant organ findings.
Target expression on one scan is not the sole criterion for treatment eligibility; integrate the disease and treatment-specific pathway.

quiz.prompt: A gallium-68 PSMA PET/CT performed for staging shows a focus of moderate uptake just lateral to the coeliac axis, along the anterior aspect of the left crus, arising from a slightly elongated 6 mm structure. The CT shows no discrete lymph node there.
quiz.answer: Report coeliac ganglion uptake rather than a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis
choices: Report coeliac ganglion uptake rather than a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis
Report a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis and upstage him to M1a disease
Report an adrenal metastasis, which characteristically lies anterior to the crus
Report a neuroendocrine tumour, since ganglia do not bind PSMA ligands at all
quiz.explain: Autonomic ganglia express PSMA, and the coeliac ganglion is the single most important false positive on these studies. The clues are morphological: a band-like or teardrop shape rather than a round node, a paired and symmetrical position hugging the crus adjacent to the coeliac trunk, uptake typically lower than a true nodal deposit, and no lymph node on the CT component. The stakes are high, because calling it a node moves a man from potentially curative local treatment to systemic therapy. Physiological uptake also occurs in lacrimal and salivary glands, liver, spleen, kidneys, small bowel and the urinary tract. Non-prostatic pathology that takes up PSMA ligands includes renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, thyroid disease, glioma, Paget disease, fibrous dysplasia, healing rib fractures and reactive nodes in sarcoidosis.

quiz.prompt: A man with Gleason 4+5 prostate cancer and a PSA of 32 ng/mL is being assessed for radical treatment. The multidisciplinary team asks whether to stage him with CT and bone scintigraphy or with PSMA PET/CT.
quiz.answer: PSMA PET/CT, which was substantially more accurate than CT with bone scan in a randomised trial
choices: PSMA PET/CT, which was substantially more accurate than CT with bone scan in a randomised trial
CT with bone scan, which was substantially more accurate than PSMA PET/CT in a randomised trial
CT with bone scan first, reserving PSMA PET/CT for cases where the bone scan is equivocal
Whole body MRI, which a randomised trial showed to be superior to PSMA PET/CT for staging
quiz.explain: The proPSMA trial randomised men with high-risk prostate cancer before curative-intent treatment to gallium-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT or to conventional imaging with CT and bone scintigraphy. PSMA PET/CT achieved around 92 per cent accuracy for nodal and distant disease against roughly 65 per cent for conventional imaging, with fewer equivocal findings, less radiation exposure and more changes in management. On that basis it is now accepted as a first-line staging investigation in high-risk disease rather than a problem-solving add-on. One consequence worth carrying into the multidisciplinary meeting: a more sensitive test causes stage migration, so a cohort staged by PSMA PET is not directly comparable with historical series staged by CT and bone scan, and apparent improvements in outcome may be partly an artefact of better staging.

quiz.prompt: Six years after radical prostatectomy a man's PSA is 0.12 ng/mL on two separate occasions. His general practitioner has referred him for PSMA PET/CT to find the site of recurrence.
quiz.answer: Explain that detection at this PSA level is poor and follow the PSA before imaging him
choices: Explain that detection at this PSA level is poor and follow the PSA before imaging him
Proceed to PSMA PET/CT now, since detection rates are high below 0.2 ng/mL
Proceed to bone scintigraphy now, which outperforms PSMA PET at very low PSA
Explain that this PSA already satisfies the Phoenix definition of biochemical failure
quiz.explain: After radical prostatectomy, biochemical recurrence requires a confirmed PSA of 0.2 ng/mL or above, so 0.12 does not yet meet the threshold. The Phoenix definition, nadir plus 2 ng/mL, belongs to patients treated with radiotherapy and does not apply after surgery. Detection rate on PSMA PET rises steeply with PSA: pooled data give roughly 40 per cent at a PSA of 0.2 to 0.5, around 60 per cent at 0.5 to 1.0, about three-quarters between 1 and 2, and over 90 per cent above 2 ng/mL. A short PSA doubling time and high Gleason grade raise the yield at any given level. Scanning too early produces a negative study that answers nothing, delays nothing useful and consumes a slot, so the sensible advice is to repeat the PSA and image when the number will support the question.

quiz.prompt: A man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer has progressed after abiraterone and docetaxel. Screening PSMA PET/CT shows avid bone and nodal disease with uptake well above liver background, but a 3 cm liver metastasis seen on CT shows no PSMA uptake at all.
quiz.answer: He is unsuitable, because a measurable metastasis without uptake would receive no treatment
choices: He is unsuitable, because a measurable metastasis without uptake would receive no treatment
He is suitable, because most of his disease shows uptake greater than the normal liver
He is suitable, because liver metastases are treated by the beta particles regardless
He is unsuitable, because previous docetaxel exposure excludes radioligand therapy
quiz.explain: The screening scan before lutetium-177 PSMA-617 asks two questions, and both must be answered favourably. First, is there at least one lesion with uptake greater than normal liver, confirming the target is expressed and bright. Second, is there any measurable lesion that lacks uptake, since a sizeable PSMA-negative deposit is disease the radioligand cannot reach and is likely to be what kills the patient. A 3 cm PSMA-negative liver metastasis fails the second test. In the VISION trial the regimen was 7.4 GBq every six weeks for up to six cycles added to standard care, improving median overall survival to about 15.3 months against 11.3. Prior taxane exposure was an entry requirement in that trial rather than an exclusion; the pre-taxane setting has been studied separately. Xerostomia from salivary uptake, fatigue and marrow suppression are the main toxicities.

quiz.prompt: A patient with a grade 3 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour has a DOTATATE PET showing only faint uptake, below that of normal liver, while an FDG PET performed a week later shows intense uptake in the same lesions.
quiz.answer: Report a discordant pattern that argues against peptide receptor therapy and suggests aggressive biology
choices: Report a discordant pattern that argues against peptide receptor therapy and suggests aggressive biology
Report a concordant pattern that supports proceeding with peptide receptor therapy at full dose
Report the DOTATATE study as technically inadequate and simply repeat it in a week's time
Report the FDG uptake as inflammatory in origin and proceed with peptide receptor therapy
quiz.explain: This is the dual-tracer flip-flop. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours express somatostatin receptor subtype 2 densely and are relatively FDG-quiet; as they dedifferentiate they lose receptor expression and switch to glycolysis. FDG-positive, DOTATATE-negative disease therefore carries a markedly worse prognosis and will not respond to peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, because there is nothing for the peptide to bind. Uptake at or below liver corresponds to a Krenning score of 2 or less and generally fails eligibility, which requires score 3 or 4. Two practical points: report the least avid lesion as well as the most avid, since heterogeneity determines what the therapy will miss; and long-acting somatostatin analogues can in principle compete for the receptor, so scans are usually scheduled shortly before the next depot injection.

quiz.prompt: A woman with papillary thyroid carcinoma underwent a staging CT with iodinated contrast three weeks ago. Her radioiodine ablation is currently booked for next week and the endocrine team asks whether to go ahead.
quiz.answer: Defer the ablation, because the stable iodine load will compete with the therapeutic dose
choices: Defer the ablation, because the stable iodine load will compete with the therapeutic dose
Proceed as booked, because iodinated contrast is fully cleared within a few days
Proceed as booked, but double the administered activity to overcome the iodine load
Defer the ablation, because iodinated contrast permanently blocks thyroidal uptake
quiz.explain: Iodinated contrast expands the stable iodide pool for weeks, and stable iodide competes with iodine-131 at the sodium-iodide symporter, so the therapeutic activity is diluted and taken up poorly. Most departments wait around four to eight weeks after contrast, some checking a urinary iodine before proceeding. Increasing the administered activity does not overcome competitive inhibition; it just increases dose to everything else. The rest of the preparation follows the same physiology: a low-iodine diet for one to two weeks, and TSH raised above about 30 mIU/L either by thyroid hormone withdrawal or by recombinant human TSH, since TSH drives symporter expression. Two further points of current practice: low-risk patients often need no radioiodine at all, and where remnant ablation is given, 1.1 GBq has been shown as effective as 3.7 GBq.

quiz.prompt: A man with castration-resistant prostate cancer has painful widespread bone metastases, no visceral disease, and a 4 cm retroperitoneal nodal mass. The oncologist asks whether radium-223 would be a reasonable choice for him.
quiz.answer: Radium-223 acts only within bone, so his bulky nodal disease would go untreated
choices: Radium-223 acts only within bone, so his bulky nodal disease would go untreated
Radium-223 treats nodal and skeletal disease alike, so it suits his pattern well
Radium-223 is unsuitable here because his skeletal disease is causing him pain
Radium-223 requires visceral metastases to be present before it can be offered
quiz.explain: Radium-223 is a calcium mimetic: it deposits at sites of high bone turnover, which in this disease means the osteoblastic reaction around metastases. Its alpha particles have a range of only a few cell diameters, under about 100 micrometres, which is exactly why it delivers high linear energy transfer damage to the tumour microenvironment while relatively sparing marrow — and equally why it does nothing whatever for soft tissue or nodal disease. The ALSYMPCA trial enrolled men with symptomatic bone-predominant disease and no visceral metastases, excluding bulky lymphadenopathy, and showed improved overall survival of roughly 14.9 against 11.3 months with fewer symptomatic skeletal events. Symptomatic bone disease is the indication, not a contraindication. Since ERA-223 found increased fractures when it was combined with abiraterone and prednisolone, that combination is avoided and bone-protective therapy is given.

quiz.prompt: A man treated with 3.7 GBq of iodine-131 for differentiated thyroid carcinoma is ready for discharge. He lives with his wife and a three-year-old daughter, and asks what he needs to do once he gets home.
quiz.answer: Sleep separately, keep his distance from the child, and use a separate toilet for some days
choices: Sleep separately, keep his distance from the child, and use a separate toilet for some days
Sleep separately for a single night, then resume close household contact from the next day
Stay away from the family home for six months, until the iodine has decayed completely
Take no precautions, since iodine-131 emits only beta particles of very short range
quiz.explain: Iodine-131 emits both a therapeutic beta particle and a 364 keV gamma photon that leaves the patient, so external dose to household contacts is real, and it is excreted in urine, saliva and sweat, so contamination matters as much as external exposure. Typical advice after ablation is to sleep alone, limit close contact time with young children and pregnant women, use a toilet carefully and flush it, wash hands thoroughly, avoid sharing utensils and towels, and avoid long journeys seated close to others. Durations are set by the dose rate measured at discharge and by local dose constraints, and run from a few days to a couple of weeks depending on activity and on who is at home. The physical half-life is around 8 days and the effective half-life shorter. Conception is deferred for about six months, and breastfeeding must cease permanently for that infant.

quiz.prompt: At discharge, the dose rate measured at 1 metre from a patient treated with iodine-131 is 45 microsieverts per hour. Assuming inverse square behaviour and no shielding, what is the dose rate at 3 metres? Answer in microsieverts per hour to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Tripling the distance divides the dose rate by nine: 45 divided by 9 gives 5.0 microsieverts per hour. This is the cheapest and most powerful protective measure available at the bedside, and it is the arithmetic behind almost every piece of household advice you will give. Since dose equals rate multiplied by time, a relative sitting on the far side of the room for an hour receives less than one sitting beside the patient for seven minutes. Discharge criteria in most jurisdictions are written in terms of measured dose rate at one metre and estimated dose to contacts and the public, rather than administered activity alone. Two caveats when you use the calculation clinically: a patient is not a point source, and self-attenuation within the body means measured rates in practice are usually lower than a pure inverse square estimate predicts.

quiz.prompt: A colleague asks what makes the PSMA and DOTATATE agents theranostic. Explain the principle in one or two sentences, and say what the diagnostic scan is actually deciding.
quiz.answer: The same targeting molecule carries either an imaging radionuclide or a therapeutic one, so the diagnostic scan shows whether the target is expressed and where, and it decides eligibility by proving the therapy will bind the patient's disease.
quiz.explain: Gallium-68 or fluorine-18 is used for imaging and lutetium-177, a beta emitter, or actinium-225, an alpha emitter, for treatment, mounted on the same vector molecule. The diagnostic study is effectively a whole-body biopsy of receptor expression, sampling every lesion at once — something no tissue sample can do, and the reason a single negative biopsy does not settle the question. It answers three things: is the target present, is it present in all the measurable disease, and is it bright enough against a reference organ. After treatment, imaging the small gamma yield of lutetium-177 confirms that the activity went where the diagnostic scan predicted, occasionally shows disease not previously seen, and provides the counts for dosimetry.

quiz.prompt: State why an amino acid infusion is given alongside lutetium-177 DOTATATE therapy, and which organ it is protecting.
quiz.answer: An infusion of lysine and arginine competitively blocks proximal tubular reabsorption of the radiopeptide, protecting the kidneys from radiation nephropathy, which is the dose-limiting organ toxicity of this treatment.
quiz.explain: Small radiolabelled peptides are freely filtered at the glomerulus and then reabsorbed by the megalin-cubilin receptor system in the proximal tubule, which concentrates activity in the renal cortex and makes the kidney the organ that limits how much can be given. Positively charged amino acids saturate that reabsorption pathway competitively, and are started before the radiopeptide and continued for several hours afterwards; the infusion is emetogenic, so antiemetic cover is routine. The NETTER-1 regimen was 7.4 GBq every eight weeks for four cycles in progressive, receptor-positive midgut neuroendocrine tumours, with a large gain in progression-free survival. Bone marrow is the other dose-limited tissue, and a small percentage of patients later develop myelodysplasia, which is worth mentioning at consent.

quiz.prompt: After each cycle of lutetium-177 PSMA therapy the patient returns for imaging at around 24 hours. Say what that post-therapy study is for.
quiz.answer: The post-therapy study images the gamma emission of lutetium-177 to confirm that the activity localised to the known lesions, to look for disease not seen before, and to provide the counts for dosimetry of the kidneys and marrow.
quiz.explain: Lutetium-177 conveniently emits low-abundance gamma photons at 113 and 208 keV alongside its therapeutic beta particles, so an ordinary gamma camera can image the treatment itself — a real advantage over pure beta and alpha emitters, where you administer the dose and hope. The study documents biodistribution and confirms delivery to the targets identified at screening; it occasionally reveals additional lesions; and with serial time points it supports patient-specific dosimetry of kidneys, marrow and salivary glands, which is moving steadily from research towards routine practice. The finding that should give you pause is a photopenic area where a known lesion sits, indicating heterogeneous target expression and a region that will not have been treated.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these reference levels of tumour uptake in the order the Krenning score ranks them, from score 1 up to score 4.
quiz.answer: very-low-uptake uptake-at-or-below-liver uptake-above-liver uptake-above-spleen
quiz.explain: The Krenning score grades somatostatin receptor expression visually against internal reference organs, with score 0 for no uptake at all, then very low uptake, uptake at or below normal liver, uptake above liver, and finally uptake exceeding normal spleen or kidney. It began with indium-111 octreotide scintigraphy and carried over to gallium-68 DOTATATE PET, where the reference organs are conveniently on the same images. Scores 3 and 4 indicate receptor density sufficient for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, and score 4 predicts the best response; score 2 or less generally fails eligibility. The discipline that separates a useful report from a decorative one is grading the least avid measurable lesion as well as the brightest, because heterogeneity is what the therapy will fail to control.

quiz.prompt: Put the steps of a first radioiodine treatment for differentiated thyroid carcinoma into the order in which they occur.
quiz.answer: total-thyroidectomy low-iodine-diet TSH-stimulation I-131-administration post-therapy-whole-body-scan
quiz.explain: Each step prepares the one after it. Surgery comes first because a bulky normal remnant takes up iodine avidly and would soak up the activity intended for residual tumour while irradiating the neck. A low-iodine diet for one to two weeks shrinks the competing stable iodide pool, for the same reason iodinated contrast must be avoided beforehand. TSH is then raised above roughly 30 mIU/L, either by withdrawing thyroid hormone or by giving recombinant human TSH, because TSH upregulates the sodium-iodide symporter that carries iodide into the cell. The capsule is administered, and a whole-body scan three to seven days later maps what actually took up the activity. That post-therapy scan is considerably more sensitive than any pre-therapy diagnostic scan, simply because far more activity is on board, and it not infrequently reveals unsuspected metastatic disease.

curriculum_modules.title: Thyroid Nodules: ACR TI-RADS and What Follows

module_contract.goal: Score a thyroid nodule with ACR TI-RADS, decide between aspiration, surveillance and doing nothing, and respond proportionately to a nodule found incidentally on CT, MRI or PET.

source.title: TI-RADS — Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System

approach.detail: Cystic/almost completely cystic and spongiform (≥50% cystic) both score 0; mixed cystic and solid scores 1; solid/almost completely solid scores 2.
Score the solid component (or the whole nodule if entirely solid): anechoic 0, hyper-/isoechoic 1, hypoechoic 2, markedly (very) hypoechoic — darker than strap muscle — 3.
Wider-than-tall scores 0; taller-than-wide scores 3, assessed on the transverse view.
Smooth or ill-defined scores 0; lobulated or irregular scores 2; extrathyroidal extension scores 3.
None, or large comet-tail artefacts, scores 0; macrocalcifications 1; peripheral (rim) calcifications 2; punctate echogenic foci 3. More than one type may be present — add every point that applies.

approach.step: Sum the points and assign the category
approach.detail: Add every point across all five categories to get the total, then read off TR1–TR5.

measure.what: Nodule size for the FNA/follow-up decision
measure.how: Measure the largest diameter on the view where it is largest.
measure.cutoff: TR3 FNA ≥ 2.5 cm, follow-up ≥ 1.5 cm · TR4 FNA ≥ 1.5 cm, follow-up ≥ 1 cm · TR5 FNA ≥ 1 cm, follow-up ≥ 0.5 cm

measure.what: Whether to size the nodule at all
measure.how: Nodules under 5 mm need no follow-up regardless of TI-RADS category.
Compare two dimensions between studies.
measure.cutoff: Significant growth = ≥ 20% increase in two dimensions (minimum 2 mm) or ≥ 50% volume increase

classify.name: ACR TI-RADS categories
classify.note: Point values and thresholds cross-checked against the ACR TI-RADS white paper (JACR 2017) — TR3 rows require no FNA below their listed size but do get surveillance at their smaller follow-up threshold. A maximum of four nodules should be fully characterised per exam, and FNA is not recommended for more than two nodules in one patient. TI-RADS does not apply to paediatric patients, FDG-PET-avid nodules, nodes, or patients with a hereditary thyroid cancer syndrome.

modifiers.meaning: A nodule stable in size over 5 years of follow-up can be considered benign and followed no further.

pitfalls: Scoring echogenicity or foci on the cystic component instead of the solid portion of a mixed nodule.
Forgetting that more than one echogenic-focus type can be present — all applicable points are added, not just the highest.
Recommending FNA on a TR3 or TR4 nodule below its size threshold because '4–6 points' felt worrying — the threshold is fixed to the category, not to gut feel.
Re-biopsying or over-following a nodule that has already been stable for 5 years.
Applying TI-RADS to a node, a paediatric patient, or an FDG-avid nodule, where the system does not apply.

radiology_reference.overview: Score a thyroid nodule with ACR TI-RADS, decide between aspiration, surveillance and doing nothing, and respond proportionately to a nodule found incidentally on CT, MRI or PET.
learning_points: Composition, echogenicity, shape, margin and foci add points.
The total expresses imaging suspicion, not certainty.
Category-specific thresholds separate aspiration from surveillance.
Review thyroid size and background parenchyma.
Review each nodule: location and three dimensions.
Review composition, echogenicity, shape, margins and echogenic foci.

A category and a management recommendation are separate outputs; the latter also depends on nodule size and clinical context.
