quiz.prompt: Ultrasound shows a solid nodule that is hypoechoic, wider-than-tall, with a lobulated margin and a single macrocalcification. Score it using the ACR TI-RADS (2017) point system. Answer as a whole number of points.
quiz.explain: Solid composition scores 2, hypoechoic scores 2, wider-than-tall scores 0, a lobulated or irregular margin scores 2, and a macrocalcification scores 1, giving 7 points. Since TR5 begins at 7 points in the ACR TI-RADS (2017) chart, this is TR5 and needs aspiration at 1.0 cm or more, and follow-up from 0.5 cm. The item worth taking away is that a nodule can reach the highest category without either of the two features people think of as the frightening ones: it is neither taller-than-wide nor speckled with punctate foci. Points accumulate. The other habit to build is scoring composition, echogenicity, shape and margin once each, taking the single highest applicable value in each column, while echogenic foci are scored cumulatively because a nodule may carry more than one kind. Levels run TR1 at 0 points, TR2 at 2, TR3 at 3, TR4 at 4 to 6, and TR5 at 7 or more.

quiz.prompt: A nodule scores 5 points on ACR TI-RADS (2017) and measures 12 mm in its greatest dimension, with no suspicious cervical nodes. By how much would it have to grow before the ACR recommends fine-needle aspiration? Answer in millimetres, as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Five points is TR4, and the ACR TI-RADS (2017) recommendation for TR4 is aspiration at 1.5 cm or more, with imaging follow-up from 1.0 cm. At 12 mm this nodule is already in follow-up but 3 mm short of the biopsy threshold. Keep the full grid available, because the whole system turns on it: TR1 and TR2 need neither aspiration nor follow-up; TR3 is aspirated at 2.5 cm and followed from 1.5 cm; TR4 is aspirated at 1.5 cm and followed from 1.0 cm; TR5 is aspirated at 1.0 cm and followed from 0.5 cm. Follow-up intervals are years 1, 3 and 5 for TR3, years 1, 2, 3 and 5 for TR4, and annually to five years for TR5. Two caveats. Growth is judged generously, usually 20 per cent in two dimensions with at least 2 mm, because inter-observer measurement error is real. And a suspicious node overrides all of this.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these four echogenic-foci findings in ascending order of the points ACR TI-RADS assigns to them.
quiz.answer: large-comet-tail macrocalcifications peripheral-calcifications punctate-echogenic-foci
quiz.explain: The echogenic foci column runs 0, 1, 2, 3. Large comet-tail artefacts, longer than about a millimetre, score 0 because they are reverberation from inspissated colloid crystals and are a positively reassuring sign, seen in benign colloid nodules. Macrocalcifications score 1: coarse and shadowing, they are mostly degenerative, though they are not innocent and can sit within a papillary or a medullary carcinoma. Peripheral or rim calcification scores 2, and the finding that raises real concern is interruption of the rim with soft tissue extruding beyond it. Punctate echogenic foci score 3, the maximum, because non-shadowing specks correspond to psammoma bodies and are the most specific ultrasound feature of papillary carcinoma. The discrimination that matters at the machine is between a punctate focus and a small comet-tail: turn up the gain, zoom in, and look for the short tail. Getting that one call wrong moves a nodule three points, which is often a whole category.

quiz.prompt: A sonographer asks why ACR TI-RADS gives three points to a taller-than-wide nodule and three to punctate echogenic foci, when a lobulated margin gets only two. Answer her, and say in which plane the shape must be judged.
quiz.answer: Both carry three points because both are highly specific for malignancy even though neither is sensitive: a taller-than-wide nodule has grown across the normal tissue planes rather than along them, which is invasive behaviour, and punctate echogenic foci correspond to the psammoma bodies of papillary carcinoma. Shape is judged on the transverse image, comparing the anteroposterior dimension with the transverse one.
quiz.explain: The point weights in ACR TI-RADS are driven by specificity, not by how often a feature turns up. Benign nodules grow with the grain of the gland and end up wider than they are deep; a nodule taller than it is wide has ignored the tissue planes, which is what invasion looks like on a two-dimensional image. Punctate non-shadowing foci are the sonographic correlate of psammoma bodies, and although they appear in only a minority of papillary carcinomas, they are rarely seen in anything else. A lobulated or irregular margin scores less because it is common, is judged less reproducibly, and occurs in benign hyperplastic nodules too. Two practical notes. Shape is assessed on the transverse plane only, because a nodule can appear taller than wide on a longitudinal image without meaning anything. And an ill-defined margin scores 0 in this system, which surprises people: a fuzzy border proved not to predict malignancy, whereas frank invasion does.

quiz.prompt: A 1.4 cm solid hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe has a smooth border except posterolaterally, where it interrupts the thyroid capsule and a small tongue of tissue lies within the strap muscle. How should the margin be scored, and what does that do?
quiz.answer: Extra-thyroidal extension, 3 points, the highest margin score there is
choices: Extra-thyroidal extension, 3 points, the highest margin score there is
Lobulated or irregular, 2 points, the commonest malignant margin
Ill-defined, 0 points, because the border is simply hard to resolve
Smooth, 0 points, because most of the border is well demarcated
quiz.explain: Margin is scored once, taking the highest applicable value, and definite invasion of tissue beyond the capsule is the top of that column at 3 points in ACR TI-RADS (2017). Do not average around the circumference: one convincing area of extension outranks a smooth remainder. The finding is worth hunting for because it is one of the few sonographic features that changes more than a category. Gross extra-thyroidal extension into strap muscle or beyond alters the operation, the stage and the risk group, so it is worth stating exactly which structure is involved and over what length. Distinguish it from simple capsular abutment, where the nodule touches the capsule without interrupting it, which does not count. An ill-defined margin, meaning a border you cannot resolve, genuinely scores 0 in this system, because it did not predict malignancy in the data the committee reviewed; the concerning border is lobulated or irregular, at 2 points.

quiz.prompt: A registrar has scored a nodule at 3 points and wants to raise it because colour Doppler shows marked central vascularity and shear-wave elastography reads it as stiff. How should the report handle that?
quiz.answer: Report it at 3 points: neither finding is part of the point system
choices: Report it at 3 points: neither finding is part of the point system
Report it at 5 points: each of the two findings adds a point
Report it at 6 points: stiffness carries the same weight as shape
Report it at 4 points: vascularity adds one and stiffness adds none
quiz.explain: ACR TI-RADS deliberately restricted itself to five grey-scale categories. Doppler patterns were left out because intranodular vascularity is common in benign hyperplastic nodules and did not add independent, reproducible value, and elastography was left out because it is machine- and operator-dependent and was not available on every system the system had to work on. Nothing stops you describing either finding in prose; they simply do not move the score, and a score that has been quietly inflated is worse than no score, because the whole point of the system is that two readers reach the same number. Two other exclusions are worth knowing. TI-RADS is for adults; paediatric nodules carry a substantially higher malignancy risk and are managed differently. And it scores the nodule, not the neck: abnormal cervical lymph nodes sit outside the system and override it entirely.

quiz.prompt: A gland contains eleven nodules. Three score 4 points and measure 1.8, 1.6 and 1.1 cm. Two score 3 points and measure 2.9 and 2.6 cm. The remainder score 2 points. Which nodules should be aspirated?
quiz.answer: The 1.8 and 1.6 cm four-point nodules, and no more than those two
choices: The 1.8 and 1.6 cm four-point nodules, and no more than those two
The 2.9 and 2.6 cm three-point nodules, since they are the largest
The three four-point nodules and the two three-point ones as well
The 1.8 cm nodule alone, since one aspirate represents the gland
quiz.explain: Score every nodule separately, then rank by level rather than by size. The three 4-point nodules are TR4, whose aspiration threshold is 1.5 cm, so the 1.8 and 1.6 cm ones qualify while the 1.1 cm one enters surveillance instead. The 2.9 and 2.6 cm nodules are TR3, and they do cross their own 2.5 cm threshold, which is why this looks like five candidates. What settles it is the ACR recommendation that no more than two nodules be aspirated in one gland, choosing those at the highest level, because sampling many nodules multiplies indeterminate cytology and surgery without improving the detection of clinically important cancer. So the TR4 pair is aspirated and the TR3 pair goes to follow-up. Sampling the largest nodule is the reflex worth unlearning: size drives the threshold within a level, never the choice between levels. And one aspirate never speaks for the gland, because each nodule is a separate clone.

quiz.prompt: A 1.3 cm nodule scoring 8 points was aspirated and the cytology returns as Bethesda category I, nondiagnostic, with too few follicular cells. The clinic asks what to do. What do you advise, and what would change that advice?
quiz.answer: Repeat the aspiration under ultrasound guidance rather than accepting the result, aiming at the solid vascularised part of the nodule and away from any cystic component, since a nondiagnostic sample carries no reassurance at all. If a second attempt is again nondiagnostic in a nodule scoring this high, move to diagnostic lobectomy rather than a third pass.
quiz.explain: Bethesda I is not a result, it is a failed test, and the commonest error is to file it as though it were negative. The malignancy risk of the nodule is unchanged by a nondiagnostic sample, so a TR5 nodule remains a TR5 nodule. Repeat sampling under ultrasound guidance resolves most of them, provided the operator targets the solid, vascular portion rather than a cystic or necrotic area, and provided there is on-site adequacy assessment where available. If it fails again, the sonographic suspicion decides: for a high-scoring nodule the route is diagnostic lobectomy, whereas a repeatedly nondiagnostic TR3 nodule can reasonably be watched. The other Bethesda categories that come back to imaging are II, benign, which returns the patient to sonographic surveillance at an interval set by the TI-RADS level, and III, atypia of undetermined significance, which typically leads to repeat aspiration, molecular testing or diagnostic lobectomy rather than to more imaging.

quiz.prompt: A 3.2 cm nodule scoring 8 points was aspirated and the cytology is reported as Bethesda category II, benign. The patient is well and euthyroid. What imaging follow-up should be arranged?
quiz.answer: Ultrasound within a year, with repeat sampling at that same visit
choices: Ultrasound within a year, with repeat sampling at that same visit
No further ultrasound, because benign cytology settles the matter
Ultrasound in five years, matching the cytological risk alone
Immediate surgery, because sonographic risk overrides the cytology
quiz.explain: This is a discordant pair: a strongly suspicious nodule with reassuring cytology. Benign cytology has a low but real false-negative rate, and that rate matters more the higher the sonographic suspicion, partly because a large nodule is easier to miss within. The standard response, set out in the 2015 American Thyroid Association guideline for a high-suspicion sonographic pattern with benign cytology, is repeat ultrasound with repeat ultrasound-guided aspiration within 12 months, rather than either discharging the patient or operating. Compare that with a benign result in a TR3 nodule, where a single ultrasound at a longer interval, or discharge, is entirely reasonable. Two habits follow. Always report the TI-RADS level alongside the cytology in your follow-up recommendation, because the pair is what determines the interval. And flag discordance explicitly in the report, since a benign cytology result filed without comment is the usual mechanism by which such nodules are lost to follow-up.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has a 1.4 cm nodule scoring 3 points, which at that size needs neither aspiration nor imaging follow-up. In the right level III chain there is a 12 mm rounded node with no fatty hilum, punctate echogenic foci within it and peripheral vascularity. What does that change?
quiz.answer: The node, not the nodule, becomes the target. A rounded shape, loss of the fatty hilum, punctate echogenic foci and peripheral rather than hilar vascularity describe a metastatic node, and nodal status sits entirely outside the TI-RADS score. Aspirate the node, send a thyroglobulin washout with the cytology, and treat the thyroid nodule as the likely primary regardless of its own points.
quiz.explain: TI-RADS scores a nodule in isolation, and this is the situation in which following it blindly does harm. The nodal features listed are the ones that matter: rounded rather than oval, absent fatty hilum, cystic change, punctate calcification, hyperechoic tissue resembling thyroid, and peripheral or chaotic rather than hilar vascularity. Punctate calcification and cystic change are the most specific of them for papillary carcinoma. When such a node is present, it is the node that is sampled, because it gives both the diagnosis and the stage in one pass, and washout of the needle for thyroglobulin markedly improves sensitivity over cytology alone, particularly in a cystic node. The 3-point nodule is then treated as the presumed primary and imaged carefully for extra-thyroidal extension, and the whole neck is mapped by level for the surgeon. Never let a low nodule score talk you out of a suspicious node.

quiz.prompt: A 62-year-old having a staging CT for colon cancer is found to have a 1.2 cm low-attenuation nodule in the right thyroid lobe. There is no local invasion and the cervical nodes are normal. What should the report recommend?
quiz.answer: No dedicated thyroid imaging: it is below the threshold at this age
choices: No dedicated thyroid imaging: it is below the threshold at this age
Dedicated thyroid ultrasound: a nodule of this size warrants scoring
Dedicated thyroid ultrasound and aspiration at the same attendance
Repeat CT of the neck in six months to look for interval growth
quiz.explain: The ACR white paper on incidental thyroid findings sets an age-dependent threshold for working up a nodule seen on CT or MRI: under 35 years, from 1 cm; at 35 and above, from 1.5 cm. At any age, a nodule accompanied by suspicious features on the same study, meaning local invasion or abnormal cervical nodes, is worked up regardless of size. At 62 with a 1.2 cm nodule and a clean neck, this falls below the threshold and the correct recommendation is none. The reasoning is proportionality: incidental thyroid nodules are extremely common, the great majority of the cancers found are indolent papillary carcinomas, and in a patient with colonic malignancy the cascade of ultrasound, aspiration, indeterminate cytology and hemithyroidectomy carries far more certain harm than the nodule does. Note also that repeating a CT characterises nothing: CT cannot assess composition, echogenicity, margin or echogenic foci, so only ultrasound can produce a TI-RADS score.

quiz.prompt: Two patients undergo PET-CT for lymphoma staging. In the first, the whole thyroid takes up FDG uniformly. In the second, a single intense 1.1 cm focus of uptake sits in the left lobe. What should each report recommend?
quiz.answer: Thyroid function tests for the first, and ultrasound for the second
choices: Thyroid function tests for the first, and ultrasound for the second
Ultrasound for the first, and thyroid function tests for the second
Ultrasound for both, since focal and diffuse uptake carry equal risk
Nothing for either, since uptake will settle after lymphoma therapy
quiz.explain: Diffuse thyroidal FDG uptake is almost always chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, and sometimes Graves disease, so it is a biochemical question and not an imaging one: thyroid function tests and antibodies, no ultrasound. Focal uptake is different. Reported malignancy rates for the focal thyroid incidentaloma cluster around a third, considerably higher than for a nodule found incidentally on ultrasound, so it earns a dedicated thyroid ultrasound and a TI-RADS score regardless of size, with aspiration if score and size call for it. Two riders. Avidity itself adds no points; it is a reason to look, not part of the score, and a benign-appearing nodule on ultrasound still carries some residual risk that many would biopsy in this setting. And proportionality applies at the other end too: in a patient with advanced disease and a short life expectancy, doing nothing may be the right answer, and the report should say so rather than leaving it unspoken.

quiz.prompt: A 3.1 cm nodule in the left lobe is anechoic with a thin smooth wall and no solid component, and several bright foci with long comet-tail artefacts drift within the fluid. The patient has no compressive symptoms and a normal TSH. What should be recommended?
quiz.answer: No aspiration and no imaging follow-up, since the nodule scores zero
choices: No aspiration and no imaging follow-up, since the nodule scores zero
No aspiration, but ultrasound at one, three and five years hence
Aspiration now, because the size has crossed 2.5 centimetres
Aspiration now, because the bright foci are worth three points
quiz.explain: Work the columns. Cystic composition scores 0, anechoic scores 0, wider-than-tall scores 0, a smooth margin scores 0, and large comet-tail artefacts score 0, giving a total of 0 points, which is TR1 in ACR TI-RADS (2017). TR1 needs neither aspiration nor follow-up at any size, so the 3.1 cm measurement is irrelevant here; the 2.5 cm threshold belongs to TR3. Aspiration may still be offered for compressive or cosmetic symptoms, but that is a therapeutic drainage and not a diagnostic test, and it is worth saying so in the report so the patient is not sent for cytology by mistake. The feature to get right is the comet tail. A bright focus with a long tapering tail, longer than about a millimetre, is reverberation from colloid crystals and scores 0; a bare non-shadowing speck is a punctate echogenic focus and scores 3. Zoom in and look for the tail before you commit.

protocol: Record pulsatile versus non-pulsatile symptom, side and hearing findings. Select temporal-bone, IAC or arterial/venous imaging accordingly.

pitfalls: A vascular loop/contact is common and may be incidental.
Routine negative MRI does not exclude all dural arteriovenous fistulas.

Is there a concerning vascular or skull-base lesion?
What remains unassessed by this protocol?

quiz.prompt: Before choosing imaging for tinnitus, which clinical distinction most directly changes the search strategy?
choices: Whether the symptom follows the pulse
The scanner manufacturer
Whether the patient prefers CT
The length of the referral letter
quiz.answer: Whether the symptom follows the pulse
quiz.explain: Pulsatility directs attention toward vascular and related structural causes. Otoscopy, laterality, hearing findings and neurological symptoms further define the appropriate pathway.

quiz.prompt: Pulsatile tinnitus accompanies a retrotympanic lesion on otoscopy. Which study best depicts the bony temporal-bone anatomy and vascular canal relationships?
choices: Unenhanced lumbar MRI
Thin-section temporal-bone CT
A skull scout alone
Routine abdominal CT
quiz.answer: Thin-section temporal-bone CT
quiz.explain: High-resolution CT evaluates bone and canal anatomy. Additional vascular or contrast-enhanced imaging depends on the suspected lesion; an apparent middle-ear mass is not automatically inflammatory.

quiz.prompt: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus occurs with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss. Which imaging target is especially relevant?
choices: The rectal wall
The rotator cuff
Internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles
The lumbar facet joints
quiz.answer: Internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles
quiz.explain: MRI can assess a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. The audiological pattern and laterality determine the focused question.

quiz.prompt: Noninvasive imaging is unrevealing, but a specialist remains concerned about a dural arteriovenous fistula. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: A normal routine brain MRI excludes every fistula
No vascular assessment can add information
Tinnitus alone proves a fistula
Selected cases may need catheter angiography after specialist review
quiz.answer: Selected cases may need catheter angiography after specialist review
quiz.explain: Small shunts can evade a routine examination. Catheter angiography is an invasive problem-solving test when the residual clinical suspicion justifies it.

quiz.prompt: CT finds a jugular-bulb variant on the same side as tinnitus. How should causality be expressed?
choices: A potential correlate requiring clinical and anatomical correlation
A proven cause solely because it is ipsilateral
A finding that excludes all other causes
A malignant tumour unless biopsied
quiz.answer: A potential correlate requiring clinical and anatomical correlation
quiz.explain: Anatomical variants can be incidental. Report their relationship to the middle ear and bony covering, without converting coexistence into proof of symptom causation.

quiz.prompt: A tinnitus referral contains no information about pulsatility, side, hearing or otoscopy. Explain why ordering the same scan for every such referral is a poor protocol strategy.
quiz.answer: These details define different diagnostic targets. Clarify pulse synchrony, laterality, hearing findings, otoscopy and neurological symptoms. Pulsatile symptoms may require vascular or temporal-bone assessment, while selected unilateral non-pulsatile presentations raise a retrocochlear question. Choose the examination to answer the resulting clinical question rather than treating tinnitus as one anatomical diagnosis.
quiz.explain: Protocol selection begins with the phenotype of the symptom. Missing referral details can change both modality and anatomical coverage.

quiz.prompt: A routine non-contrast brain MRI is reported normal in a patient with persistent pulsatile tinnitus. The clinician asks whether that excludes a vascular shunt. How would you answer?
quiz.answer: No. State which vascular information the acquired study can and cannot provide. A normal routine brain examination is not equivalent to a negative dedicated vascular investigation. The need for further targeted imaging or catheter angiography depends on clinical suspicion, prior testing and specialist assessment.
quiz.explain: A test result must be interpreted against the protocol. Exclusion claims should not extend beyond its coverage and sensitivity.

quiz.prompt: A right jugular-bulb variant is found, but the patient describes left-sided tinnitus. How should this affect the impression?
quiz.answer: Record the variant and its relevant anatomical relationships, but note that its side does not match the reported symptom. Do not present it as the established cause. Confirm the clinical laterality and consider whether the actual symptomatic side and appropriate alternative causes have been adequately assessed.
quiz.explain: An attractive imaging finding can be incidental. Side concordance is a basic check against premature causal attribution.

quiz.prompt: Temporal-bone imaging shows a retrotympanic soft-tissue lesion adjacent to vascular structures. What should a useful report establish before a definitive lesion label is applied?
quiz.answer: Localise the lesion, describe its enhancement if assessed, bony changes and relationship to vascular canals and middle-ear structures. Consider a vascular lesion in the differential and identify any need for further characterisation. Avoid a definitive inflammatory or neoplastic label unsupported by the available imaging.
quiz.explain: Anatomical relationships can determine the next safe diagnostic step even when the precise histology remains uncertain.

quiz.prompt: An internal-auditory-canal MRI finds a small lesion during assessment of unilateral tinnitus. What information should the report provide beyond the lesion name?
quiz.answer: Record side, location within the canal or cerebellopontine angle, dimensions, enhancement and relevant nerve or brainstem relationships. Compare with prior imaging where available and describe study limitations. Relate the finding to the clinical side without implying that its size alone predicts hearing loss or symptom severity.
quiz.explain: An actionable report establishes a baseline and location. Imaging anatomy and clinical function remain related but distinct observations.

quiz.prompt: A vessel touches the cisternal trigeminal nerve but does not distort it. What should the report avoid?
choices: Naming the vessel
Describing the side
Calling contact alone definitive symptomatic neurovascular compression
Reviewing high-resolution multiplanar images
quiz.answer: Calling contact alone definitive symptomatic neurovascular compression
quiz.explain: Contact can occur without symptoms. A stronger imaging argument includes morphological nerve change at a relevant site, interpreted with the clinical side and syndrome.

quiz.prompt: A patient has progressive facial numbness rather than brief triggered pain. Where should the MRI search extend?
choices: Only the root entry zone
Only the cerebellar tonsils
Only the nasal cavity
The full pathway from brainstem through skull-base foramina and peripheral branches
quiz.answer: The full pathway from brainstem through skull-base foramina and peripheral branches
quiz.explain: Trigeminal neuropathy may arise at several anatomical levels. Full pathway assessment helps detect tumour, inflammation, demyelination and perineural spread.

quiz.prompt: An enhancing lesion occupies Meckel's cave and extends through a trigeminal skull-base foramen. Which reporting detail matters?
choices: The involved branch, foramen and proximal extension
Only the largest axial diameter
Only whether the ventricles are enlarged
The absence of a scalp lesion
quiz.answer: The involved branch, foramen and proximal extension
quiz.explain: Localise the lesion along the nerve and map foraminal and cavernous-sinus extension. This anatomy guides the differential and further evaluation.

quiz.prompt: A facial malignancy is followed by new V3 numbness. MRI shows thickening and enhancement along the mandibular nerve. What must be considered?
choices: A normal consequence of ageing
Perineural tumour spread
An isolated vestibular disorder
A diagnosis excluded by a small primary tumour
quiz.answer: Perineural tumour spread
quiz.explain: Symptoms and an abnormal nerve course raise concern for perineural spread. Trace the pathway to the foramen ovale and intracranial segments rather than stopping at the primary site.

quiz.prompt: A patient with facial sensory symptoms has a focal pontine T2 lesion near the trigeminal nuclei. Which principle applies?
choices: Every trigeminal symptom arises from an arterial loop
The brainstem can be excluded if the cisternal nerve looks normal
Central pathology can explain the symptom and needs its own differential
A pontine lesion proves metastatic disease
quiz.answer: Central pathology can explain the symptom and needs its own differential
quiz.explain: The pathway begins centrally. A pontine lesion requires assessment for demyelinating, vascular, neoplastic and inflammatory causes in the clinical context.

quiz.prompt: A vascular loop indents the left trigeminal nerve, but the patient's attacks are right-sided. How would you frame the finding and the remaining search?
quiz.answer: Describe the left-sided contact and morphological change accurately, but state the side mismatch. Do not attribute the right-sided symptoms to it without additional evidence. Review the right trigeminal pathway and consider alternative causes, with clinical confirmation of symptom side and distribution.
quiz.explain: Visible compression can be important without explaining the presenting syndrome. Anatomical and clinical concordance must be tested rather than assumed.

quiz.prompt: An MRI requested for facial numbness only includes thin cisternal sequences. Explain what it could miss and how the limitation should be reported.
quiz.answer: It may incompletely assess the brainstem, Meckel's cave, cavernous sinus, skull-base foramina and peripheral branches. State the actual coverage and avoid excluding disease throughout the trigeminal pathway. If symptoms suggest neuropathy or secondary disease, a broader targeted assessment may be needed.
quiz.explain: A focused sequence can answer a narrow question well while leaving other segments unevaluated. The report must preserve that boundary.

quiz.prompt: A treated facial tumour is followed by V2 numbness and enhancement extending toward the skull base. What distribution should the report trace rather than simply measuring the primary site?
quiz.answer: Trace the abnormality along the expected V2 pathway, including the pterygopalatine region, foramen rotundum and more proximal trigeminal structures as covered. Describe thickening, enhancement, foraminal change and intracranial extent, and state concern for perineural spread in the clinical context.
quiz.explain: Nerve-related spread follows an anatomical route that can extend beyond the apparent primary lesion. A route map can be more consequential than one tumour diameter.

quiz.prompt: The symptomatic trigeminal nerve is displaced by an adjacent lesion. A colleague reports “neurovascular conflict” without identifying a vessel. Explain how to correct the reasoning.
quiz.answer: First determine the nature of the adjacent structure using the available sequences and enhancement pattern. Describe the lesion, nerve displacement and location, and distinguish a mass-related effect from vascular contact. If the structure remains uncertain, report that uncertainty and the additional characterisation needed rather than assigning a mechanism by proximity alone.
quiz.explain: The mechanism requires identification of the responsible structure. Nerve displacement does not by itself establish a vascular cause.

quiz.prompt: The referral describes both brief triggered pain and progressive persistent numbness. Why should the imaging review not stop after finding an arterial contact?
quiz.answer: The arterial contact may be incidental or explain only part of the syndrome. Progressive sensory deficit warrants assessment of the full nerve pathway for secondary disease. Describe the contact, any morphological nerve change and any other abnormality, then correlate the imaging with both the pain pattern and persistent deficit.
quiz.explain: A single finding should not erase clinical features it fails to explain. The mixed presentation broadens the question being answered.

module_contract.goal: Set frequency, focus and gain for the question in front of you, work Doppler within the limits its physics imposes, and read ultrasound artefacts as evidence rather than as noise.

also.title: Recommendations for the Identification and Mitigation of Cardiac Ultrasound Artifacts (2026)

approach.step: Decide what the artefact is telling you before you try to remove it
approach.detail: Shadowing makes the gallstone, enhancement makes the cyst, mirroring through the diaphragm excludes a pleural effusion, twinkling finds the stone you could not shadow. Some artefacts are the finding.

approach.step: Set the focal zone against the question
approach.detail: Bring the focus to the level of the object. A shadow deepens as the focal zone approaches the shadowing surface; twinkling is more obvious when the focal zone sits below the rough reflector rather than above it.

approach.step: Change the angle before you change the machine
approach.detail: Reverberation, mirroring and multipath all depend on the geometry between probe and reflector. Rocking the probe to alter the angle of insonation abolishes all three.

approach.step: On tendons, keep the beam perpendicular
approach.detail: A fibrillar structure returns maximum echo only at 90°. Off-axis it goes black and reads as tendinosis or tear. Heel-toe the probe and watch the hypoechogenicity come and go.

approach.step: Set the velocity scale to the flow, not the other way round
approach.detail: Raise the PRF/velocity scale to increase the unaliased frequency range. Moving the spectral baseline reallocates the displayed range between directions; it does not raise the sampling rate.

approach.step: Keep the angle of insonation small for velocity
approach.detail: A small beam-to-flow angle supports velocity accuracy but increases the Doppler shift at a fixed speed. A higher transmit frequency also increases the shift; greater depth limits the available PRF. Do not sacrifice angle accuracy simply to hide aliasing.

measure.how: Half the pulse repetition frequency. Doppler shifts above it are recorded with the wrong direction and velocity.
The machine converts return time to depth on a fixed velocity in soft tissue; every depth error, including speed displacement, follows from it.
Watch for red and blue directly adjacent with no intervening black line of no flow.
Set the colour velocity scale high enough that intrarenal arterial aliasing does not mimic twinkle. Colour gain, not PRF, reliably alters twinkling itself.
Time gain compensation overcompensates through a weakly attenuating structure, brightening what lies deep to it.
measure.cutoff: At 1 MHz water attenuates ~2000× less than soft tissue

classify.name: Reading the artefact
rows: Absent signal deep to an interface
Nearly all the beam reflected or absorbed — dense solid or a soft tissue/air impedance mismatch
Use it: it makes the gallstone. Move the focal zone up to the object to deepen the shadow.
Brighter tissue deep to a fluid-filled structure
Weak attenuation through fluid, overcompensated by TGC
Supports a cyst — but some solid masses, lymphoma especially, enhance too.
Equally spaced repeating echoes at increasing depth
Beam bouncing between two strong parallel reflectors, later returns read as deeper
Change the angle of insonation. Comet tail is the short-train variant, e.g. cholesterol crystals in adenomyomatosis.
A duplicate structure on the far side of a strong reflector, classically across the diaphragm
Multiply reflected echo assumed to have travelled a single longer path
Reposition and change the angle. Used deliberately, liver mirrored through the diaphragm excludes a pleural effusion.
A normal tendon or ligament turns hypoechoic
Fibrils reflect the beam away from the transducer when it is not perpendicular
Angle back to 90°. If the darkening reverses with angle, the tendon is normal.
Alternating colour behind a rough reflector, mimicking turbulent flow
Phase (clock) jitter in the Doppler electronics
More sensitive for small stones than shadowing, but roughly 50% false positive against unenhanced CT in the kidney — corroborate.
Colour wrap with no black line between hues; spectral peak cut off and wrapped to the bottom of the scale
Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit

Raise PRF/velocity scale, reduce sampling depth where possible, or use a lower transmit frequency. Baseline shift reallocates the display range without increasing PRF. Reducing the beam-to-flow angle increases the shift, not the aliasing limit. Conventional power Doppler does not encode velocity or direction.
classify.note: Aliasing is also used deliberately: the PISA method in mitral regurgitation takes the aliasing velocity as a known number.

pitfalls: Calling a hypoechoic tendon abnormal without heel-toeing the probe. Anisotropy manufactures tendinosis and tears at the slightest off-axis angle.
Reporting a renal twinkle as a stone. About half of renal twinkling artefacts are false positives against unenhanced CT, and low PRF settings raise intrarenal arterial aliasing that mimics it.
Mistaking aliasing for true flow reversal. True reversal has a black band of no flow between the colours; aliasing has red abutting blue.
Diagnosing a pleural effusion from an anechoic space above the diaphragm without checking the angle. Mirrored ascites does exactly this.
Assuming a lesion with posterior enhancement must be cystic. Lymphoma is the standing exception.
Chasing an artefact with gain when the fix is geometric. Reverberation, mirroring and anisotropy all answer to the angle of insonation, not the gain knob.

radiology_reference.overview: Set frequency, focus and gain for the question in front of you, work Doppler within the limits its physics imposes, and read ultrasound artefacts as evidence rather than as noise.
learning_points: Higher frequency improves detail but penetrates less deeply.
Angle, velocity scale and tissue boundaries shape the signal.
Artefacts can disclose interfaces, flow and hidden material.
Review transducer frequency, depth and focus.
Review gain, dynamic range and harmonic settings.
Review compression and patient positioning.
Review doppler: angle, scale, wall filter and spectral sample.
Review artefact: shadow, enhancement, aliasing or reverberation.
Absence of colour signal at insensitive settings is not proof of absent flow.

quiz.prompt: A 6 MHz transducer emits a pulse two cycles long. Taking the speed of sound in soft tissue as 1540 m/s, calculate the best achievable axial resolution. Answer in millimetres, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency: 1540 divided by 6 million is 0.257 mm. Two cycles make a spatial pulse length of 0.513 mm, and two reflectors can be separated along the beam only if they are more than half a pulse length apart, giving 0.26 mm. Two lessons follow. Higher frequency shortens the wavelength and improves axial resolution directly, and heavy damping, which shortens the pulse to one or two cycles, improves it again, which is why broadband probes resolve better than the ringing ones of an earlier generation. And axial resolution is roughly constant with depth, whereas lateral resolution depends on beam width and is best only at the focal zone, while elevational resolution depends on the thickness of the array and is the one that quietly averages a small lesion into the tissue beside it.

quiz.prompt: You are imaging to a depth of 20 cm with a speed of sound of 1540 m/s. Calculate the highest pulse repetition frequency at which every echo still returns before the next pulse is sent. Answer in hertz, to the nearest whole hertz.
quiz.explain: Each pulse travels out and back, so 0.4 m of path at 1540 m/s takes about 260 microseconds, and at most 3850 pulses can be sent per second. Depth therefore rations everything downstream. The Nyquist limit is half the pulse repetition frequency, here 1925 Hz, so deep vessels alias at velocities that would never trouble a carotid at 2 cm, which is why the renal artery in a large patient is the classic aliasing problem. Frame rate falls for the same reason, and falls further with a wide sector, deep focus or several focal zones, so a fast-moving structure imaged deep is imaged badly. Push the repetition frequency past this limit and echoes from the previous pulse arrive during the next listening interval and are placed too shallow, which is range ambiguity.

quiz.prompt: A 4 MHz pulsed Doppler beam meets blood moving at 1.0 m/s with an insonation angle of 60 degrees, in tissue with a speed of sound of 1540 m/s. Calculate the Doppler frequency shift. Answer in hertz, to the nearest whole hertz.
quiz.explain: The shift is twice the transmitted frequency, times the velocity, times the cosine of the angle, divided by the speed of sound: 2 x 4 x 10^6 x 1.0 x 0.5 divided by 1540 gives about 2597 Hz. The factor of two is there because the blood both receives and re-radiates the sound, and the answer lands in the audible range, which is why the spectral trace is also a sound worth listening to. Two consequences shape practice. At 90 degrees the cosine is zero and flow vanishes entirely, so a vessel running across the screen must be heel-toed or the beam steered. And because velocity is recovered by dividing by the cosine, the same few degrees of angle error that hardly matter at 20 degrees become a large velocity error beyond 60 degrees.

quiz.prompt: A carotid duplex is performed with the angle cursor set at 78 degrees to the vessel, because that is how the plaque sits in the available window. The peak systolic velocity reads 180 cm/s. What should be done with that measurement?
quiz.answer: Re-insonate at 60 degrees or less before quoting any velocity
choices: Re-insonate at 60 degrees or less before quoting any velocity
Report it, since the machine has already applied angle correction
Report it after multiplying the value by the cosine of that angle
Report the ratio to the distal vessel rather than the velocity
quiz.explain: Velocity is derived by dividing the measured shift by the cosine of the angle, and the cosine falls away steeply as the angle approaches 90 degrees, so the correction becomes a large multiplier applied to a small number. A few degrees of cursor error at 60 degrees produces an error of the order of ten per cent; the same error near 80 degrees can shift the velocity by tens of per cent, in either direction. Every published stenosis threshold assumes an angle of 60 degrees or less, so a velocity obtained at 78 degrees cannot be compared with them at all. The machine has indeed already applied the correction, which is precisely why re-applying a cosine by hand is wrong. Velocity ratios do cancel some systematic error and are useful in tortuous or heavily calcified vessels, but both of their components still need valid angles. The fix is a different window, beam steering, or an approach more parallel to the flow.

quiz.prompt: Colour Doppler of a native renal artery at 11 cm depth shows a mosaic of colour in mid-stream with no plaque, and the spectral trace wraps so that the systolic peaks appear below the baseline. Which single change is most likely to resolve it?
quiz.answer: Raise the velocity scale, which raises the pulse repetition frequency
choices: Raise the velocity scale, which raises the pulse repetition frequency
Raise the colour gain so that peak velocities display more brightly
Raise the wall filter so that the low-velocity signal is removed
Raise the transducer frequency so that the flow is sampled sooner
quiz.explain: Aliasing happens when the Doppler shift exceeds half the pulse repetition frequency, and the machine, sampling too slowly to know which way the phase turned, wraps the signal to the opposite direction. Raising the scale raises the repetition frequency directly and is the first move. Shifting the baseline buys the rest of the range in one direction. Choosing a lower-frequency probe helps, because the shift is proportional to the transmitted frequency, so a higher-frequency probe makes aliasing worse rather than better. Insonating at a larger angle reduces the shift as well, though it costs velocity accuracy. Reducing the imaging depth raises the ceiling on repetition frequency. And continuous-wave Doppler has no Nyquist limit at all, at the price of range resolution. Colour gain changes brightness and sensitivity, not the limit, and the wall filter removes low velocities, which is the opposite of the problem here.

quiz.prompt: A painful testis is scanned on a machine left on the preset from a carotid list. No colour flow is seen in either testis, though both look normal in grey scale. What should be done before absent perfusion is reported?
quiz.answer: Lower the velocity scale and the wall filter, and raise the colour gain
choices: Lower the velocity scale and the wall filter, and raise the colour gain
Report absent flow and refer urgently for scrotal exploration
Change to a lower-frequency curvilinear probe and rescan the scrotum
Apply harmonic imaging and spatial compounding to the whole study
quiz.explain: A carotid preset carries a high pulse repetition frequency and a high wall filter, both designed to reject exactly the slow flow that a testis has, so the study as performed is blind rather than negative. The low-flow preset drops the scale, minimises the wall filter, raises colour gain to just below the point where noise fills the box, and keeps a high-frequency linear probe. The single most valuable habit is a transverse image with both testes in the field, so the normal side proves the settings were capable of showing flow. Power Doppler is more sensitive to slow flow and is angle-independent, at the cost of direction and a tendency to flash with movement. Even then, absent flow supports torsion but a study with flow does not exclude it, since intermittent and partial torsion both occur, and a convincing clinical picture goes to theatre regardless of the pictures.

quiz.prompt: A right upper quadrant scan shows a rounded echogenic focus apparently in the lung base, the same distance above the diaphragm as a similar-looking liver lesion lies below it. What is the appropriate action?
quiz.answer: Treat it as a mirror-image artefact and scan from another window
choices: Treat it as a mirror-image artefact and scan from another window
Report a pulmonary metastasis and arrange a staging CT scan
Report a diaphragmatic hernia containing the liver lesion
Raise the output power to see through the diaphragm better
quiz.explain: The diaphragm and aerated lung form a near-total specular reflector. Sound that bounces between that interface and a structure in the liver takes a longer path home, and the machine, which assumes a single straight there-and-back journey, places the extra delay deep to the mirror, at exactly the same distance beyond it. The duplicate is identical and equidistant, which real basal lung disease never is. Confirm by scanning intercostally or from another angle, so that the geometry changes and the copy moves or disappears. The same mechanism duplicates the subclavian artery on colour above the pleura. Read positively, the artefact is useful: seeing it means aerated lung is there, so its loss can be the first clue to pleural fluid or consolidation. Raising output power adds energy and thermal index without changing geometry, and reporting a metastasis or a hernia commits a patient to a pathway built on an echo.

quiz.prompt: A liver study shows a broad bright band across the mid-field with a darker band beneath it, and the same appearance is present in every patient scanned on that machine this morning. What is the first thing to correct?
quiz.answer: Reset the time-gain compensation sliders to a smooth curve
choices: Reset the time-gain compensation sliders to a smooth curve
Reduce the overall output power and repeat the sweep
Change to a higher-frequency probe for the same views
Turn off tissue harmonic imaging for the whole study
quiz.explain: Time-gain compensation amplifies late-returning echoes more than early ones, to undo the roughly 0.5 dB per centimetre per megahertz that tissue takes out of the beam. A slider pushed out of line over-amplifies one depth and leaves the next under-amplified, producing precisely this horizontal banding, and the giveaway is that it repeats in every patient because it belongs to the console rather than to anatomy. Distinguish it from a genuine attenuating layer, such as thick subcutaneous fat, and from posterior enhancement, which is confined to the column beneath a fluid structure. Receive gain is adjusted before output power, since power raises the acoustic energy actually delivered and its thermal and mechanical indices, and the ALARA principle asks that it be the last thing raised. A steatotic liver attenuates more and needs both a steeper compensation curve and a lower frequency, and the extra attenuation is itself the diagnostic sign.

quiz.prompt: An indeterminate 3 cm renal lesion with possible enhancement is found on ultrasound in a man whose eGFR is 18 mL/min/1.73m2 and who can hold still only briefly. Which study answers the question of vascularity most safely here?
quiz.answer: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound using a microbubble agent
choices: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound using a microbubble agent
Iodinated contrast CT under intravenous hydration cover
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI with a group I agent at low dose
Unenhanced MRI with chemical shift and diffusion imaging
quiz.explain: Microbubbles are a pure blood-pool agent: they stay intravascular, they are destroyed by the beam and cleared through the lungs, and they are not excreted by the kidney, so there is no nephrotoxicity at any level of renal function. The examination is also real-time, so a patient who can co-operate for a minute is enough, and the continuous observation shows enhancement in thin septa that a single CT phase can miss. Two honest caveats: Bosniak 2019 is written for CT and MRI, so a contrast-enhanced ultrasound classification is applied by analogy rather than by that version's own criteria, and microbubbles carry a small risk of anaphylactoid reaction with cardiopulmonary cautions. Group I gadolinium agents are the higher-risk group for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, so that option is backwards; if MRI is needed, a group II agent is the appropriate choice. Unenhanced MRI simply declines to answer the question asked.

quiz.prompt: A patient with treated hepatitis C has a two-dimensional shear wave elastography result of 7.5 kPa, taken without fasting, with an interquartile range of 40 per cent of the median. How should this be handled?
quiz.answer: Repeat it fasted, since the measurement quality fails the usual criteria
choices: Repeat it fasted, since the measurement quality fails the usual criteria
Report advanced fibrosis and start endoscopic variceal surveillance
Report normal stiffness and discharge from further liver follow-up
Proceed to liver biopsy, since elastography has proved inconclusive
quiz.explain: Elastography estimates stiffness from the speed of a shear wave, and its result means nothing without its quality metrics. The widely used criterion is that the interquartile range should be no more than 30 per cent of the median, and measurement should be made fasting for at least two to three hours, because postprandial portal hyperaemia raises stiffness on its own. A spread of 40 per cent in a non-fasted patient is an uninterpretable number, not a low one. Had it been valid, the Baveno VII thresholds would apply: below 10 kPa argues against compensated advanced chronic liver disease, 10 to 15 is suggestive, and above 15 makes it highly likely. The confounders that raise stiffness without fibrosis are worth carrying: a hepatitis flare with raised transaminases, right heart failure and hepatic congestion, cholestasis, infiltration and a recent meal. Repeat properly rather than commit a patient to endoscopy or biopsy on a bad reading.

quiz.prompt: A sonographer cannot demonstrate shadowing behind a 6 mm echogenic focus in the gallbladder, and the image is being acquired with spatial compounding on and several focal zones spread through the field. State what you would change and why.
quiz.answer: Turn spatial compounding off and place a single focal zone at the level of the focus, using the highest frequency that still reaches it. Compounding insonates from several angles and averages the frames, which fills the shadow in behind a small stone, while a tight focal zone narrows the beam at that depth so less sound passes around the stone and the shadow returns.
quiz.explain: Spatial compounding is on by default because averaging several steering angles suppresses speckle and fills in angle-dependent dropout, which flatters soft tissue. The same averaging softens the very artefacts we use as evidence: acoustic shadowing behind a stone and posterior enhancement behind a cyst are both angle-dependent by nature. A small stone also fails to shadow when the beam at that depth is wider than the stone, so most of the sound simply travels around it, which is why a single focal zone placed at the stone matters more than any other setting. Tissue harmonic imaging usually sharpens shadowing rather than degrading it, because the harmonic beam is narrower and carries less clutter. When shadowing still cannot be shown, colour Doppler over the focus looking for twinkling is the next test.

quiz.prompt: A 4 mm echogenic focus in the renal sinus does not shadow convincingly, but colour Doppler over it produces a rapidly changing mosaic of colour deep to it, with a spectral trace of random noise rather than a pulsatile waveform. State what you conclude and how you would set the machine to make the sign more reliable.
quiz.answer: This is twinkling, which arises from a rough, strongly reflective surface, so the focus is a small stone rather than sinus fat or a vessel. Make it reliable by placing the colour box tightly over the focus with the focal zone at or just beyond it, raising the colour scale and pulse repetition frequency, and reducing colour gain until noise clears, since true twinkling persists while random colour noise does not.
quiz.explain: Twinkling is a rapidly alternating band of colour behind a rough calcified interface, accompanied by a spectral trace that looks like noise because there is no coherent motion generating it; the accepted explanation involves intrinsic phase jitter in the machine's own transmit and receive chain being unmasked by a strongly reflective irregular surface. It earns its place clinically because it can reveal small renal stones that are too small to shadow, and it distinguishes a stone from sinus fat, which produces no colour, and from a vessel, which produces a coherent, cardiac-cycle waveform. It is machine- and setting-dependent, so a negative result on one system means little. Other rough surfaces twinkle too, including encrusted stents, calcified plaque, and the cholesterol crystals in adenomyomatosis, where the same physics also yields comet-tail reverberation.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these transducer frequencies in order of increasing depth of penetration in soft tissue.
quiz.answer: 15-MHz 9-MHz 5-MHz 2.5-MHz
quiz.explain: Attenuation in soft tissue runs at roughly half a decibel per centimetre per megahertz, so it scales with frequency: a 15 MHz beam is losing signal about six times faster over the same path than a 2.5 MHz one, and the trade between resolution and depth is fixed by physics rather than by preference. That maps directly onto the probe you pick up: 12 to 18 MHz linear for thyroid, testis, superficial masses and vessels; 7 to 12 MHz for the paediatric abdomen and the appendix in a slim adult; 3 to 6 MHz curvilinear for the adult abdomen; and 1 to 3 MHz phased array for adult cardiac work between the ribs and for very large patients. Harmonic imaging costs a little penetration, because the received harmonic is far weaker than the fundamental, and repays it by cutting near-field clutter and reverberation, which is why a cyst looks convincingly anechoic with it switched on.

curriculum_modules.title: Uterus and Cervix: MR Staging, Endometriosis and Anomalies

module_contract.goal: Use uterine zonal anatomy on MRI to stage cervical and endometrial cancer, map fibroids and deep endometriosis for the surgeon, and separate the Mullerian anomalies that change the operation.

approach.detail: Longest diameter on T2W drives the surgery-versus-chemoradiotherapy decision — the 4 cm threshold is the one number that changes management.
An intact hypointense cervical stromal ring argues against parametrial invasion; interruption with tumour signal extending into the parametrium means stage IIB.
Upper two-thirds involvement without parametrial invasion is stage IIA and may still be resectable; lower-third involvement is stage IIIA.
Tumour abutting within 3 mm of the obturator internus, levator ani or piriformis muscles, or the iliac vessels, is stage IIIB.
Spread to nodes above the renal veins, the peritoneum or distant organs is stage IV.

approach.step: Report nodes separately from the FIGO stage
approach.detail: Nodal status is assessed alongside but does not itself define the 2018 FIGO stage the way it does for endometrial cancer.

measure.how: Longest diameter on T2W, in the plane that best shows the tumour.
measure.cutoff: < 4 cm — potentially eligible for upfront surgery

measure.how: Distance from tumour to the obturator internus, levator ani, piriformis muscles or iliac vessels.
measure.cutoff: FIGO IIIB = extension to the pelvic sidewall, and/or hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney. Tumour within 3 mm of the sidewall muscle is a proximity sign, not the stage

measure.how: Assess T2 signal continuity from cervix into vagina.
measure.cutoff: Upper two-thirds = stage IIA · lower third = stage IIIA

measure.how: Depth of tumour signal into the myometrium as a fraction of full myometrial thickness — relevant when the differential includes an endometrial rather than cervical primary.
measure.cutoff: < 50% superficial · > 50% deep, associated with higher nodal risk

classify.name: FIGO 2018 MR staging of cervical cancer
rows: Small tumours (< 4 cm) are candidates for upfront surgery
Upper two-thirds of the vagina involved, parametrium spared
May still be eligible for upfront surgery
Interruption of the hypointense stromal ring with tumour extending into the parametrium
Tumour invades or lies within 3 mm of the obturator internus, levator ani or piriformis muscles, or the iliac vessels (pelvic sidewall)
Spread to distant organs, nodes above the renal veins, or the peritoneum
classify.note: Only small (< 4 cm), early-stage tumours go to upfront surgery. Every other stage listed here is treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy or systemic therapy.

pitfalls: Measuring tumour size on a sequence degraded by motion or an overdistended bladder — this can push a resectable stage I tumour over the 4 cm surgical threshold or under it.
Calling parametrial invasion from oedema or inflammation around the cervix rather than a genuine interruption of the low-signal stromal ring.
Missing sidewall involvement because the abutment distance was not explicitly measured — 'close to' the sidewall muscles is not a stage without the 3 mm assessment.
Conflating endometrial and cervical staging systems — endometrial cancer stage depends on myometrial invasion depth (the 50% threshold) and nodal status in a way cervical staging does not.

Missing deep infiltrating endometriosis or a Müllerian anomaly on the same study because attention was fixed on the tumour — both change the surgical plan and are easy to overlook on a staging-focused read.
