quiz.prompt: In a 68-year-old being staged for endometrial carcinoma, the junctional zone cannot be identified anywhere on T2 and the myometrium is uniformly intermediate in signal. How should that affect your assessment of the depth of invasion?
quiz.answer: Measure invasion as a proportion of the whole myometrial thickness using the contrast and diffusion images, since the junctional zone is often absent after the menopause
choices: Measure invasion as a proportion of the whole myometrial thickness using the contrast and diffusion images, since the junctional zone is often absent after the menopause
Report the study as non-diagnostic for depth of invasion, since an absent junctional zone means the T2 sequence was mistimed and should be repeated
Assume deep invasion is present, since loss of the junctional zone in this setting reflects tumour having replaced the inner myometrium throughout
Report diffuse adenomyosis, since generalised loss of the junctional zone across the whole uterus is the diagnostic appearance of that disease
quiz.explain: The three-layer T2 appearance of the uterus — bright endometrium, dark junctional zone, intermediate outer myometrium — is a feature of the reproductive years. The junctional zone is the inner myometrium, where smooth muscle cells are packed more densely with less extracellular water, and it is hormonally responsive. After the menopause, and on the combined oral contraceptive or a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist, it commonly becomes thin or invisible, and the uterus looks uniformly intermediate. That is normal, not disease and not a technical failure. It does mean you lose your inner reference line, so depth is judged against total myometrial thickness on the sequences with the best tumour-to-muscle contrast. Diffuse adenomyosis is not a plausible reading in a 68-year-old with an atrophic uterus, and assuming deep invasion would overtreat. The lesson generalises: interpret zonal anatomy against the patient's hormonal state.

quiz.prompt: On sagittal T2 imaging in a 41-year-old with heavy painful periods, the junctional zone measures 7 mm at its thinnest and 14 mm at its thickest. Give the junctional zone differential in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: The junctional zone differential is simply the maximum thickness minus the minimum, here 14 minus 7, giving 7 mm. It matters because adenomyosis is judged on three related measurements rather than one. A maximum junctional zone thickness of 12 mm or more is taken as diagnostic; 8 to 12 mm is equivocal and needs supporting features; a differential of more than 5 mm and a ratio of junctional zone to total myometrial thickness above about 40% both support the diagnosis. This patient meets the maximum-thickness criterion and the differential criterion. The ancillary signs seal it: punctate high signal foci on T2 representing ectopic endometrial glands and cystic change, high signal foci on T1 from haemorrhage, linear striations radiating from the endometrium, and an ill-defined lesion that widens the myometrium without displacing the cavity. Measure perpendicular to the endometrium and avoid measuring through a contraction.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has a 3.2 cm squamous carcinoma of the cervix. On oblique axial T2 the low-signal cervical stroma forms a complete dark ring around the tumour and the parametrial fat is clean. All pelvic nodes measure under 8 mm in short axis. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Parametrial invasion is effectively excluded, the tumour is stage IB2, and radical hysterectomy remains a realistic option
choices: Parametrial invasion is effectively excluded, the tumour is stage IB2, and radical hysterectomy remains a realistic option
Parametrial invasion is present because the tumour exceeds 3 cm, the tumour is stage IIB, and chemoradiation is indicated
Parametrial invasion cannot be judged on T2 alone, so dynamic contrast imaging is needed before any stage is assigned
Parametrial invasion is probable because the dark ring is only a partial barrier, so the tumour should be staged as IIB
quiz.explain: The intact low-signal cervical stromal ring is one of the most useful negative predictors in pelvic MRI: when a complete rim of dark fibrous stroma surrounds the tumour on a properly planned oblique axial T2, parametrial invasion is very unlikely, and the negative predictive value is high enough to plan surgery on. Parametrial invasion is called when that ring is disrupted full thickness with irregular tumour signal extending into the parametrial fat, sometimes encasing vessels or reaching the ureter. Under FIGO 2018, size subdivides stage IB: IB1 is under 2 cm, IB2 is 2 cm to under 4 cm, and IB3 is 4 cm or more, so a 3.2 cm tumour confined to the cervix is IB2. Tumour size alone does not create parametrial invasion, although the probability rises with size. Stage IIB, meaning parametrial disease, generally shifts management from radical hysterectomy to chemoradiation.

quiz.prompt: In FIGO 2018 staging of cervical carcinoma, give the depth of stromal invasion above which a microscopically diagnosed tumour is no longer stage IA and becomes stage IB. Answer in millimetres, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: FIGO 2018 defines stage IA as invasive carcinoma diagnosed only by microscopy, with IA1 invading 3 mm or less in depth and IA2 invading more than 3 mm and up to 5 mm. Above 5 mm the tumour is stage IB regardless of how it was found. A notable change from earlier editions is that the horizontal extent criterion, previously 7 mm, was dropped altogether, so depth of stromal invasion is now the only measurement that separates IA1 from IA2 from IB. This matters for radiology in a mostly negative way: stage IA disease is a pathological diagnosis made on a cone or loop excision, and lesions of that depth are usually invisible on MRI. Reporting a normal-looking cervix does not exclude IA disease. MRI's contribution begins at IB, where tumour size, parametrial extension, vaginal involvement and nodal status are the questions it can genuinely answer.

quiz.prompt: A woman with a 3 cm cervical carcinoma that appears confined to the cervix on MRI has a 14 mm short-axis right external iliac node that is rounded and shows restricted diffusion. What stage should be reported and what does it change?
quiz.answer: Stage IIIC1r: nodal disease raises the stage in its own right under FIGO 2018, and the treatment shifts towards chemoradiation
choices: Stage IIIC1r: nodal disease raises the stage in its own right under FIGO 2018, and the treatment shifts towards chemoradiation
Stage IB2 with the node reported separately: nodal status does not enter the FIGO stage for carcinoma of the cervix
Stage IIIC2r: iliac nodal disease is grouped with para-aortic disease when it is detected on imaging rather than at surgery
Stage IVB: a malignant node outside the cervix constitutes distant disease, so treatment becomes palliative systemic therapy
quiz.explain: The most consequential change in FIGO 2018 was the creation of stage IIIC, which lets nodal disease raise the stage independently of the local extent of the tumour. IIIC1 is pelvic nodal disease and IIIC2 is para-aortic nodal disease. Because the finding may come from imaging or from pathology, the stage carries a suffix — r when assigned on imaging and p when assigned on histology — so this case is IIIC1r. A small primary confined to the cervix with one positive pelvic node is therefore stage III, which sounds startling until you remember that nodal status is among the strongest prognostic factors in this disease. Practically, it usually moves the patient from surgery to definitive chemoradiation, and it changes the radiotherapy volume. Judge nodes on shape, necrosis, irregular border and diffusion as well as size; PET-CT is often added to check the para-aortic chain before the field is drawn.

quiz.prompt: You are supervising the acquisition for a cervical cancer staging MRI. Say how you would plan the small field-of-view T2 stacks on the cervix, and explain why the plane matters for the numbers you will go on to report.
quiz.answer: Plan a sagittal T2 first, then prescribe an oblique axial stack perpendicular to the long axis of the endocervical canal, with an oblique coronal parallel to it. An off-axis plane cuts the cervix obliquely, which exaggerates the measured tumour diameter and blurs the low-signal stromal ring, so both the FIGO size threshold and the assessment of parametrial invasion become unreliable.
quiz.explain: Cervical staging turns on two things that are both geometry-dependent: a size measurement that decides between IB1, IB2 and IB3, and the integrity of a thin dark ring of stroma that decides between stage I and stage IIB. A straight axial stack through a cervix that is anteverted or retroverted slices it obliquely, so the cervix appears as an ellipse, the tumour is measured across its longest oblique dimension, and the stromal ring is partial-volumed into a blur that looks disrupted. Both errors push the patient up a stage. So plan from the sagittal every time: an oblique axial perpendicular to the endocervical canal, a matching oblique coronal, thin slices, small field of view, and no fat suppression on the T2 stacks, since parametrial invasion is read against bright parametrial fat. Antiperistaltic agents help, and vaginal gel can open the fornices when vaginal involvement is the question.

quiz.prompt: An endometrial carcinoma fills the uterine cavity. On sagittal T2 and on the contrast-enhanced images, tumour extends beyond half the thickness of the fundal myometrium, while the low-signal cervical stroma is intact throughout. What does the report need to convey?
quiz.answer: Deep myometrial invasion without cervical stromal involvement, a combination that raises nodal risk and shapes how extensive the surgery should be
choices: Deep myometrial invasion without cervical stromal involvement, a combination that raises nodal risk and shapes how extensive the surgery should be
Superficial myometrial invasion alone, since tumour must reach the serosal surface before invasion is graded as deep in this setting
Cervical stromal involvement is present, since tumour filling the cavity necessarily extends downward into the endocervical canal as well
Depth cannot be assessed without diffusion imaging, since T2 and contrast-enhanced images both systematically overestimate the depth
quiz.explain: The threshold that has survived every revision of endometrial staging is 50%: tumour invading less than half the myometrial thickness is superficial, and half or more is deep. Deep invasion correlates strongly with lymphovascular space invasion and nodal metastasis, which is why it influences whether nodal assessment or sentinel node mapping is performed. Cervical stromal involvement is a separate question and requires tumour to breach the dark cervical stroma; tumour merely extending along the endocervical mucosa does not count. Measure depth perpendicular to the serosa at the point of deepest invasion and express it as a fraction, not in millimetres. The traps are worth knowing: adenomyosis and fibroids distort the myometrium, the cornual myometrium is thin so invasion looks deeper than it is, and a distended cavity thins the wall. Modern FIGO staging also incorporates molecular classification, so imaging depth is one input among several.

quiz.prompt: Your endometrial MRI protocol is being rewritten. Say which sequences and which post-contrast timing you would insist on for judging the depth of myometrial invasion, and what each one contributes.
quiz.answer: Sagittal T2 plus an oblique axial T2 planned perpendicular to the long axis of the endometrial cavity for the anatomy; diffusion-weighted imaging with ADC, where tumour is bright at high b-value against darker myometrium; and dynamic contrast imaging read at the equilibrium phase around two to three minutes, when tumour-to-myometrium contrast is greatest and the subendometrial enhancing band can be followed.
quiz.explain: Three sequences, three jobs. Oblique axial T2 perpendicular to the cavity is the geometric foundation, because a tangential slice through a curved fundus manufactures apparent deep invasion. Diffusion adds lesion conspicuity: endometrial carcinoma is cellular and bright on high b-value images with a low ADC, while myometrium is not, and combining diffusion with T2 improves accuracy for depth in most series. Contrast timing is the detail people get wrong. Very early images show the thin subendometrial enhancing band, whose interruption suggests myometrial invasion, but the band is unreliable in an atrophic or fibroid uterus. The most consistently useful window is the equilibrium phase at roughly two to three minutes, when relatively hypoenhancing tumour is best set off against enhancing myometrium. Read the three together, and if they disagree, say which one you have believed and why.

quiz.prompt: A 38-year-old with heavy menstrual bleeding has a 2.6 cm fibroid whose bulk sits within the endometrial cavity, with roughly a third of its volume extending into the myometrium. She wishes to preserve fertility. What should the report drive?
quiz.answer: A FIGO type 1 submucosal fibroid, amenable to hysteroscopic resection, so report the intramural depth and the residual myometrial thickness
choices: A FIGO type 1 submucosal fibroid, amenable to hysteroscopic resection, so report the intramural depth and the residual myometrial thickness
A FIGO type 3 fibroid, which abuts the endometrium but requires abdominal myomectomy rather than any hysteroscopic approach
A FIGO type 5 fibroid, largely intramural with a subserosal component, for which uterine artery embolisation is the first-line option
A FIGO type 0 fibroid, sitting on a stalk within the cavity, for which no measurement of intramural depth is needed at all
quiz.explain: The FIGO leiomyoma subclassification runs 0 to 8 and describes position rather than size. Type 0 is entirely intracavitary on a stalk; type 1 is submucosal with less than half its volume intramural; type 2 is submucosal with half or more intramural; type 3 lies wholly within the myometrium but contacts the endometrium; type 4 is purely intramural; type 5 is subserosal with half or more intramural; type 6 is subserosal with less than half; type 7 is pedunculated subserosal; type 8 covers cervical and parasitic fibroids. Types 0 to 2 are the hysteroscopically resectable group, which is why this classification changes the operation. For type 1 and type 2 the surgeon also needs the intramural depth and the thickness of myometrium left between fibroid and serosa, because a thin margin raises the risk of perforation and fluid overload.

quiz.prompt: Arrange these FIGO leiomyoma subtypes by position, from the one lying entirely within the endometrial cavity to the one lying entirely outside the serosa.
quiz.answer: type-0 type-2 type-4 type-6 type-7
quiz.explain: The numbering is a gradient that walks outward from the cavity to the peritoneal surface, which is why it is worth learning as a sequence rather than as a list. Type 0 is pedunculated within the cavity; type 2 is submucosal with half or more of its bulk in the myometrium; type 4 is wholly intramural, touching neither surface; type 6 is subserosal with less than half embedded; type 7 is pedunculated outside the serosa. Treatment tracks the gradient. Types 0 to 2 come out hysteroscopically through the cervix. Types 3 to 6 need myomectomy, open or laparoscopic, or medical management. Type 7 is a laparoscopic problem, and a narrow-stalked type 7 is a relative caution for uterine artery embolisation, as is a type 0, which can be expelled or slough into the cavity. Before embolisation also check for coexisting adenomyosis and confirm the fibroids enhance, since a degenerated fibroid will not shrink.

quiz.prompt: A 41-year-old has an ill-defined 4 cm area of low T2 signal in the posterior myometrium containing tiny bright foci, with no cleavage plane from surrounding muscle and an endometrial stripe that runs through it undisplaced. What is the discriminating reading, and what does it mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: Focal adenomyosis: ill-defined margins with little mass effect separate it from a fibroid, so hysteroscopic resection is not an option here
choices: Focal adenomyosis: ill-defined margins with little mass effect separate it from a fibroid, so hysteroscopic resection is not an option here
An intramural fibroid: low T2 signal within the myometrium indicates smooth muscle, so myomectomy would be expected to relieve symptoms
A degenerating fibroid: bright foci within a dark myometrial lesion indicate cystic degeneration and predict a poor response to embolisation
Endometrial carcinoma invading the myometrium: an undisplaced stripe crossing a low signal myometrial lesion is the sign of invasion
quiz.explain: Fibroid and adenomyoma both look dark on T2, so the discriminators are shape and behaviour rather than signal. A fibroid is a discrete round lesion with a pseudocapsule, a visible cleavage plane, often a rim of dilated vessels, and it displaces whatever lies next to it, including the endometrial stripe. Adenomyosis infiltrates: its margins are ill-defined, it is elliptical rather than round, it widens the myometrium with minimal mass effect, and the endometrium runs through it undisturbed. The tiny T2-bright foci are ectopic endometrial glands and small cysts; corresponding T1-bright foci from haemorrhage are more specific still. The distinction changes the plan, because there is no plane to shell an adenomyoma out of and no cavity lesion to resect hysteroscopically. Options are medical treatment, focused ultrasound or ablation, embolisation with a less durable response than for fibroids, or hysterectomy.

quiz.prompt: A 33-year-old with dysmenorrhoea and dyschezia has bilateral endometriomas that meet in the midline behind the uterus. Say what that appearance predicts, and set out the specific sites your report must address before the surgical planning meeting.
quiz.answer: Kissing ovaries predict dense posterior compartment adhesions and a high likelihood of deep infiltrating disease, particularly bowel disease. The report must address the torus uterinus and uterosacral ligaments, the rectovaginal septum and posterior vaginal fornix, the rectosigmoid with lesion length, depth of wall involvement and distance from the anal verge, whether the pouch of Douglas is obliterated, the bladder dome and vesicouterine pouch, and the ureters with any hydronephrosis.
quiz.explain: Ovaries that touch across the midline are not simply two endometriomas; they are tethered there by adhesions, and the sign is strongly associated with severe deep infiltrating endometriosis, especially of the bowel. MRI is asked to map disease by compartment. Anteriorly: bladder dome, vesicouterine pouch and the distal ureters. Middle: uterus, ovaries, torus uterinus, uterosacral ligaments, the retrocervical region, the rectovaginal septum and the posterior vaginal fornix. Posteriorly: the rectosigmoid, where the surgeon needs the number of lesions, the craniocaudal length, whether the lesion reaches muscularis or mucosa, and the distance from the anal verge, since those determine shaving versus disc excision versus segmental resection. Say explicitly whether the pouch of Douglas is obliterated. Ureteric involvement and hydronephrosis change the consent conversation and may require a stent, so they must never be left implicit.

quiz.prompt: A woman with two second-trimester pregnancy losses has pelvic MRI. The cavity is divided by a low-signal T2 midline band reaching the internal os, the internal indentation is 2.2 cm deep with an acute apex, and the external fundal contour is smooth with a 4 mm dip. What operation does this support?
quiz.answer: Hysteroscopic resection of the septum, since an external fundal contour indented by less than 10 mm places this in the septate group
choices: Hysteroscopic resection of the septum, since an external fundal contour indented by less than 10 mm places this in the septate group
Abdominal metroplasty to unify two horns, since a deep internal indentation defines a bicornuate uterus whatever the external contour
No surgery at all, since a low-signal midline band in the fundus is a normal muscular variant with no reproductive consequence
Laparoscopic excision of a rudimentary horn, since a divided cavity with an indented contour indicates a unicornuate configuration
quiz.explain: The whole distinction rests on the outside of the uterus, not the inside. Both a septate and a bicornuate uterus have a divided cavity; what separates them is the external fundal contour. Under the ASRM 2021 criteria a uterus is septate when the external contour is flat or indented by 1 cm or less while the internal indentation exceeds 1 cm with an acute angle, and bicornuate when the external indentation exceeds 1 cm. Here the outer contour dips only 4 mm, so this is septate. That matters because a septum can be divided transcervically at hysteroscopy, a low-morbidity day procedure, whereas separating two true horns needs an abdominal metroplasty that is rarely performed and leaves a scarred uterus. Note that the ESHRE and ESGE classification uses different thresholds, so state which system you are applying. Always look at the kidneys, since Mullerian anomalies travel with renal agenesis.

curriculum_modules.title: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis and CSF Disorders

module_contract.goal: Recognise venous rather than arterial parenchymal injury and prove it without falling for the normal-variant traps, and work up raised and low CSF pressure and hydrocephalus to the point where management changes.

approach.step: Ask whether the parenchymal lesion obeys an artery
approach.detail: Bilateral change in a non-arterial distribution is the reason to look at the veins at all.

approach.step: Look for the clot directly on the non-enhanced CT
approach.detail: A dense cord in a cortical vein or sinus. It is present in only about one third of cases, so its absence proves nothing.
Venous occlusion gives white matter vasogenic oedema first, then a mixed cytotoxic picture with haemorrhage. Arterial infarct gives cytotoxic oedema only.
On contrast-enhanced CT, a triangle of enhancing dural collaterals around a low-attenuation thrombosed sinus.
CT venography at 45–50 seconds after the start of injection with at least 70 cc of contrast, or contrast-enhanced MR venography — the most reliable MR technique.

approach.step: Exclude the variants before you commit
approach.detail: Hypoplastic transverse sinus, arachnoid granulations, and TOF and phase-contrast flow artefacts all mimic thrombus.

measure.how: Too early and the sinuses have not filled; too late and the contrast has washed out.
Direct visualisation of clot on non-enhanced CT.
Look parasagittally, on both sides, and on blood-sensitive sequences.
Absent very early, and absent again after about two months once the sinus recanalises.
measure.cutoff: Unreliable before onset and after ~2 months

pitfalls: Excluding thrombosis because the non-enhanced CT is unremarkable. The dense clot sign appears in only a third of cases.
Calling a hypoplastic transverse sinus thrombosed. Check the jugular foramen size and go back to the source images.
T1 shine-through from methaemoglobin read as thrombus on TOF, and slow flow read as absent signal on phase contrast. Confirm with contrast-enhanced MR venography.
Dense sinuses in an infant called thrombus. The brain is less dense at that age, so the veins look relatively bright.
Reading bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia change as arterial. That is deep cerebral venous thrombosis, and it is predominantly young women.

radiology_reference.overview: Recognise venous rather than arterial parenchymal injury and prove it without falling for the normal-variant traps, and work up raised and low CSF pressure and hydrocephalus to the point where management changes.
learning_points: Prove absent or filled sinus flow while excluding variants.
Look for secondary signs and a safe venous explanation.
Brain sag and diffuse dural enhancement suggest CSF loss.
Review venous opacification and filling defects.
Review sinus/cortical vein location and extent.
Review venous infarction or haemorrhage.
Review brain sag, dural enhancement and subdural collections.
Review spinal leak localisation if studied.
Normal venous variants and flow gaps can mimic thrombosis; combine source images with the appropriate venographic sequence.

quiz.prompt: A 27-year-old woman ten days post partum has a week of worsening headache and now a seizure. CT shows swelling and patchy hyperdensity in both parasagittal frontal lobes, more on the left, with a rim of oedema that crosses from anterior to middle cerebral supply and does not match either territory. What should be arranged?
quiz.answer: CT venography now, because bilateral parasagittal change that ignores arterial boundaries points to a sinus occlusion
choices: Digital subtraction angiography now, because bifrontal swelling in pregnancy is typical of a small vessel vasculitis
CT angiography now, because bilateral frontal change of this kind indicates an anterior communicating artery aneurysm
CT venography now, because bilateral parasagittal change that ignores arterial boundaries points to a sinus occlusion
MRI with contrast next week, because posterior reversible encephalopathy resolves and needs interval confirmation alone
quiz.explain: Territory is the first question in any parenchymal insult. Arterial infarcts obey boundaries drawn by supply; venous infarcts obey boundaries drawn by drainage, so they sit where the blocked sinus collects from - parasagittal and bilateral for the superior sagittal sinus, temporal for the transverse or vein of Labbe, thalamic and basal ganglia for the internal cerebral veins and straight sinus. Oedema out of proportion to any arterial map, in a young patient with a prothrombotic state such as the puerperium, dehydration, the combined pill or an underlying cancer, should send you to the venous system. Note the sequence of events: venous obstruction raises capillary pressure, so oedema comes first and haemorrhage follows as vessels rupture, which is why the density is patchy rather than a single clean haematoma.

quiz.prompt: In that same patient a contrast-enhanced CT is performed on day one of admission and shows an enhancing dural wall around a central filling defect in the posterior superior sagittal sinus. A colleague scanned three weeks later would like to know why the appearance can be normal by then despite persisting clot. What is the sound explanation?
quiz.answer: Organising thrombus develops its own vessels and enhances, so the filling defect fades even while the sinus remains occluded
choices: Thrombus is usually fully lysed within three weeks, so a normal study means the sinus has recanalised completely
Dural walls stop enhancing after two weeks of treatment, so the surrounding rim disappears and the sign is abolished
Contrast timing in later studies is invariably too early, so the sinus opacifies poorly and the filling defect becomes invisible
Organising thrombus develops its own vessels and enhances, so the filling defect fades even while the sinus remains occluded
quiz.explain: The empty delta sign is a triangle of enhancing dura around unenhancing clot on axial contrast-enhanced imaging, and it is genuinely time-dependent in both directions. Very early it can be absent because the collateral dural venous channels have not yet dilated to give a bright rim. After roughly two to four weeks the thrombus itself becomes vascularised and enhances, so it merges with the sinus lumen and can look patent even though it is not. That is the trap for a late referral: an isolated post-contrast study is not enough. Use the non-contrast series, where acute clot is dense, and a dedicated venographic acquisition, and be aware that on MRI the signal of thrombus marches through the same deoxyhaemoglobin-to-methaemoglobin evolution as any haematoma, so an early clot can be isointense and easily missed.

quiz.prompt: A registrar reports occlusion of the left transverse sinus on a time-of-flight MR venogram. Before that report goes out, what three normal-variant or technical explanations must you exclude, and how does each one declare itself?
quiz.answer: An arachnoid granulation is a small rounded CSF-density defect inside a patent sinus, a hypoplastic transverse sinus has a correspondingly small bony groove on CT with no parenchymal change, and a flow gap on time-of-flight is a saturation artefact that disappears on contrast-enhanced venography.
quiz.explain: Over-calling transverse sinus thrombosis is one of the commonest errors in neuroradiology, because a hypoplastic or atretic transverse sinus is present in a substantial minority of normal people, usually on the right-dominant pattern's smaller left side. Three checks settle it. First, look at the skull base on bone windows: a truly hypoplastic sinus runs in a small or absent groove, whereas a thrombosed sinus of normal calibre has a normal groove. Second, arachnoid granulations are small, round, sharply marginated, follow CSF, and sit where veins enter. Third, time-of-flight venography depends on inflowing unsaturated spins, so in-plane flow produces spurious gaps; contrast-enhanced MR venography or CT venography is not subject to that. The parenchyma is the final arbiter, since a real occlusion of consequence usually leaves a mark.

quiz.prompt: CT venography confirms extensive superior sagittal sinus thrombosis in the postpartum patient, and there is a 3 cm haemorrhagic venous infarct in the left frontal lobe. The neurology team asks whether the bleed contraindicates treatment. What is the correct position to state?
quiz.answer: Full-dose anticoagulation is still indicated, because relieving venous obstruction is what stops the bleeding into congested brain
choices: Full-dose anticoagulation is still indicated, because relieving venous obstruction is what stops the bleeding into congested brain
Antiplatelet therapy should replace anticoagulation, because it lowers venous pressure with a smaller risk of extension
Anticoagulation should be deferred for two weeks, because any parenchymal haemorrhage first needs radiological stability
Immediate surgical clot retrieval should replace medical therapy, because drug treatment rarely reopens a sinus that is fully occluded
quiz.explain: This is the counterintuitive rule worth carrying: haemorrhagic transformation of a venous infarct is not a contraindication to anticoagulation, it is a consequence of the untreated occlusion. The blood is there because capillary pressure upstream of the clot has risen until vessels rupture, and the treatment for that is to stop the clot propagating and let the collateral drainage open. Heparin followed by oral anticoagulation is standard, and outcomes in the randomised and registry evidence are good even in patients who present with a bleed. Endovascular therapy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and decompressive surgery for life-threatening mass effect. The radiologist's contribution is to state the extent of the thrombus, the deep venous system involvement, and the degree of mass effect, since those drive escalation.

quiz.prompt: A 29-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 has daily headaches, transient visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus. MRI shows flattening of the posterior sclerae, an empty sella, distended and tortuous optic nerve sheaths, and smooth bilateral stenosis of the distal transverse sinuses. What should the report conclude?
quiz.answer: These findings support raised intracranial pressure but do not establish it, so an opening pressure and formal perimetry are needed
choices: These findings are within normal limits for this age and habitus, so no further neurological or ophthalmic assessment is required
These findings support raised intracranial pressure but do not establish it, so an opening pressure and formal perimetry are needed
These findings establish idiopathic intracranial hypertension on their own, so acetazolamide can be started without any further tests
These findings indicate bilateral transverse sinus thrombosis, so full anticoagulation should begin while venography is arranged
quiz.explain: The imaging signs of intracranial hypertension are supportive, not diagnostic: posterior globe flattening, an empty or partially empty sella, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space with a tortuous nerve, protrusion of the optic nerve head, and bilateral distal transverse sinus narrowing. Each occurs in people without the syndrome, and their absence does not exclude it. Diagnosis remains clinical and manometric, with papilloedema and a raised opening pressure on lumbar puncture after a normal parenchymal study. The sinus stenosis deserves a comment: it is usually smooth, bilateral and at the transverse-sigmoid junction, and it is generally a consequence of raised pressure rather than a cause, though a self-sustaining loop exists and venous stenting is used in selected refractory cases. Vision, not headache, is what is at stake, so perimetry is the urgent test.

quiz.prompt: A 44-year-old has three months of headache that comes on within minutes of standing and settles when lying flat. MRI shows smooth continuous enhancement following the falx, the tentorium and the inner table, sparing the depths of every sulcus, with bilateral thin subdural collections and a distended anterior pontine venous plexus. What should follow?
quiz.answer: Work this up as intracranial hypotension, because dural enhancement that spares the sulci reflects compensatory venous engorgement
choices: Work this up as chronic meningitis, because diffuse meningeal enhancement of this pattern usually reflects an infection
Work this up as bilateral chronic subdural haematoma, because the collections themselves account for the smooth enhancing membranes
Work this up as intracranial hypotension, because dural enhancement that spares the sulci reflects compensatory venous engorgement
Work this up as leptomeningeal metastatic disease, because enhancement along the falx and tentorium reflects tumour seeding
quiz.explain: The distribution is the whole argument. Dural, or pachymeningeal, enhancement is thick, smooth and continuous, follows the falx, tentorium and convexity dura, and never dips into a sulcus. Leptomeningeal enhancement, whether from infection or from carcinomatosis, is thin, irregular and follows the pia into sulci and around folia. In low CSF volume the Monro-Kellie doctrine explains everything you see: as CSF volume falls, blood volume rises to compensate, so the dural venous plexuses engorge and the leaky dural vessels enhance avidly, the brain sags, and subdural fluid accumulates in the space that opens up. The orthostatic history is the strongest clue of all. The subdural collections are a consequence, and draining them without finding the leak is a well-known way to make the patient worse.

quiz.prompt: You are grading that patient's brain MRI with the Bern score. Pachymeningeal enhancement is present, the suprasellar cistern measures 3.5 mm, the venous sinuses are not engorged, bilateral subdural collections are present, the prepontine cistern measures 6.0 mm, and the mamillopontine distance is 6.0 mm. Give the total Bern score. Answer as a whole number of points.
quiz.explain: The Bern score (Dobrocky and colleagues, 2019) has three major signs worth two points each - pachymeningeal enhancement, engorgement of the venous sinus, and effacement of the suprasellar cistern at 4.0 mm or less - and three minor signs worth one point each: a subdural fluid collection, effacement of the prepontine cistern at 5.0 mm or less, and a mamillopontine distance of 6.5 mm or less. Here the enhancement scores 2, the suprasellar cistern at 3.5 mm scores 2, the subdural collections score 1, and the mamillopontine distance at 6.0 mm scores 1; the prepontine cistern at 6.0 mm is above threshold and the sinuses are not engorged, so both score nothing. That is 6 of a possible 9, which falls in the high-probability band of 5 or more and justifies proceeding to specialised myelography to hunt for the leak.

quiz.prompt: The spine MRI in that patient shows no epidural fluid collection at any level, and the referring team concludes there is no leak. Explain why that conclusion is unsafe and what study you would recommend instead.
quiz.answer: A CSF-venous fistula produces no epidural fluid collection, so a normal spine MRI does not exclude it; the study to request is lateral decubitus digital subtraction myelography or dynamic CT myelography, which shows CSF draining directly from a nerve root sleeve into a paraspinal vein.
quiz.explain: Three mechanisms cause spontaneous intracranial hypotension: a ventral dural tear, usually from a calcified disc or osteophyte; a leaking meningeal diverticulum; and a CSF-venous fistula. The first two spill fluid into the epidural space and are therefore visible as an epidural collection on heavily T2-weighted spine imaging. The third does not, because CSF is shunted straight into an adjacent paraspinal vein and never enters the epidural space, so conventional spine MRI is normal. Fistulas are found with the patient in lateral decubitus - the side down matters, since the leak must be dependent - during dynamic myelography with fluoroscopic or CT acquisition timed to the intrathecal contrast bolus. They are commonly treated with transvenous embolisation or surgical ligation. A high Bern score with a normal spine MRI should raise the suspicion, not lower it.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the structures through which cerebrospinal fluid passes in normal circulation, beginning at its production in the lateral ventricle and ending at its resorption.
quiz.answer: lateral-ventricle foramen-of-Monro third-ventricle cerebral-aqueduct fourth-ventricle arachnoid-granulations
quiz.explain: Holding this sequence in mind converts a pattern of ventriculomegaly into an anatomical level. If the lateral ventricles are large and the third is normal, the block is at the foramen of Monro - a colloid cyst is the classic culprit, and it can be unilateral. If the lateral and third ventricles are large and the fourth is normal, the block is at the aqueduct. If all four are large, either the block is at the outlets of the fourth ventricle or the obstruction is beyond the ventricular system altogether, in the subarachnoid space or at the granulations. Note also that choroid plexus is not the only source of CSF, and that lymphatic routes along cranial nerves and dural vessels contribute to clearance alongside the granulations, which is why the older picture of a single drainage point is an oversimplification.

quiz.prompt: On an axial CT at the level of the foramina of Monro, the maximal width across the frontal horns measures 48 mm and the maximal internal diameter of the skull at the same level measures 148 mm. Calculate the Evans index. Answer as a ratio to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: The Evans index is the maximal width of the frontal horns divided by the maximal inner table diameter on the same axial slice, so 48 divided by 148 gives 0.32. A value above 0.3 defines ventriculomegaly and is one of the entry criteria for considering normal pressure hydrocephalus. Two cautions keep it honest. It is a crude, slice-dependent, two-dimensional surrogate, and it rises with age and with atrophy, so an index above 0.3 does not by itself mean hydrocephalus - it means the frontal horns are wide, and the reason may be lost brain. Look for the supporting features that separate pressure from atrophy: a narrow callosal angle, tight high convexity sulci with disproportionately widened Sylvian fissures, and upward bowing of the corpus callosum, together with the clinical triad of gait apraxia, cognitive decline and incontinence.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old has months of headache and blurred vision on bending forward. CT shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a rounded third ventricular recess, a normal-sized fourth ventricle, and periventricular interstitial low density around the frontal horns. Sagittal MRI shows no flow void in the aqueduct. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: The obstruction is at the aqueduct, so endoscopic third ventriculostomy is the diversion to discuss with neurosurgery
choices: The obstruction is at the arachnoid granulations, so a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is the diversion to arrange
The ventricles are enlarged from atrophy, so no diversion is needed and clinical review in six months suffices
The obstruction is at the outlets of the fourth ventricle, so posterior fossa decompression is the procedure that is needed
The obstruction is at the aqueduct, so endoscopic third ventriculostomy is the diversion to discuss with neurosurgery
quiz.explain: The level is read off the pattern. Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth places the block at the aqueduct, and loss of the normal aqueductal flow void on sagittal T2 supports it - though a flow void can also be lost from an artefact-free sequence, so it is corroborative rather than definitive, and a cine phase-contrast study settles it. Periventricular interstitial oedema, best seen as low density hugging the frontal horns, indicates transependymal CSF flow under pressure and separates active hydrocephalus from the wide ventricles of atrophy, where sulci are wide in proportion. The management consequence is real: an obstruction upstream of the fourth ventricle with a patent subarachnoid space is well suited to endoscopic third ventriculostomy, which bypasses the aqueduct without hardware, whereas communicating hydrocephalus generally needs a shunt.

quiz.prompt: A shunted teenager attends with headache and vomiting, and the CT ventricles look much the same size as on the scan from two years ago. Describe how you would nonetheless assess this shunt on imaging.
quiz.answer: Compare with the patient's own baseline scan taken when the shunt was working rather than with the largest previous ventricles, trace the whole catheter on a shunt series for disconnection, kinking or migration, and remember that stiff slit ventricles may fail to enlarge at all despite a blocked shunt.
quiz.explain: Shunt failure is a clinical diagnosis that imaging supports, and the single most useful habit is to pull up the patient's own well-functioning baseline rather than the immediately preceding study. Small interval change from a known good baseline is significant; sameness compared with a scan taken during a previous failure is meaningless. Ventricular size can mislead badly in the slit ventricle syndrome, where non-compliant ventricles do not dilate despite dangerously raised pressure, so a normal-looking CT never excludes obstruction. The shunt series covers the whole track on plain films to look for disconnection at connectors, fracture, kinking, and the tip lying outside the peritoneum. Add to that any new subdural collection, which points to overdrainage rather than blockage, and describe the valve setting if it is a programmable device that has been near a magnet.

curriculum_modules.title: Wrist and Hand: Carpal Instability and Fractures

module_contract.goal: Judge carpal alignment from the arcs and the carpal angles, chase the fracture the radiograph hides, and give the measurements and findings that decide each operation.

approach.step: Draw Gilula's three arcs on the PA
approach.detail: Arc I along the proximal convexities of scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum; arc II along their distal concave surfaces; arc III along the proximal curvatures of capitate and hamate. A break in any arc means a fracture or a ligamentous injury.
A triangular rather than quadrilateral lunate on the PA means it is tilted, and the lateral view will tell you which way.

approach.step: Go to the lateral and measure the angles
approach.detail: Scapholunate angle first, then capitolunate. The lateral has to be a true lateral or both numbers are meaningless.
Dorsal tilt of the lunate is DISI; palmar tilt is VISI. VISI is often a normal variant in lax wrists, so weigh it against the clinical picture.
In lunate dislocation the capitate is centred over the radius and the lunate has tipped out. In perilunate dislocation the lunate stays centred over the radius and the capitate displaces dorsally.
Radial inclination, radial length and volar tilt, and the articular surface — the four numbers that decide whether a reduction is acceptable.

measure.how: On a true lateral, between the long axis of the scaphoid and the long axis of the lunate.
On a true lateral, between the axes of the capitate and lunate.
PA view, angle of the radial articular surface.
PA view, height of the radial styloid above the ulnar corner.
Lateral view, tilt of the distal radial articular surface.
Greatest step across the radiocarpal articular surface after reduction.
measure.cutoff: ≥ 2 mm is not acceptable — the strongest predictor of post-traumatic osteoarthritis

classify.name: Acceptable reduction of the distal radius — International Distal Radius Fracture Study Group
classify.note: Named patterns: Colles' — dorsal angulation, the silver fork deformity. Smith's — volar displacement, typically high energy on a flexed wrist. Barton's — fracture-dislocation with dislocation of the radiocarpal joint, volar or dorsal. Chauffeur's (Hutchinson's) — isolated radial styloid fracture, displacement uncommon. Die-punch — depression of the lunate fossa from transverse loading.

IMPRESSION
1. [Injury named, with the carpal alignment.]
2. Angles: SL [n]°, CL [n]° — [normal / DISI / VISI].

4. [Occult scaphoid fracture not excluded: MRI or repeat imaging advised.]
pitfalls: Measuring carpal angles off an oblique lateral. Both the scapholunate and capitolunate angles need a true lateral; a few degrees of rotation invents instability.
Reading a scapholunate angle of 60–80° as a diagnosis. That band is questionably abnormal — above 80° is abnormal.
Calling VISI pathological by default. Palmar lunate tilt is often a normal variant in a lax wrist.
Confusing lunate with perilunate dislocation. Ask which bone is still centred over the radius: the lunate in perilunate dislocation, the capitate in lunate dislocation.

Reporting the distal radius fracture without the articular step. Incongruity of more than 2 mm is the most important factor in post-traumatic osteoarthritis, and it is the number the surgeon reduces to.

headings: Indications for Reduction in Distal Radius Fractures

protocol: Confirm correctly positioned PA, lateral and relevant targeted views; record stress or loading views. Use CT/MRI for the specified occult fracture or soft-tissue question.
Review both fracture and carpal alignment, including associated ligament injury.

checklist.label: Alignment
checklist.detail: Inspect Gilula arcs and radius-lunate-capitate relationship on true lateral.

checklist.label: Fracture
checklist.detail: Check scaphoid, triquetrum, distal radius/ulna and metacarpal/phalangeal injury.

checklist.label: Ligaments
checklist.detail: Assess scapholunate/lunotriquetral intervals and intrinsic ligament components if MRI.

checklist.label: TFCC/DRUJ
checklist.detail: Describe ulnar variance, distal radioulnar congruity and TFCC findings.

checklist.label: Soft tissue
checklist.detail: Review tendons, nerve spaces and joint degeneration.

measurements.name: Carpal alignment
measurements.method: Measure scapholunate interval and scapholunate angle on named standardised views if relevant.
measurements.pitfall: Malrotation can falsely widen intervals or alter angles.

measurements.name: Ulnar variance
measurements.method: Measure on a standard neutral PA projection with positioning recorded.
measurements.pitfall: Grip, forearm rotation and elbow position affect variance.

measurements.name: Fracture deformity
measurements.method: Record gap, displacement and articular step in mm.
measurements.pitfall: A normal initial scaphoid radiograph does not exclude occult fracture.

quiz.prompt: After a fall on the outstretched hand, a PA wrist radiograph shows a 4 mm gap between the scaphoid and lunate, a foreshortened scaphoid and a dense ring at its distal pole. The lateral shows the lunate tilted dorsally, with a scapholunate angle of 75 degrees. What does this combination tell you?
quiz.answer: The scapholunate ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a dorsal intercalated pattern
choices: The scapholunate ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a dorsal intercalated pattern
The lunotriquetral ligament has failed and the carpus has collapsed into a volar intercalated pattern
The lunate has dislocated volarly from its fossa while the capitate remains aligned with the radius
The distal radioulnar joint has dislocated, with the ulnar head displaced dorsal to the sigmoid notch
quiz.explain: Two findings on two views agree. On the PA, a scapholunate interval of 4 mm is well beyond the normal 2 mm or less, and the ring sign with a foreshortened scaphoid is the flexed bone seen end-on: freed from the lunate, the scaphoid rotates into flexion. On the lateral, the lunate is left tethered to the triquetrum and extends, giving a scapholunate angle above the normal 30 to 60 degrees, and that is the dorsal intercalated segment instability pattern. Lunotriquetral failure gives the mirror image: the lunate flexes with the scaphoid and the angle falls below 30 degrees, which is the volar pattern. A lunate dislocation would show a triangular lunate and broken arcs on the PA and a volarly tipped lunate on the lateral, not a widened interval with normal arcs. Distal radioulnar dislocation is judged on a true lateral by the position of the ulnar head, and does not alter carpal angles. Untreated, this hip of the wrist collapses into a predictable arthritis.

quiz.prompt: A distal radius fracture is reviewed on a lateral radiograph after a failed manipulation: the distal radial articular surface now tilts 12 degrees dorsally. Taking the normal palmar tilt as 11 degrees, through how many degrees would the articular fragment have to be rotated to restore that normal tilt? Answer in degrees, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: Palmar tilt is signed, so a surface tilted 12 degrees dorsally is at minus 12, and reaching plus 11 means rotating through 23 degrees. Learn the three normal values together and report all three: palmar tilt about 11 degrees, radial inclination about 22 degrees, and radial height about 11 mm. They matter because losing palmar tilt past neutral tips load onto the dorsal rim and the distal radioulnar joint, weakens grip, and provokes an adaptive midcarpal collapse that mimics dorsal intercalated instability. The commonly quoted limits that push a fracture towards fixation are dorsal tilt beyond 10 degrees, radial shortening beyond 3 mm and an intra-articular step-off beyond 2 mm, applied more strictly in a young, high-demand patient than in a frail one. Give the surgeon the numbers rather than an adjective, and say whether the distal radioulnar joint looks congruent on the lateral.

quiz.prompt: A 30-year-old carpenter has wrist pain a year after a fall. Standard PA radiographs show a 2.5 mm scapholunate interval with intact carpal arcs, and the clinical scaphoid shift test is positive. Which single additional radiograph is most likely to settle the question?
quiz.answer: A PA with the fist clenched, which drives the capitate up between scaphoid and lunate
choices: A PA with the fist clenched, which drives the capitate up between scaphoid and lunate
A lateral in full radial deviation, which flexes the scaphoid and opens the interval
A carpal tunnel view, which throws the hook of the hamate and the pisiform clear
A PA in ulnar deviation, which elongates the scaphoid and profiles its waist
quiz.explain: An interval of 2.5 mm sits in the equivocal band between the normal 2 mm and the clearly abnormal 3 mm, and a wrist with a competent secondary restraint can look normal at rest and come apart under load. The clenched-fist PA supplies that load: the capitate is driven proximally into the scapholunate space and an incompetent ligament lets the gap open, which is what dynamic instability means. Compare it with the same view of the other wrist, since intervals vary between people. Ulnar deviation elongates the scaphoid and is the view for a suspected waist fracture, not for the interval. Radial deviation flexes the scaphoid but does not stress the interval, and a lateral does not display it at all. A carpal tunnel view is for the hook of the hamate. If the stress views stay normal and suspicion persists, MR arthrography or arthroscopy is the next rung, arthroscopy still being the reference standard for a partial tear.

quiz.prompt: Arrange the stages of progressive perilunate instability in the order the ligaments fail as force travels around the lunate.
quiz.answer: scapholunate capitolunate lunotriquetral lunate-dislocation
quiz.explain: Mayfield showed that the injury propagates around the lunate from radial to ulnar in four stages, and the radiographic appearances follow the same order. Stage 1 is scapholunate failure, giving the widened interval and the flexed, ring-sign scaphoid, or its bony equivalent, a scaphoid waist fracture. Stage 2 carries the force through the space of Poirier into the capitolunate joint. Stage 3 tears the lunotriquetral ligament, and the whole carpus can now displace dorsally around a lunate that stays in its fossa, which is a perilunate dislocation. Stage 4 fails the dorsal radiotriquetral restraint and the lunate is squeezed volarly out of the fossa into the carpal tunnel, the spilled teacup on the lateral and the triangular piece of pie on the PA with all three of Gilula's arcs broken. Roughly a quarter of these are missed on the initial films, and the lateral is the view that saves you.

quiz.prompt: A motorcyclist has a swollen, painful wrist. The PA shows a triangular lunate with the three carpal arcs broken; the lateral shows the capitate in line with the radius and the lunate tipped volarly out of its fossa. Numbness is developing in the thumb and index finger. What is the priority?
quiz.answer: Urgent reduction, because the displaced lunate is compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
choices: Urgent reduction, because the displaced lunate is compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Urgent CT angiography, because the radial artery is at risk where it crosses the volar wrist crease
Outpatient MRI in two weeks, to grade the interosseous ligament injuries before any intervention
Splint and fracture clinic review, because these injuries settle as the soft tissue swelling resolves
quiz.explain: This is a lunate dislocation, the end stage of perilunate instability, and the lunate has rotated into the carpal tunnel where it presses directly on the median nerve. Developing numbness in the median distribution makes it a surgical emergency: reduction first, then ligament repair, with carpal tunnel decompression if symptoms persist. The lateral view is what separates it from a perilunate dislocation, where the lunate stays in the radial fossa and the capitate and the rest of the carpus displace dorsally; on the PA both look similar, with broken arcs and an abnormally shaped lunate, which is why these injuries are missed when only the PA is reviewed. Look also for the transscaphoid variant, in which the force passes through the scaphoid rather than around it, since a fracture will need fixing at the same operation. Delay costs nerve recovery and cartilage, so nothing here waits two weeks.

quiz.prompt: A 22-year-old has a fracture through the proximal third of the scaphoid. Explain, from the blood supply, why this site behaves so differently from a fracture of the distal tubercle, and say what your report should therefore state.
quiz.answer: Most of the scaphoid is supplied by branches of the radial artery entering the dorsal ridge distally, and flow to the proximal pole is retrograde through the bone, so a proximal fracture cuts that supply off and the proximal fragment risks avascular necrosis and non-union; the report should state the level of the fracture and the risk explicitly, because a proximal pole fracture goes to early fixation rather than a cast.
quiz.explain: The scaphoid is almost entirely covered in cartilage, so its vessels enter at two small non-articular areas, and the dominant supply comes from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery entering the dorsal ridge near the waist. Blood then runs backwards, distal to proximal, through the bone. That is why the further proximal the fracture, the worse the vascular consequence: distal tubercle fractures heal reliably, waist fractures develop necrosis in roughly a third when displaced or treated late, and proximal pole fractures are the ones that go on to necrosis and non-union most often. The practical output is the level, the displacement and any gap or angulation, since all three drive the decision between a cast and a percutaneous screw. On MRI, preserved fatty marrow signal on T1 in the proximal fragment is the reassuring finding; uniformly low T1 that fails to enhance is not.

quiz.prompt: A student falls on his hand and has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox with pain on axial loading of the thumb. Four-view scaphoid radiographs show no fracture. He is a competitive rower and wants an answer this week. What do you advise?
quiz.answer: Immobilise and arrange MRI within days, which will show or exclude the fracture straight away
choices: Immobilise and arrange MRI within days, which will show or exclude the fracture straight away
Immobilise and repeat the radiographs at two weeks, which is as accurate as early MRI
Discharge with analgesia, since four dedicated normal views exclude a scaphoid fracture
Arrange an isotope bone scan today, which is highly specific for a scaphoid fracture
quiz.explain: Initial radiographs miss a substantial minority of scaphoid fractures, and the cost of missing one is a non-union in a young hand. MRI is the most accurate early test, showing the low signal fracture line on T1 within hours, and it has the added merit of explaining the wrist when the scaphoid is intact, since distal radius, triquetral and hamate hook fractures and ligament injuries all appear in the same study. CT resolves cortical detail and displacement better and is a reasonable alternative, but it is less reliable for an undisplaced trabecular fracture. Repeating the radiographs at two weeks was the traditional pathway and is both slower and less accurate, and it leaves an athlete in a cast on a maybe. Isotope imaging is sensitive after 24 to 72 hours but is not specific, since any bone or soft tissue injury nearby takes up tracer.

quiz.prompt: A 34-year-old builder has a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture. CT shows an intra-articular step-off of 1.5 mm, radial shortening of 4 mm compared with the other side, and the articular surface tilted 5 degrees dorsally. Using the commonly quoted limits of step-off under 2 mm, shortening under 3 mm and dorsal tilt under 10 degrees, how many of the three limits does this fracture breach? Answer as a whole number.
quiz.explain: Only the shortening breaches: 4 mm against a limit of 3 mm, while the 1.5 mm step-off and the 5 degrees of dorsal tilt are both inside their limits. Reporting it that way is the point of the exercise, because one clear breach in a manual worker in his thirties is an argument for fixation, whereas a vague phrase such as mild displacement is not. Radial shortening is the measurement that tracks most reliably with ulnar-sided pain, loss of forearm rotation and grip weakness, and it is read either as radial height or as a change in ulnar variance against the uninjured side. Two further things belong in the same report: the state of the distal radioulnar joint, including a fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid or an incongruent sigmoid notch, and the number and position of the articular fragments, since a die-punch fragment of the lunate fossa changes the fixation.

quiz.prompt: A 25-year-old has ulnar wrist pain and a clunking distal radioulnar joint after a fall. MR arthrography shows contrast tracking to the ulnar side of the triangular fibrocartilage at its attachment to the fovea, with the central disc intact and neutral ulnar variance. What does this mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: A peripheral tear at a vascular attachment, which is repairable and accounts for the instability
choices: A peripheral tear at a vascular attachment, which is repairable and accounts for the instability
A central perforation in an avascular zone, which is debrided back rather than being repaired
A degenerative lesion of ulnar impaction, which is treated by shortening the ulna instead
A radial avulsion from the sigmoid notch, which needs no more than a period of splinting
quiz.explain: The Palmer classification splits traumatic class 1 lesions from degenerative class 2 lesions, and within class 1 the site is what decides the operation: 1A is a central perforation, 1B an ulnar or foveal avulsion often with a fracture at the base of the ulnar styloid, 1C a tear of the volar ulnocarpal ligaments and 1D a radial-sided avulsion. The periphery of the complex carries a blood supply and heals if it is repaired, whereas the central disc is avascular and is debrided to a stable rim. Foveal detachment is the lesion that destabilises the distal radioulnar joint, which is exactly what the clunk describes, so it goes to repair. Neutral ulnar variance and an intact central disc argue against a degenerative class 2 lesion, and ulnar shortening would be an operation for a problem this patient does not have.

quiz.prompt: A 55-year-old has chronic ulnar-sided wrist pain. Radiographs taken with the shoulder abducted and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees show the ulna projecting 3 mm distal to the radial articular surface. Say what you would look for on MRI to confirm the mechanism, and what your findings imply for treatment.
quiz.answer: Look for subchondral oedema, sclerosis and cysts in the proximal ulnar corner of the lunate and the adjacent triquetrum, with thinning or a central perforation of the triangular fibrocartilage and chondral loss on the ulnar head; that combination with positive ulnar variance confirms ulnar impaction and points towards an ulnar shortening osteotomy rather than a ligament repair.
quiz.explain: Ulnar impaction is a load problem, not a torn structure: a long ulna hammers the ulnar corner of the lunate through the triangular fibrocartilage, and the imaging signature is marrow oedema, then sclerosis and cysts, in precisely that corner. The disc thins and eventually perforates centrally, which is a Palmer class 2 degenerative lesion, and the lunotriquetral ligament may fail as a late consequence. Ulnar variance is dynamic and rises with grip and pronation, so it must be measured on a standardised PA with the shoulder abducted 90 degrees, the elbow flexed 90 degrees and the forearm in neutral rotation, otherwise you will over- or under-call it. The differentials for ulnar-sided pain that this study also addresses are extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy or subluxation, a lunotriquetral tear and a foveal triangular fibrocartilage avulsion, each with a different operation.

quiz.prompt: A skier has a swollen thumb that is unstable to radial stress at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Ultrasound shows a rounded mass of ligament tissue lying proximal and superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, with the distal insertion empty. What follows from that appearance?
quiz.answer: Surgical repair, because the retracted ligament can no longer reach its insertion to heal
choices: Surgical repair, because the retracted ligament can no longer reach its insertion to heal
A thumb spica cast for six weeks, because most of these tears heal well in a cast
Stress radiographs of the joint, to quantify the laxity before any decision is made
Aspiration of the mass with injection of corticosteroid into the joint afterwards
quiz.explain: The ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb tears at its distal insertion on the proximal phalanx, and if the torn end flips proximal to the adductor aponeurosis, the aponeurosis interposes between ligament and bone. That is the Stener lesion, and it is the reason imaging is worth doing: a non-displaced tear heals in a cast, and a displaced one will not heal at all, so the two injuries look identical clinically but are managed differently. Ultrasound shows the rounded retracted stump above the aponeurosis, sometimes described as a ball on a string, and MRI shows it equally well. The other argument for imaging first is that vigorous stress testing can itself pull a non-displaced tear proximal and convert it into a Stener lesion. Look also for an avulsed fragment from the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx, which is displaced along with the ligament.

quiz.prompt: A boxer has an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal, with a small volar-ulnar fragment left in position and the shaft displaced proximally, dorsally and radially. What should the report say about why it displaced, and what does that mean for treatment?
quiz.answer: The volar fragment is held by ligament while abductor pollicis longus drags the shaft away
choices: The volar fragment is held by ligament while abductor pollicis longus drags the shaft away
The fragment is avulsed by flexor pollicis longus and the shaft remains stable in a cast
The articular surface is comminuted into several pieces, so this needs a primary fusion
The displacement is purely rotational, so a closed reduction will hold it without fixation
quiz.explain: This is a Bennett fracture-dislocation. The small volar-ulnar fragment stays put because the anterior oblique, or volar beak, ligament anchors it to the trapezium, while abductor pollicis longus pulls the metacarpal shaft proximally, dorsally and radially, with adductor pollicis adding an adduction force. It is therefore an unstable injury by definition, and a cast will not hold it: reduction with percutaneous wires or screw fixation is the usual treatment, because residual incongruity of the trapeziometacarpal joint leads to early and symptomatic arthritis in a joint that has to take load through the thumb. Its comminuted cousin, in which the base is broken into a T or Y with several articular fragments, carries a worse outlook and needs a different fixation. An extra-articular fracture of the metacarpal base looks similar on a poor film but tolerates far more angulation, so a true lateral or a dedicated thumb view is worth the extra exposure.

quiz.prompt: Nine months after an untreated scaphoid waist fracture, CT shows a persistent lucent line with cystic change, sclerosis of the proximal fragment and a flexed humpback deformity. The surgeon asks for MRI before planning the operation. What question is MRI being asked, and what will you look at to answer it?
quiz.answer: The question is whether the proximal pole is still viable, because that decides between a conventional bone graft and a vascularised graft; look at the T1 marrow signal of the proximal fragment, since preserved fatty marrow argues for viability, and confirm the absence of enhancement after contrast before calling the fragment dead.
quiz.explain: T1 is the sequence that carries the answer, because fatty marrow is what dies. Diffusely low T1 signal throughout the proximal fragment that fails to enhance after gadolinium is the strongest non-invasive evidence of necrosis; patchy low T1 with preserved enhancement usually means oedema and reactive change rather than a dead bone. Fluid-sensitive sequences are less useful, since oedema is everywhere in a non-union. The CT contributes the structural measurements the surgeon needs: the humpback angulation, the height-to-length ratio, the extent of resorption to be filled with graft, and any dorsal intercalated collapse of the lunate. Be honest about the limits, because both MRI and CT misclassify a proportion of cases and punctate bleeding at operation remains the reference standard. Left alone, the non-union progresses to a predictable arthritis that starts at the radial styloid, spreads across the radioscaphoid joint and finally reaches the capitolunate joint.
